inside: Grand Orient lodge members secretly filed reports on army officers to the War Ministry, which used them to block Catholic officers' promotions and favour republican ones.

n: Secret NATO money funded Belgium's stay-behind network
rank: military intelligence (SDRA VIII) and State Security (STC/Mob)
d: NATO secretly paid for Belgium's 'stay-behind' network, which sat inside the country's military intelligence and State Security services. Stay-behind networks were secret organisations set up in NATO countries after the Second World War to resist a possible Soviet occupation. Belgium's was coordinated by a secretariat (SDRA XI) funded by secret NATO payments, with a military section (SDRA VIII) under military intelligence and the Defence Minister, and a civilian section (STC/Mob) under State Security and the Justice Minister. It was made public on 7 November 1990 and the government decided to disband it on 23 November 1990. A Senate commission chaired by Roger Lallemand heard 37 witnesses in 1991. It criticised the refusal to name civilian operatives; former SDRA head Paul Detrembleur refused to testify about the secretariat.
cite: Belgian Senate Commission of Inquiry into the stay-behind network (Lallemand commission), report 1991

arch.t: Italy — Operation Gladio: NATO Stay-Behind Network Used for Domestic Terrorism; 'Strategy of Tension'

inside: NATO secretly funded Belgium's stay-behind network, which sat inside the country's military intelligence and State Security services.

n: Neo-Nazi Westland New Post had members in gendarmerie and at NATO
org_note: Westland New Post: Belgian far-right paramilitary group founded by Paul Latinus with Front de la Jeunesse members.
rank: Gendarmerie (Diane anti-terror unit) and State Security
d: Westland New Post (WNP), a Belgian neo-Nazi group of the early 1980s, had members inside the Gendarmerie, Belgium's national police, and at a NATO site. Former gendarme Martin Leukeu said he was recruited into 'Group G', a neo-Nazi cell inside the Gendarmerie linked to WNP, and gendarme Madani Bouhouche was named as a member. NATO documents from the Evere transmission centre, passed by member Michel Libert, were found at member Marcel Barbier's home. Belgium's State Security service was also entangled: WNP founder Paul Latinus had been its informant, State Security agent Christian Smets admitted training members in surveillance, and the service had a mole in the group from 1981 but did not tell police. A parliamentary inquiry found no proof of a conspiracy behind the Brabant killings, a series of 1980s armed raids.
cite: Belgian parliamentary inquiries into the Nijvel (Brabant) gang and banditry; David Teacher, Rogue Agents (2003)
inside: The neo-Nazi Westland New Post had members inside the national gendarmerie and at a NATO site, where a member passed out NATO documents.

n: Reichsbürger coup plot had a sitting judge and ex-MP inside
org_note: Patriotic Union / 'Council' around Heinrich XIII Prinz Reuss: Reichsbürger network charged by the Federal Prosecutor as a terrorist association.
rank: judge at the Berlin Regional Court; former Bundestag member
d: A group of 'Reichsbürger', people who reject the legitimacy of the modern German state, around Heinrich XIII Prinz Reuss had a serving judge among its leaders. Birgit Malsack-Winkemann, a judge at the Berlin Regional Court and AfD Bundestag member for about four years, was arrested in the December 2022 raids. Prosecutors say she was to be justice minister in a new government; she admits being on the group's 'Council' with responsibility for justice. As a former MP she could bring up to six people into the Reichstag, and admits leading co-accused through it twice in September 2022. Prosecutors say up to 16 people, mainly from the KSK and other special units, were to storm it. Twenty-six defendants have been on trial since 2024; no verdict had been reported as of April 2026.
cite: Federal Prosecutor General indictment; Federal Court of Justice detention ruling (2023); Higher Regional Court Frankfurt trial from May 2024
inside: A Reichsbuerger coup group had a serving judge among its leaders, who used her former MP's access to lead co-accused through the Reichstag they planned to storm.

n: Russian-funded Voice of Europe: AfD MP Bystron investigated
org_note: Voice of Europe: Prague-based pro-Russian outlet and influence network financed by Viktor Medvedchuk, sanctioned by the Czech government in March 2024.
rank: Bundestag member, then Member of the European Parliament
d: Voice of Europe, a news website operating from Prague that Czech intelligence says was financed from Russia, is suspected of paying European politicians, including German MP Petr Bystron of the AfD party. Czech intelligence (BIS) briefed the Czech parliament's intelligence committee on a recording of a Prague meeting with Artem Marchevsky, whom the Czech government sanctioned as part of the network, in which about €20,000 was reportedly handed over. In April 2024 the Munich prosecutor's office opened a bribery and money-laundering investigation into Bystron. The Bundestag lifted his immunity and police searched his parliamentary office in May 2024. After he became a member of the European Parliament, it lifted his immunity on 6 May 2025. Bystron denies receiving money; no charge had been reported.
cite: Munich I Public Prosecutor's investigation; Bundestag immunity decision (May 2024); European Parliament immunity vote, 6 May 2025
inside: Czech intelligence says a Russian-funded website passed money to European politicians, and German prosecutors are investigating an AfD MP for bribery over it; he denies it.

n: Czech government exposes Russian-funded Voice of Europe payments
org_note: Voice of Europe: Prague-based pro-Russian outlet and influence network financed by Viktor Medvedchuk.
rank: European legislators (candidates and sitting members)
d: Voice of Europe, a news website operating from the Czech Republic, was used to pass Russian money to European politicians, according to Czech intelligence and press reports. The BIS security service said the network was financed from Russia and operated on Czech territory. On 27 March 2024 Petr Fiala's government put Voice of Europe, Viktor Medvedchuk, a pro-Russian Ukrainian politician, and Artyom Marchevsky on the Czech national sanctions list, which freezes assets and bans dealings with them. Deník N, citing a foreign ministry source, reported that payments went to politicians from Belgium, France, Germany, Hungary, the Netherlands and Poland, in particular the AfD. The case led Munich prosecutors to investigate AfD MP Petr Bystron for bribery; he denies receiving money.
cite: Czech government sanctions decision, 27 March 2024; Security Information Service (BIS) statement
inside: Czech intelligence says a Russian-funded website passed Russian money to sitting and aspiring European legislators, particularly from the AfD, according to press reports.

n: Black Hand leader Apis ran Serbia's military intelligence
rank: chief of intelligence, Serbian General Staff
d: Unification or Death, known as the Black Hand, was a secret society of Serbian army officers founded in 1911. In 1913 its leader, Dragutin Dimitrijević 'Apis', was appointed chief of General Staff intelligence of the Serbian army. Many scholars hold that he sanctioned the 1914 Sarajevo assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, with the Black Hand supplying weapons and training; the killing led to the First World War. In 1917 Prince Regent Alexander had him court-martialled at Salonika for treason; he and two others were shot on 26 June 1917 and more than 200 members were imprisoned. In 1953 the Supreme Court of Serbia retried the case and acquitted them for lack of proof of the alleged plot against the Prince Regent.
cite: Salonika court-martial, 1917; Supreme Court of Serbia retrial, 1953; Encyclopaedia Britannica
inside: A secret society of army officers had its own leader running Serbian military intelligence, and scholars hold he used that post to back the society's Sarajevo assassination plot.

n: White Hand officers' society saw its leader made Prime Minister
org_note: White Hand (Bela ruka): secret Serbian officers' group founded in 1912 by Petar Živković in opposition to the Black Hand.
rank: Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia
d: The White Hand (Bela ruka), a secret society of Serbian army officers, gained influence over the king and saw its leader appointed Prime Minister. It was founded in 1912 at the Hotel Paris in Belgrade by officers led by Petar Živković, as a rival to the Black Hand; Crown Prince Alexander later joined. After the Black Hand was broken at the 1917 Salonika trial, the White Hand gained influence over Alexander. When King Alexander I suspended the constitution on 6 January 1929 with White Hand officers' support and ruled as a dictator, General Živković was appointed Prime Minister, serving until 1932.
cite: Srejović, Gavrilović & Ćirković (eds.), Istorija srpskog naroda (1983); Milivoje Alimpić, Solunski front (1967)
inside: A secret officers' society gained influence over the king and saw its own leader made Prime Minister when its members helped him suspend the constitution.

n: Banco Ambrosiano collapse: P2 head Gelli convicted of fraud
rank: private bank used by P2 members
d: The secret P2 Masonic lodge had a member, Roberto Calvi, at the head of Banco Ambrosiano, and its leader Licio Gelli was later convicted over the bank's fraudulent collapse. In 1982 Banco Ambrosiano could not account for about US$1.287 billion, much of it routed through offshore companies tied to the Vatican Bank (IOR), its main shareholder. The Bank of Italy had warned of problems in a 1978 report. The bank was replaced by Nuovo Banco Ambrosiano in August 1982. In April 1992 a Milan court convicted 33 people of fraud; P2 head Licio Gelli's sentence was set at 12 years, confirmed by the Court of Cassation in April 1998.
cite: Milan Tribunal, fraudulent-bankruptcy verdict April 1992; Court of Cassation April 1998

arch.t: Vatican-Masonic Network — Roberto Calvi Murder; Banco Ambrosiano Collapse; P2 Lodge Member Directed Vatican Bank Investments (PROVEN)

inside: A secret lodge had its member running Banco Ambrosiano, and the lodge's own head was convicted of fraud over the money that vanished from the bank.

n: P2 membership list found: 962 names across Italy's state
rank: ministers, MPs, generals, intelligence chiefs
d: Propaganda Due (P2), a Masonic lodge run in secret by businessman Licio Gelli, had placed members throughout Italy's parliament, government, armed forces and intelligence services, as a list found in 1981 showed. On 17 March 1981 Guardia di Finanza (financial police) officers under Col. Vincenzo Bianchi, sent by Milan magistrates Gherardo Colombo and Giuliano Turone who were investigating banker Michele Sindona, searched Gelli's Giole factory at Castiglion Fibocchi (Arezzo). They found a list of 962 names. It included 44 members of parliament, ministers, 195 military officers (12 Carabinieri generals, 5 Guardia di Finanza generals, 22 army generals, 4 air force generals, 8 admirals), and the heads of all three intelligence services. The government published it on 21 May 1981.
cite: Milan investigating magistrates' search of 17 March 1981; Italian government publication 21 May 1981

arch.t: Italian Parliamentary Commission CONFIRMED — P2 Lodge Infiltrated Government, Military, Intelligence, Media, and Banking as Parallel State (962 Documented Members)

inside: A secret lodge run by a businessman enrolled 962 people across Italy's parliament, ministries, armed forces and intelligence services, giving it members inside every branch of the state.

n: Two serving ministers and five undersecretaries on the P2 list
rank: sitting cabinet ministers
d: The secret P2 Masonic lodge counted members inside the sitting Italian cabinet. When its membership list was seized in 1981, two ministers in office in Arnaldo Forlani's cabinet appeared on it as full members: Foreign Trade Minister Enrico Manca (Socialist) and Labour Minister Franco Foschi (Christian Democrat). Five undersecretaries, the junior ministers below them, were also listed: Costantino Belluscio, Pasquale Bandiera, Francesco Fossa, Rolando Picchioni and Anselmo Martoni. Publication of the list led to the fall of Forlani's government in May 1981, and a parliamentary commission later described P2 as a criminal and subversive organisation.
cite: P2 membership list published 21 May 1981; Anselmi Commission

arch.t: Italian Parliamentary Commission CONFIRMED — P2 Lodge Infiltrated Government, Military, Intelligence, Media, and Banking as Parallel State (962 Documented Members)

inside: A secret lodge counted two sitting cabinet ministers and five junior ministers among its members, giving a private organisation people inside the Italian government itself.

n: Socialist MP Fabrizio Cicchitto admits P2 membership
rank: member of parliament, Socialist Party leadership
d: The secret P2 Masonic lodge had members in Italy's parliament: the membership list seized in 1981 named 44 parliamentarians and a party secretary. Fabrizio Cicchitto, a director of the Italian Socialist Party, was the only one of about 30 parliamentarians named in early press reports who admitted being a member. A parliamentary commission chaired by Tina Anselmi later described P2 as a criminal and subversive organisation, and a 1982 law dissolved it and banned secret associations that seek to interfere with public bodies.
cite: Time, 8 June 1981; P2 list

arch.t: Italian Parliamentary Commission CONFIRMED — P2 Lodge Infiltrated Government, Military, Intelligence, Media, and Banking as Parallel State (962 Documented Members)

inside: A secret lodge, later found to be subversive and banned for interfering with public bodies, had recruited 44 members of Italy's parliament, including a Socialist Party director.

n: Italy's Chief of Defence Staff, Adm. Torrisi, on the P2 list
rank: Chief of the Defence General Staff
d: The secret P2 Masonic lodge had Italy's most senior military officer among its members. Admiral Giovanni Torrisi, Chief of the Defence Staff, the head of all the armed forces, from 1 February 1980 to 29 September 1981, and before that navy chief of staff, appeared on the P2 membership list with card no. 631. The list was found by police in March 1981 and published in May. Torrisi left the post months after the list was published. A parliamentary commission later described P2, run by businessman Licio Gelli, as an organisation aiming to undermine Italian democracy.
cite: P2 membership list 1981; Anselmi Commission

arch.t: Italian Parliamentary Commission CONFIRMED — P2 Lodge Infiltrated Government, Military, Intelligence, Media, and Banking as Parallel State (962 Documented Members)

inside: A secret lodge later found to aim at undermining Italian democracy had Italy's most senior military officer, the head of all the armed forces, enrolled as a member.

n: Military intelligence (SISMI) director Santovito on the P2 list
rank: director of military intelligence (SISMI)
d: The secret P2 Masonic lodge had the head of Italy's military intelligence service among its members. General Giuseppe Santovito led SISMI, the military intelligence service, from its creation in 1978 until August 1981 and was on the P2 membership list found in 1981. Prime Minister Giovanni Spadolini removed him during the scandal, and the Anselmi Commission, parliament's inquiry into P2, questioned him. He was arrested in December 1983 on charges of disclosing secrets and died in February 1984 before trial. The heads of Italy's other two intelligence bodies were also on the list.
cite: P2 list 1981; Anselmi Commission hearings

arch.t: Italian Parliamentary Commission CONFIRMED — P2 Lodge Infiltrated Government, Military, Intelligence, Media, and Banking as Parallel State (962 Documented Members)

inside: A secret lodge had enrolled the director of Italy's military intelligence service, so a private organisation had its member running one of the state's spy agencies.

n: Domestic intelligence (SISDE) director Grassini enrolled in P2
rank: director of civilian intelligence (SISDE)
d: The secret P2 Masonic lodge had the first head of Italy's domestic intelligence service among its members. General Giulio Grassini, appointed first director of SISDE, the civilian security service, in January 1978, was enrolled in P2 with card no. 515. He resigned when the membership list was found in 1981 and was replaced on 13 July 1981. In October 1981 the parliamentary commission on P2 heard him on possible intelligence involvement in the 1978 kidnapping of Aldo Moro, the former Prime Minister abducted and killed by the Red Brigades. The heads of Italy's other two intelligence bodies were also on the P2 list.
cite: P2 list 1981; Anselmi Commission hearing, October 1981

arch.t: Italian Parliamentary Commission CONFIRMED — P2 Lodge Infiltrated Government, Military, Intelligence, Media, and Banking as Parallel State (962 Documented Members)

inside: A secret lodge had enrolled the first director of Italy's domestic intelligence service, so a private organisation had its member running the state's civilian security service.

n: Intelligence coordinator Walter Pelosi on the P2 list
rank: secretary-general of CESIS
d: The secret P2 Masonic lodge had members at the head of all three of Italy's intelligence bodies in 1981. Walter Pelosi led CESIS, the body that coordinated the military service SISMI and the civilian service SISDE on behalf of the Prime Minister, and he was on the P2 membership list seized that year, alongside SISMI director Giuseppe Santovito and SISDE director Giulio Grassini. A private lodge run by businessman Licio Gelli therefore had members in charge of the whole intelligence system. A parliamentary commission later described P2 as a criminal and subversive organisation.
cite: P2 membership list 1981; Anselmi Commission

arch.t: Italian Parliamentary Commission CONFIRMED — P2 Lodge Infiltrated Government, Military, Intelligence, Media, and Banking as Parallel State (962 Documented Members)

inside: A secret lodge had its members at the head of all three of Italy's intelligence bodies at once, putting the whole state intelligence system in its members' hands.

n: Financial police commander Giannini on the P2 list
rank: commander-general of the Guardia di Finanza (financial police)
d: The secret P2 Masonic lodge had the commander of the Guardia di Finanza, Italy's financial police, among its members, the same force sent to search its leader's premises. Orazio Giannini appears on the P2 list with card no. 832. During the 17 March 1981 search of Licio Gelli's factory, the officer leading it, Col. Vincenzo Bianchi, received a call from the force's commander-general saying 'I am in those lists too.' The search found the membership list, which the government published in May 1981.
cite: P2 membership list 1981; Anselmi Commission

arch.t: Italian Parliamentary Commission CONFIRMED — P2 Lodge Infiltrated Government, Military, Intelligence, Media, and Banking as Parallel State (962 Documented Members)

inside: A secret lodge had enrolled the commander of Italy's financial police, the force later sent to search the lodge leader's premises.

n: 195 military officers on the P2 list
rank: generals and admirals of all services
d: The secret P2 Masonic lodge had placed members across the top of Italy's armed forces. The membership list seized in 1981 included 195 officers: 12 Carabinieri generals (the military police), 5 Guardia di Finanza generals (the financial police), 22 army generals, 4 air force generals and 8 admirals. Names included Admiral Gino Birindelli and generals Giovanni Allavena, a former head of the SIFAR intelligence service, and Giovanbattista Palumbo of the Carabinieri. A parliamentary commission later described P2 as a criminal and subversive organisation aiming to undermine Italian democracy.
cite: P2 membership list 1981; Anselmi Commission final report 1984

arch.t: Italian Parliamentary Commission CONFIRMED — P2 Lodge Infiltrated Government, Military, Intelligence, Media, and Banking as Parallel State (962 Documented Members)

inside: A secret lodge had enrolled 195 officers across the top of Italy's armed forces and police, including generals, admirals and a former intelligence chief.

n: Anselmi Commission finds P2 aimed to undermine democracy
rank: parliament-wide inquiry
d: Propaganda Due (P2), a secret Masonic lodge run by businessman Licio Gelli, had placed members in Italy's parliament, cabinet, armed forces and all three intelligence services, as its membership list showed when it was seized in 1981. Parliament then set up an inquiry under Law 527 of 23 September 1981, chaired by Christian Democrat Tina Anselmi. The commission ran until 1984 and produced six reports. The majority report described P2 as a criminal and subversive organisation aiming to 'undermine our democracy'. A minority report by Massimo Teodori argued P2 was part of the system rather than an outgrowth of it.
cite: Parliamentary Commission of Inquiry into the P2 Masonic Lodge (Anselmi Commission), final report 1984

arch.t: Italian Parliamentary Commission CONFIRMED — P2 Lodge Infiltrated Government, Military, Intelligence, Media, and Banking as Parallel State (962 Documented Members)

inside: Parliament's own inquiry found that a secret lodge had placed members in parliament, cabinet, armed forces and intelligence services, and that it aimed to undermine Italian democracy.

n: P2 head and P2 intelligence general faked Bologna evidence
rank: military intelligence (SISMI) officers
d: The head of the secret P2 Masonic lodge and a P2 member serving as a general in SISMI, Italy's military intelligence service, planted false evidence to steer the investigation into the 1980 Bologna railway station bombing. On 13 January 1981 a suitcase of explosives, weapons and false papers was placed on the Taranto–Milan train to send the inquiry toward a false foreign lead. In 1995 the Court of Cassation made final the convictions of Licio Gelli, SISMI general Pietro Musumeci (P2 list no. 487), SISMI colonel Giuseppe Belmonte and SISMI collaborator Francesco Pazienza for aggravated calumny, meaning falsely implicating others in a crime. Musumeci's final sentence was 8 years 5 months.
cite: Bologna Appeal Court 1994; Court of Cassation 1995

arch.t: Italian Parliamentary Commission CONFIRMED — P2 Lodge Infiltrated Government, Military, Intelligence, Media, and Banking as Parallel State (962 Documented Members)

inside: The secret lodge's head and his member inside military intelligence planted false evidence, so a state spy service was used to steer the Bologna bombing inquiry off course.

n: Interior Ministry intelligence chief D'Amato named in Bologna bombing
rank: head of the Interior Ministry's Ufficio Affari Riservati
d: The secret P2 Masonic lodge is reported to have had a member at the head of the Italian Interior Ministry's intelligence office. Federico Umberto D'Amato headed the ministry's confidential affairs office (Ufficio Affari Riservati), a domestic intelligence unit, and is reported as a P2 member. After his death, Bologna prosecutors in 2020 and the courts in the trial of Paolo Bellini named him among the organisers of the 2 August 1980 Bologna station bombing, which killed 85 people, and of its media handling. The same investigation named P2 head Licio Gelli as a financier of the attack.
cite: Procura generale di Bologna 2020; Bellini verdicts 2022–2025

arch.t: Italian Parliamentary Commission CONFIRMED — P2 Lodge Infiltrated Government, Military, Intelligence, Media, and Banking as Parallel State (962 Documented Members)

inside: A member of a secret lodge headed the Interior Ministry's intelligence office and is named by courts as an organiser of a bombing the lodge's head helped finance.

n: Senator Mario Tedeschi named in Bologna bombing cover-up
rank: senator (Italian Social Movement)
d: Mario Tedeschi, a senator for the neo-fascist MSI party and a journalist described as a member of the secret P2 Masonic lodge, was named by Bologna prosecutors in 2020 as having helped Interior Ministry intelligence chief Federico Umberto D'Amato manage press coverage of the 1980 Bologna station bombing, which killed 85 people, and mislead the inquiry. The same investigation named P2 head Licio Gelli as a financier of the attack. Tedeschi was dead and could not be charged.
cite: Procura generale di Bologna, 2020

arch.t: Italian Parliamentary Commission CONFIRMED — P2 Lodge Infiltrated Government, Military, Intelligence, Media, and Banking as Parallel State (962 Documented Members)

inside: A senator described as a member of a secret lodge is named as helping a fellow member inside Interior Ministry intelligence mislead the inquiry into a bombing the lodge's head financed.

n: P3 secret group convicted for seeking influence over the state
rank: network pressing on judges and state appointments
d: The 'P3', named after the earlier P2 lodge, was a secret group that prosecutors said sought undue influence on the Italian state. On 16 March 2018 a Rome court convicted eight people in the case. Businessman Flavio Carboni received 6 years 6 months for secret association; Arcangelo Martino 4 years 9 months under the Anselmi law, the 1982 law against secret societies that seek to interfere with public bodies. Senator Denis Verdini was acquitted of secret association but given 1 year 3 months for illegal party funding. In the same verdict a senior judge, Vincenzo Carbone, was convicted of abuse of office.
cite: Rome Tribunal, P3 verdict 16 March 2018
org_note: P3: secret association prosecuted under the 1982 Anselmi law, named by press after P2
inside: A secret group worked to gain undue influence over the Italian state by pressing on judges and appointments, and a senior judge was convicted in the same case.

n: Senior judge Vincenzo Carbone convicted in the P3 case
rank: senior judge (former First President of the Court of Cassation)
d: The 'P3', a secret group that prosecutors said sought undue influence on the Italian state, reached a senior judge. In the 16 March 2018 Rome verdict that convicted the group's organisers of secret association, Vincenzo Carbone received a 2-year suspended sentence for abuse of office, meaning use of a public post for improper ends. Former undersecretary Nicola Cosentino received a 10-month suspended term for defamation and private violence. Charges against Sardinia regional president Ugo Cappellacci lapsed.
cite: Rome Tribunal, P3 verdict 16 March 2018
org_note: P3: secret association prosecuted under the 1982 Anselmi law
inside: A secret group seeking influence over the Italian state reached a senior judge, who was convicted of using his public post for improper ends.

n: P4 network: MP Alfonso Papa passed secrets to fixer Bisignani
rank: member of parliament (PdL) and magistrate
d: Luigi Bisignani, a go-between, was accused of running a hidden network, called the 'P4', that reached into Italy's parliament and justice system to gather confidential information and favours. In the 2011 'P4' inquiry, Alfonso Papa, a deputy for Silvio Berlusconi's PdL party, a former Naples prosecutor and Justice Ministry director, was accused of passing confidential information to Bisignani and pressing businessmen for favours. The Chamber authorised his arrest in July 2011 and he spent 101 days in Poggioreale prison. Bisignani took a plea of 1 year 7 months. Papa was convicted in 2016 (4 years 6 months), but the charges lapsed on appeal by 2021; the judiciary's disciplinary body removed him from the bench in 2023.
cite: Naples courts 2016–2021; Superior Council of the Judiciary (CSM) disciplinary section 2023
org_note: P4: press name for the Bisignani information-trading network
inside: A fixer's hidden network had a member of parliament and former Justice Ministry director passing it confidential information and pressing businessmen for favours.

n: 'Ndrangheta trial convicts officials and ex-senator Pittelli
rank: former senator and Forza Italia regional coordinator
d: The Mancuso clan of the 'Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia, drew in civil servants, police and politicians, and prosecutors say a former senator linked it to Masonic circles and business. In the Rinascita Scott maxi-trial against the clan, more than 200 of over 300 defendants were convicted in November 2023, including civil servants, a former police chief and a former mayor. Lawyer and former Forza Italia senator Giancarlo Pittelli, described by prosecutors as a Freemason linking the clan to Masonic circles and business, received 11 years for collusion. In a separate 'Mala Pigna' trial the Palmi Tribunal gave him 14 years in 2025 for external complicity, meaning helping a mafia group without being a member.
cite: Vibo Valentia Tribunal, Rinascita Scott verdict November 2023; Palmi Tribunal 2025
inside: A mafia clan drew civil servants, a police chief, a mayor and a former senator onto its side, so officials meant to oppose it worked in its favour.

n: IDEA: secret officers' society inside Greek army led 1967 coup
rank: army officer corps
d: IDEA (Holy Bond of Greek Officers) was a secret society inside the Greek army whose members seized power in 1967. It was formed in 1945 by officers who had served in the collaborationist Security Battalions, units that worked with the German occupiers; its 1952 manifesto called dictatorship the only solution for Greece. Several leaders of the 21 April 1967 coup, including Georgios Papadopoulos, were members, and IDEA members took key posts under the military junta that ruled until 1974. In 1975 Papadopoulos and other coup leaders were sentenced to death for high treason, commuted to life imprisonment.
cite: Academic history (Kassimeris)
org_note: IDEA: Ieros Desmos Ellinon Axiomatikon, secret society of Greek army officers
inside: A secret society inside the Greek army, whose manifesto called for dictatorship, had its members lead the 1967 coup and then take key posts in the junta.

n: Golden Dawn ties inside the Greek police
rank: Hellenic Police
d: Golden Dawn, a Greek neo-Nazi party later found by a court to be a criminal organisation, had support and ties inside the Greek police. After the May 2012 election, polling stations used by officers of the Attica police directorate showed just over 20% for Golden Dawn against about 6% at civilian stations in the same district. In 2012 an officer was suspended over a raid on migrant stalls in Missolonghi carried out alongside party members. In 2013 the Council of Europe's human rights commissioner, Nils Muižnieks, said he had strong evidence of ties between police and the party. In October 2020 the Athens Court of Appeals convicted the party's leaders of directing a criminal organisation.
cite: Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights, 2013; election returns 2012
org_note: Golden Dawn: neo-Nazi party ruled a criminal organisation
inside: A neo-Nazi party built support inside the Greek police, and at least one officer joined its members in a raid on migrant stalls.

n: Hizb ut-Tahrir recruited a brigadier inside Pakistan's army
rank: brigadier, army general headquarters
d: Hizb ut-Tahrir, an international Islamist movement that seeks to set up a caliphate (a single Islamic state) and is banned in Pakistan, recruited serving Pakistani army officers. Brigadier Ali Khan was arrested in May 2011, and in August 2012 a military court convicted him and four majors of links to the group; he was sentenced to five years. The army said Hizb ut-Tahrir had tried to recruit officers to its programme of a coup and a caliphate.
cite: Pakistan Army field general court martial, August 2012; reported by Reuters, BBC, Dawn
inside: An Islamist movement seeking a coup and a caliphate recruited a serving brigadier and four majors inside Pakistan's army to its programme.

n: Hizb ut-Tahrir linked to army officers' coup plot in Bangladesh
rank: serving and retired army officers
d: Hizb ut-Tahrir, an international Islamist movement that seeks a caliphate and has been banned in Bangladesh since 2009, was named among those behind a plot by army officers to seize power. In January 2012 the Bangladesh army announced it had stopped a coup attempt by serving and retired officers it described as religious extremists, and named Hizb ut-Tahrir among those behind it. Two retired officers were arrested and a serving major was named as a fugitive.
cite: Bangladesh Army press briefing, 19 January 2012; reported by BBC, Reuters
inside: An Islamist movement seeking a caliphate was named among those behind a plot by serving and retired Bangladeshi army officers to seize power.

n: Chinese officials paid for Taiwan village chiefs' trips to sway votes
rank: village and ward chiefs (local elected officials)
d: A Chinese government office, the Taiwan Affairs Office of Taizhou City, paid for trips that Lin Hsueh-feng, a former Kuomintang (KMT) city council candidate, organised for Chiayi village and ward chiefs, who are elected local officials in Taiwan. On the 2023 trips to Zhejiang the Taizhou office covered lodging and local travel, and prosecutors said Chinese officials urged the chiefs to vote for a particular party's candidate. On 28 May 2025 Chiayi District Court sentenced Lin to four years in prison under the Anti-Infiltration Act, a law against campaigning or political donations directed by hostile foreign forces, and the presidential election law. The ruling could be appealed.
cite: Chiayi District Court, judgment of 28 May 2025; Tribune India (citing CNA), 31 May 2025
inside: A Chinese government office paid for trips by elected Taiwanese village chiefs, and Chinese officials used them to urge the chiefs to vote for a chosen party.

n: Chinese military intelligence recruited aides in Taiwan's government
rank: Presidential Office consultant; assistant to the foreign minister
d: Chinese military intelligence, working for the Central Military Commission, recruited four former members of Taiwan's governing Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) who worked close to the top of government. Huang Chu-jung, ex-assistant to a New Taipei councillor, did the recruiting. Ho Jen-chieh was an assistant to Foreign Minister Joseph Wu, Chiu Shih-yuan was deputy director of the Taiwan Foundation for Democracy, and Wu Shang-yu was a Presidential Office consultant. They passed on President William Lai's travel schedules and records of Joseph Wu's talks with foreign envoys. On 25 September 2025 Taipei District Court convicted all four of spying, jailing Huang for 10 years, Ho for 8 years 2 months, Chiu for 6 years 2 months and Wu for 4 years. The sentences could be appealed.
cite: Taipei District Court, judgment of 25 September 2025; Taipei Times, 26 September 2025
inside: Chinese military intelligence recruited aides working near Taiwan's president and foreign minister, who passed it the president's travel schedules and records of diplomatic talks.

n: Moon's church bought into a Uruguayan bank that lent to its own firms
rank: de facto president Aparicio Méndez; Uruguayan banking system
d: The Unification Church, the religious movement led by Sun Myung Moon, took part-ownership of one of Uruguay's oldest banks during military rule. In 1981 Moon's group bought 49% of Banco de Crédito and founded the daily Últimas Noticias, whose early editorial declared it 'fully identified' with the military 'process'; that year Moon's aide Bo Hi Pak met de facto president Aparicio Méndez, according to a book by Juan de Montemayor. The group also bought Montevideo's Hotel Victoria Plaza. Banco de Crédito closed in 2002. A parliamentary investigative commission on the financial and banking system found it had taken excessive risk by lending about US$100 million to Moon-linked companies, out of about US$600 million in total loans.
cite: Uruguayan parliamentary investigative commission on the financial and banking system; El Observador, 1 September 2012; Christianity Today, 13 May 1988
inside: A religious movement bought part-ownership of a Uruguayan bank, which then lent about a sixth of its loans to companies linked to that movement.

n: CIA secretly funded and ran the Congress for Cultural Freedom
rank: US Central Intelligence Agency (International Organizations Division)
d: The US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) secretly paid for and ran the Congress for Cultural Freedom, an organisation of writers and intellectuals opposed to communism. It was founded in West Berlin in June 1950 and run from Paris by Michael Josselson, a CIA officer. At its height it had offices in 35 countries and published more than 20 magazines, including Encounter (London) and Preuves (Paris). The New York Times named the CIA funding in April 1966; Ramparts and the Saturday Evening Post followed in 1967, and Thomas Braden, former head of the CIA's International Organizations Division, admitted in print that the CIA had funded the Congress and Encounter for more than ten years. CIA historians now call it one of the agency's 'more daring and effective Cold War covert operations'. After 1967 it was renamed the International Association for Cultural Freedom and funded by the Ford Foundation until it dissolved in 1979.
cite: New York Times series, April 1966; Thomas Braden, 'I'm Glad the CIA Is Immoral', Saturday Evening Post, May 1967; CIA Center for the Study of Intelligence, 'Origins of the Congress for Cultural Freedom'
inside: The CIA secretly paid for an international organisation of writers and intellectuals and had one of its own officers run it, so its work served US intelligence aims.

n: Asia Foundation set up and secretly funded by the CIA
rank: US Central Intelligence Agency (project DTPILLAR)
d: The US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) created the Asia Foundation and ran it as a 'proprietary', meaning an organisation it secretly owned and controlled while it appeared independent. A CIA memorandum to the White House 303 Committee, which approved covert operations, dated 22 June 1966, describes the foundation as 'established in 1954 to undertake cultural and educational activities on behalf of the United States Government in ways not open to official U.S. agencies'. It grew out of the Committee for a Free Asia (1951), and CIA support ran under the code name DTPILLAR. After press disclosures of CIA funding of private groups in 1966-67, a review led by Secretary of State Dean Rusk decided the foundation should be kept and funded openly by the US government.
cite: Foreign Relations of the United States 1964-68, vol. X, doc. 132 (CIA memorandum to the 303 Committee, 22 June 1966)
inside: The CIA secretly owned and controlled the Asia Foundation while it appeared independent, using it to carry out work for the US government that official agencies could not.

n: CIA secretly paid for the US National Student Association
rank: US Central Intelligence Agency
d: The US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) secretly funded the National Student Association (NSA), the federation of US college student governments, from the early 1950s until 1967. The money paid for its international programme and some domestic work, and a few NSA officers worked closely with CIA officials. Former staffer Michael Wood exposed the arrangement in Ramparts magazine in February 1967. President Johnson then set up the Katzenbach Committee to review CIA funding of US private voluntary groups, and in August 1967 the NSA formally cut its ties to the CIA.
cite: Ramparts, February 1967; New York Times, 16 Feb 1967; US Senate Church Committee Final Report, Book I (1976), on the Katzenbach Committee
inside: The CIA secretly funded the federation of US student governments, and some of its officers worked closely with CIA officials on its international programme.

n: CIA channelled money through the AFL's union committee from 1948
rank: 1948 Italian general election (party and union politics)
d: The US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) secretly passed money through the Free Trade Union Committee of the American Federation of Labor (AFL) to influence politics and unions in Europe. The committee, run by Jay Lovestone, was set up in 1944 to back non-communist unions abroad. Historian Anthony Carew found that the CIA channelled money to it for about 20 years, starting with efforts to influence Italy's 1948 elections. The committee also subsidised the French union Force Ouvrière from 1948 through its Paris representative Irving Brown, and French journalist Frédéric Charpier writes that the CIA division under Thomas Braden gave Brown and Lovestone about $1 million a year in 1951-54.
cite: Anthony Carew, 'The American Labor Movement in Fizzland: The Free Trade Union Committee and the CIA', Labor History (Feb 1998); Frédéric Charpier, La CIA en France (Seuil, 2008)
inside: The CIA secretly fed money through a US union committee to back chosen unions abroad, so a labour body's foreign work served US intelligence aims.

n: CIA-linked IBAD paid for Brazilian opposition campaigns in 1962
rank: Candidates for the National Congress and state governorships, October 1962
d: The Brazilian Institute of Democratic Action (IBAD), linked to the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and backed by multinational companies, paid for the campaigns of many opposition candidates in Brazil's October 1962 elections for Congress and eleven state governments, aiming to change who held office. A Brazilian Parliamentary Inquiry Commission (CPI) investigated the funding, and President João Goulart closed the institute the following year. In 1977 former US ambassador Lincoln Gordon admitted that the United States had funded the opposition in that election.
cite: Brazilian Chamber of Deputies Parliamentary Inquiry Commission (CPI) on IBAD, 1963; Lincoln Gordon statement, 1977
inside: A CIA-linked institute backed by multinational companies secretly paid for opposition candidates' campaigns in Brazil, aiming to choose who sat in Congress and state governments.

n: Radio Free Europe and Radio Liberty secretly run on CIA money
rank: US Central Intelligence Agency
d: The US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) secretly created and funded Radio Free Europe and Radio Liberty, which presented themselves as private stations. Radio Free Europe (1949) was set up by the National Committee for a Free Europe, a CIA front organised by Allen Dulles in New York, and Radio Liberty followed in 1951; both broadcast from Munich into the Soviet bloc. The CIA and State Department set broad policy directives for the stations. In 1971 Senator Clifford Case introduced a bill to take their funding out of the CIA budget. CIA funding ended in 1971-72, and from 1974 a Board for International Broadcasting passed open congressional appropriations to the stations.
cite: US Congress, S.18 (Senator Clifford Case, 1971); Presidential Study Commission on International Radio Broadcasting (1972-73); Board for International Broadcasting Act 1973
inside: The CIA secretly created, funded and set policy for two stations that presented themselves as private broadcasters, so their output served US intelligence aims.

n: Church Committee: CIA ran money through foundations and campus ties
rank: US Central Intelligence Agency
d: The US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) secretly routed money through private US foundations and kept covert ties to academics and journalists, according to the Senate committee that investigated US intelligence in 1975-76 (the Church Committee). It found that, leaving out Ford, Rockefeller and Carnegie, at least 108 of the 700 grants over $10,000 made by 164 other US foundations in 1963-66 involved partial or complete CIA funding, and that CIA money was in nearly half of these foundations' grants for international activities. CIA labour, student and media projects peaked in 1964-67 and were cut back after the 1967 Ramparts disclosures and the Katzenbach Committee review. The committee also reported that the CIA was then using several hundred American academics at more than 100 colleges and universities, and until February 1976 had covert ties to about 50 US journalists.
cite: US Senate Select Committee to Study Governmental Operations with Respect to Intelligence Activities, Final Report, Book I, pp. 182-192 (26 April 1976)
inside: The CIA secretly put its money into the grants of over a hundred US foundations and kept covert ties to hundreds of academics and about 50 journalists.

n: Tobacco companies secretly worked to undermine WHO from inside
rank: WHO decision-making and member-state health delegations
d: Tobacco companies ran a hidden campaign to weaken tobacco control at the World Health Organization (WHO), the UN's health agency, working through consultants, scientists and other UN bodies. At Director-General Gro Harlem Brundtland's request, a committee of experts chaired by Thomas Zeltner, director of the Swiss Federal Office of Public Health, examined company documents released in US lawsuits. Its 246-page report, received by WHO on 28 July 2000, found an 'elaborate, well financed, sophisticated and usually invisible' effort, which also worked through FAO, ECOSOC and the World Bank and through the companies' food subsidiaries, which offered partnerships to UN agencies. It urged member states to investigate tobacco-company influence on their own decisions. The report led into the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (2003).
cite: Committee of Experts on Tobacco Industry Documents, 'Tobacco Company Strategies to Undermine Tobacco Control Activities at the World Health Organization', WHO, July 2000
inside: Tobacco companies worked secretly through consultants, scientists and other UN bodies to weaken tobacco control at the World Health Organization from within.

n: Brazil's Olympic chief paid an IOC member $2m for Rio 2016 votes
rank: Head of Rio 2016 bid and Brazilian Olympic Committee, working with Rio state governor
d: Carlos Arthur Nuzman, head of the Brazilian Olympic Committee and the Rio 2016 organising committee, was found to have channelled $2 million to Lamine Diack, a member of the International Olympic Committee (IOC), to secure votes when Rio was chosen as host in 2009. The IOC is the body whose members vote on which city hosts the Olympic Games. Police arrested Nuzman in October 2017 in the 'Unfair Play' phase of Operation Car Wash, Brazil's large corruption investigation, and the IOC suspended him that month. On 26 November 2021 federal judge Marcelo Bretas sentenced him to 30 years, 11 months for corruption, organised crime, money laundering and currency evasion; he remained free while appealing.
cite: 7th Federal Criminal Court of Rio de Janeiro, sentence of 26 Nov 2021; Agência Brasil, 26 Nov 2021
inside: The head of Rio's Olympic bid channelled $2 million to a member of the International Olympic Committee to buy his vote for Rio as host city.

n: Rio governor Cabral admits paying an IOC member $2m for Olympic votes
rank: Governor of Rio de Janeiro state (2007-14)
d: Sérgio Cabral, governor of Rio de Janeiro state from 2007 to 2014, testified in July 2019 that he paid $2 million to Lamine Diack, a member of the International Olympic Committee (IOC), to buy votes for Rio's 2009 bid to host the Olympics. The money went through businessman Arthur César de Menezes Soares Filho. Cabral had been arrested in November 2016 in Operation Car Wash, Brazil's large corruption investigation, and later received sentences totalling over 400 years in many cases, some annulled in 2024. He was a co-defendant with Brazilian Olympic Committee head Carlos Nuzman in the federal case.
cite: Testimony before Judge Marcelo Bretas, 7th Federal Criminal Court, Rio, July 2019; BBC, 5 July 2019
inside: Rio de Janeiro's governor paid $2 million to a member of the International Olympic Committee to buy votes for the city's bid inside that body.

n: Milner, named by Quigley as Rhodes's secret-society heir, ran South Africa
rank: High Commissioner for Southern Africa; Governor of the Transvaal and Orange River Colony
d: Alfred Milner, whom Carroll Quigley names as a leader of Cecil Rhodes's secret society, ran British South Africa for eight years. Historian Carroll Quigley argued in The Anglo-American Establishment (1981) that Cecil Rhodes founded a secret society to extend British rule, whose circle, the Milner Group, placed members in government. Milner was High Commissioner for Southern Africa and Governor of the Cape from May 1897, administrator and then Governor of the Transvaal and Orange River Colony from 1901 to April 1905, and a Rhodes Trust trustee from Rhodes's death in March 1902; these offices are on the record. Quigley says Milner was named to the society's 'Junta of Three' in 1891, was Rhodes's chosen successor as its leader, and that the group 'caused the Boer War of 1899–1902'. The membership and the war claim rest on Quigley.
cite: Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, pp. 3–5, 33; Wikipedia 'Alfred Milner, 1st Viscount Milner' (offices)
inside: According to one historian, the leader of Cecil Rhodes's secret society to extend British rule ran British South Africa, and the group caused the Boer War.

n: Milner placed his Oxford recruits in the Transvaal government
rank: Transvaal colonial secretary, treasurer, town clerk of Johannesburg, Intercolonial Council secretary
d: Alfred Milner, Britain's High Commissioner in South Africa, filled the colonial government of the conquered Boer republics with young Oxford graduates he recruited from 1901, a group known as 'Milner's Kindergarten'. Patrick Duncan became Transvaal Treasurer and then Colonial Secretary (1903–07); Richard Feetham and Lionel Curtis served as town clerks of Johannesburg; Robert Brand was secretary of the Intercolonial Council; Geoffrey Robinson (Dawson) was Milner's secretary and then editor of the Johannesburg Star. The appointments are documented. Historian Carroll Quigley calls the group the 'Association of Helpers', the outer circle of Cecil Rhodes's secret society; that classification is his.
cite: Wikipedia 'Milner's Kindergarten'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, ch. 4
inside: Milner filled the government of the conquered Boer colonies with young Oxford recruits, putting his own circle, which one historian calls part of Rhodes's secret society, into its key posts.

n: Milner's Kindergarten pressed for South African union from inside
rank: National Convention of 1908–09; Transvaal Legislative Council
d: Members of 'Milner's Kindergarten', the young Oxford men Alfred Milner had placed in South Africa's colonial government, worked from official posts and a funded journal to bring about the union of the four colonies. Lionel Curtis founded the monthly The State, funded by mining magnate Abe Bailey, in 1908; Robert Brand served as secretary to the Transvaal delegates at the National Convention and wrote The Union of South Africa (1909); and Richard Feetham sat on the Transvaal Legislative Council (1907–10). The group wanted a federal model, but the Convention chose a unitary state, and the Union came into being in 1910. Historian Carroll Quigley writes that the group 'created the Union of South Africa in 1906–1910'; that is his summary.
cite: Wikipedia 'Robert Brand, 1st Baron Brand', 'Richard Feetham', 'Milner's Kindergarten'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, p. 5
inside: Men Milner had placed in the colonial government used their official posts and a mining magnate's journal to push for the union of South Africa's colonies.

n: Round Table editor Philip Kerr in Lloyd George's Downing Street team
rank: Private secretary to the Prime Minister; Prime Minister's Secretariat
d: Philip Kerr, founding editor of The Round Table, the journal of the Round Table movement that Alfred Milner's associates set up to promote imperial unity, was placed in the Prime Minister's personal staff. In December 1916 Lloyd George set up a secretariat in huts in the garden of 10 Downing Street, the 'Garden Suburb'. Its first members were W. G. S. Adams, David Davies, Joseph Davies, Waldorf Astor and Kerr, who edited The Round Table from 1910 to 1916. Kerr stayed as the Prime Minister's private secretary until March 1921 and wrote the Fontainebleau Memorandum of March 1919. H. W. Massingham attacked the group in The Nation (24 February 1917) as 'illuminati'. Historian John Turner (Historical Journal, 1977) found Milner's influence on its staffing; Carroll Quigley treats it as a Milner Group placement.
cite: J. A. Turner, 'The Formation of Lloyd George's "Garden Suburb": "Fabian-like Milnerite Penetration"?', Historical Journal 20:1 (1977), 165–184; Wikipedia 'Philip Kerr, 11th Marquess of Lothian'
inside: A historian found Milner's influence on the staffing of the Prime Minister's new secretariat, which placed the Round Table's own editor in Downing Street as private secretary.

n: Round Table study group with India Office officials drafted 'dyarchy'
rank: India Office; Government of India constitution (Government of India Act 1919)
d: Lionel Curtis of the Round Table movement, the imperial-unity network built by Alfred Milner's associates, ran a study group with India Office officials that worked out the 'dyarchy' system later written into law. Historian Carroll Quigley writes that Curtis formed the group inside the London Round Table about 1911, joined by three India Office officials (Sir William Duke, Malcolm Seton, Sir Lionel Abrahams), and that it settled on dyarchy, meaning some provincial functions were handed to elected Indian ministers. Lord Chelmsford, Viceroy of India, told the Lords in November 1927 he had been handed a pamphlet with the 'diarchic principle' at the India Office in 1916, thinking it came from an official committee. James Meston, a Kindergarten adviser, sat in the Imperial War Cabinet in 1917. Dyarchy was enacted in the Government of India Act 1919; Curtis described the work in Dyarchy (1920).
cite: Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, ch. 11, pp. 202–204; Lionel Curtis, Dyarchy (1920); Wikipedia 'Lionel Curtis'
inside: A private imperial network's study group, joined by India Office officials, worked out the 'dyarchy' system, which the government then wrote into the Government of India Act 1919.

n: Round Table member Geoffrey Dawson edits The Times through appeasement
rank: Editor of The Times (influence on government policy)
d: The Round Table, a private network of British imperialists around Lord Milner, placed its own members as editors of The Times, according to historian Carroll Quigley, who says it 'controlled The Times for more than fifty years' (except 1919–22). One was Geoffrey Dawson, Milner's secretary in South Africa and a lifelong Fellow of All Souls College, Oxford, who edited the paper in 1912–19 and 1923–41. During the policy of appeasing Hitler, Dawson wrote to fellow member Lord Lothian on 23 May 1937: 'I spend my nights in taking out anything which I think will hurt their susceptibilities', meaning German opinion. A Times leader of 7 September 1938 suggested Czechoslovakia might gain from ceding its German-speaking border districts. Quigley places the 'Cliveden set' of appeasers near the group's centre.
cite: Wikipedia 'Geoffrey Dawson'; The Times leader of 7 Sept 1938 as quoted at airminded.org; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, pp. 4–5
inside: According to one historian, a private imperial network placed its members as editors of The Times, and one cut stories to spare German opinion during appeasement.

n: Milner Group's Patrick Duncan, as Governor-General, installs Smuts
rank: Governor-General of the Union of South Africa
d: Historian Carroll Quigley says the Milner Group, a private network of British imperialists, had a man at the top of South Africa's state in Patrick Duncan, once Milner's Transvaal Colonial Secretary. Duncan became the first South African citizen appointed Governor-General, the Crown's representative, in 1937 and served until his death on 17 July 1943. In 1939, after Prime Minister Hertzog lost a parliamentary vote and resigned, Duncan refused his request for a general election and asked Jan Smuts to form a government instead. Quigley calls Duncan Smuts's 'chief lieutenant', inherited 'directly from Milner', and counts Smuts in the Milner Group, so on his account the decision put the group's own man in power.
cite: Wikipedia 'Patrick Duncan (governor-general)'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, pp. 78–79
inside: According to one historian, a private imperial network's man as Governor-General refused an election and installed Smuts, whom the historian counts in the same network, as Prime Minister.

n: CFR study group's Greenland memo shapes Roosevelt's policy
rank: President of the United States
d: The Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), a private New York foreign-policy club, wrote policy for the US government from outside through its War and Peace Studies. On 17 March 1940 a confidential memo from Isaiah Bowman's Territorial group argued that Greenland was strategically important and should be placed within the Monroe Doctrine, the US policy of keeping outside powers out of the Americas. CFR's 1947 anniversary book says Roosevelt summoned Bowman to the White House with the memo in hand. After Germany invaded Denmark in April 1940 Roosevelt declared Greenland part of the North American continent, and the Danish government-in-exile later granted US base rights there. The account is CFR's own.
cite: G. Gavrilis, The Council on Foreign Relations: A Short History (CFR, 2021), pp. 25–27, citing CFR's 1947 anniversary book
inside: A private foreign-policy club wrote a confidential memo on Greenland that the President took up, and the US then declared Greenland part of North America.

n: Allen Dulles carries CFR war plans into the OSS, then runs the CIA
rank: Director of Central Intelligence
d: The Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), a private New York foreign-policy club, ran War and Peace Studies in 1939–45 to draft plans for the US government. Allen Dulles, who sat on the CFR board in 1928 according to historian Carroll Quigley, led its Security and Armaments group. CFR's own history says the Office of Strategic Services, the wartime US spy agency, recruited him to carry out the group's plans for occupied Germany, so a private club's plans entered government through him. He later became the longest-serving Director of Central Intelligence, head of the CIA (1953–61).
cite: G. Gavrilis, The Council on Foreign Relations: A Short History (CFR, 2021), pp. 23–25; Quigley, Tragedy and Hope, p. 952
inside: A private foreign-policy club drew up plans for occupied Germany, and the wartime US spy agency recruited the leader of that study group to carry them out.

n: Senate inquiry says Communists used the IPR to steer Far East policy
rank: Department of State (Far Eastern policy)
d: A US Senate subcommittee concluded that Communists had used the Institute of Pacific Relations (IPR), a private research body on Asia, to steer US Far East policy. The Internal Security Subcommittee under Pat McCarran reviewed about 20,000 IPR documents in 1951–52 and reported in 1952 that it 'was a vehicle used by the Communists to orient American far eastern policies toward Communist objectives'. Owen Lattimore, editor of the IPR journal Pacific Affairs, was a central target. The IRS revoked its tax exemption in 1955, but the courts rejected all IRS allegations in 1959; the IPR dissolved in 1960. Historian Carroll Quigley, who says the Milner Group dominated its British branches, argued that Boston banker Jerome Greene, who wrote the IPR constitution in 1926 and channelled Wall Street funds into it, mattered more 'than any Communists or fellow travelers'.
cite: US Senate Internal Security Subcommittee, report on the Institute of Pacific Relations (1952); Wikipedia 'Institute of Pacific Relations'; Quigley, Tragedy and Hope, pp. 946–956; The Anglo-American Establishment, ch. 10
inside: A Senate inquiry concluded that Communists used a private research body on Asia as a vehicle to steer US Far East policy toward Communist aims.

n: Freemasons inside UK police forces, as exposed in 'The Brotherhood'
rank: Metropolitan Police and provincial police officers
d: Freemasons, members of a fraternal society organised in local lodges whose members swear to help one another, held posts throughout British police forces, according to journalist Stephen Knight's book The Brotherhood (Granada, 1983–84). It had chapters on the police, Birmingham City Police and Operation Countryman, a corruption inquiry. An extract in Police Review (28 October 1983) described City of London Freemasons helping secure a Metropolitan Police Commissioner's post for a candidate. After the book, Met Commissioner Kenneth Newman advised officers to stay away from lodges, and his Principles of Policing manual advised against joining. A lodge for Scotland Yard officers, the Manor of St James, was then formed and included chief officers. Knight died in July 1985.
cite: Stephen Knight, The Brotherhood (1984); Police Review vol. 91 no. 4733 (28 Oct 1983) via Statewatch; The Conversation, 'The Freemasons no longer have significant influence in the British police'; Wikipedia 'Kenneth Newman'

arch.t: UK Investigation: Masonic Network in Police and Judiciary Led to Parliamentary Inquiry and New Legal Disclosure Requirements

inside: A journalist's book described Freemasons spread through British police forces, with a London lodge helping secure the Metropolitan Police Commissioner's post for a chosen candidate.

n: Detective says Masonic officers took him off an Islington fraud case
rank: Detective Chief Inspector, Metropolitan Police Company Fraud Department
d: Detective Chief Inspector Brian Woollard of the Metropolitan Police said fellow officers who were Freemasons removed him from a corruption inquiry when it pointed to Freemasonry. He had been investigating corruption in Islington council's street-property renovation contracts. In a petition presented by Austin Mitchell MP on 20 December 1985 he said he was taken off the inquiry when it 'began to indicate a connection between corruption and Freemasonry', by officers who were Masons, and moved to uniform in April 1982. On 29 July 1988 Home Office minister Douglas Hogg told Jeremy Corbyn that the Home Secretary would not order an inquiry under section 32 of the Police Act 1964, and that Woollard had been dismissed by a disciplinary board on 25 May 1988 for absence from duty.
cite: HC Deb 20 December 1985 vol 89 cc671–2 (petition); HC written answer 29 July 1988

arch.t: UK Investigation: Masonic Network in Police and Judiciary Led to Parliamentary Inquiry and New Legal Disclosure Requirements

inside: A detective says fellow officers who were Freemasons took him off a corruption inquiry once it pointed to Freemasonry, so police decisions protected the lodges.

n: Wagner man Valery Zakharov becomes CAR president's security adviser
rank: national security adviser to the president
d: Russia placed Valery Zakharov, a Russian tied to the Wagner Group, inside the Central African Republic's presidency as national security adviser. Wagner is a private military company tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin that Russia used to place fighters and advisers with African governments. Zakharov served President Faustin-Archange Touadéra from 2018 and publicly told rebels in 2021 to hand over their leaders. Ukraine's SBU security service said in 2018 he headed Wagner's security firm in the country. The US Treasury put him on its sanctions list under its CAR programme with the note 'linked to: Private Military Company Wagner'; the listing shows he also held a Central African passport issued in June 2018.
cite: US Treasury OFAC sanctions list entry (CAR programme); Ukrainian SBU statement Dec 2018, as summarised on Wikipedia
inside: Russia placed a man tied to the Wagner military company inside the Central African Republic's presidency as the president's national security adviser.

n: Prigozhin's strategists pay Madagascar presidential candidates
rank: presidential election campaigns
d: Russian political strategists tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin, the businessman behind the Wagner Group, offered money to candidates in Madagascar's 2018 presidential race to shape who would hold office. The Russian investigative outlet Proekt and the BBC reported in 2019 that 15–20 such strategists dealt with as many as eight candidates, including the winner, Andry Rajoelina. Candidate André Mailhol said they gave him €5,000 in cash; ex-prime minister Omer Beriziky said he was promised $2 million. Rajoelina denied being Russia's candidate and the BBC found no evidence he took Russian money. Prigozhin's representatives denied any link.
cite: Proekt investigation (March 2019) and BBC, as reported by Meduza, 8 April 2019
inside: Russian strategists tied to the Wagner boss offered cash to several Madagascar presidential candidates, setting out to shape who would hold the country's top office.

n: Gupta family offers Mcebisi Jonas the finance ministry
rank: finance minister post offered
d: The Gupta brothers, Indian-born businessmen close to President Jacob Zuma, tried to choose South Africa's ministers by offering cabinet posts to officials who would cooperate. Deputy Finance Minister Mcebisi Jonas said the Guptas offered him the finance minister's job shortly before Zuma sacked minister Nhlanhla Nene in December 2015; former MP Vytjie Mentor testified she was offered the public enterprises ministry in 2010. The Zondo Commission, a judicial inquiry, found the Gupta network had 'captured' parts of the state, meaning it controlled appointments and contracts for its own gain. The US Treasury later cited a promised payment to a potential finance minister. The Guptas denied it.
cite: Judicial Commission of Inquiry into State Capture (Zondo Commission), report parts 1–5, Jan–June 2022
inside: A business family close to the president offered cabinet posts to officials who would cooperate, trying to choose South Africa's finance minister for its own ends.

n: Zondo report: ministers and state-firm chiefs acted for the Guptas
rank: public enterprises minister; Transnet and Eskom chief executives
d: A judicial inquiry found that South African ministers and heads of state-owned companies acted corruptly for the Gupta family, businessmen close to President Jacob Zuma. Chief Justice Raymond Zondo chaired the state capture inquiry, which heard over 300 witnesses from 2018 and published its report in five parts between 4 January and 22 June 2022. It named former public enterprises minister Malusi Gigaba and former Transnet (state rail and ports firm) chief Brian Molefe, and found that state advertising placed in the Gupta newspaper The New Age defied 'logic and legal requirements'.
cite: Zondo Commission report, 2022
inside: A judicial inquiry found that ministers and heads of state-owned companies acted corruptly for a business family, steering state decisions and spending to its benefit.

n: US sanctions the Gupta brothers for buying South African officials
rank: network that offered ministries and paid officials
d: The US Treasury found that the Gupta family, businessmen close to South Africa's President Jacob Zuma, bought influence inside the state. On 10 October 2019 it sanctioned Ajay, Atul and Rajesh Gupta and their associate Salim Essa under the Global Magnitsky programme, which freezes US assets of people accused of corruption or abuses. Treasury said the family offered government members money or posts for cooperation, paid an official to appoint people friendly to its businesses, and took hundreds of millions of dollars through state contracts. The brothers moved to Dubai in 2016; in 2023 the UAE refused to extradite Atul and Rajesh to South Africa.
cite: US Treasury press release SM789, 10 October 2019
inside: The US Treasury found that a business family paid an official to appoint people friendly to its firms and offered government members money or posts for cooperation.

n: Bain & Company helped Zuma's allies take over the tax service
rank: South African Revenue Service restructuring
d: Bain & Company, a US management consultancy, worked with President Jacob Zuma and tax commissioner Tom Moyane to take over the South African Revenue Service (SARS), the Zondo Commission found, partly to stop SARS investigating corruption. Bain had been paid for a 2015 restructuring that cut the SARS unit producing a third of revenues. Bain denied 'wilfully' facilitating capture. South Africa's National Treasury barred Bain from state contracts for 10 years on 29 September 2022, and Bain closed its South African consulting business in 2025.
cite: Zondo Commission report (2022); Nugent Commission on SARS (2018); National Treasury restriction, 29 Sept 2022
inside: A US consultancy worked inside the tax service with the president and his tax chief to restructure it, which an inquiry found partly served to stop corruption investigations.

n: McKinsey bribed South African state-firm officials, pays $122m
rank: officials at Eskom and Transnet
d: McKinsey & Company, a US consultancy, paid bribes to officials at South Africa's state power utility Eskom and rail firm Transnet to win contracts, working with Trillian, a firm owned by a Gupta associate. In 2024 McKinsey entered a three-year deferred prosecution agreement with the US Justice Department, a deal that suspends charges if the company meets conditions, and paid a $122 million penalty for bribing South African officials between 2012 and 2016; half goes to South Africa. It had earlier repaid about R1 billion to Eskom and R870 million to Transnet. South Africa's prosecutors charged McKinsey SA and former partner Vikas Sagar in 2022.
cite: US Department of Justice deferred prosecution agreement (Dec 2024); Zondo Commission part 4 (April 2022)
inside: A US consultancy bribed officials at South Africa's state power and rail companies, so those firms' contract decisions served the consultancy.

n: Iran-backed militias written into Iraq's armed forces by law
rank: Popular Mobilization Forces, a branch of the armed forces
d: Militias backed by Iran's Revolutionary Guards became a branch of Iraq's armed forces, paid by the Iraqi state. The Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) formed in June 2014 to fight Islamic State and are made up of about 67 mostly Shia factions, almost all backed by the Guards. A law passed in November 2016 and signed by President Fuad Masum on 19 December 2016 placed them under the prime minister and on the state budget. In 2024 the PMF chief of staff said publicly that it took orders from Iran's supreme leader. A 2025 reform bill to tighten state control was tabled under US pressure.
cite: Law of the Popular Mobilization Commission (2016); Washington Institute and Carnegie analyses, as summarised on Wikipedia
inside: Militias backed by Iran's Revolutionary Guards were made a paid branch of Iraq's armed forces, and their chief of staff said they took orders from Iran's supreme leader.

n: Falih al-Fayyadh: head of Iran-backed PMF sanctioned by the US
rank: chairman of the Popular Mobilization Commission; former national security adviser
d: Iran's Revolutionary Guards have allied militias inside Iraq's state through the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), militias almost all backed by the Guards and run by an Iraqi state body, the Popular Mobilization Commission. Falih al-Fayyadh, the commission's chairman, was at the same time Iraq's national security adviser, the government's senior adviser on security. On 8 January 2021 the US Treasury sanctioned him over the killing of protesters in 2019, and on 13 January it sanctioned PMF chief of staff Abu Fadak al-Mohammadawi. Iraq's foreign ministry said it was 'surprised'. Fayyadh remains PMF chairman, so the Iran-backed forces still sit under a state body he heads.
cite: US Treasury press release SM1231, 8 January 2021
inside: The chairman of the state body running Iran-backed militias was also Iraq's national security adviser, putting those forces' leader at the centre of government security policy.

n: Kata'ib Hezbollah, Iran's proxy, staffs three Iraqi state brigades
rank: PMF 45th, 46th and 47th Brigades
d: Kata'ib Hezbollah, an Iraqi Shia armed group that operates under Iran's Revolutionary Guards, staffs the 45th, 46th and 47th Brigades of Iraq's state-funded Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF). The US listed it as a terrorist organisation in 2009. It is a founding member of the PMF, and its commander Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis led the PMF in the field until a US strike killed him in January 2020. The US linked the group to the January 2024 Tower 22 drone attack in Jordan that killed three US soldiers.
cite: US State Department FTO listing (2009); US Treasury designations; Washington Institute analyses, as summarised on Wikipedia
inside: An Iraqi armed group that operates under Iran's Revolutionary Guards staffs three brigades of Iraq's state-funded forces, so state units are manned by Iran's proxy.

n: Egypt bribed Senator Bob Menendez, who was convicted as its agent
rank: US senator, chair of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee
d: Egypt's government, through businessmen, paid US Senator Bob Menendez in cash, gold bars and other gifts while he chaired the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, which shapes US arms sales and aid, including to Egypt. Prosecutors said he passed sensitive US information to aid the Egyptian government and spoke up for Qatar to help a New Jersey developer get Qatari royal funding. A halal-meat monopoly granted by Egypt to businessman Wael Hana's company was used to channel bribes. A Manhattan federal jury found Menendez guilty on all counts on 16 July 2024, including bribery, extortion, acting as a foreign agent and conspiracy. He resigned on 20 August 2024, was sentenced to 11 years on 29 January 2025 and is in prison; his wife Nadine was convicted on 21 April 2025 and sentenced to 4½ years.
cite: US v. Menendez et al., Southern District of New York: jury verdict 16 July 2024, sentence 29 January 2025; Wikipedia 'Bob Menendez'
org_note: Government of Egypt (with Qatari royal-linked funding) — foreign-state influence
inside: Egypt's government, through businessmen, paid a US senator chairing the Foreign Relations Committee, and he passed it sensitive information and acted as its agent.

n: Tom Barrack: acquitted of acting for the UAE inside Trump's circle
rank: chair of Trump's 2017 inaugural committee; US ambassador to Turkey and Syria envoy from 2025
d: US prosecutors charged that the United Arab Emirates used Tom Barrack, chair of Trump's 2017 inaugural committee, as its agent while he advised the Trump campaign and administration. The charges of 20 July 2021 were acting as an unregistered agent of the UAE, obstruction and false statements; the May 2022 indictment added that he sought hundreds of millions of dollars in UAE investment while lobbying for the UAE. A Brooklyn jury acquitted him and his aide Matthew Grimes on 4 November 2022. The Senate confirmed him as ambassador to Turkey on 29 April 2025 (60–36), and he was named special envoy for Syria in May 2025.
cite: US v. Barrack, Eastern District of New York, acquittal 4 November 2022; Senate confirmation vote 29 April 2025; Wikipedia 'Tom Barrack'
org_note: Government of the United Arab Emirates
inside: Prosecutors charged that the UAE used Trump's inaugural committee chair as its secret agent while he advised the campaign and administration; a jury acquitted him.

n: Henry Cuellar charged with taking Azerbaijan bribes; later pardoned
rank: US representative (Texas), senior member of the House Appropriations Committee
d: US prosecutors charged that the government of Azerbaijan and a Mexican bank paid Representative Henry Cuellar of Texas, a senior member of the House Appropriations Committee (which sets federal spending), to act in their interests in Congress. In May 2024 Cuellar and his wife Imelda were indicted on bribery, money-laundering and honest-services fraud counts over about $600,000 from a company controlled by Azerbaijan's government and from a bank based in Mexico City. A judge refused to dismiss the case in September 2025. On 3 December 2025, before any trial, President Trump announced a full and unconditional pardon for both.
cite: US v. Cuellar, Southern District of Texas, indictment May 2024; presidential pardon announced 3 December 2025 (Roll Call)
org_note: Government of Azerbaijan (state-controlled company) and a Mexican bank
inside: Prosecutors charged that Azerbaijan's government and a Mexican bank paid a senior congressman about $600,000 to act in their interests in Congress.

n: Cuban intelligence placed Victor Manuel Rocha in the US diplomatic service
rank: US ambassador to Bolivia; White House National Security Council staff; adviser to US Southern Command
d: Cuba's General Directorate of Intelligence (DGI) had an agent inside the US foreign service for decades, prosecutors said. Victor Manuel Rocha joined the foreign service in 1981, served at the White House National Security Council and the US Interests Section in Havana, was ambassador to Bolivia and later advised the commander of US Southern Command, the military command for Latin America. Prosecutors said he had acted for the DGI since at least 1981; in recorded conversations with an undercover agent he boasted of more than 40 years of service. He pleaded guilty and was sentenced in April 2024 to 15 years in prison and a $500,000 fine.
cite: US v. Rocha, Southern District of Florida, guilty plea and sentence April 2024 (AP via Britannica News)
org_note: Cuba's General Directorate of Intelligence (DGI)
inside: Cuba's intelligence service had its own agent inside the US foreign service for over 40 years, including as an ambassador and on the White House security staff.

n: Eric Adams charged over Turkish favours; case dismissed
rank: Mayor of New York City
d: Prosecutors charged that Turkish officials and businessmen bought favours from Eric Adams, the Mayor of New York City. In September 2024 a federal grand jury charged him with bribery, wire fraud, conspiracy and soliciting foreign campaign contributions. Prosecutors said he accepted luxury travel, took straw donations (money given in others' names) that drew city matching funds, and pressed the fire commissioner to let a Manhattan tower housing Turkey's consulate open in time for a visit by President Erdoğan. After the Justice Department asked to drop the case, Judge Dale Ho dismissed it with prejudice on 2 April 2025, so it cannot be brought again; Adams was never tried.
cite: US v. Adams, Southern District of New York, indictment September 2024, dismissal with prejudice 2 April 2025
org_note: Turkish government officials and businessmen
inside: Prosecutors charged that Turkish officials bought favours from New York's mayor, who pressed the fire commissioner to open a tower housing Turkey's consulate on time.

n: NYPD officer charged as Chinese consulate agent; charges dropped
rank: New York police officer and Army reservist
d: US prosecutors charged in 2020 that officials at China's consulate in New York directed Baimadajie Angwang, a New York police officer and Army reservist, to report on Tibetans in the United States. He was held for about six months. His lawyers said his contacts with the consulate were to get a visa to visit family. On 19 January 2023 a federal judge in Brooklyn granted the government's request to dismiss the case, prosecutors citing new, classified information. The NYPD later fired him.
cite: US v. Angwang, Eastern District of New York, dismissal 19 January 2023 (ABC7 New York)
