inside: A Google engineer secretly worked for two China-based companies while inside Google and took its confidential AI designs.

n: Russian trade envoy paid a SoftBank employee for network files
rank: employee with access to SoftBank servers
d: A Russian diplomat paid Yutaka Araki, a SoftBank Corp. employee, for company documents: in February 2019 Araki took manuals on mobile-phone base stations and other communication equipment from a company server and gave them to him, and admitted he was paid. Japanese police named Anton Kalnin, the second-ranking official of the Russian Trade Representation in Japan, as a suspect; he left for Russia when police asked to question him. Araki was arrested in January 2020 and indicted in February 2020 under the Unfair Competition Prevention Act, Japan's law on trade secrets.
cite: Tokyo District Public Prosecutors Office — indictment Feb 2020 (Japan Times)
inside: A Russian trade official paid a SoftBank employee, who took network equipment manuals from the company's server and gave them to him.

n: Motor Sich managers charged with secretly supplying Russia's Rostec
rank: president of Ukraine's main aircraft-engine maker
d: Ukrainian prosecutors charge that the management of Motor Sich, a Zaporizhzhia maker of engines for military and civil helicopters and aircraft, ran hidden channels supplying engines and parts to Russia in collusion with Rostec, Russia's state technology corporation, and that in April 2022 former president Viacheslav Bohuslaiev blocked delivery of a helicopter to Ukraine's military intelligence. The SBU security service detained Bohuslaiev and the foreign-trade director in October 2022. Assets of about US$314 million were seized and he was sent to trial for treason, the crime of betraying one's country. The state had already taken over the company in 2021 after a sale to Chinese investors was blocked.
cite: Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) and Prosecutor General — treason indictment
inside: Prosecutors charge that Motor Sich's management secretly worked with Russia's Rostec, supplying it engines and blocking a helicopter for Ukraine's military intelligence.

n: Communist Party places its cells inside China's private companies
rank: party organisation inside each firm, including foreign joint ventures
d: China's Company Law requires any company with three or more Communist Party members to set up a party organisation, giving the party its own body inside the firm. The party's Organization Department reported that 73.1% of private companies had one in 2018, up from 58.4% in 2013, and in 2017 all of the 100 largest state firms wrote the party's role into their charters. In 2017–18 Chinese state partners of some foreign joint ventures asked the foreign side to write party groups into the articles of association, the rules that govern a company. In September 2020 the party told its United Front departments, which manage relations with groups outside the party, to 'guide' the governance of private firms.
cite: PRC Company Law (party-organisation clause); CCP Organization Department statistics; CSIS analysis
inside: China's Communist Party places its own organisations inside most private firms and some foreign joint ventures, and told its departments to guide their governance.

n: Michael Calvey says a rival used FSB links to win a bank dispute
rank: control of Vostochny Bank
d: Michael Calvey, an American who founded the Baring Vostok investment fund, says a business rival used connections inside Russia's FSB security service to win a dispute over Vostochny Bank. When the FSB arrested Calvey and three colleagues on fraud charges on 14 February 2019, his fund held 52.5% of the bank and was suing a fellow shareholder, Artem Avetisyan, in London. Avetisyan is described as a friend of the son of former FSB director Nikolai Patrushev. A Moscow court gave Calvey a 5.5-year suspended sentence in August 2021; the conviction was vacated on 5 April 2024.
cite: Meshchansky District Court, Moscow — verdict Aug 2021, vacated 5 Apr 2024; London Court of International Arbitration ruling Mar 2019
inside: Calvey says a business rival used connections inside Russia's FSB to have him arrested while the two were fighting over control of Vostochny Bank.

n: Sinovel recruited an AMSC engineer to pass it turbine software
rank: insider at AMSC's Austrian subsidiary
d: Sinovel, a Chinese wind-turbine maker that bought control software from the US company AMSC, recruited an engineer at AMSC's Austrian subsidiary to pass it the source code. With the code Sinovel could stop paying AMSC; AMSC said its losses exceeded US$800 million. A federal jury in Madison, Wisconsin convicted Sinovel of trade-secret theft on 24 January 2018, and AMSC announced a settlement in July 2018.
cite: US District Court, W.D. Wisconsin — jury verdict 24 Jan 2018
inside: Chinese turbine maker Sinovel recruited an engineer inside AMSC's Austrian subsidiary to hand over the source code it needed to stop paying AMSC.

n: Tokyo Electron employee obtained TSMC's 2nm secrets from TSMC staff
rank: engineers inside TSMC
d: Taiwanese prosecutors said a Tokyo Electron employee obtained secrets about TSMC's 2-nanometre chip process from TSMC staff, to help Tokyo Electron, a Japanese chip-equipment maker, win equipment orders from TSMC. TSMC is the world's largest contract chipmaker and the 2nm process is one of Taiwan's most guarded technologies. The former TSMC staff and the Tokyo Electron employee were indicted in August 2025 under the National Security Act. On 27 April 2026 a Taiwan court sentenced the main defendant to 10 years, three other ex-TSMC staff to two to six years, and fined Tokyo Electron's Taiwan unit; two of the sentences became final in July 2026.
cite: Taiwan district court judgment, 27 Apr 2026 (Al Jazeera/Reuters); final rulings for two defendants, Jul 2026
inside: A Tokyo Electron employee obtained TSMC's 2nm chip secrets from staff inside TSMC to help his company win orders from it.

n: PCC crime group accused of controlling two São Paulo bus companies
rank: owners and directors of Transwolff and UpBus
d: São Paulo prosecutors charge that the PCC (Primeiro Comando da Capital), Brazil's largest criminal organisation, worked through the directors of the bus companies Transwolff (about 1,200 buses) and UpBus, who they say laundered PCC money from drug trafficking and robbery through city transport contracts. The charges came in Operação Fim da Linha on 9 April 2024, run by prosecutors, tax and police officials; courts froze up to R$600 million. The same day the mayor issued Decree 63.328 placing both companies under city control, and in 2025 the city moved to end their contracts and hand the lines to other operators.
cite: São Paulo Public Ministry (GAECO) — Operação Fim da Linha, 9 Apr 2024; Municipal Decree 63.328
inside: Prosecutors charge that the PCC crime group controlled two São Paulo bus companies through their directors and laundered its money through city transport contracts.

n: Sicilian Mafia clan bribed Lidl Italia insiders to win contracts
rank: four regional management offices of Lidl Italia
d: The Laudani clan of Catania, part of the Sicilian Mafia (Cosa Nostra), used bribed insiders at the supermarket chain Lidl Italia to win work such as warehouse logistics and shop fitting for firms it controlled, Milan anti-mafia prosecutors said when they arrested 15 people in May 2017. A Milan court put four Lidl Italia management offices, overseeing about 200 shops, under judicial administration (court-appointed managers) for six months, as well as the company that guarded Milan's law courts. Lidl was not itself under investigation.
cite: Milan court — judicial administration order, May 2017
inside: Prosecutors said a Sicilian Mafia clan bribed insiders at Lidl Italia so that its management offices gave contracts to firms the clan controlled.

n: 'Ndrangheta clan took over firms in Emilia-Romagna
rank: construction and haulage companies of the region
d: The Grande Aracri clan of the 'Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia, ran and took over construction and other firms in Emilia-Romagna in northern Italy, including in rebuilding after the 2012 earthquake. The Aemilia maxi-trial, a single trial of many defendants, dealt with this branch. The first final convictions of five clan leaders came in October 2018. In May 2022 Italy's Court of Cassation, its highest appeal court, confirmed more than 70 convictions, and its reasoning described a self-standing 'Ndrangheta structure in Emilia rooted among local entrepreneurs who knowingly used the clan.
cite: Court of Cassation — Aemilia rulings Oct 2018 and May 2022
inside: The 'Ndrangheta's Grande Aracri clan took over and ran construction and other firms in Emilia-Romagna, including in post-earthquake rebuilding.

n: Russian offered a Tesla worker US$1m to plant malware
rank: employee at Tesla's Nevada Gigafactory
d: In 2020 Egor Kriuchkov, a Russian national, tried to recruit an employee at Tesla's Gigafactory near Reno as an insider for a criminal group, offering US$1 million to install malware on the plant's network so the group could steal data and demand ransom; he expected US$250,000 for the recruitment. The employee told the FBI, which recorded later meetings. Kriuchkov pleaded guilty on 18 March 2021, was sentenced in May 2021 to time served and was ordered deported.
cite: US District Court, District of Nevada — plea 18 Mar 2021, sentence May 2021
inside: A Russian crime group tried to recruit a Tesla employee to install malware inside the plant's network so it could steal data and demand ransom.

n: Opus Dei-linked bloc at the core of Banco Popular
rank: board and core shareholders of Banco Popular
d: Shareholder lawsuits showed that people and foundations tied to Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation of priests and lay members, formed the core shareholder group of Banco Popular, Spain's sixth-largest bank. They included Opus Dei numerary (a celibate full member) and board secretary Francisco Aparicio Valls and the Fundación Universitaria de Navarra and Fomento de Fundaciones; Luis Valls Taberner, president from 1972 to 2004, was also a numerary. Journalist Gareth Gore's 2024 book 'Opus' says the bank channelled money to Opus Dei causes; Opus Dei and the Valls Taberner foundations call this false. The bank failed and was sold to Santander for €1 in June 2017.
cite: El Independiente, 10 Jun 2018 (shareholder lawsuits); Gareth Gore, 'Opus' (2024); Opus Dei statements 2024
inside: People and foundations tied to Opus Dei held the core of Banco Popular's board and shares, and a 2024 book says the bank sent money to Opus Dei causes, which they deny.

n: Boeing staff did FAA safety checks and played down 737 MAX system
rank: Federal Aviation Administration certification staff
d: Under the Federal Aviation Administration's Organization Designation Authorization, Boeing employees carry out much of the work of certifying Boeing's own planes as safe on behalf of the FAA, the US agency responsible. After the Lion Air (2018) and Ethiopian Airlines (2019) 737 MAX crashes killed 346 people, a June 2020 Transportation Department Inspector General report found Boeing had played down the MCAS flight-control system during certification and the FAA had missed it. The House Transportation Committee's final report of September 2020 found Boeing withheld key information from the FAA and that the delegation system weakened the agency's oversight. The delegation programme is still in use.
cite: US House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, final 737 MAX report, September 2020; US DOT Office of Inspector General report, June 2020
inside: Boeing's own employees carry out much of the FAA's safety certification of Boeing planes, and during the 737 MAX's certification Boeing played down the MCAS system.

n: Purdue helped the FDA reviewer draft his OxyContin approval
rank: FDA medical review officer
d: Purdue Pharma, owned by the Sackler family, helped write the US Food and Drug Administration's own review of its painkiller OxyContin. According to Purdue documents in a 2006 Justice Department review, Dr Curtis Wright IV, the FDA medical officer who approved OxyContin in 1995 for 'moderate to severe pain', met Purdue staff in a hotel room near FDA offices in Rockville from 31 January to 2 February 1995 and let the company help draft his review and approve label wording, including the claim that delayed absorption 'is believed to reduce the abuse liability'. Wright left the FDA about a year later and went to work for Purdue. That label sentence was quoted in Purdue's 2007 felony conviction for misbranding.
cite: US Justice Department review of Purdue documents (2006), as reported; Purdue 2007 misbranding conviction; Wikipedia 'Purdue Pharma'
inside: Purdue documents show its staff helped an FDA reviewer write his own approval of OxyContin, including label wording on abuse, and he later went to work for Purdue.

n: Ex-DEA lawyer for drug industry wrote 2016 law weakening the DEA
rank: members of Congress; DEA enforcement powers
d: D. Linden Barber, a former senior lawyer at the Drug Enforcement Administration who had become an attorney for the drug industry, wrote the text of the Ensuring Patient Access and Effective Drug Enforcement Act of 2016, the Washington Post and CBS '60 Minutes' reported in October 2017, drawing on former DEA official Joe Rannazzisi. The law, pushed by the drug industry, changed the test for seizing suspicious narcotics shipments from an 'imminent' to an 'immediate' danger, making it harder for the DEA to act against distributors. Its House sponsor, Representative Tom Marino, withdrew as President Trump's nominee for drug czar on 17 October 2017.
cite: Washington Post / CBS 60 Minutes investigation, October 2017; WGBH/NPR, 17 October 2017
inside: US media reported that a lawyer for the drug industry wrote the text of a federal law that made it harder for the DEA to act against distributors.

n: Monsanto email says EPA official offered to 'kill' a glyphosate review
rank: EPA pesticide division manager
d: Court papers unsealed in March 2017 in the US Roundup litigation include an email by a manager at Monsanto, maker of the weedkiller Roundup (glyphosate) and now owned by Bayer, saying that a senior EPA official offered to block another agency's safety review for the company. The official, Jess Rowland, chaired the EPA committee that found glyphosate unlikely to cause cancer; according to the email, he said in April 2015 'If I can kill this I should get a medal' about a planned glyphosate review by the ATSDR, a federal health agency. The ATSDR had promised its review for October 2015 and did not publish it then. Rowland had left the EPA in 2016. Monsanto said the emails showed a normal flow of information; plaintiffs' lawyers called the relationship 'highly suspicious'.
cite: In re: Roundup Products Liability Litigation, MDL 2741 (N.D. Cal.), unsealed documents; Insurance Journal (Bloomberg), 16 March 2017
inside: A Monsanto email says a senior EPA official offered to block another agency's glyphosate safety review for the company, and that review did not appear when promised.

n: Industry-written model bills copied into 10,000 US state bills
rank: state legislators in all 50 states
d: Outside groups, many funded by industry, wrote at least 10,000 bills introduced in US state legislatures from 2010 to 2018 that were almost entirely copied from their model legislation, a 2019 investigation by USA Today, the Arizona Republic and the Center for Public Integrity found after comparing nearly a million bills. More than 2,100 became law. More than 4,000 benefited industries, and over 80 limited people's ability to sue companies. Authors included the industry-funded American Legislative Exchange Council (an 'Asbestos Transparency Act' filed in at least 32 states and passed in 12), the Goldwater Institute and a for-profit cancer hospital chain, as well as the liberal State Innovation Exchange.
cite: USA Today / Arizona Republic / Center for Public Integrity, 'Copy, Paste, Legislate', 4 April 2019
org_note: alec used as the main author; the study covers several groups on both sides.
inside: Industry-funded groups wrote model bills that state legislators copied into at least 10,000 bills, over 2,100 of which became law.

n: Firms paid MP Owen Paterson, who lobbied regulators for them
rank: Food Standards Agency and Department for International Development
d: The diagnostics company Randox and the meat processor Lynn's Country Foods paid Owen Paterson, a sitting MP and former Environment and Northern Ireland Secretary, as a consultant, and he lobbied government bodies on their behalf. In October 2021 the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards found he had broken the paid-advocacy rule, which bars MPs from lobbying for those who pay them, by approaching the Food Standards Agency three times and the Department for International Development four times for Randox, and the Food Standards Agency seven times for Lynn's. A government attempt to overturn the recommended suspension collapsed, and Paterson resigned from Parliament on 5 November 2021.
cite: Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards and Committee on Standards report, October 2021
inside: Two companies paid a sitting MP as a consultant, and he lobbied the Food Standards Agency and a government department for them.

n: Peer Michelle Mone's hidden link to £200m PPE Medpro contracts
rank: Department of Health procurement
d: Conservative peer Michelle Mone, a member of the House of Lords, referred PPE Medpro into the UK government's 2020 'VIP lane', a fast track for pandemic protective equipment offers referred by ministers, MPs and officials, while denying any involvement with the firm. PPE Medpro won £200 million of contracts; its gowns were not shown to be sterile and went unused. Mone admitted her involvement in December 2023; leaked records showed £29 million of profits went to a trust she could benefit from. In October 2025 the High Court ruled PPE Medpro breached its contract and must repay about £122 million. Mone took leave from the House of Lords.
cite: High Court of England and Wales (Department of Health and Social Care v PPE Medpro), judgment October 2025; National Audit Office reports on PPE procurement
who: PPE Medpro (Michelle Mone and Doug Barrowman)
org_note: status 'convicted' used for a civil judgment against the company; not a criminal conviction.
inside: A peer with a hidden stake in PPE Medpro referred it into the government's fast track, and it won £200 million of contracts.

n: Glyphosate makers' text copied into German safety review
rank: Federal Institute for Risk Assessment (BfR) assessors
d: Text written by the glyphosate makers, led by Monsanto, ended up in the official German safety review that the EU used to renew the weedkiller. Germany's Federal Institute for Risk Assessment (BfR) wrote the draft review behind the EU's 2017 renewal of glyphosate; the renewal request came from industry. A study for Members of the European Parliament published on 15 January 2019 by Stefan Weber and Helmut Burtscher-Schaden found that BfR had taken large passages from the industry application, with up to half of some chapters written by the applicants, and presented them as its own evaluation. BfR rejected the plagiarism charge. The EU renewed glyphosate again in 2023 for ten years.
cite: Weber and Burtscher-Schaden study for MEPs, 15 January 2019; Greens/EFA release
who: Monsanto (Bayer) and the Glyphosate Task Force
inside: A study for MEPs found text written by glyphosate makers was copied into Germany's official safety review behind the EU renewal; the German institute rejects this.

n: Novartis bribed Greek public hospital staff and doctors
rank: two former prime ministers and several health ministers (alleged)
d: Novartis, the Swiss drug company, paid bribes inside Greece's public health system to sell its medicines. In 2020 Novartis paid about $347 million to US authorities to settle charges that included bribing Greek hospital staff and doctors. Greek prosecutors had gone further in 2018, alleging that Novartis bribed officials from 2006 to 2015 and naming two former prime ministers and several former health ministers from the New Democracy and PASOK parties. Those politicians denied it, and the cases against them were dropped, so the established part of the case concerns hospital staff and doctors rather than ministers.
cite: Greek prosecutors' case file sent to Parliament, February 2018; US DOJ and SEC Novartis resolution, June 2020
inside: Novartis paid bribes to staff and doctors inside Greece's public hospital system to sell its medicines.

n: Zelensky friend's network ran kickbacks at state nuclear firm
rank: energy and justice ministers; Energoatom
d: A group led by businessman Timur Mindich, a friend of President Zelensky and co-owner of the Kvartal 95 studio, took kickbacks from contractors of Energoatom, Ukraine's state nuclear power company, according to the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU). In November 2025 NABU said the scheme was worth $100 million. Mindich left Ukraine hours before NABU searched his home on 10 November 2025. Former deputy prime minister Oleksiy Chernyshov was charged with illegal enrichment. Zelensky asked justice minister German Galushchenko and energy minister Svitlana Hrynchuk to resign, and his chief of staff Andriy Yermak later became a suspect.
cite: National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU), Operation Midas, November 2025
inside: Anti-corruption investigators say a network led by the president's friend ran kickbacks from contractors of Ukraine's state nuclear company, with ministers and officials drawn in.

n: Power station director's secret company linked to Malta's top aides
rank: Prime Minister's chief of staff and energy minister
d: Yorgen Fenech, a director of Electrogas, the company that built Malta's gas power station under a state contract, secretly owned 17 Black, a company registered in the UAE, as was revealed in November 2018. Leaked documents had listed 17 Black as a 'target client' expected to pay into secret Panama companies set up for Konrad Mizzi, the energy minister, and Keith Schembri, the prime minister's chief of staff. Journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia was investigating 17 Black when she was killed by a car bomb in 2017. Fenech is charged with complicity in her murder, a trial that began in mid-2026. Schembri resigned in November 2019. In February 2025 Fenech, Mizzi and Schembri were arraigned together on corruption charges over the Electrogas project.
cite: Maltese criminal proceedings, 2019–2026; Reuters / Times of Malta 17 Black investigation, November 2018; MaltaToday, 'Dubai company 17 Black was target client of Schembri's and Mizzi's Panama set-ups', April 2018
inside: A power-station company director secretly owned a firm listed to pay into hidden companies of Malta's energy minister and the prime minister's chief of staff.

n: Bezeq owner allegedly bought favourable rulings from Netanyahu
rank: Prime Minister
d: Shaul Elovitch, controlling owner of Bezeq, Israel's largest telecoms company, is accused of obtaining regulatory decisions worth large sums from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who was also communications minister and so regulated Bezeq. Prosecutors say that in return Elovitch's news site Walla! gave Netanyahu favourable coverage. Netanyahu is charged with bribery, fraud and breach of trust in what is called Case 4000; his trial began in May 2020 and his testimony ended in June 2026. He denies the charges and in November 2025 asked President Herzog for a pardon.
cite: Indictment filed by Israel's Attorney General, 2020; Jerusalem District Court trial, 2020–2026
inside: Bezeq's owner is accused of trading favourable news coverage for regulatory decisions from the prime minister who, as communications minister, regulated Bezeq.

n: Telia paid Uzbek president's daughter for mobile licences
rank: President Islam Karimov's daughter, Gulnara Karimova
d: Telia, the Swedish-Finnish telecoms group, got into Uzbekistan's mobile market by paying companies controlled by Gulnara Karimova, daughter of then-President Islam Karimov, who in return secured licences and radio frequencies from the state. In September 2017 Telia agreed to pay about $965 million to US, Dutch and Swedish authorities to settle bribery charges. OCCRP, a network of investigative journalists, reported in 2015 that Karimova took over $1 billion in bribes from Scandinavian and Russian telecom firms. She was later jailed in Uzbekistan.
cite: US DOJ and SEC resolution with Telia Company, September 2017; OCCRP, 2015
inside: Telia paid companies controlled by the Uzbek president's daughter, who in return secured state licences and frequencies for it.

n: Airbus paid intermediaries to bribe officials for contracts
rank: airline and defence procurement officials in many countries
d: Airbus, the European aircraft maker, hired and paid intermediaries to bribe officials and win civil and military contracts in many countries. Investigators found the practice ran from 2012 onward, with suspect sales in countries including Saudi Arabia, Kazakhstan, the Philippines, Indonesia, Austria, China and Mauritius. In January 2020 Airbus agreed to pay about €3.6 billion to French, British and US prosecutors, the largest bribery settlement of its kind, under deferred prosecution agreements, deals in which charges are suspended if the company pays and reforms. The UK agreement covered bribes in Sri Lanka, Malaysia, Indonesia, Taiwan and Ghana.
cite: Deferred prosecution agreements with France's PNF, the UK Serious Fraud Office and the US DOJ, January 2020
inside: Airbus paid intermediaries to bribe officials in many countries so that their governments and airlines bought its aircraft.

n: BAE paid Saudi prince over Al-Yamamah arms deals
rank: Serious Fraud Office investigation
d: BAE Systems, Britain's largest arms maker, was reported in 2007 by BBC Panorama to have paid hundreds of millions of pounds to Prince Bandar bin Sultan, a senior Saudi royal and official, in connection with Al-Yamamah, a series of British arms sales to Saudi Arabia led by BAE since 1985. In December 2006 the Serious Fraud Office had dropped its investigation into alleged BAE slush funds, secret funds used for payments, after pressure from the Saudi and British governments; a new Typhoon fighter contract for 72 aircraft had been signed in 2006. In 2010 BAE pleaded guilty in the United States to false accounting and misleading statements and paid $400 million.
cite: UK Serious Fraud Office decision, 14 December 2006; US District Court for the District of Columbia plea, March 2010; BBC Panorama, June 2007
inside: BAE was reported to have paid a senior Saudi royal official hundreds of millions of pounds in connection with Saudi Arabia's purchases of its arms.

n: Rolls-Royce and Airbus bribes reached Garuda airline's chief
rank: president director of state airline Garuda Indonesia
d: Rolls-Royce and Airbus money reached the head of Garuda Indonesia, the state-owned national airline, while he was buying their aircraft and engines. In May 2020 the Jakarta Corruption Court sentenced former president director Emirsyah Satar to eight years in prison for taking Rp 49.3 billion (US$3.4 million) in bribes tied to those purchases, and for laundering Rp 87.5 billion. Prosecutors traced the money to the two companies through middleman Soetikno Soedarjo, who received six years. Both companies' bribery admissions to UK prosecutors covered Indonesia.
cite: Jakarta Corruption Court verdict, 8 May 2020; KPK; Jakarta Post, 9 May 2020
inside: Rolls-Royce and Airbus money reached the head of state airline Garuda Indonesia while he was buying their aircraft and engines.

n: Monsanto paid Indonesian official reviewing its GM cotton
rank: senior official, Ministry of Environment
d: Monsanto, the US seed and chemicals company, paid a high-level official at Indonesia's environment ministry while that ministry was assessing Monsanto's genetically modified cotton. In 2002 a Monsanto senior manager had an Indonesian consulting firm pay the official a $50,000 bribe, disguised as consulting fees. The US Securities and Exchange Commission also found that Monsanto's Indonesian affiliates made illicit payments of at least $700,000 to at least 140 current or former officials and their families. Monsanto settled in 2005 under a deferred prosecution agreement, a deal in which charges are suspended if the company pays and reforms.
cite: US DOJ deferred prosecution agreement and SEC settlement, January 2005
inside: Monsanto paid a senior official at Indonesia's environment ministry while that ministry was assessing its genetically modified cotton.

n: Samsung heir bribed President Park's friend for state support
rank: President Park Geun-hye
d: Lee Jae-yong, de facto head of Samsung, South Korea's largest business group, offered $38 million in bribes to entities controlled by Choi Soon-sil, a friend of President Park Geun-hye, to win government support for a merger that strengthened his control of Samsung. He was charged in 2017 and the scandal led to Park's impeachment. Lee was convicted in August 2017; after appeals he served a 2.5-year sentence from January 2021. President Yoon Suk Yeol pardoned him in August 2022, and he became Samsung chairman in October 2022.
cite: Seoul Central District Court, August 2017; Seoul High Court retrial, January 2021
inside: Samsung's heir paid money to bodies run by the president's confidante so that the government would back the merger that strengthened his control of Samsung.

n: TEPCO captured Japan's nuclear regulator before Fukushima
rank: Nuclear and Industrial Safety Agency (NISA)
d: Tokyo Electric Power Company (TEPCO) and the nuclear industry had come to steer NISA, the Japanese agency meant to regulate them, according to the National Diet's independent inquiry into the Fukushima Daiichi meltdown of March 2011. The commission, chaired by Kiyoshi Kurokawa, reported in July 2012 that the relationship amounted to 'regulatory capture', meaning the regulator served the industry. It found regulators asked operators about their wishes before writing new rules, told them they need not plan for a station blackout, and allowed TEPCO to push earthquake checks due in 2009 to 2016. NISA was abolished and replaced by the Nuclear Regulation Authority in 2012.
cite: Fukushima Nuclear Accident Independent Investigation Commission (NAIIC), National Diet of Japan, report, 5 July 2012; Nuclear Engineering International
who: TEPCO and Japan's nuclear power industry
inside: The nuclear industry came to steer the agency meant to regulate it, so regulators asked operators what rules they wanted and let TEPCO delay safety checks.

n: Coca-Cola-founded ILSI had its office inside China's CDC
rank: Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention
d: The International Life Sciences Institute (ILSI), an industry-funded science group, had its China branch housed inside the Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the national public health agency. ILSI was founded in 1978 by Coca-Cola executive Alex Malaspina and is funded by food and chemical companies. Harvard anthropologist Susan Greenhalgh reported in the BMJ and the Journal of Public Health Policy in 2019 that ILSI-China shaped China's obesity policy toward exercise rather than diet and sugary drinks. Nutrition researcher Barry Popkin said ILSI had 'an extremely harmful influence' in China. Mars left ILSI in 2018 and Coca-Cola in 2021.
cite: Greenhalgh, BMJ, January 2019; Journal of Public Health Policy, 2019
inside: An industry-funded group set up inside China's national disease-control agency and steered its obesity policy towards exercise rather than diet and sugary drinks.

n: AgustaWestland accused of bribes for Indian VIP helicopters
rank: Indian Air Force VVIP helicopter procurement
d: AgustaWestland, a helicopter maker owned by Italy's Finmeccanica (now Leonardo), was accused of paying bribes of about $60 million to win an Indian contract. India had agreed in February 2010 to buy 12 AgustaWestland AW101 helicopters to fly the president and prime minister. In February 2013 Finmeccanica chief executive Giuseppe Orsi was arrested in Italy over the alleged bribes, and India's Central Bureau of Investigation opened a case. India cancelled the $630 million deal in January 2014 and recovered its payments. Orsi was fully acquitted by Italian courts in 2019; Indian proceedings against middlemen continue.
cite: Italian courts (acquittal, 2019); Indian Ministry of Defence cancellation, January 2014; CBI case
inside: The helicopter maker is accused of paying about $60 million in bribes to win India's contract for the helicopters that fly its president and prime minister.

n: UAE oil company's chief ran COP28 and prepared oil deal talks
rank: President of the UN climate summit (COP28)
d: Sultan Al Jaber, chief executive of the UAE state oil company ADNOC and chairman of the renewable firm Masdar, was named president of the COP28 UN climate talks, and his team prepared to use meetings in that role for company business. On 27 November 2023 the BBC, with the Centre for Climate Reporting, published leaked briefing papers for his meetings with foreign governments that included talking points on ADNOC and Masdar commercial interests for more than two dozen countries and plans to discuss oil and gas deals with 15. The COP28 team did not deny using meetings for business and said 'private meetings are private'; Al Jaber called the claims false.
cite: BBC / Centre for Climate Reporting leaked documents, 27 November 2023; CBS News, 27 November 2023
inside: The UAE state oil company's chief became president of the UN climate summit, and his team prepared to use its meetings to pursue oil and gas deals.

n: Azerbaijan's COP29 chief filmed discussing oil and gas deals
rank: chief executive of the UN climate summit (COP29)
d: Azerbaijan's oil and gas interests were inside the leadership of the COP29 UN climate talks it hosted in November 2024. The summit president, Mukhtar Babayev, had been vice-president for ecology at the state oil company SOCAR. The summit's chief executive, deputy energy minister Elnur Soltanov, was secretly filmed by Global Witness campaigners posing as investors, discussing possible oil and gas deals during the run-up to the talks. Critics said this broke the code of conduct for COP presidencies, which requires them to act impartially. Azerbaijan's economy rests on oil and gas.
cite: Global Witness undercover recording, November 2024; Wikipedia '2024 United Nations Climate Change Conference'
who: SOCAR and Azerbaijan's oil and gas sector
inside: A former state oil company executive led the UN climate summit, and its chief executive was filmed discussing oil and gas deals while preparing the talks.

n: BAT arranged bribes to Comoros officials to block tobacco laws
rank: officials handling tobacco control law
d: British American Tobacco (BAT), the world's second-largest listed tobacco company, arranged bribes for officials in the Comoros Islands, Rwanda and Burundi, including payments aimed at frustrating tobacco control laws based on the WHO tobacco treaty. BBC Panorama reported this in November 2015 using documents from former BAT employee Paul Hopkins, putting the total at about $26,000. A 2021 University of Bath study of these and other leaked records counted 236 payments worth $601,502 from 2008 to 2013 in ten African countries. The UK Serious Fraud Office opened an investigation in 2017 and closed it in January 2021 without charges. BAT denied wrongdoing.
cite: BBC Panorama, 30 November 2015; University of Bath Tobacco Control Research Group, 2021; UK Serious Fraud Office closure, January 2021
inside: The tobacco company paid officials in the Comoros in ways aimed at frustrating the tobacco-control laws those officials were handling.

n: BAT payments to Burundi officials to block tobacco laws
rank: officials handling tobacco control law
d: British American Tobacco (BAT) made payments to officials in Burundi, according to the leaked company records that BBC Panorama reported in 2015. The University of Bath's 2021 analysis says payments in Burundi, Comoros, Rwanda and Uganda were aimed at frustrating tobacco control laws modelled on the WHO Framework Convention, the global treaty that commits governments to cut smoking. The UK Serious Fraud Office closed its investigation in 2021 without charges, and BAT denies the allegations.
cite: BBC Panorama, 30 November 2015; University of Bath Tobacco Control Research Group, 2021
inside: The tobacco company paid officials in Burundi in ways aimed at frustrating the tobacco-control laws those officials were responsible for.

n: Shipping industry sat inside national delegations at the UN's IMO
rank: International Maritime Organization (IMO) environment committee
d: Shipping companies and their trade groups had people inside national delegations at the International Maritime Organization (IMO), the London-based UN agency that sets rules for global shipping, which emits close to 3% of greenhouse gases. An October 2017 InfluenceMap report found that at the IMO's latest environment committee meeting, 31% of member states had delegations that included direct business interests. It found that the International Chamber of Shipping, BIMCO and the World Shipping Council sought to delay climate rules and keep measures voluntary. The industry groups said they supported cutting emissions.
cite: InfluenceMap, 'Corporate Capture of the IMO', October 2017
inside: Shipping companies and trade groups had people inside national delegations at the UN shipping agency, where the industry worked to delay climate rules.

n: ABB paid $37m to an Eskom executive for Kusile contracts
rank: senior official, state power utility Eskom
d: ABB, the Swiss-Swedish engineering group, paid more than $37 million in bribes between 2014 and 2017 to a high-ranking official at Eskom, South Africa's state-owned electricity company, to win work on the Kusile power station. ABB admitted this in December 2022 and paid $315 million to the US Justice Department, $75 million to the Securities and Exchange Commission and a Swiss fine. It also agreed to return $104 million to Eskom.
cite: US DOJ deferred prosecution agreement and SEC settlement with ABB, 2 December 2022
inside: ABB paid a senior official at the state power company more than $37 million so that Eskom would give ABB work on the Kusile station.

n: SAP bribed South African city, ministry and Eskom officials
rank: officials at Johannesburg, Tshwane, the water department and Eskom
d: SAP, the German business-software company, bribed officials at the City of Johannesburg, the City of Tshwane, the Department of Water and Sanitation and the state power company Eskom from 2013 to 2017 to win contracts, and bribed Indonesian officials from 2015 to 2018. In January 2024 SAP agreed to pay more than $220 million to US authorities and entered a three-year deferred prosecution agreement, a deal in which charges are suspended if the company pays and reforms. Up to $55.1 million was credited to a South African case. Earlier, SAP had been accused of paying a company linked to the Gupta family to win work at Transnet, the state freight company.
cite: US DOJ deferred prosecution agreement and SEC order, 10 January 2024; OCCRP, 12 January 2024
inside: SAP paid officials at South African cities, a ministry and the state power company so that those bodies would award it contracts.

n: Bosasa paid South African officials while winning prison contracts
rank: Correctional Services officials; minister Nomvula Mokonyane
d: Bosasa (later African Global Operations), a company run by the late Gavin Watson, paid benefits to politicians while it won catering, security and other contracts from the Department of Correctional Services for years. Part 3 of the Zondo Commission's report on state capture, the takeover of state bodies by private interests (1 March 2022), found prima facie evidence of corruption by former minister Nomvula Mokonyane, for whom Bosasa paid a birthday party and Christmas groceries, and recommended she be investigated. It also called for corruption charges over Bosasa's payments to former ANC MP Vincent Smith. Mokonyane denies wrongdoing and has served as the ANC's first deputy secretary-general since December 2022.
cite: Judicial Commission of Inquiry into State Capture (Zondo Commission), Report Part 3, 1 March 2022
inside: Bosasa paid benefits to a minister and an MP while it kept winning prison contracts from the department they had sway over.

n: Arms firm Thales accused of paying Zuma through his adviser
rank: Deputy President (later President) Jacob Zuma
d: The French arms firm Thomson-CSF, now Thales, is accused of paying Jacob Zuma, then a senior South African politician, through his financial adviser Schabir Shaik in connection with a R30 billion arms package South Africa signed in 1999. Shaik was convicted of corruption in 2005 for payments to Zuma linked to the deal, including an arrangement with Thomson-CSF, and President Mbeki dismissed Zuma as deputy president. Charges against Zuma were dropped in 2009 and reinstated in 2018. On 22 January 2020 the Pietermaritzburg High Court ruled that both Zuma and Thales could stand trial; the trial has been delayed repeatedly. Both deny the charges.
cite: Durban High Court, Shaik conviction, 2005; Pietermaritzburg High Court ruling, 22 January 2020
inside: The French arms firm is accused of paying Zuma through his adviser in connection with the arms deal his government signed.

n: P&ID bribed a Nigerian government lawyer during arbitration
rank: Ministry of Petroleum Resources legal adviser
d: Process & Industrial Developments (P&ID), a company registered in the British Virgin Islands, bribed Grace Taiwo, a lawyer working for Nigeria's government, while the two sides were in arbitration, a private legal process for settling contract disputes. P&ID had signed a 2010 gas-processing deal with Nigeria, did not build the plant, and won an arbitration award that grew to over $11 billion. In October 2023 Justice Robin Knowles in the London High Court set the award aside, finding P&ID obtained it by fraud: besides the bribe, it had used Nigeria's leaked privileged legal documents. Nigeria was later awarded costs.
cite: High Court of England and Wales (Commercial Court), Federal Republic of Nigeria v P&ID, judgment 23 October 2023
org_note: status 'convicted' used for a civil fraud finding; no criminal conviction of the company.
inside: P&ID bribed a lawyer working for Nigeria's government during the arbitration and used Nigeria's leaked legal papers to win an award against it.

n: OPL 245 — $1.1bn oil block money went to ex-minister's firm
rank: former oil minister Dan Etete; government officials
d: Eni and Shell paid $1.1 billion in 2011 through a Nigerian government account for the offshore oil block OPL 245, and the money went on to Malabu Oil and Gas, a company controlled by former oil minister Dan Etete. Italian prosecutors charged both companies and their executives, including Eni chief executive Claudio Descalzi, with international corruption, alleging the payment was a route for bribes to Nigerian officials. On 17 March 2021 a Milan court acquitted all defendants, and in 2022 prosecutors dropped their appeal. Nigeria's government said it was disappointed.
cite: Milan Tribunal verdict, 17 March 2021; Guardian Nigeria / Reuters, 2022
inside: Italian prosecutors alleged that Eni and Shell's $1.1 billion for the oil block was a route for bribes to Nigerian officials; a Milan court acquitted everyone.

n: Shell said it had placed its people in all Nigeria's key ministries
rank: Nigerian government ministries
d: Shell, the oldest and largest foreign oil producer in Nigeria, said it had placed its own staff inside the Nigerian government ministries that dealt with oil. A US diplomatic cable of 20 October 2009, published by WikiLeaks and The Guardian in December 2010, records Ann Pickard, then Shell's executive vice-president for Africa, telling the US ambassador that the government had 'forgotten that Shell had seconded people to all the relevant ministries', meaning Shell had lent them staff, and that Shell therefore knew what was being done in them. Shell rejected the claim.
cite: US Embassy Abuja cable, 20 October 2009, published by WikiLeaks; The Guardian and Al Jazeera, December 2010
inside: Shell said it had lent its own staff to every Nigerian ministry dealing with oil, which let it know what those ministries were doing.

n: Steinmetz bribed Guinea president's wife for iron ore rights
rank: wife of President Lansana Conté
d: BSG Resources, controlled by Israeli businessman Beny Steinmetz, paid bribes to Mamadie Touré, a wife of Guinea's President Lansana Conté, to obtain mining rights at Simandou, one of the world's largest untapped iron ore deposits. In 2008 the government took blocks I and II from Rio Tinto and gave them to BSG Resources. On 22 January 2021 a Geneva court found Steinmetz guilty of corruption over the bribes, sentencing him to five years and a fine of 50 million Swiss francs. Swiss appeal courts upheld the conviction in 2022 and 2023. Steinmetz denies wrongdoing.
cite: Geneva Criminal Court, 22 January 2021; Swiss appeal rulings, 2022–2023
inside: BSG Resources bribed a wife of Guinea's president, and the government then took iron ore rights from Rio Tinto and gave them to BSG.

n: Ericsson paid Djibouti officials for a state telecom contract
rank: officials of state-owned Djibouti Telecom
d: Ericsson, the Swedish telecoms equipment maker, paid about €2.1 million to high-ranking officials in Djibouti to win a contract with the state-owned Djibouti Telecom. It admitted this in December 2019, when it agreed to pay more than $1 billion to settle US criminal and civil cases over corruption from 2000 to 2016 in China, Indonesia, Vietnam, Kuwait and Djibouti. In 2022 leaked internal Ericsson files, published by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ), described corruption in at least ten countries; the company admitted 'serious breaches of compliance rules'.
cite: US DOJ deferred prosecution agreement and SEC settlement with Ericsson, 6 December 2019
inside: Ericsson paid high-ranking Djibouti officials about €2.1 million so that the state-owned telecom company would give it a contract.

n: Odebrecht says it paid $59m to Panamanian officials
rank: President Ricardo Martinelli (2009–2014)
d: Odebrecht, the Brazilian construction company, says it paid $59 million in bribes to Panamanian officials during Ricardo Martinelli's 2009–2014 government. Odebrecht admitted in 2016 paying $788 million in bribes in Latin America and Africa to win public contracts. Panama's main Odebrecht money-laundering trial opened on 12 January 2026 with more than 20 defendants; Martinelli, who received asylum in Colombia in 2025, took part by video and pleaded innocent. Two of his sons and former president Juan Carlos Varela, who has parliamentary immunity, are to be tried separately by the Supreme Court.
cite: Panama criminal court, Odebrecht trial opened 12 January 2026; Tico Times, 13 January 2026
inside: Odebrecht says it paid $59 million to Panamanian officials, part of bribes it admitted paying across Latin America to win public contracts.

n: Odebrecht money went into Santos's 2010 presidential campaign
rank: President Juan Manuel Santos's 2010 campaign
d: Odebrecht, the Brazilian construction company, made illegal payments to Juan Manuel Santos's 2010 presidential campaign in Colombia. On 14 March 2017 Santos, then president, acknowledged the payments and said he had not known of them. Odebrecht's bribes in Colombia were tied to the Ruta del Sol highway contract, a state road-building contract; former senator Otto Bula was among those prosecuted.
cite: Statement of President Juan Manuel Santos, 14 March 2017; Colombian Attorney General's Odebrecht cases
inside: Odebrecht's illegal money went into the president's campaign, and its bribes in Colombia were tied to a state highway contract.

n: Odebrecht executive says firm paid $35m to Maduro's campaign
rank: President Nicolás Maduro's 2013 campaign
d: Odebrecht, the Brazilian construction company, gave $35 million to Nicolás Maduro's 2013 presidential campaign in return for priority for its projects in Venezuela, according to Euzenando Prazeres de Azevedo, head of Odebrecht in Venezuela. He told Brazilian investigators in late 2017 that campaign manager Américo Mata had first asked for $50 million. Ousted Venezuelan attorney general Luisa Ortega Díaz released video of the testimony in October 2017. Maduro's government rejected the claim and no Venezuelan court has examined it. Transparency International Venezuela found Odebrecht finished 9 of its 33 contracted projects.
cite: Testimony to Brazilian prosecutors, leaked by Luisa Ortega Díaz; Washington Post, 12 October 2017
inside: Odebrecht's man in Venezuela says it paid $35 million into Maduro's campaign in return for priority for its projects from his government.

n: JBS owners accused of paying President Temer for state help
rank: President Michel Temer
d: Joesley and Wesley Batista, the brothers who control JBS, the world's largest meat company, through J&F Investimentos, are accused of paying Brazil's President Michel Temer for government help. On 26 June 2017 Prosecutor-General Rodrigo Janot charged Temer with accepting bribes, alleging $5 million in return for help with JBS tax problems and a loan. In May 2017 O Globo had published a recording Joesley Batista secretly made of Temer discussing hush money, and police filmed a Temer aide carrying a suitcase of about $150,000 from JBS. The Chamber of Deputies voted in August 2017 not to let the case proceed while he was in office. The Batistas signed plea deals.
cite: Charges filed by Prosecutor-General Rodrigo Janot with the Supreme Federal Court, 26 June 2017
inside: The owners of JBS are accused of paying the president in return for government help with the company's tax problems and a loan.

n: Notebooks case — contractors' cash to Kirchner-era officials
rank: President's office and Federal Planning Ministry (2003–2015)
d: Construction, energy and transport businessmen paid cash to officials under Presidents Néstor Kirchner and Cristina Fernández de Kirchner, prosecutors in Argentina allege, in return for public works contracts. The evidence began with notebooks kept by a driver for a senior official of the Federal Planning Ministry, which surfaced in 2018 and recorded cash deliveries. Several executives testified as 'repentants', defendants who confess in exchange for leniency. The trial opened on 6 November 2025 with 87 defendants, including Fernández de Kirchner, former ministers and company executives. She denies the charges.
cite: Federal Oral Court, Cuadernos trial opened 6 November 2025; The Star (Reuters/AFP), 6 November 2025
inside: Contractors are accused of paying cash to officials in the president's office and planning ministry in return for public works contracts.

n: Vitol bribed officials at Pemex, Petroecuador and Petrobras
rank: officials of state oil firms Pemex and Petroecuador
d: Vitol, the world's largest independent oil trader, paid bribes to officials at the state oil companies Petrobras (Brazil), Petroecuador (Ecuador) and Pemex (Mexico) to win business. In December 2020 it paid $135 million to US and Brazilian authorities over those bribes. In 2024 a US jury convicted former Vitol trader Javier Aguilar of paying more than $1 million in bribes to officials in Ecuador and Mexico.
cite: US DOJ resolution with Vitol Inc., 3 December 2020; US District Court, Eastern District of New York, Aguilar verdict, 2024
inside: Vitol paid officials inside state oil companies in Brazil, Ecuador and Mexico so that those companies would give it business.

n: Agribusiness-funded institute drafts Brazil farm caucus agenda
rank: Agricultural Parliamentary Front (FPA) in Congress
d: Agribusiness and pesticide companies write the agenda of the farm caucus in Brazil's Congress, the Frente Parlamentar Agropecuária (FPA), through a think tank they fund, according to a July 2022 report by De Olho nos Ruralistas (Agribusiness Watch). The report found the agenda is drafted by the Instituto Pensar Agro, funded by 48 business associations whose members include Bayer, BASF, Syngenta, Cargill, Bunge, ADM, Louis Dreyfus, JBS, Marfrig, Nestlé and Danone. It also counted 278 meetings between agribusiness companies and Agriculture Ministry officials from January 2019 to June 2022, led by Syngenta (81), JBS (75) and Bayer (60).
cite: De Olho nos Ruralistas, 'Os Operadores da Boiada', July 2022
who: Agribusiness and pesticide companies (via Instituto Pensar Agro)
inside: A think tank funded by agribusiness and pesticide companies drafts the agenda of the farm caucus in Brazil's Congress.

n: Fat Leonard bribed US Navy officers for ship schedules
rank: US Navy officers and Singapore contracting staff
d: Glenn Defense Marine Asia, a ship-supply contractor run by Leonard Francis ('Fat Leonard'), bribed US Navy officers with cash, travel and gifts in return for ship schedules and inside information, and overbilled the Navy for years while supplying its ships in Asian ports. A civilian Navy contracting officer in Singapore quashed an early inquiry. US prosecutors charged 33 people; 22 pleaded guilty, including Francis and 17 Navy officials. Francis fled house arrest in 2022, was caught in Venezuela and was sentenced to 15 years in November 2024.
cite: US District Court, Southern District of California, prosecutions 2013–2024
inside: A ship-supply contractor bribed US Navy officers for ship schedules and inside information, and a Navy contracting officer quashed an early inquiry.

n: Mafia groups got inside 402 Italian councils since 1991
rank: municipal councils and local health authorities
d: Italy's mafia groups, chiefly Cosa Nostra, the 'Ndrangheta, the Camorra and Puglia clans, have taken enough hold of town councils and health authorities for the national government to dissolve them 402 times. Under Law 164 of 1991, the Council of Ministers can dissolve a council after a prefect's inquiry finds it is conditioned by a mafia group; commissioners then run the town for 18 to 24 months. Il Sole 24 Ore counted 402 decrees between 2 August 1991 and 30 September 2025, covering 288 municipalities and 6 provincial health authorities; 83 bodies were dissolved more than once. Calabria, Campania and Sicily account for 360 decrees and Puglia for 26, but councils have also been dissolved in Lazio, Piedmont, Liguria, Lombardy, Emilia-Romagna and Valle d'Aosta. Courts annulled 24 decrees.
cite: Italian Interior Ministry dissolution decrees under Law 164/1991; Il Sole 24 Ore count, 2 December 2025
who: Cosa Nostra, 'Ndrangheta, Camorra and Puglia clans
inside: Mafia groups got enough hold over town councils and health authorities that the state dissolved them 402 times for being conditioned by the mafia.

n: Bari clans placed hires at city transport firm and bought votes
rank: city-owned transport company and a city councillor
d: Mafia clans in Bari, southern Italy, tried to place their people inside the city-owned transport company AMTAB and, prosecutors allege, paid to get a candidate onto the city council. In 2024 two prosecutions led to about 130 arrests. In one, three Parisi clan members working at AMTAB were charged with mafia association and extortion for pressing a manager to hire five clan-linked people; a court put AMTAB under judicial administration, later lifted after a reorganisation. In the other, Giacomo Olivieri is accused of paying the Parisi, Strisciuglio and Montani clans to get his wife Maria Carmen Lorusso elected in 2019; their trial began in July 2024. After an Interior Ministry inquiry from March 2024, the government decided on 7 February 2025 not to dissolve the council.
cite: Bari prosecutors; Bari court order on AMTAB; Council of Ministers decision of 7 February 2025, reported by Il Post
inside: Clan members working at the city transport firm pressed a manager to hire clan-linked people, and clans were allegedly paid to get a councillor elected.

n: Sicily's President passed investigation secrets to Cosa Nostra
rank: President of the Region of Sicily
d: Salvatore Cuffaro, President of Sicily from 2001 to 2008, passed information about investigations to people linked to Cosa Nostra, the Sicilian Mafia. He was convicted of aggravated aiding of Cosa Nostra (article 416-bis of the criminal code), and the sentence of 7 years and a life ban from public office became final in January 2011. He served almost five years in Rebibbia prison and was released in December 2015. Since 2020 he has led a regional party, the Christian Democracy of Sicily.
cite: Italian Court of Cassation, January 2011
inside: The President of Sicily passed information about investigations to people linked to Cosa Nostra, helping the mafia from the top of the regional government.

n: Senator Dell'Utri acted as go-between for Berlusconi and Cosa Nostra
rank: senator; aide to Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi
d: Marcello Dell'Utri, Silvio Berlusconi's long-time aide and a co-founder of the Forza Italia party, acted as mediator between Berlusconi and Cosa Nostra, the Sicilian Mafia, Italy's top court found. Dell'Utri sat in the Chamber of Deputies, the European Parliament and the Senate between 1996 and 2013. On 9 May 2014 the Court of Cassation upheld his conviction for external complicity in mafia association, meaning helping the mafia without being a member, and a 7-year sentence. In 1974 he had brought Vittorio Mangano, already charged with mafia crimes, to work at Berlusconi's villa in Arcore. A separate 12-year sentence in the State-Mafia negotiation trial was overturned on appeal in 2021.
cite: Italian Court of Cassation, 9 May 2014
inside: Berlusconi's long-time aide, who also sat in parliament, acted as Cosa Nostra's go-between with Berlusconi and was convicted of helping the mafia.

n: Economy undersecretary Cosentino protected the Casalesi clan
rank: Undersecretary of State, Ministry of Economy and Finance
d: Nicola Cosentino, an Italian deputy and undersecretary at the Ministry of Economy and Finance, protected the interests of the Casalesi clan of the Camorra, the Naples-area mafia, including in the Caserta area's waste business. He was a Forza Italia and People of Freedom deputy from 1996 to 2013 and undersecretary from May 2008 until he resigned in July 2010. On 27 April 2023 the Court of Cassation made final a 10-year sentence for external complicity in mafia association, meaning helping the mafia without being a member.
cite: Italian Court of Cassation, 27 April 2023
inside: A finance ministry undersecretary and deputy protected the Casalesi clan's interests, including in the Caserta area's waste business.

n: Mafia Capitale — Carminati and Buzzi bribed Rome officials
rank: Rome city council president and city department heads
d: A network led by Massimo Carminati, a former far-right militant, and Salvatore Buzzi, head of social co-operatives, bribed Rome city officials to win contracts including migrant reception and park maintenance. Rome prosecutors arrested them in December 2014. Among those investigated were the president of Rome's city council and the head of the public-housing department; former mayor Gianni Alemanno was indicted in December 2015 for corruption and illicit financing over €125,000 from Buzzi. The Ostia district council was dissolved for mafia infiltration in 2015. The Court of Cassation ruled in 2019–20 that the network was not a mafia-type association, so convictions stand for corruption and ordinary criminal association.
cite: Rome prosecutors (Giuseppe Pignatone); Court of Cassation ruling on the 'Mondo di mezzo' case
inside: A criminal network bribed Rome city officials, including the council president and a department head, to win city contracts.

n: Mafias secretly owned Malta-licensed online betting firms
rank: online gaming companies licensed by the Malta Gaming Authority
d: Italian mafia groups secretly owned or ran online betting companies licensed in Malta, using them to collect bets and launder money, Italian investigations from 2015 onward found. Francesco Martiradonna, said to be the hidden owner of Malta-licensed Centurionbet, was arrested in 2017 on mafia-association charges. In January 2018 Palermo's Operation 'Game Over' issued 26 arrest warrants over a Cosa Nostra-linked betting network, and the Malta Gaming Authority suspended licences including that of LB Group (Leaderbet). Some executives were later cleared: in a decade-long Calabrian case, Maltese-linked Betsolution executives were acquitted of mafia ties.
cite: OCCRP Daphne Project, 'How Maltese Online Gambling Became an ATM for the Italian Mafia', 10 May 2018; Malta Gaming Authority licence suspensions
inside: Mafia groups secretly owned or ran Malta-licensed betting firms and used them to collect bets and launder money.

n: Montenegro's top judge shielded her son's smuggling network
rank: President of the Supreme Court of Montenegro
d: Vesna Medenica, president of Montenegro's Supreme Court until 2020, used her position to protect a cigarette and narcotics smuggling network led by her son Miloš, the High Court in Podgorica found. On 28 January 2026 it sentenced her to 10 years for four counts of abuse of influence; Miloš received 10 years and 2 months. She was acquitted of creating a criminal organisation. The evidence included decrypted messages from Sky ECC, an encrypted phone service used by criminals. Miloš Medenica fled while under house arrest, and prosecutors are appealing for longer sentences.
cite: High Court in Podgorica, verdict of 28 January 2026 (Special State Prosecutor's Office case)
inside: The Supreme Court president used her office to protect the smuggling network run by her son.

n: 'The Notary' allegedly used compromising files to pressure judges
rank: judges and prosecutors
d: Martin Bozhanov, known as 'the Notary', is alleged to have collected compromising material on Bulgarian judges and prosecutors and used it to pressure them, giving him a hidden hold over decisions in the justice system. Bulgarian National Radio reported that he threatened prosecutors as well as judges, and former Prosecutor General Ivan Geshev was questioned in the case. The claims are under investigation and have not been tested in court.
cite: Bulgarian National Radio; BTA news agency reporting on the 'Notary' case
inside: A fixer allegedly gathered compromising files on judges and prosecutors and used them to pressure their decisions from the inside.

n: Global Laundromat — Moldovan judges approved fake Russian debts
rank: Moldovan district court judges
d: A Russian money-laundering network used Moldovan judges to move money out of Russia. Between 2010 and 2014 an estimated $20–80 billion left Russia this way: Russian companies 'guaranteed' fake debts, and Moldovan judges then ordered the debts paid into Moldindconbank, from where the money moved on through Latvian banks. The scheme was exposed by OCCRP, a network of investigative journalists, and the Russian newspaper Novaya Gazeta; The Guardian reported about 500 people suspected. Moldovan prosecutors later charged judges who had validated the debts.
cite: OCCRP and Novaya Gazeta 'Global Laundromat' investigation (2014, 2017); Moldovan prosecutors
inside: A Russian laundering network used Moldovan judges, who ordered fake debts paid so the money could leave Russia.

n: Kushchyovskaya — Tsapok gang ran for years under local protection
rank: district police and local officials
d: Sergei Tsapok's gang operated for years in the Krasnodar Krai village of Kushchyovskaya with protection from local authorities and police, Russian investigators found. This came out after 4 November 2010, when gang members murdered 12 people there, including four children. Tsapok was convicted and died in prison in 2014.
cite: Russian Investigative Committee and Krasnodar court
inside: Local police and officials protected the Tsapok gang, letting it operate for years until its members murdered 12 people.

n: Swedish crime networks got inside agencies and welfare firms
rank: municipalities and welfare agencies
d: Criminal networks in Sweden have got inside government agencies, run companies in the welfare sector and exploit social insurance, according to a research review by Carina Gunnarson of Uppsala University and the Swedish Defence Research Agency, published by the SNS think tank in November 2023. Incorrect welfare payments are estimated at SEK 13–16.3 billion a year. The review says municipalities are especially exposed because much public money is spent locally with weaker oversight. It cites Södertälje, where police saw warning signs in the late 1990s but decisive action came only after a double murder in 2010.
cite: SNS (Studieförbundet Näringsliv och Samhälle), 'The Vulnerable State', November 2023
inside: Criminal networks got people inside Swedish agencies and ran welfare-sector companies, drawing public money through local programmes with weak oversight.

n: Yakuza brokers placed workers in Fukushima's state-funded clean-up
rank: subcontractors on Environment Ministry decontamination contracts
d: Yakuza gangs, Japan's organised crime groups, placed workers inside the subcontracting chains of Japan's taxpayer-funded radiation clean-up after the 2011 nuclear disaster and took part of their pay. The programme, worth about $35 billion, is run through layers of subcontractors. Police arrested yakuza members at least three times in 2012 for illegally placing workers in subcontracting chains under the construction company Obayashi. In 2013 Yamagata police arrested a Sumiyoshi-kai member for sending men to decontamination work and taking about a third of their pay. A Reuters investigation in 2013 found gang-linked recruiters supplying homeless men from Sendai station.
cite: Japanese police arrests (Fukushima, Yamagata); Reuters special reports, October and December 2013
inside: Yakuza groups placed workers in the subcontracting chains of the state-funded clean-up and took part of their pay.

n: Scam-city builders partnered with Myanmar army's Karen border force
rank: commander, Karen Border Guard Force under the Myanmar army
d: Chinese-run crime groups built scam centres in Myanmar in partnership with Colonel Saw Chit Thu, leader of the Karen Border Guard Force, a militia placed under the Myanmar army. In 2017 he partnered with She Zhijiang's Yatai group to build Shwe Kokko and also dealt with Wan Kuok-koi's Dongmei Group over Saixigang; Wan, a former leader of the 14K triad, was sanctioned by the US Treasury in 2020. Saw Chit Thu received the junta's Thiri Pyanchi honour in November 2022. The UK sanctioned him in December 2023 and the US later did the same, for links to forced labour in scam centres. She Zhijiang was extradited from Thailand to China on 10 November 2025.
cite: UK sanctions designation (December 2023); US Treasury designations; reporting collected by Wikipedia
who: Yatai (She Zhijiang) and Dongmei (Wan Kuok-koi) groups
inside: Chinese crime groups partnered with the commander of an army-controlled militia, who let them build scam centres on the land his force held.

n: Iraq tax heist network had PM's office director and MP inside
rank: General Commission for Taxes and the Prime Minister's office
d: A network around businessman Nour Zuhair Jassim drew on officials inside Iraq's state, including the director of the Prime Minister's office, to take about $2.5 billion from a General Commission for Taxes account in 2021–22. The money left through 247 cheques paid to five front companies posing as oil firms owed tax refunds. In late 2024 a Baghdad court sentenced 10 people: Nour Zuhair in absentia to 10 years, former MP and finance-committee head Haitham al-Jubouri, Raed Juhi, former director of Prime Minister Mustafa al-Kadhimi's office, and a tax-commission director general and his deputy. Several former senior tax and Rafidain Bank officials have not been charged.
cite: Baghdad criminal court verdicts, November–December 2024, reported by The National
inside: A businessman's network used officials inside the tax commission and the prime minister's office to pay $2.5 billion of tax money to its front companies.

n: UN panel finds gang member on Haitian council and police aiding gangs
rank: former legislators, a municipal commissioner and police officers
d: Haiti's armed gangs have people inside the state: a 94-page report by the UN Security Council's panel of experts on Haiti, released in October 2026 and covering October 2025 to July 2026, says at least one member of a new Cité Soleil municipal commission is an active gang member and that some police officers supply gangs with weapons and information. It accuses former Kenscoff legislator Alfredo Junior Antoine of arming groups and sponsoring a 2025 attack that killed more than 100 people, and former senator Nenel Cassy of controlling a criminal group in Miragoâne. It says the 'historic use of gangs' by former senator Youri Latortue and ex-lawmaker Prophane Victor fuels violence in the Artibonite ahead of elections. Antoine and Cassy deny the allegations.
cite: UN Security Council Panel of Experts on Haiti, report of October 2026, reported by AP
who: Viv Ansanm and other Haitian gangs
inside: Haiti's gangs have a member on a municipal commission and police officers who supply them with weapons and information.

n: PCC crime group's money ran two São Paulo city bus firms
rank: city bus concession companies
d: The PCC (Primeiro Comando da Capital), Brazil's largest criminal organisation, had its money in two São Paulo bus companies that held city contracts, state prosecutors allege. In April 2024 Operation Fim da Linha alleged that Transwolff (132 lines, about 583,000 passengers a day) and UPBus (158 buses) laundered PCC money from drug trafficking and robberies; the firms had received more than R$800 million in public funds the year before. The city took over both companies on 9 April 2024, the UPBus president was arrested in December 2024, and the city moved to end both concession contracts in December 2024–January 2025.
cite: São Paulo Public Prosecutor's Office (MPSP), Operation Fim da Linha; São Paulo city government decisions, reported by CNN Brasil
inside: The PCC's money was inside two bus companies holding city contracts, which allegedly laundered its drug and robbery proceeds while taking public funds.

n: Rizzuto Mafia took a cut of Montreal public works contracts
rank: mayors of Montreal and Laval
d: The Rizzuto family, Montreal's Mafia, took a share of the city's public construction contracts through firms that also paid political parties, witnesses told Quebec's Charbonneau Commission. The commission (2011–2015) was a public inquiry into collusion and corruption in public construction contracts and organised-crime infiltration of the industry. During the inquiry Montreal mayor Gérald Tremblay resigned, and interim mayor Michael Applebaum and Laval mayor Gilles Vaillancourt were later convicted or pleaded guilty in related corruption cases. The commission reported on 24 November 2015.
cite: Commission of Inquiry on the Awarding and Management of Public Contracts in the Construction Industry (Charbonneau Commission), final report, November 2015
who: Rizzuto Mafia family and construction cartels
inside: The Mafia took a share of Montreal's public contracts through construction firms that also paid political parties, and mayors were convicted in related cases.

n: Mafia families controlled hiring on the New York docks
rank: port hiring and dock labour
d: Mafia families controlled much of the hiring of dock workers at the port of New York and New Jersey, a state crime commission found before 1953. That year the two states created the Waterfront Commission of New York Harbor to fight criminal influence over that hiring, and it licensed and screened dock workers for 70 years. New Jersey moved to leave the agreement between the states in 2018, and after the US Supreme Court allowed it in 2023 the commission was dissolved on 17 July 2023. New Jersey State Police took over its role at New Jersey ports, and New York set up a new waterfront commission.
cite: Waterfront Commission Compact (1953); US Supreme Court, New York v. New Jersey (2023)
who: American Mafia families on the docks
inside: Mafia families controlled hiring at the New York docks, deciding who worked there, until the states set up a commission to screen workers.

n: South African police minister accused of colluding with syndicate
rank: Minister of Police and national police leadership
d: A criminal syndicate had senior South African police officials working with it, including Police Minister Senzo Mchunu, KwaZulu-Natal police commissioner Lt Gen Nhlanhla Mkhwanazi alleged on 6 July 2025. Mchunu was placed on leave and President Ramaphosa set up the Madlanga Commission of Inquiry. A R228 million police health-services contract had gone to businessman Vusimuzi 'Cat' Matlala's company in 2024; he faces corruption, fraud and money-laundering charges. By July 2026, 13 police officers faced criminal charges, including National Commissioner Fannie Masemola on a public-finance charge, and 15 faced discipline. Mchunu denies wrongdoing.
cite: Madlanga Commission of Inquiry; National Prosecuting Authority charges, reported by Daily Maverick, 5 July 2026
inside: A police commissioner alleges the police minister and senior officers worked with a criminal syndicate, while a linked businessman won a police contract.

n: 'Construction mafia' bribes and threatens South African councillors
rank: ward councillors and municipal contracts
d: Extortion groups calling themselves 'business forums' try to capture ward councillors, the local elected officials, by bribery or threats, sometimes by joining local party branches, the Institute for Security Studies reported in October 2021. The forums demand a cut, often 30%, of public construction projects and shut down sites that refuse. The civil engineering contractors' body SAFCEC estimated that by March 2019 at least R25.5 billion of projects had been disrupted or halted. The ISS said three Tshwane councillors had been killed in under four years in killings linked to such syndicates. The National Prosecuting Authority agreed to prosecute violent extortion under the Prevention of Organised Crime Act.
cite: Institute for Security Studies, ISS Today, 25 October 2021; SAFCEC estimates
inside: Extortion groups bribe or threaten local councillors, sometimes by joining their party branches, to take a cut of public building projects.

n: Black Axe-linked group paid to 'protect votes', given 80 state posts
rank: state government posts and election campaigns
d: The Neo Black Movement of Africa (NBM), which the BBC linked to the Black Axe confraternity, was given 80 government roles after it was paid to 'protect votes' in Nigeria's 2012 Edo governorship election, according to leaked documents in a BBC Africa Eye investigation of December 2021. The documents suggested 35 million naira went to the NBM. Black Axe is a Nigerian confraternity, a secretive student-born brotherhood, that police in several countries treat as an organised crime group. Former members told the BBC that members hold posts in state assemblies and executives and are hired by politicians for election violence. The NBM denies any link to Black Axe.
cite: BBC Africa Eye, 'Black Axe' investigation, December 2021
inside: A group linked to Black Axe was paid to 'protect votes' in a state election and then given 80 posts in that state's government.

n: Fishrot — Samherji paid Namibian ministers' circle for quotas
rank: Minister of Fisheries and Minister of Justice
d: Samherji, an Icelandic fishing company, paid people close to Namibia's government to obtain quotas to catch horse mackerel, leaked files showed in November 2019. The files were published by WikiLeaks and investigated by Icelandic, Al Jazeera and Namibian journalists. Fisheries Minister Bernhardt Esau and Justice Minister Sacky Shanghala resigned and were arrested that month. They and other defendants are charged in Namibia with racketeering (running a criminal enterprise), corruption and money laundering under the Prevention of Organised Crime Act. Iceland also opened an investigation into Samherji.
cite: Namibian Anti-Corruption Commission and Prosecutor-General charges; Icelandic District Prosecutor investigation; Fishrot Files (WikiLeaks, November 2019)
inside: Samherji paid people close to Namibia's government, including two ministers, to obtain fishing quotas from the state.

n: 'Ndrangheta ties lead Italy to dissolve Reggio Calabria council
rank: mayor and city council of a provincial capital
d: 'Ndrangheta clans, the Calabrian mafia, had ties to councillors in Reggio Calabria, leading the Italian government on 9 October 2012 to dissolve the city council for mafia infiltration. Some councillors were suspected of links to clans during the centre-right administration of Giuseppe Scopelliti, mayor from 2002 to 2010. Mayor Demetrio Arena and all 30 councillors were removed and three commissioners ran the city. It was the first time the government of an Italian provincial capital had been dismissed over organised-crime links.
cite: Italian Council of Ministers dissolution decree, 9 October 2012 (Law 164/1991)
inside: 'Ndrangheta clans had ties to Reggio Calabria councillors, and the state dissolved the whole council for mafia infiltration.

n: Chongqing gangs paid the city's deputy police chief for protection
rank: executive deputy head of the Public Security Bureau; head of the Judicial Bureau
d: Criminal gangs in Chongqing, a city of over 30 million in south-west China, paid bribes to Wen Qiang, who was executive deputy head of the city's Public Security Bureau (its police force) for 16 years and then head of its Judicial Bureau, to protect them. His case came out during a campaign against organised crime run from October 2009 to 2011 by the city's party chief Bo Xilai and police chief Wang Lijun, which arrested 4,781 suspects, including 19 alleged crime bosses, hundreds of triad members, six district police chiefs and other officials. Wen Qiang was convicted of taking bribes and protecting criminal gangs and was executed on 7 July 2010. Lawyers and scholars raised concerns about forced confessions and due process in the campaign's trials, and Bo Xilai was himself jailed for life in 2013.
cite: Chongqing courts (2010); reporting collected by Wikipedia
inside: Chongqing's gangs paid the city's deputy police chief, who used his post to protect them for years.

n: François Pérol: Rothschild banker oversaw a bank merger, then ran it
rank: Élysée deputy secretary-general; CEO of Groupe BPCE
d: François Pérol, a French Treasury official, moved from the bank Rothschild & Cie into the president's office, where he followed a bank merger he had advised on, and then took charge of the merged bank. As a Rothschild managing partner from 2005 to 2007 he advised Banque Populaire on creating Natixis. As deputy secretary-general of the Élysée under Nicolas Sarkozy he followed the 2008–09 merger of Banque Populaire and the Caisses d'Epargne, and in February 2009 he became head of the merged group, BPCE. He was prosecuted for illegal taking of interest (prise illégale d'intérêts), the offence of an official taking a stake in a business he supervised.
