inside: Prosecutors say the Kavac clan had the chief special prosecutor and senior police officials protecting it from inside Montenegro's justice and security system.

n: Susurluk crash exposed Turkish security ties to heroin traffickers
rank: police command and legislator
d: Heroin traffickers were working with Turkey's police and security services, as a car crash near Susurluk in November 1996 revealed. The crash killed a deputy police chief and a wanted trafficker and hitman who carried a diplomatic passport, and injured a member of parliament travelling with them. Interior minister Mehmet Agar, who ran the police, resigned on 8 November 1996. The parliamentary commission that followed in 1997 documented the working relationship between the security services and heroin trafficking, but almost no one was convicted.
cite: Turkish Grand National Assembly Susurluk commission report, 1997
inside: Heroin traffickers worked with Turkey's police and security services, as a parliamentary commission documented after a crash killed a deputy police chief travelling with a wanted trafficker.

n: Crime groups paid UK police and prison officers
rank: police and prison staff
d: UK organised crime groups paid serving police and prison officers to pass them information and to move contraband. This came out through Operation Venetic, the National Crime Agency's use of EncroChat, an encrypted phone network that European police hacked in 2020. Reading the criminals' own messages led to thousands of UK prosecutions, among them those officers. The corruption was found through the traffickers' messages, not by internal checks.
cite: National Crime Agency Operation Venetic reporting, from 2020
inside: UK crime groups paid serving police and prison officers to pass them information and move contraband, as the criminals' own EncroChat messages showed.

n: Boshe meth labs were shielded by the village party secretary
rank: local party secretary
d: Methamphetamine producers in Boshe village, Lufeng, in China's Guangdong province, had the village's Communist Party secretary, Cai Dongjia, shielding the labs and warning suspects. Three thousand police raided the village in December 2013 and seized three tonnes of meth. Officials said a fifth of its households were in the trade and that Boshe had supplied a third of China's meth. Cai was sentenced to death in 2016 and executed in 2019; a Lufeng drug squad captain was detained in the same investigation.
cite: Guangdong Higher People's Court, sentence 2016; Xinhua, execution January 2019
inside: Meth producers had their village's Communist Party secretary shielding their labs and warning suspects, so local authority protected the trade it should have stopped.

n: Ahmed Wali Karzai: opium trade and CIA payroll alleged
rank: provincial council chairman and presidential family
d: Ahmed Wali Karzai, half-brother of Afghanistan's President and chair of the Kandahar provincial council, was described by US officials as taking part in the opium trade, and was reported to be on the payroll of the CIA, the US foreign intelligence agency. Both allegations put outside interests, drug traders and a foreign spy service, inside the most powerful office in southern Afghanistan. He denied the drug claims and was never charged in any court. He was shot dead by his own security chief in 2011.
cite: US State Department and military reporting, 2009–2010; SIGAR and UNODC assessments
inside: US officials alleged the Kandahar council chair took part in the opium trade, and he was reported to be on the CIA's payroll, putting both inside the region's top office.

n: Kyrgyz customs deputy chief ran a smuggling scheme from inside
rank: customs deputy chief
d: Raiymbek Matraimov, deputy head of Kyrgyzstan's customs service, used the post to run a customs scheme that moved hundreds of millions of dollars out of the country. Reporting by OCCRP (a journalists' network on organised crime) and the Kyrgyz outlet Kloop in 2019–2020 tied the scheme to a smuggling business run by a secretive Uighur family. In December 2020 the US Treasury sanctioned him under the Magnitsky Act, a law for punishing corrupt officials abroad. Journalists who documented the network were prosecuted or forced out. He settled a domestic corruption case by repayment and served no prison term at the time.
cite: OFAC Global Magnitsky designation, December 2020; OCCRP and Kloop investigations 2019–2020; OCCRP, 'U.S. Sanctions Matraimov Under Magnitsky Act', December 2020
inside: Kyrgyzstan's deputy customs chief used his post to run a scheme tied to a smuggling business, so the customs service moved money out for the smugglers.

n: Akasha brothers paid Kenyan judges, prosecutors and police
rank: judiciary, prosecution and police
d: The Akasha brothers, who ran a heroin organisation in Mombasa, Kenya, paid Kenyan judges, prosecutors and police officers over two years to block their extradition to the United States. They admitted this as part of an obstruction count when they pleaded guilty in New York in October 2018, and were sentenced in 2019. None of the Kenyan officials who took the money has been named or charged in Kenya.
cite: US v. Baktash Akasha Abdalla et al., S.D.N.Y., pleas October 2018, sentences 2019
inside: A Kenyan heroin organisation paid judges, prosecutors and police officers to block its leaders' extradition to the United States.

n: Guinea-Bissau's air force chief charged with moving cocaine
rank: armed forces chief
d: US prosecutors charged that Ibraima Papa Camara, chief of staff of Guinea-Bissau's air force, conspired with traffickers to store and move cocaine through the country, alongside the navy chief. Guinea-Bissau is a transit point for South American cocaine heading to Europe. The US Treasury had already named him a drug trafficker in 2010 under the Kingpin Act, which lets it freeze traffickers' assets. He was indicted in New York in 2013 but stayed in Bissau and was never handed over.
cite: US v. Na Tchuto and Camara, S.D.N.Y., indictment 2013; OFAC Kingpin designation 2010
inside: US prosecutors charged that traffickers had Guinea-Bissau's air force chief helping them store and move cocaine through the country.

n: Ghana police operations chief taped with MV Benjamin cocaine suspects
rank: senior police officers
d: Cocaine traffickers in Ghana were taped meeting a senior police commander after their load vanished. In 2006 seventy-seven parcels of cocaine were landed from the vessel MV Benjamin and then disappeared. A secret recording surfaced of ACP Kofi Boakye, Director of Operations at police headquarters, meeting suspects including Kwabena 'Tagor' Amaning and Alhaji Issah Abass at his home, where they discussed the missing drugs. A committee of enquiry led by Supreme Court judge Georgina Wood found the police account unsatisfactory, said Boakye's conduct damaged the integrity of the police, and recommended his prosecution; he was sent on leave. Around 2009 President John Atta Mills recalled him to duty, and he later headed the police education department.
cite: Georgina Wood Committee report, Government of Ghana, 2006; GhanaWeb, 'The 2006 MV Benjamin cocaine saga that nearly cut short COP Kofi Boakye's career' (https://mobile.ghanaweb.com/GhanaHomePage/NewsArchive/The-2006-MV-Benjamin-cocaine-saga-that-nearly-cut-short-COP-Kofi-Boakye-rsquo-s-career-1746635)
inside: Cocaine traffickers were secretly taped meeting the police director of operations at his home about their missing drugs, and an enquiry recommended he be prosecuted.

n: Air Cocaine: Mali officials alleged to protect a traffickers' flight
rank: regional administration and armed formations
d: Cocaine traffickers flying a Boeing 727 from Venezuela had protection from local officials and armed groups in northern Mali, UN and Malian investigations indicated. In 2009 the plane unloaded cocaine at a desert airstrip at Tarkint and was then burned. Arrests were made in the capital, Bamako, but they led to no senior conviction, and the owners of the aircraft were never established. The case was examined in UNODC and UN Panel of Experts reporting from 2010 and in Malian judicial proceedings.
cite: UNODC and UN Panel of Experts reporting from 2010; Malian judicial proceedings
inside: UN and Malian investigations indicated that local officials and armed groups in northern Mali protected a traffickers' cocaine flight; no senior figure was convicted.

n: Tabasco's security secretary accused of leading a CJNG-linked gang
rank: state security minister
d: Prosecutors accuse Hernan Bermudez Requena, Tabasco state's Secretary of Security and top police official from 2018 to 2024, of running La Barredora, a criminal group tied to the CJNG (Jalisco New Generation Cartel), from inside his office. He fled Mexico in early 2025, was arrested in Paraguay in September and sent back within days. He is held at the Altiplano federal prison on charges of criminal association, extortion and kidnapping.
cite: Fiscalia General del Estado de Tabasco warrant, February 2025; Paraguayan SENAD arrest and expulsion, September 2025
inside: Prosecutors say Tabasco's state security secretary ran a CJNG-linked criminal group from inside his own office as the state's top police official.

n: Los Zetas ran parts of Piedras Negras state prison
rank: state prison administration
d: Los Zetas, a Mexican cartel, used the state prison in Piedras Negras, Coahuila, as a base, a workshop and a site for disposing of bodies, after the prison administration handed it control of parts of the facility. Testimony in Texas trials of Zetas leaders and a Coahuila state investigation in 2016–2017 established the arrangement. Prosecutions reached prison staff but not the officials who authorised it.
cite: Coahuila state attorney general investigation, 2016–2017; testimony in US v. Trevino Morales, W.D. Tex.
inside: Los Zetas got the state prison administration in Piedras Negras to hand over parts of the prison, which the cartel then used as a base and for disposing of bodies.

n: Guatemalan congressman passed information and cash for a trafficker
rank: legislator
d: Jose Armando Ubico Aguilar, a member of Guatemala's Congress from 2016 to 2024, worked for a drug trafficker while in office. He admitted passing drug-related information and cash to another Guatemalan official on the trafficker's behalf. He was indicted in Texas in March 2021 while still sitting in Congress, and pleaded guilty in May 2024 to an international trafficking conspiracy.
cite: US v. Ubico Aguilar, E.D. Tex., indictment March 2021, plea May 2024
inside: A trafficker had a sitting Guatemalan congressman working for him, passing drug-related information and cash to another official on his behalf.

n: Cocaine rings used police officers in the Campo de Gibraltar
rank: municipal, national police and customs
d: Cocaine smugglers in the Campo de Gibraltar, the Spanish area around the port of Algeciras, used police officers to protect their loads. In April 2024 a municipal officer and two national police officers were sentenced to more than seven years each for guarding a 367-kilogram shipment. A separate 2022 operation arrested five municipal officers at the port with an officer stationed in Ceuta, a customs official and a former police official over 6.2 tonnes moved through the Strait of Gibraltar.
cite: Audiencia Provincial de Cadiz, sentence April 2024; Policia Nacional operation, Algeciras, 2022
inside: Cocaine smugglers used municipal and national police officers around Algeciras to guard their shipments, so officers meant to stop the loads protected them.

n: Antwerp cocaine networks had serving police officers
rank: police officers
d: Cocaine networks working through the port of Antwerp, Belgium, had serving police officers among their members. In January 2024 22 people, three of them police officers, were arrested. In October 2024 a Brussels court sentenced dozens in Belgium's largest trafficking trial, built almost entirely on decrypted messages from the Sky ECC and EncroChat encrypted phone networks. Customs seized 116 tonnes of cocaine at the port in 2023 alone.
cite: Belgian federal police operation, January 2024; Brussels correctional court verdicts, October 2024
inside: Antwerp cocaine networks had serving police officers among their own members, putting people inside the police on the traffickers' side.

n: Vietnamese drug officers shielded a Laos–Vietnam network
rank: drug squad officers
d: A drug network moving narcotics from Laos into Vietnam had protection from police drug investigators. In 2024 two former officers of a Hanoi district drug team were indicted for shielding the network, which moved 137 kilograms. In 2025 a senior officer in Viet Tri, Phu Tho province, was sentenced to life for financing the purchase of 12,000 tablets that he planned to turn into a staged arrest. Vietnam imposes the death penalty for trafficking quantities like these.
cite: Supreme People's Procuracy indictments, 2024; Hanoi People's Court verdict, 2025
inside: A Laos–Vietnam drug network had police drug investigators shielding it, so officers meant to catch it protected its shipments.

n: Venezuela's Vice-President named as protector of traffickers
rank: vice-president
d: The US Treasury found that Tareck El Aissami, appointed Venezuela's Executive Vice-President in 2017, helped cocaine shipments leave Venezuela and protected traffickers operating inside it. In February 2017, weeks after his appointment, Treasury sanctioned him under the Kingpin Act, which freezes traffickers' US assets, together with a front man and a network of petroleum, engineering and holding companies. This is a government finding, not a court verdict, and it has never been tested at trial.
cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designation, February 2017
inside: The US Treasury found Venezuela's vice-president helped traffickers' cocaine leave the country and protected them, putting the second-highest office on their side.

n: CJNG and Los Cuinis paid a Mexican federal judge for rulings
rank: appellate judge
d: The US Treasury found that Isidro Avelar Gutierrez, a sitting Mexican federal magistrate judge, took payments from the CJNG (Jalisco New Generation Cartel) and its allied group Los Cuinis in return for rulings favouring their senior members. Treasury sanctioned him under the Kingpin Act in May 2019. The case came as a US sanctions listing rather than a Mexican prosecution.
cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designation, May 2019
inside: The CJNG and Los Cuinis paid a sitting Mexican federal judge, who issued rulings favouring their senior members, the US Treasury found.

n: Nayarit governor took bribes from the CJNG and Beltran Leyva
rank: state governor
d: The US Treasury found that Roberto Sandoval Castaneda, Governor of Nayarit state from 2011 to 2017, took bribes from the CJNG (Jalisco New Generation Cartel), and earlier from the Beltran Leyva organisation, in return for information and protection, and misappropriated state assets. Treasury sanctioned him in May 2019 under the Global Magnitsky order on corruption. His state attorney general, Edgar Veytia, had pleaded guilty to drug charges in Brooklyn two months earlier.
cite: OFAC designation under E.O. 13818, May 2019
inside: The CJNG and Beltrán Leyva organisation paid Nayarit's governor, who gave them information and protection in return, the US Treasury found.

n: Haiti's former president accused of using office for traffickers
rank: head of state
d: The US Treasury found that Michel Martelly, President of Haiti from 2011 to 2016, abused his influence to help traffic cocaine to the United States, worked with Haitian drug traffickers and sponsored and financed gangs. Treasury sanctioned him in August 2024; Canada had sanctioned him in November 2022 over financing gangs. In Haiti the gangs and the cocaine transit route have become closely tied. He denies the allegations, and no court has heard them.
cite: OFAC designation under E.O. 14059, August 2024; Global Affairs Canada sanctions, November 2022; Al Jazeera, 'US sanctions former Haitian president over alleged drug trafficking', 20 August 2024
inside: The US Treasury found Haiti's president used his influence to help traffickers move cocaine to the United States and financed gangs.

n: PCC gang allegedly paid Sao Paulo police for protection
rank: police chief and investigators
d: Prosecutors allege that the PCC (Primeiro Comando da Capital), Brazil's largest criminal faction, arranged around 30 million reais in payments to a police chief, an officer and three investigators of the Sao Paulo civil police to shield its members from investigation, and that one produced a false document for the faction. The arrests came in December 2024 under Operation Tacitus. The judge who authorised them wrote that no faction reaches the PCC's size without officials in the security services. The defence says the facts were investigated and shelved before.
cite: Ministerio Publico de Sao Paulo, Operacao Tacitus, arrests December 2024
inside: Prosecutors allege the PCC paid a São Paulo police chief and investigators to shield its members from investigation, and one produced a false document for it.

n: Gulf Cartel paid Mexico's deputy attorney general
rank: deputy attorney general
d: Mario Ruiz Massieu, Mexico's Deputy Attorney General from 1993 to 1994, ran the country's drug prosecutions while taking traffickers' money. He moved about $9 million in cash into Houston bank accounts, carried by an aide on some twenty-five commercial flights. In 1997 a Houston civil jury, in a case to seize the money, found that it had been paid by traffickers, mainly the Gulf Cartel, for protection. He fought extradition under house arrest for four years and killed himself in New Jersey in 1999 before any criminal trial.
cite: US civil forfeiture proceedings, S.D. Tex., jury finding 1997; extradition litigation 1995–1999
inside: The Gulf Cartel paid Mexico's deputy attorney general, the official running drug prosecutions, for protection, a US civil jury found.

n: Cali Cartel funded Colombia's 1994 presidential campaign
rank: head of state and campaign officials
d: The Cali Cartel put money into Ernesto Samper's 1994 presidential campaign, prosecutors established in the Proceso 8000 investigation that began in 1995. The campaign treasurer, the defence minister and the comptroller were convicted. In June 1996 a congressional commission cleared Samper himself, in a vote his opponents called a whitewash. The United States revoked his visa.
cite: Fiscalia General de la Nacion, Proceso 8000, from 1995; Camara de Representantes vote, June 1996
inside: The Cali Cartel put its money into the 1994 presidential campaign, and the campaign treasurer, defence minister and comptroller were convicted over it.

n: Guinea-Bissau's army chief charged with cocaine and arming the FARC
rank: armed forces chief
d: US prosecutors charged that General Antonio Indjai, chief of staff of Guinea-Bissau's armed forces and leader of the 2012 coup, conspired with traffickers to move cocaine through the country and to arm the FARC, the Colombian guerrilla army, including a proposal to supply surface-to-air missiles in return. He was indicted in New York in 2013 and never handed over. The navy and air force chiefs were charged in the same period.
cite: US v. Indjai, S.D.N.Y., indictment 2013
inside: US prosecutors charged that Guinea-Bissau's army chief worked with traffickers to move cocaine and offered to arm the FARC in return.

n: Lungi airport staff helped land a cocaine flight in Sierra Leone
rank: aviation and security officials
d: Cocaine traffickers had airport and security staff at Lungi, Sierra Leone's international airport, working for them. With that help, in July 2008 a twin-engine aircraft painted with Red Cross markings landed there carrying around 700 kilograms of cocaine. The prosecutions that followed in Sierra Leone's High Court convicted airport and security personnel along with the foreign crew. In June 2009 testimony to the US Senate Foreign Relations Committee called the convictions historic for the region, since neighbouring Guinea-Bissau had tried no drug case since 2005.
cite: Sierra Leone High Court convictions, 2009; US Senate Foreign Relations Committee hearing, June 2009
inside: Cocaine traffickers had staff at Sierra Leone's main airport and its security working for them, which let a plane carrying cocaine land there.

n: Operation Black Tie: Bosnian officials worked for the Nizic network
rank: public officials
d: The Nizic network, a Balkan cocaine organisation whose kingpin was already sentenced in the Netherlands, had corrupt Bosnian officials working as its facilitators, according to Europol, the EU police agency. Twenty-three people were arrested in Sarajevo in April 2024 for trafficking and laundering for the kingpin's inner circle. Europol said those detained included corrupt officials as well as accomplices.
cite: Europol and Bosnian security agencies, Operation Black Tie, April 2024
inside: Europol says a Balkan cocaine organisation had corrupt Bosnian officials working as its facilitators for trafficking and laundering.

n: Cosa Nostra and Prime Minister Giulio Andreotti
rank: head of government
d: Palermo prosecutors charged that Giulio Andreotti, seven times Prime Minister of Italy, put the influence of his office at the disposal of Cosa Nostra, the Sicilian Mafia, in return for electoral support, and that the Mafia expected him to fix the Maxi Trial, which had convicted 475 of its members over a heroin trade running through New York. He was acquitted in October 1999 and again on appeal in 2003. The appeal judges found he had ties to mobsters before 1980 but held that the time limit for prosecuting them had expired. The Court of Cassation, Italy's highest court, closed the case in 2004.
cite: Tribunale di Palermo, acquittal October 1999; Corte d'Appello 2003; Corte di Cassazione 2004
inside: Prosecutors charged that Prime Minister Andreotti put his office at Cosa Nostra's disposal for its votes; he was acquitted, though appeal judges found mobster ties before 1980.

n: Traffickers bought federal judges in Oran and Salta, Argentina
rank: federal judges
d: A drug trafficker in northern Argentina's Salta province bought rulings from federal judges. In March 2019 the former federal judge of Oran, Reynoso, was sentenced to 13 years as head of a group that took money and property in return for rulings that favoured traffickers. The same trafficker had bought a different federal judge in 2007, who was removed and convicted; that judge killed himself in 2020 as his arrest approached. A federal judge in Mendoza was separately charged over links to trafficking groups.
cite: Tribunal Oral Federal de Salta, conviction of ex-judge Reynoso, March 2019; earlier conviction of judge Sola Torino, 2007
inside: A trafficker bought rulings from federal judges in Orán, so courts in northern Argentina ruled in favour of traffickers in return for money and property.

n: Caso Purga: a former legislator steered Guayas courts
rank: judges and legislators
d: Ecuadorian prosecutors say a former legislator was the power behind the courts of Guayas province, the area around the port city of Guayaquil, and arranged payments to judges to get people released. The Caso Purga file, opened in 2024, charged judges alongside him. Testimony described payments for releases, including a failed attempt to free a former vice-president. The usual method was sentence reductions granted by prison-guarantee judges (judges who oversee sentences and prison conditions), who had no power to grant them.
cite: Ecuadorian Fiscalia General del Estado, Caso Purga, from 2024
inside: Prosecutors say a former legislator ran a payment network inside the Guayas courts, paying judges to grant releases and sentence cuts they had no power to give.

n: Brazilian judge signed rulings for a cocaine trafficking route
rank: criminal enforcement judge
d: A cocaine trafficking route from Bolivia through Paraguay into Minas Gerais and on to Rio and north-east Brazil had a judge working in its favour. Federal police arrested Amaury de Lima e Souza, judge of the criminal enforcement court (which oversees sentences) in Juiz de Fora, in June 2014 during an operation against the route. Investigators found a series of rulings he had signed for traffickers, including one granting house arrest to a defendant prosecutors had charged. In October 2022 he was sentenced to 24 years and four months.
cite: Tribunal de Justica de Minas Gerais, 5th criminal chamber, sentence October 2022; Policia Federal operation, June 2014
inside: A cocaine route had a criminal enforcement judge working for it, who signed rulings for traffickers including house arrest for a charged defendant.

n: Cartel de la Toga: politicians bought Colombia's Supreme Court
rank: supreme court presidents and anti-corruption prosecutor
d: Members of Congress under investigation for ties to the AUC, a right-wing paramilitary army, paid judges of Colombia's Supreme Court, which tries sitting legislators, to shelve or steer their cases. This bribery network, known as the Cartel de la Toga (the Robes Cartel), included two former presidents of the Supreme Court, a sitting magistrate and the national anti-corruption prosecutor, all convicted. One former court president was sentenced to 16 years; another was sentenced to 10 in February 2026 and is subject to an Interpol red notice. The prosecutor was convicted in Colombia and separately in Miami.
cite: Corte Suprema de Justicia de Colombia, Sala Especial, convictions 2021–2026; US v. Moreno Rivera, S.D. Fla., 2019
inside: Legislators tied to the AUC paramilitaries paid Supreme Court judges and the anti-corruption prosecutor to shelve or steer the cases against them.

n: Colombian prosecutor held property for the Gulf Clan
rank: public prosecutor
d: A serving Colombian prosecutor was charged in July 2023 with lending her name to hide property belonging to a front man for the Gulf Clan, Colombia's largest cocaine trafficking organisation. Putting assets in her name placed the Gulf Clan's property under the protection of someone inside the prosecution service. She was placed under house arrest.
cite: Fiscalia General de la Nacion charge and house arrest order, July 2023
inside: A serving prosecutor lent her name to hide property for the Gulf Clan, putting the cartel's assets under the cover of someone inside the prosecution service.

n: Michoacanazo: officials accused of La Familia ties, all freed
rank: mayors, state and municipal officials
d: La Familia Michoacana, a cartel based in the Mexican state of Michoacan, was accused of having more than 30 state and municipal officials, including ten mayors, working for it. Mexican federal police arrested them in May 2009 in an operation that became known as the 'Michoacanazo'. Within two years every one of them had been released after federal judges found the prosecution's evidence insufficient. The case pitted the federal government against the state government and against its own courts, and ended without a single conviction.
cite: Procuraduria General de la Republica prosecutions, May 2009; federal judicial releases 2009-2011; Mexican Law Review study of the case
inside: Mexican federal police accused more than 30 Michoacán officials, including ten mayors, of working for La Familia Michoacana; judges freed them all for lack of evidence.

n: Trafficker paid South Africa's police chief and Interpol head
rank: national police chief
d: Glenn Agliotti, a drug trafficker, paid Jackie Selebi while Selebi was national commissioner of the South African Police Service and at the same time president of Interpol, the international police cooperation organisation. Selebi was convicted of corruption in July 2010 and sentenced to 15 years; the Supreme Court of Appeal upheld the conviction in 2011. In a separate case in 2011 Sheryl Cwele, wife of the state security minister, was convicted of conspiring to traffic drugs.
cite: South Gauteng High Court, conviction July 2010, sentence August 2010; Supreme Court of Appeal 2011; separate conviction of Sheryl Cwele, 2011
inside: A drug trafficker paid South Africa's national police commissioner, who was then also head of Interpol, and the commissioner was convicted of corruption over it.

n: Liberian police and airport security charged over a cocaine route
rank: police command and airport security
d: After Liberia's largest recorded seizure, close to four tonnes of cocaine bound for Europe, the police inspector general said senior government officials were involved in trafficking. The national police charged the head of its own Major Crimes Unit and another official, and named a deputy commander responsible for security at Roberts International Airport, the main airport, as an active participant. Twelve suspects were charged in the seizure case in 2026, and a former vice-president was separately indicted on trafficking charges.
cite: Liberia National Police charges and Inspector General statements, 2026; indictment of the former vice-president, 2026
inside: Traffickers had senior Liberian police officers, including the head of the Major Crimes Unit and an airport security commander, working with them on a cocaine route.

n: Sierra Leone's aviation minister cleared a cocaine flight
rank: cabinet minister
d: Proceedings in the 2008 Lungi cocaine case indicated that Sierra Leone's minister of transport and aviation had given landing clearance for the aircraft carrying around 700 kilograms of cocaine, giving the traffickers help from inside the cabinet. He was dismissed, but only by administrative decision; the allegation was never tried in court.
cite: Sierra Leone government dismissal, 2008–2009; Africa Center for Strategic Studies review of the case
inside: Lungi cocaine traffickers got Sierra Leone's transport and aviation minister to give landing clearance for their plane, giving them help from inside the cabinet.

n: Costa Rican security official and judge worked for cocaine traffickers
rank: vice-minister of public security, later judge
d: The US Treasury found that Gamboa Sanchez, a former Vice Minister of Public Security in Costa Rica who later sat as a judge, helped move tens of millions of dollars' worth of cocaine from Colombia through Costa Rica to the United States and Europe, and used his contacts inside the government to obtain information on ongoing counter-narcotics investigations. He was arrested on 23 June 2025 on a US extradition request, weeks after Costa Rica changed its constitution in May 2025 to allow extradition of its own citizens for drug trafficking and terrorism. Treasury sanctioned him on 15 August 2025.
cite: US Treasury press release sb0227 and OFAC designation under E.O. 14059, 15 August 2025; Costa Rican arrest, 23 June 2025; constitutional reform on extradition signed May 2025
inside: The US Treasury found a former vice-minister of public security helped move traffickers' cocaine and used his government contacts to get information on drug investigations.

n: Caso Colorado: traffickers recruited Costa Rican police as lookouts
rank: police officers
d: A drug-trafficking group that controlled the Caribbean lowland corridor of Costa Rica recruited police officers stationed at Guapiles and Cariari de Pococi to warn it of raids, checkpoints and investigators' movements, so drugs could be moved or hidden in time. Investigators of the OIJ, Costa Rica's judicial police, found regular telephone contact between the group and the officers. In 2026 five officers were charged before the specialised organised crime court.
cite: Organismo de Investigacion Judicial, case file 21-000115-0622-PE; Fiscalia Adjunta contra el Narcotrafico charges, 2026
inside: A trafficking group recruited police officers to warn it of raids, checkpoints and investigators' movements, so the force's own information protected its drugs.

n: Dominican drug agency and navy officers worked for traffickers
rank: anti-drug agency, navy and police
d: Traffickers in the Dominican Republic had officers of the National Drug Control Agency (DNCD) and the navy working for them. Three senior DNCD officials were arrested while providing security to traffickers waiting for a shipment bound for Puerto Rico. A navy officer in charge of port security was accused of moving 800 kilograms to Spain, and in 2008 nearly twenty officials, mostly navy, were accused of killing seven Colombian traffickers to take 1.3 tonnes. Since 2009 more than 700 DNCD staff have been removed, around 200 of them suspected of trafficking, and the national police expelled about 1,400 officers from 2010.
cite: DNCD arrests and dismissal statistics reported 2012-2013; Dominican prosecutions of navy and police personnel
inside: Dominican traffickers had officers of the national drug agency and the navy working for them, providing security for shipments the agency was meant to stop.

n: Guyanese police officer arranged safe passage for traffickers
rank: police officers
d: The US Treasury found that a serving Guyanese law enforcement officer arranged safe passage for Mexican and Venezuelan traffickers moving cocaine through Guyana. Treasury sanctioned him on 5 June 2025, along with a former officer wanted over the 2024 abduction of a policeman. Neither has been tried. Treasury noted that Guyana is a close US partner, but that the State Department treats corruption there as a significant obstacle to counter-narcotics work.
cite: US Treasury press release sb0156 and OFAC designations under E.O. 14059, 5 June 2025; ICE HSI New York investigation
inside: The US Treasury found a serving Guyanese police officer arranged safe passage for Mexican and Venezuelan traffickers moving cocaine through the country.

n: Papua New Guinea police accused of enabling cocaine flights
rank: police officers
d: Australian-based organisers flew cocaine through Papua New Guinea, and police officers there were alleged to have helped the night flights. In 2020 a Cessna loaded with 548 kilograms of cocaine crashed on a makeshift runway outside Port Moresby. The police commissioner then said publicly that there are criminals in uniform in the constabulary and promised to remove them. The organisers were convicted in Victoria, Australia, and the pilot was jailed for 18 years in PNG, but the officers were not charged. Fiji's drug intelligence chief has raised the same concern about infiltration of law enforcement there.
cite: Royal Papua New Guinea Constabulary statements, 2020; Victoria County Court sentences, July 2026; Lowy Institute analysis of Pacific trafficking
inside: Police officers in Papua New Guinea were alleged to have helped Australian-based organisers' cocaine flights, and the police commissioner said there were criminals in uniform.

n: Chapitos accused of installing Sinaloa's governor
rank: state governor
d: US prosecutors allege that the Chapitos, the faction of the Sinaloa Cartel led by sons of Joaquin 'El Chapo' Guzman, helped Ruben Rocha Moya win the 2021 election for Governor of Sinaloa and then gained control of state and local police. They say he met the faction before the election and promised to install friendly officials, and that cartel members stole ballot boxes and intimidated rivals. He and nine other current and former officials, including a senator and the mayor of Culiacan, were indicted in Manhattan in April 2026. He rejects the accusations and resigned on 1 May 2026. Mexico said the extradition request lacked evidence and opened its own inquiry; none of the ten is in custody.
cite: US v. Rocha Moya et al., S.D.N.Y., indictment unsealed 29 April 2026; Fiscalia General de la Republica statement, 2026; resignations reported 1-2 May 2026; widely reported background on the Chapitos as the faction led by Joaquin Guzman's sons
inside: US prosecutors allege the Chapitos helped get Sinaloa's governor elected after he promised to install friendly officials, and then gained control of state and local police.

n: Sinaloa Cartel protection network in Culiacan's government and police
rank: mayor, police commanders and a senator
d: US prosecutors allege that the Sinaloa Cartel had a protection network across Sinaloa state's government and police. Nine officials were charged alongside Governor Ruben Rocha Moya in an indictment unsealed in Manhattan on 29 April 2026: the mayor of Culiacan, the state capital, a sitting senator, the state deputy attorney general, a former public security secretary and several police commanders. One is also charged over the kidnapping of a source for the US Drug Enforcement Administration and a relative, both of whom died.
cite: US v. Rocha Moya et al., S.D.N.Y., indictment unsealed 29 April 2026
inside: US prosecutors allege the Sinaloa Cartel had a mayor, a senator, a deputy attorney general and police commanders working as its protection network inside the state.

n: Guatemalan anti-drug police official worked for traffickers
rank: senior police official
d: Cocaine traffickers had the leadership of Guatemala's anti-drug police working for them. The force's chief, Adan Castillo, his deputy and a third official, Rubilio Orlando Palacios, were arrested when the three travelled to the United States in November 2005, after a four-month investigation by the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) and Guatemalan authorities. A three-count Washington indictment charged them with helping traffickers ship cocaine, and they pleaded guilty in 2006. The DEA administrator called them Trojan horses for the addiction they were meant to prevent.
cite: US District Court for the District of Columbia, indictment November 2005; pleas 2006
inside: Traffickers had the chief of Guatemala's anti-drug police, his deputy and a third official helping them ship cocaine, so the force worked for those it was meant to stop.

n: Tramadol network included Chad's own security and intelligence officials
rank: senior army and intelligence officials
d: A transnational network trafficking tramadol, a prescription painkiller sold illegally across the Sahel, counted high-ranking Chadian security and intelligence officials among its members. A court in N'Djamena, Chad's capital, sentenced ten people on 24 July 2020, those officials among them. Analysts at the Institute for Security Studies and ENACT who read the court documents described a network with strong Chadian connections and large sums circulating among its members, some of which was used in attempts to corrupt judges and the security services. Because senior army and intelligence figures were inside the network, the institutions expected to enforce the law against it were the same ones it had reached.
cite: Court judgment, N'Djamena, 24 July 2020; Institute for Security Studies and ENACT analysis of the court documents, 2020; UNODC Sahel tramadol reporting, 2017
inside: A tramadol network counted senior Chadian army and intelligence officials among its members, so the bodies meant to enforce the law against it were part of it.

n: Maduro charged with using Venezuela's state to move FARC cocaine
rank: head of state
d: US prosecutors allege that Nicolas Maduro, as Venezuela's head of state, worked with the FARC, a Colombian guerrilla group, to traffic cocaine to the United States, using Venezuelan military and intelligence resources to protect shipments. The indictment, filed in the Southern District of New York in March 2020, charges him with narco-terrorism conspiracy, cocaine importation and weapons counts alongside serving and former officials. The State Department reward for his arrest was raised twice, reaching $50 million in 2025. US forces captured Maduro in Caracas on 3 January 2026; he pleaded not guilty in New York on 5 January, and a trial is set for June 2027. No trial has yet taken place and the evidence is untested; the indictment is an accusation.
cite: US v. Maduro Moros et al., S.D.N.Y., indictment March 2020; US Department of State Narcotics Rewards Program notices; Wikipedia, 'Prosecution of Nicolás Maduro and Cilia Flores' (capture 3 January 2026, not-guilty plea 5 January 2026, trial date 1 June 2027 set 22 July 2026)
inside: US prosecutors allege Venezuela's head of state worked with the FARC to traffic cocaine, using the military and intelligence services to protect its shipments.

n: Cabello accused of leading a trafficking structure from high office
rank: legislature president and interior minister
d: US authorities accuse Diosdado Cabello, one of the most powerful figures in Venezuela's ruling party, of helping lead the 'Cartel de los Soles', the name US prosecutors give to Venezuelan officials who allegedly protected and profited from cocaine trafficking. The US Treasury's sanctions office, OFAC, designated him under the Kingpin Act (a law that freezes the assets of alleged drug traffickers) in May 2018, and the 2020 New York indictment against Nicolas Maduro names him as a leader of the same structure. Cabello has held the presidency of the National Assembly, the vice-presidency of the ruling party and, from 2024, the interior ministry, which runs the police. Both US actions are executive and prosecutorial steps, not findings by a court.
cite: US Treasury OFAC Kingpin Act designation, May 2018; US v. Maduro Moros et al., S.D.N.Y., 2020
inside: US authorities accuse Cabello, who has held the assembly presidency and the interior ministry, of helping lead officials who protected and profited from cocaine trafficking.

n: Honduran ex-president Lobo named as taker of traffickers' money
rank: head of state
d: Honduran drug traffickers are alleged to have paid Porfirio Lobo Sosa, President of Honduras from 2010 to 2014. US prosecutors named him as a recipient of trafficking proceeds during the New York cases against his son, Fabio Lobo, and against his successor, Juan Orlando Hernandez. In July 2021 the State Department put him on its Engel list, a public list of officials in Central America it considers corrupt or undemocratic. He has never been charged. The allegations come from cooperating witnesses (defendants testifying in return for lighter sentences) in other people's trials, the weakest category of evidence on this map.
cite: US Department of State section 353 corrupt and undemocratic actors list, July 2021; trial testimony in US v. Fabio Lobo and US v. Hernandez, S.D.N.Y.
inside: US prosecutors named Honduras's former president as a recipient of traffickers' money, based on cooperating witnesses; he has never been charged.

n: US trial witnesses said cartels bribed a serving Mexican president
rank: head of state
d: Witnesses in two US trials testified that Mexican cartels paid bribes to a serving president of Mexico. The testimony came in the 2019 trial of Joaquin 'El Chapo' Guzman, leader of the Sinaloa Cartel, and the 2023 trial of Genaro Garcia Luna, Mexico's former federal security chief, both in Brooklyn federal court. The witnesses were cooperating with prosecutors and negotiating their own sentences, no documents corroborated the claim, and no charge has been brought. It is recorded because it was said under oath in a US federal court, not because it is established.
cite: Trial testimony, US v. Guzman Loera, E.D.N.Y., 2019, and US v. Garcia Luna, E.D.N.Y., 2023
inside: Cooperating witnesses in two US trials testified that Mexican cartels bribed a serving president of Mexico; the claim is uncorroborated and no charge has been brought.

n: Venezuela's anti-drug chief charged with tipping off traffickers
rank: counter-narcotics chief and interior minister
d: US prosecutors allege that Nestor Reverol, while head of Venezuela's national anti-drug office, worked for drug traffickers by warning them of raids and blocking seizures. He was indicted in the Eastern District of New York in 2015, with the charges made public in August 2016. Instead of being removed, he was promoted to Interior Minister the following year, putting him in charge of the police, and later moved to the electricity ministry. Venezuela does not extradite its officials, and the indictment has never been acted on.
cite: US v. Reverol Torres and Ordonez, E.D.N.Y., indictment 2015, unsealed August 2016
inside: US prosecutors allege Venezuela's anti-drug chief worked for traffickers by warning them of raids and blocking seizures, and he was then made interior minister.

n: Oran cocaine case reached officials; Algeria's police chief removed
rank: national police chief
d: A cocaine-importing network around the businessman Kamel Chikhi reached Algerian judges and officials, and its exposure brought down the head of the national police. In May 2018 Algerian authorities seized 701 kilograms of cocaine at the port of Oran, hidden in a shipment of frozen meat Chikhi had imported. Press reports said investigators found video of Chikhi meeting judges and other officials, and the case was linked to judges, prosecutors, mayors and the children of senior politicians. Abdelghani Hamel, Director-General of National Security (head of the national police), was removed after the seizure. Military and civilian courts later convicted Hamel and several generals of corruption and illicit enrichment, rather than narcotics offences; Algeria published little about the trafficking case itself.
cite: Algerian Blida military tribunal and Tipaza court judgments, 2019-2020; Algerian Ministry of Justice statements; Fanack, 'Cocaine Seizure Stirs Algerian Politics', 2018 (frozen-meat shipment, Kamel Chikhi, reported video with judges and officials)
inside: Press reports said an Oran cocaine importer's network reached judges and officials, and the national police chief was removed after the seizure.

n: Zawiya smuggling networks ran a Libyan coast guard unit
rank: coast guard commander
d: Smuggling networks in Zawiya, a port town in western Libya, had their own man commanding the local coast guard unit, the force meant to stop them. Abd al-Rahman Milad, known as 'Bija', was serving as the Zawiya coast guard commander when the UN Security Council sanctioned him in June 2018 for fuel smuggling, migrant trafficking and violence at sea. He was detained in Libya in 2020 and released without conviction in 2021, and was shot dead west of Tripoli in September 2024. The same coastal networks move hashish and medicines; the UN designation covers the smuggling economy rather than narcotics specifically.
cite: UN Security Council Committee on Libya sanctions listing, June 2018; UN Panel of Experts on Libya reports; The National, 'Notorious Libyan coastguard commander killed', 2 September 2024
inside: Zawiya's smuggling networks had their own man commanding the local coast guard, the unit meant to stop the smuggling, until the UN sanctioned him.

n: Captagon smugglers recruited Jordanian soldiers at the Syrian border
rank: armed forces officers
d: Smugglers moving captagon, an amphetamine-type pill produced in Syria, recruited serving and former Jordanian soldiers to carry the pills and weapons across the border. Jordan's State Security Court, which hears security and drug cases, has convicted soldiers in cases running from 2022 onward. The Jordanian army also carried out airstrikes inside Syria against production and storage sites. The convictions show the smugglers' protection reached into the force responsible for stopping them.
cite: Jordanian State Security Court judgments, 2022-2024; Jordanian Armed Forces statements
inside: Captagon smugglers recruited serving Jordanian soldiers to carry pills and weapons across the border the army is meant to guard.

n: Smuggling networks protected by Bulgarian customs and border officials
rank: customs and border officials
d: Smuggling networks in Bulgaria had protection from officials inside the customs and border services, according to the US Treasury. In June 2021 it named Bulgarian officials and business figures, several of them in customs and border roles, under the Global Magnitsky Act, a US law that sanctions foreign officials for corruption. It was the largest single Magnitsky action ever taken against one country. Bulgarian prosecutions largely did not follow. The customs checkpoints on the Balkan route, the main land route for drugs into the EU, are run by the same institutions.
cite: US Treasury OFAC Global Magnitsky designations, June 2021; European Commission Rule of Law reports on Bulgaria
inside: The US Treasury found Bulgarian smuggling networks had protection from officials inside the customs and border services, the bodies that run the checkpoints.

n: Belivuk crime group carried Serbian state security identification
rank: police and state security officials
d: Members of the Belivuk-Miljkovic group, a Belgrade criminal gang, held identification from Serbia's state security service and had access to protected facilities, according to evidence in their prosecution. Serbia's Special Prosecutor's Office for Organised Crime brought charges from 2021, and a former head of the security service was later charged in connection with the group. The case is still running, and the specific attributions remain contested in Serbian politics.
cite: Serbian Special Prosecutor's Office for Organised Crime indictments, 2021-2024; Belgrade Higher Court proceedings
inside: Members of a Belgrade gang carried state security identification and had access to protected facilities, and a former head of the security service was charged over the group.

n: 'Ndrangheta reached a senator, police and officials in Calabria
rank: former senator, lawyers and officials
d: The 'Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia, had people working for it inside Italian politics, policing and public offices, according to the Rinascita-Scott trial. With over 300 defendants it was Italy's largest organised crime trial since the Palermo maxi-trial of the 1980s, and in November 2023 the court in Vibo Valentia convicted 207 at first instance. Those convicted included a former senator and lawyer who had acted for 'Ndrangheta figures, along with police officers, officials and a former regional politician. Appeals are running.
cite: Tribunale di Vibo Valentia, Rinascita-Scott judgment, November 2023; Italian Direzione Nazionale Antimafia reporting
inside: The 'Ndrangheta had a former senator, police officers and officials working for it, convicted in the Rinascita-Scott trial.

n: Cocaine network A Ultranza Py had a prosecutor and court staff
rank: prosecutors, judges and legislators
d: A Ultranza Py, a cocaine network shipping product along the Hidrovia (the Paraguay-Parana river route to the Atlantic), had a serving prosecutor, court officials and figures connected to Paraguay's legislature working with it. The 2022 investigation by Paraguay's public prosecutor's office charged them alongside the traffickers. One of the case's own prosecutors was later removed, and several principals fled before arrest.
cite: Paraguayan Ministerio Publico, Operacion A Ultranza Py case file, 2022-2024; Paraguayan Jurado de Enjuiciamiento de Magistrados
inside: A cocaine network had a serving prosecutor and court officials working with it, so parts of Paraguay's justice system served the traffickers.

n: Guerreros Unidos ran Iguala's mayor and municipal police
rank: municipal mayor
d: Guerreros Unidos, a drug-trafficking gang in Guerrero state, had the mayor of Iguala, Jose Luis Abarca, and the town's municipal police acting for it. In September 2014 municipal police took forty-three students from the Ayotzinapa teacher-training college, who disappeared. Abarca was convicted of organised crime and kidnapping. The Interdisciplinary Group of Independent Experts, appointed by the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, documented federal and state forces monitoring the events in real time. It is the best-evidenced case on this map of a town government operating as an arm of a trafficking organisation.
cite: Mexican federal court judgments, 2019 and 2022; GIEI Ayotzinapa reports; Mexican Comision para la Verdad y Acceso a la Justicia, 2022
inside: Guerreros Unidos had Iguala's mayor and municipal police acting for it, and those police took the 43 students who then disappeared.

n: Rio militias' allies held seats in Congress and the police
rank: federal deputy and state officials
d: Rio de Janeiro's militias, groups that began as off-duty police running protection rackets and now control neighbourhoods, had allies holding elected and police office. In March 2024 Brazil's Federal Police arrested federal deputy Chiquinho Brazao, his brother Domingos Brazao, a former state accounts councillor, and Rivaldo Barbosa, a former head of the civil police intelligence bureau, over the 2018 killing of city councillor Marielle Franco. The Brazao brothers are alleged to have ties to militias, and Barbosa is accused of steering the investigation away from those who ordered the killing. All deny it. The case is at indictment stage.
cite: Brazilian Policia Federal and Procuradoria-Geral da Republica filings, March 2024; Supremo Tribunal Federal proceedings; Boston Globe, 'Three Rio officials arrested in connection with Marielle Franco killing', 24 March 2024
inside: Brazilian police allege that a federal deputy and his brother with militia ties had a former police intelligence chief steer the Marielle Franco murder inquiry away from them.

n: Crime boss alleged a Turkish minister protected trafficking
rank: interior minister
d: Turkish trafficking networks had protection from a former interior minister, according to Sedat Peker, a convicted Turkish organised crime figure. Turkey's interior minister commands the police. In a long series of videos posted from abroad in 2021, Peker made the claim in detail, including about a specific cocaine shipment. Opposition members raised it in parliament, but no charge followed and the allegations have never been tested. They are recorded because they were made publicly and in detail, and because the Susurluk scandal already on this map, a 1996 car crash that exposed links between police, politicians and gangsters, established the pattern they describe.
cite: Public statements by Sedat Peker, 2021; Turkish parliamentary opposition motions; no prosecution filed
inside: A convicted crime figure alleged in detail that a former Turkish interior minister, who commanded the police, protected trafficking networks; the claims are untested.

n: Mexican cartels pay US border officers to wave loads through
rank: border and customs officers
d: Mexican cartels pay officers of US Customs and Border Protection (CBP), the agency that inspects people and goods at the border, to let drug loads pass through ports of entry. CBP is the largest federal law enforcement agency in the United States, and its officers have produced more than 200 corruption convictions across a decade. In 2016 the agency's Integrity Advisory Panel found its internal affairs office too small for the caseload and said so publicly.
cite: CBP Integrity Advisory Panel final report, 2016; CBP Office of Professional Responsibility annual statistics; DOJ prosecution records
who: Mexican cartels at ports of entry
inside: Mexican cartels pay US border officers to let their drug loads pass, putting people inside the inspection agency on the cartels' side.

n: London crime families had officers inside the Metropolitan Police
rank: detectives and civilian staff
d: London organised crime families were able to place or recruit officers inside the Metropolitan Police at will, according to Operation Tiberius, an internal Met report written in 2002 that named officers connected to specific families. The report was never published; it was leaked in 2014 and the Home Affairs Select Committee of MPs questioned police about it. No prosecutions followed and its findings have not been tested in any forum. It is the most senior internal assessment of its kind in a Western police service.
cite: Metropolitan Police Operation Tiberius report, 2002 (leaked 2014); UK Home Affairs Select Committee questioning, 2014
inside: A leaked internal Met report found London crime families could place or recruit officers inside the Metropolitan Police at will.

n: Hashish importer worked with Oslo's police narcotics chief
rank: police unit commander
d: A hashish importer had the head of the Oslo police narcotics unit, Eirik Jensen, working with him. Jensen ran Oslo's narcotics section for years and was convicted of aggravated corruption and of complicity in importing around fourteen tonnes of hashish with an informant he had handled. The Borgarting Court of Appeal sentenced him to twenty-one years in 2020, and Norway's Supreme Court refused his appeal in 2021. It is the most senior police conviction of its kind in Scandinavia.
cite: Oslo District Court 2017 and Borgarting Court of Appeal 2020 judgments; Norwegian Supreme Court refusal, 2021
inside: A hashish importer had the head of Oslo's police narcotics unit working with him, and the officer was convicted of helping import around fourteen tonnes.

n: Swedish crime networks get police register data from insiders
rank: police employees and a security service officer
d: Swedish criminal networks obtain information from police databases through employees inside the police. Swedish courts have convicted police staff of passing data from law enforcement registers to networks, and separately convicted an officer of Sakerhetspolisen, the Security Service, of unauthorised disclosure. Police reporting describes insider access to registers as a systematic weakness rather than an isolated failure.
cite: Swedish district court judgments, 2021-2024; Polismyndigheten and Sakerhetspolisen public reporting
inside: Swedish criminal networks get police staff to pass them data from law-enforcement registers, so the police's own records serve the networks.

n: Cocaine importers recruit customs and terminal staff at German ports
rank: customs and terminal officers
d: Cocaine importers recruit customs officers and terminal employees at Hamburg and Bremerhaven, Germany's main container ports, to clear containers and pass on scanner information. Courts in Hamburg and Bremen have convicted such insiders in cases from 2020 to 2024. Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office treats port-side insider access as the decisive weakness in the northern European cocaine flow, as Belgian and Dutch assessments do for Antwerp and Rotterdam.
cite: Hamburg and Bremen Landgericht judgments, 2020-2024; Bundeskriminalamt Rauschgiftkriminalitat Bundeslagebild
inside: Cocaine importers recruit customs officers and terminal staff at Hamburg and Bremerhaven to clear their containers and pass on scanner information.

n: Israeli crime families received case files from serving officers
rank: police officers
d: Israeli crime organisations have obtained investigative material, such as details of cases being built against them, from serving police officers. Israeli district courts have convicted officers of passing it on, in cases brought between 2019 and 2024 by Mahash, the justice ministry department that investigates police. The organisations receiving the material are the same crime families shown on this map's group layer.
cite: Israeli Department for Investigation of Police Officers (Mahash) case records; district court judgments, 2019-2024
inside: Israeli crime organisations get serving police officers to pass them details of the cases being built against them.

n: Chilean drug distributors protected by Carabineros officers
rank: police officers
d: Drug distributors in Chile have had protection from officers of the Carabineros, Chile's national police. Chilean prosecutors have charged officers with reselling seized narcotics and protecting distribution in Santiago and the northern border region, in cases from 2020 to 2024 that ran alongside the force's wider crisis after the 2019 protests. In the same period Chile shifted from a consumer market to a transit route.
cite: Chilean Fiscalia Nacional and Fiscalia de Alta Complejidad case records, 2020-2024
inside: Chilean prosecutors have charged Carabineros officers with reselling seized drugs and protecting drug distribution, so police worked for the distributors.

n: Traffickers on the Golden Triangle route paid Malaysian drug police
rank: police and enforcement officers
d: Traffickers on the Golden Triangle export route have got Malaysian narcotics officers to work for them. The Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission has prosecuted officers for releasing suspects and reselling seized drugs, in cases from 2018 to 2024 concentrated in Johor and the Klang Valley around Kuala Lumpur. The Golden Triangle, where Myanmar, Laos and Thailand meet, is Asia's main source of methamphetamine, and Malaysia hosts the region's busiest transhipment port.
cite: Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission prosecution records, 2018-2024; Malaysian sessions court judgments
inside: Golden Triangle traffickers got Malaysian narcotics officers to release suspects and resell seized drugs for them.

n: Drug importers recruited Australian border and police officers
rank: border force and police officers
d: Drug importers have recruited Australian Border Force and state police officers to help bring drugs through Sydney and Melbourne. Courts in New South Wales and Victoria have convicted such officers in cases from 2016 to 2024, after referrals from the Australian Commission for Law Enforcement Integrity, the body that investigates corruption in federal law enforcement. Australia pays the highest wholesale drug prices of any market on this map, which is the sum against which an insider is paid.
cite: Australian Commission for Law Enforcement Integrity annual reports and referrals; NSW and Victorian court judgments, 2016-2024
inside: Drug importers recruited Australian Border Force and state police officers, who then helped bring the importers' drugs through Sydney and Melbourne.

n: Smugglers paid Canadian border officers to wave vehicles through
rank: border services officers
d: Drug smugglers have got Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) officers to wave their vehicles through at the Windsor-Detroit and Pacific Highway crossings. Ontario and British Columbia courts convicted officers in cases from 2014 to 2023. The CBSA had no independent civilian oversight body until legislation was brought forward in the 2020s, which is unusual among comparable agencies.
cite: Ontario and British Columbia court judgments, 2014-2023; CBSA internal affairs reporting; Public Safety Canada oversight legislation
inside: Drug smugglers got Canadian border officers to wave their vehicles through, so the agency meant to inspect them let the loads in.

n: Online gambling network allegedly protected by Thai deputy police chief
rank: deputy national police chief
d: An online gambling network is alleged to have had protection from Thailand's deputy national police chief. He was removed and investigated in 2023, in a case that split the police leadership publicly, with disciplinary proceedings and filings by the Office of the Attorney-General running into 2024. The charges concern gambling proceeds rather than narcotics, but the protection arrangement and the laundering routes are the same ones the drug trade uses.
cite: Royal Thai Police disciplinary proceedings and Thai Office of the Attorney-General filings, 2023-2024
inside: An online gambling network is alleged to have had protection from Thailand's deputy national police chief, who was removed and investigated.

n: Smuggling channels run through customs officers at Ukraine's western border
rank: customs and border officers
d: Smuggling networks moving contraband into the European Union work through customs and border service officers at the crossings in Zakarpattia, Ukraine's westernmost region. Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau and State Bureau of Investigation charged officers there with running those channels in cases from 2022 to 2024. The charges concern smuggling generally rather than narcotics; the crossings are the same ones used by the eastern corridor on this map's route layer.
cite: Ukrainian National Anti-Corruption Bureau and State Bureau of Investigation case records, 2022-2024
inside: Smuggling networks run their channels through customs and border officers at Zakarpattia's crossings, who were charged with running them.

n: Laundering networks bribed TD Bank staff to move $670 million
d: Money-laundering networks bribed employees of TD Bank, the US arm of Canada's Toronto-Dominion Bank, to move more than $670 million through its accounts over six years. Those bribed included a store manager; one employee took $11,000 in retail gift cards. The bank had left $18.3 trillion of activity unmonitored. In October 2024 TD Bank became the first bank in US history to plead guilty to conspiracy to commit money laundering. Penalties totalled about $3.09 billion, and regulators capped the size of its US units.
cite: US v. TD Bank NA, D.N.J., guilty plea October 2024
rank: Retail bank — branch staff and compliance (banks & money transmission)
inside: Laundering networks bribed TD Bank employees, including a store manager, to move over $670 million through the bank's accounts for them.

n: Bulgarian cocaine group had a Credit Suisse banker handling its money
d: A Bulgarian cocaine-trafficking organisation led by Evelin Banev, a former wrestler, had a Credit Suisse relationship manager (the banker who handles a client's accounts) moving its money. Elena Pampoulova-Bergomi, a former Bulgarian tennis player, built the relationship with Banev. In June 2022 the Swiss Federal Criminal Court in Bellinzona convicted her of money laundering and convicted Credit Suisse of failing to prevent it, the first criminal conviction of a major Swiss bank. The bank was fined 2 million Swiss francs and ordered to pay about 18.6 million euros; both said they would appeal.
cite: Bundesstrafgericht / Tribunal pénal fédéral, Bellinzona, June 2022; Irish Times, 'Credit Suisse found guilty over Bulgarian drug money failings', 27 June 2022
rank: Private bank — relationship management (banks & money transmission)
inside: A Bulgarian cocaine organisation had a Credit Suisse relationship manager handling its money, so a banker inside the bank laundered the group's funds.

n: Launderers for crime groups worked through Banca Privada d'Andorra's managers
d: Professional launderers acting for transnational criminal organisations had senior managers at Banca Privada d'Andorra (BPA), a private bank in Andorra, knowingly processing their transactions. The US Treasury's financial-crime unit, FinCEN, found in March 2015 that hundreds of millions had moved through four US correspondent banks. Andorra took over BPA the next day and wound it up within the week, splitting it into a continuing bank and a bad bank; clients had to prove their funds legitimate to recover them. In July 2025 a court sentenced eighteen executives, the former chief executive to seven years and a 30 million euro fine. The defendants are appealing; shareholders argue the bank was closed on an administrative finding.
cite: FinCEN Section 311 notice of finding, 10 March 2015; Andorran intervention and liquidation, March 2015; Andorran court sentences, July 2025
rank: Private bank — third-party laundering (banks & money transmission)
inside: Professional launderers for crime groups had senior managers at Banca Privada d'Andorra knowingly processing their transactions through the bank.

n: Cocaine smugglers recruited the crew of MSC Gayane
d: Cocaine smugglers recruited officers and crew of the MSC Gayane, a container ship of the Mediterranean Shipping Company, to take drugs aboard at night at sea. In 2019 about 20 tonnes were seized from the ship in Philadelphia, the largest such seizure in US history at the time. Eight seafarers pleaded guilty, among them the chief mate and second mate, and received about 50 years in prison between them. The ship was released after the operator posted security. Because the cargo bypassed the export terminal, the weakness lay in who was on the crew list, not in the container manifest. The operator called itself a victim and said it was spending over $100 million on security.
cite: US v. Vasquez Reyes, Penda, Ilic, Kavaja and others, E.D. Pa., pleas and sentences 2019-2022
rank: Container vessel — chief mate, second mate and crew (shipping, freight & ports)
inside: Cocaine smugglers recruited officers and crew of an MSC container ship, who took drugs aboard at sea for them.

n: Cocaine networks recruit staff with access at Antwerp's terminals
d: Cocaine networks recruit employees of Antwerp's terminal operators, the companies that run the container docks, to get container reference codes, gate access and scanning records. Antwerp handles the largest cocaine volumes in Europe; seizures reached 116 tonnes in 2023. The port authority and operators have since restricted access and changed codes more often. A 2025 joint report by the EU drugs agency (EUDA) and the World Customs Organization found the weakness lies in staff access rather than screening technology.
cite: Antwerp port authority and terminal operator measures, 2022-2024; EUDA and World Customs Organization joint report, 2025
rank: Container terminals — hiring, gate systems and scan records (shipping, freight & ports)
inside: Cocaine networks recruit staff of Antwerp's terminal operators to hand over container codes, gate access and scanning records.

n: Rotterdam extraction crews got container PIN codes from terminal staff
d: Crews that extract cocaine from containers at Rotterdam, known in Dutch as 'uithalers', have obtained PIN codes from terminal employees with access to the port's own container release system. The PIN releases a container for collection, so a stolen code lets the crew drive the box out. Rotterdam District Court has heard multiple prosecutions of such cases from 2019 to 2024. The weakness is administrative access rather than physical security.
cite: Rotterdam District Court proceedings, multiple, 2019–2024
rank: Terminal access and IT systems (shipping, freight & ports)
inside: Extraction crews get container PIN codes from Rotterdam terminal staff, so the port's own release system lets them drive cocaine-laden boxes out.

n: Ecuadorian cocaine exporters recruited Guayaquil port and customs staff
d: Ecuadorian cocaine exporters hide drugs in legitimate banana shipments leaving Guayaquil and have recruited port staff and customs officials to get them through. Prosecutions by Ecuador's attorney-general's office have reached exporters, port workers and customs officers, and national seizure volumes rose alongside export growth. Ecuador's criminality score on the Global Organized Crime Index rose to 7.48 in 2025.
cite: Fiscalia General del Estado prosecutions; UNODC seizure reporting
rank: Export logistics and cold chain (shipping, freight & ports)
inside: Ecuadorian cocaine exporters recruited port staff and customs officials at Guayaquil to get drugs hidden in banana shipments through.

n: 'Ndrangheta controls hiring at Gioia Tauro port
d: The 'Ndrangheta, the mafia organisation based in Calabria in southern Italy, has gained control over hiring and container handling at Gioia Tauro, Italy's largest transhipment port (a port where cargo is moved between ships rather than unloaded for the country). The port sits in the province of Reggio Calabria, where the 'Ndrangheta's hold is most complete. Deciding who works on the docks lets a crime group decide who handles which containers. This control has been documented by the Direzione Investigativa Antimafia, the Italian police directorate that investigates mafia groups, in its twice-yearly reports, and in proceedings brought by the anti-mafia prosecutors of Reggio Calabria. The drug seizures published each year at the port record only part of what passes through it.
cite: Direzione Investigativa Antimafia semi-annual reports; Reggio Calabria DDA proceedings
rank: Transhipment terminal — labour and clearance (shipping, freight & ports)
inside: The 'Ndrangheta gained control of hiring and container handling at Gioia Tauro, so it decides who works the docks and handles which containers.

n: Drug networks recruited police and customs at Algeciras port
d: Hashish and cocaine trafficking networks around the Port of Algeciras, Spain's largest container port, have recruited members of the municipal police, the customs service and the port workforce to let their shipments through. Algeciras lies on the Strait of Gibraltar, eight miles from Morocco, the main source of hashish entering Europe. Successive operations by Spain's two national police forces, the Policia Nacional and the Guardia Civil, between 2018 and 2024 have arrested serving officers, not only dock workers, and the cases have gone before the provincial court in Cadiz. The arrests show the networks reached the officials whose job is to inspect the cargo.
cite: Spanish Policia Nacional and Guardia Civil operations, 2018–2024; Audiencia Provincial de Cadiz proceedings
rank: Container port and strait crossing — access control (shipping, freight & ports)
inside: Trafficking networks at Algeciras recruited municipal police, customs officers and port workers to let their hashish and cocaine shipments through.

n: Drug networks recruited drivers in Ontario's trucking sector
d: Drug trafficking networks set up a broker-style operation inside Ontario's licensed cross-border trucking sector and recruited drivers to carry drug loads within legitimate supply chains. In trucking, a broker arranges which carrier and driver move a given load. Project Bay, a 2025–2026 investigation by Windsor Police, the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) and the Ontario Provincial Police, found drivers knowingly moving these loads. Twenty-one people were charged with 104 offences and about 1.7 tonnes of drugs were seized. Unlike a port, road freight has no single fixed checkpoint to corrupt, so the networks did their recruiting at the brokerage stage, where loads are assigned to drivers.
cite: Windsor Police, CBSA and Ontario Provincial Police, Project Bay, 2025–2026
rank: Commercial road freight — brokers and drivers (shipping, freight & ports)
inside: Drug networks set up a brokerage inside Ontario's licensed trucking sector and recruited drivers to carry drug loads hidden in legitimate freight.

n: PCC gang money placed in Sao Paulo funds, fintechs and fuel firms
d: The Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC), a gang that began in Sao Paulo's prisons and now runs much of Brazil's drug trade, placed its money inside investment funds and fintechs (online financial-technology firms) in Faria Lima, Sao Paulo's financial district. Through more than 40 funds it held a port terminal, ethanol plants, a truck fleet and over a thousand petrol stations, and ran a fuel scheme built on illegal methanol imports. Operation Carbono Oculto, launched on 28 August 2025 by Brazil's federal tax authority (Receita Federal) and the Sao Paulo prosecutors' organised-crime unit (GAECO), put the sum laundered over four years at some 26 billion reais. Fintechs were not then regulated as financial institutions, which made the transactions hard to follow. Named firms deny wrongdoing and describe themselves as used rather than complicit.
cite: Operacao Carbono Oculto, Receita Federal and Sao Paulo GAECO, from 28 August 2025
rank: Investment funds and payment fintechs (banks & money transmission)
inside: The PCC placed its money inside investment funds and fintechs, secretly holding a port terminal, ethanol plants and petrol stations to clean its drug profits.

n: Gacanin drug organisation allegedly paid Bosnian officials
d: Bosnian prosecutors allege that the drug trafficking organisation of Bosnian trafficker Gacanin paid politicians in Bosnia and Herzegovina and worked with the head of the country's state security service, the agency responsible for intelligence and protecting the state. Gacanin has been designated, meaning placed on a sanctions list that freezes assets and bars dealings, by the US in action coordinated with Europol partners the Netherlands, France and Belgium. Leaked corporate records analysed by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ) in August 2024 showed he used British Virgin Islands and Dubai free zone companies to employ men prosecutors describe as his cartel's operatives. UAE law then required a local sponsor, who was named on the filings; the sponsor's representative said she had no knowledge of narcotics or laundering.
cite: ICIJ analysis of leaked corporate records, August 2024; OFAC and Europol-coordinated designations with the Netherlands, France and Belgium
rank: Free zone company formation and local sponsorship (lawyers, brokers & formation agents)
inside: Bosnian prosecutors allege a drug organisation paid politicians and worked with the head of state security, while using Dubai firms to employ its operatives.

n: CJNG hid its money inside tequila firms and petrol stations
d: Mexico's Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), a major drug-trafficking group, secretly owned or controlled ordinary businesses in Jalisco, Nayarit, Michoacán and Zacatecas: tequila distilleries and agave producers, beverage crop companies, gas stations, a private security firm, wholesale clothing and a children's footwear store. On 23 July 2026 the US Treasury named more than fifty individuals and entities in its largest single action against CJNG, sixteen of the companies listed under both its drug and terrorism sanction programmes. Designation freezes their US assets and bars dealings with them. The action was coordinated with Mexico's Financial Intelligence Unit, followed nearly thirty earlier actions covering more than 250 targets since 2015, and also named the cartel's new leader, who took over after his stepfather was killed in a Mexican government operation in February 2026.
cite: US Treasury press release sb0573 and OFAC recent actions, 23 July 2026, under E.O. 14059 and E.O. 13224 as amended; coordinated with Mexico's Unidad de Inteligencia Financiera
rank: Agave and beverage crop production, fuel retail (gold, commodities & agribusiness)
inside: The CJNG secretly owned or controlled tequila firms, petrol stations and other ordinary businesses, which then served to hide and move its money.

n: CJNG used a Puerto Vallarta resort to feed its timeshare fraud
d: Mexico's Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) controlled Kovay Gardens, a resort near Puerto Vallarta that had run for more than two decades as an ordinary tourist business. The resort sold genuine timeshares, then passed its customer list to cartel-run call centres that sold the same owners fake resale and re-rental services. Between 2019 and 2023 the schemes cost roughly 6,000 American victims about $300 million. On 19 February 2026 the US Treasury designated (sanctioned) the resort with five individuals and seventeen companies in timeshare, real estate, tourism, travel, automotive services, accounting and financial services. It was Treasury's sixth action against CJNG timeshare fraud, bringing the total past 90 individuals and entities, and a 30-day licence was issued for others to wind down dealings with the resort.
cite: OFAC designations and Treasury statement, 19 February 2026, with General License authorising wind-down; prior CJNG timeshare designations from March 2023 and August 2025; investigation by FBI, DEA, IRS and CBP coordinated with Mexico's Unidad de Inteligencia Financiera
rank: Resort, call centres and 17 associated companies (lawyers, brokers & formation agents)
inside: The CJNG controlled an established resort, which passed its customer list to cartel call centres that defrauded the same owners.

n: PCC hid its money in forty investment funds and a port terminal
