d: Brazil's First Capital Command (PCC), a prison-born crime group from São Paulo, secretly owned businesses through about forty investment funds holding roughly 30 billion reais, some $5.5 billion: four ethanol plants, a port terminal, around 1,600 trucks and more than a thousand petrol stations across ten states. Federal Police and tax investigators uncovered the structure in Operation Carbono Oculto; the August 2025 raids ran 14 search and arrest warrants with roughly 350 searches in eight states and blocked about 1.2 billion reais. A follow-up operation found six fintechs operating as unlicensed parallel banks that had moved some 26 billion reais. Authorities named no individuals or companies, citing sealed proceedings. In May 2026 the United States designated the PCC as a terrorist organisation, exposing the holding structure to sanctions before any Brazilian trial.
cite: Operação Carbono Oculto, Brazilian Federal Police and Receita Federal, 28 August 2025; São Paulo state prosecutors; follow-up operation on fintech platforms, 2026; US Department of State designations, 28 May 2026
rank: Investment funds, ethanol plants, a port terminal, a truck fleet (banks & money transmission)
inside: The PCC secretly owned ethanol plants, a port terminal, trucks and petrol stations through about forty investment funds, so ordinary companies served its finances.

n: PCC controlled more than a thousand Brazilian petrol stations
d: Prosecutors in São Paulo allege that Brazil's First Capital Command (PCC), a prison-born crime group, controlled more than a thousand petrol stations generating some 52 billion reais in retail sales, along with fuel distributors, four ethanol plants and a transport fleet. The businesses were held through investment funds uncovered in Operation Carbono Oculto in August 2025. Owning the fuel chain let the PCC both clean drug money and earn from selling adulterated fuel to ordinary motorists, so the harm reached people with no link to the drug trade. Fuel also appears as a primary revenue source in US designations against Mexican groups. The US Department of State designated the PCC on 28 May 2026.
cite: Operação Carbono Oculto, August 2025, and São Paulo prosecutors; US Department of State designation statement, 28 May 2026
rank: Fuel retail, distribution and ethanol production (gold, commodities & agribusiness)
inside: The PCC controlled over a thousand petrol stations and fuel firms through investment funds, using them to clean drug money and sell adulterated fuel.

n: Clan del Golfo trafficker funded mayoral campaigns on its orders
d: A Colombian trafficker working for the Clan del Golfo, Colombia's largest armed drug-trafficking group, provided campaign support and funding to mayoral candidates in several Colombian municipalities on the orders of a Clan del Golfo member. The US Treasury revealed this when it designated (sanctioned) him under the Kingpin Act on 1 December 2020, together with three relatives and associates and four companies — an engineering firm, a homes business, a distributor and a general operations company — that laundered the profits with the relatives installed as figureheads and managers. Treasury assessed that he moved about 4,500 kilograms of cocaine during the autumn of 2018. The case links a crime group's front companies to its attempt to place friendly officials in local government.
cite: US Treasury press release sm1197, OFAC Kingpin Act designations, 1 December 2020, coordinated with US Southern Command; State Department statement, 1 December 2020; Clan del Golfo identified under the Kingpin Act, 31 May 2013
rank: Four companies held through relatives as figureheads (lawyers, brokers & formation agents)
inside: A Clan del Golfo trafficker funded mayoral candidates on the group's orders, an attempt to place officials friendly to it in local government.

n: Guyana police officer arranged safe passage for traffickers
d: A serving Guyanese police officer was accused by the US Treasury of arranging safe passage for Mexican and Venezuelan drug traffickers, putting trafficking groups' interests inside the police force. He was one of four Guyanese and two Colombian nationals designated (sanctioned) on 5 June 2025 after an ICE Homeland Security Investigations inquiry; the others included two men Treasury says run the largest trafficking organisations in the country, two Colombians managing clandestine airstrips, and a former officer wanted over the abduction of a policeman in 2024. The networks use semi-submersibles from Guyanese and Surinamese ports and bury cocaine at airstrips, often in Barima-Waini. In March 2025 a vessel out of Guyana was stopped off Trinidad with about 182 kilograms stamped with a Sinaloa Cartel logo. Treasury called corruption in Guyana a significant obstacle.
cite: US Treasury press release sb0156 and OFAC designations, 5 June 2025; ICE HSI New York investigation; State Department International Narcotics Control Strategy Report, 2025
rank: Semi-submersible vessels and clandestine airfields (shipping, freight & ports)
inside: The US Treasury found a serving Guyanese police officer arranged safe passage for traffickers, putting the trafficking groups' interests inside the police force.

n: Cocaine gangs recruited IT staff inside Dutch and Belgian terminals
d: Cocaine-importing gangs recruited IT contractors and terminal planners working at the container ports of Rotterdam and Antwerp. Dutch and Belgian courts have convicted these insiders of handing over PIN codes, which release containers from the terminal, and of changing where containers were stacked, so that the gangs' extraction crews could find a specific box among millions and remove the drugs before customs checks. The cases came to light through prosecutions between 2021 and 2024. Because the insiders' access to the systems is legitimate, this kind of corruption is hard to screen for in advance.
cite: Rotterdam and Antwerp court judgments, 2021-2024; Dutch Openbaar Ministerie reporting
rank: Container terminal software and planning staff (shipping, freight & ports)
inside: Cocaine gangs recruited IT contractors and planners inside Rotterdam and Antwerp terminals to hand over PIN codes and move containers where their crews could find them.

n: Traffickers recruited airport ground staff to move drugs
d: Drug-trafficking groups have recruited people already working inside airports — ground handlers, who load and unload baggage and cargo, along with cleaners and catering staff — to carry drugs past the security checkpoint for them. Prosecutors in Spain, France and Belgium, and in West African countries including Nigeria, have charged such staff between 2020 and 2024. The method works because these employees hold valid passes to secure areas, so the trafficking group does not need to beat the security check, only to pay someone who is allowed through it.
cite: Spanish, French and Belgian prosecution records, 2020-2024; Europol airport security reporting
rank: Ramp, catering and baggage staff (shipping, freight & ports)
inside: Trafficking groups recruit airport ground handlers, cleaners and catering staff, who hold valid passes, to carry drugs past security for them.

n: Crime groups bought or funded football clubs to launder money
d: Organised crime figures in Spain, Italy and Belgium have bought or funded lower-division football clubs and then used them to move drug money, according to charges brought by prosecutors between 2018 and 2024. Once in control of a club, they pass proceeds through transfer fees (the price one club pays another for a player) and sponsorship deals. Transfer values are subjective, cross-border and agreed privately between clubs, so an inflated fee is hard to prove false. The cases describe the same structure in all three countries, with the club's owners or backers serving the crime group rather than the sport.
cite: Spanish Fiscalia Anticorrupcion and Belgian federal prosecution filings, 2018-2024; Europol financial crime reporting
rank: Sports clubs and player transfers (lawyers, brokers & formation agents)
inside: Crime figures bought or funded football clubs, then used the clubs' transfer fees and sponsorship to move drug money.

n: Glencore bribed officials who allocated oil business
d: Glencore, a Swiss-based commodity trading company, paid bribes to officials in other countries who decided who got oil cargoes and contracts, so that the business went to Glencore; it also manipulated markets. The bribery came to light through US, UK and Swiss prosecutions. Glencore pleaded guilty in the United States and the United Kingdom in 2022 and paid penalties totalling around $1.5 billion; the UK case concerned bribery in Africa. A Swiss court convicted it again in 2024.
cite: US Department of Justice and CFTC resolutions, May 2022; UK Serious Fraud Office conviction and sentencing, 2022-2023; Swiss Office of the Attorney General conviction, 2024; OCCRP, Glencore pleads guilty in the UK to bribery in Africa, 2022
rank: Commodity trader (gold, commodities & agribusiness)
inside: Glencore paid officials in other countries who decided who got oil cargoes and contracts, so their decisions sent the business to Glencore.

n: Trafigura bribed an Angolan state oil official
d: Trafigura, a Swiss-based commodity trading company, paid bribes to an official at Sonangol, Angola's state oil company, to win oil business there. It was tried in Switzerland's Federal Criminal Court in December 2024, and in January 2025 the court convicted the company and a former executive, the second major trader convicted in a Swiss court. The Sonangol official was convicted alongside them. Trafigura also settled separately with Brazilian and US authorities over bribery. Physical commodity trading moves value across borders in a form that financial regulators do not see.
cite: Swiss Federal Criminal Court judgment, 2024; US Department of Justice resolution, 2024; Brazilian leniency agreement; Reuters, Trafigura and former executive found guilty of bribing Angolan official, January 2025; Ver Angola, Swiss company and former Sonangol executive convicted of corruption, January 2025; AP, Trafigura goes on Swiss trial, December 2024
rank: Commodity trader (gold, commodities & agribusiness)
inside: Trafigura paid an official at Angola's state oil company, who then helped it win oil business there.

n: Fuel smugglers had naval and customs officers inside Mexico's ports
d: A fuel-smuggling scheme in Mexico, known as 'huachicol fiscal' (tax-dodging fuel theft), had serving and former naval officers and customs officials working for it inside the ports that the Mexican Navy controls. Fuel was imported declared as lubricant additive to avoid import duty. In 2025 Mexican authorities arrested naval officers, customs officials and business figures over the scheme. It is the largest documented case of an armed force's own customs role being used for a private business, and the same terminals handle container traffic on known drug routes.
cite: Mexican Fiscalia General de la Republica and Secretaria de Marina statements, 2025; Mexican federal court filings
rank: Fuel importation and customs (gold, commodities & agribusiness)
inside: A fuel-smuggling scheme had naval officers and customs officials working for it inside Mexico's navy-run ports, letting fuel in under a false description to dodge duty.

n: Putin ally Medvedchuk led Ukraine's main opposition party, then treason charge
rank: Opposition Platform–For Life leadership; MP
d: Viktor Medvedchuk, a Ukrainian politician whose daughter has Vladimir Putin as godfather, led the pro-Kremlin party Opposition Platform–For Life and sat in Ukraine's parliament from 2019. He had earlier run President Kuchma's administration (2002–2005). In February 2021 Ukraine's security council sanctioned him and blocked three TV channels it believed he controlled. On 11 May 2021 the Prosecutor General charged him with high treason and with illegally exploiting natural resources in Russian-occupied Crimea. He escaped house arrest after the 2022 invasion, was caught in April 2022, and in September 2022 was handed to Russia in a prisoner exchange for 215 Ukrainian soldiers. Ukraine stripped his citizenship and parliament ended his mandate in January 2023.
cite: Atlantic Council UkraineAlert, 13 May 2021; Reuters, 12 Apr and 22 Sep 2022; Ukrainska Pravda, 13 Jan 2023; Wikipedia 'Viktor Medvedchuk'
inside: Ukraine charged Medvedchuk, a Putin ally who led a pro-Kremlin party and sat in parliament, with high treason, alleging he worked for Russia from inside Ukraine's politics.

n: Russia's GRU ran a network of Ukrainian MPs including Derkach and Dubinsky
rank: Members of Ukraine's parliament (Verkhovna Rada)
d: Ukrainian investigators say Russia's military intelligence service, the GRU, built a network inside Ukraine's parliament around MPs Andrii Derkach and Oleksandr Dubinsky. Derkach, an MP since 1998 and a graduate of the KGB's Dzerzhinsky school, was sanctioned by the US Treasury in September 2020 as an 'active Russian agent for over a decade' for spreading claims about Joe Biden. On 13 November 2023 Dubinsky was charged with high treason; the SBU security service said the network was set up by a GRU deputy head, Vladimir Alekseyev, received over $10 million from Russia, and gave Dubinsky the code name 'Buratino'. Derkach fled to Russia and in September 2024 was appointed to Russia's Federation Council.
cite: US Treasury press release, 10 Sep 2020; Euromaidan Press, 13 Nov 2023; Kyiv Post, 13 Nov 2023; Kyiv Independent, 16 Sep 2024
inside: Ukrainian investigators say Russia's GRU built a network of MPs inside Ukraine's parliament, paying over $10 million and giving one MP a code name.

n: Zelensky suspends security chief after 651 treason cases inside his agencies
rank: SBU security service and prosecutors' offices
d: Russian services recruited officials inside Ukraine's security service (SBU) and prosecution service before and during the 2022 invasion, according to President Volodymyr Zelensky. On 17 July 2022 he suspended SBU chief Ivan Bakanov and Prosecutor General Iryna Venediktova, saying 651 treason and collaboration cases had been opened against prosecutorial and law-enforcement officials, and that more than 60 officials from their agencies were working against Ukraine in Russian-occupied areas. The SBU is Ukraine's main domestic intelligence and counter-intelligence agency. Oleksiy Symonenko replaced Venediktova as acting prosecutor general.
cite: Al Jazeera, 17 Jul 2022; BBC News, 18 Jul 2022
inside: Russian services recruited officials inside Ukraine's security and prosecution services, and more than 60 then worked against Ukraine in occupied areas.

n: Ukraine's SBU chief for Crimea detained as suspected FSB mole
rank: Head of SBU directorate for Crimea
d: Oleh Kulinich, whom President Zelensky appointed head of the SBU security service's Crimea directorate in October 2020, is accused of working for Russia's FSB from inside the SBU. He was dismissed on 2 March 2022 and detained on 16 July 2022 on suspicion of treason. Ukraine's State Bureau of Investigation says he knew Russia was preparing to invade from Crimea, hid this from SBU leadership, passed secrets to former security-council deputy secretary Volodymyr Sivkovich, and placed Sivkovich's associates in senior SBU posts in border regions. Andriy Naumov, former head of the SBU's internal security department, is named as an accomplice and is in Serbia, where Ukraine has sought his extradition.
cite: Kyiv Independent, 16 Jul 2022; Babel, 2023 (SBI charges); Ukrainska Pravda, 3 Jul 2023
inside: Investigators say the SBU's Crimea chief worked for the FSB, hid Russia's invasion plans from his own agency and placed allies in senior SBU posts.

n: FBI agent Robert Hanssen spied for Moscow from inside US counter-intelligence
rank: FBI counter-intelligence agent
d: Robert Hanssen, an FBI agent who worked in the bureau's counter-intelligence units, sold US secrets to Moscow for about 22 years. He offered himself to the Soviet military intelligence service (GRU) in 1979, sent the KGB about 6,000 classified documents from 1985, and contacted its successor, the SVR, in 1999, without ever revealing his name. He was paid more than $1.4 million in cash, diamonds and watches. He named Sergei Motorin and Valery Martynov, KGB officers secretly working for the FBI who had also been exposed by Aldrich Ames and were executed, and revealed an FBI tunnel under the Soviet embassy. Arrested at a dead drop on 18 February 2001, he pleaded guilty and was sentenced in May 2002 to life without parole. He died in prison in 2023.
cite: US Department of Justice; Inquirer/AP, 6 Jun 2023; Wikipedia 'Robert Hanssen'
inside: Soviet and Russian intelligence had an FBI counter-intelligence agent selling them US secrets for 22 years, including the names of FBI sources.

n: CIA officer Aldrich Ames sold the agency's Soviet agents to the KGB
rank: CIA Soviet counter-intelligence officer
d: Aldrich Ames, a CIA counter-intelligence officer assigned in 1983 to the branch handling Soviet operations, began selling the agency's secrets to the KGB in April 1985. He received $4.6 million. His information compromised at least 100 US intelligence operations and led to the execution of at least ten sources, Soviet officials secretly working for the United States. He and his wife Rosario were arrested on 21 February 1994. He pleaded guilty and on 28 April 1994 was sentenced to life imprisonment without parole. Ames died in prison on 5 January 2026.
cite: Wikipedia 'Aldrich Ames' (citing court records and NYT); NBC News obituary, Jan 2026
inside: The KGB paid a CIA officer in its Soviet branch, who gave it the agency's secrets and the names of its sources, at least ten of whom were executed.

n: Klaus Fuchs passed atomic bomb designs from inside Los Alamos to Moscow
rank: Theoretical physicist, Manhattan Project (British Mission)
d: Klaus Fuchs, a German-born physicist in the British team sent to the US atomic bomb programme (the Manhattan Project), passed its secrets to Soviet intelligence. From August 1944 he worked in the Los Alamos theoretical physics division on the plutonium bomb's implosion design. By his own later statements he gave the Soviets that design, critical masses, plutonium metallurgy and US production rates, and the date and place of the July 1945 test; from 1947 to 1949, as head of theoretical physics at Britain's Harwell laboratory, he passed hydrogen bomb theory. He confessed to MI5 on 24 January 1950, pleaded guilty on 1 March 1950 and was sentenced to 14 years. Historians still debate how much he sped up the Soviet bomb.
cite: Wikipedia 'Klaus Fuchs' (citing Rhodes, Dark Sun, 1995; Holloway, Stalin and the Bomb, 1994; Greenspan, 2020)
inside: Soviet intelligence had a physicist inside the US and British atomic bomb programmes passing it the bomb's design and production details.

n: Rosenberg ring recruited engineers and a Los Alamos machinist for the KGB
rank: Army Signal Corps labs; Manhattan Project; defence firms
d: Julius Rosenberg, an engineer at the US Army Signal Corps laboratories at Fort Monmouth from 1940, ran a ring of engineers who passed military secrets to the Soviet KGB. At the direction of his Soviet handler Aleksandr Feklisov he recruited his brother-in-law David Greenglass, a machinist on the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos, who supplied a sketch of an implosion-type bomb. The ring also passed a complete proximity fuze and drawings for Lockheed's P-80 jet fighter. After arrests in 1950, Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were convicted on 29 March 1951 and executed on 19 June 1953. Venona decrypts released in 1995 confirmed Julius's role under the code name 'Liberal'; Ethel's part is still disputed.
cite: Wikipedia 'Julius and Ethel Rosenberg' (citing Haynes, Klehr & Vassiliev, Spies, 2009; NSA Venona releases)
inside: The KGB ran a ring of US engineers, including a Los Alamos machinist, who passed military secrets from their posts to their Soviet handler.

n: Venona: Soviet sources inside US Treasury, State, OSS and the White House
rank: State Dept, Treasury, OSS, White House staff
d: Venona was a US code-breaking programme, run from 1943 to 1980, that decrypted about 3,000 wartime cables of Soviet intelligence. The decrypts showed Soviet services had placed or recruited sources inside the State Department, the Treasury, the Office of Strategic Services (the wartime spy agency, which held some 15 to 20 Soviet sources), the White House and the Manhattan Project. Historians John Earl Haynes and Harvey Klehr counted about 349 Americans with covert Soviet ties in the cables, under half of them identified. Those named include Treasury's Harry Dexter White and Roosevelt aide Lauchlin Currie. The cables were released in 1995 by the Moynihan Commission on Government Secrecy; some identifications remain disputed.
cite: NSA, Benson, 'The Venona Story', 2001; Haynes & Klehr, Venona, 2000; Moynihan Commission report, 1997
inside: Decrypted cables show Soviet intelligence placed or recruited sources inside the State Department, the Treasury, the OSS, the White House and the Manhattan Project.

n: Treasury's Harry Dexter White, IMF architect, passed secrets to Soviet agents
rank: Assistant Secretary of the Treasury; US IMF executive director
d: Harry Dexter White, the US Treasury's most senior economist and the American who led the 1944 Bretton Woods conference that created the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, was a source for Soviet intelligence according to decrypted cables and archives. Venona decrypts identify him as 'Jurist'; KGB notes copied by archivist Vasili Mitrokhin list him too; courier Elizabeth Bentley named him to the FBI in 1945. The FBI warned the White House in November 1945, but President Truman still made him the first US executive director at the IMF in 1946. He denied the charges before Congress on 13 August 1948 and died three days later. The Moynihan Commission said his complicity 'seems settled'; his family and some historians dispute it.
cite: Moynihan Commission report, 1997; Steil, The Battle of Bretton Woods, 2013; Boughton, IMF working paper, 2001; Wikipedia 'Harry Dexter White'
inside: Decrypted cables and archives identify the Treasury's most senior economist as a Soviet intelligence source while he shaped US financial policy and the IMF.

n: State Department's Alger Hiss convicted of lying about passing documents
rank: State Department official; UN founding conference secretary-general
d: Alger Hiss, a State Department official who attended the Yalta conference in February 1945 and was secretary-general of the San Francisco conference that wrote the UN Charter, was accused of passing State Department documents to Soviet intelligence. In 1948 former Communist courier Whittaker Chambers produced typed State Department papers and microfilm he said Hiss had given him. Because the time limit for espionage charges had passed, Hiss was tried for perjury and convicted in January 1950, receiving five years. Some historians say Venona cable #1822 and KGB notes identify him as the agent 'Ales'; others, including Kai Bird and Svetlana Chervonnaya, dispute this. Hiss denied it until his death in 1996.
cite: Weinstein, Perjury, 1997; Haynes, Klehr & Vassiliev, Spies, 2009; Bird & Chervonnaya, The American Scholar, 2007
inside: A State Department official was accused of passing department documents to Soviet intelligence, and was convicted of lying about it.

n: NKVD paid congressman Samuel Dickstein $1,250 a month
rank: US Representative; immigration committee chair
d: Samuel Dickstein, a New York congressman from 1923 to 1945 who chaired the House immigration committee and co-led the 1934 committee investigating Nazi propaganda, took monthly payments from the Soviet secret police, the NKVD. Soviet documents found in Moscow archives in the 1990s, published by Allen Weinstein and Alexander Vassiliev in The Haunted Wood (1999), show he received $1,250 a month from 1937 to early 1940 under the code name 'Crook'. It is unclear whether he passed useful information; the payments stopped when he left the committee.
cite: Weinstein & Vassiliev, The Haunted Wood, 1999, pp. 140–150; Politico, 6 Oct 2014; NYT, 3 Jan 1999
inside: The Soviet secret police paid a sitting congressman, a committee chair, $1,250 a month, setting out to have an informant inside Congress.

n: Navy officer John Walker gave the KGB US naval cipher keys for 17 years
rank: Navy communications watch officer, submarine command
d: John Walker, a US Navy warrant officer running the communications centre of the Atlantic submarine force in Norfolk, Virginia, sold cipher material to the KGB from late 1967 until May 1985. He recruited a Navy senior chief, Jerry Whitworth, his brother Arthur and his son Michael, a seaman on the carrier USS Nimitz. The cipher cards and manuals they passed reportedly let the Soviets read more than a million encrypted naval messages. His ex-wife Barbara reported him; the FBI arrested him on 20 May 1985 after he left 124 pages from the Nimitz at a drop. He took a life sentence; Whitworth received 365 years.
cite: Earley, Family of Spies, 1989; Washington Post, 30 Aug 2014; NYT, 30 Aug 2014
inside: The KGB paid a US Navy communications officer who, with relatives and a colleague he recruited, handed over the Navy's cipher material for 17 years.

n: Trump campaign chairman shared polling data with a Russian intelligence officer
rank: Chairman, Trump 2016 presidential campaign
d: Paul Manafort, chairman of Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign, repeatedly passed internal polling data and campaign strategy to Konstantin Kilimnik, whom the US Senate Intelligence Committee called a 'Russian intelligence officer'. The data included figures for Michigan, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania. Manafort had worked from 2004 on influence operations for the Russian billionaire Oleg Deripaska and pro-Russian Ukrainian oligarchs, with Kilimnik as his liaison. The committee's fifth and final report, released in August 2020, said Manafort's access and willingness to share information with people tied to Russian intelligence 'represented a grave counterintelligence threat', though it could not determine what Kilimnik did with the data.
cite: US Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, Report Vol. 5, Aug 2020; Axios, 18 Aug 2020; Mueller Report, 2019
inside: Russian intelligence, through Manafort's long-time liaison Kilimnik, received the Trump campaign's internal polling and strategy from the campaign's own chairman.

n: Estonia's defence security chief Herman Simm sold NATO secrets to Russia
rank: Head of Defence Ministry security department
d: Herman Simm, head of the Estonian Defence Ministry's security department, the office responsible for protecting state secrets including NATO and EU classified information, passed those secrets to Russia's foreign intelligence service, the SVR, from 1995 until his arrest on 21 September 2008. He met SVR handlers three or four times a year in at least 15 European countries. The damage was judged to reach beyond Estonia to its allies. He pleaded guilty to treason and on 25 February 2009 was sentenced to 12.5 years and ordered to pay about €1.3 million in damages. NATO expelled two Russian diplomats in April 2009.
cite: Wikipedia 'Herman Simm' (citing AP, FT, Postimees, ERR); RFE/RL, 2009
inside: Russia's SVR had the Estonian official in charge of protecting state and NATO secrets passing those same secrets to it for thirteen years.

n: Estonian army major Deniss Metsavas spied for Russia's GRU for a decade
rank: Major, Estonian Defence Forces
d: Deniss Metsavas, a major in the Estonian Defence Forces, collected Estonian state secrets and classified information and passed them, for payment, to Russia's military intelligence service, the GRU. His father, Pjotr Volin, forwarded information to Russia as well. In February 2019 Harju County Court convicted both of treason: Metsavas was sentenced to 15 years and 6 months under a plea deal and Volin to six years. Prosecutors said the treason ran for about ten years. In March 2019 President Kersti Kaljulaid stripped Metsavas of all officer ranks. The case was one of a series in which Estonia, a NATO member bordering Russia, caught Russian agents inside its own security institutions.
cite: ERR News, 8 Mar 2019; RFE/RL, Feb 2019; Postimees, 2019
inside: Russia's military intelligence paid a serving Estonian army major to hand over the state secrets and classified material his post gave him.

n: Chinese military intelligence recruited NATO-linked Estonian marine scientist
rank: Defence Ministry scientific committee member
d: Tarmo Kõuts, a marine scientist at Tallinn Technical University who sat on the Estonian Defence Ministry's scientific committee and had worked with NATO's Undersea Research Centre, was recruited by China's military intelligence in 2018. He was paid about €17,000 for information and was convicted in 2021. The case was Estonia's first conviction for spying for China and showed Chinese military intelligence targeting people with access to NATO defence research in a member state.
cite: Wikipedia 'Chinese intelligence activity abroad' (citing ERR and Estonian Internal Security Service yearbook)
inside: China's military intelligence paid a member of Estonia's defence scientific committee, with NATO research links, to pass it information from that work.

n: BND's Soviet counter-intelligence chief Heinz Felfe was a KGB agent
rank: Head of BND counter-espionage against the Soviets
d: Heinz Felfe, a former SS officer, rose to lead counter-espionage against the Soviet Union in West Germany's foreign intelligence service, the BND, while working for the KGB. He became a full Soviet agent in September 1951. West Germany's Federal Court of Justice found he photographed more than 15,000 secret documents, gave Moscow the identities of 94 West German overseas officers and passed on intelligence reports prepared for the Chancellor's office. He was arrested on 6 November 1961 and on 22 July 1963 sentenced to 14 years. On 14 February 1969 he was exchanged for 21 prisoners held in the East.
cite: Wikipedia 'Heinz Felfe'; CIA FOIA reading room, 'Felfe damage assessment'
inside: The KGB had its own agent running West German intelligence's counter-espionage against the Soviets, so he handed Moscow the BND's officers and reports.

n: BND officer Carsten L. accused of selling German intelligence to the FSB
rank: BND officer due for counter-intelligence post
d: Carsten L., an employee of Germany's foreign intelligence service, the BND, is accused of passing documents from the agency to Russia's FSB security service. He was arrested in December 2022, shortly before he was due to move into the BND's counter-intelligence department, the unit that hunts foreign spies. Prosecutors say he was paid €450,000 and charged him with a particularly serious case of treason; his trial began in December 2023. The arrest came ten months into Russia's full-scale war on Ukraine.
cite: Wikipedia 'Russian espionage in Germany' (citing German federal prosecutor and press, 2022–2023)
inside: Russia's FSB is accused of paying a German BND officer to pass it agency documents just before he joined the unit that hunts foreign spies.

n: Norway's Arne Treholt, foreign ministry press chief, convicted as KGB spy
rank: State secretary; Foreign Ministry press chief
d: Arne Treholt, a Norwegian Labour Party official, worked for the KGB from 1974 to 1983 while holding senior posts. He was state secretary to minister Jens Evensen (1976–78), took part in fishing and Law of the Sea talks with the Soviet Union, served at Norway's UN mission (1979–82) and in 1983 became head of the Foreign Ministry's press department. Counter-intelligence officers arrested him at Oslo's Fornebu airport on 20 January 1984 on his way to meet KGB officers. On 20 June 1985 a court convicted him of espionage for the Soviet Union and Iraq and of high treason and sentenced him to 20 years. He was released on health grounds in 1992; review bodies rejected reopening the case in 2008 and 2011.
cite: Wikipedia 'Arne Treholt'; CIA FOIA reading room press archive, 1985
inside: The KGB had a senior Norwegian foreign ministry official, who negotiated with the Soviet Union and served at the UN, working for it for nine years.

n: Swedish intelligence officer Peyman Kia spied for Russia's GRU for a decade
rank: Officer at Säpo and military intelligence (MUST)
d: Peyman Kia worked in 2014–2015 for both of Sweden's main intelligence agencies, the Security Service (Säpo) and the armed forces' foreign intelligence service (MUST), while passing information to Russia's military intelligence, the GRU. The Stockholm District Court found that he and his younger brother Payam handed information to Russia from 2011 to 2021 for money. On 19 January 2023 it sentenced Peyman to life imprisonment and Payam to nine years and ten months; an appeals court upheld the life sentence in May 2023.
cite: NBC News/AP, 19 Jan 2023; The Local Sweden, 19 Jan 2023; Arab News/AP, 25 May 2023
inside: Russia's GRU paid an officer working inside both of Sweden's main intelligence agencies to pass it information, with his brother's help.

n: Swedish air force colonel Wennerström gave the GRU Sweden's air defence plans
rank: Air attaché; section chief in Defence Minister's office
d: Stig Wennerström, a colonel in the Swedish Air Force, served Soviet military intelligence (GRU) while holding posts as air attaché in Moscow and Washington (1952–57) and then as a section chief in the Defence Minister's military office (1957–61). He is believed to have passed about 20,000 pages of secret documents, including Sweden's air defence plans, radar defences, secret bases, mobilisation plans and the Saab Draken fighter project. His maid reported film rolls in his attic and he was arrested in Stockholm on 20 June 1963. He was sentenced to life in 1964, later commuted to 20 years, and paroled in 1974.
cite: Whiteside, An Agent in Place, 1966; Washington Post/AP, 31 Mar 2006; Wikipedia 'Stig Wennerström (colonel)'
inside: Soviet military intelligence had a Swedish air force colonel in the Defence Minister's office passing it Sweden's air defence and mobilisation plans.

n: NATO deputy press chief Georges Pâques gave Moscow NATO war plans
rank: Deputy head, NATO press service
d: Georges Pâques, a senior French civil servant recruited by Soviet intelligence in Algiers in 1944, spied for Moscow for almost two decades while holding posts in French ministries, running France's Institute for Higher National Defence Studies (1961–62) and finally serving as deputy head of NATO's press service in Paris. He gave the Soviets NATO war plans, force postures and plans for defending West Germany; an internal NATO document said he compromised 'most of the essential elements' of its defence strategy. He was arrested on 10 August 1963 after a KGB defector's warnings and sentenced to life in 1964. President Georges Pompidou pardoned him after seven years.
cite: NATO, 'Declassified: The Pâques affair'; NYT obituary, 3 Jan 1994; Wikipedia 'Georges Pâques'
inside: Soviet intelligence had a French civil servant working inside French ministries and then NATO's press service, where he gave Moscow NATO's defence plans.

n: Deputy head of Israel's secret biological institute spied for the Soviets
rank: Deputy scientific director, Israel Institute for Biological Research
d: Marcus Klingberg, deputy scientific director from 1957 to 1972 of the Israel Institute for Biological Research, the secret body responsible for Israel's chemical and biological weapons work, passed information to the Soviet Union for ideological reasons. The indictment dated his spying from 1957; his memoir said 1950. He used a Russian Orthodox church in Abu Kabir as a contact point with the KGB. Israel's Shin Bet security service caught him in January 1983 with help from a KGB double agent; he confessed after about ten days, was tried in secret and sentenced to 20 years, the first ten in solitary confinement under a false name. He is the highest-ranking Soviet spy caught in Israel.
cite: NYT obituary (Grimes), 2015; Haaretz, 2006 and 2008; Shpiro, Intelligence and National Security, 2015
inside: The KGB had the deputy scientific director of Israel's secret weapons research institute passing it information about that institute's work.

n: Gouzenko defection exposes Soviet GRU ring, including MP Fred Rose
rank: Member of Parliament; research council scientists
d: Igor Gouzenko, a cipher clerk for Soviet military intelligence (GRU) at the Soviet embassy in Ottawa, defected in September 1945 with documents showing a Soviet spy ring inside Canadian institutions. A Royal Commission under Supreme Court justices Kellock and Taschereau investigated; 21 people were arrested and 11 convicted. They included Fred Rose, a Communist member of Parliament for Montreal's Cartier riding, convicted of conspiring to pass information on the explosive RDX and sentenced to six years; he was expelled from the House of Commons on 30 January 1947 and is the only Canadian MP convicted of spying. The ring also included Raymond Boyer, a McGill chemist working with the National Research Council, and British physicist Alan Nunn May at the Montreal atomic laboratory.
cite: Kellock–Taschereau Royal Commission report, 1946; Levy, Stalin's Man in Canada, 2011; CBC archives
inside: Soviet military intelligence ran a ring inside Canada's Parliament and research bodies, including an MP and scientists who passed it military research.

n: Canadian navy analyst Jeffrey Delisle sold Five Eyes secrets to the GRU
rank: Sub-lieutenant, naval intelligence centre HMCS Trinity
d: Jeffrey Delisle, a Royal Canadian Navy sub-lieutenant and threat assessment analyst, walked into the Russian embassy in Ottawa in July 2007 and offered to sell secrets, then passed them to Russia's military intelligence, the GRU. From August 2011 he worked at HMCS Trinity, the multinational naval intelligence centre in Halifax, with access to a database shared by Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand (the 'Five Eyes'). An FBI tip led to his arrest in January 2012. In October 2012 he pleaded guilty to breach of trust and passing secret information to a foreign entity, and on 8 February 2013 he was sentenced to 20 years minus time served.
cite: Globe and Mail, 22 Oct 2012 and 8 Feb 2013; CBC News, 10 Oct 2012
inside: Russia's GRU paid a Canadian naval intelligence officer to pass it secrets from a database shared by Canada and its Five Eyes allies.

n: Sorge ring reached Japan's prime minister's circle and the German embassy
rank: Confidant of German ambassador; PM Konoe's circle
d: Richard Sorge, an officer of Soviet military intelligence working in Tokyo as a German newspaper correspondent, built a spy ring that reached into both the German embassy and the Japanese prime minister's circle. Posing as a loyal Nazi, he became a confidant of Ambassador Eugen Ott. His Japanese partner, journalist Hotsumi Ozaki, had close access to Prime Minister Fumimaro Konoe and copied secret documents. In September 1941 Sorge reported that Japan no longer planned to attack the Soviet Union, information that may have helped Moscow move troops west. Ozaki and Sorge were arrested on 14 and 18 October 1941; Sorge was hanged on 7 November 1944.
cite: Prange, Goldstein & Dillon, Target Tokyo, 1984; Whymant, Stalin's Spy, 2006; Wikipedia 'Richard Sorge'
inside: A Soviet military intelligence officer placed his ring inside the German embassy and the Japanese prime minister's circle, sending Moscow their secret plans.

n: KGB defector Levchenko names about 200 Japanese agents, including politicians
rank: Party leader; former labour minister; journalists
d: Stanislav Levchenko, a KGB major working in Tokyo under journalistic cover, defected to the United States in October 1979 and later gave the US government the names of about 200 Japanese agents of the KGB. Those he named included Seiichi Katsumata, leader of the Japan Socialist Party, then the main opposition party, and Hirohide Ishida, a former Liberal Democratic Party labour minister. A Soviet court sentenced Levchenko to death in absentia in 1981.
cite: Trahair, Encyclopedia of Cold War Espionage, 2004, pp. 166–167; Spokesman-Review, 26 Oct 1979
inside: The KGB recruited about 200 agents in Japan, including the leader of the main opposition party and a former government minister.

n: Mitrokhin archive: KGB cash taken to India's prime minister's house
rank: Prime Minister's residence; ruling Congress party
d: Notes copied from KGB files by archivist Vasili Mitrokhin, who defected to Britain in 1992, say the Soviet KGB routinely sent 'suitcases full of banknotes' to the house of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi (code name VANO). The notes, published with historian Christopher Andrew in The World Was Going Our Way (2005), also say the KGB had ten Indian newspapers on its payroll by 1973 and planted 3,789 articles in the Indian press in 1972. Congress called the claims 'pure sensationalism'; the opposition BJP demanded a judicial inquiry. Only Mitrokhin's handwritten notes exist, so the material cannot be checked against originals.
cite: Andrew & Mitrokhin, The World Was Going Our Way (Mitrokhin Archive II), 2005; Times of India; Economic Times; Rediff News
inside: KGB files say Soviet cash went to the Indian prime minister's house and that the KGB paid Indian newspapers; the notes cannot be checked against originals.

n: Kim Philby, Soviet agent since 1934, ran MI6's anti-Soviet section
rank: Head of MI6 Section IX; MI6 liaison in Washington
d: Kim Philby, recruited by Soviet intelligence at Cambridge in June 1934, rose inside Britain's foreign intelligence service, MI6, while working for Moscow. In late 1944 he became head of Section IX, the unit set up to work against Soviet and communist activity, and from 1949 to 1951 he was MI6's chief representative in Washington, liaising with the CIA and FBI. He recommended Donald Maclean and Guy Burgess to his recruiter and warned them before their 1951 flight. He resigned under suspicion in 1951, was cleared in public by Foreign Secretary Harold Macmillan in 1955, and fled from Beirut to Moscow in January 1963. He confirmed his KGB work in 1967 and was buried in Moscow with KGB honours in 1988.
cite: Macintyre, A Spy Among Friends, 2015; Boyle, The Climate of Treason, 1979; Oxford DNB (Clive, 2004)
inside: Soviet intelligence had its own agent running MI6's anti-Soviet section and then its Washington liaison post, giving Moscow British and American secrets.

n: Diplomat Donald Maclean reported Anglo-US atomic policy to Moscow
rank: Washington embassy First Secretary; head of Foreign Office American Department
d: Donald Maclean, a British diplomat recruited through the Cambridge spy ring, passed Foreign Office secrets to Soviet intelligence from inside the British embassy in Washington (1944–48) and later as head of the Foreign Office's American Department. In Washington he served as secretary of the Combined Policy Committee, the body coordinating American, British and Canadian atomic energy policy, and became Moscow's main source on it, including how much plutonium the Americans had. He reportedly passed a record of the December 1950 Attlee–Truman summit. Venona decrypts identified a source called 'Homer'; facing exposure, he fled to Moscow with Guy Burgess on 25 May 1951.
cite: Cecil, A Divided Life, 1988; Holzman, Donald and Melinda Maclean, 2014; Andrew & Mitrokhin, The Mitrokhin Archive
inside: Soviet intelligence had a British diplomat inside the Washington embassy and Foreign Office reporting Anglo-American atomic policy and summit records to Moscow.

n: John Cairncross passed Cabinet Office and Bletchley Park secrets to Moscow
rank: Private secretary to Lord Hankey; Bletchley Park; MI6
d: John Cairncross, a British civil servant recruited in 1937, worked for Soviet intelligence from posts in the Foreign Office, the Treasury, the Cabinet Office (as private secretary to minister Lord Hankey), the Bletchley Park code-breaking centre (1942–43) and MI6. Russian archives indicate he supplied 5,832 documents between 1941 and 1945. Through Hankey's office, which sat on Britain's early atomic committees, he gave Moscow early evidence that Britain was considering an atomic bomb. From Bletchley he smuggled out decrypted German messages that gave advance warning of the German offensive at Kursk in 1943. He confessed to MI5 in 1964 but was never prosecuted; in 1990 KGB defector Oleg Gordievsky confirmed him as the 'fifth man' of the Cambridge ring.
cite: Andrew & Gordievsky, The Times, 1990; Smith, The Last Cambridge Spy, 2019; Independent obituary (Bower), 1995
inside: Soviet intelligence had a British civil servant in the Cabinet Office, Bletchley Park and MI6 passing it thousands of secret documents.

n: MI5 officer Anthony Blunt passed wartime secrets to the NKVD
rank: MI5 officer; Surveyor of the King's Pictures
d: Anthony Blunt, an art historian recruited by Soviet intelligence around 1937, joined Britain's domestic security service, MI5, in 1940 and passed it secrets to the NKVD throughout the war. He handed over Ultra intelligence from decrypted German Enigma traffic on the Eastern Front, details of German spy rings in the Soviet Union and German war plans the British had chosen to withhold. After 1945 he became Surveyor of the King's Pictures, kept contact with Soviet agents and passed on gossip from MI5 colleagues until 1951. He confessed on 23 April 1964 in return for immunity, which was kept secret until Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher named him in the Commons on 15 November 1979. He was then stripped of his knighthood.
cite: Hansard, 15 Nov 1979; Carter, Anthony Blunt: His Lives, 2001; Oxford DNB
inside: Soviet intelligence had an officer inside Britain's security service MI5 passing it decrypted German traffic and other wartime secrets.

n: MI6 officer George Blake betrayed Western agents and the Berlin tunnel
rank: MI6 case officer, Berlin
d: George Blake, an officer of Britain's foreign intelligence service, MI6, volunteered to work for the Soviet MGB (the KGB's predecessor) while held prisoner during the Korean War and then served Moscow from inside MI6. He told his Soviet contacts about Operation Gold, a tunnel dug into East Berlin to tap Soviet military telephone lines, and the similar Operation Silver in Vienna. From 1955, as a case officer in Berlin recruiting Soviet officers, he exposed agents; Britain says hundreds of Western agents in Eastern Europe were compromised, some executed. Unmasked by a Polish defector, he was sentenced in May 1961 to 42 years, escaped from Wormwood Scrubs on 22 October 1966 and reached Moscow.
cite: Guardian obituary (Norton-Taylor), 2020; BBC News, 2020; Hermiston, The Greatest Traitor, 2013
inside: Soviet intelligence had an MI6 officer inside the service exposing its Berlin tunnel operation and the Western agents he was meant to run.

n: Melita Norwood passed Britain's atomic research files to Moscow for 35 years
rank: Secretary at the British Non-Ferrous Metals Research Association
d: Melita Norwood, a secretary at the British Non-Ferrous Metals Research Association from 1932, was a Soviet agent from 1937 until she retired in 1972. Her post as secretary to a department head gave her access to material from Tube Alloys, Britain's wartime atomic weapons project, which the association worked on, and she passed it to Soviet intelligence. She was exposed in September 1999 by The Mitrokhin Archive, based on notes from KGB files. She said she acted 'not to make money, but to help prevent the defeat of a new system'. British authorities decided not to prosecute her, then aged 87.
cite: Andrew & Mitrokhin, The Mitrokhin Archive, 1999; BBC News, 1999; Guardian obituary, 2005
inside: Soviet intelligence had a secretary inside a British research body working on the atomic bomb passing it the project's files for decades.

n: Moldovan president Dodon charged with treason over Russian party money
rank: President of Moldova (2016–2020); Socialist Party leader
d: Igor Dodon, president of Moldova from December 2016 to December 2020 and leader of the pro-Russian Socialist Party (PSRM), is accused of keeping his party running on money from Russia. In June 2019 videos showed him telling the oligarch Vladimir Plahotniuc that the party received monthly funding from the Russian Federation. In March 2020 three MPs presented documents they said showed Russian money reaching PSRM MPs through a Bahamas account, with Dodon as main beneficiary. He was arrested on 24 May 2022 and charged with passive corruption, illegal party financing by a criminal organisation, illicit enrichment and high treason. The US Treasury says he conspired with Russia to interfere in Moldova's elections. His trial was ordered restarted in November 2025.
cite: Wikipedia 'Igor Dodon' (citing Moldovan prosecutors, RFE/RL, US Treasury); Ziarul de Gardă
inside: Russian state money is alleged to have kept the Moldovan president's party running and reached its MPs, leading to treason charges against him.

n: Montenegro coup plot: GRU officers and pro-Russian MPs, later acquitted
rank: Democratic Front leaders, MPs
d: Prosecutors in Montenegro alleged that two officers of Russia's military intelligence (GRU), Eduard Shishmakov and Vladimir Popov, worked with leaders of the pro-Russian Democratic Front party to seize parliament on election day, 16 October 2016, kill Prime Minister Milo Đukanović and install a government that would halt Montenegro's entry into NATO. On 9 May 2019 a court convicted 13 people: the GRU officers in absentia (15 and 12 years) and Democratic Front MPs Andrija Mandić and Milan Knežević (five years each). The appeals court annulled the verdict in February 2021 for procedural violations; a retrial acquitted all defendants in July 2024, upheld in February 2026. Montenegro joined NATO in 2017.
cite: Reuters, 9 May 2019; BalkanInsight, 9 May 2019 and 12 Jul 2024; RFE/RL, 5 Feb 2021; RTCG, 20 Feb 2026
inside: Prosecutors alleged two Russian military intelligence officers worked with pro-Russian Montenegrin MPs to seize parliament and install a government that would halt NATO entry; all were later acquitted.

n: Greece expels Russian diplomats for trying to bribe state officials
rank: Greek state officials
d: In July 2018 Greece expelled two Russian diplomats and barred two others, citing threats to national security. The Greek Foreign Ministry later said Russia had attempted to bribe state officials, undermine Greek foreign policy and interfere in Greece's internal affairs. The expulsions came weeks after Greece signed the Prespa agreement with North Macedonia, which opened the way for that country to join NATO and which Russia opposed; some Greek politicians accused Russia of trying to block the deal. Russia expelled Greek diplomats in August 2018 and Greece recalled its ambassador.
cite: Reuters, 11 Jul 2018; BBC News, 11 Jul 2018; Greek Ministry of Foreign Affairs statements, 18 Jul and 10 Aug 2018
inside: Russian diplomats tried to bribe Greek state officials to undermine Greece's foreign policy, the Greek Foreign Ministry said, around a deal Russia opposed.

n: US sanctions Serbia's spy chief Vulin for aiding Russia's activities
rank: Director of Serbia's Security Intelligence Agency (BIA)
d: Aleksandar Vulin, Serbia's defence minister (2017–2020), interior minister (2020–2022) and then director of the Security Intelligence Agency (BIA), the country's main intelligence service, was sanctioned by the US Treasury on 11 July 2023. The Treasury said he carried out 'corrupt and destabilizing acts that have also facilitated Russia's malign activities in the region', and accused him of supporting a drug-trafficking network and illegal arms shipments involving Serbian arms dealer Slobodan Tešić and the Belarusian state firm Beltechexport. Vulin resigned from the BIA on 3 November 2023 under Western pressure but became deputy prime minister in May 2024.
cite: US Treasury press release jy1606, 11 Jul 2023; AP, 11 Jul and 4 Nov 2023
inside: The US Treasury says Serbia's intelligence chief, a former defence and interior minister, used his posts in ways that helped Russia's activities in the region.

n: Gazprom's Nord Stream 2 funded a German state's 'climate' foundation
rank: State government of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern
d: The state government of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern in north-east Germany, led by Minister-President Manuela Schwesig, set up a public 'Climate and Environmental Protection Foundation' whose charter stated the goal of completing the Nord Stream 2 gas pipeline from Russia. The money came from Nord Stream 2 AG, a subsidiary of Russia's state gas company Gazprom, and Reuters reported that the foundation set out to help the project get around US sanctions on firms working on the pipeline. A state body thus served as a channel for a Russian state company. In March 2024 media reported that Schwesig's office removed passages from a supposedly independent report saying closing the foundation was feasible and desirable.
cite: Reuters explainer (Escritt & Marsh), 11 Feb 2022; Business Insider Deutschland, 7 Mar 2024
inside: Money from Gazprom's pipeline company ran a German state government's public foundation, whose charter and work served completing Russia's pipeline around sanctions.

n: GRU officer with false identity nearly took a job at the ICC
rank: Position at the International Criminal Court
d: Sergey Cherkasov, an alleged officer of Russia's military intelligence (GRU), spent years in Brazil building the false identity of a Brazilian, Victor Muller Ferreira, and in April 2022 flew to the Netherlands to take up a position at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague. The ICC was then investigating war crimes in Ukraine. The Dutch intelligence service AIVD judged the threat potentially very high; he was refused entry at Schiphol airport and sent back to Brazil, where he was convicted of using forged documents. His sentence was cut from 15 years to five years and two months, and in January 2024 Brazil added a money-laundering charge.
cite: Guardian, 16 Jun 2022; BBC News, 16 Jun 2022; CNN, 28 Jul 2023; Deutsche Welle, 30 Jan 2024
inside: Russia's military intelligence built a false identity for an officer so he could take a post inside the International Criminal Court while it investigated Russia.

n: Polish judge who ruled on security clearances fled to Belarus
rank: Judge, Voivodeship Administrative Court, Warsaw
d: Tomasz Szmydt, a judge at the Voivodeship Administrative Court in Warsaw, sat in the department that ruled on whether members of the military and intelligence services could access classified information, and reportedly on access to NATO and EU top-secret material. On 1 May 2024 he left Poland and went to Belarus, Russia's close ally, where he sought asylum and appeared at a press conference by the state news agency BelTA. On 9 May the Supreme Administrative Court lifted his immunity at prosecutors' request amid espionage charges. Polish officials, including his former superior Łukasz Piebiak, said he had worked for Russia; this has not been proven.
cite: Gazeta Wyborcza, 6–9 May 2024; TVP World, 9 May 2024; BelTA, 6 May 2024
inside: Polish officials allege a judge who ruled on security clearances for military and intelligence staff was working for Russia before he fled to Belarus.

n: CIA translator Larry Wu-tai Chin spied for China for over 30 years
rank: CIA Foreign Broadcast Information Service analyst
d: Larry Wu-tai Chin, recruited by Chinese intelligence in 1944, worked as a Chinese-language translator and analyst at the CIA's Foreign Broadcast Information Service from 1952 to 1981 while spying for China. He passed CIA intelligence reports on China and East Asia, profiles of CIA employees and information that helped Chinese counter-intelligence find agents in China. In 1970 he passed CIA documents on President Nixon's plans to open relations with China, which Mao reportedly used in negotiations. A senior Chinese intelligence official, Yu Qiangsheng, defected in 1985 and exposed him. He was arrested on 23 November 1985, convicted in February 1986 and found dead in his cell on 21 February 1986.
cite: Los Angeles Times, 8 and 21 Feb 1986; Hoffman, The Spy Within, 2008; Washington Post, 6 Dec 1985
inside: Chinese intelligence had a translator inside the CIA for three decades, passing it CIA reports, staff profiles and Nixon's plans for China.

n: FBI's top China informant Katrina Leung also worked for Beijing's MSS
rank: FBI counter-intelligence asset and handler
d: Katrina Leung, a Los Angeles businesswoman whom FBI agent James J. Smith recruited as an informant code-named 'Parlor Maid' in 1982, was also recruited by China's Ministry of State Security (MSS) in 1984, according to the FBI. Smith, her handler, had a long affair with her and brought classified material to their meetings. In 1991 another agent recognised her voice on a recording of a call with an MSS official, and the FBI learned she had disclosed a classified operation. Prosecutors said she contaminated about 20 years of FBI intelligence on China. Arrested in April 2003, she had the main charges dismissed for prosecutorial misconduct and in December 2005 pleaded guilty to lying to the FBI and filing a false tax return.
cite: CNN, 2003; Wise, Tiger Trap, 2011; DOJ Office of the Inspector General review, 2006
inside: China's Ministry of State Security recruited the FBI's own top China informant, who passed it a classified FBI operation from inside the bureau's work.

n: China's MSS paid an American to apply for jobs at the State Dept and CIA
rank: Applicant to the Foreign Service and CIA clandestine service
d: Officers of the Shanghai State Security Bureau, part of China's Ministry of State Security, recruited an American student, Glenn Duffie Shriver, around 2004 and paid him to get inside US government agencies. They paid him $10,000 and $20,000 to sit the Foreign Service exam in 2005 and 2006, which he failed, and $40,000 when he applied in 2007 to the CIA's National Clandestine Service, which runs its spies abroad. He hid the contacts during CIA vetting in 2010; the CIA already knew, and the FBI arrested him in June 2010. He pleaded guilty in October 2010 to conspiracy under the Espionage Act and on 21 January 2011 was sentenced to four years.
cite: US Department of Justice, 21 Jan 2011; Reuters, 22 Oct 2010; Washingtonian (Wise), 7 Jun 2012
inside: China's Ministry of State Security paid an American to try to get jobs inside the State Department and the CIA's clandestine service so he could spy for it.

n: State Department's Candace Claiborne traded documents for Chinese agents' gifts
rank: US State Department employee
d: Candace Claiborne, a US State Department employee with top-secret clearance, hid her contacts with agents of the People's Republic of China and accepted gifts and benefits from them in return for internal State Department documents. The State Department runs US foreign policy and embassies, so its internal papers show American positions and plans on China. Claiborne was charged in 2017 and pleaded guilty in April 2019. On 9 July 2019 she was sentenced to 40 months in prison, three years' supervised release and a $40,000 fine.
cite: US Department of Justice, 9 Jul 2019; Wikipedia 'List of Chinese spy cases in the United States'
inside: Chinese agents gave a US State Department employee gifts and benefits in return for internal State Department documents.

n: US Navy sailor on USS Essex sold ship details to a Chinese intelligence officer
rank: Machinist's mate, amphibious assault ship USS Essex
d: Jinchao 'Patrick' Wei, a US Navy machinist's mate with security clearance on the amphibious assault ship USS Essex, based in San Diego, passed photos, videos and documents about Navy ships to a Chinese intelligence officer in 2022. He was charged in August 2023, convicted in August 2025 and sentenced to more than 16 years. In a parallel case, another Navy servicemember, Wenheng Zhao, sent sensitive military information, including on a radar system in Okinawa, in return for bribes, and in January 2024 was sentenced to 27 months.
cite: US Department of Justice, Aug 2023 and 2025; Wikipedia 'List of Chinese spy cases in the United States'
inside: A Chinese intelligence officer got a US Navy sailor with security clearance to pass him photos, videos and documents about Navy ships.

n: MSS agent Ji Chaoqun joined the US Army Reserve to spot recruits
rank: US Army Reserve enlistee
d: Ji Chaoqun, a Chinese citizen in Chicago, worked under a senior officer of the Jiangsu State Security Department, a provincial branch of China's Ministry of State Security, and enlisted in the US Army Reserve through a programme for foreign nationals with needed skills (MAVNI). He was tasked with gathering biographical details on eight people, including engineers and scientists working for US defence contractors, whom Chinese intelligence might recruit. Arrested on 25 September 2018, he was convicted in September 2022 of acting as an MSS agent and lying about his contacts on a military form, and in January 2023 was sentenced to eight years. He was released in a November 2024 prisoner exchange.
cite: Chicago Tribune, 26 Sep 2022; US Department of Justice, Jan 2023
inside: China's Ministry of State Security had its agent enlist in the US Army Reserve and gather details on defence engineers it might recruit.

n: Engineer Chi Mak sent US Navy technology from a defence contractor to China
rank: Engineer, Power Paragon (L-3 Communications)
d: Chi Mak, an engineer at Power Paragon, a California unit of the defence contractor L-3 Communications, passed US defence technology to China while working on Navy projects, including submarine propulsion data. The Washington Post described him as a Chinese 'sleeper' agent placed in the United States for two decades. He was convicted in 2007 of conspiring to export sensitive defence technology to China, and on 24 March 2008 was sentenced to 24 years and four months.
cite: Washington Post (Warrick & Johnson), 2008; BBC News, 2008; AP/NBC, 2007
inside: China placed a long-term agent as an engineer inside a US defence contractor, where he passed Navy technology to China.

n: Chinese agents paid aide in Taiwan's Presidential Office for documents
rank: Aide, Presidential Office
d: Wang Jen-ping, an aide in Taiwan's Presidential Office, the staff that serves Taiwan's head of state, was found in 2009 to have sold nearly 100 confidential documents to China since 2007. The People's Republic of China claims Taiwan as its territory, so documents from the presidency give Beijing a view of Taiwan's policy towards it. The case was one of a series of discoveries of Chinese agents inside Taiwan's presidency, military and intelligence services in 2009 and 2010, including a double agent in the Military Intelligence Bureau.
cite: Wikipedia 'Chinese intelligence activity abroad' (citing Taipei Times, 2009)
inside: Chinese intelligence paid an aide inside Taiwan's Presidential Office to sell it nearly 100 confidential documents.

n: Taiwan army general Lo Hsien-che spied for China; life sentence
rank: Major general, head of army electronic communications department
d: Lo Hsien-che, a major general who headed the Taiwanese army's electronic communications and information department, spied for China after being recruited around 2004 while he was military attaché in Thailand. Reports say a woman with an Australian passport drew him in, and local media cited payments of possibly US$1 million. Investigators found classified documents on military electronic warfare and strategy; concern centred on the Po Sheng command-and-control system, though the defence ministry said his access to it was limited. His office and home were raided on 27 January 2011, and on 26 April 2012 a military court sentenced him to life imprisonment.
cite: BBC News, 9 Feb 2011; Central News Agency, 26 Apr 2012; South China Morning Post, 9 and 11 Feb 2011
inside: Chinese intelligence recruited a Taiwanese army major general who headed military communications, and passed Beijing classified electronic warfare material.

n: Retired Taiwan admiral and ex-MP tried over alleged PLA recruiting; MP acquitted
who: PLA and United Front Work Department
rank: Retired rear admiral; former legislator
d: Hsia Fu-hsiang, a retired Taiwanese rear admiral, and Lo Chih-ming, a former member of Taiwan's legislature, were charged in 2023 after being recruited by China's People's Liberation Army and the United Front Work Department, the Chinese Communist Party body that cultivates people and groups outside the party to serve its aims. Prosecutors say they worked to recruit serving Taiwanese military officers. In the same year an active officer, Lieutenant-Colonel Hsieh, was detained for leaking secrets and suspected of building a network inside the armed forces. Courts have not upheld the main charge. Kaohsiung District Court found both men not guilty of recruiting spies, though it gave Hsia five months for planning to work for a Chinese state-run organisation. In April 2024 the High Court acquitted both. On 23 October 2024 the Supreme Court made Lo's acquittal final, and revoked Hsia's acquittal on the charge of attempting to form a spy ring, sending that part back for retrial.
cite: Wikipedia 'Chinese intelligence activity abroad' (citing Taiwanese prosecutors and Focus Taiwan, 2023); Taiwan News, 23 Oct 2024; Taiwan News, 9 Apr 2024
inside: Prosecutors alleged China's military and United Front body recruited a retired admiral and ex-legislator to recruit serving officers; Lo was finally acquitted and Hsia faces retrial.

n: Taiwan military intelligence officer was a double agent for China
rank: Officer, Military Intelligence Bureau
d: Lo Chi-cheng, an officer of Taiwan's Military Intelligence Bureau, the agency that runs Taiwan's spies on the mainland, was found in 2010 to have been working as a double agent for China since 2007. A double agent pretends to work for one service while reporting to another, so Chinese intelligence could learn about Taiwan's operations against it. In 2015 a Chinese officer, Zhen Xiaojiang, was convicted in Taiwan of recruiting Taiwanese officers, among them Major-General Hsu Nai-chuan; Zhen was deported in 2018.
cite: Wikipedia 'Chinese intelligence activity abroad' (citing Taipei Times and Focus Taiwan)
inside: Chinese intelligence had an officer inside Taiwan's Military Intelligence Bureau working as its double agent against Taiwan's own operations.

n: CEFC China Energy envoy offered Chad's president a $2m bribe for oil rights
rank: President of Chad
d: Patrick Ho, a former Hong Kong home affairs secretary who ran a lobbying body funded by the Shanghai-based CEFC China Energy, worked with former Senegalese foreign minister Cheikh Gadio to offer Chad's President Idriss Déby a US$2 million bribe, disguised as a donation, to win oil rights for CEFC. CEFC promoted Xi Jinping's Belt and Road Initiative. Ho was arrested in New York in November 2017 and convicted on 5 December 2018 of seven counts of bribery and money laundering under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act; Gadio testified against him. In March 2019 Ho was sentenced to three years and fined US$400,000. CEFC's chairman Ye Jianming denied authorising him.
cite: US Department of Justice, 5 Dec 2018; NYT, 5 Dec 2018; Hong Kong Free Press, 26 Mar 2019
inside: An envoy funded by the Chinese firm CEFC offered Chad's president a disguised US$2 million bribe so the state would give CEFC oil rights.

n: CEFC wired $500,000 to Uganda's foreign minister, the former UN Assembly head
rank: Foreign Minister of Uganda; President Museveni
d: Patrick Ho, working for the Chinese conglomerate CEFC China Energy, arranged in May 2016 for US$500,000 to be wired to an account provided by Uganda's foreign minister Sam Kutesa, who had served from 2014 to 2015 as President of the UN General Assembly (2014–15). Ho also urged CEFC's chairman to give President Yoweri Museveni US$500,000 in cash as a 'campaign donation' after his re-election. US prosecutors said the payments were meant to get both men to use their power to steer business to CEFC. A New York jury convicted Ho on 5 December 2018. The record contains no statement from Kutesa answering the allegation; he remained foreign minister until May 2021.
cite: US Department of Justice, 5 Dec 2018; Wikipedia 'Sam Kutesa'
inside: An envoy for the Chinese firm CEFC paid Uganda's foreign minister and offered the president cash so they would steer state business to CEFC.

n: Think-tank head Gal Luft charged with paying a Trump adviser for China
rank: Adviser to President-elect Trump
d: Gal Luft, co-director of a Washington think tank, was charged in an indictment unsealed by the US Justice Department on 10 July 2023 with acting as an unregistered agent of Chinese entities. Prosecutors say that, at their request, he recruited and paid an unnamed adviser to then President-elect Donald Trump to promote pro-China positions. The indictment also charges arms trafficking, breaking Iran sanctions and lying to federal agents. Cypriot police arrested Luft in February 2023; he vanished while on bail in March 2023. In September 2024 prosecutors said he had been re-arrested and would be extradited.
cite: US Department of Justice (SDNY), 10 Jul 2023; Washington Post, 15 Jul 2023; Reuters, 9 Sep 2024
inside: US prosecutors say Luft, at Chinese principals' request, paid an adviser to the US President-elect to promote pro-China positions from inside the transition.

n: Ecuador charges ex-president Moreno with bribery over Chinese-built dam
rank: Vice-president, later President of Ecuador
d: Ecuador's Coca Codo Sinclair hydroelectric plant, one of the country's largest, was built from 2009 to 2018 by Sinohydro, a contracting arm of China's state-owned PowerChina, with a $1.7 billion loan from China's Export-Import Bank. On 6 March 2023 a judge approved bribery charges against former president Lenín Moreno, vice-president during the build, and others over the contract. In a separate case, the 'INA Papers', prosecutors allege $76 million in kickbacks moved through an offshore company in Belize founded by Moreno's brother. Moreno, living in Paraguay, denies it. The plant later showed 7,648 cracks; in April 2026 PowerChina agreed $400 million in compensation.
cite: Reuters, 23 Feb and 6 Mar 2023; NYT, 24 Dec 2018; Reuters, 10 Apr 2026
inside: Ecuadorian prosecutors charged the former president with taking bribes over the contract for the Chinese state-built dam, with alleged kickbacks routed through his brother's offshore company.

n: ZTE broadband deal: Philippine election chief accused of seeking kickbacks
rank: Election commission chair; cabinet; presidential spouse
d: ZTE, a Chinese telecoms company controlled through state-owned shareholders, signed a US$329 million contract on 20 April 2007 to build the Philippines' government broadband network. In Senate hearings from September 2007, economic planning secretary Romulo Neri testified that election commission chairman Benjamin Abalos offered him 200 million pesos to approve it; a witness said ZTE advanced US$1 million to Abalos, and another linked President Gloria Arroyo's husband to the kickbacks. Arroyo cancelled the deal in October 2007. The Ombudsman indicted Arroyo, her husband and Abalos for graft in 2011, but the anti-graft court dismissed the case against Arroyo in 2016.
cite: GMA News, 18 Sep 2007; Reuters, Sep 2007; Rappler, 7 Mar 2012; CNN Philippines, 16 Sep 2016
inside: The Chinese firm ZTE is said to have advanced money to the Philippine election chief, who offered a cabinet secretary a bribe to approve ZTE's state contract.

n: Canada's top-security lab scientist worked to benefit China, CSIS found
who: Chinese state and military research bodies
rank: Section head, National Microbiology Laboratory
d: Xiangguo Qiu, who headed a vaccine and antiviral section at Canada's National Microbiology Laboratory in Winnipeg, Canada's highest-security pathogen laboratory, worked with Chinese state institutions while employed there. About four months before she and her husband Keding Cheng were escorted out by police in July 2019, she shipped Ebola and Henipavirus samples to the Wuhan Institute of Virology. She was co-inventor on Chinese government patents and co-wrote papers with a PLA major-general. They were dismissed in January 2021. Documents released in February 2024 included a CSIS (Canadian intelligence) report saying her work with China's government benefited China and that she 'repeatedly lied'. Neither has been charged.
cite: CBC News, Feb 2024; Globe and Mail, 2021 and 2024; National Post, 2021
inside: A section head at Canada's top-security laboratory worked with Chinese state bodies and sent them virus samples, work Canadian intelligence said benefited China.

n: Oil men Sinclair and Doheny bribed US Interior Secretary Albert Fall
org_label: Harry Sinclair's and Edward Doheny's oil companies
rank: Secretary of the Interior
d: Two oil executives, Harry Sinclair and Edward Doheny, paid the US Secretary of the Interior, Albert Fall, who then handed them navy oil reserves. Fall leased Teapot Dome in Wyoming to Sinclair's Mammoth Oil in 1922 and Elk Hills in California to Doheny's company, without competitive bidding. Doheny had given him a $100,000 interest-free loan in 1921, and gifts from the two men came to about $404,000. A Senate inquiry led by Senator Thomas Walsh uncovered the loan. In 1927 the Supreme Court ruled that the leases had been corruptly obtained and returned both reserves to the navy. Fall was convicted in 1929 of taking bribes from Doheny, the first US cabinet member to go to prison.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Teapot Dome scandal'; HISTORY.com, 'Cabinet member guilty in Teapot Dome scandal'
inside: Two oil executives paid the US Interior Secretary, who then leased them the navy's oil reserves without competitive bidding.

n: Lockheed paid ¥500m to PM Tanaka's office to sell jets to ANA
rank: Prime Minister's office
d: The US aircraft maker Lockheed paid about ¥2.4 billion in Japan to win an order from All Nippon Airways (ANA) for its L-1011 TriStar airliner, and about ¥500 million of it went to the office of Prime Minister Kakuei Tanaka. The fixer Yoshio Kodama received ¥1.7 billion and ANA officials ¥160 million. ANA announced the purchase of 21 TriStars in October 1972. The payments came out in February 1976, when Lockheed's vice-chairman told a US Senate subcommittee led by Frank Church that about $3 million had gone to Tanaka's office. Tanaka was arrested in July 1976. In October 1983 a Tokyo court found him guilty of foreign-exchange violations and sentenced him to four years, but he stayed free on appeal until his death in 1993.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Lockheed bribery scandals'; Britannica, 'Tanaka Kakuei'; Christian Science Monitor, 18 Nov 1981
inside: Lockheed paid about ¥500 million to the Japanese prime minister's office as part of the payments that won it All Nippon Airways' aircraft order.

n: Lockheed paid Dutch Prince Bernhard $1.1m over a fighter-jet choice
rank: Prince consort with senior military posts
d: Lockheed paid Prince Bernhard, husband of Queen Juliana of the Netherlands, a $1.1 million bribe in the early 1960s to help its F-104 Starfighter beat France's Dassault Mirage 5 in the Dutch fighter purchase. Bernhard held senior military and public posts and sat on more than 300 corporate boards and committees. The payment surfaced in December 1975, during US Senate hearings into Lockheed's foreign bribes, which were found to total $22 million. Prime Minister Joop den Uyl ordered an inquiry, and the queen threatened to abdicate if her husband was prosecuted. He was spared trial but had to give up several public positions and was barred from wearing military uniform. Interviews published after his death in 2004 showed he admitted taking the money.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Lockheed bribery scandals'; Time, 'The Prince Errant Loses His Epaulets' (1976); Expatica, 'Prince Bernhard admitted taking Lockheed bribe'
inside: Lockheed paid the Dutch prince consort, who held senior military posts, to help its fighter beat a rival in the Dutch government's jet purchase.

n: Lockheed bribes for Hercules planes led to Italian defence minister's jailing
rank: Minister of Defence
d: Lockheed was accused of paying Christian Democrat and Socialist politicians in Italy to favour the Italian Air Force's purchase of its C-130 Hercules transport planes. The magazine L'Espresso named former ministers Luigi Gui and Mario Tanassi, former Prime Minister Mariano Rumor and President Giovanni Leone. Leone resigned on 15 June 1978 under the pressure of the allegations. In 1979 the Constitutional Court, which then tried cases against ministers, convicted Tanassi, defence minister in 1970–1974, of bribery and sentenced him to four months in prison. He was the first former Italian minister to serve a prison sentence.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Lockheed bribery scandals'; Wikipedia, 'Mario Tanassi'; Corte costituzionale, sentenza penale Lockheed (1979)
inside: Lockheed paid Italian politicians to favour the air force buying its planes, and the defence minister was convicted of taking bribes.

n: Recruit gave cheap shares to Japan's PM and Diet members before flotation
rank: Prime Minister, cabinet and Diet members
d: Recruit, a Japanese recruitment-advertising and publishing company led by Hiromasa Ezoe, offered shares in its property subsidiary Recruit Cosmos to senior politicians and business leaders shortly before the shares went public in 1986. The share price then rose sharply, and recipients made about ¥66 million each on average. Seventeen members of the Diet, Japan's parliament, were involved, and another thirty were later found to have received favours from Recruit. They included Prime Minister Noboru Takeshita, former Prime Minister Yasuhiro Nakasone and Chief Cabinet Secretary Takao Fujinami, as well as opposition party leaders. The scandal broke in 1988 and forced Takeshita's cabinet to resign; his term ended on 3 June 1989.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Recruit scandal'; Wikipedia, 'Noboru Takeshita'
inside: Recruit gave cheap pre-flotation shares to the prime minister, cabinet and Diet members, and dozens more were later found to have received its favours.

n: Flick paid DM25m to West German parties while seeking a tax break
rank: Ministers of Economics
d: The Flick industrial group gave money to all the main parties in West Germany's parliament, about 25 million Deutsche Mark between 1969 and 1989, which its manager Eberhard von Brauchitsch called 'cultivation of the political landscape'. Cash-book entries listed payments to CSU leader Franz Josef Strauss and CDU leader Helmut Kohl. In 1976 Flick applied for a tax exemption on its sale of Daimler shares worth 1.9 billion DM to Deutsche Bank; economics minister Hans Friderichs approved it, and his successor Otto Graf Lambsdorff did too. The payments came to light in 1981 and Der Spiegel published them. Lambsdorff resigned in 1984. In 1987 both ministers were fined for tax evasion only, as a payment for the decision could not be proven.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Flick affair'
inside: The Flick group paid all main West German parties while seeking a tax exemption that two economics ministers granted; courts could not prove the payment bought it.

n: Siemens paid over $100m to Argentine officials for a $1bn ID-card deal
rank: two presidents and cabinet ministers
