d: The German engineering company Siemens paid more than $100 million in bribes to Argentine government officials, including two former presidents and cabinet ministers, to win and keep a $1 billion contract to produce national identity cards for every Argentine citizen. The scheme ran from about 1996 to 2007. Siemens won the contract in 1998, but it was suspended and then cancelled after a change of government. In December 2008 Siemens and its Argentine subsidiary pleaded guilty in the US to foreign-bribery offences over the contract, as part of a $1.6 billion settlement with the US and Germany covering about $1.3 billion in bribes worldwide. In December 2011 US authorities charged eight former Siemens executives over the Argentine payments.
cite: US SEC press release 2011-263, 13 Dec 2011; MercoPress, 13 Dec 2011; Wikipedia, 'Siemens'
inside: Siemens paid Argentine presidents and ministers more than $100 million so the state would give and keep its national ID-card contract.

n: KBR consortium paid $180m to Nigerian officials for gas plant contracts
rank: executive branch, NNPC and Nigeria LNG officials
d: A joint venture led by KBR, the engineering firm then owned by Halliburton, paid about $180 million in bribes to Nigerian officials between 1994 and 2004 to win four contracts to build the Bonny Island liquefied natural gas plant, business worth more than $6 billion. The money went through consultants: one received over $130 million to pay high-level executive branch officials, and another over $50 million for lower-level officials, including staff of the state oil company NNPC and the government-controlled Nigeria LNG. KBR pleaded guilty in the US on 11 February 2009, and with Halliburton paid $579 million in combined penalties. KBR's former chief executive Albert 'Jack' Stanley had pleaded guilty in 2008.
cite: A&O Shearman FCPA database, 'US v. Kellogg Brown & Root' and 'SEC v. Halliburton and KBR'; Government Executive, Feb 2009
inside: A KBR-led venture paid Nigerian government and state oil company officials about $180 million to win the contracts for a state gas plant.

n: Unaoil paid Iraqi oil ministry officials $17m for $1.7bn of contracts
rank: Ministry of Oil and South Oil Company officials
d: Unaoil, a Monaco-based firm that acted as a fixer for foreign oil-service companies, paid more than $17 million in bribes to officials at Iraq's Ministry of Oil and the state-owned South Oil Company to secure about $1.7 billion in contracts after the 2003 occupation. The contracts, for oil pipelines and offshore mooring buoys in the Gulf, were part of the ministry's plan to rebuild Iraq's oil export capacity. The UK Serious Fraud Office prosecuted. In July 2020 a jury convicted Ziad Akle, Unaoil's Iraq territory manager, and Stephen Whiteley, sentenced to five and three years. Unaoil's Iraq partner Basil Al Jarah, who had pleaded guilty in 2019, was jailed for three years and four months in October 2020.
cite: UK Serious Fraud Office, 8 Oct 2020 and July 2020 releases; OCCRP, July 2020
inside: Unaoil paid officials of Iraq's oil ministry and state oil company more than $17 million so they would award its clients oil contracts.

n: Elf Aquitaine's secret funds paid French parties and African contacts
rank: political parties (RPR)
d: Executives of the French state oil company Elf Aquitaine used secret company funds to buy political favour in France and Africa, along with spending on themselves. Elf acted as an unofficial arm of French policy in Africa, and its Africa specialist André Tarallo was close to Gabon's President Omar Bongo. Former chairman Loïk Le Floch-Prigent admitted secretly funding political parties and named Jacques Chirac's RPR as the main beneficiary. The scandal came to light in 1994 and was investigated by magistrate Eva Joly. On 12 November 2003 a Paris court sentenced Le Floch-Prigent and his deputy Alfred Sirven to five years in jail each and Tarallo to four, in a $350 million embezzlement case with 37 defendants.
cite: Al Jazeera, 12 Nov 2003; Transparency International, 'The Elf trial: a victory over impunity'; Wikipedia, 'Elf Aquitaine'
inside: Executives of the oil company Elf used secret company funds to buy political favour, with Chirac's RPR party named as the main recipient.

n: Gürtel: Correa's firms paid Spain's ruling party for regional contracts
rank: People's Party and PP-run regional governments
d: A network of businesses led by Francisco Correa paid kickbacks to officials of Spain's People's Party (PP) in return for public contracts from PP-run local and regional governments, including in Valencia and the Community of Madrid. On 24 May 2018 Spain's National Court (Audiencia Nacional) convicted 29 of 37 defendants: Correa received 51 years and former PP treasurer Luis Bárcenas 33 years and a €44 million fine. The court found that the PP itself had taken part in the kickback scheme since 1989. A week later, on 1 June 2018, Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy was removed by a parliamentary vote of no confidence.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Gürtel case'
inside: Correa's business network paid Spain's ruling party and its officials kickbacks so party-run governments would give his firms public contracts.

n: Mani pulite: companies' kickbacks to Italy's ruling parties for contracts
rank: governing parties and Parliament
d: Italian and foreign companies paid kickbacks, known as tangenti, to Italy's governing parties to win public works contracts; the bribes were estimated at $4 billion a year in the 1980s. Milan prosecutors uncovered the system in the 'Mani pulite' (clean hands) inquiry, which began with the arrest of Socialist official Mario Chiesa on 17 February 1992. At one point more than half the members of the Italian Parliament were under indictment, and over 400 councils were dissolved. Socialist leader Bettino Craxi admitted his party had received $93 million in illegal funds; he was convicted twice and fled to Tunisia in 1994. The Christian Democrats and Socialists, who had governed for decades, dissolved.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Mani pulite'
inside: Companies paid Italy's governing parties kickbacks for decades so that public works contracts went to them.

n: Lobbyist Abramoff bought favours from Congressman Ney and officials
rank: House Administration Committee chair
d: Jack Abramoff, a Washington lobbyist who charged Native American tribes with casinos an estimated $85 million, gave trips, meals, event tickets and campaign money to officials in return for official favours. Representative Bob Ney, chair of the House Administration Committee, put statements into the Congressional Record to help Abramoff's SunCruz casino deal and pursued legislation to reopen a casino for the Tigua tribe. Abramoff pleaded guilty to conspiracy, fraud and tax evasion on 3 January 2006 and was sentenced to four years in 2008. Ney pleaded guilty in October 2006 and got 30 months. Former deputy interior secretary Steven Griles and more than a dozen congressional aides and officials were also convicted or pleaded guilty.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Jack Abramoff Indian lobbying scandal'; Wikipedia, 'Bob Ney'; Fox News/AP, 'People caught up in the Abramoff corruption probe'
inside: Lobbyist Abramoff gave a congressman and officials trips, money and favours, and the congressman then used his office to push Abramoff's clients' deals.

n: Defence contractors paid Congressman Cunningham $2.4m for earmarks
rank: House Defence Appropriations Subcommittee member
d: Two defence contractors, Mitchell Wade of MZM and Brent Wilkes of ADCS, gave US Congressman Randy 'Duke' Cunningham about $2.4 million in cash and benefits to steer Pentagon money to their companies. Cunningham sat on the House Defence Appropriations Subcommittee, which sets military spending, and slipped earmarks, spending lines reserved for a named purpose, into bills that led to contracts for Wilkes's firms. Wade provided a yacht and other perks tied to about $150 million in contracts, and Wilkes received nearly $90 million in defence work. Cunningham pleaded guilty and was sentenced to seven years for bribery and tax evasion. Wade pleaded guilty in February 2006, and Wilkes was sentenced to 12 years in 2008.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Cunningham scandal'; NPR, 4 June 2013; NBC News, 'Defense contractor gets 12 years in bribery case' (Feb 2008)
inside: Two defence contractors paid a congressman on the defence spending committee, who then wrote spending lines that sent Pentagon contracts to their firms.

n: Air Force buyer Druyun took a Boeing job while handling Boeing deals
rank: Air Force principal deputy for acquisition
d: Boeing hired Darleen Druyun, the US Air Force's senior civilian acquisition official, who had been handling Boeing business, including a plan to lease 100 Boeing KC-767 refuelling tankers. Acquisition is the office that buys the Air Force's aircraft and weapons. Druyun joined Boeing in 2003 at $250,000 a year with a $50,000 signing bonus. She pleaded guilty to a felony in 2004 and was sentenced in October 2004 to nine months in prison. Boeing fired its chief financial officer Michael Sears, who was sentenced to four months in February 2005, and Boeing paid $615 million in fines. The tanker plan, revised in 2003 to 20 leased and 80 bought planes, was put under investigation.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Darleen Druyun'; Government Executive, Oct 2004
inside: Boeing recruited the Air Force's senior buyer with a well-paid job while she was handling Boeing's tanker deal, a conflict she pleaded guilty over.

n: Keating Five: S&L owner's senators pressed US bank regulators
rank: five US senators
d: Charles Keating, chairman of Lincoln Savings and Loan, gave about $1.3 million in political contributions to five US senators, who then pressed federal regulators on his behalf. In April 1987 Senators Alan Cranston, Dennis DeConcini, John Glenn, John McCain and Donald Riegle met Edwin Gray, chair of the Federal Home Loan Bank Board, which supervised savings banks, and later San Francisco regulators, seeking a lenient outcome in the investigation of Lincoln. The regulators backed off. Lincoln collapsed in 1989, costing the federal government $3.4 billion and leaving about 23,000 bondholders with worthless investments. In 1991 the Senate Ethics Committee reprimanded Cranston and criticised the other four.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Keating Five'
inside: A savings bank owner gave five senators $1.3 million, and they pressed the bank regulators investigating his firm, who then backed off.

n: Oil firms' gifts and favours inside the US drilling regulator MMS
rank: Minerals Management Service officials
d: Oil and gas companies got close enough to officials of the Minerals Management Service (MMS), the US agency that leased offshore drilling areas, collected oil royalties and inspected rigs, that staff took gifts, holidays and favours from them. In September 2008 the Interior Department's inspector general, Earl Devaney, reported that more than a dozen MMS officials had engaged in unethical and criminal conduct, including drug use and sex with energy company representatives, in 'a culture of ethical failure'. A May 2010 report found that Gulf region inspectors had let industry officials fill in inspection reports themselves. After the Deepwater Horizon oil spill, Interior Secretary Ken Salazar ordered MMS split into three agencies in May 2010.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Minerals Management Service' (citing Interior Inspector General reports, Sept 2008 and May 2010)
inside: Oil and gas companies gave staff of the US drilling regulator gifts and favours, and its inspectors let industry fill in their own inspection reports.

n: Bofors paid kickbacks in India's 1986 howitzer deal
rank: politicians and defence officials
d: The Swedish arms maker Bofors paid kickbacks to win a contract signed on 24 March 1986 to supply India's army with 410 155mm field howitzers. Swedish Radio reported the payments on 16 April 1987, based on a leak from Swedish police investigator Sten Lindström, and Chitra Subramaniam of The Hindu then obtained over 350 documents. Payments to Indian politicians and defence officials were put at about ₹640 million. India's Central Bureau of Investigation named the Italian middleman Ottavio Quattrocchi, arms agent Win Chadha and the late Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi in a 1999 charge sheet. The Delhi High Court quashed the charges against Gandhi in 2004 and no one was finally convicted. The scandal contributed to Congress's defeat in the 1989 election.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Bofors scandal'
inside: Bofors paid kickbacks to Indian politicians and defence officials to win the army's howitzer contract, investigators found, though no one was finally convicted.

n: Kazakhgate: US adviser charged with paying Nazarbayev for oil deals
rank: President and Prime Minister
d: James Giffen, an American businessman who advised Kazakhstan's President Nursultan Nazarbayev, was charged by US prosecutors in 2003 with paying bribes to Nazarbayev and former Prime Minister Nurlan Balgimbayev to win oil contracts, including in the Tengiz field, for Western companies in the 1990s. Prosecutors alleged he moved $20 million through Swiss bank accounts. A former Mobil executive, J. Bryan Williams, was charged with tax evasion over kickbacks from Mobil's Kazakh business. In August 2010 Giffen pleaded guilty only to a tax misdemeanour and his company Mercator pleaded guilty to a foreign-bribery offence; the other charges were dropped and in November 2010 the judge gave him no prison term or fine.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Kazakhgate'
inside: An American adviser to Kazakhstan's president was charged with paying the president and prime minister so Western firms got oil contracts; his company admitted foreign bribery.

n: Denis O'Brien paid Irish minister Lowry, who delivered a mobile licence
rank: communications minister
d: An official tribunal found that Irish businessman Denis O'Brien made payments to Michael Lowry, the minister responsible for communications, who 'not only influenced, but delivered the result' of the 1995 competition for Ireland's second mobile phone licence to O'Brien's consortium, Esat Digifone. The licence was awarded in May 1996. The Moriarty Tribunal's final report in March 2011 found two payments from O'Brien to Lowry, in 1996 and 1999, and support for a £420,000 loan, which it treated as a benefit. It said Lowry bypassed his cabinet colleagues and gave O'Brien valuable information, a 'cynical and venal abuse of office'. O'Brien rejected the findings, and the tribunal judge later admitted some mistakes.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Moriarty Tribunal' (final report, March 2011)
inside: Businessman O'Brien made payments to Ireland's communications minister, who an official tribunal found delivered the national mobile licence to O'Brien's consortium.

n: Harrods owner Al-Fayed paid British MPs to table questions
rank: Conservative MPs
d: Mohamed Al-Fayed, owner of the London department store Harrods, paid Conservative MPs to ask questions in the House of Commons on his behalf. The Guardian reported in October 1994 that the lobbyist Ian Greer had paid MPs Neil Hamilton and Tim Smith about £2,000 each to table questions for Al-Fayed. Smith admitted taking payments from Al-Fayed directly and resigned his government post. In July 1997 the parliamentary standards commissioner, Sir Gordon Downey, called the evidence of cash payments to Hamilton 'compelling', and a Commons committee found Smith had taken £18,000 to £25,000. The affair led Prime Minister John Major to set up the Committee on Standards in Public Life. Hamilton lost his seat in 1997.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Cash-for-questions affair'
inside: Harrods' owner paid Conservative MPs to table questions in the House of Commons on his behalf.

n: Holyland developers bribed Jerusalem's mayors, including Ehud Olmert
rank: Mayor of Jerusalem
d: Developers of Holyland, a large housing project in Jerusalem, bribed city officials to get planning approvals, including two mayors: Ehud Olmert, who later became Israel's prime minister, and his successor Uri Lupolianski. On 31 March 2014 a Tel Aviv court convicted 10 of 13 defendants. Olmert was convicted of receiving NIS 560,000 in bribes, acquitted of two other bribery charges, and given a prison term and a NIS 1 million fine. Developer Hillel Charney was convicted of bribing Olmert, his aide Shula Zaken and Lupolianski, and was sentenced to three and a half years. Lupolianski was convicted of accepting bribes totalling more than NIS 2 million.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Holyland Case'
inside: Developers paid Jerusalem's mayors and officials bribes so the city would approve their Holyland housing project.

n: Tycoon Truong My Lan secretly controlled Saigon Commercial Bank
rank: owner and lender of Saigon Commercial Bank
d: Truong My Lan, chair of the Vietnamese property group Van Thinh Phat, secretly controlled Saigon Joint Stock Commercial Bank (SCB) from 2012 to 2022 through more than two dozen middlemen who held its shares for her. She owned over 90 percent of the bank, and 93 percent of its loans reportedly went to her company and to shell companies. Prosecutors said she used 916 fake loan applications to take more than 304 trillion dong (US$12.5 billion) from the bank between February 2018 and October 2022, and the case caused a run on SCB. On 11 April 2024 a court sentenced her to death for embezzlement, in a first trial of 85 defendants.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Truong My Lan'
inside: A property tycoon secretly owned and ran a Vietnamese bank through middlemen and used it to lend billions to her own companies.

n: Viet A paid officials $35m to sell overpriced Covid tests to the state
rank: Health Minister and Hanoi mayor
d: Viet A Technology, a Vietnamese company, admitted bribing officials with more than US$35 million in total so that they would buy its Covid-19 test kits. Between September and December 2021 it imported rapid tests from China at about US$0.96 each, marketed them as Vietnamese-made and sold them to local officials for about US$20.75. The scandal became public in December 2021. By June 2022 dozens of officials had been arrested and charged, including Health Minister Nguyen Thanh Long and Hanoi's mayor Chu Ngoc Anh, both of whom were expelled from the Communist Party and dismissed. In January 2023 the National Assembly removed two deputy prime ministers and President Nguyen Xuan Phuc resigned.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Viet A scandal'
inside: Viet A paid health officials, including the minister, more than $35 million so the state would buy its overpriced Covid test kits.

n: e-KTP contractors paid Indonesia's House Speaker Setya Novanto
rank: Speaker of the House of Representatives
d: Members of the business consortium that won Indonesia's tender for electronic identity cards, known as e-KTP, paid Setya Novanto, Speaker of the House of Representatives, while the project's budget and tender went through parliament. Prosecutors said he received Rp 300 billion and a $135,000 wristwatch. The Corruption Eradication Commission (KPK) named him a suspect in July 2017 in a Rp 2.3 trillion corruption case, and he resigned as Speaker after his arrest. On 24 April 2018 the Jakarta Corruption Court sentenced him to 15 years in prison, finding corruption in the budgeting and tender processes from 2011 to 2013, and barred him from public office for five years after his sentence ends.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Setya Novanto'
inside: Members of the consortium that won Indonesia's ID-card tender paid the House Speaker while the project's budget and tender went through parliament.

n: Napoles' fake NGOs drew Philippine lawmakers' pork-barrel funds
rank: Senators and members of Congress
d: Businesswoman Janet Lim-Napoles was accused of arranging for members of the Philippine Congress to send money from their Priority Development Assistance Fund, known as 'pork barrel', to fake foundations run by her JLN Group, which carried out no projects. The Philippine Daily Inquirer exposed the scheme in July 2013, and losses were estimated at about ₱10 billion. Plunder charges were filed against Napoles and Senators Juan Ponce Enrile, Jinggoy Estrada and Ramon 'Bong' Revilla. In November 2013 the Supreme Court declared the fund unconstitutional. In 2024 Napoles was convicted on seven counts of corruption of public officials, while Estrada and Enrile were eventually acquitted.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Priority Development Assistance Fund scam'
inside: Napoles arranged for lawmakers to send their public development funds to her fake foundations, which did no work.

n: Gold trader Zarrab accused of bribing Turkish ministers and Halkbank's chief
rank: ministers and Halkbank general manager
d: Reza Zarrab, an Iranian-born gold trader, was accused by Turkish prosecutors in December 2013 of paying bribes to cabinet ministers and to the general manager of the state-owned Halkbank to run a scheme that moved gold and money to Iran through the bank, around international sanctions. Police reported finding US$4.5 million in shoeboxes at the home of Halkbank's Süleyman Aslan, and the indictment alleged that Economy Minister Zafer Çağlayan received $52 million. Çağlayan resigned on 25 December 2013. Zarrab was freed after 70 days, and in January 2015 parliament declined to lift the ministers' immunity, ending the case. Zarrab later took a plea deal in the US and testified against a Halkbank deputy chief executive.
cite: Wikipedia, '2013 corruption scandal in Turkey'; Wikipedia, 'Reza Zarrab'
inside: Gold trader Zarrab is accused of paying Turkish ministers and the state bank's chief so the bank would move money to Iran around sanctions.

n: Gorilla file: Penta partner recorded discussing kickbacks with ministers
rank: Deputy Prime Minister and officials
d: A leaked file called 'Gorila', said to be drawn from a 2005–2006 wiretap by the Slovak Information Service of a Bratislava flat, reportedly records officials, politicians and executives of Penta Group, one of Slovakia's two biggest investment companies, discussing kickbacks for privatisation and procurement contracts. Penta partner Jaroslav Haščák allegedly spoke there with Deputy Prime Minister Jirko Malchárek, and Robert Fico and others are also named. The file appeared online on 21 December 2011. Penta called it fiction, its accuracy has not been officially confirmed and no convictions followed, but in January 2012 a court confirmed it had authorised the wiretaps, and 'Protest Gorila' rallies shaped the 2012 election.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Gorilla scandal'
inside: A leaked wiretap file reportedly records a partner of Penta Group discussing kickbacks for privatisation and state contracts with Slovakia's deputy prime minister; Penta calls it fiction.

n: Agusta and Dassault bribe forced NATO chief Willy Claes to resign
rank: Minister of Economic Affairs
d: The Italian helicopter maker Agusta and the French aircraft maker Dassault were linked to a bribe of over 50 million Belgian francs accepted while Willy Claes was Belgium's economy minister, during negotiations on defence contracts with the two companies. The bribe came to light during the investigation into the murder of former deputy prime minister André Cools. Claes had become Secretary General of NATO in 1994 and resigned on 20 October 1995. The Court of Cassation, which tries ministers, convicted him; he received a three-year suspended sentence, a fine and a five-year ban on standing for office, and the European Court of Human Rights upheld the sentence.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Willy Claes'
inside: The arms makers Agusta and Dassault were linked to a bribe taken by Belgium's economy minister during his negotiations on their defence contracts.

n: Construction firms paid kickbacks to Laval and Montreal city halls
rank: mayors and city parties
d: Construction and engineering firms in Quebec formed a bid-rigging cartel and paid city politicians to win public works contracts. At the Charbonneau Commission, a public inquiry set up in 2011, a former construction boss testified that for years 3 percent of the value of his Montreal contracts went to the mayor's party and 1 percent to a city official. Montreal mayor Gérald Tremblay resigned in November 2012, and interim mayor Michael Applebaum was convicted on eight corruption-related charges in 2017. Gilles Vaillancourt, mayor of Laval from 1989 to 2012, pleaded guilty in December 2016 to fraud, breach of trust and conspiracy over city construction contracts from 1996 to 2010, and was jailed for six years.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Charbonneau Commission'; Wikipedia, 'Gilles Vaillancourt'
inside: Quebec construction firms paid city mayors' parties and officials a share of contract values so the cities kept giving them public works.

n: Brazil's meatpackers paid farm ministry inspectors to pass unfit meat
rank: Agriculture Ministry inspection service
d: Brazilian meatpacking companies, chiefly JBS and BRF, were accused by the Federal Police in March 2017 of paying officials of the Ministry of Agriculture's inspection service to approve unfit meat. Prosecutors said the bribes bought adulterated quality certificates. A 2018 offshoot, Operation Trapaca, led to the arrest of BRF's former president and a former vice-president. The federal court at Curitiba has since passed at least seven sentences on the scheme: one convicted seven people and acquitted five, and ordered the convicted officials to lose their posts; a later one convicted six more. BRF's production director was acquitted of active corruption. In December 2022 BRF agreed to pay the state 583,977,360.48 reais, of which 259,928,388.50 is the fine under the Clean Company Act.
cite: Tribunal Regional Federal da 4a Regiao, reports of the sentences of the 14th Federal Court of Curitiba in Operation Carne Fraca - 29 July 2020, seven convicted and five acquitted with loss of office, the sixth sentence in the operation, and a later sentence convicting six, acquitting one and declaring one punishability extinguished; Estado de S. Paulo, 28 April 2017, carried by Terra and Exame, on an earlier sentence and the acquittal of BRF's production director of active corruption; and the Acordos de Leniencia dataset of Brazil's Portal da Transparencia, process 00190.109990/2018-98, for the BRF agreement of 28 December 2022 and its figures
inside: Meatpackers including JBS and BRF are accused of paying Brazil's farm ministry inspectors to approve unfit meat.

n: Fishing firm Corpesca paid Chilean senator Orpis over the fishing law
rank: Senator
d: The fishing company Corpesca paid Jaime Orpis, a senator of Chile's UDI party, 230 million pesos in exchange, prosecutors said, for favourable votes on fishing quota legislation. The 2012 fisheries law, promoted by minister Pablo Longueira, allocated a large share of Chile's national fishing quota to companies controlled by a few families on an indefinite basis. The citizens' group Fundación Ciudadano Inteligente filed a bribery complaint in 2015. Orpis lost his parliamentary immunity in January 2016 and left the UDI. In April 2021 a court sentenced him to prison for bribery and fraud against the Treasury, and an appeals court upheld the sentence in January 2022.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Corpesca case'; Wikipedia, 'Jaime Orpis'; Radio Universidad de Chile, 16 Apr 2021; Radio Cooperativa, 6 Jan 2022
inside: The fishing company Corpesca paid a Chilean senator, who voted its way on the law handing out the national fishing quota.

n: Coal lobbyist Andrew Wheeler became head of the US EPA
rank: EPA Administrator
d: Andrew Wheeler, who lobbied for the coal producer Murray Energy from 2009 to 2017, moved into the leadership of the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), which regulates pollution from coal mining and coal-fired power plants. Murray was his best-paying client and lobbied against Obama-era climate rules for power plants; in March 2017 Wheeler arranged a meeting between Robert Murray and Energy Secretary Rick Perry at which Murray pressed for rollbacks. Wheeler was confirmed as EPA deputy administrator in April 2018, became acting head when Scott Pruitt resigned in July 2018, and was confirmed as administrator in February 2019. In April 2020 the EPA weakened mercury regulation by narrowing the health benefits counted in rule-making.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Andrew R. Wheeler'
inside: A coal company's lobbyist moved into the leadership of the agency that regulates coal pollution, which then weakened the mercury rules his former client opposed.

n: Oil and water lobbyist David Bernhardt became US Interior Secretary
org_label: Westlands Water District and oil-industry clients
rank: Secretary of the Interior
d: David Bernhardt, a lawyer and lobbyist whose clients included the Westlands Water District, a large California farm-water supplier, the oil-sector firms Halliburton, Cobalt International Energy and Samson Resources, and the Independent Petroleum Association of America (IPAA), moved into the leadership of the US Interior Department, which manages federal land, water and drilling leases. He became deputy secretary in August 2017, acting secretary in January 2019 and secretary in April 2019. He had said he would not involve himself in former clients' matters unless authorised. During his tenure Interior substantially increased fossil fuel sales on public land and cut regulation, and in 2019 Politico reported IPAA leaders celebrating their ties to him.
cite: Wikipedia, 'David Bernhardt'
inside: A lobbyist for oil firms and a water district moved into the leadership of the Interior Department, which then increased fossil fuel sales and cut regulation.

n: Monsanto's lawyer and executive Michael Taylor held top US food posts
rank: FDA Deputy Commissioner
d: Michael Taylor moved several times between US food regulators and the side of the biotech company Monsanto. From 1981 to 1991 he worked at the law firm King & Spalding, which represented Monsanto. As the Food and Drug Administration's deputy commissioner for policy from 1991 to 1994 he oversaw biotechnology policy, including 1992 guidance on genetically modified foods and guidance that milk from cows treated with bovine growth hormone, a Monsanto product, need not be labelled. He was Monsanto's vice-president for public policy from 1998 to 2000, and the FDA's deputy commissioner for foods from January 2010 to 2016. US government reviewers found he had complied with his recusal agreement on the hormone approval.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Michael R. Taylor'
inside: A lawyer on Monsanto's side moved into the US food regulator, where he oversaw guidance that milk from cows given Monsanto's hormone need not be labelled.

n: Ex-Verizon lawyer Ajit Pai chaired the FCC and repealed net neutrality
rank: Chairman of the Federal Communications Commission
d: Ajit Pai, associate general counsel at the telecoms company Verizon from 2001 to 2003, chaired the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), the US regulator of telephone, broadband and broadcasting companies, from January 2017 to January 2021. On 14 December 2017 the FCC under his leadership voted to stop regulating internet service providers under Title II of the Communications Act, ending the 'net neutrality' rules that barred providers such as Verizon from blocking or slowing traffic or selling priority. Broadband companies had fought the rules since they were adopted in 2015. The decision changed how internet access is regulated across the United States.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Ajit Pai'
inside: A former Verizon lawyer took charge of the regulator of telecoms companies and ended the net neutrality rules that Verizon and its industry had fought.

n: Alcatel accused of paying Costa Rica's president for a phone contract
rank: President
d: Prosecutors in Costa Rica alleged that the French telecoms company Alcatel paid more than US$800,000 to Miguel Ángel Rodríguez while he was president, in return for help winning a government contract to supply 400,000 mobile phone lines. Rodríguez had been elected Secretary General of the Organization of American States (OAS) in 2004 and stepped down in October 2004, about a month into the job, after a former political associate accused him. In April 2011 a Costa Rican court sentenced him to five years in prison, but in December 2012 an appeals court acquitted him, citing problems with the main witness, who had immunity and changed his account several times. Rodríguez denied wrongdoing throughout.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Miguel Ángel Rodríguez'
inside: Costa Rican prosecutors said Alcatel paid the sitting president to help it win a state phone contract; an appeals court later acquitted him.

n: Businessmen paid Politburo member Bo Xilai and his family
org_label: Businessmen Xu Ming and Tang Xiaolin
rank: Politburo member and Chongqing party chief
d: Two Chinese businessmen, Xu Ming and Tang Xiaolin, gave Bo Xilai and his family money and benefits worth about 21.79 million yuan (US$3.56 million), prosecutors said. Bo had been Minister of Commerce from 2004 to 2007 and was Communist Party secretary of Chongqing and a member of the Politburo, the party's top leadership body, from 2007 to 2012. At trial Xu said he gave Bo's wife Gu Kailai $3.23 million in 2000 to buy a villa in Nice, and paid for their son's travel and credit card bills. On 22 September 2013 a court in Jinan found Bo guilty on all counts, including bribery, and sentenced him to life imprisonment.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Bo Xilai'
inside: Two businessmen gave a Politburo member and former commerce minister and his family millions in money and benefits, which a court ruled were bribes.

n: Drug firms bribed the head of China's drug regulator, Zheng Xiaoyu
rank: head of the State Food and Drug Administration
d: Eight pharmaceutical companies paid Zheng Xiaoyu, head of China's drug regulator, more than 6.49 million yuan (about US$850,000) in bribes, and in return he personally approved unproven and unsafe medicines. Zheng led the State Drug Administration from 1998 and its successor, the State Food and Drug Administration, from 2003 to 2005. Over eight years he ordered approval of more than 150,000 new medicines, most of them from the companies that had paid him. One unsafe drug killed 14 people, and his approvals were linked to cough syrup that killed more than 800 people in Panama. He was convicted of bribery and dereliction of duty, sentenced to death on 29 May 2007 and executed on 10 July 2007.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Zheng Xiaoyu'
inside: Eight drug companies paid the head of China's drug regulator, who in return approved their unproven and unsafe medicines.

n: Railway minister Liu Zhijun took bribes while building China's fast rail
rank: Minister of Railways
d: Liu Zhijun, China's Minister of Railways from 2003 until his dismissal in February 2011, took more than 64 million yuan in bribes, according to the charges brought in April 2013, while overseeing the fast expansion of the country's high-speed rail network. Ding Shumiao, a Shanxi business magnate whose Boyou investment group gained greatly from high-speed rail construction, was linked to his fall. State media said the ministry had illegitimate business ties with large companies and used illegal subcontracting. In July 2013 Liu was convicted and sentenced to death with a two-year reprieve, a sentence commuted to life imprisonment in December 2015.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Liu Zhijun'
inside: China's railway minister was convicted of taking more than 64 million yuan in bribes while overseeing rail building, with a businessman who profited from the contracts linked to his fall.

n: Hanbo Steel bribed politicians and bankers for loans in South Korea
rank: Home Minister, presidential aides and state-influenced bank chiefs
d: Hanbo, a small South Korean steelmaker that began building a huge plant in 1992, got bank loans by bribing politicians and bankers, who pressed banks to lend to it. Hanbo went into receivership on 28 January 1997 with losses estimated at US$6 billion. In June 1997 a court found that it had received illegal preferential treatment from President Kim Young-sam's government, mainly through these loans. Founder Chung Tae-soo was sentenced to 15 years. Those convicted included former Home Minister Kim Woo-suk, presidential aides, lawmakers and two former presidents of Korea First Bank, and the president's son Kim Hyun-chul was sentenced to three years in a related case. The collapse added to the country's economic troubles that year.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Hanbo scandal'
inside: Hanbo Steel paid politicians, presidential aides and bankers, who then pressed banks to give it loans.

n: Samsung paid legal fees for ex-president Lee Myung-bak's family firm
rank: President
d: South Korean courts convicted former President Lee Myung-bak of taking bribes from Samsung, the country's largest business group, in the form of nearly $6 million in legal fees paid for DAS, a car-parts maker owned by Lee's brother, according to prosecutors. They said the money was meant to win a presidential pardon for Samsung chairman Lee Kun-hee, who had been convicted of tax evasion and stock fraud. On 5 October 2018 Lee was convicted of bribery, embezzlement and abuse of power and sentenced to 15 years; an appeals court raised it to 17 years and the Supreme Court upheld that on 29 October 2020. President Yoon Suk-yeol pardoned him in December 2022. Samsung and Lee denied the charges.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Lee Myung-bak'
inside: Samsung paid legal fees for the South Korean president's family firm, money courts found was meant to win a pardon for Samsung's chairman.

n: Businesses paid Taiwan's President Chen Shui-bian and his wife
rank: President
d: Taiwanese business owners paid former President Chen Shui-bian and his wife Wu Shu-chen in connection with government decisions, including millions from the owners of a company after the government bought its land at Longtan for a science park. Chen was president from 2000 to 2008. On 11 September 2009 the Taipei District Court sentenced him to life in prison and a NT$200 million fine for embezzlement, bribery and money laundering involving about US$15 million during his presidency, and found that the couple had amassed NT$800 million. In June 2010 the High Court reduced the sentence to 20 years. He was the first Taiwanese president imprisoned; his supporters called the case political.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Chen Shui-bian'
inside: Taiwanese business owners paid the president and his wife in connection with government decisions, including after the state bought one company's land.

n: Sagawa Kyubin payments reached LDP vice-president Shin Kanemaru
rank: Vice President of the Liberal Democratic Party
d: Shin Kanemaru, vice-president of Japan's governing Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) and a former deputy prime minister, was indicted in the 1992 Sagawa Kyubin scandal over payments from the parcel delivery company and from construction companies seeking political influence. Kanemaru, a senior figure in Noboru Takeshita's faction, resigned and was arrested on 13 March 1993 on charges of evading taxes on those payments. Investigators reported finding at least $51 million in bearer bonds and hundreds of pounds of gold at his home. He died in March 1996.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Shin Kanemaru'
inside: A parcel delivery company and construction firms seeking political influence made payments to the governing party's vice-president, a former deputy prime minister.

n: SNC-Lavalin paid C$47.7m to Libyan officials linked to Saadi Gaddafi
rank: officials linked to the ruling Gaddafi family
d: The Canadian engineering company SNC-Lavalin paid about C$47.7 million in bribes between 2001 and 2011 to Libyan officials linked to Saadi Gaddafi, a son of Libya's ruler Muammar Gaddafi, and defrauded Libyan organisations of about C$130 million. The money went through two companies whose sole beneficial owner was Riadh Ben Aissa, a former SNC-Lavalin executive. The prosecution in Canada led to the 2019 political crisis in which Prime Minister Justin Trudeau's office pressed the attorney general to offer the company a deferred prosecution agreement. In December 2019 SNC-Lavalin Construction pleaded guilty to fraud and was fined C$280 million.
cite: Wikipedia, 'SNC-Lavalin affair'
inside: SNC-Lavalin paid about C$47.7 million in bribes to Libyan officials tied to the ruling Gaddafi family, a court case it pleaded guilty in.

n: BAE paid £115m in commissions to win South Africa's arms deal
rank: arms-deal bid evaluators (alleged)
d: BAE Systems, the British arms maker, paid about £115 million in commissions to advisers to help win contracts in South Africa's 1999 arms package, valued at R29.992 billion at signing, the UK Serious Fraud Office found. One adviser, Fana Hlongwane, received over R100 million from BAE, which the SFO said was for corrupt ends, and South Africa's Scorpions investigators found 'at the very least a reasonable suspicion' that he used money to reward officials who evaluated the bids. BAE denied paying bribes. The government's Seriti Commission found no corruption in 2016, but in August 2019 the High Court set its findings aside for failing to pursue relevant evidence.
cite: Wikipedia, 'South African Arms Deal'
inside: BAE paid an adviser over R100 million that the UK found was for corrupt ends, and South African investigators suspected he used it to reward officials judging the bids.

n: Angolagate: arms dealers' money reached French political figures
rank: senator and former minister; president's son
d: Arms dealers Pierre Falcone and Arcadi Gaydamak, who sold $633 million of weapons to Angola's government by late 1994, paid French political figures to promote their interests, a Paris court found in 2009. Jean-Christophe Mitterrand, son of former president François Mitterrand, was found guilty of receiving $2 million and given a suspended sentence, and former interior minister Charles Pasqua was convicted of taking money from the two men. In all 36 people were convicted, and Falcone and Gaydamak got six years. On 29 April 2011 the Paris Court of Appeal overturned the convictions of Pasqua and his aide Jean-Charles Marchiani and dropped charges against the dealers, accepting that they had acted under an Angolan state mandate.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Angolagate'
inside: Arms dealers selling weapons to Angola paid French political figures, including a former minister and the president's son, to promote their interests; some convictions were overturned.

n: Ex-deputy mayor gave Kansai Electric bosses ¥320m for contracts
rank: Kansai Electric Power executives
d: Eiji Moriyama, a former deputy mayor of Takahama, the town that hosts one of Kansai Electric Power's nuclear plants, gave cash and gifts worth about ¥320 million to executives of the utility, which awarded contracts to local firms including Yoshida Kaihatsu, a company linked to him. Kansai Electric, known as Kanden, supplies electricity to the Osaka, Kyoto and Kobe region and runs nuclear plants in Fukui Prefecture. Investigations found more than 380 cases of gifts. The scandal broke in 2019; chairman Makoto Yagi resigned that year and president Shigeki Iwane in 2020.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Kansai Electric Power Company'
inside: A local power broker gave Kansai Electric's executives cash and gifts, and the utility gave contracts to local firms including one linked to him.

n: S. Alam Group took control of Islami Bank and other Bangladeshi banks
rank: board and management of Islami Bank Bangladesh
d: S. Alam Group, a Bangladeshi conglomerate founded by Mohammed Saiful Alam, took over Islami Bank Bangladesh in 2017 under the Awami League government, installing a new chairman and remaking the bank's board, management and hiring. It also came to control First Security Islami Bank, Union Bank and Global Islami Bank, and bought half of Social Islami Bank through 19 subsidiaries, beyond the 5 percent limit in banking law. Media reported that the group took Tk 300 billion in loans from Islami Bank, which the bank denied, and Islami Bank needed Tk 80 billion of emergency central bank money in January 2023. After the government fell in August 2024 the interim government opened investigations; the group denies wrongdoing.
cite: Wikipedia, 'S. Alam Group'
inside: S. Alam Group installed its own chairman, board and managers inside Islami Bank and other banks, beyond legal limits, and is reported to have drawn huge loans from them.

n: Penta group funded Chilean UDI politicians through fake invoices
rank: UDI party politicians
d: Grupo Penta, a Chilean holding company, used fake invoices, with help from employees of the tax service (SII), to pass money to the campaigns of politicians, mainly from the right-wing UDI party. Penta's directors Carlos Alberto Délano and Carlos Eugenio Lavín were charged in March 2015; they were fined, spent a few days in prison and were ordered to attend ethics classes. Former UDI president Jovino Novoa received a three-year suspended sentence in December 2015 for tax crimes, and SII employees Iván Álvarez and Sergio Díaz were given prison terms, fines and asset forfeitures. Several Penta employees and relatives were convicted of tax evasion, bribery and money laundering.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Penta case'
inside: Grupo Penta used tax service employees inside the state to help pass money through fake invoices to the campaigns of politicians it funded.

n: US charges Firtash's group with $18.5m bribe to Indian officials
rank: officials granting titanium mining licences
d: A US grand jury in Chicago indicted Dmytro Firtash, a Ukrainian businessman who heads Group DF, and five others in 2014 on bribery, racketeering and money-laundering charges over an alleged $18.5 million bribe to Indian officials to obtain titanium mining licences. Firtash, co-owner of the gas trader RosUkrEnergo, was influential under Ukrainian presidents Viktor Yushchenko and Viktor Yanukovych and reportedly helped finance Yanukovych's 2010 campaign. Arrested in Vienna in 2014, he fought extradition to the US for years, and in November 2024 a Vienna court ruled extradition not permissible. He denies the charges. In June 2021 Ukraine's security council sanctioned him.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Dmytro Firtash'
inside: US prosecutors say Firtash's group arranged an $18.5 million bribe to Indian officials so they would grant it titanium mining licences.

n: Juárez Cartel had Mexico's drug czar, General Gutiérrez Rebollo
rank: Head of the National Institute to Combat Drugs (INCD)
d: The Juárez Cartel of Amado Carrillo Fuentes had Mexico's top anti-drug official working for it. General Jesús Gutiérrez Rebollo was named head of the National Institute to Combat Drugs (INCD), the federal anti-narcotics agency, in December 1996; weeks later the US drug czar Barry McCaffrey praised his 'impeccable integrity'. On 6 February 1997 the defence minister had him arrested and said he had protected Carrillo Fuentes for several years. Investigators acted on a tip that he lived in an expensive apartment supplied by a Carrillo associate. He was sentenced to more than 31 years for weapons offences, and in 2007 a court added 40 years. He died in custody in December 2013.
cite: Transnational Institute, 'Mexico: The Narco General Case' (1997); Wikipedia, Jesús Gutiérrez Rebollo
inside: The Juárez Cartel had Mexico's top anti-drug official protecting its leader, so the agency meant to fight it worked for it.

n: General Navarro Lara offered Tijuana's anti-drug chief $1m a month
rank: Army brigadier general
d: An army general tried to buy Mexico's top counter-narcotics official in Tijuana on behalf of a drug cartel. On 17 March 1997, a month after the arrest of the national drug czar, Mexico jailed Brigadier General Alfredo Navarro Lara on charges of drug corruption, bribery and criminal association. Prosecutors said he had offered the Tijuana anti-drug official $1 million a month to protect one of the country's largest trafficking groups, and threatened to kill him and his family if he refused. Prosecutors separately linked the general to the Tijuana mafia of the Arellano Félix brothers. He was the second general jailed in the same high-security prison in a month.
cite: Spokesman-Review / AP, 'Mexico busts general for drug bribe' (18 Mar 1997)
inside: An army general, on behalf of a drug cartel, offered Tijuana's anti-drug official $1 million a month to protect the cartel's trade.

n: Generals Acosta Chaparro and Quirós convicted of working for Carrillo
rank: Army generals
d: Two senior Mexican army generals helped the drug lord Amado Carrillo Fuentes, leader of the Juárez Cartel, move drugs. In 2002 a military court found Generals Arturo Acosta Chaparro and Francisco Quirós Hermosillo guilty of drug smuggling and related charges; Quirós was also convicted of taking the trafficker's bribes. Quirós received 16 years and Acosta 15. Both also faced separate charges over the deaths of more than 130 people during the 1970s 'dirty war' against leftist rebels. Acosta Chaparro was later cleared of the drug charges and was shot dead in Mexico City in 2012.
cite: VOA (2 Nov 2002); Al Jazeera (21 Apr 2012); Fox News/AP on Acosta Chaparro's killing
inside: The Juárez Cartel had two senior army generals helping it move drugs, with one taking its bribes.

n: Beltrán Leyva cartel paid officials inside Mexico's organised-crime unit
rank: SIEDO, federal organised-crime prosecution unit
d: The Beltrán Leyva cartel bought officials inside SIEDO, the elite unit of Mexico's federal attorney general's office that prosecutes drug trafficking and organised crime. In October 2008 the government admitted that at least 35 SIEDO officials and agents, including a senior intelligence director, had leaked operations, raids and evidence to the cartel for up to four years, for $150,000 to $450,000 a month each. The inquiry began on tips from an informant who walked into the Mexican embassy in Washington. Noé Ramírez Mandujano, SIEDO's head from 2006 to August 2008, was accused of taking $450,000 a month to tip off traffickers. Several later cases collapsed, and Ramírez called the operation a farce.
cite: Los Angeles Times via Spokesman-Review, 'Drug gang breaches top agency' (28 Oct 2008); Wikipedia, Noé Ramírez Mandujano; Reforma interview via vLex
inside: The Beltrán Leyva cartel paid at least 35 officials inside Mexico's organised-crime prosecution unit to leak raids, operations and evidence to it.

n: Ex-deputy defence secretary charged with aiding Beltrán Leyva cartel
rank: Former Deputy Secretary of National Defence and generals
d: Mexican prosecutors charged a former deputy defence secretary and four other senior officers with selling military intelligence to the Beltrán Leyva cartel. In August 2012 a federal judge ordered Tomás Ángeles Dauahare, former army under-secretary and military attaché in Washington, to stand trial with Brigadier Generals Roberto Dawe González and Rubén Pérez Ramírez, retired General Ricardo Escorcia Vargas and a retired lieutenant colonel who had run Sinaloa's state police. They were accused of taking cartel bribes in 2007 and 2008 in return for information on military operations and protection for cocaine shipments. The officers denied the charges, one said he was coerced, and the defence attacked shifting witness accounts.
cite: Justice in Mexico, 'Six current and former military officials formally charged with aiding Beltrán Leyva Cartel' (9 Aug 2012)
inside: The Beltrán Leyva cartel is accused of paying a former deputy defence secretary and generals for military intelligence and protection for its shipments.

n: El Chapo bribed Puente Grande prison staff to walk out in 2001
rank: Puente Grande maximum-security prison staff and director
d: Joaquín 'El Chapo' Guzmán of the Sinaloa Cartel bought the staff of the maximum-security prison holding him. On 19 January 2001 a guard opened his electronic cell door at Puente Grande, Jalisco, and a maintenance worker wheeled him out in a laundry cart that bribed guards did not search. Officials later said 78 people were implicated and that the escape cost him about $2.5 million; the prison's director was jailed for aiding it, and Jalisco police were reportedly paid to give him 24 hours to leave the state.
cite: Wikipedia, Joaquín 'El Chapo' Guzmán (citing contemporary reporting)
inside: The Sinaloa Cartel's leader bribed staff of the prison holding him, including the director, so they let him walk out.

n: 'El Mayo' Zambada admits paying Mexican police and army commanders
rank: Police and military commanders
d: Ismael 'El Mayo' Zambada, co-founder of the Sinaloa Cartel, admitted in a US court that his organisation bought Mexico's security forces. Pleading guilty in Brooklyn on 25 August 2025 to running a continuing criminal enterprise from 1989 to 2024 and to racketeering, he said people working for him paid bribes to Mexican police and military commanders so the cartel could operate freely. Mexican press accounts of the hearing reported he also named corrupt politicians. His cartel moved at least 1.5 million kilograms of cocaine between 1980 and 2024. The plea is the cartel's own leader confirming the protection system that Mexican and US cases had described for decades.
cite: NPR (26 Aug 2025); Al Jazeera (25 Aug 2025); Zeta Tijuana (25 Aug 2025)
inside: The Sinaloa Cartel's own leader admitted it paid Mexican police and military commanders so it could operate freely.

n: Congressman Julio César Godoy accused of serving La Familia Michoacana
rank: Federal deputy (Chamber of Deputies)
d: A man charged with working for the La Familia Michoacana cartel got into Mexico's federal Congress. Julio César Godoy Toscano, half-brother of Michoacán's governor, was elected a federal deputy for the PRD party in 2009, and that July was charged with ties to La Familia and money laundering. He evaded arrest, then on 23 September 2010 slipped past police checkpoints into the Chamber of Deputies to be sworn in, gaining parliamentary immunity. In October recordings surfaced of him talking with the cartel leader Servando 'La Tuta' Gómez; he left the PRD, and on 14 December 2010 Congress voted 384 to 2 to strip his immunity. He remains a fugitive.
cite: Wikipedia, Julio César Godoy Toscano (citing El Universal, Proceso and others)
inside: A man charged with working for La Familia Michoacana cartel was elected to Mexico's Congress and sworn in, gaining immunity from arrest.

n: Michoacán's interim governor Jesús Reyna met Knights Templar leaders
rank: Interim Governor and Secretary of Government of Michoacán
d: The Knights Templar Cartel, which grew out of La Familia Michoacana, reached the top of Michoacán's state government. Jesús Reyna García of the PRI was the state's secretary of government and served six months as interim governor in 2013. In April 2014 federal prosecutors detained him; Attorney General Jesús Murillo Karam said the investigation confirmed he had met cartel leaders, and a 2012 state security document described three meetings with the leader Servando 'La Tuta' Gómez. In May 2014 he was sent to the Altiplano prison on organised-crime charges. That August the governor's son, Rodrigo Vallejo, was arrested after a video showed him meeting Gómez.
cite: Al Jazeera/AFP (8 Apr 2014); InSight Crime (May 2014); Wikipedia, Fausto Vallejo
inside: The Knights Templar Cartel's leader met Michoacán's secretary of government and interim governor, who was then jailed on organised-crime charges.

n: Allende police rounded up victims for Los Zetas, rights commission finds
rank: Allende and northern Coahuila municipal police
d: Los Zetas, a cartel founded by army deserters, used the municipal police of Allende, a town in northern Coahuila, as its own force. From 18 to 20 March 2011 Zetas gunmen and local police rounded up families sharing a surname, apparently to punish a suspected betrayal. In 2018 Mexico's National Human Rights Commission found the police complicit in at least 38 abductions and killings, carried out 'with the authorization, support or acquiescence' of local police. A 2017 Colegio de México study led by Sergio Aguayo said numerous mayors' offices and police departments in the region operated at the Zetas' direction, and put the dead and missing above 100.
cite: AP via Fox News, 'Mexico rights agency: police were complicit in 2011 killings' (19 Mar 2018); ProPublica (21 Nov 2017)
inside: Los Zetas used Allende's municipal police as their own force, so local police helped carry out the cartel's abductions and killings.

n: Zetas witnesses say they paid Coahuila's governor for control of the state
rank: Governor of Coahuila and state attorney general
d: Former members of Los Zetas testified in US courts that the cartel paid Coahuila's state government to let it operate. At a 2016 trial in San Antonio, Texas, the convicted trafficker Rodrigo Uribe Tapia said he helped deliver $2 million in bribes for then-Governor Humberto Moreira; a 2017 University of Texas law school review of the testimony recorded two $2 million payments routed through Moreira's secretary and the state attorney general Jesús Torres Charles 'for control over Coahuila'. Another ex-Zeta said cash was loaded at a ranch in 2012 as campaign money for Governor Rubén Moreira. Both Moreiras and the state government denied the claims, and no court has ruled on them.
cite: Borderland Beat (July 2016); El Financiero, 'Los Zetas pagaron a gobernadores de Coahuila y Veracruz' (7 Nov 2017)
inside: Former Zetas testified that the cartel paid Coahuila's governor and attorney general for control of the state; the officials deny it.

n: Operación Enjambre: 19 mayors among 85 officials held for crime ties
org_label: La Familia Michoacana, CJNG, Sinaloa Cartel and local gangs
rank: Mayors, councillors and municipal police chiefs
d: Mexico's federal security ministry is prosecuting municipal governments that it says criminal groups had taken over. Operación Enjambre ('Swarm') began on 22 November 2024 in the State of Mexico, targeting officials accused of running extortion, kidnapping and murder alongside groups such as La Familia Michoacana. By July 2026 more than 85 public servants had been detained, among them at least 19 serving or former mayors, plus councillors and police commanders, in at least 28 municipalities across nine states. Excélsior calculated that the municipalities affected hold more than 2.2 million people, most of them in the State of Mexico.
cite: Excélsior, 'Operación Enjambre rompe el control criminal sobre 2 millones de habitantes' (19 Jul 2026); UnoTV
inside: Criminal groups took over municipal governments, prosecutors say, with mayors, councillors and police chiefs running extortion and kidnapping alongside them.

n: Federal Security Directorate agents served the Guadalajara Cartel
rank: Federal Security Directorate (DFS), national intelligence police
d: The Guadalajara Cartel, Mexico's first large trafficking organisation, worked with officers of the Federal Security Directorate (DFS), the national political police and intelligence agency. On 7 February 1985 several DFS officers took part in kidnapping the US drug agent Enrique 'Kiki' Camarena and pilot Alfredo Zavala in Guadalajara; both were tortured and killed. The journalist Manuel Buendía, murdered in 1984, had been investigating ties between DFS director José Antonio Zorrilla and the cartel. The government formally dissolved the DFS on 29 November 1985. The Camarena case strained US–Mexico relations for decades.
cite: Wikipedia, Dirección Federal de Seguridad; Wikipedia, Guadalajara Cartel
inside: The Guadalajara Cartel had officers of Mexico's national intelligence police working with it, including in kidnapping a US drug agent.

n: Police chief took $300,000 to let Caro Quintero fly out of Guadalajara
rank: Commander, Federal Judicial Police
d: The Guadalajara Cartel bought the federal police commander leading the hunt for its own leader. After the kidnapping of US drug agent Enrique Camarena in February 1985, Rafael Caro Quintero was found at Guadalajara airport, but Armando Pavón Reyes, the Federal Judicial Police commander, reportedly took a $300,000 bribe and let him leave on a private jet on 9 March 1985. Caro Quintero was arrested in Costa Rica on 4 April. Pavón Reyes was fired, charged with bribery and complicity in the Camarena murder, and convicted of bribery in 1986, according to the Associated Press.
cite: Wikipedia, Rafael Caro Quintero and Guadalajara Cartel (citing AP 1986)
inside: The Guadalajara Cartel paid the federal police commander hunting its leader, who then let him fly away.

n: Mexico City police chief Durazo took cocaine-trade kickbacks
rank: Chief of Mexico City police
d: Cocaine traffickers paid the chief of police of Mexico's capital. Arturo Durazo Moreno, a childhood friend of President José López Portillo, ran Mexico City's police from 1976 to 1982 and reported directly to the president. A US grand jury had indicted him on narcotics charges about eleven months before he took the post. On a salary under $1,000 a month he acquired two large homes, vintage cars and property abroad, attributed to police bribes and payments from the cocaine trade. The FBI arrested him in Puerto Rico in 1984; after extradition in 1986 he was convicted of corruption, extortion and cocaine-trade kickbacks and sentenced to 16 years.
cite: Wikipedia, Arturo Durazo Moreno (citing New York Times, Los Angeles Times)
inside: Cocaine traffickers paid the chief of Mexico City's police, who was convicted of taking kickbacks from the cocaine trade.

n: Three Tamaulipas ex-governors held in Mexico over Gulf Cartel ties
rank: Governors of Tamaulipas, 1993–2010
d: Mexico's federal prosecutors investigated whether the Gulf Cartel and its former armed wing Los Zetas had the governors of Tamaulipas, the border state where the cartel was based. On 30 January 2012 the Attorney General ordered three former governors, Manuel Cavazos Lerma (1993–1999), Tomás Yarrington (1999–2004) and Eugenio Hernández Flores (2005–2010), and their families not to leave the country while they were investigated for possible cooperation with cartels. The PAN politician Santiago Creel said the PRI in Tamaulipas had protected the Gulf Cartel for years. In May 2015 the US indicted Hernández for laundering about $30 million; a Mexican judge refused to extradite him.
cite: Wikipedia, Gulf Cartel (citing Excélsior, 30 Jan 2012); Wikipedia, Eugenio Hernández Flores
inside: Mexican prosecutors investigated whether three former Tamaulipas governors cooperated with the Gulf Cartel, which a senior politician said the state's ruling party had long protected.

n: Batista gave Meyer Lansky's mafia Cuba's casinos for kickbacks
rank: President Fulgencio Batista; government gambling adviser
d: The American Mafia, through its financier Meyer Lansky, reached the head of Cuba's government. In the late 1940s Fulgencio Batista agreed to give Lansky and the Mafia control of Cuba's casinos and racetracks in return for kickbacks. After seizing power in a 1952 coup, Batista made Lansky an adviser on gambling reform. In 1955 the law was changed so any hotel worth $1 million could host a casino, and the state matched large hotel investments. Lansky put most of the roughly $14 million into the Havana Riviera, opened in 1957. The arrangement ended with the 1959 revolution, when casinos were looted and then nationalised.
cite: Wikipedia, Meyer Lansky (citing Lacey, 'Little Man'; English, 'Havana Nocturne')
inside: The American Mafia paid Cuba's ruler for control of the casinos, and he made its financier his gambling adviser and changed the law to suit casino investment.

n: Pablo Escobar elected to Colombia's Congress with parliamentary immunity
rank: Alternate member, Chamber of Representatives
d: Pablo Escobar, leader of the Medellín Cartel, got himself into Colombia's Congress. In the March 1982 election he won a seat as an alternate (substitute) member of the Chamber of Representatives for Medellín on a Liberal list, which automatically gave him parliamentary immunity and a diplomatic passport. Justice Minister Rodrigo Lara Bonilla accused him of crime from the first days of Congress, and the Liberal leader Luis Carlos Galán expelled him from his movement. Escobar's term ended in October 1983 and he announced his retirement from politics in January 1984. Lara Bonilla was murdered on 30 April 1984 and Galán in August 1989, both by the cartel.
cite: Wikipedia, Pablo Escobar; Wikipedia, 1982 Colombian parliamentary election; Wikipedia, Medellín Cartel
inside: The Medellín Cartel's leader won himself a seat in Colombia's Congress, which gave him parliamentary immunity.

n: Drug lords suspected of swaying the 1991 assembly that banned extradition
rank: Constituent Assembly
d: Colombia's drug lords were suspected of influencing the assembly that wrote the country's 1991 constitution. The Medellín Cartel had fought extradition to the United States with bribery, threats and killings of judges and ministers. The Constituent Assembly wrote a ban on extraditing Colombian citizens into the new constitution, approved in 1991, and Pablo Escobar surrendered that year under a deal that let him be held in La Catedral, a prison he built himself. Suspicions that traffickers paid or pressed assembly members were widely reported but not proven.
cite: Wikipedia, Pablo Escobar; Wikipedia, Medellín Cartel
inside: Colombia's drug traffickers were widely suspected of paying or pressing members of the constitutional assembly that then banned extraditing Colombians, though this was never proven.

n: Uribe's intelligence chief Noguera put the DAS at paramilitaries' service
rank: Director, Administrative Department of Security (DAS)
d: The AUC, Colombia's paramilitary and drug-trafficking federation, had the head of the national intelligence agency working for it. Jorge Noguera, a regional campaign manager for Álvaro Uribe, ran the Administrative Department of Security (DAS) from August 2002 to October 2005. A former DAS IT chief testified that Noguera made DAS resources available to the AUC's Northern Bloc under 'Jorge 40', including information used to kill trade unionists. On 14 September 2011 the Supreme Court convicted him of conspiracy, conspiracy to murder, destroying public documents and leaking secret information, and sentenced him to 25 years.
cite: Wikipedia, Jorge Noguera Cotes; Colombia Reports (Sept 2011); CTV/AP (14 Sep 2011)
inside: Paramilitaries had the head of Colombia's intelligence agency put its resources at their service, including information used to kill trade unionists.

n: Former DAS chief Maza Márquez jailed for role in Galán assassination
rank: Director, Administrative Department of Security (DAS)
d: Colombia's Supreme Court found that the director of the national intelligence agency took part in the cartel-ordered killing of a presidential frontrunner. General Miguel Maza Márquez ran the Administrative Department of Security (DAS) from 1985 to 1991. The Liberal presidential candidate Luis Carlos Galán was assassinated in August 1989 on the orders of the Medellín Cartel's leader. In November 2016 the Supreme Court sentenced Maza Márquez to 30 years for participating in the assassination. The Medellín Cartel had also tried to kill him, including with the December 1989 DAS building bombing.
cite: Wikipedia, Miguel Maza Márquez (citing BBC Mundo, Nov 2016)
inside: Colombia's Supreme Court found the head of the national intelligence agency took part in the Medellín Cartel's killing of a presidential frontrunner.

n: Medellín's chief prosecutor shielded 'Don Mario' drug gang
rank: Chief prosecutor of Medellín
d: The drug gang of Daniel Rendón Herrera, alias 'Don Mario', a former paramilitary commander, had Medellín's chief prosecutor protecting it. Guillermo León Valencia Cossio, brother of the then Minister of Interior and Justice Fabio Valencia Cossio, was arrested on 25 September 2008. The Supreme Court found he had ordered a police commander to leave Don Mario's second-in-command off an investigation chart of the gang, and convicted him of conspiracy, suppression of documents and illicit enrichment, with a 15-year sentence. In October 2010 the US listed him as a Specially Designated Narcotics Trafficker. His sentence was later extended as more criminal ties emerged.
cite: Colombia Reports, 'Former chief prosecutor sentenced to 15 years'; El Colombiano (25 Sep 2008)
inside: A drug gang had Medellín's chief prosecutor protecting it, so he kept its second-in-command off an investigation.

n: Cali Cartel had insiders in the police Search Bloc and phone company
rank: Search Bloc police unit; Bogotá–Cali telephone exchange
d: The Cali Cartel, which preferred bribery to violence, placed people inside the bodies hunting it. It recruited Jorge Salcedo, a Colombian military member, to run its intelligence and build a hidden radio network across Cali. A 1995 raid showed its counter-intelligence unit had been monitoring calls in and out of Bogotá and Cali, including those of the US Embassy and the Ministry of Defence, with help from an insider at the phone company. A high-ranking member of the Search Bloc, the police unit formed to catch the cartel's leaders, hid Miguel Rodríguez Orejuela in his car during a 1995 raid. Six of the seven leaders were arrested that year.
cite: Wikipedia, Cali Cartel (citing Time, 1991; Chepesiuk, 'The Bullet or the Bribe')
inside: The Cali Cartel placed insiders in the police unit hunting it and in the phone company, so it could tap calls and hide its leaders.

n: Norte del Valle Cartel bribed police and legislators to block extradition
rank: Colombian police and Congress
d: The Norte del Valle Cartel, a cocaine group based in Colombia's Valle del Cauca, tried to buy the state's protection against extradition. A 2004 US racketeering indictment said its leaders 'bribed and corrupted Colombian law enforcement and Colombian legislators' to block extraditions, and ran their own wiretaps on rivals and on Colombian and US police. The cartel's lawyer Gabriel Puerta Parra, arrested in October 2004, reportedly influenced the government on extradition. Laureano Rentería, accused of bribing high officials for the leader Juan Carlos Ramírez Abadía, was found dead of cyanide poisoning in his cell on the day of his extradition in February 2007.
cite: Wikipedia, Norte del Valle Cartel (citing US DOJ indictment, 2004)
inside: The Norte del Valle Cartel bribed Colombian police and legislators to block the extradition of its leaders, a US indictment said.

n: Trafficker Alexander Ardón ran El Paraíso as mayor and funded the party
rank: Mayor of El Paraíso, Copán; National Party campaigns
d: A cocaine trafficker took over a Honduran border town by becoming its mayor and used the post to buy national protection. Alexander Ardón, a go-between for Colombian and Mexican traffickers, was mayor of El Paraíso, Copán, on the Guatemalan border, and was re-elected in 2009 with 94.7% of the vote; police said he posted cameras and armed guards at the town's entrances. US prosecutors said that from 2008 Tony Hernández offered protection in return for National Party campaign money, and that Ardón paid $1.5 million into Juan Orlando Hernández's 2013 campaign. Indicted in 2019, Ardón became the key US witness against both Hernández brothers.
cite: InSight Crime, 'How an ex-mayor could bring down Honduras' president' (Aug 2019); El Heraldo (Aug 2026)
inside: A cocaine trafficker became mayor of a border town and paid a presidential campaign in return for protection, US prosecutors said.

n: Texis Cartel: a mayor and a football boss accused, later acquitted
rank: Mayor of Metapán; legislators, police, judges
d: El Faro reported in 2011 that a trafficking network called the Texis Cartel, which moved drugs along El Salvador's northern border, was led by a sitting mayor and protected by officials. It named as founders José Adán Salazar ('Chepe Diablo'), president of the national football league, and Juan Umaña Samayoa, mayor of Metapán, and alleged support from other mayors, a legislator, and police, soldiers, judges and prosecutors paid to let shipments pass or drop charges. President Mauricio Funes ordered an investigation, and the US listed Salazar as a drug kingpin in 2014, then delisted him in 2017. In May 2021 a court acquitted all nine defendants of laundering $500 million.
cite: El Faro (2011); Wikipedia, Texis Cartel
inside: El Faro reported that a trafficking network was led by a sitting mayor and protected by paid police, judges and prosecutors; a court later acquitted the accused.

n: Haiti's police chief Michel François indicted for cocaine bribes
rank: Chief of National Police
d: US prosecutors charged that Colombian drug lords paid the head of Haiti's police under the military regime. Colonel Joseph-Michel François helped lead the 1991 coup against President Jean-Bertrand Aristide and then ran the police and secret police under General Raoul Cédras. In March 1997 the US indicted him for allegedly smuggling 33 tons of cocaine and heroin into the United States from his private airstrip in Haiti while taking bribes from Colombian traffickers. He denied the charges. Honduras, where he had fled, refused to extradite him in July 1997 for lack of evidence, and he died there in 2017.
cite: Wikipedia, Michel François (citing New York Times, 1997)
inside: Colombian traffickers paid the head of Haiti's police, US prosecutors charged, while he moved their drugs through his airstrip.

n: Royal Commission finds drug money ran through Pindling's cabinet
rank: Prime Minister, cabinet and police
d: Colombian cocaine smugglers paid members of the Bahamian government to use the islands as a route to the US. Carlos Lehder, a Medellín Cartel co-founder, controlled Norman's Cay in the Exumas as a smuggling base. After an NBC report, 'The Bahamas: A Nation For Sale', a Royal Commission of Inquiry into Drug Trafficking and Government Corruption reported in 1984 wide corruption in the cabinet and police. It found that Prime Minister Lynden Pindling's spending from 1977 to 1984 was eight times his reported income and that he and his wife had received at least $57.3 million in cash. The commission did not find Pindling guilty, but five ministers resigned or were dismissed.
cite: Wikipedia, Lynden Pindling and Illegal drug trade in the Bahamas (citing New York Times; Royal Commission report 1984)
inside: Cocaine smugglers' cash reached the Bahamian cabinet and police, so the islands' own government let them use the country as a route to the US.

n: Minister Vere Bird Jr let Israeli guns pass Antigua to the Medellín Cartel
rank: Cabinet minister
d: Agents of the Medellín Cartel used an Antiguan cabinet minister to obtain military weapons. Maurice Sarfati and the Israeli mercenary Yair Klein ordered Israeli arms in Antigua's name, with forged papers, as part of a plan to train and supply the forces of the cartel leader Gonzalo Rodríguez Gacha. An Israeli diplomatic note said the guns were shipped at the apparent instruction of minister Vere Bird Jr, son of the prime minister. After Colombia complained, an inquiry under Sir Louis Blom-Cooper, ordered in April 1990, reported that November and recommended Bird be barred from public office for life. He was removed from cabinet on 10 May 1990.
cite: Wikipedia, Vere Bird Jr. (citing Blom-Cooper inquiry report, 1990)
inside: Medellín Cartel agents used a serving Antiguan cabinet minister to order Israeli military weapons in the state's name for a cartel leader's forces.

n: Cocaine Coup: trafficker Roberto Suárez financed Bolivia's 1980 junta
rank: Military junta; Minister of the Interior
d: Bolivia's leading cocaine trafficker helped pay for a military coup and then had his cousin in charge of the police. On 17 July 1980 General Luis García Meza seized power in what became known as the 'Cocaine Coup'. Roberto Suárez Gómez helped finance it, and many officers had ties to traffickers, with parts of the army acting as their protectors for bribes. Suárez's cousin, Colonel Luis Arce Gómez, became Minister of the Interior, giving Suárez political protection. US pressure isolated the regime, which fell in 1981. Arce Gómez was later jailed in the US for drug trafficking, and García Meza received a 30-year sentence for human rights crimes.
cite: Wikipedia, Luis García Meza; Wikipedia, Luis Arce Gómez; Wikipedia, Roberto Suárez Gómez
inside: A cocaine trafficker paid for the coup that put the junta in power, and his cousin then ran the Interior Ministry and gave him protection.

n: Bicho bosses' ledgers named 12 congressmen and 125 police in Rio
rank: Police, judges, congressmen and state officials
d: The bosses of the jogo do bicho, Rio de Janeiro's illegal numbers lottery, kept police and politicians on their side. Rio's attorney general Antônio Carlos Biscaia called the bosses' central commission 'a true Brazilian Mafia' that aimed to corrupt authorities and police, and in 1993 Judge Denise Frossard convicted the commission's members of criminal association. In March 1994 police raided Castor de Andrade's base in Bangu and seized 200 account books. The material implicated a former president, Rio's governor, the mayors of São Paulo and Rio, three judges, 12 congressmen, seven state legislators, 25 police commissioners and 100 police officers. Those named were not convicted.
cite: Wikipedia, Jogo do bicho (citing Folha de S.Paulo, Veja, New York Times 1994)
inside: Seized account books of the numbers-game bosses named police, judges and politicians they were said to pay to keep the authorities on their side.

n: Federal raid finds bicho and slot-machine bosses paying judges and police
rank: Judges, prosecutors and police
d: Brazil's federal police found that the bosses of Rio's illegal numbers game and slot-machine trade were paying people inside the justice system. On 12 April 2007 they arrested Antonio Petrus Kalil, Anísio Abraão David and Capitão Guimarães, then president of the league of Rio samba schools, with 24 others over illegal lotteries, bingo halls and slot machines. The raids allegedly uncovered payoffs to judges, police officers, prosecutors and lawyers, and about $6 million in cash was seized. The same families had been jailed in 1993 and freed on parole within three years.
cite: Wikipedia, Jogo do bicho (citing O Globo, Folha de S.Paulo, April 2007)
inside: Illegal lottery and slot-machine bosses paid judges, prosecutors and police, putting people inside the justice system on the side of their trade.

n: Rio state deputy TH Joias arrested as Comando Vermelho's man in assembly
rank: Rio de Janeiro State Legislative Assembly (Alerj)
d: Comando Vermelho (Red Command), Rio de Janeiro's oldest drug faction, is accused of having a representative in the state legislature. In 2025 police placed state deputy TH Joias in preventive detention for ties to the group, alleging he acted as its arm in the Legislative Assembly of Rio de Janeiro (Alerj). That September the MDB party's president said a state deputy allegedly involved with the faction would be expelled. A September 2025 report also cited investigations showing police officers escorting the faction's drug shipments. In October 2025 a police operation against the group in the Penha and Alemão favelas left more than 120 dead.
cite: Wikipedia, Comando Vermelho (citing G1, Folha de S.Paulo, 2025)
inside: Police allege the Comando Vermelho drug faction had a state deputy acting as its arm in Rio's legislature, while police officers escorted its drug shipments.

n: Caso Encuentro: Albanian mafia link reached Lasso's family circle
rank: State companies and President Lasso's campaign
d: Reporting in 2023 alleged that a drug-trafficking network linked to the Albanian mafia reached Ecuador's presidency through a businessman close to the president's family.
