The outlet La Posta published audio of Rubén Cherres, an associate of President Guillermo Lasso's brother-in-law Danilo Carrera, describing a scheme in state companies and saying he provided $1.5 million to Lasso's 2021 campaign; investigators later reported Cherres linked the Albanian mafia to Lasso's circle. A police inquiry into Cherres's drug ties had been dropped. Cherres was murdered on 31 March 2023. Facing impeachment, Lasso dissolved the National Assembly on 17 May 2023, forcing early elections.
cite: Wikipedia, Guillermo Lasso (citing La Posta, Primicias, El Universo 2023)
inside: Reporting alleged that an associate of the president's brother-in-law, later tied by investigators to the Albanian mafia, ran a scheme in state companies and funded the campaign.

n: Los Choneros leader 'Fito' walks out of La Roca prison
rank: Prison service and guards
d: Los Choneros, the gang that has held sway in Ecuador's prisons since 2011, ran its operations from inside them and is accused of buying the staff. Its leader José Adolfo Macías ('Fito'), serving 34 years, directed the gang by phone and internet from his cell. In January 2024 he vanished from La Roca prison in Guayaquil; guards were suspected of complicity, a perimeter fence had been cut days earlier, and a boat with guard uniforms and ammunition was found nearby. About 30 officials were arrested in a linked anti-corruption operation, and the government declared an 'internal armed conflict'. Fito was recaptured in June 2025 and agreed to extradition to the US.
cite: Wikipedia, Los Choneros (citing Primicias, Reuters, AP 2024–25)
inside: Los Choneros ran its operations from inside Ecuador's prisons, and guards suspected of being bought helped its leader escape from La Roca.

n: US names three of Chávez's security chiefs as FARC drug helpers
rank: Military intelligence chief, DISIP intelligence director, former interior minister
d: The US Treasury said the FARC, the Colombian guerrilla army that financed itself through cocaine, had senior Venezuelan security officials working for it. On 12 September 2008 it sanctioned Hugo Carvajal, head of military intelligence; Henry Rangel Silva, director of the DISIP intelligence service; and Ramón Rodríguez Chacín, a former Minister of the Interior. It accused Carvajal of protecting FARC drug loads from seizure, supplying weapons and giving it Venezuelan official documents. Rangel Silva later became defence minister and governor of Trujillo.
cite: US Treasury press release (12 Sep 2008), via Wikipedia, Hugo Carvajal
inside: The FARC had Venezuela's intelligence chiefs working for it, protecting its cocaine loads and supplying it with weapons and official documents.

n: Corleonesi ally Vito Ciancimino ran Palermo's building permits
rank: Palermo public works assessor and mayor
d: Cosa Nostra, the Sicilian Mafia, had its own man in charge of Palermo's building permits. Vito Ciancimino, from Corleone and close to the Corleonesi bosses Bernardo Provenzano and Totò Riina, became the city's assessor for public works and building permits in 1959 and was mayor in 1970–71. The construction boom of those years, known as the 'Sack of Palermo', destroyed the city's green belt. After the informer Tommaso Buscetta testified, Ciancimino was arrested in 1984. In 1992 he was sentenced to 13 years for Mafia association and laundering, the first time an Italian politician was found guilty of working with the Mafia. In 2002 the city sought €150m in damages from him.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Vito Ciancimino' and 'Sack of Palermo' (citing Italian court records and press)
inside: The Corleonesi bosses' ally ran Palermo's building permits and later the mayor's office, so the city's planning powers served the Mafia's construction boom.

n: Mafia cousins Nino and Ignazio Salvo held Sicily's tax collection
rank: Sicilian regional tax-collection concession
d: Two members of Cosa Nostra, the cousins Nino and Ignazio Salvo, held the private concession to collect taxes for the region of Sicily. The concession, arranged through the Christian Democrat leader Salvo Lima, paid them 10% of what they collected, about three times the 3.3% national average. The informer Tommaso Buscetta revealed that both men belonged to the Mafia, and they were arrested on 12 November 1984. Nino died in 1986; Ignazio was convicted of Mafia association at the 1987 Maxi Trial and sentenced to seven years. Photographs from 1979 showed Prime Minister Giulio Andreotti with Nino Salvo, though Andreotti denied knowing the cousins. Ignazio was murdered by the Mafia in 1992.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Ignazio and Nino Salvo' (citing police and Maxi Trial records)
inside: Two sworn Mafia members held Sicily's tax-collection concession, arranged through a party leader, and kept three times the usual national commission.

n: Mafia votes put Antonio D'Alì in the Senate and Interior Ministry
rank: Under-secretary of the Interior
d: Cosa Nostra helped elect a senator who then became a junior minister at Italy's Interior Ministry, the ministry that runs the police. Italy's highest court, the Court of Cassation, confirmed in December 2022 a six-year sentence for Antonio D'Alì, a Forza Italia senator for 24 years, for 'external complicity' in a mafia association (helping the Mafia without being a sworn member). The court found that in 2001 he made a pact under which the Mafia delivered votes for his re-election, which led to his appointment as interior under-secretary from 2001 to 2006. It also found he took part in a sham land sale arranged by the Trapani boss Matteo Messina Denaro. D'Alì surrendered at Opera prison.
cite: L'Indipendente, 15 Dec 2022; LiveSicilia (D'Alì surrenders at Opera prison)
inside: Cosa Nostra delivered votes to a senator under a pact, which led to his post at the Interior Ministry, and he joined a sham land deal for its boss.

n: Intelligence deputy Bruno Contrada convicted of aiding the Mafia
rank: Deputy director, SISDE civil intelligence
d: Former Mafia members said Cosa Nostra had a source high in Italy's civil intelligence service, SISDE. Bruno Contrada had headed Palermo's judicial police and later rose to deputy director of SISDE. He was arrested on 24 December 1992 after the informers Gaspare Mutolo and Giuseppe Marchese accused him of tipping off the Mafia about police operations and obstructing the capture of the boss Totò Riina. He was sentenced to ten years, a verdict upheld by the Court of Cassation in 2007. In 2015 the European Court of Human Rights ruled he had been convicted for conduct that was not clearly a crime at the time, and in 2017 Italy's top court annulled the conviction. He died in March 2026.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Bruno Contrada'; ANSA, 14 Apr 2015 (ECtHR ruling)
inside: Informers said Cosa Nostra had the deputy head of civil intelligence as its source, tipping it off about police operations and obstructing a boss's capture.

n: Salvo Lima, Andreotti's man in Sicily, killed after Maxi Trial loss
rank: Palermo mayor, MP and MEP
d: Cosa Nostra treated Salvo Lima, Palermo's mayor in 1958–63 and 1965–68, later an MP, budget under-secretary and member of the European Parliament, as its link to national power. Lima was the Sicilian broker for Prime Minister Giulio Andreotti's faction of the Christian Democrats. A 1964 indictment described Palermo bosses seeking favours from him, and the Italian parliament's Antimafia Commission found in 1993 strong signs of his relations with Cosa Nostra. The informers Tommaso Buscetta and Gaspare Mutolo said Lima was expected to get the Maxi Trial convictions overturned. When the Supreme Court upheld them in January 1992, he was shot dead on 12 March 1992; Totò Riina and other bosses got life sentences for the killing.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Salvo Lima' (citing 1993 Antimafia Commission report and 2004 Cassation ruling on Andreotti)
inside: Cosa Nostra treated a mayor and MP as its link to national power, bringing him requests for favours and expecting him to get its convictions overturned.

n: Judge 'the sentence-slayer' Carnevale tried for helping the Mafia
rank: President, First Criminal Section, Court of Cassation
d: Prosecutors charged that Cosa Nostra had influence over the judge who heard Mafia appeals at Italy's highest court. Corrado Carnevale presided over the First Criminal Section of the Court of Cassation and overturned so many Mafia convictions that he was nicknamed 'l'ammazzasentenze', the sentence-slayer. Because of suspected collusion, he was kept off the final ruling in the Maxi Trial of hundreds of mafiosi in 1992 and another judge took his place. He was suspended in 1993 and in June 2001 sentenced to six years for 'external complicity' in a mafia association. The Court of Cassation acquitted him in October 2002, and he returned to work as a civil judge in 2007.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Corrado Carnevale'
inside: Prosecutors charged that Cosa Nostra had influence over the supreme court judge hearing its appeals, who overturned many Mafia convictions.

n: Lombardy regional minister Zambetti bought 4,000 'Ndrangheta votes
rank: Lombardy regional assessore (minister)
d: The 'Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia, sold a block of votes to a politician who then sat in the government of Lombardy, Italy's richest region. Prosecutors said Domenico Zambetti paid €200,000 to two 'Ndrangheta figures, Eugenio Costantino and Giuseppe D'Agostino, for about 4,000 preference votes in the 2010 regional election, which he won with 11,217 votes before becoming a regional assessore (minister). He was arrested in October 2012. In February 2017 a Milan court sentenced him to 13 years and six months for a 'political-mafia exchange', and the prosecutor said the deal had distorted the 2010 result. Costantino, described as a contact of the Di Grillo-Mancuso clan, received 16 and a half years.
cite: Il Fatto Quotidiano, 8 Feb 2017; LaPresse, 8 Feb 2017
inside: The 'Ndrangheta sold a politician a block of 4,000 votes, which helped put him in Lombardy's regional government through a 'political-mafia exchange'.

n: 'Ndrangheta clans steered Reggio Calabria's public health authority
rank: Reggio Calabria provincial health authority (ASP)
d: The 'Ndrangheta got inside the public body that runs hospitals for Reggio Calabria province. On 13 March 2019 Italy's cabinet dissolved the provincial health authority (ASP) for mafia infiltration and put it under commissioners, at the request of the prefect, the national government's local representative. In March 2021 Carabinieri arrested 14 people. Investigators said the Piromalli clan, with the Molè family, steered appointments of health directors, and firms linked to it monopolised supply of medical products to hospitals in Locri, Gioia Tauro, Polistena and Melito Porto Salvo through direct awards, with staff taking 2.5–5% commissions. Earlier reporting found convicted mafia employees still drawing pay and debts above €420m.
cite: ANSA, 13 Mar 2019; Domani, 23 Mar 2021; Il Fatto Quotidiano, 13 Mar 2019
inside: 'Ndrangheta clans steered the appointment of health directors in a public health authority, and their firms won its hospital supply contracts without tender.

n: Ostia's council dissolved for mafia infiltration; Fasciani clan convicted
rank: Rome Municipio X (Ostia) council
d: Crime groups got inside the local government of Ostia, Rome's seaside district (Municipio X, a borough council of the city). On 27 August 2015 the national government dissolved the Ostia council for mafia infiltration, after its former chairman Andrea Tassone was arrested in June with 43 others in the 'Mafia Capitale' inquiry into a ring of gangsters, businessmen and politicians. In November 2019 Italy's Court of Cassation confirmed that the Fasciani family ran a mafia-type association in Ostia, with ten final convictions, including over 27 years for Carmine Fasciani. Rome's mayor called it the first clear recognition that a mafia existed in Rome. Police had seized €18.5m of assets, including beach businesses, in 2018.
cite: ANSA, 27 Aug 2015; Open, 29 Nov 2019
inside: A mafia-type clan and its partners got inside Ostia's borough council, and the national government dissolved the council for mafia infiltration.

n: Sicily's President Raffaele Lombardo tried for Mafia ties, acquitted
rank: President of the Region of Sicily
d: Prosecutors charged that the elected head of Sicily's regional government had dealings with Cosa Nostra. Raffaele Lombardo became President of Sicily in April 2008 and resigned on 31 July 2012 while under investigation for external complicity with the Mafia and for handing out public money for political favours. On 19 February 2014 a court sentenced him to six years and eight months for mafia association. The case went through several appeals: he was acquitted at a second appeal trial in 2022, and in 2023 the Court of Cassation confirmed the acquittal. This was a separate case from that of his predecessor Salvatore Cuffaro, who was jailed for leaking investigation secrets.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Raffaele Lombardo'
inside: Prosecutors charged that Sicily's elected regional president worked with Cosa Nostra; he was convicted of mafia association at first and later acquitted.

n: Interior Minister Antonio Gava accused of trading favours for Camorra votes
rank: Minister of the Interior
d: Prosecutors in Naples accused a former Italian interior minister, the minister in charge of the police, of being tied to the Camorra, the Naples-area mafia. Antonio Gava, a Christian Democrat from Campania, was interior minister from April 1988 to October 1990. He was charged in 1993 with membership of a criminal organisation and arrested on 21 September 1994, accused of trading favours for votes gathered by the Camorra. He had also been involved in the 1981 release of the politician Ciro Cirillo, kidnapped by the Red Brigades, when politicians visited the jailed Camorra boss Raffaele Cutolo to ask him to negotiate. After 13 years of proceedings Gava was acquitted of all Camorra charges.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Antonio Gava'
inside: Prosecutors accused the interior minister, who ran the police, of trading favours for votes the Camorra gathered for him.

n: Casalesi clan bribed Campania officials for 20 years to take toxic waste
rank: Campania local politicians and officials
d: The Casalesi clan of the Camorra paid local officials in Campania so that toxic waste could be dumped in their areas. The clan's waste broker Gaetano Vassallo admitted that for about 20 years he bribed local politicians and officials to accept the dumping. Industrial waste from northern Italy, including heavy metals, was mixed with household rubbish, buried or burned around Acerra, Nola and Marigliano, the area called the 'triangle of death'. From about 2005 the Camorra also bought land rented to the state waste contractor FIBE for storing waste bales. In June 2008 President Giorgio Napolitano said the Camorra had systematically moved toxic waste from northern industry into Campania.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Naples waste management crisis' (citing Vassallo testimony and D'Alisa et al.)
inside: The Casalesi clan bribed Campania's local politicians and officials for about 20 years so that they accepted the clan's toxic-waste dumping.

n: Montenegro's leader Djukanovic indicted in Italian cigarette-mafia case
rank: Prime Minister / President of Montenegro
d: Italian anti-mafia prosecutors in Bari charged that Montenegro's state, under its leader Milo Djukanovic, protected cigarette smugglers working with Italian crime groups. In October 2008 they indicted Djukanovic, then prime minister, with seven Serbian and Montenegrin and seven Italian suspects, over smuggling cigarettes from Montenegro to Puglia between 1994 and 2002 and helping talks between the Montenegrin mafia and a Puglia crime group over control of the trade. The EU estimated the smuggling cost it billions of euros in taxes. Prosecutor Giuseppe Scelsi said Djukanovic would not stand trial because of his immunity; a 2003 Italian ruling had already found he had head-of-state immunity. Djukanovic went on to lead Montenegro until 2023.
cite: OCCRP, Oct 2008 ('Djukanovic Indicted; Avoids Trial'); ICIJ/OCCRP 'The Montenegro Connection'
inside: Italian prosecutors charged that Montenegro's leader used the state to protect cigarette smugglers working with Italian crime groups and helped broker their deals.

n: Businessman Marian Kočner's messages expose 13 Slovak judges
rank: Judges and the deputy justice minister
d: Marian Kočner, a Slovak businessman later charged with ordering the 2018 murder of the journalist Ján Kuciak, had judges and a deputy justice minister working for him, according to messages taken from his phone. On 11 March 2020 the National Criminal Agency detained 13 judges and a lawyer in 'Action Storm'. Those charged with corruption, interfering with court independence and abuse of power included former deputy justice minister Monika Jankovská and acting Supreme Court President Jarmila Urbancová. Former judges Vladimír Sklenka and Miriam Repáková confessed to cooperating with Kočner, and five accused were held in custody. The case led to a wider clean-up of Slovakia's courts.
cite: Slovak Spectator, 12 and 15 Mar 2020; RTVS, 16 Mar 2020
inside: A businessman had judges and a deputy justice minister working for him, according to his phone messages, so courts served his interests.

n: Oligarch Bödör's group allegedly ran Slovakia's police leadership
rank: Police President, NAKA and financial police chiefs
d: Slovak prosecutors charge that a businessman, Norbert Bödör, ran a criminal group whose members included the country's top police officers. In 'Očistec' (Purgatory), police detained eight former senior officials on 5 November 2020, including former Police President Tibor Gašpar, allegedly Bödör's right-hand man, and former heads of the National Criminal Agency (NAKA) and its financial and anti-corruption units. The group allegedly used police powers to blackmail businesspeople, obtain information on investigations and pass it to people close to the ruling Smer party. Two former officers confessed. The Special Prosecutor Dušan Kováčik was also charged with supporting the group. The trial continues.
cite: Slovak Spectator, Nov 2020; RTVS, 'Očistec trial' reports
inside: Prosecutors charge that a businessman's criminal group counted the top police chiefs as members and used police powers for blackmail and leaking investigations.

n: Jovanjica: police and intelligence officers guarded a cannabis farm
rank: Serbian police and BIA intelligence officers
d: A Serbian businessman close to the ruling party is accused of running a cannabis farm with help from police officers and agents of the BIA, Serbia's security intelligence agency. Predrag Koluvija's company Jovanjica presented itself as an organic food producer; in November 2019 police raided it and found about 650 kg of dried marijuana and 65,000 stems. Koluvija had travelled in President Aleksandar Vučić's delegation to a 2019 Moscow business forum. Prosecutors charged him with leading a criminal group with police and intelligence officers among its members. He is on trial in two cases at Belgrade's Special Court for Organised Crime, and courts ordered many of his properties seized in 2023.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Jovanjica case' (citing KRIK, BIRN, N1)
inside: A businessman's cannabis operation allegedly had police and state intelligence officers among its members, guarding the farm instead of stopping it.

n: Marbella council dissolved after planning chief's bribery ring
who: Property developers via Juan Antonio Roca
rank: Marbella City Council
d: A network built around Marbella's urban planning adviser, Juan Antonio Roca, took property developers' money in return for planning decisions from the city council. The council had been run since 1991 by Jesús Gil's GIL party; Gil himself was jailed in 2002 for diverting public funds. In March 2006 police arrested Roca, Mayor Marisol Yagüe, the deputy mayor and many councillors in 'Operación Malaya'. On 7 April 2006 Spain's government dissolved the council, the first time that power had been used against a council in Spanish democracy. In October 2013 a court convicted 53 people of bribery, fraud and laundering; Roca got 11 years and a fine of about US$300m.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Marbella City Council dissolution'; OCCRP, Oct 2013
inside: Property developers' money passed through the planning adviser to the mayor and councillors, so Marbella's planning decisions were sold to them.

n: Delyan Peevski made Bulgaria's security chief; US cites bribes
rank: Head of DANS state security agency
d: Delyan Peevski, a Bulgarian MP and media owner, was elected by parliament on 14 June 2013 to head DANS, the State Agency for National Security. Mass protests in Sofia followed, with crowds chanting 'Mafia', and he resigned the next day. By then his family's media group owned six of the 12 largest newspapers and controlled nearly 80% of print distribution. In June 2021 the US Treasury sanctioned him under the Global Magnitsky Act, which targets serious corruption. It said he had used influence peddling and bribes to protect himself from scrutiny and to control key institutions in Bulgaria. The UK later imposed its own anti-corruption sanctions.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Delyan Peevski' (citing US Treasury, June 2021)
inside: The US says a media owner used bribes and influence peddling to control key Bulgarian institutions, and parliament made him head of state security.

n: Mkhedrioni militia of Jaba Ioseliani became Georgia's interior forces
rank: Interior forces and parliament
d: An armed group accused of extortion and drug smuggling was given a place inside Georgia's state after it helped overthrow the government. Jaba Ioseliani founded the Mkhedrioni in 1989. It joined the 1991–92 coup against President Zviad Gamsakhurdia and was then given the role of interior forces and, later, semi-official status as the 'Georgian Rescue Corps'. Ioseliani sat in parliament with armed Mkhedrioni men as 'bodyguards'. Members ran roadblocks where drivers were 'fined', and were accused of extortion, robbery and drug smuggling. In 1995 Eduard Shevardnadze ordered the group disarmed; it was outlawed and Ioseliani was jailed until an amnesty in 2000.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Mkhedrioni' (citing Jamestown Foundation and contemporary reports)
inside: An armed gang that helped topple the president was taken inside the state as its interior forces, and its members used that position for extortion.

n: Tambov gang's Kumarin ran St Petersburg's city fuel company
rank: Deputy president, Petersburg Fuel Company
d: The Tambov gang, a St Petersburg crime group, got control of the city's main fuel trader. The Petersburg Fuel Company (PTK) was formed in 1994 and administered by the city government; from 1998 to 1999 its deputy president was Vladimir Kumarin, named as the gang's leader. In 2001 Russia's interior minister Boris Gryzlov said the gang controlled up to 100 industrial enterprises, including PTK. The city legislature's speaker, Viktor Novosyolov, was alleged to be close to Kumarin before he was killed in a 1999 car bombing. Kumarin, jailed for racketeering in 1990–93, was sentenced in November 2009 to 14 years. A Spanish case against the gang's Spanish branch ended in acquittals in 2018.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Tambov Gang' (citing Vedomosti, 2009, and Gryzlov statement, 2001)
inside: The Tambov crime group's named leader became deputy president of St Petersburg's city fuel company, one of up to 100 enterprises the gang controlled.

n: Crime groups controlled AvtoVAZ car sales through its managers
rank: AvtoVAZ management and dealer network
d: Criminal groups got control of sales at AvtoVAZ, maker of Lada cars and then Russia's largest carmaker, through close ties with part of its management. By 1995 car sales, distribution and spare parts were controlled by criminal organisations, which were also used to control workers and break strikes; some dealerships simply stole cars from the factory. Operation Cyclone, a 1997 investigation by Russia's Interior Ministry, found evidence that gangsters connected to AvtoVAZ had committed at least 65 murders of managers, dealers and rivals. By late 1996 the company was Russia's largest tax debtor, owing $2.4 billion, and workers went unpaid for months.
cite: Wikipedia, 'AvtoVAZ' (citing Interior Ministry Operation Cyclone, 1997)
inside: Crime groups took control of AvtoVAZ car sales through ties with its managers, and the company was used to break strikes while cars were stolen.

n: Mogilevich alleged to control Ukraine's gas middleman RosUkrEnergo
rank: RosUkrEnergo (sole gas importer)
d: Ukrainian politicians and US diplomats suspected that the crime boss Semion Mogilevich, once on the FBI's Ten Most Wanted list, controlled the company that supplied all of Ukraine's imported gas. RosUkrEnergo was half-owned by Russia's Gazprom and half by a group of Dmytro Firtash and Ivan Fursin; from 2006 to January 2009 it supplied all of Ukraine's gas imports from Russia and Central Asia and resold them to the state firm Naftogaz, earning over $785 million in profit in 2006. In November 2006 Yulia Tymoshenko said it was controlled by Mogilevich, and leaked US cables showed diplomats shared her suspicion. Mogilevich denies any link. A January 2009 deal cut RosUkrEnergo out.
cite: Wikipedia, 'RosUkrEnergo' and 'Semion Mogilevich' (citing leaked US diplomatic cables)
inside: Ukrainian politicians and US diplomats suspected a crime boss secretly controlled the company that supplied all of Ukraine's imported gas and earned large profits from it.

n: Hong Kong police officer Godber's flight exposed police graft syndicates
org_label: Illegal gambling, vice and drug operators
rank: Royal Hong Kong Police senior officers
d: In colonial Hong Kong, operators of illegal gambling, prostitution and drugs paid police, and stations were organised to profit from them. The system came to light in 1973 when Chief Superintendent Peter Godber, deputy commander for Kowloon, was found to hold about HK$4.3 million in overseas accounts and fled to London when asked to explain it. The public outcry led to the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) being founded on 15 February 1974, reporting to the Governor rather than the police. Godber was extradited and jailed for four years in 1975. In 1978, 119 officers were made to leave the force and 24 were held on conspiracy charges.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Independent Commission Against Corruption (Hong Kong)' and 'Peter Godber'
inside: Gambling, vice and drug operators paid senior Hong Kong police, so whole stations were organised to protect and profit from their trade.

n: Smuggler Lai Changxing bought Xiamen's officials and a police vice-minister
rank: Vice-minister of public security and Xiamen officials
d: A smuggling ring based in Xiamen corrupted hundreds of Chinese officials, up to a vice-minister of public security. Lai Changxing's Yuanhua Group was believed to have smuggled about US$10 billion of goods, including luxury cars and oil, into China, avoiding US$3.6 billion in taxes and fees. Officials were won over with bribes, banquets, jobs for relatives and blackmail; those named included Li Jizhou, deputy minister for public security. About 300 officials were put on trial and 14 people were executed in connection with the case. Lai fled to Canada in August 1999, was deported in July 2011 after a 12-year fight, and was sentenced to life in May 2012.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Lai Changxing' (citing Xinhua and Canadian court records)
inside: A smuggling ring bribed and blackmailed hundreds of officials up to a vice-minister of public security, so the state let billions in goods through untaxed.

n: Saigon gang boss Nam Cam bought a police chief and a top prosecutor
rank: Police chief, deputy chief prosecutor, state radio head
d: Truong Van Cam, known as Năm Cam, ran Ho Chi Minh City's gambling dens, extortion and loan-sharking for about 15 years with officials on his side. At his 2003 trial, then Vietnam's largest, about 155 defendants included 13 senior police officers and two expelled members of the Communist Party's Central Committee. Phạm Sỹ Chiến, former deputy national chief prosecutor, and Trần Mai Hạnh, former head of state radio, were found guilty of taking bribes from Cam. Bùi Quốc Huy, city police chief in 1996–2001, was found guilty of negligence that enabled Cam's operations. Cam was executed in June 2004 for ordering a rival's killing in 2000.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Năm Cam' (citing 2003 trial reporting)
inside: A gang boss paid a deputy chief prosecutor, senior police officers and a state radio head, so the authorities protected his crime operations.

n: Afghan counter-narcotics chief Daud accused of protecting smugglers
rank: Deputy Interior Minister for Counter-narcotics
d: The official in charge of fighting Afghanistan's drug trade was accused of working for it. General Mohammad Daud Daud, a former commander under Ahmad Shah Massoud, became Afghanistan's Deputy Minister of Interior for Counter-narcotics and head of its Counter Narcotics Police. A 2009 Globe and Mail report and two books accused him of involvement in the narcotics trade and of using his post to give smugglers safe passage. His campaigns were also credited with cutting poppy cultivation in some provinces. He was never charged. Daud was killed in a bombing in Taloqan on 28 May 2011, claimed by the Taliban.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Mohammad Daud Daud' (citing The Globe and Mail, 2009)
inside: The official in charge of fighting Afghanistan's drug trade was accused of using his post to give smugglers safe passage.

n: Brothels and casinos paid Queensland's police commissioner $700,000
who: Brothel, SP bookmaker and casino operators
rank: Queensland Police Commissioner
d: Operators of brothels, illegal casinos and off-course 'SP' bookmakers paid Queensland's top police officer to protect them. The Fitzgerald Inquiry (1987–89) found long-term police and political corruption; detective Jack Herbert, the 'bagman' who collected bribes for Commissioner Terry Lewis from 1980, became its key witness. A jury found Lewis, commissioner from 1976 to 1987, had accepted bribes totalling $700,000 to protect these businesses and to block legal poker machines. He was sentenced to 14 years and stripped of his knighthood in 1993. Premier Joh Bjelke-Petersen resigned, ministers were jailed, and the inquiry led to the Criminal Justice Commission, a standing anti-corruption body.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Fitzgerald Inquiry' and 'Terry Lewis (police officer)' (citing Fitzgerald report, 1989)
inside: Brothel, casino and bookmaking operators paid Queensland's police commissioner to protect their businesses and to block legal poker machines.

n: Drug dealers paid Sydney's Kings Cross detectives, royal commission finds
rank: NSW Police Kings Cross detectives and Drug Squad
d: Drug traffickers in Sydney's Kings Cross paid regular cash to the detectives meant to police them. The Wood Royal Commission (1994–97) examined whether corruption in the New South Wales Police was 'systemic and entrenched'. Detective Trevor Haken, who collected payments from dealers including Bill Bayeh, agreed to work for the commission; recordings from his car contradicted detectives' sworn denials in 1995. The commission found hundreds of cases of bribery, drug dealing and evidence tampering in the Kings Cross detective division, and specialist units including the Drug Squad were implicated. Hundreds of officers were forced out, the police commissioner resigned, and its staff formed the Police Integrity Commission.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Wood Royal Commission' (citing the Royal Commission into the NSW Police Service final report, 1997)
inside: Drug traffickers paid regular cash to the Kings Cross detectives meant to police them, so those detectives protected the drug trade.

n: NSW Premier Askin alleged to take weekly payoffs from Abe Saffron
org_label: Abe Saffron and Sydney crime syndicates
rank: Premier of New South Wales and police commissioner
d: Sydney's organised crime figures were alleged to have paid the premier of New South Wales and his police commissioner. After Sir Robert Askin, premier from 1965 to 1975, died in 1981, the National Times ran 'Askin: friend of organised crime', and David Hickie's book The Prince and the Premier alleged long-running payoffs, with Police Commissioner Norman Allan assisting. The Australian Taxation Office found that much of Askin's estate came from undisclosed income. In 2008 Alan Saffron, son of the crime boss Abe Saffron, wrote that his father paid Askin and Allan A$5,000 to $10,000 a week for years for illegal liquor, prostitution and gambling. None of this was tested in court.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Robert Askin' (citing National Times, 1981; Hickie; Alan Saffron, 2008)
inside: A crime boss was alleged to have paid the premier and police commissioner weekly for years to protect his liquor, prostitution and gambling businesses.

n: Vohra report: crime syndicates ran a 'parallel government' in India
rank: Politicians, police and civil servants
d: An official Indian report found crime syndicates had got inside politics and the civil service. After the March 1993 Bombay bombings, the government asked former Home Secretary N. N. Vohra to examine the links between criminals, politicians and officials, starting from intelligence on Dawood Ibrahim's gang. His October 1993 report said criminal networks were 'virtually running a parallel government', protected by politicians of all parties and by officials, with criminals elected to local bodies, state assemblies and Parliament. It said agencies kept such information to themselves and recommended a single point to collect it. Its annexes were never published; in 1997 the Supreme Court recommended a high-level committee to pursue prosecutions.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Vohra Report'
inside: An official report found crime syndicates protected by politicians and officials of all parties and placed in elected bodies, running a 'parallel government'.

n: Customs and police bribed to land RDX for the 1993 Bombay bombings
rank: Customs and police officers, Raigad coast
d: Smugglers working for Dawood Ibrahim's crime syndicate, D-Company, paid customs and police officers to let about 3,000 kg of RDX explosive and weapons land at Shekhadi on the Raigad coast in February 1993. The explosives were used in the Bombay bombings of 12 March 1993. A special anti-terror (TADA) court convicted the officials in 2006–07: assistant customs commissioner R. K. Singh took over ₹780,000 and got nine years; customs superintendents and an inspector got seven to eight years; police sub-inspector Vijay Patil got life; and four constables got six years. Senior customs officer S. N. Thapa was also given life. Dawood Ibrahim and Tiger Memon have never been tried.
cite: Wikipedia, '1993 Bombay bombings' (citing TADA court verdicts, 2006–07)
inside: D-Company's smugglers paid customs and police officers to let explosives and weapons land on the coast, the explosives later used in the Bombay bombings.

n: Nepali minister Mirza Dilshad Beg tied to Dawood Ibrahim's D-Company
rank: Nepali MP and minister
d: A member of Nepal's parliament who held ministerial posts was reported to work with Dawood Ibrahim's Indian crime syndicate, D-Company. Mirza Dilshad Beg, born in India, was elected from Kapilvastu in 1994, held posts in two governments and won two terms for the Rastriya Prajatantra Party. Reports linked him to D-Company and its lieutenant Chhota Shakeel, and to Pakistan's ISI intelligence agency, with activities including gun-running, drug trafficking, document forgery and sheltering fugitives. He was shot dead in Kathmandu on 29 June 1998; the rival gangster Chhota Rajan claimed the killing in an India Today interview, saying Beg was spreading terror in India for the ISI.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Mirza Dilshad Beg' (citing India Today, 1998)
inside: A Nepali MP and minister was reported to work for Dawood Ibrahim's D-Company and Pakistan's ISI, in gun-running, forgery and sheltering fugitives.

n: Tajikistan's drug agency chief Mirzoyev jailed, drug ties alleged
rank: Head of the Drug Control Agency
d: The head of Tajikistan's Drug Control Agency, on the main route for Afghan heroin north, was charged with drug trafficking. General Ghaffor Mirzoyev had commanded the Presidential Guard from 1995 and later ran the drug agency. He was arrested in August 2004 with 15 supporters and charged with abuse of power, seizing state property and drug trafficking; about 3,000 weapons were found in Drug Control Agency stores. He was sentenced to life and stripped of his rank. Many said the arrests were political, while critics who accepted he was a corrupt official also said he had links to the narcotics trade.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Ghaffor Mirzoyev'
inside: The head of Tajikistan's drug agency was charged with drug trafficking, and critics said the official meant to stop the heroin trade had links to it.

n: Fugitive Djoko Tjandra bribed police generals and a prosecutor
rank: Police generals and a state prosecutor
d: A fugitive tycoon paid Indonesian police generals and a prosecutor to help him escape a prison sentence. Djoko Tjandra fled in 2009, the day before the Supreme Court gave him two years over the Bank Bali scandal. In 2020, through the businessman Tommy Sumardi, he paid police Inspector General Napoleon Bonaparte and Brigadier General Prasetijo Utomo to remove his Interpol Red Notice and issue a travel letter that let him fly inside Indonesia. Prosecutor Pinangki Sirna Malasari took $500,000 for a plan to obtain a Supreme Court ruling clearing him. In 2021 Napoleon got 4.5 years, Prasetijo 3.5 years, Pinangki 10 years and Tjandra 4.5 years for bribery.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Djoko Tjandra' (citing Jakarta court verdicts, 2020–21)
inside: A fugitive tycoon paid police generals to drop his Interpol notice and give him travel papers, and a prosecutor to seek a court ruling clearing him.

n: Illegal jueteng gambling bosses paid President Estrada ₱5m a month
rank: President of the Philippines
d: Operators of jueteng, an illegal numbers game run across the Philippines, were accused of paying the country's president for protection. In October 2000 Luis 'Chavit' Singson, governor of Ilocos Sur, alleged that President Joseph Estrada received 5 million pesos a month in jueteng protection money and that Singson had given him 400 million pesos in gambling profits. On 13 November 2000, 115 members of the House signed an impeachment complaint. The Senate trial collapsed in January 2001, mass protests followed, the armed forces withdrew support and Gloria Macapagal Arroyo was sworn in on 20 January 2001. Estrada was later convicted of plunder in 2007 and pardoned weeks later.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Impeachment of Joseph Estrada' and 'Joseph Estrada'
inside: Illegal jueteng operators were accused of paying the president monthly protection money, putting the head of state on the side of their gambling trade.

n: Zimbabwe's envoy Uebert Angel filmed offering gold-laundering route
rank: Ambassador-at-large and presidential envoy
d: An Al Jazeera investigation alleged that criminal money-launderers had Zimbabwe's own presidential envoy on their side. In March 2021 President Emmerson Mnangagwa appointed the preacher Uebert Angel as ambassador-at-large and presidential envoy to seek trade and investment. In 'Gold Mafia', broadcast in March 2023, undercover reporters posing as clients recorded Angel apparently offering to use his diplomatic status to bring illicit cash into Zimbabwe, swap it for mined gold and sell the gold abroad as clean money, saying 'gold we can do it right now'. Zimbabwe's Financial Intelligence Unit said in March 2023 that it found no evidence to support the claims.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Uebert Angel' (citing Al Jazeera Investigative Unit, March 2023)
inside: An undercover investigation alleged that gold launderers had the presidential envoy on their side, filmed offering his diplomatic status to move illicit cash.

n: Czech fugitive Krejčíř allegedly bought a judge and South African warders
rank: Extradition judge and prison warders
d: Radovan Krejčíř, a Czech organised-crime figure, was accused of buying his way through two countries' justice systems. In 2005 he escaped during a police raid on his villa near Prague, an escape that led Czech Police President Jiří Kolář to resign. He moved to South Africa in 2007. The Czech Republic said South Africa refused his extradition because he had bribed the judge involved. Convicted in Johannesburg of attempted murder and kidnapping, he was sentenced to 35 years in February 2016. A September 2015 cell raid found weapons, and reports said R246 million was available for an escape plan that included R1.5 million paid to three prison warders.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Radovan Krejčíř'
inside: A Czech crime figure allegedly bribed the judge handling his extradition and paid prison warders for an escape plan.

n: Executed trafficker Freddy Budiman said he paid Indonesian drug agencies
rank: Police, BNN drug agency and customs
d: An Indonesian drug trafficker on death row claimed he had worked with the agencies meant to stop him. Freddy Budiman was sentenced to death in 2012 for importing 1.4 million ecstasy pills from China, and from prison he reportedly ran a dealer network and made his own drugs, while getting preferential treatment. In 2014 he told the human rights lawyer Haris Azhar that he had asked the police, the National Narcotics Agency (BNN) and the customs directorate to bring drugs into Indonesia for him. Azhar published the account shortly before Budiman was executed on Nusa Kambangan on 29 July 2016. The claims were not tested in court.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Freddy Budiman' (citing Haris Azhar/KontraS statement, July 2016)
inside: A trafficker said the police, the narcotics agency and customs, the bodies meant to stop him, brought drugs into Indonesia for him.

n: Countrywide gave cut-price 'VIP' mortgages to US lawmakers and officials
rank: Senators, House members, Fannie Mae and agency staff
d: Countrywide Financial, then the largest US mortgage lender, gave hundreds of discounted 'VIP' home loans to members of Congress, their staff and other government employees, including staff of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, the state-backed firms that bought its loans. A three-year investigation by the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, led by Darrell Issa, reported on 5 July 2012 that the programme was used to buy influence in Washington and to protect Countrywide's special arrangement with Fannie Mae, which gave it fee discounts. Recipients named included Senators Christopher Dodd and Kent Conrad and four House members. Countrywide's chief, Angelo Mozilo, called it another channel to compete for loans.
cite: House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, 'How Countrywide used its VIP loan program to influence Washington policymakers' (5 July 2012); CNNMoney (5 July 2012)
inside: A House inquiry found the mortgage lender gave cut-price loans to lawmakers and staff of the state-backed firms that bought its loans, to buy influence and protect its fee discounts.

n: Citigroup's lobbyists wrote most of a House bill on bank derivatives
rank: House Financial Services Committee bill
d: Citigroup, one of the largest US banks, drafted much of a bill passed by the House Financial Services Committee in 2013 to weaken a rule it opposed. The 'push-out' rule in the Dodd-Frank Act, passed after the 2008 crash, required banks to move certain risky derivatives trades out of units backed by federal deposit insurance. On 23 May 2013 the New York Times reported that Citigroup's recommendations appeared in more than 70 lines of the committee's 85-line Swaps Regulatory Improvement Act (H.R. 992). The committee approved the bill 53 to 6. It would have let banks keep a wider range of derivatives in their insured arms.
cite: New York Times (23 May 2013), as reported by Mother Jones (24 May 2013); NPR, 'When lobbyists literally write the bill' (11 November 2013)
inside: Citigroup's own drafting made up more than 70 of the 85 lines of a House committee bill weakening a rule the bank opposed.

n: JPMorgan's chief sat on the New York Fed board as it rescued his bank's deals
rank: Board of directors, Federal Reserve Bank of New York
d: Jamie Dimon, chief executive of JPMorgan Chase, sat on the board of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York while the Fed gave his bank emergency help during the 2008 crisis. Regional Fed banks are partly governed by directors drawn from the banks they oversee. A Government Accountability Office audit released on 19 October 2011 found at least 18 current and former Fed directors were tied to banks and firms that received emergency Fed loans. JPMorgan received $29 billion in financing to take over Bear Stearns in 2008, acted as a clearing bank for Fed lending programmes, and was given an 18-month exemption from risk-based capital rules. The audit called for tighter conflict-of-interest rules for Fed directors.
cite: US Government Accountability Office, GAO-12-18 (19 October 2011), summarised in Sen. Bernie Sanders press release; ABC News (October 2011)
inside: JPMorgan's chief sat on the board of the regional Fed that oversees banks while the Fed gave his bank emergency financing and a capital-rule exemption.

n: Payday-lender donor Mulvaney ran the US consumer finance watchdog
rank: Acting Director, Consumer Financial Protection Bureau
d: Mick Mulvaney, who received nearly $63,000 from payday lenders for his congressional campaigns, was named acting director of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), the US agency that polices lenders, in November 2017. At the bureau he froze new investigations, slowed existing ones and scaled back enforcement against payday, car-loan and other lenders. In April 2018 he told about 1,300 bankers at an American Bankers Association conference that as a congressman he had met lobbyists who gave him money and mostly not those who did not. Senator Elizabeth Warren asked for an ethics inquiry into whether donations shaped CFPB decisions.
cite: CNBC (24 April 2018); Office of Sen. Elizabeth Warren, letter to Mulvaney (27 April 2018)
inside: A congressman funded by payday lenders took charge of the agency that polices lenders and scaled back its investigations and enforcement against them.

n: Japan's banks paid Finance Ministry inspectors for advance tip-offs
org_label: Sanwa Bank, Asahi Bank affiliate and other banks
rank: Finance Ministry bank inspection office
d: Japanese banks entertained and paid Ministry of Finance bank inspectors in return for advance notice of inspections. On 26 January 1998 Tokyo prosecutors arrested Koichi Miyagawa, chief of the ministry's finance inspection office, and his colleague Toshimi Taniuchi. Miyagawa allegedly took ¥1,804,838 in bribes from an Asahi Bank affiliate plus a ¥4.4 million discount on a flat; Taniuchi allegedly took ¥1.61 million in meals and golf from Sanwa Bank. In return they told banks the dates of inspections and which branches would be checked. Prosecutors raided the ministry and several banks, and Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka resigned two days later.
cite: Japan Times (26, 27 and 28 January 1998); Spokesman-Review (28 January 1998)
inside: Banks paid finance ministry inspectors, who in return told them in advance when inspections would happen and which branches would be checked.

n: Latvian bank's owners bribed central bank chief and ECB member
rank: Governor, Bank of Latvia; ECB Governing Council
d: Shareholders of Trasta Komercbanka, a Riga bank, paid Ilmārs Rimšēvičs, governor of the Bank of Latvia and a member of the European Central Bank's Governing Council, for help with Latvia's financial regulator. In 2010 a shareholder offered him a paid fishing trip to Kamchatka; in 2012 two shareholders approached him again and he asked for €500,000, of which €250,000 was paid. Bank representatives later went to Latvia's anti-corruption bureau, which detained Rimšēvičs in February 2018. On 20 December 2023 the Riga District Court sentenced him to six years in prison and confiscated property; businessman Māris Martinsons, the go-between, got five years.
cite: LSM, 'Former Latvian central bank governor Rimšēvičs sentenced to 6 years in prison' (20 December 2023); Baltic Times (December 2023)
inside: Bank shareholders paid the central bank governor, who sat on the ECB's governing council, for help with Latvia's financial regulator.

n: Banker Ilan Shor paid Moldova's ex-PM Filat to let him take a state bank
rank: Former Prime Minister; government decision on Banca de Economii
d: Ilan Shor, a businessman named by investigators as the main figure in Moldova's $1 billion bank fraud, testified that he paid former prime minister Vlad Filat $250 million. About $190 million was for the government not to use its pre-emptive rights in Banca de Economii, the state-controlled savings bank, which let Shor's investors take control of it. The $1 billion vanished from Banca de Economii, Unibank and Banca Socială in 2014, a loss equal to about 12 percent of Moldova's GDP. On 27 June 2016 a Chișinău court sentenced Filat to nine years for corruption and abuse of office. The central bank governor resigned in 2015 saying politicians had interfered in the inquiry.
cite: bne IntelliNews, 'Moldovan ex-premier Filat jailed for 9 years in $1bn bank fraud case' (June 2016); Wikipedia, '2014 Moldovan bank fraud scandal'
inside: A businessman paid the former prime minister so the government would not use its rights in the state savings bank, letting his investors take control.

n: Tycoon Truong My Lan paid Vietnam's bank inspection chief $5.2m
rank: Head of inspection and supervision, State Bank of Vietnam
d: Truong My Lan, chair of the property group Van Thinh Phat, paid the head of the State Bank of Vietnam's inspection and supervision department to protect Saigon Commercial Bank (SCB), which Lan secretly controlled. The State Bank is Vietnam's central bank and banking supervisor. Do Thi Nhan received $5.2 million through an intermediary after meeting Lan, then told her inspection team to adjust data and keep SCB off the list of banks under special monitoring, though she knew its condition. On 11 April 2024 a court sentenced Nhan to life in prison and Lan to death, alongside about 85 other defendants.
cite: The Investor (Vietnam), 'Former State Bank of Vietnam inspection chief receives life sentence in Van Thinh Phat scandal' (11 April 2024); RFA (11 April 2024)
inside: A tycoon paid the central bank's chief inspector, who then had her team adjust data and keep the bank the tycoon secretly controlled off the watch list.

n: Financier Xiao Jianhua paid Chinese officials to evade financial supervision
rank: Financial regulators and officials
d: Xiao Jianhua, a Chinese-Canadian billionaire, and his conglomerate Tomorrow Holdings, which owned banks, insurers and brokerages, gave Chinese officials shares, property, cash and other assets worth more than 680 million yuan (about $100 million) between 2001 and 2021. A Shanghai court said on 19 August 2022 that the payments were meant to 'evade financial supervision and seek illegitimate interests'. Xiao was convicted of bribery, illegally taking public deposits and misusing entrusted funds, and sentenced to 13 years; Tomorrow Holdings was fined a record 55.03 billion yuan ($8.1 billion). Xiao had not been seen in public since 2017, and in July 2020 regulators seized nine of the group's financial institutions.
cite: Al Jazeera / Reuters (19 August 2022); NBC News (19 August 2022)
inside: A financier's conglomerate gave officials shares, property and cash worth over 680 million yuan to evade financial supervision.

n: Goldman bankers bribed Malaysian and Abu Dhabi officials for 1MDB bonds
rank: Officials of Malaysia's 1MDB fund and Abu Dhabi state funds
d: Goldman Sachs bankers paid bribes to officials in Malaysia and Abu Dhabi to win the bond business of 1MDB, a Malaysian state investment fund. Between 2011 and 2013 Goldman sold about $6.5 billion of 1MDB bonds and earned about $600 million in fees, around ten times the normal rate; billions were then stolen from the fund. Tim Leissner, Goldman's Southeast Asia chairman, pleaded guilty in 2018 to paying the bribes and was sentenced to two years in May 2025. His deputy Roger Ng was convicted in 2022. In October 2020 Goldman agreed to pay $2.9 billion to authorities in the US, Malaysia, Singapore and the UK, and its Malaysian arm pleaded guilty.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Goldman Sachs' and 'Tim Leissner'; US Department of Justice (October 2020); Wikipedia, '1MDB scandal'
inside: Goldman bankers paid officials at Malaysia's state fund and Abu Dhabi's state funds so that those officials gave Goldman the fund's bond business.

n: National City Bank took Haiti's gold, central bank and finances for decades
who: National City Bank of New York
rank: Haiti's national bank and public finances
d: National City Bank of New York, forerunner of Citigroup, took control of Haiti's national bank and, with US troops, of its public finances. It bought into the bank from 1910 and owned all its shares by 1920. Its lobbyist Roger Farnham pressed Washington to intervene, and in December 1914 eight US Marines removed $500,000 in gold from the bank to a Wall Street vault. US forces occupied Haiti from 1915 for 19 years. A 1922 New York loan, approved by a president the US installed, came with US management of Haiti's finances until repaid; over a decade about a quarter of revenue went on debts held by National City and an affiliate. US financial control lasted until 1947.
cite: New York Times, 'Invade Haiti, Wall Street urged. The U.S. obliged.' ('The Ransom' series, 2022), republished by bdnews24
inside: A New York bank came to own Haiti's national bank and, with US control of its finances, a quarter of revenue went on debts held by that bank.

n: European bondholders took over Ottoman tax collection
rank: Ottoman tax and customs revenues
d: European holders of Ottoman government bonds, chiefly British and French, got their own body placed inside the Ottoman state to collect its revenue. The Ottoman Empire had stopped paying its foreign debt, and the Decree of Muharrem of 15 October 1881 created the Ottoman Public Debt Administration. Bondholders from Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Austria and the Netherlands, along with Ottoman bondholders, were represented on it, and it was given special rights to collect various taxes and customs duties inside the empire to pay creditors. It turned part of the empire's tax system into an agency run for foreign lenders.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Ottoman public debt'; Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Decree of Muharrem'
inside: The creditors' own Public Debt Administration sat inside the Ottoman state and collected taxes and customs duties to pay foreign bondholders.

n: Creditor powers placed commissioners over Egypt's debt payments
rank: Egyptian public finances
d: Egypt's European creditors placed their own commissioners over its finances through the Caisse de la Dette Publique (Public Debt Fund), set up by a decree of Khedive Isma'il on 2 May 1876 after Egypt fell behind on its loans. The commissioners represented Austria-Hungary, France and Italy, joined by Britain in 1877 and Russia and Germany in 1885. Its work covered collecting debt payments, how taxes were raised and what Egypt could afford to pay. Alongside it France and Britain ran 'dual control' of Egypt's finances until Britain occupied the country alone in 1882. The Caisse lasted about 64 years, until an Anglo-Egyptian agreement abolished it on 17 July 1940.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Caisse de la Dette Publique'
inside: Creditor powers placed their commissioners inside Egypt's finances to collect debt payments and decide how taxes were raised for the lenders.

n: Six creditor powers' commission ran Greek tax revenue for 38 years
rank: Greek state monopolies and taxes
d: Greece's creditor states placed a six-member International Financial Commission inside the Greek state to take its revenues and repay loans. Greece had declared bankruptcy in 1893 and then lost the 1897 war with the Ottoman Empire, which required reparations and a new loan of 151.3 million francs. Law 2519 of 23 February 1898 gave the commission, representing Britain, France, Austria-Hungary, Germany, Russia and Italy, control of the salt, oil, match, playing-card, cigarette-paper and Naxos emery monopolies, the tobacco tax, stamp duties and Piraeus port duties. It also assessed state agencies' tax collection. It stayed in Athens until 1936 and in the 1920s handled League of Nations lending.
cite: Wikipedia, 'International Financial Commission'
inside: The creditor powers' commission sat in Athens and took control of Greek state monopolies, taxes and port duties to repay their loans.

n: Dawes Plan put creditor nominees on half the Reichsbank's board
org_label: Allied creditor states and Wall Street lenders (Dawes Plan)
rank: Reichsbank board; German national railway
d: Under the Dawes Plan, Germany's First World War creditors placed their own representatives inside its central bank and railway to secure reparation payments. Germany had been declared in default in January 1923. The Reichstag passed the plan on 29 August 1924 and it took effect on 1 September. The Reichsbank was reorganised under creditor supervision and made independent of the German government, with a board of seven creditor-state representatives and seven Germans, and the national railway became a corporation under creditor supervision. Germany received an 800 million Reichsmark loan as the central bank's capital, about half raised through Wall Street bond issues. The Young Plan replaced it in 1929.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Dawes Plan'
inside: Creditor-state representatives took half the seats on Germany's central bank board and supervised its railway so they would serve reparation payments.

n: New York bankers took Nicaragua's national bank, railway and customs
rank: National Bank, National Railway and customs of Nicaragua
d: New York bankers, backed by the US government, took control of Nicaragua's main financial institutions in exchange for loans. Around the 1911 Knox-Castillo proposal they lent $15 million and later advanced another $1.5 million, took Nicaragua's National Bank as collateral and gained a 51 percent stake in the National Railway, while President Taft appointed the collector of Nicaragua's customs. When President Adolfo Díaz faced a revolt in July 1912 and asked for help, US Marines landed in August 1912; they stayed until 1925, returned in 1926 and remained until 1935. US diplomatic records describe the loan contracts with American bankers.
cite: Historical Text Archive, 'Nicaragua and U.S. intervention'; US Office of the Historian, Foreign Relations of the United States 1913, 'Financial affairs: conclusion of a loan contract with American bankers'
inside: New York bankers took Nicaragua's national bank and a majority of its railway, and the US president appointed the collector of its customs.

n: IMF and World Bank placed foreign co-signers inside Liberia's state firms
rank: Co-signatory controllers in state enterprises
d: Under the Governance and Economic Management Assistance Program (GEMAP), launched in September 2005, foreign financial controllers were placed inside Liberia's main state enterprises with power to co-sign their major transactions. The programme was designed and funded by the IMF, the World Bank, the US Treasury and USAID, and agreed between Liberia's government and an international contact group, after a 2005 European Commission audit of the central bank and five state firms. Non-Liberian controllers sat in the National Port Authority, the Liberia Petroleum Refining Company, Roberts International Airport and the Forestry Development Authority. Signing authority returned to the Liberian government in October 2009.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Governance and Economic Management Assistance Program'
inside: Foreign controllers designed and funded by the IMF, World Bank and US agencies sat inside Liberia's main state firms and co-signed their major transactions.

n: Jakob Fugger's money bought Charles V's election as emperor
rank: Prince-electors of the Holy Roman Empire
d: Jakob Fugger, an Augsburg banker, financed the payments that made Charles of Habsburg Holy Roman Emperor. More than 850,000 guilders went to the prince-electors, the seven rulers who chose the emperor; Fugger supplied about 550,000, the Welser house about 150,000 and Italian bankers the rest. The rival, Francis I of France, had offered 300,000. Charles was elected unanimously on 28 July 1519. By 1521 he owed Fugger more than 600,000 guilders and repaid part by giving his firm the silver and copper mines of Tyrol, and in 1523 a quicksilver concession at Almadén. At the 1523 Imperial Diet Fugger reminded Charles that he could not have won the crown without Fugger's help.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Jakob Fugger'
inside: A banker's money paid the prince-electors to choose Charles as emperor, and Charles then repaid him by handing his firm state mines.

n: Banca Romana's secret loans to Italian politicians toppled Giolitti
rank: Prime ministers and parliament
d: Banca Romana, one of Italy's note-issuing banks, lent money, often interest-free, to politicians for their election campaigns and to newspapers, in return for favours. Under its governor Bernardo Tanlongo it had 135 million lire in notes in circulation against a legal limit of 75 million, and had printed another 40 million in duplicate-numbered notes. The bank failed in January 1893. Documents implicated Prime Minister Giovanni Giolitti, who had tried to make Tanlongo a senator, which would have given him immunity, and former premier Francesco Crispi. Giolitti resigned on 24 November 1893. Tanlongo was acquitted in 1894, but the scandal led to the founding of the Bank of Italy.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Banca Romana scandal'
inside: A note-issuing bank lent money to politicians for their campaigns in return for favours, and the prime minister tried to make its governor a senator.

n: Second Bank of the United States paid and lent to members of Congress
who: Second Bank of the United States
rank: Members of Congress
d: The Second Bank of the United States, a privately run national bank headed by Nicholas Biddle, used loans and retainer fees to win support in Congress for renewing its charter. Senator Daniel Webster reportedly received an annual fee for defending the bank. Senator George Poindexter of Mississippi received a $10,000 loan after backing renewal, and another $8,000 while the first was unpaid, in breach of the bank's charter. The bank also gave money to Henry Clay and to pro-bank newspaper editors before the 1832 election. Congress passed the renewal, but President Andrew Jackson vetoed it on 10 July 1832 and in 1833 removed federal deposits from the bank.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Bank War'
inside: The national bank paid fees and loans to members of Congress to win their votes for renewing its charter, which Congress then passed.

n: Panama Canal financiers paid off French deputies and a minister
rank: Deputies and a minister
d: The French Panama Canal Company, through the financiers Jacques de Reinach and Cornelius Herz, paid bribes to members of parliament and a minister to get approval to raise money from the public. Ferdinand de Lesseps was accused of paying bribes in 1888 to permit a stock issue; Reinach handled right-wing deputies and Herz the radicals. When the company collapsed, about 800,000 French investors lost around 1.8 billion gold francs. Before his death in 1892 Reinach gave a list of bribed deputies to the newspaper La Libre Parole, and inquiries found 104 legislators involved. Former minister Charles Baïhaut was sentenced to five years; most others were acquitted.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Panama scandals'
inside: The canal company's financiers bribed deputies and a minister to approve its raising money from the public.

n: Financier Stavisky's protection reached France's prime minister
rank: Prime minister; courts
d: Alexandre Stavisky, a financier who sold worthless bonds tied to the municipal pawnshop of Bayonne, had protection from people in the French state. His fraud trial, opened in 1927, was postponed again and again, and he was granted bail 19 times. He fled in December 1933 and was found dead in Chamonix on 8 January 1934. His dealings with many officials then came to light, and Prime Minister Camille Chautemps resigned after it emerged that he had shielded Stavisky. Right-wing protests followed; on 6 February 1934 police fired on a crowd in Paris and killed 17 people, and Chautemps's successor Édouard Daladier was also forced out.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Stavisky Affair'
inside: A fraudster financier had protection from people in the French state, with his trial postponed repeatedly and the prime minister shielding him.

n: Bank of Crete owner Koskotas paid Greek ministers; two convicted
rank: Prime Minister and ministers
d: George Koskotas, owner of the Bank of Crete, said he paid Greek ministers and Prime Minister Andreas Papandreou in return for state money. He claimed PASOK government figures ordered state companies to deposit about $35 million in his bank, which went on bribes and media purchases, and that over $200 million missing from the bank was taken with ministers' help. On 28 September 1989 parliament indicted Papandreou and four ministers, the first indictment of a Greek prime minister. In 1992 a special court acquitted Papandreou by seven votes to six, but sentenced former finance minister Dimitris Tsovolas to two and a half years and George Petsos to ten months. Koskotas got 25 years.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Koskotas scandal'
inside: A bank owner said he paid the prime minister and ministers, who in return had state companies deposit public money in his bank.

n: Pakistan's spy agency paid politicians through Mehran Bank in 1990
rank: Politicians in the 1990 election
d: Pakistan's military intelligence agency, the ISI, used Mehran Bank and its owner Yunus Habib to pass money to politicians in the 1990 election to stop Benazir Bhutto winning. Payments of up to 140 million rupees were reportedly made through Habib, authorised by ISI chief Lieutenant-General Asad Durrani, in a scheme started by army chief General Mirza Aslam Beg. The officers formed the Islami Jamhoori Ittehad alliance with Nawaz Sharif as leader. Mehran Bank later collapsed and Habib was jailed for fraud in 1995. On 19 October 2012 Pakistan's Supreme Court, ruling on a petition by Air Marshal Asghar Khan, found Beg and Durrani had violated the constitution.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Asghar Khan case'
inside: The ISI spy agency passed money through a private bank to chosen politicians in the 1990 election to build an alliance and stop Benazir Bhutto winning.

n: Golkar treasurer's firm drew $80m from Indonesia's bank rescue agency
rank: Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency (IBRA)
d: Era Giat Prima, a debt-collecting firm owned by tycoon Djoko Tjandra and run by Setya Novanto, deputy treasurer of the ruling Golkar party and part of President B.J. Habibie's re-election team, used officials of the Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency (IBRA) to extract a fee from Bank Bali. IBRA held Bank Bali's Rp904.6 billion claim on two failed banks; its deputies approved payment on 1 June 1999 while its chairman was abroad, and the firm took Rp546 billion (about $80 million). Part went to Habibie's campaign. After the scandal broke the fee was returned, parliament rejected Habibie's accountability speech, and an IBRA deputy, Pande Lubis, was later jailed for four years.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Bank Bali scandal'
inside: A party treasurer's debt-collecting firm used officials of the bank rescue agency to approve a payment that gave it about $80 million.

n: IMF official Ouattara was pressed on Côte d'Ivoire as its economic chief
rank: Prime Minister
d: Alassane Ouattara, director of the IMF's African Department from 1984 to 1988 and then governor of the regional central bank BCEAO, was placed at the head of Côte d'Ivoire's economic policy under IMF pressure. In April 1990 the IMF pressed President Félix Houphouët-Boigny to accept him as chair of a committee on economic stabilisation, and on 7 November 1990 he became prime minister, still under the IMF's programme. He later returned to the IMF as Deputy Managing Director from 1994 to 1999, and has been president of Côte d'Ivoire since April 2011.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Alassane Ouattara'
inside: The IMF pressed for its own former department director to be put in charge of Côte d'Ivoire's economic policy, where he ran the country under its programme.

n: Croatia's Sanader accused of Hypo bank commission; later acquitted
rank: Deputy Foreign Minister
d: Ivo Sanader, later Croatia's prime minister, was charged with taking a commission of nearly $695,000 from Austria's Hypo Alpe-Adria-Bank for arranging a loan from it in 1995, when he was deputy foreign minister. Croatia's anti-corruption office USKOK investigated payments from Hypo in the 1990s. In November 2012 he was sentenced to ten years in a combined verdict covering the Hypo case and a separate MOL case; the Supreme Court cut the term in 2014, and the Constitutional Court quashed the verdict in 2015 over procedural errors. On retrial he was acquitted in the Hypo case, and in 2025 the High Criminal Court upheld the acquittal.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Ivo Sanader'
inside: Prosecutors charged that an Austrian bank paid a deputy foreign minister a commission for arranging a state loan from that bank; he was later acquitted.

n: Chinese energy firm's NGO paid ex-UN Assembly president Kutesa $500,000
rank: President of the UN General Assembly (just ended term)
d: Patrick Ho, head of a Hong Kong charity funded by the Shanghai oil conglomerate CEFC China Energy, used the charity's standing at the United Nations to reach Sam Kutesa, Uganda's foreign minister, who had just finished a term as President of the UN General Assembly. Ho had $500,000 wired through New York to an account Kutesa named, dressed up as a gift to a charitable foundation, and Kutesa later steered a Ugandan bank acquisition towards CEFC. Ho also offered Chad's president $2 million in cash hidden in gift boxes for oil rights, which was refused. The charity held special consultative status with the UN Economic and Social Council. A New York jury convicted Ho of bribery and money laundering on 5 December 2018.
cite: US Department of Justice, SDNY press release, 5 Dec 2018; OCCRP, Dec 2018
inside: A Chinese oil company's charity paid a former UN Assembly president, who then steered a Ugandan bank acquisition towards that company.

n: Saddam's Iraq gave the UN Oil-for-Food chief oil allocations, inquiry found
rank: Executive Director, UN Oil-for-Food Programme
d: Saddam Hussein's government is accused of buying the head of the United Nations programme meant to control its oil sales. The Oil-for-Food Programme, launched in December 1996, let sanctioned Iraq sell oil to buy food and medicine under UN supervision. Its director, Benon Sevan, solicited oil allocations from Iraq between 1998 and 2001 for a small trading company, African Middle East Petroleum, according to the inquiry led by former US Federal Reserve chairman Paul Volcker. Kofi Annan suspended Sevan in February 2005 and he resigned. In January 2007 US prosecutors indicted him for bribery and wire-fraud conspiracy, alleging about $160,000 in kickbacks. Sevan denied wrongdoing and stayed in Cyprus, out of reach of extradition.
cite: JURIST, Jan 2007; Fox News/AP, 5 Aug 2005 (Volcker interim findings)
inside: The Iraqi government gave oil allocations to the head of the UN programme meant to control its oil sales, according to the UN inquiry.

n: Contractors paid UN procurement officer Yakovlev nearly $1m for contracts
rank: UN procurement officer; chair of UN budget oversight committee
d: Companies seeking United Nations supply contracts paid a UN purchasing officer, the Russian Alexander Yakovlev, to help them win. The UN's inquiry into the Oil-for-Food Programme found $950,000 in illegal payments from winners of UN contracts worth $79 million, paid into an offshore account he controlled in Antigua. The UN lifted his diplomatic immunity and he pleaded guilty to conspiracy, wire fraud and money laundering in August 2005. A second Russian diplomat, Vladimir Kuznetsov, who had chaired the UN's budget oversight committee, was convicted in March 2007 of laundering Yakovlev's bribes through an offshore company he set up in 2000. The case led the UN to order a review of its procurement office.
cite: Al Jazeera, 9 Aug 2005; Fox News/AP, 7 Mar 2007; Probe International, Aug 2005
inside: Companies seeking UN contracts paid a UN purchasing officer to help them win, and a UN budget committee chair laundered the payments.

n: CIA's agent Arkady Shevchenko served as UN Under-Secretary-General
rank: UN Under-Secretary-General for Political Affairs
d: The US Central Intelligence Agency had a source in the second rank of the United Nations Secretariat. Arkady Shevchenko, a Soviet diplomat, was the UN's Under-Secretary-General for Political Affairs from July 1973 to June 1978, a post the Soviet Union filled by custom. From about 1975 he passed Soviet secrets to the CIA while working in the UN's top political office and formally representing Moscow's interests there. When Moscow recalled him on 31 March 1978 he defected to the United States on 10 April 1978. He described the arrangement in his 1985 book 'Breaking With Moscow'. The case showed how national intelligence services used UN posts.
cite: Wikipedia 'Arkady Shevchenko'; Shevchenko, Breaking With Moscow (Knopf, 1985)
inside: The CIA recruited a senior UN official, the Secretariat's head of political affairs, to pass it Soviet secrets while he held that post.

n: East German spy 'Topaz' took NATO's war plans from inside its headquarters
rank: NATO headquarters staff
d: East Germany's foreign intelligence service, the HVA, placed a spy inside NATO's headquarters in Brussels. Rainer Rupp, a West German hired by NATO in 1977, rose quickly through its staff and, under the code names Mosel and later Topaz, passed material to East Berlin until 1989. He photographed about 10,000 pages, including deployment plans for cruise and Pershing II missiles, and handed over MC 161, the document summarising NATO strategy and its assessment of the Warsaw Pact. He was arrested in 1993 while on holiday in Germany, and sentenced to 12 years in prison in 1994.
cite: Wikipedia 'Rainer Rupp'; Reuters archive, 1994
inside: East German intelligence placed a spy on NATO's headquarters staff, who passed it NATO's war plans and strategy documents.

n: Soviet spy Georges Pâques became deputy head of NATO's press service
rank: Deputy head, NATO press service
d: Georges Pâques, a French official who had spied for the Soviet Union since 1944, joined NATO in October 1962 as deputy head of its press service. He was arrested on 10 August 1963 in the wake of the 'Martel affair', a Soviet defector's disclosures to the West. At his 1964 trial in Paris he admitted espionage and was sentenced to life imprisonment. He served seven years before being pardoned by his old friend Georges Pompidou, by then President of France. The case was one of several in the 1960s that showed Soviet services placing long-term agents in Western governments who could then be posted into NATO itself.
cite: Wikipedia 'Georges Pâques', citing French trial reporting 1964
inside: A long-term Soviet agent moved into a senior post in NATO's press service, putting Soviet intelligence inside the alliance's headquarters.

n: CIA used UN weapons inspectors in Iraq to spy on Saddam, reports said
rank: UN Special Commission (UNSCOM) inspection teams
d: United States intelligence is reported to have used UNSCOM, the United Nations commission that inspected Iraq's weapons after the 1991 Gulf War, as cover to spy on Iraq's leadership. In January 1999 the Washington Post reported that CIA engineers posing as UN technicians had installed eavesdropping equipment at Iraqi sites without the knowledge of UNSCOM's chairman, Richard Butler, and that the system helped track Saddam Hussein's movements. Former inspector Scott Ritter made similar accusations. Butler denied that foreign agencies 'piggybacked' on the commission. Iraq had long said UNSCOM was a cover for espionage. Inspectors had withdrawn in 1998 and UNSCOM was disbanded in 1999 and replaced by a new body, UNMOVIC.
cite: Wikipedia 'UNSCOM', citing Washington Post, Jan 1999
inside: US intelligence was reported to have used CIA engineers posing as UN technicians inside the weapons inspection teams to spy on Iraq's leadership.

n: Nazi SS chiefs took over Interpol and ran it from Berlin
rank: Presidency and headquarters of the ICPC (Interpol)
d: Nazi Germany took control of the International Criminal Police Commission, the body that became Interpol, which shares police information between countries. After Germany annexed Austria in 1938 the Vienna-based commission came under German control and most member states stopped supporting it. From 1938 to 1945 its presidents were all SS generals: Otto Steinhäusl, Reinhard Heydrich, Arthur Nebe and Ernst Kaltenbrunner, the last executed after the Nuremberg trials. By November 1941 it had offices at Am Kleinen Wannsee 16 in Berlin, and its headquarters moved to Berlin in 1942. The organisation was re-founded after the war, and Interpol's own history acknowledges the period.
cite: Wikipedia 'Interpol', citing Interpol history and academic sources
inside: Nazi SS generals took over the international police commission's presidency and moved its headquarters to Berlin, putting it under the SS.

n: Microsoft partners joined national committees to vote its format into ISO
rank: National committees voting in the ISO standards process
d: When Microsoft sought approval of its Office Open XML document format as an international standard at ISO, the Geneva-based body that sets world standards, national committees that cast each country's vote saw sudden new members. In Sweden, Microsoft admitted an employee had asked two partner companies to join the Swedish Standards Institute committee and vote yes in return for 'marketing contributions'; the institute annulled Sweden's vote in 2007. In Norway the committee grew from about seven members to 30, and 13 of 23 members resigned in October 2008 after the vote was changed to approval. Similar complaints of 'committee stuffing' came from Switzerland, Poland and Portugal. The format was approved in April 2008 and published in November 2008.
cite: Wikipedia 'Standardization of Office Open XML', citing Computer Sweden, SIS statement 2007 and national press
inside: Microsoft had partner companies join national standards committees and vote for its format, in Sweden in return for 'marketing contributions'.

n: NSA steered a weakened encryption standard through NIST and ISO
rank: Editor of national and international encryption standards
d: The US National Security Agency used its place in standards-setting bodies to have a random-number generator it could likely predict, Dual_EC_DRBG, adopted as an encryption standard by the US standards agency NIST in 2006, and by ANSI and ISO. Encryption depends on unpredictable random numbers. Leaked NSA documents reported by the New York Times in September 2013 showed the agency had become the sole editor of the standard.
