After an opposition CHP deputy, Atilla Kart, complained that 20 named candidates had seen the questions, expert reports from prosecutors and the national testing centre (ÖSYM) found the candidates had marked the same questions wrong. In June 2015 the Supreme Board of Judges and Prosecutors (HSYK) dismissed 37 judges and prosecutors on that evidence. The board linked the suspects to the movement, which was already accused over the 2010 civil-service exam leak. The case was used as evidence of a wider practice of placing members in state institutions.
cite: Daily Sabah, 11 Jun 2015
inside: Gülen followers became judges and prosecutors through a leaked entrance exam, placing the movement's members inside Turkey's courts, the judicial board found.

n: Gülen-linked prosecutor summoned Turkey's spy chief in 2012 'MİT crisis'
rank: Istanbul special prosecutor and police chiefs
d: Prosecutors and police chiefs that a Turkish court later tied to the Gülen movement used their posts to target the head of the national intelligence agency (MİT). On 12 February 2012 Istanbul prosecutor Sadrettin Sarıkaya, running a probe into the Kurdish KCK network, summoned MİT undersecretary Hakan Fidan over his talks with the PKK. Prime Minister Erdoğan ordered Fidan not to appear and passed a law requiring the prime minister's permission to prosecute intelligence officers. On 3 March 2021 the Istanbul 23rd High Criminal Court gave 10 of 18 defendants, including former police chiefs Yurt Atayün and Ali Fuat Yılmazer, aggravated life sentences for attempting to overthrow the government. Sarıkaya was jailed.
cite: Turkish Minute, 3 Mar 2021; Hürriyet Daily News (Sarıkaya arrest)
inside: Prosecutors and police chiefs tied by a court to the Gülen movement used their posts to summon and target the head of Turkey's intelligence agency.

n: Gülen-linked gendarmes and prosecutors stopped Turkish spy-agency trucks
rank: Gendarmerie commanders and Adana prosecutors
d: Gendarmerie officers and prosecutors whom Turkish courts tied to the Gülen movement used their posts in 2014 to stop and search trucks of the national intelligence agency (MİT) heading to Syria near the border, against government orders to let them pass. The government said the search was part of the movement's campaign from inside the state. On 28 June 2019 Ankara's 16th High Criminal Court convicted seven gendarmes and prosecutors of obtaining and disclosing confidential state documents. Former Adana chief prosecutor Süleyman Bağrıyanık received over 22 years, prosecutors Ahmet Karaca and Aziz Takcı 26 years each, and former brigadier general Hamza Celepoğlu about 20 years.
cite: Hürriyet Daily News, 29 Jun 2019
inside: Gendarmes and prosecutors tied to the Gülen movement used their posts to stop intelligence-agency trucks against government orders, which the government said served the movement's campaign.

n: Court ties Istanbul police intelligence chiefs to Hrant Dink murder
rank: Istanbul police intelligence chief and deputy
d: An Istanbul court ruled in March 2021 that the 2007 killing of Hrant Dink, an Armenian-Turkish newspaper editor, was carried out in line with the aims of the Gülen movement, which it found had members inside the police and security services who let the plot go ahead. Of 76 defendants, former Istanbul police intelligence chief Ramazan Akyürek and his deputy Ali Fuat Yılmazer were given life sentences for premeditated murder, as were two former Istanbul interior-ministry officers. A former Trabzon commander, Ali Öz, got 28 years. The gunman, Ogün Samast, had been sentenced in 2011. Other defendants were convicted of membership of what Ankara calls 'FETÖ' and of destroying documents.
cite: Voice of America (AP), Mar 2021; Duvar English
inside: A court found Gülen movement members inside the police and security services let the plot to kill Hrant Dink go ahead in line with the movement's aims.

n: Aide to Turkey's armed forces chief confessed to bugging for Gülenists
rank: Aide-de-camp to the Chief of General Staff
d: Lieutenant Colonel Levent Türkkan, aide-de-camp to Turkey's Chief of General Staff Hulusi Akar, told investigators after the July 2016 coup attempt that he had been a follower of the Gülen movement since school and had carried out its orders inside the military. He said movement members gave him the questions for his 1989 military academy entrance exam, and that he planted listening devices in the office of the previous chief, Necdet Özel, with a device supplied by a contact at Türk Telekom. State media published the confession as key proof of the movement's role. On 23 May 2017 he told an Ankara court the statement was false and given under torture; photos had shown him bruised.
cite: Hürriyet Daily News, 21 Jul 2016; Stockholm Center for Freedom, 24 May 2017
inside: The armed forces chief's aide said the Gülen movement placed him in the military through leaked exam questions and had him bug the previous chief's office; he later retracted it.

n: Menzil Sufi order said to fill Turkish police posts vacated by Gülenists
rank: Police appointments; health and energy ministers
d: Menzil, a branch of the Naqshbandi Sufi order, moved its followers into Turkish state posts emptied by the purge of Gülen followers, according to journalists and the order's own leader. The book Metastaz by Barış Terkoğlu and Barış Pehlivan says that from 2014 new police recruits came largely from Naqshbandi and other sects, with Menzil dominant, and T24 reported police promotions made by reference to Menzil membership. Menzil chief Fevzeddin Erol told Sözcü that health minister Recep Akdağ and energy minister Taner Yıldız were members and that the order had 'men everywhere in the state'. Interior Minister Süleyman Soylu denied it, and a court ordered T24's article removed.
cite: Foreign Policy, 15 Jan 2020
inside: Journalists and the order's own leader say the Menzil order moved its followers into Turkish police and state posts, with police promotions made by reference to membership.

n: RSS sends its own organiser to run the BJP as 'general secretary'
rank: BJP national general secretary (organisation)
d: The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), a Hindu nationalist volunteer organisation, places one of its full-time organisers, called pracharaks, inside India's ruling BJP as its general secretary (organisation), a post reserved by convention for senior RSS men. In July 2019 the RSS recalled Ram Lal after 13 years in the post and replaced him with B. L. Santhosh. The holder makes sure the BJP leadership carries out the RSS chief's instructions, reports to the RSS head and mobilises RSS workers at elections. In 2004 the then holder, Sanjay Joshi, drafted a resolution against party leader L. K. Advani over his praise of Jinnah, and Advani was forced to resign as party president.
cite: ThePrint, Jul 2019; Asian Age, 14 Jul 2019
inside: The RSS places one of its own organisers in the ruling BJP's top organisational post, where he makes sure the party carries out the RSS chief's instructions.

n: Liberhan inquiry: RSS groups and UP government enabled Babri demolition
rank: Uttar Pradesh chief minister, bureaucracy and police
d: The Liberhan Commission, a 17-year official inquiry into the 1992 demolition of the Babri Mosque at Ayodhya, found that the RSS and its allied groups, together with Uttar Pradesh's BJP government, made it possible. Its report, given to the prime minister on 30 June 2009, named the RSS, VHP, Bajrang Dal, BJP and Shiv Sena, and called chief minister Kalyan Singh the 'pivotal figure'. It said his government transferred officers who opposed the plan, worked through handpicked bureaucrats, and that about 90% of the police sent to guard the mosque were sympathisers, the rest told not to use force. The demolition was followed by violence that killed hundreds.
cite: ThePrint, summary of Liberhan Commission report (2009)
inside: An official inquiry found RSS-family groups worked with a state government that moved aside opposing officers and used sympathetic police, so the state let the mosque be demolished.

n: VHP officials made public prosecutors in Gujarat 2002 riot trials
rank: Special public prosecutors in riot cases
d: Gujarat's government appointed lawyers from the Vishva Hindu Parishad (VHP), a Hindu nationalist body in the RSS family, as public prosecutors in trials over the 2002 Gujarat riots, in which VHP members were among the accused. Citizens for Justice and Peace told the Supreme Court that Dilip Trivedi, general secretary of the VHP's Mehsana unit, prosecuted the Sardarpura massacre case and that Chetan Shah, a VHP supporter, handled the Gulbarga Society case. A Special Investigation Team report of 17 May 2010 said political affiliation appeared to have influenced the appointments. In 2021 Kapil Sibal told the court that 55 accused were bailed after Trivedi's appointment.
cite: Zee News (Supreme Court hearing, Oct 2003); LiveLaw, 11 Nov 2021
inside: Gujarat appointed VHP lawyers to prosecute riot cases in which VHP members were accused, putting the group's people in charge of cases against its own members.

n: RSS history wing's leader made chair of India's history research council
rank: Chair, Indian Council of Historical Research
d: Y. Sudershan Rao, head of the Andhra Pradesh branch of the Akhil Bharatiya Itihas Sankalan Yojana (ABISY), a history body set up by the RSS, was made chair of the Indian Council of Historical Research (ICHR), the state body that funds and directs historical research, in July 2014. In March 2015 three ABISY-linked historians were nominated to the council on his recommendation. Critics, including historian Romila Thapar, said he had no peer-reviewed publications and saw the appointments as placing RSS-aligned people in state institutions. Rao said the Ramayana and Mahabharata were accurate history and announced a study of whether Adam's Bridge was man-made. He served until 2017.
cite: Wikipedia (Yellapragada Sudershan Rao, citing Indian press); Tribune, 27 Nov 2015
inside: The leader of an RSS history body was made head of the state history research council and brought in more of that body's historians, critics say to serve the RSS line.

n: VHP men took 9 of 11 key seats on the state-formed Ram temple trust
rank: Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust
d: The Vishva Hindu Parishad (VHP), the Hindu nationalist body that led the campaign for a Ram temple at Ayodhya, took control of the trust India's government formed on the Supreme Court's orders to build it. In February 2020, nine of the 11 trustees with a decisive role were from the VHP or RSS, including its chairman Nritya Gopal Das, a member of the VHP's guidance council, and general secretary Champat Rai, a VHP vice-president. Former Modi aide Nripendra Misra chaired the construction committee, and four ex-officio members are senior government officers. Only two trustees had no RSS or VHP link.
cite: IANS via Lokmat Times, 21 Feb 2020; The Week, 19 Feb 2020
inside: VHP and RSS figures took nine of eleven decisive seats on the state-formed trust building the Ayodhya temple, the project the VHP had campaigned for.

n: Army officers and Harkat-ul-Jihad plotted Islamist coup in Pakistan, 1995
rank: Army general headquarters
d: Serving Pakistani army officers working with Qari Saifullah Akhtar, chief of the militant group Harkat-ul-Jihad al-Islami, planned to seize power from inside the army in 1995. They intended to storm a corps commanders' meeting at army headquarters in Rawalpindi on 30 September, kill Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto, the army chief and other leaders, and proclaim an Islamic caliphate with Major General Zahirul Islam Abbasi as its emir. Officers were detained on 26 September 1995 after Akhtar turned informer, and weapons and uniforms were seized. A court martial gave Abbasi seven years and Brigadier Mustansir Billah 14 years; two colonels were dismissed and jailed.
cite: Dawn (Supreme Court appeal coverage, Feb 2022); Wikipedia (Zahirul Islam Abbasi)
inside: A militant group's chief worked with serving army officers on a plan to seize power from inside the army by killing the country's leaders.

n: Saudi-inspired Madkhali Salafis entrenched in Libya's forces and mosques
rank: Special Deterrence Force; LNA brigades; religious endowments authority
d: Followers of Rabee al-Madkhali, a Saudi cleric whose ultra-conservative Salafi teaching demands obedience to rulers, built positions inside both of Libya's rival governments after 2011, the International Crisis Group reported in April 2019. In Tripoli they are strong in the Special Deterrence Force (Rada), nominally under the interior ministry and given a national remit by decree in May 2018. In the east they form units of Khalifa Haftar's Libyan National Army and dominate the eastern religious endowments authority, which runs mosques and issues fatwas. In late 2018 the Tripoli government named a Madkhali-sympathetic head of its endowments office; a former official estimated most Tripoli mosques were under Madkhali influence.
cite: International Crisis Group, Addressing the Rise of Libya's Madkhali-Salafis, 25 Apr 2019
inside: Followers of a Saudi-inspired Salafi current hold posts in Libyan security units and run the eastern religious authority that controls mosques and issues fatwas.

n: Al-Shabaab agents inside Mogadishu's city hall, spy agency and chamber
rank: Mogadishu mayor's office; intelligence agency (NISA)
d: Al-Shabaab, the al-Qaeda-linked Islamist insurgency, placed agents inside Somalia's institutions. On 24 July 2019 a blind woman using a false name, who worked as a disability coordinator in the office of Mogadishu mayor Abdirahman Omar Osman, blew herself up at a security meeting there, killing six officials; the mayor died of his wounds on 1 August. Al-Shabaab said the target was UN envoy James Swan. The National Intelligence and Security Agency (NISA) later paraded a government band singer it said was al-Shabaab's accountant, and the government dissolved the Chamber of Commerce board after finding the group had representatives on it.
cite: Daily Nation (Nairobi), Jan 2020; Al Jazeera, 25 Jul 2019
inside: Al-Shabaab placed its agents in Somali institutions, including a worker in the Mogadishu mayor's office who bombed a meeting there and members on the Chamber of Commerce board.

n: Unification Church members signed up en masse to South Korea's ruling party
rank: People Power Party membership and leadership vote
d: A South Korean special counsel found that about 3,500 Unification Church followers joined the then-ruling People Power Party (PPP), about 3,100 of them between October 2022 and March 2023, ahead of the party convention that chose its leader. Prosecutors raided the firm holding the PPP membership list on 18 September 2025 and matched about 120,000 names against 1.2 million church records. They suspect the church first sought to help lawmaker Kweon Seong-dong and then backed Kim Gi-hyeon, who won the leadership. A former church official had texted a shaman about '11,101 new members'. Party figures said the overlap was statistically expected; the law requires proof members were coerced.
cite: Korea JoongAng Daily, 26 Sep 2025
inside: A special counsel found thousands of Unification Church followers joined the ruling party before its leadership vote, which prosecutors suspect was an effort to choose the party's leader.

n: Assembly of God pastor Everaldo allegedly steered Rio's health posts
rank: Rio de Janeiro State Health Secretariat; Cedae; Detran
d: Everaldo Pereira, an Assembly of God pastor and national president of the Social Christian Party (PSC), was arrested on 28 August 2020 in Operation Tris in Idem, a federal police inquiry into corruption in Rio de Janeiro state's health secretariat during the COVID-19 pandemic under PSC governor Wilson Witzel. Reports cited by Congresso em Foco said Everaldo, who held no government post, was the most powerful figure in Witzel's government and influenced appointments to the Health Secretariat, the state water company Cedae and the vehicle agency Detran. Witzel was suspended from office the same day and later removed. Everaldo had baptised Jair Bolsonaro in the Jordan River in 2016.
cite: Congresso em Foco, 28 Aug 2020 (citing O Dia); Channels TV/AFP, 28 Aug 2020
inside: A pastor and party chief with no government post is reported to have controlled appointments in Rio's health secretariat and other state bodies, which were then under corruption investigation.

n: Greek junta's officers in Cyprus's National Guard overthrew Makarios
rank: Cypriot National Guard command
d: Greece's military government used the Greek officers it had posted to Cyprus's army, the National Guard, to overthrow the Cypriot government. About 650 Greek officers were serving in the National Guard, and the junta also supplied, controlled and funded EOKA-B, an armed group that wanted Cyprus joined to Greece. On 2 July 1974 President Makarios wrote publicly to the Greek president demanding the officers' withdrawal and accusing the junta of plotting against him. On 15 July, on orders from junta leader Dimitrios Ioannidis, the National Guard attacked the presidential palace and installed Nikos Sampson. Turkey invaded on 20 July and came to hold 37 per cent of the island, which remains divided.
cite: Library of Congress Country Studies, 'Cyprus: The Greek Coup and the Turkish Invasion'; Wikipedia, '1974 Cypriot coup d'état'
inside: Greece's junta used the Greek officers it had posted inside Cyprus's National Guard to turn that army on the Cypriot president and overthrow him.

n: KGB 'home Russians' cultivated Finland's leaders, including Kekkonen
rank: President and party leaders
d: The Soviet KGB assigned its officers in Helsinki to individual Finnish politicians and officials, who each came to have a personal Soviet contact known as a 'kotiryssä', or 'home Russian'. Dozens of KGB officers worked under diplomatic cover at the Soviet embassy. Viktor Vladimirov, a KGB general posted there in 1955–60, 1970–71 and 1977–84, began the system and dealt with elite politicians, including President Urho Kekkonen. A former Soviet diplomat later said Vladimirov reported straight to the Soviet leadership and backed Ahti Karjalainen to succeed Kekkonen. The public learned of the system through a 1981 book. It is tied to 'Finlandization', the bending of Finnish policy to Moscow's wishes; Helsingin Sanomat reported in 2015 that the practice had almost ended.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Kotiryssä' (citing Helsingin Sanomat 2003, 2009, 2015; Koivisto memoirs); Barents Observer (5 Nov 2012)
inside: The Soviet KGB gave Finnish politicians and officials personal KGB contacts and worked on the country's leaders, linked to Finnish policy bending to Moscow's wishes.

n: TV figure 'Boki 13' bribed North Macedonia's special prosecutor
rank: Head of the Special Prosecution Office
d: Bojan Jovanovski, a television personality known as 'Boki 13', used his closeness to Katica Janeva, head of North Macedonia's Special Prosecution Office, to sell the country's richest man, Jordan Orce Kamčev, milder treatment in his criminal case. The Special Prosecution Office had been set up to pursue high-level crimes after a wiretapping scandal. Kamčev had been detained in November 2018 on extortion and money-laundering charges and was released in March 2019. In July 2019 Jovanovski and his security chief were arrested at the Greek border carrying €1.5 million. In June 2020 a court found he had bribed Janeva with €50,000 and jailed him for nine years; Janeva got seven years for misuse of office.
cite: OCCRP (22 Jun 2020); RFE/RL (2020)
inside: A TV personality bribed the head of the special prosecution office to sell a tycoon milder treatment in his criminal case, so a prosecutor's decisions served the payers.

n: Serbian intelligence officer gave instructions to a Macedonian MP
org_label: Serbian Security Information Agency (BIA) and Russian intelligence
rank: Member of parliament
d: Leaked files of Macedonia's own counter-intelligence service say a Serbian intelligence officer at Serbia's embassy in Skopje steered a pro-Russian Macedonian MP. The documents, prepared in 2017 for the service's director and published by OCCRP partners on 4 June 2017, say Goran Živaljević of Serbia's Security Information Agency (BIA) gave instructions to Ivan Stoilković, an MP who led the Democratic Party of Serbs in Macedonia, a partner in the ruling coalition, and that Stoilković was in contact with Russian diplomats. They also say three officers of Russia's foreign intelligence service (SVR) worked from the Russian embassy and tried to recruit current and former army and interior ministry staff. Stoilković declined to discuss the contacts; Serbia said Živaljević broke no rules.
cite: OCCRP / Spooks and Spin (4 Jun 2017)
inside: North Macedonia's counter-intelligence files say a Serbian intelligence officer gave instructions to a coalition MP, while Russian intelligence officers tried to recruit army and interior ministry staff.

n: Tycoon Savvidis paid Macedonian politicians to fight the name deal
rank: Politicians from several parties
d: Ivan Savvidis, a Russian-Greek billionaire and former member of Russia's parliament for the ruling United Russia party, paid at least €300,000 to opponents of the agreement that renamed Macedonia 'North Macedonia', a deal needed for it to join NATO. According to Macedonian interior ministry documents seen by OCCRP partner IRL, the money, some carried in cash across the Greek border, went to more than a dozen Macedonian politicians from several parties, to new nationalist groups and to football hooligans linked to the opposition VMRO-DPMNE party, ahead of protests in which a petrol bomb was thrown at parliament. Greece separately expelled two Russian diplomats for paying opponents of the deal. Savvidis denied funding the protests.
cite: OCCRP (16 Jul 2018); Eurasia Review (18 Jul 2018)
inside: A Russian-Greek billionaire paid Macedonian politicians from several parties to oppose the name deal Macedonia needed to join NATO, according to interior ministry documents.

n: Mafia banker Michele Sindona became the Vatican's financial adviser
rank: Financial adviser to the Holy See
d: Michele Sindona, a Sicilian banker who laundered heroin money for Mafia families, was hired by the Holy See to manage its investments. After Italy ended the Vatican's tax exemption on Italian investment income in 1968, the Holy See took Sindona on as financial adviser, and his work with the Vatican Bank (the IOR) began in 1969; large sums moved from his banks through the Vatican to Swiss banks. He was also a member of the secret P2 Masonic lodge. When his Franklin National Bank in New York failed in 1974, the Vatican lost an estimated 35 billion lire. In 1986 an Italian court jailed Sindona for life for ordering the 1979 murder of Giorgio Ambrosoli, liquidator of his banks; he died of cyanide poisoning in prison days later.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Michele Sindona'; Wikipedia, 'Institute for the Works of Religion'
inside: A banker who laundered Mafia money was made the Holy See's financial adviser, giving him control of Vatican investments through which large sums moved from his banks.

n: Polish communist secret police had an informant in the Vatican
rank: Pope John Paul II's circle
d: Poland's communist Security Service (SB), the secret police, had an informant close to Pope John Paul II in Rome. In April 2005, weeks after the Pope's death, Poland's Institute of National Remembrance, the state body that holds communist-era police files, announced that about 700 pages showed Father Konrad Hejmo, a Dominican priest who ran pastoral care for Polish pilgrims at the Vatican, had been a secret collaborator under the code names 'Hejnal' and 'Dominik' during the 1980s. Hejmo's Dominican superior, who reviewed the files, called them convincing. It was not established how much secret information he passed on. The case was part of a wider picture of communist services trying to watch the Polish-born Pope.
cite: NBC News / Associated Press (Apr 2005); Mail & Guardian (28 Apr 2005)
inside: Poland's communist secret police had a priest working inside the Vatican's pastoral care for Polish pilgrims as its secret informer near the Pope.

n: Iranian agents worked alongside Bosnian Interior Ministry staff
rank: Interior Ministry and AID intelligence agency
d: Iran built a presence inside Bosnia's wartime security apparatus. On 15 February 1996 NATO-led troops raided a ski chalet at Fojnica that they called a terrorist training cell, arresting three Iranians and several Bosnians who worked for the Interior Ministry, and finding explosives, weapons and models of UN buildings. Western officials said the Bosnian intelligence agency AID, under former interior minister Bakir Alispahić, worked largely beyond government control and close to Iran, one of Bosnia's few wartime allies. The United States made ending Iran's military role a condition of a $400 million programme to train and equip the Bosnian army, and demanded that AID be shut down.
cite: Christian Science Monitor (12 Mar 1996)
inside: Iranian agents worked alongside Bosnian Interior Ministry staff, and the Bosnian intelligence agency operated close to Iran and largely beyond government control.

n: MG Baltic bribed Lithuania's Liberal leader and parties for votes
rank: Liberal Movement leader and Labour Party MP
d: MG Baltic, one of Lithuania's largest business groups, paid politicians and their parties to get decisions it wanted in parliament. On 12 May 2016 anti-corruption officers searched Eligijus Masiulis, leader of the Liberal Movement, and detained MG Baltic vice-president Raimondas Kurlianskis; prosecutors said Masiulis had taken a bribe from Kurlianskis, and €242,000 was found in his possession. A lower court acquitted everyone in 2022, but the Court of Appeal convicted them in 2023 and the Supreme Court made it final on 24 October 2024. Masiulis got five and a half years in prison, Labour MP Vytautas Gapšys four years and three months, and Kurlianskis five and a half years. The Liberal Movement, the Labour Party and MG Group were fined as organisations.
inside: A business group paid a party leader and other MPs to get the decisions it wanted in parliament, and courts convicted them of bribery.

n: Russia's GRU recruited a Lithuanian Air Force officer
rank: Air Force officer, Šiauliai airbase
d: Sergey Moiseyenko, an army surgeon at a military hospital in Šiauliai who worked for Russia's military intelligence service, the GRU, recruited a Lithuanian Air Force officer in 2012. The officer, Sergej Pusin, served at Šiauliai airbase, which hosts NATO's Baltic air-policing mission, and was paid 500 to 1,000 euros at secret meetings in Moiseyenko's garage. Moiseyenko passed Russian intelligence copies of Lithuanian defence ministry documents and personal files of airbase officers, and sought details of NATO flights and training. He was detained in late 2014 and a Šiauliai court sentenced him to ten and a half years; appeals failed. Lithuania pardoned him in November 2019 as part of a spy swap with Russia.
cite: LRT (15 Nov 2019)
inside: Russia's military intelligence paid a Lithuanian Air Force officer at a NATO airbase to pass defence documents and officers' files.

n: FSB officer tried to recruit Lithuania's presidential guards
rank: VIP Protection Department
d: Nikolai Filipchenko, an officer of the Kaliningrad branch of Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) who used a false identity, tried to recruit officers of Lithuania's VIP Protection Department, the unit that guards the president, in order to plant listening devices in the office and home of President Dalia Grybauskaitė. Lithuanian authorities said the operation aimed at infiltrating state institutions, law enforcement and intelligence services. He was detained on 29 April 2015 on a train from Kaliningrad, the first FSB officer caught spying in Lithuania. A Vilnius court jailed him for ten years on 7 July 2017. He was pardoned in November 2019 in a prisoner swap with Russia.
cite: LRT (15 Nov 2019); RFE/RL (7 Jul 2017)
inside: Russia's FSB tried to recruit officers of the unit guarding Lithuania's president so they would plant listening devices in her office and home.

n: Insurer ICBL paid Barbados's industry minister for state contracts
rank: Minister of Industry
d: Senior executives of the Insurance Corporation of Barbados Limited (ICBL) paid Barbados's Minister of Industry, Donville Inniss, to use his post to win the company government business. In 2015 and 2016 Inniss helped ICBL get two Barbadian government insurance contracts covering more than $100 million of state property, and took about $36,000 in bribes, routed through a US bank account in the name of a friend's dental company in New York. Because the money passed through the United States, US prosecutors charged him. A federal jury in Brooklyn convicted him of money laundering on 16 January 2020, and on 27 April 2021 he was sentenced to two years in prison.
cite: US Department of Justice (27 Apr 2021)
inside: Insurance company executives paid Barbados's industry minister, who used his post to win the company government contracts.

n: Contractors and Trinidad's finance minister rigged Piarco airport bids
rank: Minister of Finance
d: Contractors building the new Piarco International Airport terminal in the late 1990s worked with Trinidad and Tobago's then finance minister, Brian Kuei Tung, to rig bids and charge inflated prices. Raul Gutierrez Jr, president of the Miami firm Calmaquip Engineering, and five co-defendants pleaded guilty in US courts in 2006; prosecutors said the group hid the scheme through offshore companies and bank accounts, and Gutierrez was jailed for six years in 2007. The government sued 52 people and firms in Miami in 2004. In March 2023 a jury found Gutierrez, Kuei Tung and businessman Steve Ferguson liable for racketeering and fraud, and in May 2023 a judge entered a final judgment of US$131.3 million for Trinidad and Tobago.
cite: Caribbean Today (May 2023); White & Case / Law360 (Mar 2023); FreightWaves (18 Jan 2007)
inside: Airport contractors worked with Trinidad's finance minister to rig the bidding, so the state paid them inflated prices for the new terminal.

n: Trafigura paid $31m into a Jamaican ruling-party account
rank: Governing People's National Party
d: Trafigura, a Dutch-registered oil trading company that held an agreement to lift oil for the Jamaican government, paid $31 million into an account linked to the then governing People's National Party (PNP) in 2006. Three payments of just over $10 million each were wired on 6 and 12 September 2006 to an account named CCOC ('Colin Campbell Our Candidate'), and about $30 million then went to the party's campaign account. The PNP called it a donation, Trafigura called it a commercial payment, and the party said the money was returned. Dutch prosecutors investigated possible bribery of Jamaican officials; after the UK Privy Council ruled in April 2021 that five PNP figures, including former prime minister Portia Simpson Miller, must answer questions, Trafigura went on trial in the Netherlands.
cite: Jamaica Gleaner (11 Mar 2022); Stabroek News (20 Apr 2021)
inside: Trafigura, which lifted oil for Jamaica's government, paid $31m into an account linked to the ruling party, and Dutch prosecutors investigated it as possible bribery of officials.

n: Senior Bahamian police officers indicted for protecting cocaine flights
rank: Senior Royal Bahamas Police Force officers
d: A cocaine trafficking network got senior Bahamian police and military officials working for it, according to a US indictment filed on 27 November 2024. Prosecutors say that since at least May 2021 two high-ranking officers of the Royal Bahamas Police Force and a Bahamian military official helped cocaine arriving on charter flights from Colombia and Venezuela pass through Bahamian airports, and let boats carry it on to Florida, for bribes of $10,000 to $2 million. One officer allegedly demanded $2 million on behalf of an unnamed 'high-ranking Bahamian politician'. Others allegedly shared US Coast Guard information with traffickers and misled the DEA. Police Commissioner Clayton Fernander, who was not accused, resigned on 4 December 2024.
cite: InSight Crime (12 Dec 2024); WLRN (9 Dec 2024)
inside: Cocaine traffickers paid senior Bahamian police and military officers to let their flights and boats through and to pass them Coast Guard information, US prosecutors allege.

n: Plan to pay 40 Maldivian MPs with Indian money to impeach Muizzu
rank: People's Majlis (parliament)
d: The Washington Post reported on 30 December 2024 that Maldivian opposition politicians had planned to bribe 40 members of parliament, including some from President Mohamed Muizzu's own People's National Congress, to vote to impeach him, using about $6 million to be sought from India. Muizzu had won office on a platform of reducing India's influence. The paper cited an internal document titled 'Democratic Renewal Initiative' and said an officer of India's foreign intelligence agency, the Research and Analysis Wing (RAW), explored ways to remove Muizzu through two intermediaries, who confirmed the plan existed. There is no report that money was paid; Muizzu's coalition won a parliamentary majority in April 2024. Former president Mohamed Nasheed denied any Indian role.
cite: ThePrint (30 Dec 2024), citing The Washington Post; Business Standard (31 Dec 2024)
inside: An Indian intelligence officer is reported to have explored a plan to pay Maldivian MPs, including the president's own, with Indian money to vote to impeach him.

n: ERHC may have paid São Tomé officials for oil rights, inquiry says
rank: Oil licensing officials
d: ERHC, a small Houston oil company controlled from 2001 by Nigerian businessman Emeka Offor, a major donor to Nigeria's ruling party, secured favourable oil rights from São Tomé and Príncipe, including the right to pick the best blocks without the usual one-time fee. A 1997 contract had already given ERHC exploration rights for 25 years for $5 million. In 2005 São Tomé's attorney general reported that bidding for blocks in the zone shared with Nigeria showed 'serious procedural deficiencies and political manipulation' and that ERHC 'may have made improper payments to government officials'. US federal authorities investigated whether ERHC bribed São Tomé officials, and the FBI raided its Houston offices in 2006. ERHC denied wrongdoing, and no charges were reported.
cite: CorpWatch / Washington Post (2007); Offshore Magazine
inside: An oil company is alleged to have made improper payments to São Tomé officials, who gave it favoured oil rights through a bidding process the attorney general called manipulated.

n: Russian intelligence agent worked inside a Danish energy firm
rank: Employee at an energy technology firm
d: A Russian intelligence service paid a Russian man who worked in Denmark to collect information from inside a Danish company and a university. A court in Aalborg found that over several years he gathered information, mainly on energy technology, from the Technical University of Denmark and from a business in north-west Denmark, and passed it to Russian intelligence for payment. The Danish fuel cell maker SerEnergy confirmed it had employed him. He was arrested in July 2020, and after a closed trial the court on 10 May 2021 sentenced him to three years in prison followed by permanent expulsion. Russia called the case a 'witch hunt'.
cite: Moscow Times / AFP (10 May 2021); The Local Denmark (9 Dec 2020)
inside: Russian intelligence paid a man working inside a Danish energy company and a university to pass it information on energy technology.

n: Drug traffickers reached Fiji's narcotics police and customs
rank: Counter Narcotics Bureau and customs
d: Drug trafficking networks moving methamphetamine through the Pacific got officers of Fiji's police and customs working for them. In May 2025 two officers of the police Counter Narcotics Bureau and a senior customs border manager were among seven people charged after more than 4 kg of methamphetamine was found in air cargo at Nadi airport; the bureau was later disbanded. In December 2025 Police Commissioner Rusiate Tudravu confirmed that seven senior officers, including Fisi Nasario, director of the serious organised crime and intelligence department, were under investigation after leaked chats appeared to show officers discussing drug shipments and payments with traffickers. Fiji's policing minister said 27 police officers were involved in 33 drug cases between January 2023 and October 2025.
cite: RNZ (27 May 2025); OCCRP (10 Dec 2025)
inside: Methamphetamine traffickers had officers of Fiji's drugs police and customs working with them, so the units meant to stop shipments helped move them.

n: Angolan banker's charity card funded Mauritius president's spending
rank: President of Mauritius
d: Álvaro Sobrinho, an Angolan banker, gained influence over Mauritius's president, Ameenah Gurib-Fakim, through his charity, the Planet Earth Institute (PEI). Gurib-Fakim was the charity's vice-chair and used a PEI credit card for private spending, and PEI paid for business trips that the government approved. Sobrinho was seeking a banking licence from Mauritius's Financial Services Commission, and Gurib-Fakim asked the regulator to issue it. After the newspaper L'Express published her card statements, she repaid the spending and resigned on 23 March 2018. Before leaving she named a judge to inquire into Sobrinho's activities without consulting the cabinet, and in June 2018 the government set up a commission of inquiry into her own conduct.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Ameenah Gurib-Fakim' (citing L'Express, Le Mauricien)
inside: An Angolan banker's charity paid for the Mauritian president's private spending, and she asked the regulator to give him the banking licence he wanted.

n: Foreign dam contractors bribed Lesotho water project chief Masupha Sole
org_label: Acres International, Lahmeyer and other foreign contractors
rank: Chief executive, Lesotho Highlands Development Authority
d: Foreign engineering and construction firms working on the Lesotho Highlands Water Project, a World Bank-backed scheme of dams and tunnels that sells water to South Africa, paid Masupha Sole, chief executive of the state authority running it, through intermediaries. A 1993 audit led to his dismissal, and Swiss bank records later showed millions of maloti he could not explain. In 2002 Lesotho's High Court convicted Sole of bribery; his 18-year sentence was cut to 15 on appeal. The Canadian firm Acres International was convicted the same year and fined CAD 3.8 million, and the German consultancy Lahmeyer was convicted in 2003. In 2004 the World Bank barred Acres from Bank-funded contracts for three years.
cite: Pambazuka News, 'The Lesotho Highlands Water Project: Bribery on a massive scale'; Probe International, 21 May 2002, 18 Sept 2002, 18 June 2003
inside: Foreign dam contractors paid the chief of Lesotho's state water project authority through intermediaries, and courts convicted him and two firms of bribery.

n: BAE's agent took 30% of Tanzania radar price; attorney general implicated
rank: Attorney General (later infrastructure minister)
d: BAE Systems, the British arms maker, sold Tanzania a Watchman radar system for about $40 million in 1999 and paid about $12 million, roughly 30 per cent of the price, through its offshore company Red Diamond into a Swiss account controlled by its local agent, Sailesh Vithlani. Andrew Chenge, Tanzania's Attorney General when the deal was made, is alleged to have received $1.5 million for his support; he stepped down as infrastructure minister in 2008 after a British request for legal help was leaked. In 2010 BAE pleaded guilty in Britain only to an accounting offence, was fined £500,000 and paid £29.5 million for Tanzanian schools. The Serious Fraud Office did not establish that the money was passed on as bribes, and no one in Tanzania was prosecuted for taking them.
cite: corruption-tracker.org, 'Tanzania's air traffic control system'; World Bank StAR Asset Recovery Watch, BAE Systems Tanzania case; The Corner House, BAE-Tanzania SFO plea bargain
inside: BAE paid its agent about 30 per cent of the radar price, and Tanzania's attorney general at the time is alleged to have received $1.5 million for supporting the deal.

n: Tegeta escrow: $122m power fund moved; businessman paid Tanzania minister
org_label: Pan Africa Power (Harbinder Singh Sethi) and businessman James Rugemalira
rank: Lands minister; Attorney General; energy minister
d: At least $122 million of public money held in an escrow account, an account jointly held by TANESCO, Tanzania's state power company, and the private power producer IPTL, was moved to IPTL's new owner, Pan Africa Power, run by Kenyan businessman Harbinder Singh Sethi. Parliament's Public Accounts Committee called for Sethi's arrest and for two cabinet ministers to be removed. James Rugemalira, a businessman linked to the deal, had paid $1 million to lands minister Anna Tibaijuka; President Jakaya Kikwete sacked her in December 2014 for breaching leadership ethics. Attorney General Frederick Werema resigned, energy minister Sospeter Muhongo quit in January 2015 denying wrongdoing, and 12 donors held back almost $500 million in budget support. Prosecutors dropped charges against Rugemalira in 2021.
cite: Reuters via This Is Africa, 25 Jan 2015; Business Daily Africa, 23 Dec 2014; The EastAfrican, 20 Dec 2014; The Citizen (Tanzania), 17 Sept 2021
inside: Officials were alleged to have let $122m of public escrow money pass to the power firm's new owner, while a businessman linked to the deal paid a cabinet minister $1m.

n: Saipem accused of bribing Algeria's oil officials; acquitted on appeal
rank: Sonatrach and Algerian government officials
d: Italian prosecutors charged Saipem, the oil-services arm of Italy's Eni group, with paying bribes to officials of Sonatrach, Algeria's state oil and gas company, and of the Algerian government to win oil and gas contracts; the alleged bribes were valued at €197 million. A Milan court convicted Saipem and its former chief executive Pietro Tali in September 2018, sentencing Tali to four years and nine months. The Milan Court of Appeal acquitted Saipem and the managers in January 2020, and Italy's highest court upheld the acquittals, including that of the Algerian intermediary Farid Bedjaoui, in December 2020. In Algeria, Chakib Khelil, energy minister from 1999 to 2010 and for a time also head of Sonatrach, was sentenced in absentia in February 2022 to 20 years for corruption.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Saipem' and 'Chakib Khelil'; Echorouk Online, 'Italian Saipem wraps up 13-year legal battle in Algeria'; GlobeNewswire, 18 Dec 2020
inside: Italian prosecutors charged Saipem with bribing Algerian state oil company and government officials to win contracts; the company and its managers were acquitted on appeal.

n: Chinese contractor's adviser and Algeria's highways chief jailed
org_label: East-West motorway contractors (CITIC-CRCC, Cojaal) and their agents
rank: Director of highways, Ministry of Public Works
d: Contractors building Algeria's 1,200 km East-West motorway, begun in 2006 by a Japanese consortium (Cojaal) and a Chinese one (CITIC-CRCC), paid officials of the public works ministry through agents. In May 2015 an Algiers court jailed 14 people in the case. Chani Mejdoub, an adviser to the Chinese group, and Mohamed Khelladi, a former director of highways, each received ten years for corruption, money laundering and embezzlement; two other former ministry staff got seven years and a former intelligence officer three. Seven foreign firms, including Cojaal and CITIC-CRCC, were found guilty and fined. A defendant accused former public works minister Amar Ghoul of taking a quarter of the kickbacks, which he denied. The road's cost rose from $6 billion to at least $13 billion.
cite: Middle East Eye, May 2015; World Highways, 15 May 2015
inside: Motorway contractors paid public works ministry officials through agents, and an Algiers court jailed the director of highways and others for the kickbacks.

n: Alcoa paid Bahraini royals via a middleman to keep Alba supply deals
rank: Alba tender officials, senior royal family members
d: Alcoa, the US aluminium company, kept long-term contracts to supply alumina to Aluminium Bahrain (Alba), a smelter controlled by Bahrain's government, by placing a London-based middleman with close ties to senior members of Bahrain's royal family between itself and Alba as a sham sales agent. Sales went through his offshore shell companies, which marked up prices by about $188 million between 2005 and 2009, and he used the margin to pay tens of millions of dollars in kickbacks to Bahraini officials who controlled the tenders, through accounts in Guernsey, Luxembourg, Liechtenstein and Switzerland. In January 2014 Alcoa World Alumina pleaded guilty to bribery under the US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, and Alcoa paid $384 million in US criminal and regulatory penalties.
cite: US Department of Justice, 9 Jan 2014; Business Insurance, 9 Jan 2014
inside: Alcoa put a middleman with royal ties between itself and Bahrain's state smelter, and he paid kickbacks to officials who controlled its tenders so Alcoa kept the contracts.

n: Bolloré group ran Togo president's campaign cheaply, then got Lomé port
rank: President Faure Gnassingbé's election campaign
d: French investigators allege that subsidiaries of the Bolloré Group, the conglomerate of French billionaire Vincent Bolloré, gave under-priced campaign communication services through its agency Euro RSCG (later Havas) to Faure Gnassingbé, Togo's president, for the 2010 election, and that the group then secured control of the port of Lomé. A similar deal is alleged with Alpha Condé in Guinea and the port of Conakry. The inquiry opened in 2013, and Bolloré and two Euro RSCG executives were charged in 2018. In 2021 Bolloré admitted the facts in a guilty-plea procedure with a €375,000 fine, but the Paris court refused the deal. In March 2026 he was ordered to stand trial in Paris in December. The group sold its African ports and logistics business in 2022.
cite: Africanews, 20 Mar 2026; Euronews, 11 Oct 2023; Financial Afrik, 26 Feb 2021
inside: French investigators allege the Bolloré group gave Togo's president cheap campaign services and then got control of the state's port of Lomé.

n: Gunvor paid fixers close to Sassou-Nguesso's family for Congo oil cargoes
rank: Congolese National Oil Company (SNPC)
d: Gunvor, the Geneva oil trader, obtained crude oil from the Congolese National Oil Company (SNPC) of the Republic of Congo between 2010 and 2012 by lending it six advances of $125 million each, repaid in oil, while paying nearly $30 million in commissions to two intermediaries close to President Denis Sassou-Nguesso's family, Jean-Marc Henry and Maxime Gandzion. According to the case record, the bribes were meant for the president's relatives. Credit Suisse reported suspicious payments in late 2011 and Swiss police searched Gunvor's headquarters in January 2012. A Gunvor employee admitted five corrupt agreements in Congo and Côte d'Ivoire involving $43 million and received a suspended sentence in 2018. On 17 October 2019 Gunvor was convicted in Switzerland and ordered to pay CHF 94 million.
cite: Public Eye, 'Gunvor in Congo'; Energy Intelligence, Oct 2019; Africanews, 27 Sept 2018
inside: Gunvor paid intermediaries close to the Congolese president's family, with bribes meant for his relatives, to get crude oil from the state oil company.

n: Odebrecht admitted paying $50m in bribes to Angolan officials
rank: Unnamed government officials and a state company executive
d: Odebrecht, the Brazilian construction group, admitted in a December 2016 guilty plea in a New York court that it paid about $50 million in bribes to Angolan officials to win public works contracts, gaining about $261.7 million in benefits. The plea describes $8 million paid through an Odebrecht employee to one Angolan official to secure an infrastructure project, and $1.19 million to a senior official at a state-controlled company to steer business to Odebrecht. The officials were not named. Angola's government did not respond publicly when the plea was released, and the anti-corruption campaigner Rafael Marques de Morais, who had demanded an investigation, described 'absolute silence' from officials.
cite: Reuters via Club of Mozambique, March 2017; US v. Odebrecht plea (E.D.N.Y., Dec 2016)
inside: Odebrecht paid Angolan officials, including a senior official at a state company, to steer public works contracts to it.

n: China International Fund and Angola's top generals indicted
org_label: China International Fund (Sam Pa's Queensway group)
rank: Generals 'Kopelipa' and 'Dino', President dos Santos's inner circle
d: China International Fund (CIF), a Hong Kong company linked to the Chinese fixer Sam Pa, ran Chinese-financed reconstruction projects in Angola in partnership with generals close to President José Eduardo dos Santos. In July 2022 Angola's prosecutors indicted Generals Manuel Hélder Vieira Dias Júnior ('Kopelipa') and Leopoldino Fragoso do Nascimento ('Dino'), a lawyer, a Chinese national and CIF itself for criminal association, money laundering, fraud and influence-peddling. The indictment alleges that public money for housing at Zango was used for private ends and that CIF sold state-funded buildings back to Sonangol, the state oil company. It also says about $1.5 billion of Chinese payments for Angolan oil never reached Angola. The two generals went on trial in 2024.
cite: Maka Angola, July 2022; Ver Angola, Feb 2024; Wikipedia, 'Sam Pa'
inside: A Chinese-linked company ran Angolan state-funded projects in partnership with the president's generals, and the indictment says public money was used for their private ends.

n: SBM Offshore bribed at least nine officials of Angola's Sonangol
rank: Sonangol officials
d: SBM Offshore, a Dutch company that builds and leases floating oil production vessels, paid 'commissions' to local sales agents in Angola between 1997 and 2012 knowing that part would be passed to at least nine officials of Sonangol, Angola's state oil company, and its US subsidiary, which award offshore contracts. Agents' fees usually went first to Swiss or Monaco bank accounts and were then wired on. Across Angola, Brazil, Equatorial Guinea, Kazakhstan and Iraq, SBM paid more than $180 million to intermediaries and gained at least $2.8 billion of business from state oil companies. It paid $240 million to Dutch prosecutors in 2014, and in November 2017 agreed a $238 million US criminal penalty; its former chief executive Anthony Mace pleaded guilty.
cite: A&O Shearman FCPA database, US v. SBM Offshore; gCaptain, 30 Nov 2017
inside: SBM Offshore paid agents knowing part would reach officials of Angola's state oil company, which then awarded it offshore contracts.

n: SBM Offshore bribed Equatorial Guinea's oil ministry and GEPetrol officials
rank: Ministry of Mines, Industry and Energy; GEPetrol
d: SBM Offshore, a Dutch company that leases floating oil production vessels, paid commissions to local agents in Equatorial Guinea between 2008 and 2012 knowing that part would reach at least nine officials of the Ministry of Mines, Industry and Energy and of GEPetrol, the state oil company, which control offshore oil contracts. The money usually passed through Swiss or Monaco bank accounts first. US prosecutors found SBM paid more than $180 million to intermediaries across five countries and won at least $2.8 billion of business from state oil companies. SBM paid $240 million to Dutch prosecutors in 2014 and agreed a $238 million US criminal penalty in November 2017, when its former chief executive Anthony Mace pleaded guilty.
cite: A&O Shearman FCPA database, US v. SBM Offshore; gCaptain, 30 Nov 2017
inside: SBM Offshore paid agents knowing part would reach officials of Equatorial Guinea's oil ministry and state oil company, which control the offshore contracts it won.

n: US oil firms paid Obiang's family and officials, Senate inquiry found
org_label: ExxonMobil, Amerada Hess and Marathon Oil
rank: President Teodoro Obiang, his family and officials
d: A 2004 report by the US Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations found that ExxonMobil, Amerada Hess and Marathon Oil, which produced most of Equatorial Guinea's offshore oil, made payments to President Teodoro Obiang, his relatives and officials for land, office leases and security services, with single payments of up to $250,000. One company paid over $450,000 over four years to a 14-year-old relative of the president for office space, and the firms paid over $4 million to send more than 100 students abroad, most of them officials' children or relatives. Obiang and his family held secret shares in joint ventures between US oil firms and the government; Marathon's supposedly state-owned partner GEOGAM was 75 per cent owned by Abayak, a company Obiang controlled. The money moved through Riggs Bank in Washington.
cite: The New Humanitarian (IRIN), 16 July 2004; Multinational Monitor, July 2004
inside: US oil firms paid Equatorial Guinea's president, his relatives and officials, and the president secretly owned stakes in the firms' joint ventures with the state.

n: Embraer paid $1.65m to a Saudi state company official for an aircraft sale
rank: Official at a Saudi state-owned company
d: Embraer, the Brazilian aircraft maker, paid $1.65 million in 2010 to an official of a Saudi Arabian state-owned and state-controlled company, disguising it with a false agency agreement, to secure that company's purchase of three aircraft for about $93 million. The payment was one of several that the US Justice Department set out when Embraer agreed, on 24 October 2016, to a deferred prosecution agreement and a criminal penalty of about $107 million; others went to officials in the Dominican Republic, Mozambique and India in return for military and airline orders.
cite: US Department of Justice, 24 Oct 2016; US SEC press release 2016-224
inside: Embraer paid an official of a Saudi state-owned company to secure that company's purchase of its aircraft.

n: Airbus unit GPT paid Saudi National Guard officials to keep its contract
rank: Deputy head, Saudi Arabian National Guard
d: GPT Special Project Management, a British company then owned by Airbus, held a UK Ministry of Defence contract from 1994 to supply and run communications for the Saudi Arabian National Guard, the force that protects the Saudi royal family. The Serious Fraud Office investigated £9.7 million in payments made between 2007 and 2012 through offshore firms and intermediaries; prosecutors said about 12 per cent of GPT's revenue went to Saudi officials to keep contracts worth at least £1.6 billion, and SFO findings named Prince Miteb bin Abdullah, then deputy head of the National Guard, among the recipients. GPT pleaded guilty and paid £27.5 million. In 2024 two executives were acquitted of bribery after arguing the British government required the payments; one, a former ministry official, was jailed for misconduct.
cite: OCCRP, 2024; Bloomberg via BNN, 12 Apr 2024; Serious Fraud Office, 2024
inside: GPT paid Saudi National Guard officials, including its deputy head, to keep its communications contracts with the force.

n: Bangladeshi MP Papul bribed Kuwait interior ministry officials for visas
rank: Assistant Under-Secretary, Ministry of Interior
d: Mohammad Shahid Islam, known as Kazi Papul, a Bangladeshi member of parliament whose companies supplied cleaners for Kuwaiti government contracts, paid officials of Kuwait's Interior Ministry, which controls work and residence visas, to bring in Bangladeshi workers and win contracts. He reportedly confessed to giving one official 1.1 million Kuwaiti dinars by cheque and another KD1 million in cash. Arrested in June 2020, he was sentenced in January 2021 to four years and fined KD1.97 million for bribery, later extended to seven years. Major General Mazen Al-Jarrah, an assistant under-secretary at the Interior Ministry, was among those convicted. Prosecutors said his firms brought in more than 20,000 workers, some on fake visas. He lost his seat in Bangladesh's parliament.
cite: The Daily Star (Bangladesh), 29 Jan 2021 and Feb 2021; The Business Standard, 2021
inside: A Bangladeshi MP and labour contractor paid Kuwaiti Interior Ministry officials, who controlled visas, to bring in his workers and win contracts.

n: Iran's Revolutionary Guards ran a spy cell inside Kuwait's army
rank: Serving Kuwaiti army personnel
d: Men serving in Kuwait's army passed information about Kuwaiti and US military forces to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the Iranian military force that also runs intelligence and foreign operations, a Kuwaiti court found on 29 March 2011. The group had been arrested in May 2010. Two Iranians and one Kuwaiti were sentenced to death, and a Syrian and a stateless former soldier received life sentences; the three sentenced to death and the Syrian were serving in Kuwait's army when arrested. Another Iranian and a woman defendant were acquitted. Iran denied that the men were its spies. The death sentences were later commuted.
cite: RFE/RL and VOA via GlobalSecurity.org, 29 Mar 2011; Hands Off Cain, 'Kuwait: spies' sentences commuted'
inside: Iran's Revolutionary Guards had men serving in Kuwait's army pass them information on Kuwaiti and US forces.

n: Kuwait inquiry: Airbus paid commissions on €1bn Caracal helicopter deal
rank: Ministry of Defence officials
d: Airbus Helicopters sold Kuwait's Ministry of Defence 30 military Caracal helicopters in August 2016, in a deal reported at about €1 billion, while discussing payments to Farid Abdelnour, a consultant who had worked on the negotiations; Airbus had declared to Kuwaiti authorities that no commissions were paid. Kuwait began investigating in late 2017. In January 2024 a Kuwaiti parliamentary inquiry found that Airbus had paid commissions for the contract and that €349 million of public money had been wasted, and a draft report named eight senior officials, seven of them suspected of profiteering. Parliament was dissolved in May 2024 and it is unclear whether any prosecution followed. The Kuwait deal was not part of Airbus's 2020 bribery settlements in France, Britain and the US.
cite: OCCRP, 'As bribery probe unfolded, Airbus kept in touch with middleman on Kuwait helicopters deal'; The National, 11 Jan 2024
inside: A Kuwaiti parliamentary inquiry found Airbus paid commissions on the helicopter deal it won, and named senior officials suspected of profiting from it.

n: Baker Hughes paid $4.1m meant for a Kazakh state oil official
rank: Official of Kazakhoil, the state oil company
d: Baker Hughes, a US oilfield services company, won a contract in October 2000 for services on the Karachaganak oil and gas field in north-western Kazakhstan after agreeing to pay commissions to a consulting firm on the Isle of Man, understanding that part or all of the money would go to an official of Kazakhoil, then Kazakhstan's state oil company. It paid about $4.1 million between May 2001 and November 2003. In April 2007 the company agreed to pay $44 million in US criminal fines, civil penalties and disgorgement, then a record sum under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, the US law against bribing foreign officials.
cite: US Department of Justice, 26 Apr 2007; Oil & Gas Journal, 2007
inside: Baker Hughes paid commissions it understood would reach an official of Kazakhstan's state oil company, and won the oilfield contract.

n: Rolls-Royce paid advisers to bribe Kazakh state pipeline officials
rank: Officials over a Kazakh-Chinese state pipeline venture; a senior official
d: Between 2009 and 2012 Rolls-Royce, the British engineering group, paid about $5.4 million to advisers in Kazakhstan, knowing that at least part would be used to bribe officials with influence over a joint venture owned by the Kazakh and Chinese governments that was building a gas pipeline; the venture awarded Rolls-Royce several contracts. In 2012 Rolls-Royce also took on a local distributor secretly owned by a high-ranking Kazakh official who could affect its ability to keep operating in the country. The Guardian and BBC Panorama reported that the Monaco firm Unaoil represented Rolls-Royce in Kazakhstan from 2008. The conduct formed part of Rolls-Royce's January 2017 settlement of about $800 million with US, British and Brazilian authorities.
cite: The Diplomat, Jan 2017; A&O Shearman FCPA database, US v. Rolls-Royce
inside: Rolls-Royce paid advisers knowing part would bribe officials with influence over a Kazakh state pipeline venture, which then awarded it contracts.

n: Daimler gave a top Turkmen official an armoured Mercedes
rank: High-level executive official
d: Daimler, the German maker of Mercedes-Benz vehicles, gave a high-level official of Turkmenistan's executive branch an armoured Mercedes S-class worth about $300,000 as a birthday present in 2000, because its managers believed all its sales to the Turkmen government were otherwise at risk, according to US court papers filed in March 2010. It also paid about $250,000 to translate and print 10,000 German copies of the Ruhnama, the spiritual guide written by President Saparmurat Niyazov, booking it as market development, and made other payments to Turkmen officials to win government vehicle orders. Daimler settled the US case for $185 million in 2010; prosecutors said it had paid officials in at least 22 countries between 1998 and 2008.
cite: Eurasianet, March 2010; RFE/RL, March 2010
inside: Daimler gave a top Turkmen official an armoured car and paid other officials so the government would keep buying its vehicles.

n: Kozeny's investors made Azerbaijani officials secret SOCAR partners
org_label: Viktor Kozeny and Oily Rock investors
rank: Senior Azerbaijani government officials
d: Viktor Kozeny, a Czech financier, and investors in his company Oily Rock tried in 1997–98 to gain control of SOCAR, Azerbaijan's state oil company, through a privatisation auction they expected to be rigged, by making senior Azerbaijani government officials their secret partners. According to US prosecutors, Kozeny agreed in August 1997 to give the officials two-thirds of the privatisation vouchers and profits, flew millions of dollars in cash into Azerbaijan on private planes, and in 1998 raised Oily Rock's share capital so that $300 million in shares could go to the officials; Oily Rock also paid for two officials' medical treatment in New York. In July 2009 a New York jury convicted American investor Frederic Bourke of conspiring to break the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act; Kozeny remained a fugitive.
cite: US Department of Justice, 10 July 2009; Oil & Gas Journal, 2009
inside: Kozeny's investors made senior Azerbaijani officials their secret partners, paying them cash and shares, to win control of the state oil company in a rigged privatisation.

n: Russia's GRU recruited Georgian air force pilots and a navy radio operator
rank: Air force pilots; navy radio operator
d: Georgia's Interior Ministry said in November 2010 that it had arrested people spying for the GRU, Russia's military intelligence agency, among them six Georgian air force pilots, a naval radio operator accused of passing secret military codes, and four Russian citizens. Most were accused of giving Russia information on the combat readiness of Georgia's forces, two years after the 2008 war between the countries. The ministry said its counter-intelligence had placed its own agent, a former Soviet army officer, inside the GRU, and that people who took an amnesty offered since 2006 for confessing to foreign spying had supplied leads. Fifteen were arrested in October 2010 and two released under plea bargains. Russia's Foreign Ministry called it 'chronic spy mania'.
cite: The Moscow Times, 7 Nov 2010; Christian Science Monitor, 5 Nov 2010
inside: Russia's military intelligence recruited Georgian air force pilots and a navy radio operator to pass it information on Georgia's forces and military codes.

n: Azerbaijani intelligence recruited Armenian officers through fake profiles
rank: Armed forces officers with access to state secrets
d: Armenia's National Security Service said in February 2022 that Azerbaijani intelligence had recruited members of Armenia's armed forces who held posts with access to state secrets. Operatives posed as Armenian women on social media, built close relationships with officers and then offered money for information; checks confirmed one fee received in foreign currency. The officers allegedly passed on troop locations, the number and types of equipment, details of unit commanders and the layout of defences through mobile apps. Nineteen people were detained, some confessed, more than 30 searches were made, and the service said dozens of servicemen were involved. It came after the 2020 war in which Azerbaijan retook much of the territory around Nagorno-Karabakh.
cite: JAMnews, 10 Feb 2022 (citing Armenia's National Security Service); Armenpress, Feb 2022
inside: Azerbaijani intelligence used fake profiles and money to recruit Armenian officers with access to secrets, who passed it troop and defence details.

n: Leaked papers alleged Tullow Oil paid Uganda's prime minister and ministers
rank: Prime Minister; foreign minister; energy minister
d: During an October 2011 debate in Uganda's parliament, MPs produced documents alleging that Tullow Oil, the British company developing Uganda's Lake Albert oil fields, had bribed Prime Minister Amama Mbabazi, Foreign Minister Sam Kutesa and former energy minister Hilary Onek; Onek was accused of receiving about €17 million and strongly denied it. On 11 October 2011 parliament voted to halt all oil deals until new laws were passed, to review existing contracts and to have the accused ministers step aside pending investigation. The government ignored the resolutions, signed new production-sharing agreements with Tullow, and the ministers stayed in office and oversaw the new contracts. The bribery claims were not tested in court.
cite: Foreign Policy, 10 Feb 2012; Irish Times, Oct 2011
inside: Leaked papers alleged Tullow paid Uganda's prime minister and ministers, who then stayed in office and signed new oil agreements with the company.

n: Standard Bank's Tanzanian arm paid $6m to a firm with an official inside
rank: Finance ministry bond deal; former tax authority chief
d: Stanbic Bank Tanzania, part of South Africa's Standard Bank group, paid $6 million to a local 'partner' firm that had a serving member of the Tanzanian government among its directors, while it was winning the job of raising $600 million for the government through a sovereign note. The partner, Enterprise Growth Market Advisors (EGMA), was paid 1% of the money raised after the bank's fee was raised from 1.4% to 2.4%; the cash was withdrawn and no evidence showed EGMA did any work. In November 2015 the UK Serious Fraud Office reached its first deferred prosecution agreement (a deal suspending prosecution in return for penalties) with the bank, which paid about $32.6 million. In April 2016 Tanzania charged former tax authority head Harry Kitilya and two Stanbic executives with laundering the $6 million.
cite: Morgan Lewis, 'Serious Fraud Office reaches an agreement with Standard Bank', Dec 2015; The Citizen (Tanzania), 2 Apr 2016
inside: Standard Bank's Tanzanian arm paid $6 million to a firm with a government official on its board while winning the job of raising money for the government.

n: BAE paid its Tanzania agent $12m to win a $40m military radar deal
rank: Government radar purchase; Attorney General
d: British arms maker BAE Systems paid about $12.4 million to companies of its Tanzanian agent, Sailesh Vithlani, while selling Tanzania's government a military air traffic radar for $39.97 million in 1999. Almost all of the money went through Red Diamond, a BAE-controlled offshore company. Sentencing BAE in London on 21 December 2010, the judge found a high probability that part of the money would be used to favour BAE in the negotiations, and rejected the idea that the agent was merely a lobbyist. BAE pleaded guilty only to an accounting offence, was fined £500,000 and agreed to pay the balance of £30 million to Tanzania. In 2008 Andrew Chenge, Attorney General when the deal was made, resigned as a minister after UK investigators found $1 million in his offshore account; Tanzania's anti-corruption bureau later cleared him.
cite: R v BAE Systems plc, sentencing remarks, Southwark Crown Court, 21 Dec 2010 (World Bank StAR); Corner House; Wikipedia, 'Andrew Chenge'
inside: BAE paid its Tanzanian agent about $12 million on a radar sale, which a British judge found likely to be used to favour BAE in the government's negotiations.

n: Uganda's police chief charged with helping Rwandan agents seize exiles
rank: Inspector General of Police
d: Uganda's military prosecutors charged Kale Kayihura, Inspector General of Police (head of the national police) from 2005 to March 2018, with aiding officers under him to kidnap Rwandan exiles and send them back to Rwanda between 2012 and 2016, working with Rwandan agents. One of those returned, former presidential bodyguard Joel Mutabazi, was given a life sentence in Rwanda. Kayihura was arrested in June 2018 and charged in a military court in August 2018; several senior officers seen as his loyalists were also detained. Kayihura was reported to be close to Rwanda's President Kagame, and the arrests came amid mistrust between the two governments. The US sanctioned him in September 2019 for corruption and abuses by units under him. The army withdrew all charges in August 2023.
cite: African Arguments, Sep 2018; US Treasury via The EastAfrican, 13 Sep 2019; The Observer (Uganda), 31 Aug 2023
inside: Uganda's police chief was charged with having officers under him help Rwandan agents seize Rwandan exiles, so Uganda's police served Rwanda's government; charges were later withdrawn.

n: MPs alleged Tullow Oil paid Uganda's PM and two ministers for oil deals
rank: Prime minister, foreign minister, internal affairs minister
d: In October 2011 Ugandan MP Gerald Karuhanga tabled documents in parliament alleging that the British-Irish oil company Tullow Oil had paid officials, including Prime Minister Amama Mbabazi, Foreign Minister Sam Kutesa and Internal Affairs Minister Hilary Onek, to secure its oil concessions. MPs alleged payments of up to $100 million between June and July 2010, sent from Tullow accounts in Malta. Parliament voted for the three ministers to step aside during an inquiry and delayed Tullow's $2.9 billion sale of a one-third stake to Total and CNOOC until oil laws were passed. Tullow called the claims defamatory. President Museveni said the documents were forgeries and denied that he had taken money from the Italian firm Eni, which had also bid.
cite: The Irish Times, 14 Oct 2011
inside: MPs alleged Tullow paid Uganda's prime minister and two ministers to secure its oil concessions, putting the officials in charge of the deals on the company's side.

n: North Korean spy agency ran Malaysian firms behind arms seller Glocom
rank: Malaysian registered companies
d: North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau, its main foreign intelligence agency, controlled Malaysian-registered companies that fronted for Glocom, a seller of military radios, according to a draft UN sanctions panel report described by Reuters in February 2017. Two Malaysian firms with North Korean directors and shareholders, International Global System and International Golden Services, registered Glocom's website from an unmarked office in Kuala Lumpur in 2009. A North Korean, Kim Chang Hyok, was a founding director; a member of the ruling UMNO party, Mustapha Ya'akub, had been a director since 2014 and said North Koreans controlled Glocom. Glocom exhibited at Malaysia's Defence Services Asia arms show at least three times. In July 2016 a shipment of its battlefield radios bound for Eritrea was seized.
cite: Reuters, 27 Feb 2017 (via The Daily Star)
inside: North Korea's spy agency secretly controlled Malaysian companies that fronted for its military radio business, run with North Korean directors.

n: North Korean front firms placed 130 IT workers in US companies for $88m
rank: Staff posts at US companies and non-profits
d: Two companies controlled by North Korea, Yanbian Silverstar in China and Volasys Silverstar in Russia, employed at least 130 North Korean IT workers who took remote jobs inside US companies and non-profits under stolen or borrowed American identities, according to an indictment in a Missouri federal court reported on 12 December 2024. The 14 North Koreans charged were accused of earning at least $88 million between April 2017 and March 2023 for Pyongyang, including its weapons programmes. Workers were told to earn more than $10,000 a month and some held several jobs at once. Some stole source code and threatened to leak company data unless paid. The US State Department offered $5 million for information on the 14 men.
cite: The Record (Recorded Future News), 12 Dec 2024; NBC News, Dec 2024
inside: North Korean front firms placed IT workers inside US companies under false identities, earning money for Pyongyang and in some cases stealing company data.

n: Azerbaijan paid adverts in German MP Mark Hauptmann's newspaper
rank: Member of the Bundestag
d: Azerbaijan's government paid money to German MP Mark Hauptmann, a CDU member of the Bundestag (the federal parliament) from Thuringia, through tourism advertisements in a local newspaper he published, the Südthüringer Kurier, Der Spiegel reported in March 2021. Investigators claimed he had tried to influence policy on Azerbaijan's behalf. Hauptmann admitted that Azerbaijan, Vietnam and Taiwan had paid for advertorials (paid articles made to look like editorial content) in the paper, but denied that the money affected his political actions. He resigned his seat on 11 March 2021, the third conservative MP to leave that week. The case came days after the Bundestag lifted the immunity of fellow CDU MP Axel Fischer over alleged Azerbaijani payments.
cite: Euronews, 12 Mar 2021; The Irish Times, Mar 2021; Armenpress citing Deutsche Welle and Der Spiegel, 12 Mar 2021
inside: Azerbaijan paid a German MP through adverts in his newspaper, and investigators claimed he tried to influence policy on its behalf.

n: Arms dealer paid Museveni's brother $800,000 in Uganda's helicopter deal
rank: President's brother and special adviser; army procurement
d: Ugandan arms broker Emmanuel Katto paid an $800,000 bribe to Major General Salim Saleh, President Museveni's brother and a special adviser, over a deal in which Uganda's army bought four Mi-24 helicopter gunships from Belarus's state arms company for $12.26 million in February 1997, a judicial commission found. The commission, led by High Court Justice Julia Sebutinde and appointed in 2000, found the helicopters were in a poor state when deployed, put the government's losses at at least $6.8 million, and recommended prosecuting Saleh and Katto, saying Saleh had shown 'the highest form of greed, self interest and corruption'. Katto was charged and acquitted in 2005. OCCRP's 2022 Suisse Secrets reporting showed his Credit Suisse account stayed open until late 2005.
cite: OCCRP, Suisse Secrets, Feb 2022; Daily Monitor, 12 Dec 2002
inside: An arms broker paid the president's brother and adviser a bribe over the army's helicopter purchase, a judicial commission found.

n: Bujagali dam contractor paid $10,000 to Uganda's energy minister
rank: Minister of Energy
d: The manager of Norcil, the UK subsidiary of Norwegian builder Veidekke, paid $10,000 in 1999 to a Ugandan official named in published reports as Richard Kaijuka, then Uganda's energy minister, while Veidekke was a contractor on the planned Bujagali hydropower dam. Veidekke said the payment was unauthorised and did not say what it was for. Kaijuka said it paid for his son's work. When the allegations became public in 2002, Kaijuka was serving as an alternate executive director of the World Bank, which had approved loans and a guarantee for the dam in December 2001. The Bank referred the matter to US, UK, Norwegian and Ugandan authorities, and in June 2002 suspended further action on the project. Veidekke announced in August 2002 that it was withdrawing from the Bujagali site.
cite: US Congressional Research Service, 'World Bank: Bujagali Hydropower Project', RS21501, 22 Apr 2003; Probe International, 11 Sep 2002
inside: A Norwegian dam contractor's subsidiary paid Uganda's energy minister $10,000 while working on the state dam project, a payment the company said was unauthorised and never explained.

n: Japanese IT firm passed Japanese clients' work to North Korean engineers
rank: Japanese software firms and their clients
d: North Korean IT engineers got inside software projects for Japanese companies through a Japanese firm that acted as their front, police in Japan alleged in March 2024. Robast, a company in Fukuyama, won app-development work from Japanese customers through a business-brokering website and passed it on to North Korean engineers; the customers were unlikely to have known. Police found suspicious payments from Robast to the engineers. On 27 March 2024 Kanagawa and Hiroshima police issued arrest warrants for Robast's head, Toshiron Minomo, and his former employer Pak Hyon-il, a South Korean national who ran the IT firm ITZ, on charges of falsifying company records. Police were checking whether Pak had ties to a person raising foreign currency for North Korea. A day earlier the National Police Agency warned firms against hiring North Korean IT workers.
cite: The Register, 28 Mar 2024, citing Jiji, Asahi and Mainichi
inside: North Korean engineers got inside Japanese companies' software projects through a Japanese front firm that passed the work on to them.

n: Taiwan soldiers guarding the Presidential Office sold secrets to China
rank: Presidential Office security unit
d: Chinese intelligence agents recruited soldiers inside the military unit that guards Taiwan's Presidential Office, the seat of Taiwan's president. In March 2025 the Taipei District Court convicted four soldiers, three from the Presidential Office security unit and one from the defence ministry's information and telecommunications command, of passing confidential military information to Chinese agents between 2022 and 2024. Prosecutors said they photographed material on their phones and were paid NT$260,000 to NT$660,000 (about US$7,850 to US$20,000) each. A tip-off to the defence ministry in August 2024 started the investigation. They received five years and ten months to seven years in prison.
cite: The Defense Post / AFP, 28 March 2025
inside: Chinese intelligence paid soldiers inside the unit that guards Taiwan's Presidential Office to pass it confidential military information.

n: China's spy recruiting in Taiwan: 64 charged in 2024, most of them soldiers
rank: Taiwan's armed forces
d: China's Communist Party recruits serving and retired members of Taiwan's armed forces to spy and build networks inside them, according to Taiwan's National Security Bureau, the island's main intelligence agency. Its report of January 2025 said 64 people were prosecuted for Chinese espionage in 2024, up from 48 in 2023, and that spy cases rose from three in 2021 to 15.
