Serving military personnel made up 43% of those prosecuted and retired personnel 23%. The bureau said recruiters work through local gangs, underground banks, shell companies and temples, and use old comradeship between former colleagues to pull serving officers into networks.
cite: Taiwan News, 13 January 2025, citing National Security Bureau report
inside: China's Communist Party recruits serving and retired Taiwanese military personnel to spy and to pull serving officers into its networks.

n: Latvian ex-minister and MP Ādamsons jailed for spying for Russia's FSB
rank: Member of the Saeima (parliament), defence committee
d: Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) obtained information from Jānis Ādamsons, a sitting member of Latvia's parliament, the Saeima, who had been interior minister in 1994–95 and sat on its defence, internal affairs and anti-corruption committee. Courts found he passed material on NATO units and compromising details about Latvia's State Security Service to a former KGB officer, Gennady Silonov, who handed it to the FSB; investigators recorded more than 100 meetings since at least 2015, and money was sent to his daughter in Russia. He was arrested in 2021 and sentenced in November 2023 to eight and a half years. In January 2026 the appeal court gave eight years and two months.
cite: LSM (Latvian Public Broadcasting), 9 November 2023 and 16 January 2026
inside: Russia's FSB obtained NATO and security-service information from a sitting Latvian MP on the defence committee through a former KGB officer.

n: Guard at the US embassy in Oslo spied for Russia and Iran
rank: US embassy security guard
d: Russian and Iranian intelligence services each obtained the help of a Norwegian security guard working inside the US embassy in Oslo. Between March and November 2024 he gave them embassy floor plans, security routines, and the names, addresses, phone numbers and car number plates of diplomats, staff and their families, as well as a list of mail services used by Norway's intelligence service. He was paid 0.17 Bitcoin by Iranian intelligence and €10,000 by Russian intelligence. An Oslo court convicted him on 15 October 2025 and sentenced him to three years and seven months. He said he acted in protest at US backing for Israel's offensive in Gaza.
cite: The National, 16 October 2025; AP, 16 October 2025
inside: Russian and Iranian intelligence each paid a guard inside the US embassy in Oslo for floor plans, security routines and staff details.

n: Hong Kong trade office manager ran a UK Border Force officer as a spy
rank: UK Border Force officer and special constable
d: Bill Yuen, a former Hong Kong police superintendent working at the Hong Kong Economic and Trade Office in London, the Hong Kong government's official office in Britain, directed Peter Wai, a serving UK Border Force officer who was also a volunteer City of London police constable. Prosecutors said the pair carried out 'shadow policing' of Hong Kong dissidents, including former lawmaker Nathan Law, and that Yuen told Wai to target MPs and government staff. Wai was paid from a trade office account and misused police computer systems. In May 2026 an Old Bailey jury convicted both of assisting a foreign intelligence service under the National Security Act. Britain summoned China's ambassador.
cite: AP via WTOP, May 2026; SCMP 2024
inside: A Hong Kong government office in London directed and paid a serving UK Border Force officer to spy on dissidents and misuse police systems.

n: Australian army private and husband charged with spying for Russia
rank: Australian Defence Force private
d: Australian police allege that Kira Korolev, a Russian-born private in the Australian Defence Force (ADF), and her husband Igor used her ADF work login to obtain sensitive defence information intended for Russian authorities. The Australian Federal Police say she made undeclared trips to Russia from 2023 while on long leave, and that her husband accessed her account and emailed material to her private address while she was there. Both were arrested in Brisbane in July 2024. In June 2026 police upgraded the charges to conspiracy to commit espionage, which carries a maximum life sentence; it is the first use of that offence since Australia's 2018 foreign interference laws. The case is before the courts.
cite: JURIST, 12 July 2024; Cyber Daily, June 2026
inside: Police allege a Russian-born private in Australia's army and her husband used her defence login to obtain information meant for Russia.

n: Russian spy ring inside Bulgaria's defence ministry and parliament registry
rank: Defence ministry official, military intelligence officers, parliament's classified registry
d: Bulgarian prosecutors say Russia's military intelligence ran a ring of insiders in Bulgaria's defence establishment, led by a former senior Bulgarian military intelligence official trained at a GRU school in Moscow. Those charged in March 2021 included a senior defence ministry planning and budget official, two serving military intelligence officers, and a former military attaché who headed parliament's registry of classified information. Prosecutors said the ring passed classified NATO and EU documents, through the leader's dual-national wife, to the Russian embassy, coordinated by Russia's military attaché. Bulgaria expelled Russian diplomats. The case was re-submitted to the Sofia Military Court in February 2024 and the accused remain on trial.
cite: AP, 19 March 2021; BTA, 14 February 2024
inside: Russia's military intelligence ran a ring of insiders in Bulgaria's defence ministry, military intelligence and parliament's classified registry, prosecutors say.

n: Iranian agents recruited Israeli soldiers in Iron Dome and air force HQ
rank: Iron Dome unit and Air Force operational headquarters
d: Iranian intelligence recruited Israeli soldiers inside air-defence units, Israeli prosecutors say. In January 2025 they indicted two 21-year-olds from Kiryat Yam: Yuri Eliasfov, who served in the Iron Dome missile-defence unit, and Georgi Andreyev, who served in the Air Force's operational headquarters. The charge sheet says they were in contact with an Iranian handler called 'Boaz', and that Eliasfov passed photos and video of an Iron Dome radar screen and offered footage for $10,000, receiving $800 in advance. The case is one of a run: police arrested nearly 30 Israelis over Iran-linked spying in December 2024 alone, most recruited online for small payments.
cite: Times of Israel, 31 January 2025
inside: Iranian intelligence recruited Israeli soldiers in the Iron Dome unit and air force headquarters to pass it images of military systems for payment.

n: Chinese agent bought the list of South Korea's undercover military spies
rank: Korea Defense Intelligence Command
d: A suspected Chinese intelligence agent recruited a civilian employee of the Korea Defense Intelligence Command, South Korea's military spy agency, after the employee was detained at a Chinese airport in 2017. The employee sent the agent personal details of South Korean undercover agents working abroad, known as 'black agents', in 30 documents and voice messages, and received 162 million won while asking for about 400 million won on 40 occasions. A court martial sentenced him on 21 January 2025 to 20 years in prison and a 1.2 billion won fine. The leak forced South Korea to pull back agents, and reporting said rebuilding its overseas networks could take years.
cite: Korea JoongAng Daily, 21 January 2025; SCMP, 2024
inside: A Chinese agent paid a South Korean military intelligence employee, who sent him the personal details of South Korea's undercover agents abroad.

n: Pakistani intelligence paid a CRPF officer posted in Pahalgam
rank: Assistant sub-inspector, Central Reserve Police Force
d: Pakistani intelligence officers paid Moti Ram Jat, an assistant sub-inspector in India's Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), the country's largest armed police force, for information, according to India's National Investigation Agency (NIA). The NIA says that from 2023 he passed details of troop movements and deployments in Jammu and Kashmir, intelligence on security operations and the locations of installations, receiving Rs 3,000 a month from a foreign account into his wife's account and further money through Indian go-betweens. He served with a battalion in Pahalgam until five days before the April 2025 attack there that killed 26 people. He was arrested in May 2025, dismissed, and charged in November 2025 at Patiala House Court in Delhi.
cite: ThePrint, 15 November 2025; The Week, 27 May 2025
inside: Pakistani intelligence paid an Indian armed police officer in Kashmir to pass details of troop movements and security operations, investigators say.

n: Russia's FSB recruited two colonels in Zelensky's State Guard
rank: Colonels in the State Guard (protection of top officials)
d: Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) recruited two colonels in Ukraine's State Guard, the agency that protects the president and other top officials, according to Ukraine's Security Service (SBU). The SBU said in May 2024 that the colonels had been recruited before Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, and that the FSB plan, run from Moscow, sought soldiers close to President Zelensky's security detail who could take him hostage and kill him, alongside rocket and drone strikes on senior officials. The two were detained on suspicion of treason, which carries a life sentence. SBU chief Vasyl Maliuk said he oversaw the counter-operation personally.
cite: Global News / AP, 7 May 2024
inside: Russia's FSB recruited two colonels in the guard that protects Ukraine's president, as part of a plan to use his security detail against him, Ukraine says.

n: Italian navy officer Walter Biot sold classified documents to Russia
rank: Frigate captain, General Staff of Defence planning office
d: Russian military intelligence officers at the embassy in Rome paid Walter Biot, an Italian navy frigate captain working in the political-military planning office of Italy's General Staff of Defence, for classified documents. On 30 March 2021 police caught him in a Rome car park handing a memory card hidden in a medicine box to Dmitrij Ostroukhov, a Russian military officer at the embassy, who gave him €5,000. Italy expelled Ostroukhov and his superior two days later. A military court and a civilian assize court both convicted him. On 6 May 2026 Italy's Court of Cassation rejected his last appeal, making a 20-year sentence final.
cite: Il Post, 15 March 2022; ANSA, 6 May 2026
inside: Russian military intelligence officers paid an Italian navy officer in the defence general staff for classified documents.

n: French finance ministry employee passed data on dissidents to Algeria
rank: French finance ministry employee
d: An Algerian contact at Algeria's consulate in Créteil, near Paris, obtained information on Algerian asylum seekers and known opponents of Algeria's government from an employee of France's finance ministry, French prosecutors say. The employee was placed under formal investigation, a step in French law meaning there is serious evidence of likely involvement, for spying for Algeria; prosecutors made it public in March 2025. A social worker at the French Office for Immigration and Integration was also accused of sharing asylum seekers' confidential files. The case added to a crisis in relations between France and Algeria.
cite: Arab News / AFP, 13 March 2025
inside: Algeria's consulate got information from an employee inside France's finance ministry about Algerian dissidents and asylum seekers, data the French state was meant to protect.

n: Hydro-Québec researcher accused of passing work to China's talent scheme
rank: Researcher at Hydro-Québec (state power utility)
d: Canadian prosecutors say Yuesheng Wang, a researcher at Hydro-Québec, Quebec's state-owned power company, shared its proprietary battery research with Chinese entities and applied to Chinese universities through a Chinese government programme for recruiting foreign-trained scientists. Arrested in November 2022, he was the first person charged with economic espionage under Canada's Security of Information Act. He has pleaded not guilty. His trial ended in 2026, but the judge postponed the verdict in June 2026 and the case returned to court in September.
cite: Global News, 5 June 2026; CTV News, 2022–2025
inside: Chinese state bodies recruited a researcher inside Quebec's state power company, who allegedly passed them its proprietary battery research through a Chinese government talent programme.

n: Iran hanged a nuclear institute scientist as a Mossad agent
rank: Nuclear Science and Technology Research Institute, Atomic Energy Organisation
d: Iran's judiciary says Israel's foreign intelligence service, Mossad, recruited Rouzbeh Vadi, a scientist at the Nuclear Science and Technology Research Institute of the Atomic Energy Organisation of Iran. Officials said he was recruited online, vetted by a Mossad officer called 'Alex', met handlers in Vienna, and passed information on an Iranian nuclear scientist later killed in the 12-day war with Israel in June 2025. He was hanged in August 2025 after Iran's Supreme Court upheld the sentence. The case was one of several espionage executions after the war; the evidence was not made public and rights groups count a steep rise in Iran's executions in 2025.
cite: Iran International, 6 August 2025; The National, 6 August 2025
inside: Iran says Israel's Mossad recruited a scientist inside Iran's nuclear research institute, who passed it information on a fellow scientist later killed in the war.

n: Long-serving Polish defence ministry employee held as Russian-Belarusian spy
rank: Ministry of National Defence employee
d: Poland's Military Counterintelligence Service suspects that Russian and Belarusian intelligence recruited a long-serving employee of Poland's Ministry of National Defence. The man, reported to be 60 and to have worked in various ministry posts since the 1990s, was detained at the ministry's Warsaw headquarters on 3 February 2026 as he arrived for work, after months of surveillance. The ministry confirmed he is suspected of collaborating with foreign intelligence and that prosecution proceedings are under way. The case is one of a series of Russian and Belarusian recruitment cases inside Poland's state since 2022.
cite: Notes from Poland, 3 February 2026, citing Onet and the defence ministry
inside: Russian and Belarusian intelligence allegedly recruited a long-serving employee inside Poland's defence ministry to work for them from within the ministry.

n: Cologne policewoman suspected of feeding police files to Turkey's MIT
rank: Police officer, Cologne police headquarters
d: German prosecutors suspect Turkey's national intelligence agency, MIT, of obtaining internal police information through a policewoman at Cologne police headquarters. According to rulings of Germany's Federal Court of Justice in August and September 2025, which upheld searches and seizures, the officer, identified as T., sent internal police information and assessments to an administrative employee of the Turkish Consulate General in Cologne between March 2024 and February 2025, covering the PKK (a Kurdish militant group), incidents seen as hostile to Turkey and unrelated police matters. The consular employee is suspected of reporting, at least indirectly, to MIT. North Rhine-Westphalia's interior ministry authorised prosecution in July 2025.
cite: Middle East Forum, 2025, citing Federal Court of Justice rulings StB 37/25 and StB 42/25; Stockholm Center for Freedom
inside: Turkey's intelligence service allegedly got a Cologne police officer to send internal police files, including on Kurdish militants, to a Turkish consular employee.

n: Congo sentences ex-president Kabila to death for working with Rwanda and M23
rank: Former president, senator
d: Congo's government accuses Joseph Kabila, president from 2001 to 2019 and afterwards a member of the Senate, of collaborating with Rwanda and the Rwanda-backed M23 rebel group, which seized Goma and other eastern cities in January 2025. In May 2025 the Senate lifted his immunity from prosecution, and in April he appeared in rebel-held Goma. On 30 September 2025 a military court in Kinshasa convicted him in absentia of treason, insurrection, conspiracy and supporting terrorism, and sentenced him to death. Kabila denied the charges and called the Senate vote 'dictatorial'. His whereabouts are unknown.
cite: AP via Arab News, 30 September 2025
inside: Congo's military court convicted a former president and sitting senator of treason for working with Rwanda and the Rwanda-backed M23 rebels against the state.

n: Ukrainian MP Nestor Shufrych on trial as an FSB recruit
rank: Member of the Verkhovna Rada (parliament)
d: Ukraine's prosecutors say Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) recruited Nestor Shufrych, a sitting member of Ukraine's parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, from the pro-Russian Opposition Platform – For Life. They allege he carried out tasks set by a former deputy secretary of Ukraine's National Security and Defence Council who moved to Moscow in 2014, spread Russian narratives, and in 2016 paid over 648,700 roubles to Russia's National Guard in occupied Crimea for protection of his property there. The Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) searched his home and charged him with treason on 15 September 2023, and a court held him in custody. Prosecutors sent the case to court on 3 September 2024.
cite: NV (New Voice of Ukraine), September 2024
inside: Russia's FSB allegedly recruited a sitting Ukrainian MP, who carried out tasks set by his Russian-based contact and spread Russian narratives from inside parliament.

n: 'Cobalt': Russian intelligence said to have recruited an Irish legislator
rank: Member of the Oireachtas (parliament)
d: The Sunday Times reported in October 2024 that Russian intelligence had recruited a serving member of the Oireachtas, Ireland's parliament, through a 'honeytrap', code-named the person 'Cobalt', and said one aim was to strain relations between Britain, Ireland and the EU during the Brexit talks. It said Irish military and security services had identified the person, who was not named. Justice Minister Helen McEntee declined to say whether she had been briefed; Tánaiste and defence minister Micheál Martin said he had never been told. Several senators stood up in the Seanad to say they were not Russian spies. TheJournal's sources said Russia and other states had approached Oireachtas members and senior officials.
cite: TheJournal.ie, 13 October 2024, citing The Sunday Times
inside: Russian intelligence reportedly recruited a serving member of Ireland's parliament, partly to strain British, Irish and EU relations during the Brexit talks.

n: ASIO: foreign spy 'A-Team' recruited a former Australian politician
rank: Former member of parliament
d: Mike Burgess, director-general of ASIO, Australia's domestic security agency, said in his annual threat speech in February 2024 that a unit of a foreign intelligence service, which ASIO calls 'the A-Team', had cultivated and recruited a former Australian politician several years earlier. He said the politician had sold out the country and had even proposed bringing a family member of a prime minister into the spies' orbit, a plan that did not go ahead. Burgess said the A-Team uses social networking sites and offers money to people with access to privileged information. He did not name the country or the politician, and no one was charged because the person was no longer active.
cite: Al Jazeera, 29 February 2024
inside: A foreign intelligence service recruited an Australian politician, who sold out the country and even proposed bringing a prime minister's relative into the spies' reach.

n: Iranian intelligence ran British soldier Daniel Khalife from inside the army
rank: British Army soldier with NATO security clearance
d: Iranian intelligence obtained information from Daniel Khalife, a serving British Army soldier who had joined at 16 in 2018 and held the second-highest NATO security clearance. Over about two and a half years, while posted in Britain and at Fort Hood in Texas, he passed material including a handwritten list of 15 soldiers, among them special forces personnel, with service numbers, ranks and units. He twice collected cash and travelled to Turkey to meet his handlers. He escaped from Wandsworth prison in September 2023 while awaiting trial and was caught days later. Convicted in November 2024 of espionage and a terrorism offence, he was sentenced at Woolwich Crown Court on 3 February 2025 to 14 years.
cite: Al Jazeera, 3 February 2025
inside: Iranian intelligence paid a serving British soldier with high security clearance to pass it army material, including names and details of special forces personnel.

n: Guard inside Britain's Berlin embassy photographed secrets for Russia
rank: British embassy security guard
d: Russia's military attaché's office in Berlin obtained secrets from David Smith, a former Royal Air Force serviceman working as a security guard at the British embassy in Berlin. From about 2018 he used his access to enter offices at night and photograph classified documents, some marked secret, including a report sent to Prime Minister Boris Johnson; he also filmed the building and sent annotated photos of new staff. He had written to a Russian major general serving as attaché at Russia's Berlin embassy, and the judge found Russia paid him. Arrested in August 2021, he pleaded guilty to eight Official Secrets Act offences and was sentenced at the Old Bailey on 17 February 2023 to 13 years.
cite: Civil Service World, 17 February 2023
inside: Russia's military attaché's office paid a guard inside Britain's Berlin embassy to photograph classified documents the embassy was meant to keep secret.

n: Russia's GRU ran an Austrian army colonel for 26 years
rank: Austrian Army colonel
d: Russia's military intelligence service, the GRU, recruited an Austrian Army colonel who, according to his indictment, passed it military secrets from 1992 until September 2018 in return for about €280,000. He was arrested in November 2018, after he had retired, and the case became public that month. A jury in Salzburg convicted him on 9 June 2020. He was sentenced to three years in prison but released for the time he had already spent in custody. His defence argued that he had passed only publicly available information and put the payments at €220,000.
cite: RFE/RL via GlobalSecurity, 10 June 2020
inside: Russia's military intelligence paid a serving Austrian army colonel for 26 years to pass it military secrets from inside the armed forces.

n: AfD Bundestag aide Sergienko reported to take tasks from an FSB officer
rank: Aide to AfD Bundestag member Eugen Schmidt
d: Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) directed Vladimir Sergienko, an aide and speechwriter to Eugen Schmidt, a member of the German Bundestag for the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, according to leaked emails published by The Insider and Der Spiegel on 1 February 2024. The documents showed him in contact with an FSB officer, Ilya Vechtomov, and taking actions at his request, including filing a lawsuit to delay German military aid to Ukraine. He had visited Russia 18 times since the full-scale invasion. Sergienko called the claims unfounded and Schmidt called them 'without substance'. German authorities later moved to strip Sergienko of his citizenship.
cite: Kyiv Independent, 2 February 2024, citing The Insider and Der Spiegel; beck-aktuell (OVG Berlin-Brandenburg)
inside: Russia's FSB allegedly directed an aide inside the German Bundestag, who acted at its request, including filing a lawsuit to delay German military aid to Ukraine.

n: China says CIA recruited a military-industry worker, 'Zeng', in Italy
rank: Employee of a Chinese military-industrial group
d: China's Ministry of State Security (MSS) said in August 2023 that the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) had recruited Zeng, a 52-year-old employee of a Chinese military-industrial group, while he was studying in Italy. It said a CIA officer at the US embassy in Rome befriended him, offered 'a huge amount of compensation' and help moving his family to the United States in return for sensitive military information, and that Zeng signed an espionage agreement, was trained and returned to China to spy. State media said 'compulsory measures' had been taken and the case sent to prosecutors. The claim came soon after CIA director William Burns said the agency had rebuilt its network in China. The US did not comment and no evidence was published.
cite: Al Jazeera, 11 August 2023
inside: China says the CIA recruited an employee of a Chinese military-industrial group, who signed on and returned home to pass it sensitive military information.

n: Russian intelligence recruited a US Army officer who became a Green Beret
rank: US Army Special Forces captain
d: Russian intelligence agents recruited Peter Debbins, who then served as a US Army officer from 1998 to 2005, first in chemical units and then in Army Special Forces, where he reached the rank of captain. The US Justice Department said the conspiracy ran from December 1996 to January 2011: he was given a code name in 1997, passed details about his units and deployments, and supplied names of former Special Forces team members so the Russians could try to recruit them. He was arrested in 2020, pleaded guilty, and on 14 May 2021 was sentenced in Virginia to 188 months, almost 16 years, in prison.
cite: US Department of Justice, Eastern District of Virginia, 14 May 2021
inside: Russian intelligence recruited a man who then served as a US Army officer and passed it details of his units and names of soldiers it could approach.

n: Fed adviser accused of giving China's spies Fed rate deliberations
rank: Senior adviser, Federal Reserve Board's international finance division
d: US prosecutors say Chinese government intelligence officers obtained confidential Federal Reserve information from John Harold Rogers, a senior adviser in the Fed Board's Division of International Finance from 2010 to 2021. The Fed is the US central bank. The indictment, announced on 31 January 2025, alleges that from at least 2018 he passed proprietary data, deliberations on tariffs against China, governors' briefing books and sensitive Federal Open Market Committee (interest-rate committee) deliberations to officers posing as graduate students, meeting them in hotel rooms in China under cover of teaching. He was reportedly paid about $450,000 in 2023 as a part-time professor at a Chinese university. He is charged with conspiracy to commit economic espionage and lying to the Fed's inspector general.
cite: US Department of Justice, 31 January 2025
inside: Chinese intelligence officers allegedly obtained confidential interest-rate and trade deliberations from a senior adviser inside the US Federal Reserve, who was also paid by a Chinese university.

n: Greek air force colonel arrested for passing NATO plans to China
rank: Hellenic Air Force colonel, unit commander
d: Greek investigators say Chinese handlers obtained classified NATO operational plans from a serving Greek air force colonel who commanded a unit in the coastal district of Kavouri, near Athens. He was arrested inside a military facility in February 2026, in the presence of a military prosecutor. Reports said he sent material on air-defence systems and NATO regional strategy using specialised encryption software, and that he tried to recruit other personnel. He was charged with espionage, reportedly confessed, and was jailed pending trial; Greek media later reported he claimed he had been coerced and used a burner phone with a digital wallet to receive Chinese payments.
cite: iefimerida.gr, 6 February 2026; To Vima, February 2026
inside: Chinese handlers allegedly paid a serving Greek air force colonel to pass them classified NATO plans and to try to recruit other personnel.

n: Iran's intelligence ministry paid a German army interpreter
rank: Bundeswehr military translator and cultural adviser
d: Iran's Ministry of Intelligence (MOIS) recruited Abdul Hamid S., an Afghan-German translator working for the Bundeswehr, Germany's armed forces. Between 2013 and 2017 he met Iranian intelligence officers in European cities and gave them site plans of German military facilities and defence ministry analyses of certain countries and topics, for about $37,000. He was arrested in January 2019. In March 2020 the court in Koblenz convicted him of treason and sentenced him to six years and ten months, saying he had abused his position of trust; his wife received a suspended sentence for helping him.
cite: FDD / Jerusalem Post, 25 March 2020; The Local, 15 January 2019
inside: Iran's intelligence ministry paid an interpreter inside Germany's armed forces to hand over plans of military sites and defence ministry analyses.

n: Mossad reportedly hired IRGC guards to plant the bombs that killed Haniyeh
rank: IRGC Ansar al-Mahdi protection unit
d: Israel's foreign intelligence service, Mossad, recruited agents from the Ansar al-Mahdi protection unit of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), the unit that guards senior officials, according to Iranian officials quoted by The Telegraph in August 2024. They said the agents planted explosives in three rooms of an IRGC guesthouse in north Tehran, which were detonated remotely on 31 July 2024, killing Hamas political leader Ismail Haniyeh, who was in Tehran for President Pezeshkian's inauguration. Officials said further devices were found in two other rooms and that an earlier plan for May had been dropped. Israel neither claimed nor denied responsibility.
cite: Asharq Al-Awsat, 3 August 2024, citing The Telegraph
inside: Mossad reportedly recruited guards inside the Revolutionary Guards unit that protects Iran's officials, and they planted the bombs that killed a guest in its guesthouse.

n: Pakistani general and brigadier jailed for spying for foreign agencies
rank: Lieutenant-general and brigadier, Pakistan Army
d: Foreign intelligence agencies obtained sensitive information from two senior Pakistan Army officers and a civilian working at a sensitive state organisation, according to Pakistan's military, which tried them under the Pakistan Army Act and the Official Secrets Act. On 30 May 2019 army chief Qamar Javed Bajwa confirmed a 14-year prison sentence for Lieutenant-General Javed Iqbal and death sentences for retired Brigadier Raja Rizwan and the civilian doctor, Wasim Akram, for espionage and leaking information to foreign spy agencies. The army did not name the agencies. The case had been made public that February.
cite: Al Jazeera, 30 May 2019
inside: Foreign spy agencies obtained sensitive information from a serving Pakistani general, a brigadier and a civilian at a sensitive state body, according to Pakistan's military.

n: State Department employee photographed secret files for suspected Chinese agents
rank: State Department employee with top-secret clearance
d: People Michael Schena believed worked for China's government recruited him, a US State Department employee with a top-secret clearance. From April 2022 he was in contact with online acquaintances who said they worked for consulting firms; in August 2024 one met him in a hotel in Peru and gave him $10,000 and a phone for taskings. In October 2024 he photographed at least four secret documents at work and sent them. The FBI watched him photograph seven more in February 2025 and arrested him before he could send them. He pleaded guilty and on 4 September 2025 was sentenced to 48 months in prison.
cite: US Department of Justice, 4 September 2025
inside: People he believed were Chinese agents paid a US State Department employee with top-secret clearance to photograph and send them secret documents from his workplace.

n: Cuban officers guarding Maduro: Cuba confirms 32 killed in the US raid
rank: Venezuelan president's security apparatus
d: Cuban military and police officers worked inside Venezuela's security system around President Nicolás Maduro. After US forces seized Maduro in Caracas on 3 January 2026, Cuba's government said 32 Cuban officers had been killed in the operation while on a mission carried out at the request of Venezuela's government, and declared two days of mourning. It did not give their names or posts. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Maduro's internal security apparatus was headed by Cubans who were 'propping up Maduro'. Cuba has sent military and police personnel to Venezuela for years, including to help run its military counterintelligence.
cite: AP, 4–5 January 2026
inside: Cuba's own military and police officers worked inside Venezuela's security system, heading Maduro's internal security and helping run military counterintelligence.

n: CIA had a source inside Venezuela's government tracking Maduro
rank: Source inside the Venezuelan government
d: The US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) recruited a person inside Venezuela's government who reported President Nicolás Maduro's whereabouts in the days and moments before US special forces seized him in Caracas on 3 January 2026, The New York Times reported, citing people familiar with the operation. It said CIA officers had worked clandestinely inside Venezuela from August 2025 to map Maduro's movements and routine, after President Trump authorised more aggressive CIA action and, in November, planning for operations in the country. The US had offered a $50 million reward for information leading to his capture. The source's identity and how they were recruited have not been disclosed, and the US government has not confirmed the account.
cite: L'Orient Today, January 2026, citing The New York Times
inside: The CIA reportedly recruited a source inside Venezuela's government who reported Maduro's whereabouts so US forces could seize him.

n: Mali's junta says French intelligence recruited two generals for a plot
rank: Army generals, including a former regional governor
d: Mali's military government accuses French intelligence of trying to get inside its armed forces. In August 2025 it arrested Generals Abass Dembélé, a former governor of the central Mopti region, and Nema Sagara, along with a French national, Yann Vezilier, whom it said acted for French intelligence services to rally political figures, civil society and military officers against the government of General Assimi Goïta. Sources told Reuters more than 30 soldiers and officials were detained. France's foreign ministry gave no official comment. The arrests followed Mali's break with France and its turn to Russian military support since 2021.
cite: Reuters via Arab News, 15 August 2025
inside: Mali's junta says French intelligence worked through a French agent to win over two generals and other officers inside its armed forces against the government.

n: Slovak military academy vice-rector charged as a GRU contact
rank: Vice-rector, Slovak military academy
d: Slovak police say Russia's military intelligence, the GRU, had Pavol B., a former vice-rector of a Slovak military academy, as a contact from 2013, gathering and passing it information of strategic importance. He was detained and charged in March 2022 together with Bohuš G., a contributor to a pro-Russian website, who admitted seeking material from classified intelligence reports prepared for parliament. Slovakia expelled three Russian diplomats the day before the charges were announced. Bohuš Garbár later received a suspended sentence after admitting the offence.
cite: Reuters via Euronews, 16 March 2022; TASR, 28 February 2023
inside: Russia's military intelligence had a vice-rector of a Slovak military academy as its contact, passing it information of strategic importance from inside the defence establishment.

n: Chinese agents paid aides working inside Taiwan's legislature
rank: Legislative aides, including to a former Speaker
d: Chinese intelligence agents paid aides working in Taiwan's legislature, the Legislative Yuan, for information, prosecutors say. In April 2025 they accused a former aide to You Si-kun, Speaker from 2020 to 2024, of selling confidential legislative information for cash and virtual currency received at meetings in China; he admitted taking money but said he shared only public material. In April 2026 prosecutors indicted Chu Cheng-chi, a former aide to legislator Ho Chih-wei who had won a ruling party primary for Taipei city council, for photographing documents marked confidential in August 2022 and sending them to a Chinese contact for 20,000 yuan. Both worked for the governing Democratic Progressive Party, which expelled Chu.
cite: CNA via GlobalSecurity, 2 April 2025; Taipei Times, 3 April 2026
inside: Chinese intelligence paid aides working for legislators inside Taiwan's legislature to photograph and hand over confidential legislative documents for cash.

n: Russia's FSB tasked a member of Estonia's Defence League in Narva
rank: Member of the Estonian Defence League
d: An officer of the operational department of Russia's FSB Border Service, Aleksandr Bobkov, tasked Ivan Dmitrijev, an active member of the Estonian Defence League, the volunteer force that forms part of Estonia's national defence, to supply information between March and May 2025. Prosecutors said the FSB wanted details on Defence League members, Estonian Defence Forces personnel in the border city of Narva and local political life. Estonia's Internal Security Service arrested him before he could travel to Russia to meet his handler after a training exercise. In October 2025 the Viru District Court convicted him under a plea agreement and sentenced him to four years and eleven months in prison.
cite: Estonian Prosecutor's Office, 8 October 2025
inside: An officer of Russia's FSB tasked a member of Estonia's volunteer defence force to report on its members, Estonian soldiers and politics in Narva.

n: Chinese intelligence recruited Philippine defence, navy and coast guard analysts
rank: Analysts in the Department of National Defense, Navy and Coast Guard
d: Chinese intelligence recruited three Filipino analysts working in the Philippines' Department of National Defense, Navy and Coast Guard, according to the country's National Security Council (NSC). In March 2026 the NSC said it had 'addressed and terminated' the operation: the three had given Chinese handlers lists of military personnel and operational details of resupply missions to Philippine outposts in the South China Sea, where the two countries are in a territorial dispute. A spokesman said they were 'low-level analysts' recruited over time for money, had confessed and were cooperating. China's embassy did not respond. The case followed arrests of Chinese nationals for spying near military sites and election offices in 2025.
cite: Philstar / AFP, 6 March 2026
inside: The Philippine security council says Chinese intelligence recruited and paid analysts inside the Philippine defence department, navy and coast guard to hand over personnel lists and details of resupply missions.

n: Congo tries General Yav, ex-eastern commander, for treason linked to Rwanda
rank: Commander of the third defence zone (Ituri, North Kivu, Maniema)
d: Congo's authorities accuse Lieutenant-General Philémon Yav, who commanded the army's third defence zone covering Ituri, North Kivu and Maniema in the east, of working with neighbouring Rwanda, which UN experts say backs the M23 rebels. He was detained in September 2022 for 'connivance with a foreign country'; Congolese media reported he had been in regular contact with General James Kabarebe, security adviser to Rwanda's President Kagame. His trial for treason and taking part in an insurrection began at the High Military Court in December 2025. Reports from the hearings said the prosecution struggled to prove contact with Rwanda. On 3 September 2026 the army's auditor general asked for life imprisonment, and a verdict was awaited.
cite: North Africa Post, 22 September 2022; AllAfrica, 28 January and 4 September 2026
inside: Congo accuses a general commanding its eastern army zone of secretly working with Rwanda, which backs the rebels his forces were fighting.

n: Navy HQ clerk in Delhi passed information to an ISI handler
rank: Clerk, directorate of dockyard, Indian Navy headquarters
d: Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), its main spy agency, recruited Vishal Yadav, an upper division clerk in the directorate of dockyard at Nausena Bhawan, the Indian Navy's headquarters in New Delhi, according to Rajasthan Police's intelligence wing. Officers said a female ISI handler using the name 'Priya Sharma' paid him for sensitive and strategically significant information over several years, including during Operation Sindoor, India's strikes on Pakistan in May 2025. He was arrested in June 2025 after surveillance of people linked to Pakistani networks. The case was one of several arrests of Indian security personnel for passing information to Pakistan that year.
cite: The Week, 26 June 2025
inside: Pakistan's ISI allegedly paid a clerk inside the Indian Navy's headquarters to pass it sensitive information, including during India's strikes on Pakistan.

n: FSB mole headed the staff of the SBU's Anti-Terrorist Center in Ukraine
rank: Chief of staff, SBU Anti-Terrorist Center
d: Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) recruited Dmytro Kozyura, a colonel in Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) who later headed the staff of its Anti-Terrorist Center, during a trip to Vienna in 2018. When his Russian handlers resumed contact in December 2024 they tasked him with gathering information on troop deployments, Ukrainian weapons, critical infrastructure, the effects of Russian strikes and senior military and political leaders. The SBU says it watched him and used him to feed the FSB disinformation before SBU chief Vasyl Maliuk personally detained him in February 2025. On 25 June 2026 Ukraine's prosecutor-general announced he had been sentenced to life imprisonment for high treason under martial law.
cite: Kyiv Post, 2026; Liga.net, 25 June 2026
inside: Russia's FSB recruited a Ukrainian security service colonel who headed its anti-terrorist staff and tasked him with gathering military and leadership information from inside.

n: Temple head recruited Taiwanese soldiers for China's 'surrender' videos
rank: Active-duty and retired Taiwanese military personnel
d: Chinese handlers used Lee Hui-hsin, head of a temple in New Taipei's Luzhou district, to recruit serving and retired Taiwanese military personnel. Prosecutors said she received tasks during religious exchange trips to China to build a pro-China organisation in Taiwan, and in 2023 used her temple and organised-crime contacts to recruit soldiers, many in financial need. Recruits filmed 'psychological warfare' videos in uniform holding the Chinese flag and pledging to surrender, and handed over confidential military documents. Soldiers reported the scheme in October 2023 and March 2024. Ten people were indicted in October 2024, and on 5 June 2025 Taiwan's Supreme Court upheld their sentences, including six years and eight months for Lee.
cite: CNA via GlobalSecurity, 5 June 2025
inside: Chinese handlers used a temple head to recruit serving Taiwanese soldiers, who filmed surrender videos for China and handed over confidential military documents.

n: Hungary's foreign minister reportedly briefed Lavrov from EU meetings
rank: EU Foreign Affairs Council (via Hungary's foreign minister)
d: Russia had a channel into the closed meetings of the EU's Council of ministers through Péter Szijjártó, Hungary's foreign minister from 2014, according to a Washington Post investigation of 21 March 2026 citing a European security source. It said that for years he phoned Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov during breaks to brief him on what EU ministers had discussed and to suggest possible Russian responses; the source said every EU meeting 'has basically had Moscow behind the table'. Szijjártó first called the report fake news, then confirmed he routinely calls Lavrov before and after closed EU meetings, while denying passing secrets. The EU Commission and Germany demanded explanations. Hungarian media later published recordings of him promising Lavrov help. His Fidesz party lost the April 2026 election.
cite: Euronews, 22 March 2026; EU Alive, 24 March 2026; Ukrainska Pravda, 23–24 March 2026; 444.hu, 31 March 2026; RFE/RL, 13 April 2026 (election result)
inside: Hungary's foreign minister reportedly briefed Russia's foreign minister from closed EU meetings and suggested Russian responses, giving Moscow a channel into EU decision-making.

n: Russia's SVR paid a Czech foreign ministry official with top-secret clearance
rank: Foreign Ministry official with top-secret clearance
d: Russia's foreign intelligence service, the SVR, obtained classified Czech diplomatic information from a long-serving employee of the Czech Foreign Ministry who had top-secret clearance and had worked at headquarters and embassies, including in Africa. Czech counter-intelligence, BIS, monitored him for several years and told Prime Minister Petr Fiala and Foreign Minister Jan Lipavský in the first half of 2022. The news site Deník N reported in September 2022 that he had repeatedly accepted money; Fiala, Lipavský and BIS confirmed the case. He was removed from the ministry. A judicial source said prosecution was unlikely because intelligence material could not be used in court.
cite: ČTK via Expats.cz, 16 September 2022, citing Deník N
inside: Russia's foreign intelligence service paid a Czech foreign ministry official with top-secret clearance for classified diplomatic information.

n: Chinese-run ring recruited serving Taiwanese officers for secrets and pledges
rank: Active-duty Taiwanese military officers
d: A network working for Beijing recruited serving officers in Taiwan's armed forces, according to Taiwan's High Prosecutors' Office, which in November 2023 indicted ten former and current officers. Prosecutors said three defendants recruited active-duty servicemen to collect military information and build a network for China; four officers they enlisted handed over military secrets for money; two active-duty officers recorded a 'psychological warfare' video for Beijing saying they would surrender to China's army; and one stole secrets from a safe at his workplace. The month before, a retired air force colonel had been sentenced to 20 years for spying for Beijing. On 14 February 2025 the Supreme Court made final the convictions of eight of them, with terms of up to 13 years; one defendant was found not guilty and one remains wanted. The court record says the Chinese side tried to persuade Hsieh Meng-shu, who was given nine years, to defect by flying a CH-47 Chinook helicopter to China.
cite: The Defense Post / AFP, 27 November 2023; CNA via GlobalSecurity, 14 Feb 2025
inside: A Beijing-run network recruited serving Taiwanese officers, who handed over military secrets for money; eight men's convictions are final, with terms of up to 13 years.

n: Belarus's military spies joined Lithuania's Riflemen's Union
rank: Lithuanian Riflemen's Union (state volunteer defence force)
d: The Main Intelligence Directorate of Belarus's General Staff recruited two Lithuanian citizens, Mindaugas Januitis and Tatjana Beleckaja, after they travelled to Minsk in May 2022, and one of them joined the Lithuanian Riflemen's Union, a volunteer defence organisation linked to the armed forces, in order to spy. They gathered information in Lithuania and Latvia on the Lithuanian armed forces, the Riflemen's Union, NATO allies' equipment and the Belarusian opposition, and received at least €8,500. They were arrested in November 2023, and the union expelled the member in 2024. On 15 April 2026 the Klaipėda Regional Court sentenced them to seven and six and a half years.
cite: LRT, 15 April 2026
inside: Belarus's military intelligence recruited a Lithuanian who joined a defence volunteer body linked to the armed forces in order to spy on it for Belarus.

n: Cocaine network allegedly had Madrid police economic-crime chief as partner
rank: Head of the Madrid police economic and tax crime unit (UDEF)
d: A cocaine-importing network allegedly had the head of the Madrid police unit that investigates money laundering working with it. Óscar Sánchez Gil led the economic and tax crimes unit (UDEF) of Spain's National Police in Madrid. He was arrested in November 2024, after police seized about 13 tonnes of cocaine hidden in Ecuadorian bananas at the port of Algeciras, and €20 million in cash was found in the walls and cupboards of his home. Investigators say he shielded the network from inquiries and helped decide which port containers were opened. In March 2026 a judge at the National Court indicted him for drug trafficking, money laundering, bribery and revealing secrets; investigators estimate the network brought in about 58 tonnes. He has been held in custody since his arrest.
cite: The Week, 'The Spanish cop, 20 million euros and 13 tonnes of cocaine' (Nov 2024); Vozpópuli, 'La Audiencia Nacional procesa al narcopolicía...' (6 Mar 2026)
inside: A cocaine network allegedly had the head of Madrid's anti-money-laundering police unit as a partner, shielding it from inquiries and helping decide which port containers were opened.

n: Gambling sites paid Indonesian ministry staff to stay off the block list
rank: Communications ministry staff; minister named in indictment
d: Illegal online gambling operators paid staff of Indonesia's communications ministry, the body that blocks banned websites, to keep their sites running. Online gambling is illegal in Indonesia. Police arrested ministry officials in late 2024. In an indictment read at the South Jakarta District Court on 14 May 2025, prosecutors said ministry employees took about Rp 8 million (US$487) from each site they protected; one defendant, a former state-company commissioner, allegedly received more than Rp 52 billion, and a member of the ministry's expert staff shared the money. The indictment also alleged that Budi Arie Setiadi, minister from July 2023 to October 2024, let the sites operate and would receive half of their earnings. He has been questioned and denies wrongdoing.
cite: Jakarta Post, 'Minister Budi Arie in hot water over online gambling indictment' (22 May 2025); The Star, 'Indonesian police widen online gambling probe...' (10 Dec 2024)
inside: Illegal gambling operators allegedly paid staff of Indonesia's communications ministry, the body meant to block their sites, to keep them off the block list.

n: Ankara crime boss Kaplan's ties led to nine senior police suspended
rank: Senior Ankara police officers
d: A crime group led by Ayhan Bora Kaplan in Turkey's capital is alleged to have had protection inside the Ankara police. Kaplan was arrested on 8 September 2023. Turkey's financial intelligence unit, MASAK, said 56 investigations had been opened into him between 2017 and 2019 without a conviction. In October 2023 Interior Minister Ali Yerlikaya said nine police officers who held key posts under his predecessor, Süleyman Soylu, had been suspended over mafia connections. In December 2024 an Ankara court sentenced Kaplan to 68 years in a trial of 61 defendants. A separate case against police officers who ran the investigation, accused of pressuring witnesses, has added claims that implicate politicians; these remain unproven.
cite: Bianet, 'Leader of Ankara crime ring sentenced to 68 years in prison' (4 Dec 2024); Duvar English, 'Turkish authorities detain four high-ranked police officers...' (May 2024)
inside: An Ankara crime group allegedly had protection inside the city police, where dozens of investigations into its leader went nowhere and nine senior officers were suspended.

n: Guatemalan prison guards charged over escape of 20 Barrio 18 leaders
rank: Guard unit at Fraijanes II prison
d: The Barrio 18 street gang, a transnational gang the United States designated a terrorist organisation in September 2025, had guards at a Guatemalan prison help its leaders walk out. Twenty high-risk Barrio 18 members left Fraijanes II, near Guatemala City, over several days between 8 and 11 October 2025; the escape was found during a prisoner count. On 25 October authorities arrested 23 guards from the unit that watched the prison's 256 Barrio 18 inmates, on warrants for cooperating in the escape and failing in their duties. The interior minister, Francisco Jiménez, resigned with his deputies for prisons and counter-narcotics, and the prison system's director was dismissed. Only some of the escapees had been recaptured by late October.
cite: La Prensa (Honduras)/EFE, 'Detenidos 23 guardias penitenciarios por fuga de pandilleros en Guatemala' (25 Oct 2025); AP via KDH News, 'Guatemala's president accepts resignations...' (Oct 2025); Tico Times/AFP (15 Oct 2025)
inside: Barrio 18 allegedly had guards inside the prison unit holding its members cooperate in letting 20 of its leaders walk out.

n: 'Pastillas' bribes let Chinese workers past Manila airport immigration
rank: Bureau of Immigration officers at Manila airport
d: Brokers bringing Chinese nationals into the Philippines paid immigration officers at Manila's airport to wave them through without checks. Senator Risa Hontiveros exposed it in February 2020 and said many arrivals went to work in Philippine offshore gaming operators (POGOs), Chinese-run online gambling hubs later tied to scams. Bosses or Chinese suppliers acted as go-betweens for travel agencies and officers, mostly through group chats. By November 2020, 86 people had been charged. In 2022 the Ombudsman dismissed 45 Bureau of Immigration officers for grave misconduct over 143 Chinese nationals admitted at airport terminals 1 and 2 The Justice Department separately dismissed 18 immigration personnel.
cite: Inquirer, 'Ombudsman sacks 45 BI officers over links to Pastillas scheme' (2022); Philstar, 'DOJ fires 18 immigration personnel over pastillas scheme' (10 Jun 2022)
inside: Brokers paid immigration officers at Manila's airport to wave Chinese workers through without checks, so the state's border control served their trade.

n: Tren de Aragua ran Venezuela's Tocorón prison as its headquarters
rank: Tocorón prison, under the prison ministry
d: The Tren de Aragua gang controlled Tocorón prison in Venezuela's Aragua state, with the prison ministry long leaving its leader, Héctor Guerrero Flores ('Niño Guerrero'), in charge as the inmates' boss. The prison served as the gang's base for recruiting, planning and income: inmates paid a regular fee called 'la causa' worth millions of dollars a year. On 21 September 2023 about 11,000 soldiers and police took the prison back, and the government said the gang was dismantled. Guerrero was not caught; the Venezuelan Prison Observatory estimated more than 1,500 inmates escaped, and sources described the takeover as a negotiated handover. From that base the gang had spread into Colombia, Peru and Chile.
cite: InSight Crime, 'Operativo en prisión de Venezuela...' (25 Sep 2023)
inside: Tren de Aragua's leader was left in charge inside Tocorón prison, so a state prison became the gang's headquarters, recruiting ground and income source.

n: US says Sinaloa faction had Rosarito's mayor, now a federal deputy
rank: Mayor of Rosarito (2021–24), later federal deputy
d: The US Treasury says Los Mayos, a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, had ties to the mayor of the Baja California city of Rosarito. On 18 September 2025 the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), which runs US sanctions, added Hilda Araceli Brown Figueredo of the ruling Morena party to its sanctions list. OFAC said her ties to Los Mayos dated from her term as mayor in 2021–2024, that she had a close personal relationship with Candelario Arcega, a Los Mayos member also sanctioned, and that both were linked to the faction's Arzate brothers. By then she was a federal congresswoman. Mexico's Financial Intelligence Unit froze 22 accounts of the people and companies named, while noting the US listing is not a court ruling.
cite: Mexico News Daily, 'Mexico freezes funds of Morena lawmaker...' (Sep 2025); Expansión Política (18 Sep 2025)
inside: US sanctions officials say a Sinaloa Cartel faction had ties to Rosarito's mayor during her term, giving it a friend inside the town hall.

n: Seized FARC-dissident files name a Colombian general and intelligence official
rank: Army general and National Intelligence Directorate (DNI) official
d: Files seized from a FARC dissident group suggest it sought allies inside Colombia's army and intelligence agency. The material came from phones and computers taken in July 2024 when the commander known as 'Calarcá' and six fighters were stopped at an army checkpoint. Caracol television reported in November 2025 that a February 2024 letter described a meeting at which General Juan Miguel Huertas proposed a legal security company that would let the group buy weapons and armoured cars, with Huertas obtaining permits for a share. Wilmar Mejía of the National Intelligence Directorate (DNI) and the head of the state arms maker were also named. Huertas denies the claims; the defence minister ordered an investigation and the inspector-general opened one.
cite: Colombia Reports, 'FARC dissidents infiltrated Colombia's military, intelligence agency: report' (24 Nov 2025); Blu Radio, 'Procuraduría abre investigación contra Wilmer Mejía y general Huertas' (Nov 2025); El Colombiano, 'General Huertas negó vínculos con disidencias'
inside: Seized files suggest a FARC dissident group sought allies inside Colombia's army and intelligence agency, with a general allegedly proposing a scheme to arm it for a share.

n: Los Ardillos gang met Chilpancingo's mayor and has kin in Chilapa's town hall
rank: Mayors and town-hall staff in Guerrero
d: Los Ardillos, a crime group in Mexico's Guerrero state led by the Ortega family, has had close links to local office-holders. In July 2023 a video leaked showing Norma Otilia Hernández, Morena mayor of the state capital Chilpancingo, meeting Celso Ortega, the group's presumed leader; she admitted the meeting but denied any pact, and the state prosecutor opened an investigation. Morena expelled her in September 2024. In May 2026 La Silla Rota reported that the mayor of nearby Chilapa, Mercedes Carballo, is Celso Ortega's sister-in-law and that his son is the town hall's private secretary. A former president of Guerrero's state congress, Bernardo Ortega Jiménez, is from the same family and denies any criminal links.
cite: El Financiero, 'Quién es Norma Otilia Hernández...' (2 Aug 2023); Expansión Política (8 Sep 2024); La Silla Rota, 'Mercedes Carballo, mayor of Chilapa and sister-in-law of the top Ardillo leader' (26 May 2026)
inside: Los Ardillos' leader's own relatives hold the mayoralty and the mayor's private office in Chilapa, and he met the mayor of the state capital.

n: Cocaine gangs recruit and coerce dockers at France's Le Havre port
rank: Dockers and badge holders at Le Havre port
d: Cocaine traffickers get dockers at Le Havre, France's largest container port, to move drugs out of the terminals. Few people can enter the port, so traffickers need insiders among its roughly 2,200 dockers. A price list found in 2017 offered up to €75,000 to help get a container out, €50,000 to move one and €10,000 to lend a security badge. Lawyers say many dockers are threatened rather than paid; about two dozen were kidnapped or held hostage after 2017, and docker Allan Affagard was found murdered in June 2020. Several dockers have been jailed for working with gangs. Seizures at the port reached a record 10 tonnes in 2021, and the prosecutor warned Le Havre was nearing Antwerp's level of violence.
cite: AFP via Channels TV, 'Dockers killed, kidnapped and corrupted by drugs mafia' (16 Jan 2023)
inside: Cocaine gangs pay or coerce dockers inside Le Havre port to move containers and lend security badges, turning port staff to the traffickers' service.

n: Caso Plaga: Ecuadorian judges sold prisoners' release by habeas corpus
rank: Judges and court staff
d: A criminal network in Ecuador paid judges to free prisoners, prosecutors say. The 'Plaga' case concerns a structure led by Cristian Romero, a former lawyer for the drug figure Leandro Norero and for ex-vice-president Jorge Glas, which allegedly obtained releases for money by having judges grant habeas corpus petitions, a court order to free someone held unlawfully. Fifteen people, including judges, lawyers, former officials and a police officer, admitted guilt and were sentenced to between 10 and 44 months. In July 2025 five judges and a judicial secretary were on trial at the National Court of Justice in Quito, with prosecutors asking for seven years each. Romero remained a fugitive.
cite: Primicias, 'Caso Plaga: juicio a jueces...' (23 Jul 2025); Expreso, 'Dos jueces y tres exjueces detenidos en Ecuador en Caso Plaga'
inside: A criminal network allegedly paid judges to grant habeas corpus petitions, so courts released prisoners for money.

n: PCC allegedly placed allies in São Paulo-area town halls
rank: Appointed posts in municipal governments
d: The Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC), Brazil's largest crime group, is accused of placing allies in municipal governments around São Paulo. In Operation Contaminatio on 27 April 2026, São Paulo's civil police said the group sought posts in city administrations to ease business, move illicit money and gain political influence. Investigators identified at least six politically exposed people, some in senior appointed posts, and said the group financed candidates in the 2024 municipal elections to win access to future contracts. Alleged methods included a digital platform used to collect municipal fees, shell companies and simulated contracts. Courts froze R$513.6 million in assets; a former Santo André councillor was named as the alleged organiser.
cite: Correio da Manhã, 'Polícia faz operação contra infiltração do PCC em prefeituras de São Paulo' (27 Apr 2026)
inside: The PCC allegedly placed allies in São Paulo-area town halls and financed candidates, to move illicit money and win access to municipal contracts.

n: Rio assembly president and a federal judge accused of tipping off CV's deputy
rank: President of Rio state assembly; federal appeals judge
d: The Comando Vermelho (CV), a Rio de Janeiro drug faction, is accused of having had help from the head of the state's legislature and a federal judge. Federal police say state deputy TH Joias, arrested in September 2025, was a CV member who laundered money and brokered arms. They say Rodrigo Bacellar, president of Rio's legislative assembly, warned him before the raid and told him to hide evidence, and that appeals judge Macário Ramos Júdice Neto, the case's rapporteur, leaked the operation. Bacellar was arrested on 3 December 2025, freed when the assembly voted 42–21, and re-arrested on 27 March 2026 after losing his seat. On 16 March 2026 the prosecutor-general charged all three with obstruction; they deny it.
cite: BBC Brasil via O Povo, 'Rodrigo Bacellar é preso novamente...' (1 Apr 2026); Wikipedia, 'Rodrigo Bacellar'
inside: The Comando Vermelho had a member sitting as a state deputy, and the assembly's president and a federal judge allegedly tipped him off before a police raid.

n: Sky ECC messages lead Albania to arrest senior police and a prosecutor
rank: Senior police officers, a prosecutor and judicial staff
d: Albanian crime groups had senior police officers, a prosecutor and members of the judiciary working with them, according to Albania's special anti-corruption prosecutor, SPAK. In July 2023 SPAK's 'Metamorphosis' operation arrested eight people and sought nine more, among them underworld figures, top police officers and officials, on charges including murder, corruption, abuse of office, drug trafficking and membership of a criminal organisation. The evidence came largely from Sky ECC, an encrypted phone service used by criminals whose messages Belgian, Dutch and French police had read; SPAK received them through European courts and Eurojust.
cite: VRT News, 'Top Albanian police officers and members of the judiciary arrested' (31 Jul 2023)
inside: Albanian crime groups had senior police officers, a prosecutor and members of the judiciary working with them, prosecutors say, based on intercepted encrypted messages.

n: Trinidad detains prison superintendent as an associate of a jailed gang
org_label: Radical Islamic Criminal Gang and allied gangs
rank: Prison superintendent
d: Gangs in Trinidad and Tobago allegedly had a senior prison officer working for them while their jailed leaders plotted attacks. The government declared a state of emergency on 18 July 2025 after police said they had uncovered a plot, hatched in prison, to kill officials. On 27 August 2025 it published a detention order against a prison superintendent, saying he was an associate of the Radical Islamic Criminal Gang and other networks and had used his position to get contraband to inmates planning violent attacks, including the killing of public officials with high-powered rifles, and to support jailed gang leaders. More than 160 people had been detained under the emergency by then.
cite: Jamaica Observer, 'Trinidad prison superintendent detained under SoE' (27 Aug 2025); AP via The Week (18 Jul 2025)
inside: Jailed gang leaders allegedly had a prison superintendent use his position to bring them contraband while they plotted to kill public officials.

n: Sydney drug importers bribed a Border Force supervisor to clear cocaine
rank: Australian Border Force supervisor; logistics insiders
d: Organised crime groups importing drugs into Sydney recruit 'trusted insiders' in Australia's border agency and freight firms. In March 2025 a new federal and New South Wales police strike team, set up in November 2024 to target such insiders, charged a 50-year-old Australian Border Force supervisor with taking bribes and abuse of public office. Police allege she was paid in cash and goods over several months to make sure a parcel holding 6.9 kg of cocaine avoided inspection, checking agency systems to see whether parcels were flagged. A 67-year-old man said to have organised-crime links was charged with bribing her. The team also charged a father and son who allegedly swapped legal cargo for two tonnes of illegal cigarettes.
cite: Australian Federal Police, 'New strike team targets double-dealers working for organised crime' (12 Mar 2025); The Nightly (12 Mar 2025)
inside: Drug importers allegedly paid an Australian Border Force supervisor to check agency systems and make sure their cocaine parcel avoided inspection.

n: Operation Apocalypse: 42 guards at Chile's Santiago 1 jail served gangs
who: Tren de Aragua and prison gangs
rank: Guards at Santiago 1 prison
d: Crime groups held in Chile's Santiago 1 prison, including leaders of the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua, are accused of buying the help of about a tenth of its guards. On 16 December 2025, 690 detectives and prison officers raided sites in seven regions in 'Operation Apocalypse'; 77 people were charged, at least 42 of them current or former Santiago 1 guards. Prosecutors say guards smuggled in drugs and mobile phones for set fees, arranged visits with gang members and supplied a WiFi network that bypassed signal jammers. The case began after gunmen attacked a guard's home in April 2024 using personal details colleagues had allegedly leaked to Tren de Aragua. Authorities froze 183 bank accounts.
cite: El Ciudadano, 'Major corruption crackdown: 42 Santiago 1 guards investigated...' (16 Dec 2025)
inside: Prison gangs including Tren de Aragua allegedly paid about a tenth of Santiago 1's guards, who smuggled in drugs and phones and leaked a colleague's details.

n: Ecuadorian soldiers at Peru border paid to pass Los Choneros' fuel
rank: Soldiers at the Puyango border control
d: Los Choneros, the Ecuadorian gang led by Adolfo Macías ('Fito'), allegedly paid soldiers guarding the border with Peru to let its smuggling run. In the 'Estrella Verde' operation announced on 3 September 2025, police arrested 24 people, 16 of them serving members of the armed forces, one of whom was said to belong to Los Choneros. Investigators say soldiers at the Puyango border control in Loja province let vehicles through for about US$6,500 per trip, enabling some 142 smuggling runs and about 497,000 gallons of fuel every two months. They warned the network which officers to avoid. Preliminary estimates put the state's losses at about US$20 million.
cite: Extra, 'Corrupción en FF.AA.: las operaciones que militares y Los Choneros ejecutaban juntos' (3 Sep 2025)
inside: Los Choneros allegedly paid soldiers at Ecuador's border control to let its fuel-smuggling vehicles through and warn it which officers to avoid.

n: Clan del Golfo paid a Colombian police captain and his team monthly
rank: Police captain and SIJIN investigators
d: The Clan del Golfo, Colombia's largest drug-trafficking group, allegedly kept eight police officers on its payroll in the Caldas region. In September 2024 investigators arrested a captain, a lieutenant and six other members of the police criminal-investigation unit (SIJIN). They say the officers were paid by 'La Empresa', the group's armed wing in the area, to ignore its crimes and drug sales, freed its members when patrols caught them, and made false arrests to divert attention from real culprits. The captain allegedly received about 8 million pesos a month and sent the group's local leader details to identify people detained. The officers faced charges of extortion by a public official and criminal conspiracy.
cite: El Espectador, 'Capturan ocho policías de la Sijín que estarían relacionados con el Clan del Golfo' (18 Sep 2024)
inside: The Clan del Golfo allegedly kept police investigators on a monthly payroll, so they ignored its crimes, freed its members and passed it details of detainees.

n: Court removes Ceará mayor elected with Comando Vermelho's help
rank: Mayor and deputy mayor of Santa Quitéria
d: Brazil's Comando Vermelho drug faction helped put a mayor in office in the north-eastern state of Ceará, an electoral court found. José Braga Barrozo ('Braguinha') won Santa Quitéria in the 2024 municipal elections and was held in pre-trial detention. Ceará's regional electoral court upheld his detention and unanimously revoked his and his deputy's mandates, calling it the most serious case it had faced. Investigators say the faction bought votes with drugs, coerced voters and rivals, threatened electoral staff and paid large sums to traffickers in Rio's Rocinha. Police are investigating faction interference in several other Ceará towns, including Sobral, where candidates were charged 'tolls' of up to R$60,000 to campaign.
cite: Diário do Nordeste, column by Inácio Aguiar on the Santa Quitéria ruling (2025); Diário do Nordeste, 'TRE-CE mantém prisão de prefeito de Santa Quitéria...'
inside: The Comando Vermelho helped elect a mayor through vote-buying and coercion, an electoral court found, getting its candidate into the town hall.

n: Gold smugglers had Kathmandu airport customs and an ex-Speaker on side
rank: Airport customs chief and officers; former Speaker
d: A gold-smuggling network allegedly had customs officers at Kathmandu's international airport and a former Speaker of parliament working for it. On 25 December 2022 customs seized about 9 kg of gold hidden in 730 vapes from Dubai; much of it was later swapped for ordinary vapes inside the sealed customs warehouse. A security guard who took one home found gold inside and exposed the switch, and police opened an inquiry in May 2023. On 9 April 2026 Nepal's anti-graft commission charged 28 people, including the airport's chief customs administrator and other officers, ex-Speaker Krishna Bahadur Mahara and his son, who allegedly pressed for the goods' release, and Chinese national Daojin Wang, the alleged ringleader.
cite: Kathmandu Post, 'Anti-graft body files corruption charges against former Speaker Mahara...' (9 Apr 2026)
inside: A gold-smuggling network allegedly had airport customs officers and a former Speaker working for it, and its seized gold was swapped inside the sealed customs warehouse.

n: Athens protection ring for brothels and casinos had at least 11 police
rank: Police officers, including a juvenile-division officer
d: A criminal ring that sold 'protection' to brothels, casinos and clubs in Athens had at least 11 police officers among its members, according to the Greek police internal affairs unit. The case broke in January 2025, when 19 people were arrested. Investigators say the ring, of at least 70 people, had operated since February 2014 and made more than €85 million, and that its leaders included men known as 'Cretan' and 'Uncle'. A 37-year-old officer from the juvenile division is accused of passing internal police information to the leaders. The internal affairs spokeswoman said the investigation did not at that point implicate senior officers or politicians.
cite: Greek City Times (citing In.gr), 'Greek police protection ring' (14 Jan 2025)
inside: Investigators say a protection racket had at least 11 police officers among its members, one of them allegedly passing internal police information to its leaders.

n: Camorra clan ran services and false papers inside a Naples hospital
rank: San Giovanni Bosco public hospital staff and doctors
d: The Contini clan of the Camorra, the Naples mafia, is accused of running parts of the city's San Giovanni Bosco public hospital through its staff. On 25 February 2026 police arrested four people; 76 are under investigation, including six current or former public officials. Prosecutors say the clan took over the hospital's café and vending machines through threats and the complicity of some administrators, and moved dead patients out by private ambulance, bypassing the mortuary, for €700 to €1,200 a family. An emergency doctor allegedly falsified a discharge for a patient already dead, and a health-authority psychiatrist allegedly wrote false certificates that got at least one prisoner released. A state witness's testimony began the inquiry.
cite: ANSA, 'Arrests in Naples over hospital in hands of mafia' (25 Feb 2026); AP via Irish Examiner (26 Feb 2026)
inside: A Camorra clan allegedly worked through administrators and staff inside a Naples public hospital to take over its services and obtain false medical papers.

n: Rio's police chief Turnowski convicted as double agent for lottery bosses
rank: Secretary (head) of Rio's Civil Police
d: Bosses of Rio de Janeiro's jogo do bicho, an illegal animal-themed lottery run by crime families, are accused of having the head of the state's Civil Police on their side. Allan Turnowski led the force in 2010–11 and again as state secretary from 2020 to March 2022, when he left to run for Congress. Rio prosecutors arrested him on 9 September 2022, alleging he took bribes from the lottery bosses. He was later sentenced to nearly ten years for obstruction of justice, with investigators saying he acted as a double agent for the bosses Rogério de Andrade and Fernando Ignácio. He was jailed again in May 2025 in a further case over a lottery-linked criminal organisation, then freed by a higher court in August 2025.
cite: Brasil de Fato, 'Quem é Allan Turnowski...' (9 Sep 2022); Agência Brasil, 'STJ manda soltar ex-secretário de Polícia Civil do Rio' (14 Aug 2025)
inside: Illegal lottery bosses allegedly bribed the head of Rio's Civil Police, who acted as their double agent inside the force, a court found.

n: Malaysian scam boss Nicky Liow had dozens of police on his side
rank: Police officers, anti-corruption officers and an ex-prosecutor
d: A Malaysian syndicate run by businessman Nicky Liow Soon Hee, which ran 'Macau scams' (phone fraud in which callers pose as officials), had police officers working for it, the national police chief said. After Operation Pelican 3.0 in March 2021, which arrested 68 people, Inspector-General Abdul Hamid Bador said 34 members of the force were suspected of colluding with 'Geng Nicky' and called them 'turncoats'. A former deputy public prosecutor was also arrested. In April 2021 ten police officers and two officers of the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission were detained over links to the group. Liow fled abroad, and an opposition politician later asked publicly what had become of charges against the officers.
cite: The Vibes, '68 held in Geng Nicky bust, 34 cops in cahoots to be rounded up' (30 Mar 2021); Free Malaysia Today, '10 cops, 2 MACC officers arrested over Nicky Liow links' (27 Apr 2021)
inside: A phone-scam syndicate had dozens of police officers and anti-corruption officers colluding with it, according to Malaysia's police chief.

n: Teuchitlán mayor charged with taking a CJNG salary near its ranch
rank: Mayor of Teuchitlán
d: The Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) allegedly paid the mayor of the town where it ran a recruitment and training ranch. In March 2025 relatives searching for missing people found shoes, clothing and charred bones at the Izaguirre ranch outside Teuchitlán, Jalisco, which soldiers had first entered in September 2024. Federal prosecutors arrested Mayor José Asunción Murguía in May 2025, alleging he received 70,000 pesos a month from the CJNG, was seen at the ranch several times and was linked to the cartel's recruiter 'El Lastra'. A judge charged him with organised crime and forced disappearance. He denies any connection; the attorney-general disputed that the ranch was an extermination site.
cite: Mexico News Daily, 'Authorities arrest Teuchitlán mayor' (6 May 2025); Euronews (5 May 2025)
inside: The CJNG allegedly paid the mayor of the town where it ran a recruitment ranch a monthly salary, prosecutors say.

n: Sinaloa Cartel paid a US border officer $10,000 a car at Tecate
rank: US Customs and Border Protection officer
d: A Sinaloa Cartel-linked smuggling group paid a US border officer to let drug-laden cars through his inspection lane. Jesse Garcia, an officer of US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) at the Tecate port of entry east of San Diego, gave the group his duty schedules and lane assignments from at least 2021 to 2024, switched himself into lanes he was not due to work and falsely claimed technical faults to skip checks. He was paid $10,000 for each vehicle and admitted bringing in at least 100 kg of fentanyl, 107 kg of methamphetamine and 270 kg of cocaine. He pleaded guilty in July 2025 and was sentenced to nine years in prison. A co-conspirator worked at the Otay Mesa crossing.
cite: Courthouse News, 'Former San Diego border officer sentenced to 9 years for Sinaloa cartel drug smuggling scheme' (2025)
inside: A Sinaloa Cartel-linked group paid a US border officer to switch into lanes and skip checks so its drug-laden cars passed through.

n: Mahadev betting app accused of paying Chhattisgarh's police and leaders
rank: Chief minister (alleged), police and officials
d: An illegal online betting syndicate, Mahadev Online Book, is accused of paying police, officials and politicians in India's Chhattisgarh state to avoid action. Indian investigators say the app, run from Dubai by promoters from Bhilai, took in about Rs 450 crore a month. A state anti-corruption chargesheet in June 2024 alleged the promoters paid protection money to police, administrators and influential politicians through hawala dealers, with police employees passing money on to other officers.
