The Enforcement Directorate alleges then chief minister Bhupesh Baghel received about Rs 508 crore. The federal CBI took over in 2024, named Baghel in its case and searched about 60 places on 26 March 2025. Baghel denies the allegations and calls them political.
cite: ThePrint, 'As CBI raids Bhupesh Baghel's residence in Mahadev betting app case...' (27 Mar 2025)
inside: An illegal betting syndicate allegedly paid Chhattisgarh's police, officials and politicians protection money so the state took no action against it.

n: Italy dissolves Foggia council over 'Società foggiana' infiltration
rank: Foggia city council and administration
d: The Società foggiana, the organised crime group of the southern Italian city of Foggia, had got into the city's administration, the Italian government found. On 5 August 2021 the Council of Ministers dissolved Foggia's council for mafia infiltration and put the city under special commissioners, cancelling the October election. An inquiry commission reported links between local administrators and the group, which had influenced the council's work for years: contracts for video surveillance, council housing given to people tied to crime groups, and public-service firms without anti-mafia clearance. The Lega mayor, Franco Landella, had resigned after majority councillors were arrested for corruption. Foggia was the second provincial capital dissolved this way, after Reggio Calabria in 2012.
cite: Il Post, 'Il comune di Foggia è stato sciolto per mafia' (6 Aug 2021); Il Fatto Quotidiano (5 Aug 2021)
inside: A Foggia crime group got into the city administration, influencing contracts and council housing, until the government dissolved the council for mafia infiltration.

n: Bolivian identity-office worker gave trafficker Marset a false ID
rank: Employee of the national identity service (SEGIP)
d: The Uruguayan cocaine trafficker Sebastián Marset lived openly in Bolivia with help from inside its state. He moved to Santa Cruz in late 2022 and bought a football club. An employee of Bolivia's personal identification service issued him a false national identity card, which let him travel to Paraguay undetected; the employee was detained in August 2023. Marset escaped a police operation on 29 July 2023; lawyers and experts said he appeared to have been warned, and Paraguay said it had alerted Bolivia months earlier. He was captured in Santa Cruz on 13 March 2026 and sent to the United States. In Paraguay, a senator was sentenced in March 2026 to 13 years for laundering linked to his network.
cite: Montevideo Portal, 'Familiares, socios y efectos mariposa: uno por uno, los implicados en la red de Marset' (2026); Los Tiempos (28 Jul 2024)
inside: A cocaine trafficker had an employee of Bolivia's identity service issue him a false ID, letting him travel undetected.

n: Fracking chief Chris Wright became US Energy Secretary
rank: Secretary of Energy
d: Chris Wright, founder and chief executive of the fracking-services company Liberty Energy, moved straight into the post of US Secretary of Energy, which sets federal energy policy and funds energy research. The Senate confirmed him by 59 votes to 38 on 3 February 2025. As secretary he has ordered several coal power plants to stay open, citing grid reliability, and his department published reports in August 2025 questioning mainstream climate science, which scientists disputed. In October 2025 the department cancelled 321 clean-energy grants worth $7.56 billion in states that had voted for Kamala Harris. Wright told Congress the cuts were not political, but officials said in a July 2026 court filing that they were based on the states' political identity.
cite: American Nuclear Society Newswire, 4 Feb 2025; Wikipedia 'Chris Wright' (citing Senate record and court filings)
inside: A fracking company's chief became the US energy secretary and then kept coal plants open and cancelled clean-energy grants, favouring the fossil-fuel industry over its rivals.

n: Chemical lobby's Nancy Beck again runs EPA chemical-safety rules
rank: Senior official, EPA chemicals office
d: Nancy Beck, a former senior executive at the American Chemistry Council, the lobby group for US chemical makers, has twice been put in charge of chemical-safety rules at the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the federal body that decides which chemicals can be sold and how they are controlled. In 2017, in Donald Trump's first term, career staff objected to her rewrites of toxic-chemical rules. She returned in January 2025, gaining decision-making power in the chemicals office and later oversight of pesticide rules. The New York Times, Washington Post and ProPublica have reported her moves to make PFAS 'forever chemicals' harder to track, to scale back proposed bans on asbestos, methylene chloride and the solvent TCE, and to loosen formaldehyde limits.
cite: Politico, 22 Jun 2017; New York Times, 22 Jan 2025; Washington Post, 23 Jan 2025; E&E News, 6 Mar 2025; ProPublica, 8 Dec 2025
inside: A former chemical-industry lobby executive was put in charge of EPA chemical rules and moved to weaken bans and limits her former industry opposed.

n: Crypto adviser Paul Atkins became SEC chair; crypto lawsuits dropped
org_label: Patomak Global Partners and Token Alliance (Paul Atkins)
rank: Chair, Securities and Exchange Commission
d: Paul Atkins, whose consultancy Patomak Global Partners advised financial firms such as Goldman Sachs and Fidelity, and who co-chaired the crypto advocacy group Token Alliance, became chair of the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the regulator of stock and investment markets, on 21 April 2025. He arrived owning about $6 million in crypto-related businesses and pledged to divest them; his later filings listing sold assets did not include those businesses. He sold his stake in Patomak in July 2025 for between $25 million and $50 million. Under his chairmanship the SEC dropped or settled many lawsuits against cryptocurrency companies, ProPublica reported in December 2025.
cite: SEC press release, 21 Apr 2025; Washington Post, 2024; The Lever, 30 Jul 2025; ProPublica, 22 Dec 2025
inside: An adviser to financial firms who held crypto stakes became the securities regulator, which then dropped or settled many lawsuits against crypto companies.

n: Investor David Sacks set US AI policy while holding hundreds of AI stakes
rank: White House AI and crypto czar
d: David Sacks, co-founder of the venture fund Craft Ventures, became the White House 'AI and crypto czar' in January 2025 as a 'special government employee', a status that allows up to 130 days' work a year without Senate confirmation and with lighter financial disclosure. He kept his investments in technology start-ups. A New York Times analysis of his disclosures, published on 30 November 2025, counted 708 technology investments, 449 of them in AI companies that could gain from policies he backed, and described his role in lifting restrictions on Nvidia chip sales abroad. He had received two ethics waivers. Sacks called the report a 'nothing burger'. He left the czar post in March 2026 but still co-chairs the President's science and technology advisory council.
cite: New York Times, 30 Nov 2025; TechCrunch, 30 Nov 2025; Bloomberg
inside: A venture investor holding hundreds of AI stakes set White House AI policy and helped lift limits on chip sales that could benefit companies he owned.

n: Peer Michelle Mone pushed a PPE contract for her husband's firm
rank: House of Lords member; Covid 'high priority lane'
d: Michelle Mone, a Conservative member of the House of Lords, used her access to ministers to win Covid-era government contracts for PPE Medpro, a company in which her husband, Doug Barrowman, was involved. On the day the firm was incorporated in May 2020 she referred it to the government's 'high priority lane', a fast track for suppliers recommended by MPs, peers and officials. She arranged a call between the Department of Health and the firm and pressed the Cabinet Office on its behalf, and contracts were awarded despite concerns about the conflict of interest. In October 2025 the High Court ruled that 25 million surgical gowns PPE Medpro supplied were not sterile and ordered it to repay almost £122 million.
cite: Express & Star/PA, 1 Oct 2025; Civil Service World, Oct 2025; Good Law Project
inside: A peer used her place in the House of Lords to fast-track government contracts for a company linked to her husband, which then supplied unusable gowns.

n: E.ON subsidiary chief Katherina Reiche became Germany's energy minister
rank: Minister for Economic Affairs and Energy
d: Katherina Reiche, chief executive since January 2020 of Westenergie, the largest subsidiary of the energy company E.ON, became Germany's Minister for Economic Affairs and Energy on 6 May 2025. She had earlier led the lobby group for municipal utilities. As minister she planned 8 gigawatts of new gas power stations, against about 5 under her predecessor, and a draft that ends fixed payments for small rooftop solar from 2027. A 2025 monitoring report on the energy transition came from an institute whose founding funders include E.ON and RWE; Greenpeace documented 28 changes between its draft and final versions. In February 2026 Green MP Michael Kellner said her draft grid package served E.ON, citing nine meetings with E.ON representatives.
cite: Frankfurter Rundschau/leinetal24, 26 Feb 2026; Xpert.Digital, 2026; LobbyControl
inside: An E.ON subsidiary chief became Germany's energy minister and pursued gas and grid plans that an MP said served E.ON, after nine meetings with it.

n: German MPs took commissions for brokering Covid mask sales to the state
rank: Members of the Bundestag and Bavarian parliament
d: Members of Germany's governing CDU and CSU parties took commissions from mask suppliers for brokering sales to federal and state authorities in the first months of the Covid pandemic in 2020. Prosecutors alleged that Georg Nüßlein, a CSU member of the Bundestag, received about €660,000 and Alfred Sauter, a former Bavarian justice minister, about €1.2 million; the company of CDU MP Nikolas Löbel took about €250,000. The affair broke in February 2021, and Löbel left his party and parliament. On 5 July 2022 the Federal Court of Justice ruled that brokering deals outside parliamentary work was not bribery of MPs under the law, so the men could keep the money. Parliament then created a new offence of improper paid lobbying by MPs.
cite: OCCRP, 30 Mar 2021; Legal Tribune Online, 12 Jul 2022; CMS, 2024
inside: Mask suppliers paid sitting German MPs commissions to broker their sales to federal and state authorities.

n: Port tycoon paid Liguria's governor's campaigns for a terminal concession
rank: President of Liguria region; Genoa port authority
d: Aldo Spinelli, a Genoa port-terminal entrepreneur, paid money towards the election campaigns of Giovanni Toti, president of the Liguria region in north-west Italy, in exchange for favours including the extension of a port terminal concession, prosecutors alleged. Toti was placed under house arrest in May 2024 and resigned as governor in July. The three main defendants took plea bargains. Toti's, for corruption and illegal party funding, was ratified on 18 December 2024: two years and one month, converted into 1,620 hours of community service. Spinelli agreed to three years and three months, and Paolo Emilio Signorini, former chairman of the Western Ligurian Sea Port Authority, to three years.
cite: ANSA, 16 Sep 2024; ANSA, 18 Dec 2024; Il Post, 13 Sep 2024
inside: A port tycoon paid towards the Liguria governor's campaigns in exchange for favours, including extending his terminal concession, the governor's plea bargain confirmed.

n: Businessman Aldama paid Spain's transport minister; Ábalos jailed 24 years
rank: Minister of Transport
d: Víctor de Aldama, a businessman, paid José Luis Ábalos, Spain's transport minister and organisation secretary of the governing Socialist Party, and his adviser Koldo García in return for public business, including mask contracts during the Covid pandemic. In June 2026 Spain's Supreme Court convicted Ábalos of membership of a criminal organisation, bribery, embezzlement and influence peddling, finding he took €10,000 a month from October 2019 to June 2022, and sentenced him to 24 years and three months. García received 19 years and eight months, with the court finding he used his closeness to the ministry. Aldama, who cooperated extensively with prosecutors, received four years and six months, suspended. The case is known in Spain as the 'Koldo case'.
cite: OCCRP, 22 Jun 2026; Euronews, 22 Jun 2026; Ara, Jun 2026
inside: A businessman paid Spain's transport minister monthly in return for public contracts, the Supreme Court found.

n: Gas firms paid ex-minister Montoro's consultancy to get tax laws changed
rank: Minister of Finance and his ministry
d: Industrial-gas companies paid a consultancy founded by Cristóbal Montoro, Spain's finance minister under José María Aznar and Mariano Rajoy, to have tax laws written in their favour, according to a Tarragona investigating judge, Rubén Rus Vela, who charged Montoro and some 30 others in July 2025. The judge says the firm, Equipo Económico, obtained quick changes to the special electricity tax for companies including Air Liquide, Messer, Praxair and Carburos Metálicos, acting through their association AFGIM, and that bills passed by the People's Party government were drafted with the companies' 'active collaboration' in exchange for payments. The case was investigated in secret for seven years. Montoro left the party and says there is no evidence against him.
cite: Orain/EITB, 16 and 18 Jul 2025; Ara, Jul 2025
inside: Industrial-gas companies allegedly paid an ex-minister's consultancy to have tax law changed, with bills drafted with the companies' active collaboration.

n: Data-centre firm's lobbying reached Portugal's PM's office; Costa quit
rank: Prime Minister's chief of staff; infrastructure minister
d: Start Campus, the company behind a €3.5 billion data-centre project at Sines, sought favourable government decisions through people close to Prime Minister António Costa, prosecutors allege. It hired Diogo Lacerda Machado, a lawyer and friend of Costa, as a consultant. Police searches in November 2023, in the inquiry called 'Operation Influencer', found €75,800 in envelopes in the office of Costa's chief of staff, Vítor Escária, and named infrastructure minister João Galamba a suspect. Costa, who was not named a suspect, resigned on 7 November 2023, bringing down the government. A judge found evidence of influence peddling by Machado, Escária and two Start Campus executives but dismissed other corruption charges. All deny wrongdoing.
cite: Irish Times, 3 Dec 2023; Euronews, 17 Nov 2023
inside: A data-centre company allegedly worked through the prime minister's friend and chief of staff to win favourable government decisions.

n: Croatia's health minister arrested over bribes from equipment sellers
rank: Minister of Health
d: Croatia's health minister, Vili Beroš, was arrested on 15 November 2024 and sacked the same day by Prime Minister Andrej Plenković, accused of taking bribes in a scheme run with medical-equipment sellers. Prosecutors allege that between June 2022 and November 2024 a group sought undue profits from selling medical robotic devices to Croatian hospitals and offered bribes at least four times to fix public tenders. In three cases, they say, the minister took a bribe to approve purchases of operating microscopes for Zagreb hospitals at prices inflated by about $654,000. Eight people, including two hospital directors, and two companies were accused. An indictment against Beroš and eight others was later confirmed. He denies the charges.
cite: Al Jazeera, 15 Nov 2024; HRT, Nov 2024; Ground News/N1, 2025
inside: Medical-equipment sellers allegedly bribed Croatia's health minister, who approved hospital purchases at inflated prices.

n: Drug distributors' kickbacks alleged inside Argentina's disability agency
rank: National Disability Agency (ANDIS); presidency
d: Pharmaceutical suppliers allegedly paid kickbacks to officials at ANDIS, Argentina's national disability agency, which buys medicines for disabled people, in exchange for contracts, according to leaked audio recordings attributed to its head, Diego Spagnuolo, a former lawyer for President Javier Milei. In the recordings, made public in August 2025, a voice says the president's sister Karina Milei, secretary-general of the presidency, 'gets three percent' of purchases through the distributor Suizo Argentina. Police seized about US$700,000 in cash from one suspect's home and notebooks allegedly recording payments. In February 2026 Judge Sebastián Casanello charged Spagnuolo and 18 others and froze over 200 billion pesos in assets. Those accused deny wrongdoing.
cite: Buenos Aires Times, 21 Nov 2025; El Cronista, 9 Feb 2026
inside: Pharmaceutical distributors allegedly paid officials inside Argentina's disability agency kickbacks in exchange for its medicine contracts.

n: Contractors' kickbacks to Philippine lawmakers in flood-control works
rank: House of Representatives; public works department
d: Construction firms building flood-control works for the Philippines' Department of Public Works and Highways paid lawmakers and public-works officials to get and keep contracts, according to testimony that opened a national scandal in 2025. On 8 September 2025 the contractors Sarah and Pacifico 'Curlee' Discaya, owners of at least nine companies, told a Senate committee that officials demanded 10–25% of project costs as 'advance commissions'. They named House Speaker Martin Romualdez, the president's cousin, and former appropriations chair Zaldy Co among some 20 representatives. Romualdez denied it but stepped down as speaker that month. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr had named 15 contractors at the centre of the projects, and graft charges followed.
cite: Gulf News, Sep 2025; Manila Bulletin, 8 Sep 2025; Philippine Daily Inquirer, Sep 2025
inside: Contractors paid lawmakers and public-works officials a share of project costs to win and keep flood-control contracts, according to their testimony.

n: Sugar-mill owners in Imran Khan's coalition gained from export subsidy
rank: Federal cabinet and Economic Coordination Committee
d: Owners of sugar mills who sat in or alongside Pakistan's governing coalition benefited from government decisions to allow sugar exports and pay export subsidies, an inquiry led by the Federal Investigation Agency's director-general found in April 2020. The JDW group of Jahangir Tareen, a senior figure in Prime Minister Imran Khan's party PTI, received about Rs3.06 billion, 12.28% of all export subsidy, in 2015–18, and 22.71% in 2018–19. The RYK group, linked to coalition MP Moonis Elahi and to a relative of food-security minister Khusro Bakhtiar, received about Rs3.94 billion. The committee found the 2018–19 exports were not justified; local prices rose from Rs55 to Rs71.44 a kilo. Khan reshuffled his cabinet.
cite: Dawn, 5 Apr 2020; Arab News, Apr 2020
inside: Sugar-mill owners sitting in or alongside the governing coalition received large shares of export subsidies their government approved, which an inquiry found unjustified.

n: Banco Master's owner paid Brazilian politicians and judges' relatives
rank: Senate, Supreme Court circle, state bank BRB
d: Daniel Vorcaro, owner of the Brazilian bank Banco Master, made payments to politicians and officials and to relatives of Supreme Court justices while his bank sought a rescue by BRB, the state bank of the Federal District, Federal Police investigations allege. The central bank rejected the BRB purchase in September 2025 and liquidated Banco Master on 18 November 2025, the day after Vorcaro was arrested trying to fly to Malta. Police estimate missing funds may reach R$12 billion. Reported payments include R$300,000 a month to Senator Ciro Nogueira, who police say pushed to raise deposit-insurance cover, and a contract worth about R$130 million with the law firm of Justice Alexandre de Moraes's wife. Those named deny wrongdoing.
cite: Bloomberg, 18 Nov 2025; Wikipedia 'Banco Master scandal' (citing Federal Police, Folha, Estadão)
inside: A bank owner allegedly paid a senator who pushed a rule change helping banks like his, and paid relatives of Supreme Court justices while seeking a state rescue.

n: Wind-power firm paid Japanese vice-minister Akimoto over ¥60 million
rank: Lower House member; parliamentary vice-minister
d: Masayuki Tsukawaki, president of the offshore-wind developer Japan Wind Development, paid more than ¥60 million between March 2019 and June 2023 to Masatoshi Akimoto, a Liberal Democratic Party member of Japan's lower house, prosecutors charged in September 2023. About ¥30 million in 2019 helped Akimoto register as a racehorse owner, and ¥31 million came through a racehorse owners' group the two shared. Prosecutors say Akimoto in return used Diet speeches in 2019 and 2020 to press the government to review how offshore-wind sites off Aomori and Akita were assessed, the second after the company had lost a bid. He resigned as parliamentary vice-minister for foreign affairs on 4 August 2023. Tsukawaki reportedly admitted the payments; Akimoto denies bribery.
cite: Japan Times, 7 Sep 2023 and 27 Sep 2023; Nippon.com/Jiji, 25 Nov 2024
inside: Prosecutors say a wind-power developer paid a vice-minister, who used Diet speeches to press for a review of site assessments after the company lost a bid.

n: Smartmatic executives charged with bribing the Philippine election chief
rank: Chairman, Commission on Elections
d: Executives of Smartmatic, a voting-technology company, paid more than $1 million in bribes between 2015 and 2018 to Andres Bautista, then chairman of the Philippines' Commission on Elections (Comelec), the body that runs national elections, to win a $199 million contract for 94,000 vote-counting machines for the 2016 presidential election and to secure timely payment, US prosecutors charge. A federal grand jury in Florida indicted Bautista and three Smartmatic executives, including co-founder Roger Piñate, in August 2024, and a superseding indictment in October 2025 charged the company itself. Prosecutors allege money was moved through shell companies and false invoices. Bautista, Piñate and Smartmatic deny the charges, and Smartmatic calls the case political.
cite: Philippine Daily Inquirer, Oct 2025; Daily Tribune, 8 Aug 2024; Philstar, 9 Aug 2024
inside: Smartmatic executives allegedly bribed the Philippine election chief to win a voting-machine contract and timely payment from his commission.

n: Raytheon paid a Qatari air-force procurement chief for contracts
rank: Qatar Emiri Air Force procurement official
d: Raytheon, the US missile maker now part of RTX, paid bribes from 2012 to 2016 to a high-ranking Qatari military official who ran procurement for the Qatar Emiri Air Force and represented Qatar on a Gulf air-defence contract, the US Justice Department found. At least $2 million reached him through sham contracts with a company he owned. Raytheon won four additions to the air-defence upgrade contract, earning about $36.7 million in profit, and a $510 million contract for a Qatari joint-operations centre that Qatar did not go ahead with. In October 2024 RTX agreed to pay over $950 million to resolve this and separate US fraud cases, including a $252 million criminal penalty for the bribery.
cite: Defense News/AP, 16 Oct 2024; US Immigration and Customs Enforcement release, Oct 2024
inside: Raytheon paid a Qatari air-force procurement chief through sham contracts and won contracts he oversaw, the US Justice Department found.

n: Freepoint Commodities bribed Petrobras staff for rivals' bid information
rank: Petrobras traders and officials
d: Freepoint Commodities, a trading house based in Stamford, Connecticut, paid bribes from about 2012 to 2018 to officials at Petrobras, Brazil's state-controlled oil company, in return for confidential information about competitors' prices and bids, which helped it win business. Freepoint made over $30 million in profit from the scheme. On 14 December 2023 it agreed with the US Justice Department to pay more than $98 million, a $68 million criminal penalty and about $30.6 million in forfeiture, under a three-year deferred-prosecution agreement, and to pay over $7.6 million to the US commodities regulator. Trader Glenn Oztemel was convicted at trial in September 2024 and sentenced on 9 December 2025 to 15 months in prison and a $300,000 fine. Trafigura, Vitol and Glencore have also admitted bribing Petrobras staff.
cite: US Department of Justice, 14 Dec 2023; Compliance Week, Dec 2023; US Department of Justice, 9 December 2025
inside: Freepoint paid officials inside Brazil's state oil company for rivals' confidential bid information, which helped it win business.

n: Mining and gas executives ran Australia's Covid recovery commission
org_label: Gas and mining executives (Nev Power, Andrew Liveris)
rank: National COVID-19 Coordination Commission
d: Prime Minister Scott Morrison's government put business executives in charge of the National COVID-19 Coordination Commission, set up in 2020 to advise on Australia's economic recovery. Its chairman, Nev Power, a former chief executive of the iron-ore miner Fortescue, was a director of 18 companies, including the gas company Strike Energy. Andrew Liveris, a former head of the chemicals firm Dow with energy interests, chaired its manufacturing taskforce, which urged the government to underwrite new gas fields and pipelines. Power stood down as chair of Strike Energy over perceived conflicts, and in June 2020 the commission told a Senate inquiry it would not publish members' declarations of interest. The government went on to promote a 'gas-led recovery'.
cite: Canberra Times, 4 Jun 2020; RenewEconomy, May 2020; Guardian Australia, 21 Sep 2020
inside: Mining and gas executives were put in charge of the national recovery commission, which urged state support for new gas fields that the government then promoted.

n: Business chamber chief led consultation on Indonesia's omnibus jobs law
rank: Government task force on the omnibus law
d: Indonesia's government gave business leaders the leading role in consultation on its Omnibus Law on Job Creation, a single law amending dozens of existing laws on labour, investment, land and environmental permits. In December 2019 Coordinating Minister for Economic Affairs Airlangga Hartarto appointed Rosan Roeslani, chairman of the Indonesian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (Kadin), to chair the bill's task force; its members included 14 Kadin members and heads of hotel and exporters' associations, alongside regional officials and university rectors. Labour unions were still demanding a role in deliberations in June 2020. The law passed in October 2020 amid mass protests, and environmental groups alleged conflicts of interest with coal and energy businesses.
cite: Jakarta Globe, 16 Dec 2019 (via APSN); Hukumonline, Dec 2019; Jakarta Post, 12 Jun 2020; APSN, 19 Oct 2020
inside: The head of Indonesia's business chamber chaired the task force drafting the jobs law, with business associations filling its seats while unions sought a role.

n: Nigeria's ex-oil minister acquitted in London over oil businessmen's gifts
rank: Minister of Petroleum Resources
d: Diezani Alison-Madueke, Nigeria's petroleum minister from 2010 to 2015, was tried at Southwark Crown Court in London in 2026 on charges that oil and gas businesspeople seeking or keeping contracts with the state oil company NNPC gave her a life of luxury in London between 2011 and 2015, including the use of properties, a chauffeur-driven car, private jets, a Harrods shopping trip and her son's school fees. Oil executive Olatimbo Ayinde was charged with bribing her. Prosecutors did not allege she awarded contracts improperly. On 17 June 2026 the jury acquitted her, her brother Doye Agama and Ayinde of all charges. The US Justice Department had said in 2017 that she steered oil contracts to executives who paid her.
cite: Reuters via The Star, 18 Jun 2026; Reuters via Citizen Digital, 28 Jan 2026
inside: Prosecutors charged that oil businesspeople seeking state oil contracts paid for Nigeria's petroleum minister's luxuries; US officials said she steered contracts to them. She was acquitted.

n: Qatar and Amazon lobbyist Pam Bondi became US Attorney General
org_label: Ballard Partners clients (Qatar, Amazon, GEO Group)
rank: Attorney General
d: Pam Bondi, a registered lobbyist at the Washington firm Ballard Partners for more than 30 clients, including Amazon, Uber, the private-prison company GEO Group and the government of Qatar, for which she was registered as a foreign agent and was reported to earn $115,000 a month, became US Attorney General in February 2025. The Attorney General runs the Justice Department, which prosecutes federal crimes and enforces the Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA), the law requiring people who lobby for foreign governments to register. On 5 February 2025 Bondi issued a memo limiting criminal FARA charges to conduct 'similar to more traditional espionage' and disbanded the FBI's Foreign Influence Task Force.
cite: Senate Judiciary Committee Democrats, 15 Jan 2025; Semafor; Skadden, Feb 2025; CyberScoop, Feb 2025
inside: A registered agent of Qatar's government became Attorney General and then narrowed prosecutions under the law policing foreign lobbying.

n: Telefónica's Venezuelan arm bribed officials for access to dollar auctions
rank: Venezuelan officials running currency auctions
d: Telefónica Venezolana, the Venezuelan subsidiary of the Spanish telecoms group Telefónica, paid bribes to Venezuelan government officials so that it could take part in a state-run auction that let companies exchange bolivars for US dollars, at a time when Venezuela tightly rationed access to foreign currency, the US Justice Department found. In November 2024 the company agreed to pay more than $85 million to resolve the US investigation under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, the US law against bribing foreign officials.
cite: AP via WTOP, 8 Nov 2024; Dow Jones via Tiger Brokers, Nov 2024
inside: Telefónica's Venezuelan arm bribed government officials to gain access to state dollar auctions, the US Justice Department found.

n: Associations allegedly paid insiders to take R$6.3bn from Brazil's pensioners
rank: National Social Security Institute (INSS) leadership
d: Private associations claiming to represent retired people took an estimated R$6.3 billion from Brazilian pensioners between 2019 and 2024 through unauthorised 'membership' deductions taken directly from their state pensions, which can only be made with approval inside the National Social Security Institute (INSS), the agency that pays pensions. On 23 April 2025 the Federal Police and the Comptroller-General's office launched 'Operation No Discount', investigating active and passive corruption among other crimes, and a court removed INSS president Alessandro Stefanutto and six other officials from their posts. President Lula ordered Stefanutto's dismissal, and courts froze more than R$1 billion in assets. The former INSS president was later arrested in the investigation.
cite: InfoMoney, 23 Apr 2025; Congresso em Foco, Apr 2025; O Imparcial, Nov 2025
inside: Private associations allegedly paid insiders at Brazil's pension agency to approve deductions, letting them take billions from pensioners.

n: America First Policy Institute leaders took nine top Trump posts
rank: Attorney General, FBI and CIA directors, four cabinet secretaries
d: The America First Policy Institute (AFPI), a Texas-based think tank set up in 2021 by former Trump officials, supplied much of the top tier of Donald Trump's second administration. Its president Brooke Rollins became Agriculture Secretary and its board chair Linda McMahon Education Secretary; Pam Bondi (Attorney General), Kash Patel (FBI), John Ratcliffe (CIA), Lee Zeldin (EPA), Scott Turner (Housing), Doug Collins (Veterans Affairs) and Matthew Whitaker (NATO ambassador) had also worked for it. Financial disclosures showed AFPI had paid incoming officials nearly $2.6 million, including $1.61 million to Rollins over two years. The group raised about $30 million in 2023, and Rollins said in April 2024 it had '298 executive orders drafted' for a new president's first day.
cite: ABC News, 18 Jan 2025
inside: A think tank paid future officials, filled nine top posts with its own people and drafted executive orders for the new administration to adopt.

n: WallBuilders model bills put the Ten Commandments in Texas classrooms
rank: Texas Legislature (Senate Bill 10)
d: Christian nationalist groups wrote ready-made 'model bills' for state lawmakers, and in 2025 Texas passed one: Senate Bill 10, signed by Governor Greg Abbott, requires a poster of the Ten Commandments in every public-school classroom. Project Blitz, a playbook exposed in 2018, offered such bills off the shelf; the Congressional Prayer Caucus Foundation's texts were used word for word in some states. Reporting by The 74 traced the Texan activist David Barton of WallBuilders, the law's main promoter, to 28 bills in 18 states in a single year. Similar laws passed in Louisiana and Arkansas. All three were challenged in state and federal courts, while posters went up in East Texas classrooms by December 2025.
cite: Baptist News Global, 20 Oct 2025; KLTV, 4 Dec 2025
inside: Christian nationalist groups wrote ready-made bills for state legislators, and Texas lawmakers passed one of them into law.

n: Leonard Leo routed fees to Justice Thomas's wife, 'no mention of Ginni'
rank: US Supreme Court (spouse of Justice Clarence Thomas)
d: Leonard Leo, the long-time Federalist Society leader who steered the choice of Republican Supreme Court nominees, secretly arranged consulting money for Ginni Thomas, wife of Justice Clarence Thomas. In January 2012 Leo told the pollster Kellyanne Conway to bill the Judicial Education Project, a non-profit he advised, and pass money to Thomas, writing 'No mention of Ginni, of course.' Conway's firm billed $25,000 that day; between June 2011 and June 2012 it paid Thomas's firm $80,000, with $20,000 more expected. In December 2012 the same non-profit filed a brief in Shelby County v. Holder, the case in which the court, with Justice Thomas in the majority, struck down a core part of the Voting Rights Act. The Washington Post published the documents in May 2023.
cite: Washington Post, 4 May 2023 (via Boston Globe)
inside: Leonard Leo secretly routed money to a Supreme Court justice's wife while a non-profit he advised argued a case before that justice.

n: Iraq gave Iran-backed militias a state firm, the Muhandis Company
rank: State-owned Muhandis General Company
d: Iraq's cabinet created a state-owned company for the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), the umbrella of militias, many of them Iran-backed, that are paid as part of the armed forces. Approved on 28 November 2022, the Muhandis General Company was given capital of 100 billion dinars (about $67 million) and is run by the PMF. It is named after Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis, the PMF's de facto commander and leader of Kataib Hezbollah, killed by a US strike in 2020. Analysts compared it with Khatam al-Anbiya, the business arm of Iran's Revolutionary Guards. The company gave the militias a legal channel to win state contracts; it later signed a memorandum with the Chinese firm CMEC.
cite: The National, 29 Nov 2022; Washington Institute, 2023
inside: Iran-backed militias got a state-owned company run by their own command, giving them a legal channel to win state contracts.

n: US-designated militia Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq ran Iraq's higher education
rank: Minister of Higher Education
d: Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq (AAH), an Iran-backed Iraqi militia that the US designated a terrorist organisation in 2020, held a cabinet seat in Prime Minister Mohammed Shia al-Sudani's government formed in October 2022. Naeem al-Aboudi, an aide to AAH leader Qais al-Khazali, became Minister of Higher Education and Scientific Research, in charge of Iraq's universities. The Washington Institute described him in October 2024 as 'the cabinet member controlled by' AAH, noting that he toured the United Kingdom to agree joint education programmes with hosts who likely did not know of the link. In May 2026 al-Aboudi, speaking for AAH's party Sadiqoun, said it would join the next government only after talks on disarmament.
cite: Washington Institute (Michael Knights), 15 Oct 2024; Shafaq News, 13 May 2026
inside: An Iran-backed militia placed one of its leader's aides as higher-education minister, a cabinet member analysts say the militia controls.

n: Badr and Kataib Hezbollah nominees in Iraq's 2026 cabinet
rank: Ministers of Transport, Water Resources, Communications
d: Iran-aligned armed groups placed nominees in the cabinet of Iraq's new prime minister Ali al-Zaidi, which parliament approved with only 14 of 23 ministers on 14 May 2026. The Badr Organisation, a militia founded in Iran, nominated the ministers of transport (Wahab Salman Muhammad) and water resources (Muthanna Ali Mahdi). The communications minister, Mustafa Jabbar Sand, was reportedly linked to Kataib Hezbollah, which the US designates as terrorist. The Trump administration had told Baghdad it would not deal with a government that included affiliates of Iran-backed terror groups, and the US Treasury sanctioned figures from such groups earlier that month. Al-Zaidi set up a committee telling factions in government to end armed activity outside the state.
cite: FDD's Long War Journal, 15 May 2026; Shafaq News, 13 May 2026
inside: Iran-aligned armed groups placed their own nominees as ministers in Iraq's cabinet while keeping their armed wings.

n: Radaa militia held Tripoli's airport and prisons as a state force
rank: Mitiga airport, prisons and detention centres
d: Radaa, a Tripoli militia led by Abdel Rauf Kara that operates as part of the state's security forces, controlled Mitiga, the only airport in Libya's capital handling commercial flights, from 2011, along with prisons and detention centres. In July 2025 Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah said militias had become 'a state within the state', demanding that Radaa hand the airport, seaport and prisons to the state, give up wanted men and disband; the Attorney General had issued about 125 arrest warrants for suspects around Mitiga. After clashes in May 2025, a Turkish-brokered deal in September 2025 provided for a neutral force to run four western airports, including Mitiga, and for prisons to pass to the Attorney General's office.
cite: Libya Herald, Jul 2025; Arab News (AFP), 13 Sep 2025
inside: A militia operating as a state force held the capital's airport and prisons, running state functions under its own command.

n: Tripoli militia chief al-Kikli's force became a state agency
rank: Stability Support Apparatus under the Presidential Council
d: Abdel Ghani al-Kikli, a former baker who built an armed group in Tripoli's Abu Salim district in 2011, turned it into the Stability Support Apparatus (SSA), a body placed under Libya's Presidential Council when the UN-backed unity government took office in 2021. Analysts called him the 'de facto king of Tripoli': his associates controlled the internal security agency, public companies and ministries, and cash transfers from the central bank. Amnesty International documented disappearances, deaths in custody and torture of migrants by SSA members, and a UN panel said in December 2024 he played a key role in militia financing through corrupt practices. He was killed at a rival brigade's base on 12 May 2025, setting off clashes across Tripoli.
cite: The National, 14 May 2025; Atlantic Council, May 2025
inside: A militia leader turned his group into a state agency, and his associates took control of security agencies, ministries and central-bank cash transfers.

n: Bashir's Islamists returned to Sudan's central bank and courts
rank: Central bank, judiciary, prosecution, foreign ministry, state media
d: After General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan's coup of 25 October 2021, members of the National Congress Party (NCP), the Islamist party of the ousted ruler Omar al-Bashir, banned in 2019, returned to state posts. A special court reinstated scores of officials whom a civilian taskforce had dismissed, in the central bank, judiciary, public prosecution, prime minister's office, foreign ministry and state media. Returning diplomats were sent to lead missions abroad, the civilian-appointed head of state broadcasting was replaced, and NCP leader Ibrahim Ghandour was acquitted and freed while taskforce leaders were jailed. Reuters reported in 2022 that NCP figures were rebuilding under military protection; Islamist brigades later fought for the army in the war with the RSF.
cite: Reuters analysis, Apr 2022
inside: Members of Bashir's banned Islamist party were reinstated across the central bank, courts and ministries after the coup and rebuilt under military protection.

n: Darfur rebel leaders given Sudan's finance ministry and Darfur governorship
who: Justice and Equality Movement and SLM-Minawi
rank: Finance Minister; Governor of Darfur region
d: The Juba Peace Agreement of 3 October 2020 gave Sudan's armed rebel movements three seats on the ruling Sovereign Council, five ministries (about a quarter of the cabinet) and a quarter of the transitional legislature. Gibril Ibrahim, leader of the Justice and Equality Movement (JEM), became Finance Minister in 2021 and staffed the ministry with JEM members; he still held the post in May 2025. Minni Minawi, head of a Sudan Liberation Movement faction, was named Governor of the Darfur region on 29 April 2021. When Prime Minister Kamil Idris promised a non-partisan cabinet in mid-2025, the movements insisted on keeping the finance and mining ministries, the main point of dispute.
cite: Dabanga, 29 Apr 2021; Atalayar, 7 Jul 2025; Sudans Post, 6 May 2025
inside: Darfur rebel movements took ministries, and the JEM leader staffed the finance ministry with his own members and refused to give it up.

n: Rabbis' council ordered Haredi ministers out of Netanyahu's government
rank: Knesset coalition and ministries
d: Israel's ultra-Orthodox (Haredi) parties take their decisions from councils of senior rabbis, not from members or voters, and those rabbis used the parties' place in government to protect exemptions from military service for yeshiva (seminary) students. After the Supreme Court ordered the Defence Ministry in 2024 to start drafting them, United Torah Judaism's seven MKs left Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition on 15 July 2025; Degel HaTorah said the move was made 'in accordance with the directive' of its spiritual leader, Rabbi Dov Lando. The exit left Netanyahu with 61 of 120 seats. Shas, another Haredi party guided by its own Council of Torah Sages, then quit its government posts too, while staying in the coalition.
cite: Al Jazeera, 15 Jul 2025; Times of Israel, Jul 2025
inside: Rabbinical councils direct the ultra-Orthodox parties, and used the parties' place in government to protect seminary students from military service.

n: Tufton Street think-tank staff became Liz Truss's special advisers
who: Free-market think tanks around 55 Tufton Street
rank: Special advisers in the Treasury, Cabinet Office and five ministries
d: When Liz Truss became UK prime minister in September 2022, staff from free-market think tanks based around London's Tufton Street took advisory posts across her government. Adam Memon, formerly of the Centre for Policy Studies, became the Chancellor's special adviser; James Price of the TaxPayers' Alliance became Cabinet Office chief of staff; Victoria Hewson, until then head of regulatory affairs at the Institute of Economic Affairs (IEA), and Radomir Tylecote, an IEA fellow, advised the Foreign Office and Business Department. Others went to Education, Work and Pensions, Housing and the Wales Office. The 23 September 'mini-budget' of unfunded tax cuts, which the groups had applauded, set off a market crisis, and Truss resigned after 49 days.
cite: Byline Times, 4 Oct 2022; Left Foot Forward, Sep 2022
inside: Staff of free-market think tanks became advisers across Truss's government, which delivered the tax-cutting budget the groups had called for.

n: America First Legal's founders moved into Trump's White House
rank: White House deputy chief of staff; deputy counsel
d: America First Legal (AFL), a legal group set up after Donald Trump's first term to sue over diversity, immigration and election policies, moved its top people into his second White House. Its co-founder Stephen Miller became deputy chief of staff for policy, and its president Gene Hamilton became special assistant to the president and deputy counsel. Before leaving, Miller received a $75,000 bonus and a $100,000 'adjustment' payment, and Hamilton $125,000 and $150,000; Miller's 2024 pay topped $567,000. AFL had filed more than 100 cases against diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programmes, and in January 2025 Trump ordered such programmes ended across the federal government. It raised $31.5 million in 2024, $21.3 million through the donor fund DonorsTrust.
cite: NOTUS, 10 Dec 2025
inside: America First Legal's founders, paid large exit sums, moved into the White House, which then ordered an end to the DEI programmes the group had sued over.

n: US group Family Watch coached Ugandan MPs behind the 2023 anti-gay law
rank: Parliament of Uganda; President Museveni
d: Family Watch International (FWI), an Arizona-based Christian lobby group led by Sharon Slater, worked with Ugandan legislators on the Anti-Homosexuality Act of 2023, which allows life imprisonment and, in some cases, the death penalty. A 2020 openDemocracy investigation had found FWI coaching senior African politicians for a decade. Slater organised a private WhatsApp group of over 150 campaigners in which Uganda's Deputy Speaker Thomas Tayebwa wrote on 25 January 2023 that 'the ground is now ripe to re-table the anti-homosexuality bill'; she also met President Yoweri Museveni to press for a conversion-therapy clause. Parliament passed the bill in March and again in May 2023. FWI said it did not support the final version.
cite: Mail & Guardian / Fronteras, 11 May 2023; CNN, 18 Dec 2023
inside: A US Christian lobby group coached Ugandan legislators and ran a private group in which the Deputy Speaker planned the re-tabling of the anti-gay bill.

n: 30 of 47 new Bangladeshi vice-chancellors tied to BNP or Jamaat groups
rank: Public university vice-chancellors and pro-vice-chancellors
d: After Sheikh Hasina's government fell in August 2024, the interim government filled Bangladesh's public universities with people from the networks of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) and the Islamist movement Jamaat-e-Islami. A Daily Star investigation in December 2024 found that 30 of 47 newly appointed vice-chancellors, and 18 of 40 pro-vice-chancellors and treasurers, had close ties to teachers' groups linked to the BNP or Jamaat. In June 2025 the planning adviser who had overseen education said he had asked the BNP secretary general for names of candidates; Awami League-linked academics were excluded. A formal search committee was set up only in May 2025, after the main appointments had been made.
cite: The Daily Star, Dec 2024 and 1 Jul 2025
inside: The interim government took names from the BNP leadership and filled most new university vice-chancellor posts with people from BNP and Jamaat networks.

n: Leipzig airport logistics worker gave China's spy details of arms flights
rank: Employee of a Leipzig airport logistics firm
d: Chinese intelligence used Yaqi X., an employee of a firm providing logistics services at Leipzig/Halle airport, as a source on what was flown through the airport. She admitted giving Jian Guo, an aide to an AfD member of the European Parliament, flight schedules and cargo details; prosecutors said these included military planes, troops and drones, some bound for Israel. On 30 September 2025 the Higher Regional Court in Dresden convicted Jian Guo of acting as an agent for a Chinese intelligence service and jailed him for four years and nine months; Yaqi X. received a suspended sentence of one year and nine months. Leipzig airport is a major cargo hub that handles military shipments.
inside: Chinese intelligence, through its agent Jian Guo, used a worker inside an airport logistics firm to learn which German arms and troops were being flown out.
cite: Times of Israel / AFP, 30 Sep 2025; The Local Germany, 30 Sep 2025; Federal Prosecutor General press release, 29 Apr 2025

n: US Army intelligence analyst sold 92 documents to a contact in China
org_label: Contact in China believed tied to the Chinese government
rank: US Army intelligence analyst (sergeant)
d: A person in China whom the soldier believed was tied to the Chinese government recruited Korbein Schultz, a US Army intelligence analyst, after first approaching him on a freelance work website while posing as a client of a geopolitical consulting firm. From May 2022 until his arrest in March 2024 Schultz sold at least 92 sensitive documents for about $42,000. They included his unit's order for a deployment to Eastern Europe, Army lessons from the war in Ukraine relevant to Taiwan, and technical material on the F-22A, ICBMs, HIMARS rockets and THAAD missile defence. He pleaded guilty in August 2024 and on 23 April 2025 was sentenced to seven years in prison.
inside: A handler tied to China's government paid a serving US Army intelligence analyst to pass on military documents from inside his unit.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Middle District of Tennessee, 23 Apr 2025; CBS News, 23 Apr 2025; KFVS12, 23 Apr 2025

n: Bundeswehr procurement captain handed internal files to Russia's consulate
rank: Captain, Bundeswehr procurement office, Koblenz
d: Thomas H., a captain at the procurement office of Germany's armed forces (Bundeswehr) in Koblenz, the agency that buys the military's equipment, took internal documents to Russia's consulate in Bonn in 2023 and offered to supply more. He admitted the charges at his trial, saying he acted out of fear of nuclear escalation over the war in Ukraine. On 27 May 2024 the Higher Regional Court in Düsseldorf sentenced him to three years and six months in prison. The case was one of several in 2023–24 in which Russian state offices received material from people inside German security institutions.
inside: Russia's consulate took in an officer from inside the German army's buying office who offered it internal files and more to come.
cite: Reuters / Yahoo News, 27 May 2024; Novaya Gazeta Europe, 27 May 2024; Kyiv Independent, Apr 2024

n: US soldiers at Lewis-McChord charged with selling secret drives to China
rank: Active-duty Army supply sergeant and officer
d: US prosecutors say buyers in China paid serving US Army soldiers at Joint Base Lewis-McChord in Washington state for military material. In March 2025 they charged Sergeant Jian Zhao, a battery supply sergeant, with selling about 20 hard drives marked SECRET and TOP SECRET, an encrypted Army computer and information on US readiness for a possible conflict with China for at least $15,000 from around July 2024. In a separate indictment, officer Li Tian and former soldier Ruoyu Duan were accused of passing information on weapons systems including Bradley and Stryker armoured vehicles from around November 2021. The arrests followed an FBI and Army counter-intelligence investigation. These are charges, not convictions.
inside: Prosecutors say buyers in China paid serving soldiers inside a major US Army base for classified drives and weapons information.
cite: Colorado Politics / AP, 7 Mar 2025; Stars and Stripes, 20 Jun 2025; The Record, Mar 2025

n: China's spy ministry ran a Verizon and Infosys worker as an informant
rank: Employee at Verizon, then Infosys
d: China's Ministry of State Security (MSS), its main civilian intelligence agency, used Ping Li, who worked for about two decades at the US telecom company Verizon and then at the Indian IT firm Infosys, as a 'cooperative contact' from at least 2012. He passed material from his employer, including internal cybersecurity training files and details of hacks against US companies such as the SolarWinds attack, and gathered personal information on Chinese dissidents and Falun Gong members in the United States. He pleaded guilty to conspiring to act as an agent of China and in November 2024 was sentenced to four years in prison and a $250,000 fine.
inside: China's spy ministry used an employee inside two large technology companies to pass it their internal security material and information on dissidents.
cite: The Record, 25 Nov 2024; VOA, Nov 2024; The Hacker News, Nov 2024

n: Ukraine detains SBU general Shaytanov as an FSB agent
rank: Major general, Security Service of Ukraine (SBU)
d: Ukraine's Security Service (SBU), the country's main domestic intelligence agency, said on 14 April 2020 that one of its own top officials, Major General Valeriy Shaytanov, had worked for Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) since 2014. It said he gave Moscow information on secret operations against Russia-backed separatists in eastern Ukraine, recruited other agents, and helped plan attacks, including a plot to kill Adam Osmayev, a commander of Chechen volunteers fighting for Ukraine. He was detained on suspicion of high treason and terrorism, and the SBU cited audio and video recordings as evidence. The case came two years before Russia's full-scale invasion.
inside: Russia's FSB is accused of having a general inside Ukraine's own security service who passed it secret operations and recruited more agents.
cite: RFE/RL, 14 Apr 2020; Hromadske, Apr 2020; The Moscow Times, 14 Apr 2020

n: Two former DGSE officers jailed for passing French secrets to China
rank: Officers of the DGSE, France's foreign intelligence service
d: China's intelligence services obtained information from two officers of France's foreign intelligence agency, the DGSE. Henri M. had been the DGSE's man at the French embassy in Beijing in 1997–98, later married a former embassy interpreter and moved to China; Pierre-Marie H., who had never been posted abroad, was arrested at Zurich airport carrying cash after meeting a Chinese contact. Both were charged in December 2017. On 10 July 2020 a Paris court sitting in secret convicted them of sharing intelligence with a foreign power, identified as China, and sentenced them to eight and twelve years. Pierre-Marie H.'s wife received four years, two suspended, for concealment.
inside: China drew two officers from inside France's foreign intelligence service into passing it information that the service existed to keep secret.
cite: AFP / Ahram Online, 10 Jul 2020; South China Morning Post, Jul 2020; The Local France, 5 Jul 2020

n: China's agents tried to bribe an IRS agent to strip Shen Yun's tax status
rank: US Internal Revenue Service (IRS) agent
d: Agents working for China's government tried to buy an official inside the US tax authority, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS). Acting on directions from a Chinese official, John Chen and Lin Feng filed a complaint and then paid $5,000 in cash in May 2023 to a man they believed was an IRS agent, to have the agency revoke the tax-exempt status of Shen Yun Performing Arts, which is run by practitioners of Falun Gong, a movement banned in China. Chen also offered $50,000 to open an audit. The 'agent' was an undercover officer. Chen was sentenced to 20 months in prison on 19 November 2024, and Feng to time served.
inside: China's government set out to buy an official inside the US tax agency so that the agency would punish a group Beijing persecutes.
cite: US Department of Justice, 19 Nov 2024; KTLA, Nov 2024

n: China says MI6 recruited a married couple inside its central state agencies
rank: Staff of central state agencies
d: China's Ministry of State Security (MSS) said on 3 June 2024 that Britain's foreign intelligence service, MI6, had planted two moles inside Chinese government agencies. It said Wang, who held a post with access to core confidential information in a central state body, was studying in Britain in 2015 when MI6 befriended him, paid him for 'consulting' that moved on to internal state matters, trained him and sent him back to gather intelligence, and that MI6 then had him recruit his wife Zhou, who worked at a 'core' government agency. The claims could not be independently checked, and Britain did not comment. The MSS said the case was still under investigation.
inside: China says British intelligence recruited two officials inside its central government so that they would gather state secrets for Britain.
cite: CNN, 3 Jun 2024; Dawn / Reuters, 3 Jun 2024; Taipei Times, 4 Jun 2024

n: China says the CIA placed a recruit, 'Hao', in a government ministry
rank: Cadre in a government ministry
d: China's Ministry of State Security said on 21 August 2023 that the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) had recruited Hao, a 39-year-old Chinese national, while he studied in Japan, and steered him into a government job. It said a US embassy official befriended him while he applied for a visa, paid him to help write a research paper and introduced him to a CIA officer, who asked him to return to China and work for a 'core and critical department'. Hao allegedly signed an espionage agreement, was trained, took a post in a ministry and met CIA officers several times to hand over intelligence and collect money. The claims could not be independently verified.
inside: China says the CIA recruited a student abroad and had him take a ministry job so that he would pass it intelligence from inside.
cite: CNN, 21 Aug 2023; Global Times, 21 Aug 2023; Arab News / Reuters, Aug 2023

n: Moldova's parliament legal chief charged as a Russian embassy source
rank: Head of the Parliament's Legal Division
d: Prosecutors in Moldova say an assistant to Russia's military attaché in Chișinău recruited Ion Creangă, head of the legal division of Moldova's parliament, and a senior Border Police officer at Chișinău airport. They allege that in 2023–24 Creangă passed internal and secret information on Moldova's defence measures, its security cooperation with other states and the work of institutions in that field, and discussed with the diplomat why a planned referendum on joining the EU was bad for Russia. He was detained in July 2024 while receiving $500, and $1,100 more was found at his home. Moldova expelled the Russian embassy employee. Both men were sent to trial for treason.
inside: Prosecutors say Russia's embassy recruited the head of the Moldovan parliament's legal division and an airport border officer to pass it state information.
cite: IPN Moldova, 2024; Ukrinform, 2 Aug 2024; RFE/RL, Jul 2024; Novaya Gazeta Europe, 1 Aug 2024

n: SBU says Russia's FSB had agents inside Ukraine's anti-corruption bureau
rank: Officers of the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU)
d: Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) said on 21 July 2025 that Russia's FSB had built influence inside the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU), the independent agency that investigates senior officials. It detained Viktor Husarov, an officer in a closed NABU unit, saying he passed information on officials and civilians to the FSB at least 60 times for pay through a former Yanukovych bodyguard, and Ruslan Magamedrasulov, a NABU department head, over alleged business with Russia. It charged former MP Fedir Khrystenko with treason as an FSB agent strengthening Russian influence on NABU. In December 2025 Ukraine's prosecutor general confirmed an unpublished agreement with Khrystenko, whose case was then sent quickly to court. The other cases were still under investigation.
inside: Ukraine's security service says Russia's FSB recruited officers inside the anti-corruption bureau and paid them for information on Ukrainian officials and citizens.
cite: Euromaidan Press, 22 Jul 2025; Babel, 21 Jul 2025 and 4 Dec 2025; Kyiv Post, Jul 2025

n: Intern at NATO's military headquarters arrested as suspected Chinese spy
rank: IT intern at SHAPE, NATO's military headquarters
d: Belgian prosecutors arrested a Canadian national of Chinese origin in July 2026 who had been working as an intern in the IT department of SHAPE, NATO's military headquarters in Mons, on suspicion of spying for a 'third country' and belonging to a criminal organisation. Two sources told Reuters the country was China. SHAPE had reported her to Belgian intelligence after noticing her behaviour and said there was no sign NATO's readiness or missions were affected. She had earlier worked at the European Space Agency and the World Trade Organisation. Canada, which is responsible for vetting its NATO interns, said it would review its screening.
inside: Prosecutors suspect a foreign state, which sources name as China, had a person working inside NATO's military headquarters to spy for it.
cite: Reuters / CP24, 30 Jul 2026; The Defense Post, 25 Jul 2026; Euronews, 29 Jul 2026

n: Chinese intelligence paid a South Korean sergeant for US–Korea drill secrets
rank: Sergeant, 21st Infantry Division
d: A man who said he belonged to a Chinese intelligence organisation recruited an active-duty sergeant in South Korea's 21st Infantry Division after contact on social media and a meeting in Beijing in August 2024. He gave the sergeant 15,000 yuan, a spy camera disguised as a wristwatch and an iPhone, which the soldier smuggled onto his base, and over about seven months paid him 80,000 yuan more. The sergeant passed classified data on Korea–US joint exercises, UN Command material and Korean troop movements. A military court gave him five years, cut to four on appeal, and the Supreme Court confirmed the sentence on 18 September 2026.
inside: Chinese intelligence paid a serving South Korean sergeant to take a spy camera onto his base and hand over allied military plans.
cite: Korea JoongAng Daily, 18 Sep 2026; The Star / Korea Herald, 19 Sep 2026

n: Chinese military intelligence sought THAAD plans through a Korean soldier
rank: Active-duty South Korean soldier
d: A team linked to a Chinese military intelligence department recruited a serving South Korean soldier to obtain allied secrets, according to prosecutors who disclosed an indictment in May 2025. They said the soldier leaked 21 military secrets for about 50 million won (about $35,000), and that the Chinese side sought data on THAAD, the US missile-defence system deployed in South Korea, nuclear-operations guidelines and plans involving US Forces Korea. The Defense Counterintelligence Command caught the Chinese contact on Jeju Island in March 2025 as he tried to collect USB drives from the soldier. Because Korea's espionage law covers only 'enemy' states, he was charged under the military secrets law.
inside: A Chinese military-intelligence team paid a soldier inside South Korea's army to hand over secrets on US missile defence and war plans.
cite: Korea Herald, 15 May 2025; Korea Times, 27 May 2025; Stars and Stripes, 27 May 2025

n: Russian SVR officer at trade mission recruited a Tokyo machine-tool manager
rank: Sales manager at a machine-tool maker
d: An officer at Russia's trade representation in Japan, believed by police to belong to a division of the SVR, Russia's foreign intelligence service, that collects science and technology, recruited a sales manager at a Tokyo-area machine-tool manufacturer. Police say that after arriving in April 2023 the officer posed as a Ukrainian, met the manager repeatedly at family restaurants and paid about 700,000 yen plus meals, receiving catalogues, internal training material and, in November 2024 and February 2025, spoken trade secrets on product development. The officer left Japan in March 2025. On 20 January 2026 Tokyo police referred both men to prosecutors, citing the firm's technologies with possible military uses.
inside: Russia's foreign intelligence service paid a manager inside a Japanese machine-tool company for trade secrets with possible military uses.
cite: Kyodo / Adnkronos, 20 Jan 2026; The Nation (Thailand), 20 Jan 2026

n: China's spy ministry network tried to recruit US Navy personnel
rank: US Navy personnel (recruitment targets)
d: US prosecutors say China's Ministry of State Security (MSS) ran Liren 'Ryan' Lai and Yuance Chen in an effort to gather information on the US Navy and recruit its personnel. They allege Lai began cultivating Chen around 2021; Chen met MSS officers abroad, collected Navy information including personal details of Navy employees, toured the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln in San Diego with a Navy employee, and discussed recruitment targets with the MSS. In 2022 the pair left $10,000 in cash in a California locker as payment for intelligence gathering. The Justice Department charged both on 1 July 2025 with acting as unregistered agents of China.
inside: Prosecutors say China's spy ministry set out to recruit people inside the US Navy and paid for information gathered on its personnel.
cite: US Department of Justice (N.D. Cal.), 1 Jul 2025; Al Jazeera, 2 Jul 2025; Military Times, 2 Jul 2025

n: SBU officers in Kherson and Kharkiv accused of aiding Russia's invasion
rank: SBU regional officers (Kherson, Kharkiv)
d: Russian services are accused of having recruits inside regional offices of Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) when Russia invaded in February 2022. Kherson's regional council head said in June 2022 that Ihor Sadokhin, head of the anti-terrorist centre in the Kherson SBU office, had been recruited beforehand, gave Russian forces a map of minefields and coordinated air strikes on an evacuating SBU column; he was detained in March 2022. The former head of the Kharkiv SBU office, Roman Dudin, was charged with high treason, prosecutors alleging he sabotaged defence preparations. Kherson's SBU chief Serhiy Kryvoruchko was stripped of his general's rank.
inside: Russia is accused of having officers inside Ukraine's regional security service offices who helped its army take territory in 2022.
cite: Fakty / Ukrinform, 18 Jun 2022; Hromadske, Sep 2023; Babel, Jun 2022

n: BrahMos missile engineer jailed for life for leaking to Pakistan's ISI
rank: Engineer, BrahMos Aerospace missile centre
d: Pakistan's military spy agency, Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), obtained sensitive technical information from Nishant Agarwal, an engineer in the technical research section of BrahMos Aerospace's missile centre in Nagpur. BrahMos Aerospace is the Indian–Russian joint venture that makes the BrahMos cruise missile used by India's armed forces. He was arrested in 2018 in a joint operation by military intelligence and the anti-terrorism squads of Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra. Reports said he was drawn in by the same ISI handlers who had entrapped a Border Security Force constable. On 3 June 2024 a Nagpur sessions court sentenced him to life imprisonment and 14 years' rigorous imprisonment under the Official Secrets Act.
inside: Pakistan's spy agency drew an engineer inside India's cruise-missile maker into passing it technical secrets from the company's research section.
cite: The Week, 3 Jun 2024; Scroll.in, 3 Jun 2024; LiveLaw, Jun 2024

n: DRDO guest house manager at a missile range arrested as an ISI source
rank: Manager, DRDO guest house at Chandan firing range
d: Rajasthan police say handlers from Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI) recruited Mahendra Prasad, the contract manager of the guest house run by India's Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) near the Chandan Field Firing Range in Jaisalmer, where missiles and other weapons are tested. DRDO is the state agency that develops India's weapons. Police say that, after contact through social media, he passed details of the movements of DRDO scientists and army officers who stayed there for weapons tests, and that his phone held sensitive information on DRDO and the army. He was arrested on 12 August 2025 and charged under the Official Secrets Act.
inside: Police say Pakistan's spy agency recruited the manager of a defence-research guest house to report on scientists and officers arriving for missile tests.
cite: ThePrint, 13 Aug 2025; The Week, 13 Aug 2025; India TV, 13 Aug 2025

n: Polish territorial-defence soldier charged with espionage for Russia
rank: Radio operator, 12th Territorial Defence Brigade
d: Prosecutors in Poznań charged a serving soldier of Poland's Territorial Defence Forces (WOT), the volunteer branch of the army, with espionage in April 2026, after his arrest in March. Gazeta Wyborcza named him as Jarosław K., a radio operator in the 12th Wielkopolska Territorial Defence Brigade since March 2024, and reported that he sought to spy for Russian intelligence; he was active in a pro-Russian far-right group. WOT dismissed him at once. A court spokesman said the offence was most likely declaring readiness to work for, or gathering data for, foreign intelligence; the court refused pre-trial detention and prosecutors appealed.
inside: Prosecutors say a soldier inside Poland's territorial defence force offered to work for Russian intelligence, which would have given it a source in the army.
cite: Notes from Poland, 17 Apr 2026; Gazeta Wyborcza, Apr 2026

n: Iran paid an Iron Dome reservist for battery and air-base locations
rank: Reservist, Iron Dome air-defence system
d: An Iranian intelligence handler recruited Raz Cohen, a reservist who served as a command-and-control technician and launcher operator in Israel's Iron Dome missile-defence system, according to an indictment filed in Jerusalem on 18 March 2026. Prosecutors say the handler contacted him on Telegram in December 2025 and paid about $1,000 in cryptocurrency, and that he passed how Iron Dome works, the locations of seven air-force bases and two Iron Dome batteries, 27 photos and videos, and contact details of others including a guard at the President's Residence. He was called up for reserve duty in January 2026. Israeli authorities had cleared 35 Iranian espionage cases for publication by December 2025.
inside: Prosecutors say Iranian intelligence paid a reservist inside Israel's missile-defence force for the positions of batteries and air bases.
cite: Times of Israel, 20 Mar 2026; Ynet, 27 Dec 2025

n: Hong Kong agent's ring paid Taiwanese officers for secrets and surrender
org_label: PLA political department, Nanjing work station (reported)
rank: Serving and retired Taiwanese military officers
d: Taiwan's High Prosecutors' Office indicted seven people on 18 November 2025 over a spy ring that recruited current and former military personnel for China. Prosecutors said Ting Hsiao-hu, a Chinese national with Hong Kong citizenship believed to be directed by the Nanjing work station of the People's Liberation Army's political department, made repeated trips to Taiwan, recruited retired officers who then recruited former colleagues and subordinates, and paid them according to the value of classified military information. Members were urged to persuade serving personnel to resist passively or surrender in a war. More than NT$11.12 million was moved in illegally. The defence ministry said two active-duty officers were among those held.
inside: Prosecutors say a Chinese military agency built a paid network of serving and retired officers inside Taiwan's armed forces to collect secrets and prepare surrender.
cite: Taipei Times / ANI via Tribune India, 18 Nov 2025

n: Taiwan coast guardsman paid every quarter to pass vessel data to China
rank: Coast Guard, Southern Sector Flotilla
d: Chinese intelligence recruited a member of Taiwan's Coast Guard Administration, surnamed Lee, who served with the Kaohsiung-based Southern Sector Flotilla, through a contact known as 'Tony' in September 2022, Kaohsiung prosecutors said when they indicted him on 25 June 2025. For about two years he passed information on coast guard vessels in the waters between Taiwan and the Philippines, graphics of missile-launch warning zones and other military intelligence, and was paid NT$60,000 every three months plus year-end bonuses. He resigned in 2024 after learning he was being investigated. He reportedly admitted the allegations and was charged with treason and national security offences.
inside: Chinese intelligence put a serving coast guardsman on a quarterly retainer to pass it information from inside Taiwan's coast guard.
cite: Central News Agency (Taiwan), 25 Jun 2025, via GlobalSecurity.org; Focus Taiwan, 25 Jun 2025

n: Armenian army commander passed troop data to Azerbaijan in 2020 war
rank: Commander of an Armenian army detachment
d: Armenian investigators said in June 2021 that Azerbaijani special services had obtained military and state secrets from a former Armenian serviceman, reported to have commanded an army detachment, and an acquaintance during the autumn 2020 war over Nagorno-Karabakh. The information included the deployment of Armenian troops, the names of commanders of the Armenian and Nagorno-Karabakh armies and the number of weapons. The two were arrested on espionage charges. The 44-day war ended in November 2020 with Azerbaijan retaking large areas, and Armenia opened several treason and spying cases against its own personnel afterwards.
inside: Armenian investigators say Azerbaijan's secret services had a source inside an Armenian army unit who passed troop positions during the 2020 war.
cite: Caucasian Knot, 7 Jun 2021

n: Cartels had staff inside Mexican banks CIBanco and Intercam, US says
org_label: Mexican cartels (CJNG, Gulf, Sinaloa, Beltrán Leyva)
rank: Managers and staff at CIBanco, Intercam and Vector
d: The US Treasury's financial-crimes unit, FinCEN, said in June 2025 that Mexican cartels had people inside three Mexican financial firms. It said mid-level managers at the bank Intercam met alleged members of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) at the end of 2022 to discuss laundering schemes, including transfers from China, and that a CIBanco employee knowingly helped open an account to launder US$10 million for a Gulf Cartel member in early 2023. It linked the brokerage Vector to transactions involving Sinaloa Cartel bribes paid to former security chief Genaro García Luna. The orders, the first under the 2024 FEND Off Fentanyl Act, cut the three firms off from US transfers from July 2025. Mexico's finance ministry said no evidence had been shown, and the firms denied wrongdoing.
inside: US officials say cartels reached managers and staff inside Mexican banks, who then opened accounts and moved cartel money instead of reporting it.
cite: FinCEN orders of 25 June 2025 (summary by Miller & Chevalier); Bloomberg Línea, June 2025

n: Saharan cocaine network drew in Moroccan regional chiefs and gendarmes
org_label: Haj Ahmed Ben Brahim's trafficking network ('Escobar of the Sahara')
rank: Oriental regional council president, an ex-MP, gendarmes and local officials
d: A drug-trafficking network linked to the Malian trafficker Haj Ahmed Ben Brahim, nicknamed the 'Escobar of the Sahara', drew Moroccan elected officials and security staff into its operation, a Casablanca court found. The main suspects were detained in December 2023. On 25 June 2026 the court jailed Saïd Naciri, former president of the Wydad Casablanca football club, for 10 years and Abdenbi Bioui, former president of the Oriental regional council, for 12 years, both for conspiring in international drug trafficking. A former member of parliament got 10 years, partly for corruption, and local officials, security officers and gendarmes (a military police force) got four to five years for helping drug lorries pass through. There were 28 defendants. An appeal opened in August 2026.
inside: The court found a Saharan trafficking network had regional politicians, gendarmes and local officials working with it, so state posts helped move its drug lorries.
cite: Hespress, 26 June 2026; Le360, 26 June 2026; TelQuel, 5 August 2026

n: Gold-heist ring had Air Canada cargo staff on the inside at Pearson
rank: Air Canada cargo employee and former manager
d: Thieves who took about C$20 million in gold, 6,600 bars, plus C$2.5 million in foreign currency from Air Canada's cargo building at Toronto Pearson airport on 17 April 2023 had people inside the airline, Peel police say. Nine people face 19 charges. They include a serving Air Canada employee, Parmpal Sidhu, charged with theft and conspiracy, and a former manager, Simran Preet Panesar, who resigned in summer 2023 and was named on a Canada-wide warrant. 'They needed people inside Air Canada to facilitate this theft,' a detective said when the arrests were announced in April 2024. Police believe the gold was melted down and sold and some proceeds bought guns: the alleged lorry driver was arrested in Pennsylvania with 65 illegal firearms.
inside: Police say the theft ring recruited people inside Air Canada's cargo operation, who helped it take a gold shipment the airline was meant to guard.
cite: CTV News, 17 April 2024; CBC News, April 2024

n: Visa brokers got clients' lists pushed through Poland's foreign ministry
rank: Deputy foreign minister and consulates
d: Intermediaries who sold faster Polish visas got their clients' names passed from the foreign ministry to consulates for quick approval, Polish investigators and auditors say. The 'cash-for-visas' affair surfaced in 2023. Deputy foreign minister Piotr Wawrzyk was dismissed on 31 August 2023 and charged with accepting bribes in January 2024; he denies it. The Supreme Audit Office (NIK), in a report completed in July 2024 covering 2018 to 2022, found that Wawrzyk had forwarded to consuls lists of people for whom 'third parties' expected faster visas, and called the system a 'non-transparent and corruption-prone mechanism for influencing some consuls'. Poland issued about 6.5 million visas in that period, valid across the EU's Schengen area. The new government suspended the programme concerned in early 2024.
inside: Prosecutors say visa brokers paid a deputy foreign minister, whose office then pushed their paying clients through Poland's consulates with fewer checks.
cite: Notes from Poland, 24 September 2024 (NIK report); Polish cash-for-visa scandal summary of charges (Wikipedia)

n: Gambling tycoon's network allegedly used police to abduct cockfight workers
rank: Philippine National Police officers (14 charged)
d: Philippine prosecutors say a network around Charlie 'Atong' Ang, a businessman tied to cockfighting arenas, used serving police officers to abduct cockfighting workers (sabungeros) who went missing in 2021 and 2022. In December 2025 the Department of Justice ordered charges of kidnapping with homicide and kidnapping with serious illegal detention against Ang and 21 others, to be filed in three courts in Batangas and Laguna. Fourteen of those named are police officers, from a lieutenant colonel down to a corporal, several of them assigned to anti-crime units. The case rests partly on Julie Patidongan, a former security chief at arenas linked to Ang, who claims more than 100 people were killed; that figure is unproven. Ang's defence called the ruling flawed and unfair.
inside: Prosecutors say a gambling boss's network had police officers act on its behalf, turning members of anti-crime units into its instruments for abducting people.
cite: PTV News, December 2025; Daily Tribune, 9 December 2025

n: Cocaine ring recruited airport-services staff at Paris Roissy
rank: Employees and managers of an airport services company
