d: A network moving cocaine from Brazil to Paris used employees and managers of a company working at Roissy-Charles-de-Gaulle, France's largest airport, the gendarmerie says. The case began after airport security found two boxes holding 45 blocks, about 50 kg of cocaine, in late 2024. Investigators believe the ring brought in 20 to 50 kg a month. On 3 June 2025, 105 gendarmes arrested eight people across six départements around Paris and seized nearly €500,000 in assets, including over €100,000 in cash, five vehicles, a house and a handgun. The gendarmerie described the case as 'airport compromise' and noted that crime groups look to bribe airport staff, especially mid-level managers who are unknown to the police.
inside: Investigators say a trafficking ring recruited staff inside an airport services company, who used their jobs to get its cocaine past airport controls.
cite: Brussels Times, 7 June 2025; Gendarmerie nationale (Gendinfo), June 2025

n: Georgia's ex-security chief accused of taking scam call-centre bribes
rank: Head of the State Security Service
d: Georgian prosecutors say Grigol Liluashvili, who ran the State Security Service, the country's main security and intelligence agency, from 2020 to April 2025, took bribes to protect scam call centres, which phone people abroad and talk them into fake investments. He was detained in December 2025 and faces four corruption charges. Prosecutors say about US$1.365 million reached him through a relative, partly from tenders and partly from a businessman in exchange for protecting 'a relatively smaller portion' of call centres between 2021 and 2023. Earlier in 2025 OCCRP's 'Scam Empire' investigation, with Sweden's SVT and more than 30 partners, had exposed a Tbilisi call centre near the service's headquarters that took US$35.3 million from more than 6,100 victims. Liluashvili belongs to the ruling Georgian Dream party.
inside: Prosecutors say scam call-centre money reached the head of Georgia's security service, whose agency then protected the centres instead of closing them.
cite: OCCRP, 23 December 2025

n: Chinese gangs had Thai police inside; 80 immigration officers charged
rank: Immigration Bureau officers incl. three generals; Royal Thai Police officers
d: Chinese criminal groups in Thailand had police officers working for them, Thai investigators said during a crackdown that began in late 2022. Chaiyanat 'Tuhao' Kornchayanant, a Chinese businessman accused of drug and money-laundering crimes, had gained Thai citizenship by marrying a senior police officer; she and five other officers were dismissed over links to his case, five of them accused of demanding bribes. In January 2023 investigators charged at least 80 immigration police, including three generals, with malfeasance and demanding bribes over visas issued to about 5,000 Chinese nationals in 2020 and 2021. The visas let them stay and run illegal businesses, among them a Pattaya club police suspect is a triad base. Authorities seized 5.3 billion baht of Tuhao's assets. On 11 February 2025 the South Bangkok Criminal Court acquitted Tuhao, his former wife and 17 others for insufficient evidence, finding no clear proof of a criminal organisation or of laundering; six defendants were convicted of drug offences.
inside: Thai investigators said Chinese gangs paid or married into the police, so officers gave their members visas and protection; a court later acquitted Tuhao and his former wife.
cite: The Nation (Thailand), 17 January 2023; Bangkok Post, 2023; Nation Thailand and Bangkok Post, 11 Feb 2025

n: Cocaine network had 26 workers inside Panama's Balboa port
rank: Port of Balboa workers and contractors
d: A criminal network shipping cocaine to Australia and Europe used corrupt workers and contractors at the Port of Balboa, on the Pacific end of the Panama Canal, Australian and Panamanian police say. On 7 July 2026 Panamanian authorities arrested 26 people described as Balboa port workers in 37 searches across the country, after a two-year joint investigation with the Australian Federal Police (AFP) and Australian Border Force. Police allege the workers hid cocaine in refrigerated containers before export. More than a tonne of cocaine linked to the group has been seized in Australia and Europe since October 2024. An AFP commander said the operation had 'struck at the heart' of a major criminal organisation.
inside: Police say a trafficking group recruited workers inside a major canal port, who loaded its cocaine into other firms' export containers.
cite: Australian Federal Police media release, 9 July 2026; Marine Insight, 11 July 2026

n: Albanian-led gang recruited Piraeus port workers to pull cocaine
rank: Cargo-handling workers at Piraeus port
d: An international cocaine ring allegedly led by an Albanian gang used workers at Piraeus, Greece's largest port, to get drugs out of containers, Greek police say. Six employees of a private company handling cargo at the port were jailed pending trial on 25 July 2025. Police say they used their access and their knowledge of loading and unloading to find the ships carrying the drugs and remove cocaine parcels hidden in refrigerated containers of bananas from Ecuador; one was in contact with buyers in Albania. The suspects, who deny wrongdoing, had allegedly taken part since at least 2024. The case began with a tip from the US Drug Enforcement Administration and was the third investigation since 2023 into Piraeus port workers on drug charges.
inside: Police say an Albanian-led gang recruited dockers inside a cargo firm at Piraeus, who used their access to get its cocaine out of the port.
cite: Reuters via gCaptain, 26 July 2025

n: PCC and Colombian cartels allegedly paid Portuguese customs and port staff
rank: Tax and Customs Authority officers and port officials
d: Brazil's Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC), the country's biggest crime group, and Colombian cartels allegedly paid officials at Portugal's ports to let several tonnes of cocaine from Latin America in, according to Portugal's Judicial Police (PJ). In Operation Porthos on 25 February 2025, about 150 PJ officers and four prosecutors carried out 32 searches in Lisbon, Setúbal, Sines and Leiria. Four people were detained, two of them officials of the Tax and Customs Authority, and 15 were made formal suspects, including officials at the ports of Lisbon, Setúbal and Sines. Police seized over €500,000 in cash, ten vehicles and five guns. The inquiry, which began more than two years earlier with help from the US Drug Enforcement Administration, covers corruption, drug trafficking and money laundering.
inside: Investigators say Brazilian and Colombian cocaine groups paid customs and port officials, who then let their containers into Europe without checks.
cite: Renascença, 25 February 2025; Portugal Resident, February 2025

n: Tequila's mayor accused of running a CJNG-linked extortion ring
rank: Mayor and three municipal department heads
d: Mexican authorities say the mayor of Tequila, the Jalisco town that gives the drink its name, ran a corruption ring from the town hall that worked with the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG). Mayor Diego Rivera was arrested on 5 February 2026 with the town's security director and its heads of public works and the land registry. Security minister Omar García Harfuch said the ring targeted beer and tequila producers. Becle, maker of José Cuervo, complained that the administration charged property tax up to 20 times the legal rate, withheld permits, tried to shut one of its plants and imposed a fine of over 60 million pesos; the Jalisco governor said at least 10 companies had complained. A town concert had earlier projected images of the CJNG's fugitive leader.
inside: Prosecutors say a cartel-linked network ran Tequila's town hall, so local taxes, permits and police were used to squeeze distillers for its benefit.
cite: Reuters via The Star, 6 February 2026; Mexico News Daily, February 2026

n: Prison staff took cash to smuggle phones and drugs in Auckland jails
rank: Corrections officers and Serco reintegration staff
d: Prisoners coordinating drug importations from inside Auckland jails were helped by staff who took cash to smuggle in phones and drugs, New Zealand police allege. In Operation Jasper, which began at Mount Eden Corrections Facility in July 2025, police in May 2026 charged 20 people with 108 offences: nine Corrections officers from Mount Eden, one from Spring Hill, five reintegration officers employed by the private operator Serco at Auckland South Corrections Facility, and five members of the public. A detective inspector said 'some of those prisoners were coordinating drug importations' from prison. The Corrections Association, the officers' union, called it the largest operation of its kind it had seen.
inside: Police say drug networks run from custody paid prison staff, who brought in the phones and drugs that let those networks keep operating from jail.
cite: 1News, 21 May 2026

n: Paper-leak gang got inside India's NEET medical exam via a test-centre chief
rank: National Testing Agency city coordinator and centre superintendent
d: A gang that sold leaked exam papers got inside the 2024 NEET-UG, the national entrance test for India's medical colleges, sat by over 2.3 million candidates, through the officials running one test centre, India's Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) says. The National Testing Agency had made Ahsanul Haque, principal of Oasis School in Hazaribagh, Jharkhand, its city coordinator, and his vice-principal was the centre superintendent. The CBI alleges that on 5 May 2024 they let Pankaj Kumar, an alleged mastermind, into the room holding the paper trunks, where he opened one and took the paper. Medical students brought in for the purpose solved it, and the answers went to candidates who had paid. By September 2024 the CBI had arrested 48 people and filed three charge sheets.
inside: Investigators say a paper-leak gang recruited the officials the testing agency had put in charge of a test centre, so the national exam paper reached its paying clients.
cite: ThePrint / PTI, 20 September 2024; The Week / PTI, 5 October 2024

n: Syndicates paid KLIA immigration officers to wave foreigners through
rank: Immigration and border-agency officers at KLIA
d: Syndicates bringing foreigners into Malaysia paid immigration officers at Kuala Lumpur International Airport (KLIA) to let their clients through without proper checks, the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) says. The practice is known as 'counter setting': an agent sends officers the travellers' passport numbers and flight details, then tells them which counters to use, and the officers let them skip thorough checks. In September 2025 the MACC detained 19 officers of the immigration department and the new Border Control and Protection Agency, including team leaders and supervisors, in four states. MACC chief Azam Baki said officers took RM1,800 to RM2,500 per foreigner, paid in cash or through mule accounts, and earned RM10,000 to RM50,000 a month.
inside: Smuggling syndicates paid officers inside Malaysia's border agencies, who then cleared the syndicates' clients at the airport counters meant to check them.
cite: Free Malaysia Today, 13 September 2025

n: Tokyo organised-crime detective leaked surveillance to the 'Natural' gang
rank: Inspector, Tokyo police organised-crime division
d: An inspector in the Tokyo Metropolitan Police's organised-crime division leaked investigation details to Natural, one of Japan's largest illegal 'scout' groups, which recruits women on the street and places them in sex parlours and hostess bars. Daisuke Jinbo had worked on the inquiry into Natural from 2023. He was arrested in November 2025, accused of sending the group, through its own smartphone app, images showing where police had installed surveillance cameras for the investigation. Natural is believed to have earned about ¥4.5 billion in kickbacks in 2022. In March 2026 a Tokyo court gave Jinbo an 18-month suspended prison sentence, saying the leak would 'greatly undermine society's trust' in police. He said he had received no money or goods from the group.
inside: A crime group got an officer inside the police unit investigating it, who passed it the locations of the surveillance aimed at the group.
cite: Japan Times, 13 November 2025; Jiji Press via Nippon.com, 25 March 2026

n: PCC recruited ground staff at São Paulo's Guarulhos airport to move cocaine
rank: Outsourced ground-handling employees
d: A Federal Police report obtained by CNN Brasil in April 2023 said the Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC), Brazil's largest crime group, had recruited outsourced workers with access to restricted areas at São Paulo-Guarulhos, Latin America's largest airport, since 2019, paying about R$30,000 per suitcase of cocaine sent abroad. In March 2023 two Brazilian women were jailed in Frankfurt for over a month after bags of cocaine were tagged in their names; video showed two employees of the ground-handling firm WFS Orbital handling their luggage. In Operation Bota Fora on 7 December 2023 police arrested nine people, saying colluding employees were recruited soon after being hired and some joined before getting their jobs. That ring was linked to about 700 kg of cocaine seized in Brazil, Germany, Portugal and Ethiopia.
inside: Police say a crime group recruited and placed airport ground staff, who retagged bags so its cocaine flew under innocent passengers' names.
cite: Rádio Itatiaia (citing CNN Brasil), 16 April 2023; One Mile at a Time, 11 April 2023; Agência Brasil, 8 December 2023

n: Istanbul police and a court clerk held for leaking to the Casperlar gang
rank: Police officers, a court clerk and a customs official
d: Casperlar ('the Caspers'), an Istanbul crime group that recruits young people, many of them minors, through social media, had police officers and a court clerk feeding it information, Turkish prosecutors say. In February 2026 police detained 17 suspects, including nine police officers, a court clerk and a customs official, and on 23 February a Bakırköy court placed 14 people in pretrial detention, among them seven officers and the clerk. Prosecutors say the officials gave the gang advance warning of arrest warrants and planned operations, letting it act first, and searched official databases for criminal records and vehicle registrations, in what they called a 'benefit-based relationship'. The case grew from WhatsApp messages between officers and gang figures found on devices seized in a 9 January raid.
inside: Prosecutors say the gang had police officers and a court clerk working for it, so warrants and raids meant to stop it were leaked in advance.
cite: Hürriyet Daily News, 19 February 2026; Turkish Minute, 23 February 2026

n: Cocaine gang recruited a Sheerness port guard to let its vans through
rank: Port security guard
d: An organised crime group trying to collect 1.2 tonnes of cocaine, worth over £90 million, hidden in a banana shipment from Costa Rica at Sheerness Port in Kent recruited a port security guard to get it past the gates, the National Crime Agency (NCA) says. The NCA said Sam Elphick 'was recruited specifically for his knowledge of Sheerness Port and the security systems'. In the early hours of 20 December 2021 he let the gang's two vans through a security checkpoint. At Maidstone Crown Court in November 2024 Elphick was jailed for two years for taking part in an organised crime group, and the seven defendants received more than 74 years in all.
inside: A smuggling gang recruited a guard inside the port's own security, who opened the checkpoint he was employed to keep closed.
cite: National Crime Agency, 3 December 2024

n: Clan del Golfo paid soldiers through a go-between for operations plans
rank: Army and security-force personnel
d: The Clan del Golfo, Colombia's largest drug-trafficking armed group, used a community leader in Valdivia, Antioquia, to bribe members of the security forces for confidential information, Colombia's prosecutor's office says. Teresa Jaramillo Giraldo, alias 'La Tía', presided over local community boards while secretly working as the group's link. Prosecutors say her network offered money for troop movements and planned operations against the group in the Magdalena Medio and southern Bolívar regions, which helped it evade the authorities; in one instance a former army corporal allegedly offered an officer 100 million pesos, and two men in Medellín paid 25 million pesos each between October 2024 and January 2025. The case was announced in February 2025, and in September 2025 she was sentenced to four years under a plea deal.
inside: The armed group paid soldiers through a go-between to pass it the plans of operations against it, so it could escape them.
cite: Minuto60, 21 September 2025

n: Smuggling boss 'Papá Pitufo' charged with buying Colombia's customs police
rank: Fiscal and Customs Police (POLFA) officers
d: Colombian prosecutors say a smuggling network led by Diego Marín Buitrago, alias 'Papá Pitufo', set out to co-opt the officials who control customs, handing money and gifts to current and former members of the Fiscal and Customs Police (POLFA), the National Police branch that fights contraband. In November 2025 prosecutors formally charged him with bribery and conspiracy to smuggle; several POLFA members have also been charged. He appeared at the hearing by video from Portugal, where extradition proceedings were under way. In 2024 prosecutors set up a special task group to examine mentions of police generals and other senior officials in the case. Marín is also reported to have given 500 million pesos to Gustavo Petro's 2022 campaign through Xavier Vendrell, who says the money was returned.
inside: Prosecutors say a contraband network paid members of the police unit that guards customs, so officers meant to stop smuggling worked for it.
cite: Blu Radio, 13 November 2025; El Tiempo, 12 February 2025

n: Slovenian prosecutor's office worker leaked search orders to Kavač clan
rank: Official at the Specialised State Prosecutor's Office
d: The Kavač clan, a Montenegrin cocaine-trafficking syndicate with a cell in Slovenia, received secret case material from inside Slovenia's Specialised State Prosecutor's Office, which handles organised crime, Slovenian police said in November 2021. An official who had worked there for about five years photographed documents on ongoing investigations, including orders for house searches and covert surveillance, and sent them through her partner to three people in the Ljubljana area. Four people were arrested in the leak case. Two key members of the clan's Slovenian cell, Luka Arapovič and Blaž Kadivec, avoided arrest. The head of the prosecutor's office said the official had passed all background checks, the last of them three years earlier.
inside: A crime syndicate got material out of the prosecutor's office investigating it, so its members learned of planned searches and surveillance in advance.
cite: Total Slovenia News / STA, 10 November 2021

n: Drug gang's contact in Border Force waved its courier through Portsmouth
rank: Border Force officer at Portsmouth port
d: A London drug-smuggling group had a Border Force officer, from the UK agency that runs passport and customs checks at ports, working for it at Portsmouth. Kevin Smith met the group's ringleader, David Johnson, while working as an officer at the prison where Johnson was serving a drugs sentence. After joining Border Force, Smith met Johnson in Portsmouth, messaged him on an encrypted phone and let a courier, Caprice Thompson, through his booth when she arrived on a ferry from France; police later found 15 kg of MDMA, worth about £400,000, in her car. In June 2024 Smith was jailed for two years for misconduct in public office. The National Crime Agency said such insiders are 'invaluable to organised crime groups'.
inside: A drug gang cultivated an officer inside Britain's border agency, who then let its courier pass the check he was posted to carry out.
cite: Portsmouth News, June 2024; National Crime Agency, 10 June 2024

n: Los Lobos allegedly had a prosecutor's office worker in Babahoyo
rank: Employee of the Los Ríos prosecutor's office
d: Los Lobos, one of Ecuador's largest gangs, had a woman linked to the Los Ríos provincial prosecutor's office working for it, Ecuador's police say. In Operation Jauría in Babahoyo on 12 December 2025, police detained her with seven others, several of them with records for drug trafficking, extortion, murder or weapons offences. Police say she 'operated to favour members' of the gang: she advised it, passed it sensitive information and intervened in legal proceedings to benefit its members. Officers seized a computer and phones from an archive office of the prosecutor's office in Babahoyo. The case is one of a series of Ecuadorian investigations since 2023 into gangs' reach inside courts, prosecutors' offices and prisons.
inside: Police say a gang had a worker inside the prosecutor's office that pursues it, who leaked case information and steered proceedings in its members' favour.
cite: Primicias, 12 December 2025

n: Sri Lankan army officers and police allegedly armed and aided Padme's gang
rank: Army colonels, a police sub-inspector, immigration officials
d: The arrest of Kehelbaddara Padme, an organised-crime leader returned from Indonesia with four other gang members in 2025, led Sri Lankan investigators to officials who allegedly worked for his network. Police arrested a sub-inspector in Gampaha Division's crime investigation unit, identified from the gang members' statements, on suspicion of close ties with Padme. An army lieutenant colonel was detained over allegedly selling firearms to Padme and his associate 'Commando Salintha', and an army colonel over allegedly selling 260 rounds of T-56 rifle ammunition to people including Salintha, who had served under him. A former local councillor is accused of overseeing drug and arms operations on Padme's orders. The public security minister said there was evidence that police and immigration officials helped the gang obtain forged passports.
inside: Investigators say a crime gang reached officers in the army, police and immigration service, who supplied it with weapons, passports and protection.
cite: Sunday Times (Sri Lanka), 14 September 2025; Ada Derana, 11 September 2025

n: Peruvian army lieutenant accused of supplying ammunition for Ecuador's gangs
rank: Lieutenant, Peruvian Army (Chorrillos fort)
d: A Peruvian army lieutenant is accused of taking about 4,000 rounds of 5.56 mm rifle ammunition out of a military fort in Lima for sale to cells of Los Choneros and Los Tiguerones, Ecuadorian gangs operating on the border with Peru. Peruvian police stopped a car carrying the ammunition in Lima's La Victoria district on 5 January 2025. The two people in it said it came from Lieutenant Christian Revilla Barzola, who supplied it from inside the Chorrillos fort, and police arrested him outside the army's Special Forces Brigade two days later. Police said the rounds were destined for the Ecuadorian gangs; the two detainees said only that they were to go to a third person. Investigators were examining whether other soldiers were involved.
inside: Police say buyers for Ecuadorian gangs reached an officer inside Peru's army, who took ammunition from a military fort to arm them.
cite: Primicias, 7 February 2025

n: Recology and contractors paid San Francisco's public works chief
rank: Director, San Francisco Department of Public Works
d: Contractors and the city's rubbish company, Recology, paid Mohammed Nuru, director of San Francisco's Department of Public Works from 2011, to steer city business their way. The US Justice Department says contractor Walter Wong gave him cash, more than $260,000 of building work on his home and ranch, and paid travel; in return Nuru shaped city tenders so that Wong's company would win, shared rivals' confidential bids and sped up permits. Recology supplied meals, a New York trip, money for department parties and a job for a relative, and Nuru gave it favourable treatment on the 'tipping fee' rates it charged. Arrested in January 2020, he pleaded guilty and on 25 August 2022 was sentenced to seven years in prison.
inside: Contractors and the city's waste company paid the official who ran San Francisco's public works, and he rigged tenders and rates in their favour.
cite: US Attorney's Office, N.D. California, 25 Aug 2022

n: Chinese billionaire's firm paid LA's planning committee chair over a tower
org_label: Shen Zhen New World I (Wei Huang)
rank: Chair, LA City Council planning committee
d: Property developers paid José Huizar, the Los Angeles city councillor who chaired the council's Planning and Land Use Management Committee, which reviews large building projects, to help their projects in his downtown district. Prosecutors said he secured more than $1.5 million in illegal payments and helped the payers with council votes, by speeding up or delaying approvals and by pressing other officials and unions. The biggest payer was Shen Zhen New World I, owned by Chinese billionaire Wei Huang, which paid more than $1 million in bribes for help with a planned 77-storey tower; Huang also gave Huizar casino trips and $600,000 to settle a lawsuit. The company was fined $4 million in 2023, and on 26 January 2024 Huizar was sentenced to 13 years. Huang fled to China.
inside: Developers' money bought the councillor who chaired Los Angeles's planning committee, and he used votes and approvals to push their buildings through.
cite: LAist, 26 Jan 2024

n: Banker offered Puerto Rico's governor campaign cash to replace his regulator
rank: Governor of Puerto Rico; bank regulator's post
d: Prosecutors say Julio Herrera Velutini, owner of the Puerto Rico bank Bancrédito, set out to get his own choice installed as the island's bank regulator. His bank was being audited by the Office of the Commissioner of Financial Institutions (OCIF), which supervises banks. According to the 2022 indictment, he and a former FBI agent promised to fund Governor Wanda Vázquez's 2020 campaign if she replaced the OCIF head; the commissioner resigned in February 2020, and in May Vázquez appointed a former adviser to Herrera Velutini. More than $300,000 allegedly went to consultants through a political action committee. Vázquez later pleaded guilty only to a campaign-finance offence, and after a pardon from President Trump the case was dismissed on 27 January 2026.
inside: Prosecutors say a banker under audit offered the governor campaign money to remove his regulator, and the new commissioner was his own former adviser.
cite: Governing / AP, Aug 2022; Zol FM (Puerto Rico), 27 Jan 2026

n: Sargeant Marine bribed PDVSA, Petrobras and Petroecuador staff for asphalt
rank: Officials of PDVSA, Petrobras and Petroecuador
d: Sargeant Marine, a Florida asphalt trading company, paid people inside three South American state oil companies to win asphalt business. Pleading guilty in New York on 22 September 2020, it admitted an eight-year scheme from 2010 to 2018. In Venezuela it paid four officials of PDVSA, the state oil company, for inside information and to steer asphalt contracts to a company it nominated. At Brazil's Petrobras it bribed senior executives, as well as a government minister and a senior member of Congress, and at Ecuador's Petroecuador it paid an official for a 2014 supply contract. The company paid a $16.6 million fine, and five people, including former PDVSA official Hector Nuñez Troyano, pleaded guilty.
inside: An asphalt trader paid officials inside three state oil companies, who passed it inside information and steered their purchasing contracts to it.
cite: US Department of Justice, 22 Sep 2020

n: Waste firm Stericycle paid officials in Mexico, Brazil and Argentina
rank: Officials of government agencies and state bodies
d: Stericycle, a US medical-waste company, paid officials at government agencies and state-owned bodies in Brazil, Mexico and Argentina to win and keep waste-collection business. According to the US Justice Department and Securities and Exchange Commission, between 2011 and 2016 its staff made hundreds of bribe payments, usually in cash and worked out as a percentage of what government customers owed the company, totalling more than $10.5 million; Stericycle earned at least $21.5 million in profit from the business. On 20 April 2022 it agreed to pay more than $84 million, including a $52.5 million criminal penalty under a deferred prosecution agreement, a deal in which charges are dropped if the company meets set conditions. The Brazilian strand, hospital waste contracts with institutions of the national health service, has its own record on this map.
inside: A waste company put officials in three countries' public bodies on its payroll, so contracts and payments from those bodies flowed its way.
cite: US DOJ and SEC, 20 Apr 2022 (via McGuireWoods, 25 Apr 2022)

n: Honeywell UOP offered a Petrobras executive $4m for a refinery contract
rank: Senior Petrobras executive
d: Honeywell UOP, a US oil-refining technology firm owned by Honeywell, conspired to pay a then senior executive of Petrobras, Brazil's state oil company, to win work there. The US Justice Department said that between 2010 and 2014 UOP offered the executive a bribe of about $4 million to help it obtain a contract worth about $425 million to design and build the Premium refinery, and that UOP made about $105.5 million in profit from the business. On 19 December 2022 it agreed to pay more than $160 million to US and Brazilian authorities, including a criminal penalty of about $79 million under a deferred prosecution agreement, a deal in which charges are dropped if the company meets set conditions.
inside: A US supplier bought the help of a senior executive inside Brazil's state oil company to win a refinery contract from it.
cite: US Attorney's Office, S.D. Texas, 19 Dec 2022

n: Albemarle's agents bribed state refinery officials in Vietnam, India, Indonesia
rank: Officials of state oil companies and refineries
d: Albemarle, a US chemicals company that sells refinery catalysts, used sales agents to bribe officials at state-owned oil companies in Vietnam, Indonesia and India between 2009 and 2017. The US Justice Department said that in Vietnam an agent asked for higher commissions to pay officials at two state refineries and to shape tender requirements in Albemarle's favour; in Indonesia an agent kept winning business after warning that bribes were needed; and in India an intermediary helped it keep business with the state oil company and avoid being blacklisted. Albemarle made about $98.5 million in profit from the scheme. In September 2023 it agreed to pay more than $218 million to settle US criminal and civil investigations.
inside: Through paid agents, a chemicals company got officials inside Asian state oil companies to tailor tenders and keep buying its products.
cite: US Department of Justice, Sep 2023 (via Mondo Visione, 29 Sep 2023)

n: Corficolombiana and Odebrecht paid Colombian officials $23m for a toll road
rank: Officials in government, Congress and the infrastructure agency
d: Corficolombiana, an investment company in the Colombian banking group Grupo Aval, joined Brazil's construction firm Odebrecht in paying high-ranking Colombian officials to win a highway contract. The US Justice Department said that between 2012 and 2015 the company conspired to pay more than $23 million in bribes to officials in Colombia's executive and legislative branches and to an executive of the state infrastructure agency, to secure the Ocaña–Gamarra extension of a toll road. The money was passed on through intermediaries under fictitious contracts. On 10 August 2023 Corficolombiana agreed to pay more than $80 million to US and Colombian authorities; the Justice Department called it its first foreign bribery resolution coordinated with Colombia.
inside: A bank-owned investment company and Odebrecht paid officials in Colombia's government, Congress and road agency, who gave them the toll-road contract.
cite: US Department of Justice, 10 Aug 2023

n: Airline Gol bribed Brazilian officials to pass two tax-cutting laws
rank: Brazilian officials who passed legislation
d: Gol, the Brazilian airline, paid Brazilian officials to get laws passed that cut its taxes. The US Justice Department said that in 2012 and 2013 a member of Gol's board caused the airline to sign sham contracts with companies tied to the officials, and about $3.8 million in bribes flowed through them. In return the officials secured the passage of two pieces of legislation giving payroll-tax and fuel-tax reductions that benefited Gol and other Brazilian airlines. On 15 September 2022 Gol agreed to pay more than $41 million to US and Brazilian authorities, a total reduced because the airline could not afford more.
inside: An airline paid Brazilian officials through sham contracts, and they delivered two laws cutting taxes for Gol and the rest of the industry.
cite: US Department of Justice, 15 Sep 2022

n: AAR paid Nepali officials over Nepal Airlines' Airbus purchase
rank: officials over Nepal Airlines Corporation
d: AAR Corp, a US aviation services company, paid officials in Nepal to win the sale of two Airbus A330-200 aircraft to Nepal Airlines Corporation, the state-owned carrier. The US Justice Department said that from 2015 to 2020 AAR paid through intermediary companies to reach the officials deciding the purchase. On 19 December 2024 AAR accepted a non-prosecution agreement and agreed to pay more than $55 million, covering this and a parallel scheme in South Africa, from which it made nearly $24 million in profit in total. A former subsidiary executive pleaded guilty.
inside: An aviation company paid the officials who controlled Nepal's state airline purchasing, and the airline then bought two of the jets it was selling.
cite: US Department of Justice, 19 Dec 2024

n: Phuc Son Group paid Vietnamese provincial leaders $5m for projects
rank: Provincial party leaders and officials
d: Phuc Son Group, a Vietnamese property company, paid provincial party leaders and officials to give it preferential treatment in bidding for public projects. A Hanoi court found that its chairman, Nguyen Van Hau, paid more than 132 billion dong (about $5.1 million) in bribes from 2010 to 2023 and made more than 1.16 trillion dong in illicit profit. On 11 July 2025 he was sentenced to 30 years. Hoang Thi Thuy Lan, a former senior party official in Vinh Phuc province, received 14 years for taking bribes to favour the company in provincial tenders, and nearly 30 other former officials from three provinces were jailed or given suspended terms. In all 41 people were sentenced; an appeal trial has since opened.
inside: A property company paid the party leaders who ran provincial bidding, and they gave it preferential treatment for lucrative public projects.
cite: The Star / AFP, 11 Jul 2025; VietnamPlus (appeal)

n: Thuan An Group used bribes and ties to win Vietnamese road and bridge tenders
rank: Project boards, provincial committees, National Assembly Office
d: Thuan An Group, a Vietnamese construction company, won public road and bridge contracts by offering bribes to officials on project management boards and provincial people's committees and by using its connections with central and local leaders. In September 2025 Hanoi's People's Court found its former chairman, Nguyen Duy Hung, guilty of breaking bidding rules and sentenced him to ten and a half years. Among 28 others sentenced was Pham Thai Ha, a former deputy chairman of the National Assembly Office, whose influence Hung used; he received five and a half years. The projects included the Dong Viet Bridge, the first phase of the Tuyen Quang–Phu Tho expressway and the second phase of Hanoi's Vinh Tuy Bridge. The state lost over 120 billion dong; sentences were later reduced on appeal.
inside: A builder paid officials who ran tenders and used a senior parliamentary official's influence, so state road and bridge contracts went to it.
cite: VietnamPlus / VNA, 18 Sep 2025; Vietnamnet (appeal)

n: AIC bribed Dong Nai's party chief to win hospital equipment deals
rank: Party secretary and chairman, Dong Nai province
d: AIC, a Vietnamese medical-equipment supplier, bribed the top leaders of Dong Nai province and its general hospital to win supply contracts. In January 2023 a Hanoi court found that AIC's chairwoman, Nguyen Thi Thanh Nhan, had rigged bids to win 16 contracts to supply equipment to Dong Nai General Hospital, earning about 150 billion dong ($6.3 million). Tried in absentia because she is hiding abroad, she was sentenced to 30 years for bid-rigging and bribery. The province's former Communist Party secretary, Tran Dinh Thanh, got 11 years and its former chairman, Dinh Quoc Thai, nine years for taking bribes; the hospital's director received 19 years. Thirty-five others were also sentenced.
inside: A supplier paid Dong Nai's party chief, provincial chairman and hospital director, who then let it win rigged contracts for hospital equipment.
cite: Radio Free Asia, 4 Jan 2023

n: Firms paid Vietnamese ministry officials to approve Covid repatriation flights
rank: Vice Foreign Minister and officials of three ministries
d: During the Covid-19 pandemic, when Vietnamese citizens abroad could return home only on approved 'repatriation flights', businesses paid officials in the foreign affairs, health and public security ministries to get their flights approved. On 28 July 2023 Hanoi's People's Court convicted 54 people, including 23 business executives for giving bribes and 21 officials for taking them. A group of 20 businesses with more than 100 companies paid about 226 billion dong in roughly 400 payments and then raised ticket prices to recover the cost. Vice Foreign Minister To Anh Dung received 16 years for taking about $907,000, and Pham Trung Kien, an assistant to a deputy health minister, was jailed for life.
inside: Charter-flight businesses paid officials in three ministries, including a vice foreign minister, who then approved the flights they sold seats on.
cite: Viet Nam News, 28 Jul 2023; The Diplomat, Jul 2023

n: Tin smelters got PT Timah's directors to open its concessions to them
rank: Directors of state tin company PT Timah
d: Private tin smelting companies, represented by businessman Harvey Moeis of PT Refined Bangka Tin, reached a deal with directors of PT Timah, Indonesia's state tin company, to mine illegally inside Timah's concessions on the Bangka Belitung islands from 2015 to 2022. According to the case record, in 2018 Moeis discussed the arrangement with Timah director Mochtar Riza Pahlevi Tabrani, disguised as the leasing of smelting equipment, and organised profit-sharing among the smelters, which also sold tin to Timah. The Attorney General's Office put state losses at about 300 trillion rupiah, most of it environmental damage. Moeis was sentenced in December 2024 to six and a half years, raised on appeal on 13 February 2025 to 20 years.
inside: Private smelters reached a deal with the state tin company's own directors, who opened its concessions to their illegal mining and bought their tin.
cite: The Jakarta Post, 13 Feb 2025; Wikipedia 'Indonesian tin mining scandal'

n: Palm oil firms' lawyers allegedly paid Jakarta judges to acquit them
org_label: Wilmar, Permata Hijau and Musim Mas (lawyers)
rank: Deputy head and judges, Central Jakarta District Court
d: Indonesian prosecutors say lawyers acting for three large palm oil groups, Wilmar, Permata Hijau and Musim Mas, paid judges to clear the companies in a corruption case. The firms were on trial over permits to export crude palm oil in 2022, when shipments were restricted, and on 19 March 2025 the Central Jakarta District Court acquitted them. On 12–14 April 2025 the Attorney General's Office arrested the court's former deputy head, Muhammad Arif Nuryanta, and the three judges on the panel. Prosecutors allege Arif accepted 60 billion rupiah (about $3.5 million) from two of the companies' lawyers, chose the judges and passed money to them. Wilmar has denied involvement.
inside: Prosecutors say the companies' lawyers paid a court's deputy head, who picked the judges and paid them to acquit the palm oil groups.
cite: The Jakarta Post, 15 Apr 2025; Reuters via The Star, 14 Apr 2025

n: ThyssenKrupp's agent allegedly bribed Israeli officials over submarine deals
rank: the prime minister's bureau chief, the prime minister's pick to head the National Security Council, and former navy command
d: Miki Ganor, the Israeli agent of German shipbuilder ThyssenKrupp, is accused of paying officials and political figures to help him win the agency and to promote Israel's purchases of ThyssenKrupp submarines and patrol boats. Ganor was appointed in October 2009, entitled to a commission on each deal, and earned about 10.4 million euros. In December 2019 Israel's State Attorney announced charges against Ganor for bribery and money laundering, against former navy commander Eliezer Marom and David Sharan, former head of Prime Minister Netanyahu's bureau, for taking bribes, and against former minister Eliezer Zandberg. The indictments filed at the Tel Aviv District Court on 10 May 2021 also charge Avriel Bar-Yosef, then on the National Security Council and Netanyahu's pick to head it, with taking about 420,000 shekels from Ganor disguised as consultation fees; prosecutors say Bar-Yosef pushed for Ganor's appointment in 2009 on an understanding that commissions would come back to him. Prosecutors closed the case against Marom in May 2021. Netanyahu was not charged. In January 2026 a state commission of inquiry found systemic failings in the procurement that endangered state security. ThyssenKrupp denies wrongdoing.
inside: Prosecutors say a shipbuilder's agent paid the prime minister's bureau chief and an official on the national security council who had pushed for his appointment, to promote the purchases he earned commissions on.
cite: Globes, 5 Dec 2019; The Times of Israel, 'Several indicted in submarine affair; ex-navy chief, Netanyahu's cousin off hook', 10 May 2021; The JC, 26 Jan 2026; The Jerusalem Post, 'Israel's communications adviser convicted of bribe brokering in Submarine Affair', 26 October 2026
undone: On 26 October 2026 the Tel Aviv District Court convicted the communications adviser Yitzhak Liber of brokering bribes, money laundering and helping to prepare false accounts, finding that nearly 94,000 shekels from Ganor's company passed through companies owned by Liber and his business partner and reached Sharan in cash, disguised by false invoices. The proceedings against Ganor and Sharan are still running.

n: Builders paid Martín Vizcarra as Moquegua governor; ex-president jailed
rank: Regional Governor of Moquegua (later President)
d: Two construction companies paid Martín Vizcarra while he was governor of Peru's Moquegua region, from 2011 to 2014, to win public works, a court found; he later served as Peru's president from 2018 to 2020. On 26 November 2025 the Fourth National Criminal Court convicted him of aggravated passive bribery and sentenced him to 14 years. Witnesses said he asked the firm Obrainsa for 2% of the budget of the Lomas de Ilo irrigation project, worth 80.9 million soles, and was paid 1 million soles in two instalments in 2014. The court found that ICCGSA agreed to pay him 1.3 million soles, through a former minister, over the expansion of Moquegua's regional hospital. He is appealing.
inside: Construction firms paid the regional governor who awarded Moquegua's public works, and he gave them an irrigation scheme and a hospital contract.
cite: bne IntelliNews, 26 Nov 2025

n: Bribes bought loans and contracts from China's central bank deputy Fan Yifei
rank: Deputy Governor, People's Bank of China
d: People seeking loans and contracts paid Fan Yifei, a deputy governor of the People's Bank of China, the country's central bank, more than 386 million yuan (about $53 million). The Huanggang Intermediate People's Court found that from 1993 to 2022, in posts at China Construction Bank, as chairman of Bank of Shanghai, as vice-president of the sovereign wealth fund China Investment Corporation and at the central bank, he used his position to benefit others in loan financing, business contracting and job transfers. On 10 October 2024 he received a death sentence suspended for two years, which becomes life imprisonment without parole if he behaves well. He was the most senior central bank official arrested in a decade.
inside: Those who paid the central bank's deputy governor got loans, contracts and jobs from the state financial bodies he helped run.
cite: China Daily, 10 Oct 2024; Reuters via VOA, 10 Oct 2024

n: Firms paid Bank of China's chairman $167m to obtain loans
rank: Chairman, Bank of China
d: Businesses paid Liu Liange, chairman and Communist Party secretary of Bank of China, one of the country's largest state-owned banks, and earlier president of the Export-Import Bank of China, to obtain loans and deals. The Jinan Intermediate People's Court found that from 2010 to 2023 he took bribes worth more than 1.2 billion yuan (about $167 million) and improperly helped companies obtain loan financing, project partnerships and personnel arrangements. He also pushed through 3.2 billion yuan of loans to companies he knew did not meet the requirements, causing losses of about 191 million yuan. On 26 November 2024 he was sentenced to death with a two-year reprieve.
inside: Companies paid the head of a major state bank, who then lent them money they did not qualify for and arranged deals in their favour.
cite: Yicai Global, 27 Nov 2024

n: Core Pacific Group bribed Taipei mayor Ko Wen-je for building rights
rank: Mayor of Taipei
d: Core Pacific Group, a Taiwanese property developer, paid Ko Wen-je while he was mayor of Taipei so that the city would let it build far more on its Core Pacific City site. On 26 March 2026 the Taipei District Court found that bribes from chairman Sheen Ching-jing and his executives directly affected the city government's decision to raise the project's floor area ratio, the limit on how much floor space may be built on a plot, to as much as 840%, increasing potential returns. Ko, who founded the Taiwan People's Party and ran for president in 2024, was sentenced to 17 years in total on four charges, 13 of them for corruption. Sheen was sentenced to ten years. Both can appeal.
inside: A developer paid Taipei's mayor, and the city government then raised the building limit on the developer's site, increasing what it could earn.
cite: Taipei Times, 27 Mar 2026; Focus Taiwan, 26 Mar 2026

n: Tycoon's land for Imran Khan's trust; his government settled the tycoon's fine
rank: Prime Minister
d: A Pakistani court found that real-estate developer Malik Riaz Hussain gave land to the Al-Qadir Trust, a charity set up in 2018 by Prime Minister Imran Khan and his wife, and that Khan's government in return let money belonging to the state pay the developer's own court fines. Britain had sent £190 million to Pakistan in 2019 after Hussain forfeited cash and assets to settle a British investigation; prosecutors said Khan's government used it to pay fines a Pakistani court had imposed on Hussain for acquiring government land in Karachi below market value. On 17 January 2025 an accountability court in Islamabad sentenced Khan to 14 years and his wife Bushra to seven. Hussain denies wrongdoing, and Khan's party calls the case baseless.
inside: The court found a developer gave land to the prime minister's trust, and his government then used state money to cover the developer's fines.
cite: Arab News Pakistan, 17 Jan 2025; Dawn, Jan 2025

n: Builder Acciona allegedly paid kickbacks through the PSOE's number three
rank: PSOE organisation secretary; transport ministry
d: Spain's Supreme Court is investigating whether the construction company Acciona paid kickbacks to win public works through a network led by Santos Cerdán, organisation secretary and third-ranking official of the governing Socialist Party (PSOE). On 30 June 2025 judge Leopoldo Puente jailed Cerdán pending trial, citing strong signs that he acted as intermediary with paying companies, mainly Acciona, and knew the details of each contract; Acciona won works worth more than €537 million in the period investigated. Seized recordings suggest former transport minister José Luis Ábalos and his aide Koldo García received €550,000 and were owed €450,000 more. Cerdán, freed in November 2025 after 142 days in custody, denies the charges.
inside: Investigators say a construction company paid the governing party's number three and the transport minister's circle, who steered public works its way.
cite: elDiario.es, 30 Jun 2025; El Independiente, 19 Nov 2025

n: Lobbyist Redl's group allegedly steered Prague transport company contracts
rank: Deputy mayor and managers, Prague Public Transit Company
d: Czech police say a group led by Michal Redl, a businessman and lobbyist from Zlín linked to the STAN party, influenced contracts and finances at the Prague Public Transit Company (DPP), the city-owned firm that runs the metro, trams and buses, to benefit businessmen connected to it. Deputy mayor Petr Hlubuček allegedly used his influence over the city and DPP's supervisory board, working with senior DPP managers. Police raided City Hall and DPP on 15 June 2022 and charged 13 people, including four DPP officials; Education Minister Petr Gazdík resigned over his contacts with Redl. Another branch concerns contracts at the state health insurer VZP. The trial was under way in October 2025, with Redl and Hlubuček denying guilt.
inside: Police say a lobbyist's group worked through a deputy mayor and senior managers inside Prague's transit company to steer its contracts to allied businessmen.
cite: Wikipedia 'Operation Dozimetr' (citing Czech media); Ground News / ČTK, 2 Oct 2025

n: Fuel importers and navy officers allegedly ran 'fiscal huachicol' in ports
rank: Navy officers and customs staff at ports
d: In the scheme Mexicans call 'huachicol fiscal', companies import petrol and diesel declared as lubricants or additives to avoid fuel taxes, with help from inside the ports and customs, which the armed forces took over between 2020 and 2022. After the navy seized the tanker Challenge Procyon at Tampico in March 2025 carrying about 10 million litres of diesel declared as additives, federal authorities on 7 September 2025 announced 14 arrests of customs staff, businessmen and six military members, including Vice Admiral Manuel Roberto Farías Laguna, and sought more than 200 further warrants. Prosecutors cite testimony that bribes were paid to let vessels dock at a Tampico pier without inspection. Officials say each untaxed cargo costs the state about 1 billion pesos.
inside: Investigators say fuel importers had navy officers and customs staff inside the ports on their side, letting untaxed fuel through inspections those officers controlled.
cite: Mexico News Daily, 8 Sep 2025; Wikipedia 'Huachicol fiscal'

n: 'Audios' case: lawyer's business clients' bribes reached Chile's tax service
org_label: Luis Hermosilla and the Sauer group
rank: Officials of the tax service (SII) and Treasury
d: In a recording made by businesswoman Leonarda Villalobos and leaked to the news site Ciper in November 2023, Luis Hermosilla, a prominent Santiago lawyer, was heard discussing bribes to public officials for the benefit of clients including the Sauer brothers, who ran the finance firm Factop. The 'Audios' case that followed has already produced convictions for bribery of officials at the tax service (SII) and the national Treasury: former SII official Patricio Mejías was sentenced to four years, and a former Treasury official received supervised release for taking bribes from other defendants. The investigation closed on 16 January 2026, and prosecutors are seeking 14 years for Hermosilla, 18 for Villalobos and 20 for Daniel Sauer.
inside: Prosecutors say a lawyer and his business clients paid officials inside Chile's tax service and Treasury to deal with the clients' affairs in their favour.
cite: The Clinic, 14 Nov 2023; El Dínamo, 28 Jan 2026

n: Belarusian-Chilean consortium allegedly paid Supreme Court judge Vivanco
rank: Supreme Court justice
d: Chilean prosecutors say Belaz Movitec, a consortium of the Belarusian mining-truck maker Belaz and the Chilean firm Movitec, paid Ángela Vivanco, then a Supreme Court justice, over a ruling against Codelco, Chile's state copper company. An appeals court in Copiapó had ordered the consortium to pay Codelco $20 million for breach of contract; the Supreme Court's Third Chamber, provisionally chaired by Vivanco, reversed it and ordered Codelco to pay the consortium that sum instead. Prosecutors estimate she received about 57 million pesos plus $15,600 in cash, routed through third parties; the consortium was represented by lawyers Mario Vargas and Eduardo Lagos. She was detained on 25 January 2026, and Codelco has filed a criminal complaint.
inside: Prosecutors say a consortium paid a Supreme Court justice, whose chamber then reversed a ruling and ordered the state copper company to pay it $20 million.
cite: T13, 26 Jan 2026; Diario Financiero, Nov 2025

n: Road builders MECO and H Solís allegedly paid Costa Rica's roads agency staff
rank: Officials, National Roads Council (CONAVI)
d: Costa Rican prosecutors say construction companies, centrally MECO and H Solís, gave officials of the National Roads Council (CONAVI), the agency that pays for and supervises road works, gifts and cash to favour them in publicly funded projects. Raids on 14 June 2021 led to 30 detentions, 14 of them public officials. Investigators counted payments of at least 62 million colones over 21 months, including liquor, cash and vehicles, and accuse the two firms, which received about 64% of CONAVI's road-work funds, of agreeing to divide contracts between them. MECO's president Carlos Cerdas and H Solís's owner Mélida Solís were released on bail of $5 million and $3 million. In 2024 prosecutors formally accused the first 12 suspects.
inside: Prosecutors say road builders paid staff inside the agency that awards and checks road works, who then favoured their bids and payments.
cite: La Nación, 28 Jun 2021; Delfino, Apr 2024

n: Kyiv developer allegedly offered ex-deputy PM Chernyshov cheap flats for land
rank: Minister for Communities and Territories (later Deputy PM)
d: Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) says the owner of a Kyiv construction company offered officials of the Ministry for Communities and Territories Development heavily discounted flats in return for help securing a land plot in Kyiv for a housing project. The minister at the time, Oleksiy Chernyshov, later became deputy prime minister. He was formally named a suspect in June 2025, accused of seeking improper benefits worth 18.4 million hryvnia through flats priced at 1,000–8,000 hryvnia per square metre against a market price of about 30,000. Other suspects include a former state secretary of the ministry and the developer. NABU completed its investigation in December 2025, sending the case to trial; Chernyshov denies wrongdoing.
inside: Investigators say a developer offered cheap flats to the minister and officials who controlled a Kyiv land plot, so they would hand it to him.
cite: LIGA.net, 31 Dec 2025; Babel, Jun 2025

n: Businessmen allegedly paid Tirana mayor Veliaj's family while he gave permits
rank: Mayor of Tirana
d: Albania's Special Anti-Corruption Structure (SPAK) says four businessmen gave Erion Veliaj, mayor of the capital Tirana, and his wife Ajola Xoxa illegal benefits, directly or through non-governmental organisations, while he approved construction permits and moved city funds to companies controlled by his wife and her associates. Prosecutors say the benefits, including property, luxury travel and payments for fictitious services, came to more than €1 million over four years, part of it used to buy a villa. Veliaj was arrested on 10 February 2025 and kept in custody; in September 2025 prosecutors sent him to trial for corruption and money laundering. He denies the charges and calls the evidence fabricated.
inside: Prosecutors say businessmen paid the Tirana mayor's family through charities and firms while he approved construction permits and moved city money.
cite: OCCRP, 11 Feb 2025; Citizens.al, 10 Sep 2025

n: Contractors paid Muhyiddin's party for Jana Wibawa contracts, trial hears
rank: Prime Minister
d: Malaysian prosecutors say companies seeking contracts under Jana Wibawa, a Covid-era government programme of public works for Bumiputera (Malay and indigenous) contractors, paid money to Bersatu, the party of Prime Minister Muhyiddin Yassin, while he used his office to help them. He faces four counts of abuse of power for allegedly soliciting 232.5 million ringgit for Bersatu from four companies and individuals between March 2020 and August 2021, and three counts of money laundering. At his trial in July 2026 a company founder testified that Nepturis, which won a 141 million ringgit contract to build a police headquarters, gave Bersatu a 1 million ringgit cheque that he regarded as payment for the contract. Muhyiddin denies the charges.
inside: Prosecutors say contractors paid the prime minister's party, and he used his office to make sure their bids for public works succeeded.
cite: The Star, 28 Jul 2026; The Edge, 2023

n: President's secretary's husband took 60% of Argentine state insurance fees
rank: President's office and state insurer Nación Seguros
d: An Argentine federal judge found that insurance broker Héctor Martínez Sosa, a long-time client of Alberto Fernández, profited from state business after Fernández became president, while Martínez Sosa's wife, María Cantero, served as the president's private secretary. In 2021 Fernández signed Decree 823/2021 requiring state bodies to take all their insurance from the state-owned insurer Nación Seguros; brokers earned commissions on those policies, and Martínez Sosa's came to 2,252 million pesos, nearly 60% of all commissions Nación Seguros paid. On 10 July 2025 judge Sebastián Casanello indicted Fernández and 33 others, finding the process was undermined by private dealings that benefited the president's circle; an appeals court confirmed the decision in November 2025.
inside: A broker whose wife was the president's secretary gained a hold on state insurance, and the president's decree channelled most of its commissions to him.
cite: La Gaceta, 10 Jul 2025; Canal 26, 18 Nov 2025

n: Developers and a Seongnam official rigged the Daejang-dong project's profits
rank: Head of planning, Seongnam Urban Development Corporation
d: Private developers led by Kim Man-bae, majority owner of Hwacheon Daeyu Asset Management, worked with Yoo Dong-gyu, head of planning at the Seongnam Urban Development Corporation, a city-owned developer, to set the terms of the Daejang-dong housing project in their own favour. On 31 October 2025 the Seoul Central District Court found that they drafted consortium guidelines ensuring the Hwacheon Daeyu-led consortium was chosen, and fixed the public body's share of profit below half of what was expected, leaving the rest to the private partners. The court put illicit gains at 788.6 billion won and the corporation's losses at 489.5 billion won. Kim and Yoo were each sentenced to eight years for breach of trust. The project was approved while Lee Jae-myung, now president, was Seongnam's mayor.
inside: Developers worked with an official inside a city-owned development company to write bidding rules and profit terms that handed them most of the gains.
cite: Asia Economy, 31 Oct 2025; Korea JoongAng Daily, Feb 2026

n: Aides said Texas's attorney general used his office for developer Nate Paul
rank: Attorney General of Texas
d: Eight senior aides to Ken Paxton, attorney general of Texas and the state's chief lawyer, reported him to the FBI in September 2020, saying he had used his office to do favours for Nate Paul, an Austin property investor and friend, including hiring an outside lawyer to pursue Paul's complaints and giving him confidential law-enforcement files. House investigators said Paul paid for renovations to a house Paxton owned and employed a woman with whom Paxton was having an affair. The Texas House impeached Paxton in May 2023 and the Senate acquitted him in September 2023. On 4 April 2025 a court found his office had broken the whistleblower law by firing the aides and awarded them $6.6 million. Paxton denies wrongdoing.
inside: Aides said a property investor's favours to the attorney general were repaid with the state legal office being used to pursue the investor's own disputes.
cite: KUT / Texas Tribune, 5 Apr 2025

n: 'Construction club' firms allegedly paid Peru's transport ministry for 30 works
rank: Transport ministry and Provías officials
d: Peruvian prosecutors say a cartel of construction companies known as the 'Club de la Construcción' paid about 46 million soles in bribes to senior officials of the Ministry of Transport and Communications and its roads agency Provías, so that 30 public works tendered between 2011 and 2014 went to its members. In February 2025 prosecutor Germán Juárez Atoche filed charges of criminal association, bribery, collusion and money laundering against 29 people and 14 companies, among them former President Ollanta Humala, for whom 13 years are sought, and former transport minister Carlos Paredes. Four firms, Cosapi, ICCGSA, Graña y Montero and Obrainsa, have admitted responsibility, been sentenced and are paying compensation.
inside: Prosecutors say a cartel of builders paid officials inside Peru's transport ministry, who then shared out public road contracts among its members.
cite: La República, 25 Feb 2025

n: Rio Tinto's consultant offered a Guinean official $822,000 over Simandou
rank: Guinean government official
d: Rio Tinto, the Anglo-Australian mining company, hired a French investment banker who was a close friend of a former senior Guinean government official to help it keep its rights to the Simandou iron-ore deposit in Guinea. The US Securities and Exchange Commission found that Rio Tinto, which took him on in July 2011, paid him $10.5 million without a written agreement or any check on his work, and that, acting as its agent, he offered and tried to make an improper payment of at least $822,000 to a Guinean government official. On 6 March 2023 Rio Tinto agreed to pay a $15 million penalty without admitting or denying the findings.
inside: The mining company's paid go-between tried to buy a Guinean official's help so the government would let Rio Tinto keep its mining rights.
cite: US SEC press release 2023-46, 6 Mar 2023

n: Amec Foster Wheeler used agents to bribe oil officials in five countries
rank: Oil and gas sector officials
d: Amec Foster Wheeler Energy, a British engineering company now owned by John Wood Group, used corrupt agents to bribe officials in the oil and gas sectors of Nigeria, Saudi Arabia, Malaysia, India and Brazil to win contracts. The ten offences, committed by the former Foster Wheeler business between 1996 and 2014, were admitted in a deferred prosecution agreement with the Serious Fraud Office, a deal under which prosecution is suspended while the company meets set terms, approved by a London court on 1 July 2021. The firm agreed to pay £103 million in the UK, including compensation for Nigerian victims, as part of a $177 million settlement with US and Brazilian authorities. The Brazilian strand, the UFN-IV design contract at Petrobras, has its own record on this map.
inside: Through paid agents, an engineering company got officials in five countries' oil sectors to award it contracts.
cite: UK Serious Fraud Office, 2 Jul 2021

n: BCG's Lisbon office paid an agent $4.3m to win Angolan state contracts
rank: Ministry of Economy and National Bank of Angola
d: The Boston Consulting Group (BCG), a US management consultancy, paid an agent in Angola to win consulting contracts with the Angolan Ministry of the Economy and the National Bank of Angola, the country's central bank. In a letter in August 2024 the US Justice Department said it would not prosecute BCG for bribing Angolan officials under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, because the firm had reported the conduct itself and corrected its controls; BCG's Lisbon office had given the agent $4.3 million. BCG agreed to give up $14.4 million. A Portuguese association later asked Portugal's prosecutors to investigate.
inside: A consultancy paid an agent to bribe Angolan officials so that the economy ministry and central bank would hire it.
cite: Compliance Week, 30 Aug 2024; JD Supra, Aug 2024

n: Lobbyist allegedly bought draft rulings from Brazil's STJ court offices
rank: Staff in Superior Court of Justice (STJ) offices
d: Brazil's Federal Police say lobbyist Andreson de Oliveira Gonçalves and lawyer Roberto Zampieri paid staff in the offices of judges at the Superior Court of Justice (STJ), Brazil's highest court for non-constitutional cases, to obtain draft rulings and sealed warrants for agribusiness clients in Mato Grosso bankruptcy cases. Investigators say a chief of staff accessed and helped prepare an unsigned draft favourable to a client in 2019, while Zampieri moved about 600,000 reais to firms linked to Andreson and a 6 million reais payment indexed to soybean prices was agreed. The inquiry, Operation Sisamnes, began in November 2024 after messages on the phone of Zampieri, murdered in 2023, came to light. Police say the judges took no part. In May 2026 the prosecutor-general charged the lobbyist and two STJ employees.
inside: Police say a lobbyist paid staff inside judges' offices at a top Brazilian court to obtain draft rulings and secret warrants for his clients.
cite: Poder360, 2025; Diario de Pernambuco, May 2026

n: Supplier syndicates paid officials to drain R2bn from Tembisa Hospital
rank: Gauteng health department and hospital staff
d: South Africa's Special Investigating Unit (SIU), a state body that probes corruption in public institutions, reported in September 2025 that three coordinated syndicates of suppliers drained more than R2 billion meant for health care at Tembisa Hospital, a large public hospital in Gauteng province. The largest is linked to businessman Hangwani Maumela, with at least 41 supplier companies. The SIU identified at least 15 current and former officials, from clerks to senior managers, and corrupt payments of R122.2 million to staff of the Gauteng health department and the hospital, while suppliers used fake quotes and split orders below R500,000 to avoid competitive bidding. Babita Deokaran, a senior provincial finance official who was exposing the payments, was shot dead in August 2021.
inside: Supplier syndicates paid hospital and health-department staff, who approved split orders and fake quotes that sent the hospital's money to their companies.
cite: The Herald / TimesLIVE, 29 Sep 2025

n: Odebrecht's highway bribes allegedly reached Guatemala's minister Sinibaldi
rank: Minister of Communications
d: Guatemalan prosecutors and the former UN-backed anti-impunity commission, CICIG, say the Brazilian construction company Odebrecht paid bribes to win the contract to expand the CA-2 Occidente highway, and that Alejandro Sinibaldi, Minister of Communications under President Otto Pérez Molina, managed at least $17.9 million of the money and kept $9.3 million himself. Sinibaldi, a former presidential candidate of the now-defunct Partido Patriota, was sent for trial in 2023 on charges including passive bribery and money laundering. In March 2024 the Supreme Court granted him a provisional order upholding the dismissal of the case, but in June 2025 the Constitutional Court reportedly revoked it, so he must face trial.
inside: Prosecutors say Odebrecht paid the minister who controlled Guatemala's road contracts, and the company won the highway expansion it was paying for.
cite: La Hora, 4 Jun 2025

n: Sudanese Islamists placed fighters and ex-spies inside Sudan's army at war
rank: Sudanese Armed Forces and allied brigades
d: Sudan's Islamist movement, which ran the state under Omar al-Bashir until 2019, put its fighters and former spies inside the army's war against the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the paramilitary it has fought since April 2023. In June 2023 Reuters cited military sources saying about 6,000 members of Bashir's former intelligence service, men with ties to his Islamist movement, joined the army weeks before the war. On 12 September 2025 the US sanctioned the Islamist Al-Baraa Bin Malik Brigade, saying it had supplied more than 20,000 fighters, trained and armed by Iran's Revolutionary Guards, and that Islamists were obstructing a ceasefire. AFP reported in December 2025 that army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan relies on Islamist backing and had removed only a handful of Islamist-linked officers.
inside: Sudan's Islamist movement placed thousands of its fighters and former intelligence men inside the army, and the US says it uses that weight to block a ceasefire.
cite: Reuters, 28 June 2023 (via ThePrint); US Treasury and State Department, 12 September 2025; AFP, 3 December 2025 (via EWN)

n: Colorado clerk let an election-denial activist copy county voting systems
rank: Mesa County clerk and recorder's office
d: Tina Peters, the elected clerk who ran elections in Mesa County, Colorado, used her office to let an outside activist of the movement claiming the 2020 election was stolen copy the county's voting system. About six months after the 2020 vote, security credentials were made for a local man, Gerald Wood, and used to admit Conan Hayes to a secure software update. Hayes copied data, which was later posted online and shown at a 'cyber symposium' hosted by MyPillow chief Mike Lindell. A jury convicted Peters on seven counts in August 2024 and she was sentenced to nine years. In April 2026 an appeals court upheld the conviction but ordered resentencing; Governor Jared Polis cut her sentence, and she was due for parole on 1 June 2026.
inside: Activists pushing claims of a stolen 2020 election got inside a county election office through its own clerk, who gave them false credentials to copy the voting system.
cite: Colorado Public Radio, 3 October 2024; WFAE/NPR, 15 May 2026

n: Trump lawyer's team let into Georgia county election office to copy machines
rank: Coffee County elections office
d: Operatives working to overturn Donald Trump's 2020 defeat were let into the elections office of Coffee County, Georgia, by local party and election officials, and copied its voting equipment. Security video showed that on 7 January 2021 Cathy Latham, then the county Republican chair and one of 16 Republicans who signed a false certificate of Trump's win, admitted a team from the data firm SullivanStrickler, whose trip Trump lawyer Sidney Powell helped arrange. On 18 January elections director Misty Hampton unlocked the office for Doug Logan of Cyber Ninjas and Jeff Lenberg. In October 2023 Powell pleaded guilty to six misdemeanour counts of conspiring to interfere with election duties. The wider Georgia case against Trump and others was dropped in November 2025.
inside: A campaign to overturn the 2020 result got its operatives inside a county elections office with help from local officials, and copied the voting machines' software and data.
cite: AP via PBS NewsHour, 6 September 2022; Courthouse News, 19 October 2023; WUNC/NPR, 26 November 2025

n: Pennsylvania county let a Trump-allied firm inspect its voting machines
org_label: Election-denial campaign around State Sen. Doug Mastriano
rank: Fulton County board of commissioners
d: County commissioners in Fulton County, Pennsylvania, let an outside company, Wake TSI, inspect and copy parts of the county's Dominion voting equipment weeks after the 2020 election, under pressure from the campaign to dispute the result. The county's election director said the paperwork was 'sent by Senator Mastriano', a state senator who pushed claims of fraud. The state decertified the machines in July 2021 and won a Supreme Court order barring further outside access, but the county then let another firm, Speckin Forensics, examine them. After about two years of litigation a special master ordered the county and its lawyer to pay about $1.04 million to the state and Dominion. The county was still appealing in 2025.
inside: A political campaign disputing the 2020 election got outside examiners into a county's voting machines through sympathetic commissioners, breaking state rules that protect election equipment.
cite: Pennsylvania Capital-Star, 2025

n: Trump allies charged with taking five Michigan vote tabulators from clerks
org_label: Matthew DePerno, Stefanie Lambert and Daire Rendon
rank: Local election clerks' offices in three counties
d: Michigan prosecutors say activists disputing the 2020 election got voting tabulators out of local election offices and broke into them. In August 2023 a special prosecutor, acting on a citizens' grand jury, charged lawyer Stefanie Lambert, Matthew DePerno and Daire Rendon. Michigan's attorney general said they 'orchestrated a coordinated plan to gain access to voting tabulators'. Investigators say five tabulators were taken from three counties to a hotel room, where they were opened and 'tested'. Some defendants say local clerks gave permission; a judge ruled that taking a machine without a court order or the Secretary of State's approval is a felony. Lambert's trial was moved to 2026.
inside: Prosecutors say election-denial activists got voting machines out of local clerks' offices and opened them, using access that the law reserves for election officials.
cite: AP via CBS News Detroit, 3 August 2023; Michigan Advance, 3 November 2025

n: Washington police lieutenant fed Proud Boys leader inside information
rank: Lieutenant, Metropolitan Police Department
d: Shane Lamond, a lieutenant in Washington DC's Metropolitan Police Department, passed confidential police information to Enrique Tarrio, then leader of the Proud Boys, a far-right street group. Lamond told Tarrio about the department's investigation into the burning of a church's Black Lives Matter banner at a 2020 rally, including that a warrant had been issued for his arrest. In December 2024 a judge convicted Lamond of obstruction of justice and three counts of lying to investigators about the contacts. On 6 June 2025 he was sentenced to 18 months in prison. President Trump commuted Tarrio's separate 22-year prison sentence in 2025.
inside: A far-right group's leader had a police lieutenant inside the capital's force who warned him about the investigation and arrest warrant targeting him.
cite: CNN via KRDO, 6 June 2025

n: Neo-Nazi O9A member joined US Army and passed his unit's plans for an attack
rank: Private, 173rd Airborne Brigade
d: Ethan Melzer joined the US Army around 2018 in what US prosecutors called an 'insight role' for the Order of Nine Angles (O9A), a neo-Nazi and Satanist network that tells members to infiltrate institutions such as the military. Deployed to Italy with the 173rd Airborne Brigade in 2019, in May 2020 he sent O9A contacts details of his unit's coming deployment to Turkey, including troop movements, locations, weapons and security, so they could plan a mass-casualty 'jihadi attack' on it. He pleaded guilty on 24 June 2022 to attempting to murder US service members, supporting terrorists and passing national defence information, and was sentenced to 45 years on 3 March 2023.
inside: An extremist network that tells followers to infiltrate the military had a member enlist, who then sent it his own unit's deployment secrets to plan an attack.
cite: US Department of Justice, 3 March 2023

n: Settlers serving in Israel's West Bank defence units accused of attacks
rank: IDF regional defence (Hagmar) reserve units
d: After the 7 October 2023 attack, thousands of Israeli settlers called up as reservists were placed in the army's West Bank regional defence units, known as Hagmar, which are staffed largely by residents of the settlements they guard. Rights groups and Palestinian residents say settlers in uniform have used army authority and weapons against Palestinian villagers. The army says it issued about 7,500 weapons to Hagmar personnel by the end of 2024 and that dozens have been dismissed for violations, including attacks on Palestinians. Cases reported in 2025–26 include a reservist who opened fire and wounded two Palestinians at Deir Jarir. The army's chief of staff called such attacks unacceptable in March 2026, and the army has cut the number of active Hagmar personnel.
inside: Rights groups say settlers drafted into army units guarding their own areas used military weapons and authority to push their movement's aims against Palestinian villagers.
cite: Times of Israel, 9 June 2026

n: Jemaah Islamiyah leader sat on Indonesia's top clerical fatwa commission
rank: Fatwa commission, Indonesian Ulema Council (MUI); party leadership
d: Indonesian police say Jemaah Islamiyah (JI), the network behind the 2002 Bali bombings, had its leaders inside mainstream bodies. On 16 November 2021 counter-terrorism police arrested Ahmad Zain an-Najah, a member of the 75-strong fatwa commission of the Indonesian Ulema Council (MUI), the state-recognised body that issues religious rulings. Police said he sat on JI's advisory council and chaired the sharia board of a charity raising money for JI. They also arrested Farid Okbah, chairman of a small Islamic party, as another JI adviser. MUI suspended an-Najah. The counter-terrorism agency said JI had tried for over a decade to infiltrate the military, police and ministries, and in 2022 it said JI suspects were joining political parties.
inside: Police say a banned militant network placed its own advisers on Indonesia's state-recognised fatwa council and at the head of a political party, while raising money for it.
cite: BenarNews, 17 November 2021 and February 2022; Jakarta Post, 17 November 2021

n: Leaked files say Erdogan-linked foundation TUGVA placed members in state posts
rank: Army, police, Justice Ministry and judiciary recruitment
d: Documents published on 12 October 2021 by journalist Metin Cihan suggest that TÜGVA, a conservative religious youth foundation whose advisory council includes President Erdoğan's son Bilal, worked to place its members in state jobs. The files included lists of candidates for the armed forces, police, Justice Ministry and judicial bodies, marked as officer, non-commissioned officer and special-operations candidates with exam and interview dates, and references from TÜGVA executives and a former ruling-party MP. They also listed hundreds of public buildings allocated to the foundation. TÜGVA said the papers were forged. A former executive, Ramazan Aydoğdu, was later sentenced to two years for accessing and manipulating the documents and passing them on; he told the court TÜGVA had close links to intelligence and police.
inside: Leaked papers, which the foundation calls forged, suggest a religious foundation close to the president's family put its members forward for army, police and judicial posts.
cite: Bianet, 13 October 2021; Turkish Minute, 4 September 2023

n: Iran-aligned Babylon militia took Iraq's Christian seats and Nineveh council
rank: Christian quota seats; Nineveh Provincial Council
