d: The Babylon Movement, political arm of the 50th Brigade of Iraq's Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF, the state-funded umbrella for mostly Shia militias), used seats reserved for Christians to gain power in Nineveh province. Its leader Rayan al-Kildani was sanctioned by the US in 2019 over abuses including extortion and land seizure. Because anyone may vote for the quota seats, the movement mobilised mostly Shia Arab voters and in the December 2023 provincial elections took all four Christian seats, in Baghdad, Nineveh, Kirkuk and, after a rival's disqualification, Basra. On 2 July 2024 the Nineveh council, where it controls 16 of 29 seats, voted to remove 15 mayors and directors in Christian and Yazidi towns; opponents went to the federal court.
inside: An Iran-aligned militia's party captured council seats reserved for Christians using other voters, then used its council majority to replace local Christian and Yazidi officials.
cite: Washington Institute, 2 January 2024; Wilson Center, 19 August 2024

n: Kataib Hezbollah's state brigades stormed a Baghdad office to keep their man
rank: PMF 45th and 46th Brigades; Baghdad agriculture directorate
d: Kataib Hezbollah, an Iran-backed militia whose fighters serve in state-paid brigades of Iraq's Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), used those units to fight over control of a government office. On 27 July 2025 gunmen from the PMF's 45th and 46th Brigades raided the agriculture directorate in Baghdad's Karkh district after its director was replaced, and clashed with federal police; three people were killed. A government inquiry found that the former director, linked to forged contracts to seize farmland, had called in Kataib Hezbollah members to stop his successor taking office. Prime Minister Mohammed Shia al-Sudani removed both brigade commanders, and in November 2025 a court sentenced the former director to death.
inside: An Iran-backed militia's fighters, serving inside Iraq's state security forces, used those state units to keep their ally in charge of a government office.
cite: AP via Arab News, 10 August 2025; 964 Media, 25 November 2025

n: China's loans bought nine Taiwanese officers' secrets and pledges
rank: Army, navy, air force and coast guard officers up to major
d: Chinese intelligence recruited a Taiwanese man surnamed Chen through social media in September 2024 and paid him to run a bank account used for bribes and loans to Taiwanese military officers in financial trouble, prosecutors in Kaohsiung's Ciaotou district said in April 2026. They indicted nine serving and former officers of the army, navy, air force and coast guard, up to the rank of major, and one accomplice. Prosecutors say the officers sent phone videos of military operations and photos of documents, some classified, for money, and that borrowers were pressured to film videos 'switching allegiance' to China. It is Taiwan's first national security trial with citizen judges.
inside: Prosecutors say Chinese intelligence used loans and bribes to turn indebted officers inside Taiwan's armed forces and coast guard into paid sources.
cite: Taipei Times, 15 Apr 2026

n: FirstEnergy paid $4.3m to the man who became Ohio's utility regulator
rank: Chair, Public Utilities Commission of Ohio
d: FirstEnergy, a large Ohio electricity company, paid more than $4.3 million to Sam Randazzo, according to a federal indictment, and he went on to chair the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio (PUCO), the state body that regulates utilities and sets what customers pay. Prosecutors say the money passed through a consulting firm he controlled, in return for favourable actions in PUCO cases, including wording he put into a commission order to deal with a FirstEnergy problem expected in 2024. He led the commission from April 2019 and resigned in November 2020, days after the FBI searched his home. Indicted on 11 counts in December 2023, he died before trial. The case belongs to the same scandal as FirstEnergy's secret $60 million funding of Ohio's House Speaker.
inside: Prosecutors say FirstEnergy's money reached the head of Ohio's utility regulator, who then wrote rulings that served the company he was meant to oversee.
cite: WVXU / Ohio Public Radio, 4 Dec 2023; News 5 Cleveland, 2024

n: Somalia's spy agency arrests ten al-Shabaab agents inside government bodies
rank: Somali government agencies
d: Al-Shabaab, the al-Qaeda-linked group fighting Somalia's government, had informants working inside state agencies, according to the government's own intelligence service. In August 2023 the National Intelligence and Security Agency (NISA) said its agents had arrested ten 'spies for al-Shabaab within government agencies' in Mogadishu, accused of leaking information, and named two more government employees it was hunting. The arrests followed an attack on an army training centre in which at least 25 trainees were killed; a preliminary inquiry suggested an insider had given the militants information or access. Somali opposition parties had earlier urged the president to purge NISA itself of al-Shabaab operatives.
inside: An armed group placed informants on the government's own payroll, who passed it information from inside state agencies; one inquiry suggested an insider helped an attack.
cite: Garowe Online, 5 August 2023; Garowe Online, 3 May 2020

n: Retired colonel's eight-year ring recruited serving Taiwan air force officers
rank: Air force lieutenant colonel and majors
d: Chinese intelligence officers recruited Liu Sheng-shu, a retired Taiwanese air force colonel working for a Taiwanese firm in China, and he built a spy network inside Taiwan's forces. He ran it for eight years, took NT$16.7 million from China through a shell company, and paid NT$100,000 to NT$200,000 per classified document. Recruits included Lieutenant Colonel Sun Wei and his wife, Major Liu Yun-ya, who was still serving when the investigation began. In June 2024 the Supreme Court upheld Liu's 20-year term, the heaviest in recent years for an officer, though it ordered some charges against the couple re-examined. One major was acquitted.
cite: Taipei Times, 15 June 2024; Taipei Times, 29 January 2025
inside: Chinese intelligence recruited a retired colonel, who paid serving air force officers for classified documents from their own units, so Taiwan's secrets went to Beijing.

n: Chinese officials recruited a deputy news chief at Taiwan's military news agency
who: PLA Eastern Theater Command officials in Xiamen
rank: Deputy news-desk chief, Military News Agency
d: Officials in Xiamen linked to China's People's Liberation Army (PLA) recruited Lieutenant Colonel Kung Fan-chia, deputy chief of the news desk at Taiwan's Military News Agency, a state media outlet run by the defence ministry. He took US$6,000 in 2006 and US$5,700 in 2008 to arrange trips where Chinese officials could host serving and retired personnel. He retired in 2012 and received 60,000 yuan between 2014 and 2016. He kept trying until 2020, but the High Court said his recruiting failed. He pleaded guilty and returned the money. In 2026 the Supreme Court made final a sentence of five years and four months.
cite: Taipei Times, 8 April 2026; Taipei Times, 19 July 2024; Taiwan News, 2025 (High Court ruling)
inside: PLA-linked officials paid a serving officer at the defence ministry's Military News Agency to bring fellow officers to Chinese hosts, aiming to build a spy network in Taiwan's forces.

n: Kinmen TV correspondent recruited a Taiwanese colonel for China on a monthly fee
rank: Kinmen Garrison Battalion commander (former)
d: Shao Wei-chiang, a retired army lieutenant who was a television correspondent on Kinmen, the Taiwanese island beside China's coast, worked for China for about 20 years and recruited Taiwanese officers on its behalf, a court found. One recruit was Colonel Hsiang Te-en, a former commander of the Kinmen Garrison Battalion, who received NT$40,000 a month, NT$560,000 in all, for military information. He signed a pledge to surrender and was photographed holding a document promising help to China in an invasion. Hsiang was jailed for seven and a half years in February 2023. In May 2023 Shao got 15 years, subject to appeal. He failed with at least three other colonels.
cite: Taipei Times, 6 May 2023; Central News Agency, 24 February 2023
inside: China used a local correspondent to pay an army colonel for military information and for a signed pledge to help China if it invaded Taiwan.

n: Kao An-kuo, retired Taiwan general, jailed over armed group for China
rank: Army lieutenant general (retired)
d: Chinese intelligence recruited Kao An-kuo, a retired Taiwanese army lieutenant general, in 2019, prosecutors said, and he and others sought active-duty and retired personnel for a network serving China. The High Court found he tried to build an armed group, the 'Republic of China Taiwan Military Government', to attack government bodies and help invading Chinese forces. In October 2025 it gave him seven and a half years, making him Taiwan's highest-ranking officer convicted of espionage. His partner Liu Yi-chen got more than six years, with reports differing on the months, and spokesman Hou Shao-kang six. Kao denied all charges, and Taiwan News reported that appeals were still possible.
cite: Taipei Times, 23 October 2025; ANI via The Tribune, January 2025; UDN, October 2025; Taiwan News, October 2025
inside: Chinese intelligence recruited a retired general who, a court found, sought serving and former soldiers for a group meant to help Chinese forces during an invasion of Taiwan.

n: PLA officers in Bali recruited an Air Force Academy department head with a bonus
rank: Department director, Air Force Academy
d: Three officers of China's People's Liberation Army, attached to a Guangdong government office in Bali, Indonesia, recruited Chang Ming-che, a former colonel and department director at Taiwan's Air Force Academy, in 2019. He received a US$10,000 signing bonus and NT$1.34 million up to 2023, with some monthly payments reaching NT$65,000, for intelligence and for recruiting others. A businessman, Chung Shun-he, arranged the meeting and died during the case. In September 2025 the High Court gave Chang 16 years in total. In January 2026 the Supreme Court made an 11-year term final and sent two other charges back for retrial. An active-duty officer, Yeh, was acquitted.
cite: Taipei Times, 31 January 2026; Central News Agency via GlobalSecurity, January 2026
inside: Chinese army officers paid a Taiwanese colonel from the air force academy a signing bonus and regular fees to supply intelligence and recruit other officers for China.

n: Hong Kong front man used retired officers to reach Taiwan's air commanders
rank: Air force major general and lieutenant colonel (retired)
d: A Hong Kong man surnamed Tse, posing as a businessman, used two retired Taiwanese air force officers to reach serving and former senior officers. Prosecutors said he worked for a front set up by the Central Military Commission, China's top military body. Lieutenant Colonel Wei Hsien-yi and former Major General Chien Yao-tung took gifts and paid trips to China and introduced him to at least five high-ranking officers, among them Chang Che-ping, later deputy defence minister. The rulings concerned Wei and Chien, not those they introduced. Tse stopped visiting in 2019. In June 2024 the Supreme Court upheld suspended sentences of two years for Wei and 16 months for Chien, plus fines.
cite: Taipei Times, 22 June 2024; Central News Agency via GlobalSecurity, 21 June 2024
inside: A Chinese military front paid retired officers with gifts and trips to open doors to serving and former senior officers, giving it a route towards the top of Taiwan's air force.

n: Ex-major paid a Taiwan air force controller for missile and air-defence data
rank: Air force air intercept controller
d: Chinese intelligence officers recruited Shih Chun-cheng, a former Taiwanese air force major, to run a ring. He persuaded Hsu Chan-cheng, a serving air intercept controller, to supply information from 2021 to August 2024, falsely claiming links to the US forces. Hsu leaked details on air-launched Hsiung Feng III anti-ship missiles and on deployments answering Chinese incursions into Taiwan's air defence identification zone. Shih took NT$2.1 million from his Chinese contacts and gave Hsu NT$200,000. In August 2025 the Supreme Court upheld a 26-month term for Shih and sent a 10-month term back for retrial. The defence minister said the missile data was not combat-related.
cite: Central News Agency via GlobalSecurity, 21 August 2025
inside: Chinese intelligence recruited a former major, who paid a serving air controller for details of how Taiwan's air force responds to Chinese incursions.

n: Loan shark working for a Chinese handler bought Taiwan air force secrets
rank: Air force captain and staff sergeants
d: Prosecutors said a loan shark surnamed Huang, acting under a Chinese intelligence handler, ran an illegal lending business in Taiwan from 2019 as a front to reach active-duty soldiers in urgent need of money. He advertised online, paid gambling debts or gave bonuses in return for classified material, including documents on the Han Kuang, Taiwan's annual military exercises. On 15 July 2026 the High Court in Kaohsiung sentenced an air force captain to eight and a half years, one staff sergeant to eight years and another to two. Huang's sister, a bank employee, was convicted of laundering. Huang is a fugitive, and the rulings can be appealed.
cite: Taipei Times, 16 July 2026
inside: A money lender run by a Chinese handler used soldiers' debts to buy classified documents from serving air force personnel, so exercise documents could reach Chinese intelligence.

n: Retired airman accused of passing Taiwan tank and exercise data to China
rank: Army serviceman; retired officers
d: Prosecutors say a retired Taiwanese air force member surnamed Chen took instructions and money from late 2020 from an intelligence agency under a provincial committee of China's Communist Party, and tried to build an organisation for China. The indictment, announced on 1 October 2026 by the High Prosecutors' Kaohsiung branch, alleges that a serving soldier surnamed Lu gave him confidential tank specifications and details of the Han Kuang, Taiwan's annual military exercises. It also alleges that a retired officer surnamed Mao attended a 2024 banquet with Chinese intelligence officials in Zhuhai and agreed to approach serving personnel. No verdict has been given.
cite: Central News Agency, 1 October 2026; Taiwan News, 2 October 2026
inside: Prosecutors say a Chinese Communist Party intelligence body funded a retired airman, who got confidential tank and exercise details from a serving soldier in Taiwan's army.

n: Ex-soldier and army officer accused of leaking artillery course files to China
rank: Army lieutenant, 21st Artillery Command veteran
d: Taipei prosecutors allege that a Chinese intelligence operative, 'Wang', used a debt-ridden former soldier, Chen Tai-yin, to reach a serving officer. Chen introduced Lee Chun-ta, once his colleague at the Army's 21st Artillery Command and now a lieutenant, to Wang over WeChat in March 2024. Lee reportedly declined an offer of twice his monthly salary. Prosecutors say that on 7 April 2024 the two met in a Beitou car park, where Chen photographed unreleased classified course materials and sent them to Wang, and that Chen later received 2,500 USDT, a cryptocurrency. Both were indicted on 12 May 2026 under the National Security and Anti-Corruption Acts, and no verdict has been reported.
cite: Central News Agency, 12 May 2026
inside: Prosecutors say a Chinese operative used a former soldier in debt to obtain classified training material from a serving army officer who had access to it.

n: Fake reporter from China's armed police bought Taiwan missile unit's manuals
rank: Navy Hai Feng missile group serviceman
d: An intelligence officer of China's People's Armed Police, posing as a Hong Kong reporter for The Epoch Times, recruited a member of the Taiwanese navy's Hai Feng group, which operates shore-based anti-ship missiles. She met a discharged navy man, Lin, on a dating app in 2023, and he introduced a serving colleague, Tsai. Tsai got NT$8,000 for details of himself and his unit, then NT$30,000 for photos of Hsiung Feng II launcher manuals. Prosecutors said the manuals were not classified but still harmed national security. In August 2026 the Taichung court gave Tsai two years and seven months, subject to appeal. Lin is investigated separately.
cite: Central News Agency, 7 August 2026; Taiwan News, 7 August 2026 and 12 October 2025
inside: An undercover Chinese intelligence officer paid a serving Taiwanese missile-unit member for unit details and launcher manuals, using a former colleague as the go-between.

n: CTi reporter accused of paying Taiwanese soldiers for secrets and pledges
rank: Six active and retired service members
d: Prosecutors say Lin Chen-you, a host and reporter at Taiwan's CTi News, passed bribes from an agent surnamed Huang to active and retired soldiers in return for classified information and videos saying they would surrender to China's army. Six service members were indicted with him on 6 May 2026 by the Ciaotou prosecutors in Kaohsiung, who want 12 years for Lin. They say he received 4,325 Tether, a cryptocurrency, for videos attacking a recall campaign. A Marine Corps officer, Chen, allegedly took NT$210,000 to film a pledge. Reports citing sources say leaked material covered the Han Kuang military exercises and troop deployments. No verdict has been given.
cite: Taipei Times, 7 May 2026; Taipei Times editorial, 26 January 2026; Herald Business, 22 June 2026
inside: Prosecutors allege a foreign agent's money went through a television reporter to serving and retired soldiers, who supplied classified information and filmed pledges to surrender to China.

n: Taiwan vice admiral Ko Cheng-sheng agreed to work with China's United Front
rank: Deputy commander, naval fleet
d: Chinese authorities began courting Ko Cheng-sheng, deputy commander of Taiwan's naval fleet, in 1998, and he agreed to cooperate with the United Front Work Department, the Communist Party body that cultivates people outside the party. A friend, businessman Shen Ping-kang, arranged all-expenses-paid trips for Ko and his family until 2007. Ko passed classified information and tried to recruit officers under his command into an internal network. A navy source said the Gu An plan for defending Taiwan could have been compromised, though other officers said damage was limited. In 2014 a court gave Ko 14 months and Shen 12; the Supreme Court rejected Ko's appeal in March 2015.
cite: Taipei Times, 3 October 2014; Central News Agency, 16 March 2015
inside: China's United Front won over a navy vice admiral with paid trips, and he passed on classified information and tried to enlist officers serving under him.

n: Ex-servicemen used paid tours to recruit Taiwanese officers for China
rank: Navy lieutenant; missile command centre; meteorology office commander
d: Two former Taiwanese servicemen recruited officers for China by arranging overseas tours paid for by Chinese officials, a Kaohsiung court found. Lu Chun-chun, who retired from the military's missile command centre in 2005, drew in navy lieutenant Chien Ching-kuo, who left the service in 2009 and received a trip and cash gifts that year. On the tours, other officers were approached to become spies, and one former commander at the navy's meteorology and oceanography office agreed to cooperate. On 21 February 2014 each man got ten months, Lu's suspended for three years. Chien had a separate 2013 conviction for leaking warship deployments and missions.
cite: AFP via Yahoo News, 21 February 2014
inside: Chinese officials paid for tours that two former servicemen used to approach Taiwanese officers, and one former navy commander agreed to cooperate with China.

n: PLA officer Zhen Xiaojiang recruited Taiwan air force officers for radar secrets
rank: Air force officers; retired major general
d: Zhen Xiaojiang, a retired captain in China's People's Liberation Army working in intelligence, built a ring inside Taiwan's military after gaining Hong Kong residency. Prosecutors indicted him in January 2015 with five Taiwanese defendants, including retired Major General Hsu Nai-chuan, later a Kinmen county official. Free trips and cash reached serving and former air force officers, and China sought data on Mirage 2000 fighters and the Leshan long-range radar. Reports put payments at about US$9,400, and Zhen offered up to US$10,000 for top-secret material. In 2024 a retrial gave former Lieutenant Colonel Lou Wen-ching 17 years, while former Colonel Ko Chi-hsien's acquittal was upheld. A third retrial in November 2025 cut Lou's term to 12 years.
cite: Defense News, 24 January 2015; Taipei Times, 1 October 2024 and 28 November 2025; Liberty Times, 10 April 2015
inside: A Chinese military intelligence officer paid serving and retired Taiwanese air force officers with money and trips for classified information on fighter jets and a key radar.

n: Chinese ex-student Zhou Hongxu offered Taiwan foreign ministry official cash
rank: Junior official, Ministry of Foreign Affairs
d: Zhou Hongxu, a former Chinese student in Taiwan, tried to recruit a junior official at Taiwan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Li Bin, a Shanghai liaison officer for a group the Communist Party runs, told him to befriend Taiwanese politicians and people in the military, police, intelligence and foreign affairs. Zhou offered the official at least US$10,000 a quarter for classified information and suggested expenses-paid trips to Japan and other countries to meet Chinese officials. The official reported him, and he was detained in March 2017. Zhou confessed in detention but later told the High Court the confession was coerced. A Taipei court gave him 14 months in September 2017, reportedly a lighter term because he obtained nothing, and the Supreme Court upheld it in 2019.
cite: Central News Agency via GlobalSecurity, 6 July and 15 September 2017; Taipei Times, 15 March 2019; Asia Times, 15 December 2017
inside: A Chinese liaison officer directed a former student to buy a foreign ministry insider for classified material; the attempt failed because the official reported it.

n: Brothers used pawn shops to recruit debt-ridden Taiwanese officers for China
rank: Eight serving army, navy, air force and coast guard officers
d: Prosecutors in Tainan charged 23 people on 18 September 2024 over a ring they say two brothers surnamed Hsu ran for Chinese intelligence. They included eight serving officers from the army, navy, air force and coast guard, most of low rank. Prosecutors say the brothers met two Chinese agents in Macau and Zhuhai from 2021, and used advertisements and pawn shop owners to find officers in financial trouble, promising to resolve their debts. China reportedly paid NT$5 million over more than two years, with NT$2,000 to NT$30,000 per new recruit. Prosecutors seized nine secret military documents. The report recorded no verdict.
cite: Taiwan News, 18 September 2024
inside: Prosecutors say Chinese agents paid two brothers a fee per recruit to find indebted officers across Taiwan's armed services and coast guard and obtain sensitive information.

n: Father and son recruited Taiwanese missile officers for Han Kuang secrets
rank: Air defence and missile unit officers
d: A father and son surnamed Huang, who met Chinese intelligence officials in 2015 while doing business in Xiamen, recruited two serving officers in Taiwanese air defence and missile units, Yeh and Su. Both recruits signed pledges of allegiance and went abroad to meet Chinese officials. They passed eight secret documents about the Han Kuang, Taiwan's annual military exercises, in person or by phone messages. The Huangs received NT$1.71 million, Yeh NT$210,000 and Su NT$100,000. On 29 August 2024 the Supreme Court upheld eight-year terms for both Huangs. Reports differ on the officers: Taiwan News says their terms were overturned for a new trial, while the Taipei Times says terms of seven and six years were upheld as final.
cite: Taiwan News, 30 August 2024; Taipei Times, 31 August 2024
inside: Chinese intelligence paid two businessmen, who recruited serving missile-unit officers to sign allegiance pledges and hand over secret documents on Taiwan's main military exercises.

n: Diabolo teacher jailed for paying serving Taiwanese personnel for China
rank: Active-duty military and coast guard personnel
d: Taiwan's courts convicted Lu Chi-hsien, a well-known instructor of the diabolo, a juggling toy, of building a spy organisation for China among military and coast guard personnel. Prosecutors said he was recruited during a 2020 trip to China, received NT$5.7 million and used his diabolo association as cover. They said that from 2022 he paid seven active-duty officers for education materials, training lectures, plans and meeting reports, reaching personnel through online games, banquets, loan sharks and cash rewards. Taipei District Court gave him ten and a half years on 30 June 2025. In June 2026 the Supreme Court made this final, reporting that twelve people agreed to join and hand over documents and twelve refused. Lu admitted the offences.
cite: Taiwan News, 19 November 2023; CNA via GlobalSecurity, 30 June 2025; United Daily News, 26 and 27 June 2026
inside: Courts found China funded a sports instructor who used his association as cover to obtain military documents from serving personnel.

n: Reuters: CIA recruited an aide to a Chinese state security vice-minister
rank: Aide to a vice-minister of State Security
d: An aide to a vice-minister in China's Ministry of State Security, the body running its domestic and overseas intelligence, was arrested on suspicion of spying for the US, Reuters reported on 1 June 2012, citing three anonymous sources. One source said the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) had recruited him. The aide, who was not named, allegedly supplied political, economic and strategic intelligence for hundreds of thousands of US dollars. He was reportedly detained between January and March 2012, and the vice-minister was suspended and questioned. The sources said it could be China's worst known intelligence breach in two decades. Neither government confirmed the case, and the sources said it was unrelated to the Bo Xilai scandal.
cite: Reuters via The Guardian, 1 June 2012
inside: Reuters sources said the CIA paid a man inside a vice-minister's office at China's spy ministry to pass it political, economic and strategic intelligence.

n: NYT: CIA's sources deep in China's bureaucracy were killed or jailed, 2010-2012
rank: Disaffected insiders in the Chinese bureaucracy
d: The US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) had recruited disaffected insiders deep in China's bureaucracy, some upset by corruption, according to a New York Times report of May 2017 citing ten current and former US officials. It said China dismantled this network from 2010, killing at least a dozen sources between late 2010 and the end of 2012. Two former senior officials put those killed or jailed at 18 to 20. One source was reportedly shot in front of colleagues in a government building's courtyard. Officials were unsure whether a CIA mole or a hacked communication system was responsible. The CIA declined to comment.
cite: New York Times via Al Jazeera, 21 May 2017
inside: US officials told reporters the CIA had recruited sources deep inside China's bureaucracy, who gave it inside information until Beijing found and removed them.

n: China says foreign agency recruited secret-comms researcher Huang Yu; executed
rank: Researcher, top-secret communication system
d: China's Ministry of State Security says a foreign spy agency, which it did not name, recruited Huang Yu, a researcher on a top-secret communication system project. In a documentary aired by state broadcaster CCTV in April 2024, the ministry said he sold core secrets, including military codes, sent them through the agency's website, trained in Hong Kong and Bangkok, and had his wife copy confidential material. It said he was convicted in 2015 and executed in May 2016. The reports present this as the ministry's account, with no independent confirmation.
cite: South China Morning Post, 16 April 2024; Bangkok Post, April 2024
inside: China's security ministry says a foreign spy agency recruited a researcher on a secret communications project and trained him to sell it military codes.

n: China says foreign spies turned former state agency staffer Zhang; sentenced to death
rank: Core confidential staff, state agency (former)
d: China's Ministry of State Security said on 6 November 2024 that a foreign intelligence agency recruited a former employee of a state agency, surnamed Zhang, whom it called 'core confidential personnel'. It said a foreign spy surnamed Li lured him abroad with promises of 'experiencing exotic customs', made him sign a cooperation agreement and seized his USB work drive and belongings. The ministry said Zhang could not resist the temptation of money and leaked a large number of state secrets. He was sentenced to death. A colleague, Zhu, got six years for helping him. The ministry named neither the agency nor the country, gave no sum, and no independent confirmation was reported.
cite: Al Jazeera, 6 November 2024; AFP, 6 November 2024
inside: China's security ministry says a foreign service pressured a former holder of state secrets into a signed agreement and that, tempted by money, he leaked secrets; a colleague also helped.

n: China says a foreign spy steered Shanghai graduate Dong into a civil-service job
rank: Civil servant, Shanghai
d: Chinese national security authorities said in November 2023 that a foreigner, who was in fact a spy, cultivated a man surnamed Dong, born in the 1990s, who joined a Shanghai research institute after graduating in 2019. They said Dong was offered payments, copied and photographed documents, and became a civil servant under the spy's guidance, which gave him access to more sensitive internal information. The offence was uncovered in August 2022, and he got four years and nine months in November 2022. The account came from the authorities through Shanghai Media Group and Global Times. It named no foreign service, and no independent confirmation was reported.
cite: Global Times via GlobalSecurity, 8 November 2023
inside: Chinese authorities say a foreign spy offered a young researcher payments and guided him into the civil service to reach more sensitive documents.

n: WSJ: China's top general Zhang Youxia accused of passing nuclear data to the US
rank: Vice chair, Central Military Commission
d: The Wall Street Journal reported in January 2026 that Zhang Youxia, senior vice chair of China's Central Military Commission, the body that commands its armed forces, was accused at a briefing of top officers of sharing technical data on China's nuclear weapons with Washington. It cited people familiar with the briefing, who gave no further detail, and said Gu Jun, a former state nuclear company head under investigation, supplied some evidence. In September 2026 the Communist Party expelled Zhang and sent his case to military prosecutors, citing factions, money for promotions and gifts. The report of that statement mentions neither nuclear data nor the US. The allegation is unproven.
cite: Wall Street Journal via The Times of Israel, 26 January 2026; The Star, 23 September 2026
inside: Unnamed sources allege China's most senior general secretly gave Washington nuclear weapons data from inside its top military body; the party's published case against him, as reported, does not mention this.

n: Two heads of a Korean secret-operations team suspected of selling documents to foreign agents
rank: Secret operations team chiefs, Defense Intelligence Command
d: Seoul prosecutors in June 2018 held two former officers of South Korea's Defense Intelligence Command, the military spy agency, on suspicion of selling secrets to foreign agents. Hwang led its secret operations team from 2013 until April 2018, and Hong was his predecessor. Hwang allegedly photographed classified material with his phone and sold it to Hong, and about 100 military secrets were allegedly sold on for tens of millions of won to agents of two unnamed countries. One allegedly received details of Korean agents working there. A suspected recipient, a diplomat in Korea, had returned home. The National Intelligence Service tipped off the military in April, which waited a month to investigate.
cite: Korea JoongAng Daily, 5 June 2018
inside: Prosecutors suspected foreign agents paid for classified documents taken from inside South Korea's military spy agency by the officers running its secret operations team.

n: South Korean navy officer at Defense Security Command held for spying for China
rank: Lieutenant commander, Defense Security Command
d: A South Korean navy lieutenant commander assigned to the Defense Security Command, the military's own counter-espionage and security body, was arrested on suspicion of giving classified information to a suspected Chinese agent, the defence ministry announced in July 2015. He allegedly passed military materials to a university student in China whom authorities suspected of being a spy, and received money in return, though no sum was reported. Military prosecutors indicted him on 10 July 2015. No foreign service or handler was named. The reports recorded no verdict. AFP noted that two other officials of the command had been jailed the month before for passing classified information to arms dealers.
cite: AFP via Yahoo, 3 July 2015; Korea Times, 10 July 2015
inside: The defence ministry suspected a Chinese agent was paying an officer inside the military's own security command for classified information and materials.

n: South Korean two-star general charged with leaking secrets that reached North Korea
rank: Two-star army general
d: South Korean prosecutors and the Defense Security Command were reported in June 2010 to be investigating a two-star army general named only as Kim, suspected of passing classified information on military management and operations to North Korea between 2005 and 2007. The report said a former South Korean agent who had run missions against the North in the 1990s was recruited by Pyongyang and won the general over. Prosecutors and the National Intelligence Service arrested that former agent and a former defence-firm executive. The defence ministry later said Kim had been detained and charged with leaking secrets, including the contingency war plan, but not spying, because he did not know they would reach the North. No verdict was found.
cite: Aju Business Daily, 4 June 2010; Zee News, 2010 (undated page, defence ministry statement)
inside: Prosecutors suspected North Korea used a former South Korean agent it had recruited to obtain military secrets from a two-star general.

n: Japan's ex-Eastern Army chief suspected of getting manual for a GRU officer
rank: Commander, Ground Self-Defense Force Eastern Army (former)
d: A former Russian military attaché in Tokyo, Sergey Kovalev, believed to be an officer of the GRU, Russia's military intelligence service, is suspected of asking Kazushige Izumi to obtain a restricted booklet of Japan's Ground Self-Defense Force, the country's army. Izumi, a former commander of its Eastern Army, admitted asking subordinates in May 2013 for the booklet, which described how divisions and brigades operate. In December 2015 police referred the case to prosecutors, along with five current and former officers. No payment was confirmed. Kovalev had returned to Russia, and Moscow did not respond to a request to summon him.
cite: The Japan Times, 4 December 2015
inside: Police suspected a Russian military intelligence officer used a former Japanese army commander to get restricted army material from serving officers, who were bound to keep it confidential.

n: TIGO bribed Guatemalan Congress members, drug cash alleged
rank: members of Congress
d: TIGO Guatemala, a mobile phone company owned by Luxembourg-based Millicom, paid monthly cash bribes to Guatemalan members of Congress from 2012 to 2018, and they backed laws that helped the company. US prosecutors say a then-Guatemalan shareholder and senior staff ran the scheme. A law-firm account of the case says cash reached the offices by helicopter and in duffel bags, and that some came from a banker laundering a drug trafficker's money. In November 2025 TIGO paid over $118 million under a deferred prosecution agreement, a deal that holds off charges if the company meets its terms for two years. No bribed official has been named.
inside: A phone company paid Guatemalan legislators monthly, some of it reportedly laundered drug money, so that Congress passed laws serving the company rather than the public.
cite: US Justice Department, 12 December 2025; Cleary Gottlieb client memo, 2025

n: Miami telecoms firms bribed Haiti's state phone company directors
org_label: Terra Telecommunications and other Miami-based carriers
rank: directors, Haiti Teleco
d: Miami telephone companies paid bribes to directors of Haiti Teleco, the state-owned company that was Haiti's only landline provider, to get cheaper rates and keep their connection to Haiti. Terra Telecommunications passed more than $890,000 through shell companies between 2001 and 2005, recorded as consulting. Director Robert Antoine admitted taking over $1 million and got four years; his successor Jean Rene Duperval got nine in 2012. Former director general Patrick Joseph pleaded guilty and agreed to testify that bribes were shared with other senior officials. His father was then shot dead, and the killing is unsolved. Terra's president Joel Esquenazi got 15 years in 2011, which US prosecutors called the longest sentence yet under the US foreign bribery law.
inside: Foreign carriers paid the directors running Haiti's state phone company, so that the company's rates and contracts favoured those carriers.
cite: US Justice Department, 25 October 2011 and May 2012; Associated Press via Fox News, 21 May 2012

n: Haiti's palace security chief allegedly armed and helped Viv Ansanm gangs
rank: head, National Palace General Security Unit
d: Dimitri Hérard, head of the unit guarding Haiti's National Palace from 2017 to 2021, is accused by the UN of working for criminal groups from inside the state. The UN listing, repeated by the UK, says he diverted police weapons, imported arms illegally and moved drugs for criminal groups. A UN panel says he and the palace security coordinator imported more than 200 firearms in November 2020 without government oversight, most going to unknown buyers. He was jailed over the killing of President Moïse, escaped in March 2024, and is accused of helping plan attacks by Viv Ansanm, a gang alliance. The US and UN sanctioned him in October 2025. He says he is wrongly accused, and the sources cited report no verdict.
inside: The UN alleges that the head of Haiti's palace security used his post to divert police weapons and move drugs for criminal groups, then helped gangs attack the state.
cite: UK Sanctions List notice (UN listing), 20 October 2025; UN Panel of Experts S/2024/704; Latin Times, 26 October 2025

n: Witnesses said Haitian palace guards took the Manzanares drugs from port
rank: presidential palace guard and police
d: Witnesses said men in Haitian presidential guard and police uniforms took drugs from the port after the arrival of a ship called the Manzanares. In April 2015 the ship, carrying sugar from Colombia, was found to hold a large cocaine and heroin load, and only a fraction was recovered. Witnesses said Dimitri Hérard, then a palace guard officer, gave orders. He admitted being at the terminal but said he was there to discuss a firearms and security business, and he denied any link to the drugs. A former US Drug Enforcement Administration agent said he interviewed Hérard at least twice, and a former Haitian official said antinarcotics police searched his home. Hérard was never charged, and became head of palace security in 2017.
inside: Witnesses allege that traffickers had uniformed presidential guards and police collecting their drugs from the port, which would put state security staff to work for them; Hérard was never charged.
cite: Univision News, 2021

n: US accused members of Haiti's ruling council of supporting gangs
rank: Transitional Presidential Council members
d: The United States alleges that members of Haiti's Transitional Presidential Council, the body then running the country, supported gangs from inside it. In November 2025 it barred one member for "supporting gangs and other criminal organizations"; Fritz Alphonse Jean said he was the one, called the claim false, and said US and Canadian envoys had threatened council members with visa cancellations while they reviewed election candidates. In January 2026, days after a council vote to fire the prime minister, which Washington called illegal, it restricted the visas of two more unnamed members, citing "involvement in the operation of gangs". The State Department gave no details.
inside: The US alleges that gangs had allies on the council governing Haiti; Jean denies it, and the State Department has given no details.
cite: Al Jazeera, 25 November 2025; AOL/Miami Herald, January 2026; Le Quotidien 509, 25 January 2026

n: Importer Reynold Deeb allegedly swayed who staffed Haiti's port customs
rank: customs officers at major ports
d: A UN panel of experts says Haitian businessman Reynold Deeb, general manager of Deka Group, gained influence inside Haiti's customs service. Its report, made public in October 2023, says he paid gang members to protect his business and in 2017 paid a gang leader so he could operate at a main port. It says he used gang members to press customs officials not to inspect his containers, which let him avoid import duties, and that he "continues to unofficially influence the choice of customs officers" at major ports. It also alleges that he helped finance the 2019 protest movement and later bribed members of parliament. Canada has sanctioned him. The Miami Herald's report on the findings gives no reply from Deeb.
inside: A UN panel alleges that a private importer used gang pressure and influence over postings to control customs officers, so that the agency stopped checking and taxing his goods.
cite: Miami Herald (Jacqueline Charles) via Yahoo, 19 October 2023, on the UN Panel of Experts report

n: UN panel: business owners bribed Haitian customs to release and block containers
rank: deputy customs director and customs agents
d: Importers in Haiti pay customs officials to work for them, according to a 2024 report by the UN panel of experts on Haiti. The panel says some business people bribe customs officials to release containers without the required procedures, and that competitors bribe agents to block a rival's containers. It cites the dismissal in July 2023 of a deputy customs director in Port-au-Prince who had authorised the release of several containers from two private ports. Elsewhere the panel says gangs have also been used to deter customs officials from inspecting some containers. The report names no official or company, and says the panel was still investigating.
inside: Private importers paid customs staff, according to UN experts, so that a state agency decided which goods were checked according to who had paid, including to harm their competitors.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, S/2024/253, paras 92-93

n: Haitian police officers caught carrying thousands of rounds for gangs
rank: Haitian National Police, palace unit and central armoury
d: Haitian police officers have been caught moving ammunition to the gangs they are meant to fight, according to the UN panel of experts on Haiti. On 31 October 2024 an officer of a counter-ambush team based at the Presidential Palace was arrested with 2,695 rounds intended for a member of the Krache Dife gang. On 8 November 2024 an officer in a temporary anti-gang unit was arrested with 2,400 rounds traced to the police central armoury, where his partner, a secretary, was allegedly stealing from stock. A source said those rounds were for a main leader of the Viv Ansanm gang alliance. The panel's earlier report says close to 1,000 firearms were diverted from police stocks in four years.
inside: UN experts say gangs had police officers, including one in a palace unit and a staff member at the central armoury, supplying them with the force's own ammunition.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, S/2025/356, paras 62-64; S/2024/704, para 77

n: Guy Philippe and gangs allegedly used Haiti's protected-areas brigade
org_label: Guy Philippe's movement and allied gangs
rank: Protected Areas Security Brigade
d: Former police commander Guy Philippe and allied gangs got use of a state security force, according to UN experts. The Protected Areas Security Brigade is an armed unit created by Haiti's protected-areas agency, part of the environment ministry. The panel says it grew to about 6,000 members, 95 per cent not on any payroll, outside government control. It says the agency's then director, Jeantel Joseph, used armed agents to guard Philippe, and that in February 2024 agents went with Philippe to meet two Gonaïves gangs, where weapons were reportedly handed out under the guise of recruiting agents. It also says Philippe reportedly tried to bribe police to let gangs into the National Palace. A 2026 panel report says some agents work with local gangs on land seizures.
inside: UN experts report that a former police commander and his gang allies gained the use of a state brigade, with its name offering cover for handing weapons to gang members.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, S/2024/704, paras 31, 42, 83-85; S/2024/253, paras 23-24; S/2026/241, para 26

n: Former mayor of Arcahaie allegedly gave logistical help to Haitian gangs
rank: mayor of Arcahaie
d: A former mayor of the Haitian town of Arcahaie was close to gang leaders and gave them logistical support, according to sources quoted by the UN panel of experts on Haiti in its 2026 interim report. The same report says collusion and infiltration in some police and government institutions mean gang leaders are often warned before security operations. The former mayor was arrested in the Dominican Republic on 10 August 2025 on charges of holding undeclared foreign currency and cheques, and was handed to Haitian authorities. Those charges do not concern gangs. The part of the panel's report cited does not give the name, and no court finding on the gang claims is recorded there.
inside: Sources told UN experts that a former mayor of a Haitian town was close to gang leaders and gave them logistical support; no court finding on this is recorded in the report.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, interim report S/2026/241, paras 19, 69, via ecoi.net

n: Honduran police officer fed the Cachiros traffickers police information
rank: Honduran National Police officer
d: Los Cachiros, a Honduran drug trafficking group, had Honduran National Police officer Juan Manuel Avila Meza working for it. US prosecutors say that from about 2004 to 2014 he gave the group sensitive police information, helped it launder money and brokered meetings with other corrupt officials. In February 2014 he helped arrange a meeting between a Cachiros leader and Tony Hernández, brother of the Honduran president, about laundering money between a Cachiros front company and the government. In June 2014 he led a discussion with other officers on using the force to give a large cocaine shipment safe passage. He pleaded guilty, and in 2021 a New York judge sentenced him to 12 years.
inside: A drug syndicate kept a police officer working for it for about a decade, so police information and fellow officers served its shipments and its money laundering.
cite: US Attorney SDNY, March 2021; DEA, 29 March 2021

n: Honduran police officer Hernández Pineda guarded cocaine for traffickers
rank: deputy commissioner, Honduran National Police
d: Traffickers had a senior Honduran police officer, Mauricio Hernández Pineda, protecting their cocaine. Prosecutors said he led other officers in escorting tons of cocaine and tipped traffickers off about police operations, working with Tony Hernández, the president's brother, and moving loads through north-western Honduras towards Guatemala for the Sinaloa Cartel. Trafficker Alexander Ardón testified that Hernández Pineda guarded loads and passed on details of checkpoints and investigations. Reports describe him as a cousin of President Juan Orlando Hernández; in 2020 the president's office denied any family tie. He pleaded guilty on 2 February 2024, days before the trial, and was sentenced to 15 years on 2 July 2024. He filed an appeal on 10 July 2024.
inside: Traffickers had a deputy police commissioner using his rank to escort their cocaine and warn them of operations, so a police force served the shipments it should have stopped.
cite: El Heraldo, 2024 (including 10 July 2024); Univision, 2020; LatinNews, 2024; Inner City Press, July 2024

n: Nicaraguan electoral magistrate supplied false ID to El Palidejo's network
rank: substitute magistrate, Supreme Electoral Council
d: A drug trafficking network led by Costa Rican Alejandro Jiménez, known as "El Palidejo", had a magistrate of Nicaragua's Supreme Electoral Council, the body that oversees elections, working for it. Julio César Osuna was charged with giving members of the group false identification cards, and the report of the verdict says he provided Jiménez with a Nicaraguan identity card. Colombian police caught Jiménez in March 2012 as he entered the country with false documents. A Guatemalan court convicted him in April 2016 of the 2011 murder of singer Facundo Cabral and gave him 50 years. Police arrested Osuna in May 2012. A Nicaraguan court convicted him with Henry Fariñas, and in October 2012 sentenced Osuna to 17 years and Fariñas to 30.
inside: A trafficking network had an electoral magistrate supply false identification cards to its members, including a Nicaraguan identity card for its Costa Rican leader.
cite: La Estrella de Panamá, 12 October 2012; InSight Crime, 28 May 2012 and 2012; Notimex via El Siglo de Torreón, 25 June 2012; Envío, April 2012; Tico Times, 13 Mar and 28 May 2012; La Prensa (Nicaragua), 7 Apr 2016

n: Minister said Nicaraguan judges freed traffickers; cables allege party pay
org_label: International drug traffickers, including Sinaloa Cartel members
rank: judges and magistrates
d: International drug traffickers allegedly got Nicaraguan judges to release them. In 2010 Interior Minister Ana Isabel Morales told the weekly Confidencial she held a list of judges and magistrates who had granted releases or shorter sentences to 1,000 traffickers, reportedly including Sinaloa Cartel members. She later refused to release prisoners whose sentences had been reduced. The article reporting this names no judge. Leaked 2010 US embassy cables, as reported by the newspaper La Prensa, said Daniel Ortega's Sandinistas received money from traffickers in return for freeing detained members. No payment to a judge has been proven in the sources cited, and they give no reply from the party or the judges.
inside: A minister's list and US cables allege that traffickers' money reached Nicaragua's ruling party and that courts then freed traffickers, though no court has ruled on a payment.
cite: InSight Crime (Meléndez and Orozco), 2013; La Prensa (Nicaragua), 4 February 2025

n: Embraer promised Dominican military official $3.5m for Super Tucano sale
rank: armed forces projects director; defence minister and senator alleged
d: Brazilian aircraft maker Embraer admitted promising $3.52 million to a Dominican official to win a sale of eight Super Tucano aircraft worth about $92 million. The official was to help win Senate approval of financing, and the money went through shell companies in 2009 and 2010. Embraer settled with US and Brazilian authorities for $205 million in 2016, and $7 million with Dominican authorities in 2018. Brazil convicted Embraer staff that year. Dominican prosecutors accused retired colonel Carlos Piccini Núñez and former defence minister Pedro Rafael Peña Antonio, who denied any bribe; Senator Luis René Canaán was named but not charged. A court acquitted both in 2022. After an annulment and a 2023 time-limit ruling, an appeal court ordered a fresh trial in December 2024. No verdict since was found.
inside: An aircraft maker promised a Dominican military official money, sent through shell companies, to get a military aircraft purchase through government and Senate, so the decision served the seller.
cite: Tufts University, Compendium of Arms Trade Corruption; Diario Libre, 30 May 2022 and 21 December 2024; El Nuevo Diario, 14 September 2023; El Día, 25 October 2016

n: Stef Goris named as pivot of Azerbaijan's lobbying inside PACE
rank: Former PACE member and lobbyist
d: Stef Goris, a former Belgian member of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE), was described by witnesses to its 2018 inquiry as a "key or pivotal figure" in Azerbaijan's lobbying inside the assembly. Witnesses told the inquiry he handed out envelopes of money within the European People's Party group, and that he invited an Irish member to Azerbaijan on business-class tickets. He gave Polish member Tadeusz Iwiński a pre-written statement to send to the PACE Bureau. Goris and Alain Destexhe were also in charge of the European Academy of Election Observation, which the European Stability Initiative called a sham election-observation organisation. The money claims rest on witness evidence, not a court ruling.
inside: Witnesses told the inquiry a former member worked for Azerbaijan inside the assembly, passing envelopes and ready-written statements to members so the body would treat Baku more favourably.
cite: European Stability Initiative summary of the PACE Independent Investigation Body report, April 2018

n: Azerbaijan rapporteur Destexhe quit PACE over reported Baku money
rank: PACE rapporteur on Azerbaijan (Belgian member)
d: Belgian media reported that Alain Destexhe, a Belgian member of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) working on a human rights report about Azerbaijan, had been paid for seven years by Azerbaijan's ruling family to help legitimise its elections. He announced his resignation in 2017, saying debates would focus on him rather than the report. The 2018 PACE inquiry found he had breached the rapporteur code and PACE's Code of Conduct. It noted that the European Academy of Election Observation had its registered seat at his address until September 2016, and called his claim of non-involvement implausible. The payment claim is reported, not proven.
inside: Press reports allege Azerbaijan's ruling family paid an assembly member writing about its rights record; an inquiry found he broke the rules and was tied to an election-observer group.
cite: Armenpress, September 2017, citing Belgian media and the OCCRP Azerbaijani Laundromat; European Stability Initiative summary of the PACE inquiry report, April 2018

n: Kazakh billionaires' fixers reached Belgian Senate over a settlement law
org_label: Kazakh billionaires Chodiev, Mashkevitch and Ibragimov
rank: Vice-president of the Belgian Senate
d: Three billionaires linked to Kazakhstan, facing money-laundering charges in Belgium, were helped by Armand De Decker, then vice-president of the Belgian Senate, who joined their legal team. In February 2011 he visited Justice Minister Stefaan De Clerck at home. Belgium adopted a wider settlement law in 2011, and on 17 June Patokh Chodiev paid €22.5 million to close the case. France agreed a sale of helicopters and locomotives to Kazakhstan worth over €2 billion. Le Canard Enchaîné reported that De Decker received over €700,000 from the case's French lawyer; he called this very exaggerated. A parliamentary inquiry, set up in late 2016, found he breached professional ethics. He was charged with influence peddling in 2018 and denied wrongdoing. The case against him ended when he died in 2019.
inside: Billionaires facing Belgian charges put a sitting Senate vice-president on their legal team; he visited the justice minister at home as a new settlement law let them close the case.
cite: La Libre Belgique, 13 June 2019; DH, 8 December 2016; L'Avenir, 23 Nov 2016; Paris Match Belgique, 31 Jan 2017; RTBF on the Canard Enchaîné report; Brussels Times, 26 Apr 2018; VRT, 28 Mar 2018

n: Tenaris paid staff of Uzbek state oil firm to rig four pipe bids
rank: Officials of state oil and gas firm O'ztashqineftgaz
d: Tenaris, a Luxembourg-based steel pipe supplier, made improper payments to officials of O'ztashqineftgaz, a state-controlled Uzbek oil and gas producer, to win contracts. For four public bids on oilfield pipe and services, Tenaris hired an agent to obtain competitors' bid information, then secretly submitted better revised bids. It agreed to pay the agent 3.5% of the contracts' value, while aware or substantially certain that the agent would pass all or part of the money to the firm's employees. In May 2011 Tenaris agreed a $3.5 million penalty with the US Justice Department and paid the US Securities and Exchange Commission $5,428,338. It had reported the conduct itself.
inside: A foreign pipe supplier paid staff of a state oil company through an agent, and received rivals' bid details so that public tenders went its way.
cite: US Department of Justice press release 11-629, 17 May 2011; Eurasianet, 2011

n: Tobacco firm Dimon carried bags of cash to a top Kyrgyz official
rank: High-ranking Kyrgyz government official; tax officials
d: Dimon, a global tobacco trader that later became part of Alliance One International, paid more than $3 million in bribes to Kyrgyz government officials so that its Kyrgyz subsidiary could buy local tobacco. According to the US Securities and Exchange Commission, most of the money was delivered in bags of $100 bills to a high-ranking official, and tax officials were also paid. The conduct began as early as 1996. The agency announced the case in August 2010. Alliance One paid $10 million in disgorgement to the agency and accepted an independent monitor for three years. Its subsidiaries paid a $9.45 million criminal fine in separate US Justice Department proceedings.
inside: A tobacco trader paid a senior official and tax officers in Kyrgyzstan so its local subsidiary could keep buying the country's tobacco crop.
cite: US Securities and Exchange Commission press release 2010-144, 6 August 2010

n: Leaks say arbitrators weighed bribery of Kazakh officials over Karachaganak
rank: Kazakh officials approving oilfield costs
d: Kazakhstan claims that foreign oil contractors bribed its officials to approve costs at the Karachaganak gas field that the state should not have covered. Kazakhstan cited documents from 2017 Italian criminal cases in which, according to the report, contractors admitted bribing Kazakh officials over Karachaganak and Kashagan; the contractors are not named. In January 2026 Bloomberg and Reuters reported that a London arbitration had recognised some of Kazakhstan's claims and taken the bribery into account, with possible compensation of $2-4 billion. This comes from leaks: the hearing is confidential and no ruling has been published. Karachaganak is run by a group including Shell, Eni, Chevron and Lukoil, and the report ties no single company to bribery.
inside: Kazakhstan alleges oil contractors paid its officials so they would sign off costs the state then bore; a leaked arbitration ruling reportedly took this into account.
cite: Mts.kg, 2026, citing Bloomberg and Reuters

n: Oyu Tolgoi money reached Mongolia's finance minister, court reportedly ruled
rank: Minister of finance
d: Sangajav Bayartsogt, Mongolia's finance minister, signed the 2009 agreement for the Oyu Tolgoi copper and gold mine after, investigators say, money had reached him from people connected to it. Swiss prosecutors allege that businessman Borkhuu Delgersaikhan received about $45 million from a Chinese investor in 2007-08 and paid €8.2 million into Bayartsogt's Credit Suisse account. Offshore Leaks exposed his Swiss accounts in 2013 and he resigned as parliament's vice-president. In 2020 a Mongolian court reportedly convicted him of taking kickbacks and sentenced him to 10 years; one account says the bribes came from Ivanhoe, the mine's then owner. He had denied all charges, and OCCRP reported in 2022 that he had been released. The Swiss proceedings were still open in June 2020.
inside: Money tied to a giant mine deal reached the minister who signed it, a court reportedly found; prosecutors say it came through intermediaries who stood to gain.
cite: Swissinfo, June 2020; Reuters via Mining.com, 29 January 2019; OCCRP Suisse Secrets, 2022; Global Anticorruption Blog, 8 December 2020

n: Ex-PM Batbold accused of secret deals with mine interests and shells
rank: Prime minister
d: Filings by Mongolian state bodies in New York alleged that Sukhbaatar Batbold, while prime minister, took kickbacks in 2010 from people associated with Ivanhoe in exchange for favours over the Oyu Tolgoi mine. They also alleged that shell companies bought about $400 million of copper concentrate from a state-owned mine. His adviser said he received no kickbacks and that the case was politically motivated. The blog that reported the case says the Mongolian and New York cases were shut down after a Batbold protégé won the 2021 presidential election. In March 2024 the US Justice Department sued to seize two New York flats bought for $14 million, alleging he used his post to award those copper contracts to associates and his son.
inside: Mongolian bodies and US prosecutors allege a sitting prime minister gave favours to people associated with Ivanhoe and copper contracts to his associates and son for hidden gains; he denies this.
cite: Global Anticorruption Blog, 8 December 2020, 6 January 2021 and 27 March 2024

n: Georgian NATO mission adviser Maisaia jailed for spying for Russia
rank: Counsellor at Georgia's mission to NATO
d: Tbilisi City Court found that Vakhtang Maisaia, a former counsellor at Georgia's mission to NATO from 2004 to 2008, had spied for Russia, and sentenced him to 20 years in January 2010. He was accused of giving Russian secret services classified information about arms purchases and troop movements during the August 2008 war; President Mikheil Saakashvili said he reported army positions every two hours or more often. Maisaia was arrested in May 2009 and the trial was held behind closed doors. He denied the charges, said his televised confession was made under duress, and his lawyer planned an appeal.
inside: A court found that Russia's secret services got wartime military secrets from a former Georgian diplomat who had served at the country's mission to NATO.
cite: Civil Georgia, 29 January 2010; The Moscow Times, 1 February 2010; RFE/RL, 20 October 2009

n: Kazakh presidential institute's China expert jailed for treason
rank: Senior researcher, Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies
d: Konstantin Syroyezhkin, a China expert at the state-run Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies and a reported adviser to Kassym-Jomart Tokayev on border talks, was sentenced to 10 years for treason in October 2019. He also lost his citizenship. The security service did not say who he spied for. Activists citing law enforcement sources said the case concerned his work with China, and media reports said he was accused of passing secret documents to China or Chinese nationals for money. Details were never published. He pleaded not guilty, academics asked for a transparent investigation, and Chinese authorities called the case made up. He was paroled in April 2024 and pardoned that September.
inside: Reports say Chinese nationals got secret documents from a researcher advising Kazakhstan's government, but the charges were never published and he pleaded not guilty.
cite: RFE/RL, October 2019, April and September 2024; South China Morning Post, 10 October 2019; Eurasianet, 7 May 2019; CABAR, October 2019

n: Moldovan MP Nesterovschi jailed over Shor party money, fled via embassy
rank: Member of parliament
d: A Moldovan court sentenced MP Alexandr Nesterovschi in his absence to 12 years on 19 March 2025 for illegally channelling money to a pro-Russian party linked to fugitive businessman Ilan Shor. The funding concerned the 2023 local elections, the 2024 presidential vote and a referendum on joining the EU. The security service released video of him entering the Russian embassy on 18 March, and says he was driven to Transnistria in a car with diplomatic plates. It says he is part of a criminal network coordinated by Shor and under Russian protection. Moldova expelled three Russian diplomats. Nesterovschi denies the charges, and Russia's ambassador rejects the accusation.
inside: A sitting MP moved money for a fugitive's pro-Russian network into Moldova's elections, a court found; security officials say Russia's embassy then helped him escape.
cite: Reuters via The Star, 31 March 2025; Moldpres, 31 March 2025

n: Tajik anti-drug police chief jailed for drug trafficking tied to smuggler 'Hummer'
rank: Head of district police anti-narcotics department
d: Investigators in Tajikistan said Faridun Umarov, head of the police anti-narcotics department in Farkhor district, protected the smuggling group of Rustam Haitov, known as "Hummer", and helped carry drugs from the Afghan border at least once, apparently for bribes. The anti-corruption agency arrested Haitov on 6 January 2012 and reportedly found about 42 kg of opium and heroin at his house. The chief of the Interior Ministry's anti-narcotics police and other senior officers were arrested in the same investigation. On 7 August 2012 a court in Dushanbe's Sino district convicted Umarov of drug trafficking and jailed him for seven years, and Haitov for 24 as ringleader. Umarov, brother of a deputy head of the security committee, was paroled in August 2014 after an amnesty halved his term.
inside: Investigators said a smuggling group bought the police officer meant to stop it, so the state's anti-drug unit protected and helped move its shipments; a court convicted him of drug trafficking.
cite: Jamestown Foundation, Eurasia Daily Monitor vol. 9 issue 29, February 2012, via ecoi.net; Asia-Plus, 8 Aug 2012 and 19 Aug 2014

n: Ex-rebel Ayombekov ran Tajik border unit while accused of smuggling
rank: Chief of the Ishkashim border unit
d: Tolib Ayombekov, a former civil war rebel leader, was chief of the Ishkashim border unit on the Afghan frontier and in government service from 2008 while, authorities said, leading a smuggling operation. In 2012 he faced charges of drug smuggling, contraband cigarettes, human trafficking and leading an illegal armed group, which Eurasianet reported he did not deny. He was also accused of involvement in the July 2012 killing of General Abdullo Nazarov, the regional security chief; he said, "We didn't need it." About 2,000 troops entered Khorog on 24 July. He surrendered on 12 August. Wikipedia says cases against him were dropped in 2018 and that he received a life sentence in November 2022.
inside: A warlord's armed group was given a state post guarding the Afghan border, and authorities later charged that he used it to run drug and cigarette smuggling.
cite: Eurasianet via ecoi.net, 2012; RFE/RL, 13 August 2012; Wikipedia, Tolib Ayombekov

n: Bribes for medical contracts reached Belarus's deputy health minister
rank: Deputy Health Minister; state hospital and import chiefs
d: Belarusian health officials allegedly took bribes of $10,000 to $450,000 from those seeking medical equipment and drug contracts, with prices inflated by up to 60%. The KGB, the state security service, began detentions in June 2018. Thirty-three officials and others were held, including former Deputy Health Minister Ihar Lasitski and Alyaksandr Sharak, head of the state medical importer Belmedtechniki. Three former hospital officials were convicted that August, with sentences of up to seven years. Sharak received 6.5 years for bribe-taking on 11 May 2020. Experts estimated that 10 private firms controlled about 75% of drug imports.
inside: Suppliers allegedly paid officials in Belarus's health ministry and hospitals, so purchasing decisions went to them at inflated prices.
cite: RFE/RL, 29 August 2018; Zerkalo, on Sharak's sentence

n: Russian firm paid Lukashenko's former guard chief about $148,000, Belarus court found
rank: Deputy state secretary, Security Council
d: A Russian company paid Andrei Vtiurin, deputy state secretary of Belarus's Security Council and former head of President Aleksandr Lukashenko's protection service, to promote its interests in Belarus, a Belarusian court found. He was detained in spring 2019, in April or on 3 May according to differing reports, after receiving about $148,000 from a company representative, who was also charged. One report says KGB officers kept the arrest secret for a long time. In July 2020 the Supreme Court sentenced him to 12 years, with confiscation of property, and stripped his colonel's rank. Lenta put the bribes at $192,000 in total. The KGB said he pleaded guilty.
inside: A Russian company paid a senior Security Council official, once the president's guard chief, to push its business interests inside Belarus, a Belarusian court found.
cite: Adevărul, 5 May 2019; The Insider and Lenta, 27 July 2020

n: Beltelecom chief jailed in bribery case including €15,000 from Russian firm
rank: Director general of Beltelecom
d: Representatives of the Russian firm UGMK-Telecom, Kazantsev and Gorbachev, gave Sergei Sivodedov, director general of Beltelecom, Belarus's state telecommunications operator, 15,000 euros in January 2019, according to the charges, over equipment supplies for modernising its Zala television service. He was charged with three counts of taking bribes totalling $470,000 and 15,000 euros, including money from tender winners while he chaired Beltelecom's tender commission, and admitted guilt on the first day of trial in March 2020. The case had 16 defendants under Belarus's bribery articles, among them Andrei Vtiurin, a senior Security Council official. In July 2020 it was reported that the Supreme Court had sentenced Sivodedov to seven years.
inside: Representatives of a Russian telecoms firm paid the head of Belarus's state telecoms operator over equipment supplies to the company; he admitted guilt and was jailed.
cite: Adevărul, 5 May 2019; Onliner, 10 March 2020; dev.by, 27 July 2020

n: US base fuel supplier allegedly paid Kyrgyz president's son
rank: President's family
d: Officials of Kyrgyzstan's provisional government said in 2010 that Mina Corp, which supplied jet fuel to the US air base at Manas, paid Maxim Bakiyev, son of the ousted president Kurmanbek Bakiyev. Prosecutors separately said six local suppliers of Mina and its affiliate Red Star, all belonging to Maxim Bakiyev, evaded about $90 million in excise over five years, and that the president engineered a zero rate from 2005 to help them. Mina had won a no-bid contract worth up to $730.9 million in 2009. The new government's chief of staff said the US had bribed the ruling family. A US congressional committee opened an investigation; its findings are not covered by these sources.
inside: Kyrgyz officials allege a fuel contractor paid the president's son while his father set tax rules that benefited suppliers feeding that contract; these claims remain unproven.
cite: Eurasianet, 26 April 2010 and May 2010

n: Armenian foreign ministry employee charged with treason for foreign state
rank: Foreign Ministry employee
d: Armenian investigators charged an unnamed Foreign Ministry employee with state treason, accusing the person of passing or giving access to state secrets for a foreign state. The case opened on 20 June 2025 and the suspect is in pre-trial detention. Officials said no other ministry staff were implicated, and rejected claims that the accused was a consul or senior official. The state concerned has not been named. The newspaper Hraparak, citing unnamed sources, linked the detention of a consul to spying for Azerbaijan, which has not been confirmed.
inside: Investigators allege a foreign state obtained secrets through an employee inside Armenia's Foreign Ministry; the state and the employee have not been officially named.
cite: Orda.kz, 30 August 2025

n: Congo MP and coltan mine owner sentenced to death as an M23 collaborator
rank: National Assembly member for Masisi
d: A Congolese military court found that a sitting member of parliament worked with M23, the rebel movement fighting Congo's army, which UN experts say Rwanda backs. Édouard Mwangachuchu represented Masisi in North Kivu and owned Société minière de Bisunzu, which mines coltan at Rubaya. He was arrested in Kinshasa on 1 March 2023, and the case followed the discovery of weapons at a company site. On 6 October 2023 the High Military Court sentenced him to death for treason, taking part in M23 and holding weapons. It said his minerals went to Rwanda. His lawyers said no link to Rwanda was proved. He appealed to the Court of Cassation that month; it was still pending in March 2024, and no result was found.
inside: A Congolese military court found a sitting MP and mine owner took part in the M23 rebel movement and sent minerals to Rwanda; his lawyers dispute any Rwanda link.
cite: Africanews, 7 Oct 2023; Actualite.cd, 14 Mar 2024; Wikipedia, Édouard Mwangachuchu (citing Huggins 2022 and Radio Okapi); Rebelion summary of UN Group of Experts report, Dec 2024

n: Och-Ziff money funded bribes to Congo's officials for mining assets
rank: High-ranking DRC officials
d: A New York hedge fund's money went through a business partner in Congo to pay senior officials for access to state-controlled mines, US regulators said. Och-Ziff settled for $413m in September 2016 under the US foreign bribery law; a subsidiary pleaded guilty. The Securities and Exchange Commission said a significant part of the fund's loans to its "DRC partner" paid bribes to high-ranking officials, with more than $100m alleged over ten years. One reported $11m went to the official Augustin Katumba Mwanke. A person familiar with the matter identified the partner as the Israeli billionaire Dan Gertler, who denied the allegations and had not been charged. The partner's companies repaid Och-Ziff in full.
inside: US filings say a hedge fund's loans passed through a Congo partner to pay senior officials, so state mining assets went to that partner and the fund.
cite: Global Witness, 29 Sep 2016; Bloomberg via Mining Weekly, 30 Sep 2016; Quartz, 30 Sep 2016

n: Belgian firm Semlex sent to trial over $60 cut of each Congo passport
rank: Congo's passport contract; relative of President Kabila (alleged)
d: Belgian prosecutors allege that the identity-document company Semlex paid its way into Congo's passport contract through people close to the president. Semlex made Congo's biometric passports from 2015 to 2025, sold at $185 each. Reuters reported in 2017 that $60 of each went to a United Arab Emirates company believed to be owned by a relative of President Joseph Kabila; Brussels prosecutors opened an inquiry that year. In late August 2026 a Brussels court sent Semlex and 13 others to trial for alleged bribery, money laundering and tax fraud. Civil parties say nearly $60m was diverted. Authorities have not conclusively linked the company to the relative, the accused are presumed innocent, and Semlex called the reports a smear in 2017.
inside: Prosecutors allege a foreign company channelled part of each passport fee to a firm tied to the president's circle, so a state contract served the company and that circle.
cite: Reuters via Internazionale, 1-2 Sep 2026; FIDH press release, 31 Aug 2026; Reuters via Yahoo, 20 Apr 2017

n: Griffiths Energy paid Chad's ambassador's wife $2m to win oil rights
rank: Ambassador to the US and Canada
d: A Calgary oil company put money and shares in the hands of Chad's top diplomat in North America while seeking an oil contract from Chad. Griffiths Energy paid a US$2m success fee to Chad Oil Consulting, controlled by the wife of Ambassador Mahamoud Adam Bechir; she and two people she nominated also subscribed for founders' shares. New management that took over in summer 2011 reported this, and on 22 January 2013 the firm pleaded guilty in Alberta and was fined C$10.35m. A US indictment, unsealed in 2021, says the consulting services were never provided. Co-founder Naeem Tyab pleaded guilty and agreed to forfeit about US$27m. Bechir, his deputy and his wife were at large in 2021 and face charges that remain unproven.
inside: An oil company paid money and shares to an ambassador's wife while negotiating a state oil contract, which the company admitted in court was a bribe to a foreign official.
cite: Bennett Jones, Jan 2013; Global News/Canadian Press, 25 May 2021; CBC, 2021

n: UN: Somali president's alleged adviser sent state arms to al-Shabaab
rank: Presidential adviser and official liaison (alleged)
d: UN arms monitors alleged that a man working for Somalia's government steered state weapons to al-Shabaab, the al-Qaeda-linked insurgency it was fighting. Their 2014 reporting named Musa Haji Mohamed Ganjab, a businessman, as having acted as an adviser to President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud. A government document made him a liaison to South Africa from 2010. The Wall Street Journal reported that emails from October 2013 ordered a government arms shipment split between a regional official and al-Shabaab commander Yusuf Isse, and the UN confirmed Isse received weapons. Ganjab called the emails fakes and denied dealing in arms. The president said he had no such adviser and denied that anyone close to him passed arms to the group.
inside: UN monitors allege a man with government standing diverted state arms to an al-Shabaab commander, so supplies meant for the army served the insurgents; he and the president deny it.
cite: Wall Street Journal via Goobjoog, 29 Dec 2014; Al Jazeera, 15 Feb 2014; Garowe Online, 18 Oct 2014

n: UN: al-Shabaab infiltrated Mogadishu port and read its cargo manifests
rank: Mogadishu port institutions
d: Al-Shabaab, the al-Qaeda-linked insurgency, got inside the institutions running Mogadishu's port and the city's shipping agents, the UN Panel of Experts on Somalia reported in 2019. This gave it cargo manifests, the documents listing the type, value and owner of imported goods. In April 2019 the group told Mogadishu businesses that all imports would be taxed by it. After a Gulf-based company imported several thousand tons of building materials in late July 2019, al-Shabaab used the manifest to summon the company's agent to its court at Mubarak and demand over $70,000, which the agent paid by bank transfer. The panel said the agent was told to pay future taxes in advance.
inside: UN experts report that an insurgent group got inside the institutions running Mogadishu's port, then used the port's import records to tax businesses for itself.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Somalia, S/2019/858, paras 11, 31-32

n: Hormuud Telecom staff prosecuted for helping al-Shabaab's truck bomb
rank: Hormuud Telecom employees
