d: Two employees of Hormuud Telecom, a Somali phone and mobile-money company, were prosecuted for helping al-Shabaab's truck bomb of 14 October 2017 pass the Sinka Dheere checkpoint. Al-Shabaab is the al-Qaeda-linked insurgency. One employee, Abdiweli Ahmed Diriye, received three years in prison. UN monitors reported in 2018 that a federal investigator believed the group "had infiltrated Hormuud", an opinion they attributed to him and did not state as their own finding. The monitors said Hormuud declined on 12 May 2018 to give them phone data on the plot's organisers. They also found ledgers showing al-Shabaab moved funds through the company's EVC Plus mobile-money service.
inside: A telecom company's staff were prosecuted for helping an insurgent group's truck bomb, and one investigator believed the group had infiltrated the firm.
cite: UN Monitoring Group on Somalia and Eritrea, S/2018/1002, paras 72-73, 89

n: UN: al-Shabaab bribes to border officials eased 2018 Kenya bomb plot
rank: Kenyan and Somali security officials
d: Al-Shabaab, the Somali al-Qaeda-linked insurgency, paid security officials on both sides of the Kenya-Somalia border to let a car-bomb plot through, UN monitors reported. The plot of February 2018 was organised from Somalia by an operative of Amniyat, the group's intelligence wing, known only as "Dere", who arranged about $30,000 in informal hawala money transfers to an operative named Abdimajit Adan. The monitors wrote that the plot crossed with little interference, helped by bribes to various security officials. They did not name any official or give the size of the bribes. Six people were prosecuted in Kenya, and the monitors said several plotters escaped and the attack team might still be at large.
inside: UN monitors report that an insurgent group paid unnamed border security officials in Kenya and Somalia, so forces meant to stop its bomb plot let it pass.
cite: UN Monitoring Group on Somalia and Eritrea, S/2018/1002, paras 78-80

n: UN: Somali commanders' arms and ammunition reached al-Shabaab
rank: Transitional Federal Government military commanders
d: Al-Shabaab, then an insurgency fighting Somalia's Transitional Federal Government, was buying weapons from the commanders of the forces it fought, according to the UN Monitoring Group on Somalia in 2008. The monitors recorded a sale on 27 November 2007 in which an arms trader acted as go-between for al-Shabaab and government commanders over arms taken from the group's caches, and al-Shabaab's representatives bought them back. They added, without naming a source, that commanders supplied trusted dealers with their own ammunition, listed it as used, and that al-Shabaab was the largest buyer. The report records no response from the commanders.
inside: An insurgent group's money reached government commanders through arms dealers, UN monitors report, so weapons and ammunition the state held went back to the enemy it was fighting.
cite: UN Monitoring Group on Somalia, S/2008/274, paras 120, 123-124, 137

n: British printer Smith & Ouzman bribed Kenya's election and exam bodies
rank: Interim electoral commission; national exams council
d: A British security printer paid officials at Kenya's electoral commission and national exams council to win printing contracts for ballot papers and exam materials, using the code word "chicken" for the bribes. After a Serious Fraud Office investigation, a London court convicted the firm and its owner Nicholas Smith, who served three years. Evidence alleged Sh66m went to Interim Independent Electoral Commission officials between June 2009 and October 2010 through middlemen. Smith & Ouzman was ordered to pay about £2.2m in a fine, confiscation and costs, reported as the first British company convicted of bribing foreign officials. Kenya received Sh52m in 2017 and bought ambulances. Former commission chief James Oswago was charged in Kenya and denies it; the anti-corruption body cleared commission chair Ahmed Issack Hassan.
inside: A foreign printing company paid staff inside the bodies running Kenya's elections and exams, so public printing contracts went to it; a British court convicted it.
cite: Daily Nation (Briton jailed for IEBC Chickengate scandal walks to freedom); The Citizen (Kenya); The Standard, 24 Dec 2014

n: Areva's paid go-between reached two senior Mongolian officials
rank: Two senior Mongolian public officials
d: The French nuclear group Areva got money to two senior Mongolian officials through a chain of consultants while building its uranium business there. According to the Paris court president, Areva signed a €4 million contract with the firm Eurotradia International, which signed a consultancy deal with a Mongolian businessman who received €1.275 million. He invested in a property project controlled by one senior official and paid a second; both had helped Areva set up in Mongolia. In December 2024 Areva agreed a €4.8 million fine under a CJIP, a French settlement that avoids trial and conviction. Orano Mining accepted three years of anti-corruption audits and says it does not admit responsibility.
cite: Reuters via Easybourse, 9 Dec 2024; Pinsent Masons Out-Law, 17 Dec 2024
inside: The Paris court president said Areva's consultants passed money to two senior Mongolian officials who had helped the company establish its uranium mining operations there.

n: Sediver's commissions reached officials around Congo's state power firm
rank: Officials linked to SNEL, the state electricity company
d: The insulator maker Sediver allegedly paid commissions to officials in the Democratic Republic of Congo while supplying a power line for SNEL, the state electricity company. Sediver was a subcontractor on a World Bank-financed contract signed in 2012 between SNEL and an Indian firm. The money allegedly went through a consultancy the World Bank had commissioned to assist SNEL and through a Swiss agent and his company. The French settlement, approved on 4 December 2023, set a €13,373,000 fine and required a compliance programme under French anti-corruption agency supervision. It also covers similar facts in 19 countries from 2009 to 2015. Two SEVES subsidiaries had already paid the World Bank €6.8 million in 2017.
cite: International Bar Association, 'France: CJIPs and Sediver'
inside: French settlement papers say Sediver's commissions reached Congolese officials through agents, including a consultancy hired to assist the state power company buying its insulators.

n: ADP's engineering arm paid commissions to a Fujairah representative
rank: Representative of the Emirate of Fujairah
d: ADP Ingénierie, the engineering arm of the Paris airports group, allegedly gave a representative of the Emirate of Fujairah a personal share of its work there. Under an agreement with him, he and his company received commissions of 5% and 21.5% on payments to ADPI for Fujairah work. In 2011 ADPI also gave an excessively priced housing estate contract, with no deliverables found, to a subcontractor he majority-owned. The French settlement, signed on 29 November 2023 and approved on 4 December, set a €14.6 million fine. It also covered a Libyan airport tender, where ADPI had confidential tender information and intermediaries may have helped it win.
cite: International Bar Association, 'France: CJIPs and Sediver'
inside: French settlement papers say ADPI paid a Fujairah representative personal commissions on the emirate's own work and gave his company an overpriced subcontract.

n: Société Générale paid for access to Libya's state investment money
rank: Libyan Investment Authority director and senior officials
d: The French bank Société Générale paid bribes to senior Libyan officials through a Libyan intermediary to win investments from Libya's state financial institutions. From 2004 to 2009 it paid him more than $90 million in commissions of 1.5% to 3% on fourteen transactions, and part of that money was diverted to officials. The transactions earned the bank $523 million in profit. In 2018 it settled with US prosecutors and France's financial prosecutor, whose CJIP settlement set a fine of €250,150,755. It was the fourth CJIP in France and the first negotiated in cooperation with the US Justice Department.
cite: Paul Weiss client memo, 7 June 2018; JD Supra, 'A closer look: France - U.S. and French coordinated settlements with Société Générale'; Les Petites Affiches, 2018
inside: A French bank's commissions reached senior Libyan officials through a go-between, and Libya's state financial institutions then placed investments with the bank.

n: Total convicted over payments for Iran's South Pars gas field
rank: Head of National Iranian Oil Company subsidiaries
d: The French oil company Total paid about $30 million, disguised as a consulting contract with a firm called Baston, to help secure a deal on Iran's South Pars gas field. Prosecutors said much of the money was meant for Mehdi Rafsanjani, son of former president Hashemi Rafsanjani, who then ran subsidiaries of the National Iranian Oil Company. Total signed the South Pars contract with that company on 28 September 1997. On 21 December 2018 a Paris court convicted Total of corrupting foreign officials over the payments made from 2000 to 2004 and fined it €500,000, rejecting a request to confiscate €250 million. Total had paid US authorities $398 million in 2013.
cite: AFP via Tradingsat, 21 Dec 2018; RFE/RL, 21 Dec 2018
inside: A French oil company paid money through a consultancy, which prosecutors said was largely meant for a state oil executive, to secure Iran's South Pars gas contract.

n: Systra paid a railway official's secret firm in Uzbekistan
rank: Official at UTY, the national railway; tender committee members
d: The French rail engineer Systra paid an official at UTY, Uzbekistan's national railway company, through a firm he secretly owned, in a rigged tender. A complaint from Japanese authorities said the official asked a Japan Transportation Consultants employee to submit an inappropriate bid so Systra would win a railway electrification project. Systra would do the same on another line. Both had to use a UK company, Kirkliston Development, as subcontractor. Investigators found Systra paid nearly $576,000 to a Kirkliston account in Latvia whose beneficial owner was the official, and Kirkliston rented out overpriced flats owned by tender committee members. Systra agreed a €7,496,000 French settlement in July 2021, which also covered the Baku metro.
cite: Willkie Compliance Concourse, July 2021; Parquet National Financier press release, 13 July 2021
inside: A French engineering firm paid a railway official through his hidden company, and that official arranged a rigged bid so the firm won Uzbekistan's tender.

n: Systra paid 30% commissions to a Baku metro agent close to a minister
rank: Agent of the Baku public metro company, close to the minister
d: The French rail engineer Systra won an engineering contract for the Baku metro in May 2009, and French investigators determined the contract was obtained corruptly. A Systra subsidiary in Azerbaijan paid so-called commissions, through intermediaries in the US and Scotland, to an agent of the public metro company who had close access to the minister in charge of the metro. These came to about 30% of all invoices on the project, which ran from 2009 to 2017 and brought gross revenue of over €44 million. The contracts ended after a management change at the metro company. Systra agreed a €7,496,000 settlement with France's financial prosecutor in July 2021, which also covered Uzbekistan.
cite: Willkie Compliance Concourse, July 2021; Parquet National Financier press release, 13 July 2021
inside: A French engineering firm paid about 30% of its invoices to an agent of Baku's public metro company to obtain and keep the metro contract.

n: Technip's Brazilian units admitted unlawful acts and repaid bribes to Petrobras
rank: Petrobras, the state oil company
d: Technip Brasil and Flexibrás, Brazilian units of the Technip engineering group, admitted unlawful acts, including improper advantages to public agents, in a leniency deal, an agreement to cooperate in exchange for lighter penalties. It was announced on 25 June 2019 by Brazil's federal comptroller (CGU), its attorney general's office, federal prosecutors and the US Justice Department, who described it as the first global deal of Operation Car Wash. The companies agreed to pay about R$1.13 billion. Of the R$819 million paid in Brazil, all to the state oil company Petrobras, R$191 million was restitution of bribes and damages and R$439 million was improper profit. They gave evidence on more than 40 people and companies. The reports cited do not name the bribed officials.
cite: CGU/AGU leniency agreement, 2019; Legismap, 26 June 2019; Suno Notícias, 25 June 2019; Felsberg Advogados, 12 July 2019
inside: An engineering group's Brazilian units admitted unlawful acts and agreed to repay bribes and damages on Brazilian projects, with Petrobras named as the injured party.

n: MullenLowe and FCB paid bribes for Brazilian state advertising accounts
rank: Federal deputy André Vargas; state advertising contracts
d: The advertising agencies MullenLowe Brasil and FCB Brasil accepted responsibility for paying bribes to win advertising bids at federal bodies: the state bank Caixa, the health ministry and the fuel distributor BR Distribuidora. In September 2015 Judge Sergio Moro convicted former federal deputy André Vargas and Ricardo Hoffmann, a former director of MullenLowe, then called Borghi Lowe, over about R$1.1 million paid to two companies controlled by Vargas and his brothers. In May 2017 a federal appeal court upheld the convictions, setting nearly 14 years for each. On 16 April 2018 the federal comptroller, the attorney general's office and prosecutors announced a joint leniency deal, with R$53.1 million going to the bodies affected. A public servant the companies identified faced an improbity suit and a disciplinary case.
cite: IstoÉ Dinheiro, 16 Mar 2018; Tribuna do Paraná/Estadão, 16 Apr 2018; Exame and Congresso em Foco, Sept 2015; Jornal do Comércio, 31 May 2017
inside: Advertising agencies admitted paying bribes to win state advertising accounts, and a court convicted one executive and a federal deputy over money sent to the deputy's companies.

n: Braskem's improper payments produced Brazilian government rules
rank: Federal contracts and normative acts
d: The petrochemical company Braskem settled with Brazil's federal comptroller (CGU) and attorney general's office over contracts and official rules obtained with improper payments. The leniency deal, a cooperation agreement that reduces penalties, was signed on 31 May 2019. Braskem agreed to pay R$2.87 billion by January 2025. The CGU said the sum covers damage, illicit enrichment and fines relating to fraudulent contracts using federal funds and to normative acts, meaning official rules, produced from improper payments. Braskem gave information and evidence on more than 60 people and companies. The deal recognises its earlier agreements with US and Swiss authorities and Brazil's federal prosecutors. The report cited does not name the officials or the rules.
cite: Estadão via Tribuna do Paraná, 3 June 2019
inside: Brazil's comptroller said a petrochemical company's improper payments produced official rules and fraudulent federally funded contracts, and the company agreed to repay R$2.87 billion.

n: French firms accused of Scorpene submarine kickbacks in Malaysia
rank: Defence ministry under minister Najib Razak
d: French investigators allege that the shipbuilder DCN and the defence group Thales paid kickbacks through Abdul Razak Baginda, an adviser to Najib Razak, to sell Malaysia submarines in 2002, when Najib was defence minister. A firm whose main shareholder was Baginda received €30 million for consultancy that investigators believe was a front, and €114 million allegedly went to Perimekar, controlled by his wife at the time. A complaint by rights group Suaram began the inquiry in 2010. France charged Baginda and four former executives in 2017 and Thales in 2022; all deny wrongdoing. Prosecutors later recommended a trial for Baginda, others and the firms, and a magistrate must decide. They claim Najib helped prepare the contracts, but seek no trial for him, and Bloomberg reported no evidence he received payments.
cite: AFP via Free Malaysia Today, 19 July 2017; The Malaysian Insight, 1 Aug 2017; The Edge Malaysia (citing Financial Times); dettedelafrance.fr; Free Malaysia Today, 27 Apr 2022; The Vibes citing Bloomberg, 21 May 2025
inside: French investigators allege two defence firms paid kickbacks through the defence minister's close adviser to win Malaysia's submarine purchase; those charged deny wrongdoing.

n: Russia's SVR recruited Portuguese intelligence officer Carvalhão Gil
rank: Officer of the SIS, Portugal's security intelligence service
d: Russia's SVR, its foreign intelligence service, recruited Frederico Carvalhão Gil, an officer of Portugal's Security Intelligence Service (SIS), to hand over state secrets for money. Italian police caught him in Rome with an SVR officer, Sergey Pozdnyakov, on 21 May 2016, and he was extradited to Portugal. Police seized 10,000 euros that the SVR officer had paid him, and a handwritten document holding state secrets was found on Pozdnyakov. Diário de Notícias says a 2015 tip put him under surveillance. On 8 February 2018 a Lisbon criminal court sentenced Carvalhão Gil to seven years and four months for espionage and corruption. The Lisbon appeal court upheld the term and he was jailed to serve it.
cite: Diário de Notícias, 8 Feb 2018 and 9 Feb 2018; Sábado, profile of Carvalhão Gil
inside: Russia's foreign intelligence service recruited and paid an officer inside Portugal's own intelligence service, so secrets he was meant to protect went to Moscow.

n: Polish defence ministry officer Zbigniew J. jailed as a Russian spy
rank: Lieutenant colonel, defence ministry education and promotion department
d: Russian military intelligence, the GRU, had a source inside Poland's defence ministry: Lieutenant Colonel Zbigniew J., who worked in its education and promotion department. Poland's Internal Security Agency arrested him in October 2014, using material from military counter-intelligence. Prosecutors indicted him on 11 February 2016 for working with a foreign intelligence service, and members of the parliamentary special services committee said that service was the GRU. A military court in Warsaw heard the case behind closed doors and on 30 May 2016 sentenced him to six years, well below the 15-year maximum, reportedly because he cooperated. Reports give only his first name and an initial.
cite: Defence24, 23 Feb 2016; SpaceDaily, 30 May 2016
inside: Russian military intelligence gained a serving officer inside Poland's defence ministry, who passed it information from a post he held for the Polish state.

n: Russia's GRU had a source in Poland's ministry handling gas supplies
rank: Ministry employee on energy infrastructure projects
d: Russian military intelligence, the GRU, obtained information from inside a Polish ministry through an employee named as Marek W., who worked on strategic energy projects and on seeking EU money to reduce Poland's reliance on Russian gas. Court records place him at the economy ministry; other reports say energy. The Internal Security Agency detained him on 23 March 2018. Prosecutors charged that he passed the GRU information from his job between 2014 and 2016, and Polish media reported it concerned the Nord Stream 2 pipeline from Russia to Germany, which Poland opposed. On 5 July 2019 Warsaw District Court, dating the activity to March 2015 to January 2016, sentenced him to three years, and Defense News reports a 10-year ban from public administration.
cite: RFE/RL, 6 Jul 2019; AP via Washington Times, 6 Sep 2018; Belsat; Defense News, 2 Dec 2019; Polsat News, 5 Jul 2019
inside: Russian military intelligence had a ministry employee working on cutting Poland's dependence on Russian gas pass it information from his job, on policy against Moscow's interests.

n: Warsaw registry official Tomasz L. accused of feeding records to Russian spies
rank: Warsaw city hall official in the civil registry archives
d: Polish prosecutors say Russian intelligence recruited Tomasz L., a Warsaw city hall official with access to the capital's civil registry archives, and worked with him from 2017 until the Internal Security Agency detained him in March 2022. The indictment, filed on 11 September 2025, alleges he copied records and official templates and sent them to Russian officers by covert radio. Prosecutors say the data helped produce false identities for deep-cover officers, known as illegals. Rzeczpospolita reported that he copied hundreds of certificates from parish registers of former Polish territories. TVN24 reported that in 2006 he sat on the commission winding up Poland's old military intelligence services. He has not admitted guilt.
cite: Notes from Poland, 9 Oct 2025; citing National Prosecutor's Office, Rzeczpospolita and TVN24
inside: Prosecutors say Russian intelligence recruited a Warsaw archive official, who used his access to official records to help build false identities for its deep-cover officers.

n: Belarus's military spies recruited a worker at Lithuania's air traffic firm
rank: Employee of state air navigation company Oro Navigacija
d: Belarusian military intelligence obtained information from inside Oro Navigacija, the state company that runs air traffic services over Lithuania, through its employee Romualdas Lipskis. Prosecutors said he secretly photographed documents and passed details about Lithuania's army and strategically important state companies to the Main Intelligence Directorate of Belarus's General Staff. He was arrested in 2013 after a counter-intelligence operation lasting about three years, and the case was announced in November 2014. On 5 November 2015 a Vilnius court sentenced him to three years and three months. The judge called the term close to the minimum because the documents had almost no intelligence value. Lipskis denied guilt and said he would appeal. In May 2016 the Court of Appeals raised the term to five years.
cite: Fox News, 5 Nov 2015; RFE/RL, Nov 2015; Baltic Course, 11 Nov 2014; Belsat; The Lithuania Tribune, 24 May 2016
inside: Belarus's military intelligence used an employee inside Lithuania's state air traffic company, who photographed documents there and passed on information about the country's army and state firms.

n: Worker at Lithuania's Šiauliai air base photographed orders for Russia
rank: Employee at the Lithuanian Air Force base in Šiauliai
d: A Russian intelligence organisation paid a man working at the Lithuanian Air Force's base in Šiauliai, and a retired accomplice, for information from inside it. From autumn 2014 the two photographed official documents, premises, airport and base layouts, plans and command orders, material that was not public though not classified. They made more than 35 handovers and met their contacts in Russia or other countries. Lithuanian intelligence passed the case to law enforcement, and both were detained on 11 December 2017. On 20 June 2019 Šiauliai Regional Court, in a closed hearing, gave each four years and nine months after they pleaded guilty. The court confiscated almost 6,500 euros. The men were not named.
cite: BNS via LRT, 20 Jun 2019
inside: Russian intelligence paid a worker inside a Lithuanian air force base to photograph its layouts, plans and command orders, so a military base's internal records reached Moscow.

n: Former Latvian interior ministry official Buraks got 15 years for spying for Russia
rank: Official at the Interior Ministry's Information Centre
d: A Latvian court convicted Oļegs Buraks, a former official at the interior ministry's Information Centre, of long-running and systematic espionage for Russian special services. He retired in late 2006 and was detained in October 2018. Riga's Vidzeme Suburbs Court gave him 15 years in August 2020, and the sentence became final in 2023. Latvian public media LSM said in January 2024 that this was the heaviest term among the ten people found guilty of espionage in Latvia. Baltic Sentinel described the sentence as being for mishandling classified state materials and said he died in 2024 at Riga Central Hospital; European Pravda placed the death at Riga Central Prison.
cite: LSM, 23 Jan 2024; TASS, Aug 2020; European Pravda, 24 Sep 2024; Baltic Sentinel, 19 Mar 2025
inside: A Latvian court convicted a former interior ministry official of long-running, systematic espionage for Russian special services.

n: Latvia's security service says a Russian recruiter targeted its officer
rank: Official of the State Security Service (VDD)
d: Latvia's State Security Service (VDD), the country's counter-intelligence agency, said a Latvian citizen acting for Russian intelligence tried to recruit one of its own officials. The official was to have gathered and passed on secret information available through their duties. The VDD opened criminal proceedings on 8 July 2019, asked the Prosecutor General's office to prosecute the suspect on 17 February 2020, and made the request public on 2 March 2020. The suspect was then under arrest and neither person was named. The allegation comes from the VDD and had not been tested in court at that point. The source cited does not give the outcome of the case.
cite: LSM, Mar 2020, citing the VDD
inside: Latvia's security service alleges a Latvian citizen working for Russian intelligence tried to recruit one of its officials, to get the agency's own secrets through someone already inside.

n: Latvian Railways employee jailed for sending NATO train videos to Moscow
rank: Employee of Latvian Railways
d: A contact in Moscow received information from inside Latvian Railways, the national rail company, through its employee Aleksandrs Krasnopjorovs, a resident without Latvian citizenship. He was charged with sending videos of NATO military supply trains to Moscow. He denied the accusation and said he had only shared footage with a friend. The investigative centre Re:Baltica found that he had also sent lists of unusual train routes. He was sentenced to three years in prison in 2019. Baltic Sentinel reports the case as part of Russian spying in Latvia but does not name the Russian service behind the contact.
cite: Baltic Sentinel, 19 Mar 2025, citing Re:Baltica
inside: A contact in Moscow got footage of NATO supply trains and route lists from a worker inside Latvia's national railway, which carried those shipments.

n: Bulgarian reserve general at defence ministry accused of spying for Russia
rank: Reserve general employed by the Defence Ministry
d: Bulgarian prosecutors said in March 2022 that a Russian embassy adviser in Sofia had a source inside the Defence Ministry: a reserve general employed there, who had served on missions abroad. They alleged he passed state secrets to the adviser from 2016 onward. The general, who was not named, was placed in 72-hour custody and faced espionage charges. On 2 March 2022 the Foreign Ministry gave two Russian diplomats 48 hours to leave and summoned Russia's ambassador. The source cited does not say how he was recruited or how the case ended. The allegations had not been tested in court at that time.
cite: Sofia Globe, 2 Mar 2022, citing Bulgaria's Prosecutor's Office and Foreign Ministry
inside: Prosecutors allege a Russian embassy adviser received state secrets for years from a reserve general working inside Bulgaria's Defence Ministry, so those secrets served Moscow.

n: Two senior officers of Bulgaria's security agency investigated as Russian spies
rank: Sector head and department head, State Agency for National Security
d: Bulgarian prosecutors said on 1 April 2022 they were investigating whether Russia had sources inside the State Agency for National Security (SANS), the country's counter-intelligence service. The suspects were a SANS sector head, a department head and an employee of a government ministry. SANS chief Plamen Tonchev said both officers had worked there for over five years and had been dismissed after an internal inquiry. A prosecution spokesperson alleged they passed information using special technical means rather than meeting in person. No arrests had been made. Prosecutors also said the first secretary at Russia's embassy had committed espionage. The source cited does not give the outcome, and no one was named.
cite: Sofia Globe, 1 Apr 2022, citing the Specialised Prosecutor's Office and SANS
inside: Prosecutors suspect Russia had two senior officers inside Bulgaria's counter-intelligence agency and a ministry employee passing it information from the bodies meant to stop such spying.

n: Russian diplomat paid a consultant at Swedish truckmaker Scania for secrets
rank: Consultant at Scania
d: A Russian diplomat suspected of being an intelligence officer obtained information from inside Swedish truckmaker Scania through a 47-year-old tech consultant. Prosecutors said he copied material on manufacturing, including source code, from his work computer and photographed his screen to avoid the IT logs. He was arrested in February 2019 while dining with the diplomat in Stockholm, having just received 27,800 kronor. The diplomat was released because of diplomatic immunity, and Sweden and Russia then acted against each other's envoys. In September 2021 Gothenburg District Court sentenced the consultant to three years over Scania and acquitted him over Volvo Cars. He denied wrongdoing and his lawyer said he would appeal.
cite: Sveriges Radio, 15 Sep 2021; The Moscow Times, 22 Feb 2021; The Local, 26 Aug 2021
inside: A suspected Russian intelligence officer paid a consultant working inside Scania, who took company material from his work computer, so industrial information reached Russia.

n: Austrian ex-operations chief Weiss allegedly relayed Marsalek's orders
who: Jan Marsalek network, linked to Russia's FSB
rank: Head of operations at Austria's intelligence agency, the BVT
d: Austrian prosecutors allege that Martin Weiss, a former operations chief at the BVT, Austria's domestic intelligence agency, helped Russia-linked Jan Marsalek reach inside it. Marsalek, the former Wirecard executive, is suspected of working for Russian intelligence. An arrest warrant described in Britannica's news report alleges Weiss began working for Marsalek after leaving the BVT in 2018 and relayed orders from Marsalek and Russian operatives to his former subordinate, Egisto Ott. Profil reports Weiss was allegedly close to Marsalek from 2015 and told investigators he passed on Marsalek's orders. Weiss was briefly arrested, then fled to Dubai, and was not tried. On 20 May 2026 a Vienna court convicted Ott of spying against Austria and other offences and gave him four years and one month. He plans to appeal.
cite: Britannica news report on the Ott warrant; Profil, Jan and May 2026; Brussels Signal, May 2026
inside: Prosecutors allege a former Austrian intelligence operations chief worked for a Russia-linked fugitive and passed his orders to an officer he once supervised.

n: Elbasan cocaine group allegedly paid Albanian judges and police chiefs
rank: Judge and former senior police officials
d: Prosecutors say a cocaine-trafficking group from the Albanian city of Elbasan paid judges and senior police officers to work for it. SPAK, Albania's special anti-corruption and organised-crime prosecutor, said in November 2024 that the group, led by Suel Çela, bought cocaine in Latin America and sold it across Europe. Messages from Sky ECC, an encrypted phone service used by criminals, allegedly showed officials suppressing charges and cutting sentences for money. Twenty-one arrest warrants were issued, and 18 people were ordered into prison, among them former senior police officials and a judge. Two journalists were also summoned over allegedly paid coverage. In February 2026 SPAK sent 21 defendants to trial; no verdict had been reported.
inside: Prosecutors say a cocaine group paid Albanian judges and senior police, so that charges were suppressed and sentences cut in the traffickers' favour.
cite: Albanian Times, 26 Nov 2024, on SPAK investigation; Shqiptarja, 22 Feb 2026

n: Albanian police crime chiefs charged with tipping off cannabis trafficking groups
rank: Police crime chiefs of Himara and Lushnja; head of Saranda border police
d: Albanian prosecutors say police commanders worked for two cannabis-trafficking groups. In an operation reported on 1 March 2025, SPAK, the special anti-corruption prosecutor, and the State Police acted on ten arrest warrants after reading Sky ECC messages, an encrypted phone service used by criminals. SPAK says Shkëlzen Ruska and Ervis Alisinanaj, crime chiefs of the Himara and Lushnja police, former officer Erdit Hazizaj, and Dervishi, head of the Saranda border police, passed the groups details of anti-drug operations. The cannabis was grown around Saranda and Gjirokastër for sale in Greece. Three of the men denied the charges through lawyers. In May 2026 SPAK sent those three to trial, Alisinanaj on abuse of duty only. No verdict was found.
inside: Prosecutors say cannabis traffickers had police chiefs and a border commander telling them about anti-drug operations, so the officers' work protected the groups they should have stopped.
cite: A2 CNN Albania, 1 and 3 Mar 2025; Balkanweb, 29 May 2026

n: Albania's IT agency tenders allegedly steered to a contractor group
rank: Director of AKSHI, the state IT agency
d: Prosecutors say two entrepreneurs, Ergys Agasi and Ermal Beqiri, worked with the director of Albania's state IT agency in a structured criminal group that steered public contracts to their firms. The agency, AKSHI, has had a budget of about €500 million since 2017. SPAK, the anti-corruption prosecutor, suspects at least 19 tenders worth about €60 million were written for a predetermined winner under director Mirlinda Karçanaj, placed under house arrest in December 2025. The firms gained access to police and prison security systems and allegedly made tens of millions of euros. Both entrepreneurs evaded that operation. Beqiri was arrested in France in July 2026 and Agasi in Durrës that August; his lawyer says he is innocent. An opposition MP claims Agasi chose a police director. No verdict has been reported.
inside: Prosecutors say private contractors worked with the head of a state agency so that public tenders were written for them, also giving them access to police systems.
cite: Citizens.al, 30 Dec 2025; Tirana Times, 28 Aug 2026; Balkanweb, 28 Aug 2026; Wikipedia, AKSHI public procurement scandal

n: US says Bosnia's intelligence chief Mehmedagić worked with criminal networks
rank: Director General, Intelligence and Security Agency (OSA)
d: The United States says criminal networks had the head of Bosnia's state intelligence service working with them. In March 2023 the US Treasury sanctioned Osman Mehmedagić, Director General of the Intelligence and Security Agency (OSA), citing credible information that he worked with criminal networks to enrich himself and his party, the SDA. It also said he used state-owned BH Telecom to collect phone activity on politicians outside the SDA. The State Department added a corruption designation in December 2023. That month Bosnian police arrested him and the president of the state court on suspicion of wiretapping judges and prosecutors in 2020; the prosecutor said organised-crime cases were the target. He entered no plea, recorded as not guilty, and his trial began on 8 April 2026. No verdict was found.
inside: US sanctions cite credible information that the state spy chief worked with criminal networks; Bosnian prosecutors suspect organised-crime cases were targeted by illegal eavesdropping.
cite: US Treasury, 15 Mar 2023; N1, 11 Dec 2023; RFE/RL, 19 Dec 2023 and 29 Oct 2025; Fena, 8 Apr 2026

n: US says Bosnian state prosecutor Kajmaković hid evidence for traffickers
rank: Prosecutor, State Prosecutor's Office
d: The US State Department says a Bosnian state prosecutor worked in support of drug traffickers. In December 2023 it designated Diana Kajmaković, a former deputy chief prosecutor, for significant corruption, saying that, for personal gain, she helped hide evidence and prevent prosecution in support of narcotics traffickers and other criminals, and tried to block an investigation into associates. She had been on the team handling the Sky and Anom cases, built on encrypted messages. N1 reported that she was taken off the team after her name came up in a conversation between two alleged criminals. In December 2023 a Bosnian disciplinary commission found she abused her office and demoted her to ordinary prosecutor, which a second commission upheld. The US designation is not a court verdict.
inside: The US says traffickers had a prosecutor inside the state office meant to charge them, who hid evidence and obstructed cases for personal gain.

n: Sky and Anom messages: Bosnian judge and 14 police among 100 suspects
rank: Judge in Bijeljina; 14 officers of police and law-enforcement agencies
d: Messages on Sky and Anom, two encrypted phone services used by criminals, led Bosnian prosecutors to suspect that crime groups had contacts inside the police and courts. By January 2023 more than 100 suspects had been detained over 16 months. Fourteen came from police and law-enforcement agencies, along with a judge in Bijeljina and a former adviser to the Ministry of Security. The judge, Jovan Savić, was suspected of leaking information to criminals. Republika Srpska's interior minister, Dragan Lukač, said in 2022 that some officers had supported criminals and committed crimes with them. Chief Prosecutor Milanko Kajganić warned that anti-crime institutions were contaminated. Two indictments had been filed; these are suspicions, not verdicts.
inside: Prosecutors suspect crime groups had a judge and police officers passing them confidential information from inside the bodies meant to investigate them, as encrypted messages later appeared to show.

n: Montenegro's ex-police chief Veljović accused of aiding cigarette smugglers
rank: Director of the Police Directorate; security adviser to the president
d: Montenegrin prosecutors say a cigarette-smuggling group had the country's former police chief among its members. Veselin Veljović ran the police directorate in two terms between 2007 and 2020 and then advised President Milo Djukanovic. He was arrested in July 2023 and charged with creating a criminal organisation, abuse of position and smuggling. The indictment says Aleksandar Mrkić organised smuggling from the free customs zone at the Port of Bar and that Veljović passed secret information to the group over Sky ECC, an encrypted phone service. Prosecutors also say Mrkić told him in 2020 he could become police director. Veljović has denied such accusations in the past.
inside: Prosecutors say smugglers had Montenegro's former police director passing them secret information, so that the force meant to stop them protected their business.
cite: AP via WTOP, 24 Jul 2023; Kurir, 30 Jan 2024

n: Slovak Special Prosecutor Kováčik accused of taking bribe to free underworld boss; conviction annulled
rank: Special Prosecutor
d: Slovak prosecutors allege that people acting for organised criminals bought the head of the office that prosecutes organised crime. Ľudovít Makó, a former financial administration criminal office chief, testified that in 2017 he gave Special Prosecutor Dušan Kováčik €50,000 over the release of underworld boss Ľubomír Kudlička. In May 2022 the Supreme Court upheld convictions for bribery and leaking, cut the sentence from 14 years to eight with a €100,000 fine, and acquitted him of supporting a criminal group. Justice Minister Boris Susko suspended the sentence in 2024, freeing him. In December 2025 the Supreme Court annulled those judgments and ordered a retrial. In May 2026 the trial court sent the case back to pre-trial; prosecutors appealed. A separate 2024 guilty verdict, over €50,000 hidden in a book, was appealed.
inside: Prosecutors allege criminals' intermediaries paid the top organised-crime prosecutor to free a boss and bury cases; his final conviction was annulled in 2025 and the case is unresolved.
cite: Slovak Spectator, 2021, 2022, 3 Sep 2024; RTVS; Euronews, 2 Jun 2022; China-CEE, Nov 2020; SITA, 11 Dec 2025; Noviny, 19 Oct 2026; Noviny, 3 Sep 2024; SITA, Kováčik trial testimony by Makó

n: Portuguese prosecutor convicted of taking money linked to Angola's vice-president
rank: Prosecutor, Public Ministry
d: A Lisbon court found that a Portuguese prosecutor took money linked to a foreign vice-president to close an inquiry into him. In Operation Fizz, former magistrate Orlando Figueira was sentenced to six years and eight months for corruption, money laundering, breaching judicial secrecy and forgery. Prosecutors said he received more than €760,000 from Manuel Vicente, then Angola's vice-president, to shelve an inquiry into €3.8 million that Vicente used to buy property in Estoril. All denied the charges. Vicente's case was sent to Angola. Lisbon's appeal court confirmed the term in 2021. Figueira entered Évora prison on 2 October 2024 and the Supreme Court refused his release. In January 2025 the appeal court ruled the secrecy offence time-barred and ordered a new sentence; no figure was found.
inside: A court found a foreign politician's money reached a prosecutor inside Portugal's justice system, who shelved the inquiry into that politician's own property purchase.
cite: Portugal Resident; Observador, 24 Nov 2021, 16 Oct 2024 and 17 Jan 2025; RTP, 2 Oct 2024

n: De Silva review: 85% of UDA intelligence came from security forces
rank: Army, RUC Special Branch and Security Service sources
d: A British government review found that the UDA, a loyalist paramilitary group, drew most of its targeting information from people inside the security forces. Sir Desmond de Silva reported in 2012 on the 1989 murder of Belfast solicitor Patrick Finucane. The Security Service had assessed in 1985 that 85% of UDA intelligence came from security force sources, and he found that largely unchanged by 1989. Army informer Brian Nelson and state-paid agent William Stobie were involved in the killing. RUC Special Branch knew of the threat and did not act, and in 1991 recruited Ken Barrett as an agent rather than let detectives prosecute him; he was convicted in 2004. Prime Minister David Cameron apologised. De Silva found no overarching state conspiracy.
inside: A loyalist armed group had sources in the army and police feeding it target information, and agents it shared with the state were shielded from prosecution.
cite: UK Government, Prime Minister's statement to Parliament, 12 Dec 2012

n: Smithwick Tribunal: someone in Dundalk Garda station tipped off the IRA
rank: Garda station, Dundalk
d: An Irish judicial tribunal found that someone in Dundalk Garda station, an Irish police post, was helping the IRA when two senior Northern Ireland police officers were killed. Chief Superintendent Harry Breen and Superintendent Bob Buchanan were shot dead near the border on 20 March 1989, shortly after meeting Irish police in Dundalk. Mr Justice Peter Smithwick reported in December 2013 after eight years, with no direct evidence against a named officer. He found Detective Sergeant Owen Corrigan had inappropriate dealings with the IRA and that there was some evidence he passed it information, not enough to tie him to the murders; Corrigan rejected the finding of an inappropriate relationship. The Irish government apologised to the families.
inside: An armed group outside the state had a source inside an Irish police station, the tribunal found, who tipped it off before it killed two visiting police officers.
cite: Irish Times, 4 Dec 2013 and later report on Corrigan's response; RTÉ, 3 Dec 2013

n: Neo-Nazi National Action's recruiter was a serving British Army corporal
rank: Corporal, Royal Anglian Regiment
d: The banned neo-Nazi group National Action tried to build membership inside the British Army, and a serving corporal acted as its recruiter. Mikko Vehviläinen joined the Army in 2012 and served in the Royal Anglian Regiment. Prosecutors described him as a key part of the group's strategy to grow in the armed forces; other members tried and failed to enlist. He was arrested in September 2017, convicted in March 2018 of belonging to National Action, and sentenced to eight years. He was cleared of possessing a document useful to a terrorist and of stirring up racial hatred, and was discharged from the Army.
inside: A banned neo-Nazi group had a serving corporal inside the army, working to its plan of drawing soldiers into its ranks.
cite: ITV News, 12 Nov 2018

n: Naumann Circle of ex-Nazi officials accused of setting out to infiltrate the FDP
rank: Free Democratic Party (FDP), North Rhine-Westphalia
d: A group of former Nazi officials were accused of setting out to infiltrate West German parties, above all the liberal Free Democratic Party (FDP). The Naumann Circle was led by Werner Naumann, last state secretary in the Nazi Propaganda Ministry, and included seven former Gauleiter (regional party chiefs). It planned to place trusted men in veterans' groups and local administrations. Around fifty former Nazi officials were elected as FDP candidates in North Rhine-Westphalia's November 1952 municipal elections. British forces, who had been tapping the group, arrested Naumann and six others in January 1953. In December 1954 a court dismissed the charges for lack of evidence, saying the group had no political effectiveness.
inside: Former Nazi officials worked to place their men in a governing coalition party, aiming to steer it from inside; a court later found no effect shown.
cite: Wikipedia (citing Frei 2002; Baldow 2012; The Times), Naumann Circle

n: IRA got false Irish passports through Garda sergeants, tribunal found
rank: Garda sergeants, Dundalk
d: An Irish tribunal found that the IRA got help from Irish police officers to obtain passports. Mr Justice Peter Smithwick, whose inquiry into two 1989 police murders reported in December 2013, found that Sergeant Leo Colton assisted the Provisional IRA in 1995 and 1996 by having a former colleague, Sergeant Finbarr Hickey, sign false passport applications. Hickey signed eight blank forms between January 1995 and April 1996, was convicted and jailed. He said he got no benefit and did not know who the forms were for. Colton denies any IRA involvement. Smithwick said the evidence did not show that Colton colluded in the 1989 murders.
inside: An armed group outside the state had a police sergeant arranging signatures from inside the force, so that its members could obtain false Irish passports.
cite: Irish Times, 4 Dec 2013; RTÉ, 3 Dec 2013

n: US says Veselinović group bribed Kosovo and Serbian security officials
rank: Kosovar and Serbian border and security officials; Srpska Lista vice-president
d: The US Treasury says a crime group run by Kosovo Serb businessman Zvonko Veselinović bribed security officials and backed politicians to protect its trade. In December 2021 it sanctioned him, his brother, and Milan Radojičić, vice-president of Srpska Lista, a Belgrade-backed Kosovo Serb party. It also listed Željko Bojić, former police operations chief for northern Kosovo. Treasury said the group bribed Kosovar and Serbian officials to smuggle goods, money, drugs and weapons, and that politicians gave it business control and protection in return for campaign support. A 2019 indictment alleged Radojičić and Veselinović led a group behind the killing of politician Oliver Ivanović. They denied it. In June 2024 a Pristina court convicted four others, two of them policemen; neither leader had been charged.
inside: The US says a smuggling group paid border and security officials and backed politicians, who then shielded its trade and gave it control of business areas.
cite: Prishtina Insight, 9 Dec 2021, on US Treasury OFAC action; Prishtina Insight, 28 Jun 2024

n: Bar's criminal police chief arrested in Montenegro cigarette-smuggling probe
rank: Head of the criminal police, Bar
d: Prosecutors allege that the former head of criminal police in the port city of Bar, Montenegro, worked with cigarette smugglers. Ilija Vasović was arrested on 6 June 2024 and indicted on 5 December 2024 for creating a criminal organisation and abuse of office. Published messages from Sky, an encrypted phone service used by criminals, date from January 2021. They appear to show Aleksandar Mrkić, a fugitive, instructing Vasović before a meeting with Miodrag Davidović, a businessman on the US sanctions list. In February 2025 Vasović pleaded not guilty and said he never disclosed official data. His case was merged with that of former police director Veselin Veljović. No verdict was reported by February 2026.
inside: Prosecutors allege a smuggling group had the local criminal police chief in the port it used acting on its instructions and passing it police information; he denies it.
cite: Vreme, 7 Jun 2024; Primorski, 5 Dec 2024 and 26 Feb 2025; ETV, 6 Feb 2026

n: Bosnia's state court president accused of taking a bribe from Zdravko Mamić
rank: President, Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina
d: Bosnian prosecutors say outside money reached the president of the state-level Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Ranko Debevec was arrested on 18 December 2023 and suspended. Prosecutors allege he took a bribe from Zdravko Mamić, a former Dinamo Zagreb football director convicted in Croatia, to help him in extradition-related proceedings in Bosnia, and another from a car dealership in Ljubuški. They also allege he and intelligence chief Osman Mehmedagić illegally wiretapped court and prosecution staff in 2020, and that wiretap orders vanished from court records. An indictment was confirmed on 12 August 2025, with media reporting a watch worth about €15,000 from Mamić. The trial opened on 8 April 2026, and no verdict had been found.
inside: Prosecutors allege a man convicted in Croatia paid the head of Bosnia's state court, so that the court would help him in his extradition proceedings.
cite: China-CEE Weekly Briefing, Feb 2024; Index.hr/Hina, 2 Jul 2025; FENA, 12 Aug 2025 and 8 Apr 2026

n: Serbia's deputy organised-crime police chief convicted over Belivuk associate
rank: Deputy head, organised-crime police service (SBPOK)
d: A Serbian court convicted a senior organised-crime police officer of acting for an associate of a crime group. Goran Papić, former deputy head of SBPOK, Serbia's organised-crime police service, demanded against regulations that a seized car be returned to a close associate of Veljko Belivuk. Belivuk is accused of leading a Belgrade criminal group whose indictment covers seven murders, and the group was arrested in February 2021. In August 2022 the Higher Court in Belgrade gave Papić one year and four months in prison and a ten-year ban on police work. In December 2022 the appeals court raised the prison term to two years. An N1 reporter said the gang's indictment contains nothing about its ties to the state.
inside: A senior officer of the police unit meant to fight organised crime used his post to get a seized car back for a gang leader's close associate.
cite: N1 Serbia, 11 Oct 2023; N1, 22 Feb 2022; N1, 9 Jan 2023; N1, 24 Dec 2022; Kurir, 24 Aug 2022

n: Former Tirana police chief Breçani sent to trial in cocaine group case
rank: Former Tirana police chief; head of crimes, Commissariat No. 6
d: Albanian prosecutors suspect that former police officers helped a cocaine group. SPAK, the special anti-corruption prosecutor, says the group moved 931 kg of cocaine in four episodes through Brazil, the Netherlands and Germany. Its case grew from decrypted messages on Sky ECC, an encrypted phone service used by criminals. On 20 November 2023 it issued eleven arrest warrants, and five people were arrested. They included Erzen Breçani, a former Tirana police chief, accused of aiding a crime's perpetrator and of money laundering, and Dedan Gjoni, a former head of crimes at a commissariat, accused of drug trafficking, providing the means for murder and abuse of duty. On 27 December 2024 the special court sent the case to trial. No verdict was found.
inside: Prosecutors suspect a cocaine group had former police, including a former Tirana chief, helping its crimes and laundering money, rather than investigating them.
cite: Shqiptarja, 2024, on Supreme Court decision; Shqiptarja, 27 Dec 2024, on referral to trial

n: Senior Tirana police officer accused of passing TIMS system data to a suspect in a drug inquiry
rank: Chief of criminal police; deputy chief, Tirana Police Station No. 3
d: Albanian prosecutors say a senior Tirana police officer gave data from a system called TIMS to a suspect in a drug-trafficking inquiry. SPAK, the special anti-corruption prosecutor, raided sites in Shkodër, Elbasan, Vlora and Tirana in July 2025. It identified 13 suspects in a group moving cocaine, cannabis and heroin from South America to the EU, with 3,585 kg of cocaine seized in 2020 and 2021. In October 2025 SPAK split off part of the case and sent six people to trial, including Erjon Dani, then criminal police chief and deputy head of Police Station No. 3. All six are charged with unlawful influence, allegedly taking €4,000 to €7,500 from citizens in 2020 by promising to sway justice officials. Dani also faces abuse of office. No verdict was found.
inside: Prosecutors say a senior officer passed data from the TIMS system to a suspect, and that he and others took money by promising to sway justice officials.
cite: Vox News Albania, 11 Jul 2025; Alfa Press and Shqiptarja, 28 Oct 2025

n: Vlora drug network allegedly had police officer leaking checks and border data
rank: State Police officer
d: Albanian prosecutors say a drug and murder network based in the coastal city of Vlora had a police officer working for it. A special court ordered eight suspects held on 5 March 2026, on a case from SPAK, the special anti-corruption prosecutor. The network allegedly funded cocaine purchases in Latin America and moved drugs to the EU, with 750 kg seized at Rotterdam. Two suspects allegedly organised the 2021 killing of Gentjan Qarri. The officer, named only as R.K., allegedly arranged drug transport, leaked details of police checks, deleted phone data, and misused TIMS, the national border-control database. He was placed in pre-trial detention. These are allegations.
inside: Prosecutors allege a trafficking network had a police officer arranging its transport, warning it of checks and searching the border database on its behalf.
cite: Albanian Daily News, 7 Mar 2026; Balkanweb, 7 Mar 2026

n: Slovak spy chief Pčolinský accused of taking €40,000 from lawyer Kollár, acquitted in 2025
rank: Director, Slovak Information Service (SIS)
d: Slovak prosecutors said a lawyer charged with corrupting judges bought protection from the head of the country's intelligence service. Vladimír Pčolinský, former director of the Slovak Information Service (SIS), was accused of taking part of a €40,000 bribe from Zoroslav Kollár in August 2020, split with his deputy Boris Beňa, to stop SIS officials wiretapping Kollár. Ľudovít Makó allegedly carried the money. Beňa and Makó confessed, and Kollár admitted the bribe in a plea deal. Pčolinský denied it. He was held for months, a first case ended in acquittal, and he was charged again in February 2022. On 16 June 2025 a court acquitted him, finding no clear evidence he took part or received money. Prosecutors appealed.
inside: Prosecutors said an outsider facing investigation paid the intelligence chief and his deputy to stop the service's agents listening to his phone; a court acquitted the chief in 2025, subject to appeal.
cite: Slovak Spectator, 2022; SITA and Noviny, 16 Jun 2025

n: Operation Gale: lawyer Kollár allegedly paid Slovak Supreme Court judges
rank: Supreme Court judges; former Supreme Court vice-chair
d: Slovak police charged a lawyer and senior judges in a case of bribes paid to judges. In late October 2020 the National Criminal Agency's Operation Gale detained former Supreme Court vice-chair Jarmila Urbancová, Supreme Court judge Jozef Kolcun, former Bratislava district court vice-chair Katarína Bartlaská, judge David Lindtner and lawyer Zoroslav Kollár. On 31 October a specialised court ordered Urbancová, Lindtner and Kollár held, citing possible witness tampering. They were charged with accepting bribes and interfering with judicial independence, and Kollár was reported as charged with corrupting judges. Kolcun, charged with accepting €30,000 and €10,000, was to be prosecuted at liberty after the Constitutional Court refused custody. An outcome was not confirmed.
inside: Police allege money from outside the courts reached Supreme Court judges through a lawyer, in a case charged as interference with the independence of the judiciary.
cite: China-CEE, Slovakia report, Nov 2020; Slovak Spectator, 11 Mar 2021

n: Far-right Nordkreuz network drew police ammunition and data from inside
rank: Special operations police unit (SEK), Mecklenburg-Vorpommern
d: A far-right network preparing for social collapse had officers of a German police commando unit inside it. Nordkreuz was a Telegram group of about 30 people, founded by Marko G., a former SEK officer. Prosecutors alleged three serving commandos stole police ammunition for it. Cartridges at his home were traced to about a dozen police and military depots, and another member's binder of political opponents contained data from a police computer. An inquiry found eight of the unit's 12 members were linked to the network. Marko G. got a 21-month suspended sentence, made final in February 2021. Saxony investigated 17 officers over ammunition paid to a range where the group trained; one was fined in 2025, and experts saw no evidence of far-right links.
inside: A far-right network with police among its members drew state ammunition and police data out of the force, using the state's own stores for its plans.
cite: VICE, 27 Nov 2019; NZ Herald, 2020; Nordkurier, Feb 2021; dpa via t-online, 31 Mar 2021; taz, 17 Mar 2022; Nordkurier, 14 Apr 2025

n: Samsung Heavy paid two Petrobras officials over a $636m drillship deal
rank: Two Petrobras officials
d: Samsung Heavy Industries, a South Korean shipbuilder, got money to two officials of Petrobras, Brazil's state oil company, while seeking a drillship deal. A drillship is a vessel that drills for oil at sea. It agreed a $20 million commission to a Brazilian agent and raised the drillship's price by $20 million. From 2008 to 2011 at least $4 million reached accounts the two officials controlled, described as repayment of a sham loan. A non-binding agreement with Petrobras came on 18 December 2007, and the $636,040,000 purchase agreement with a Houston drilling company on 21 December. On 22 November 2019 the company made a deferred prosecution agreement with the US Justice Department, meaning charges are held back if it meets the terms, with a $75,481,600 penalty.
inside: A foreign shipbuilder routed money to two Petrobras officials through an agent, in a deal where Petrobras signed a non-binding agreement and a drilling company bought the $636 million vessel.
cite: Miller & Chevalier, FCPA Winter Review 2020 (summarising US DOJ and SEC filings)

n: Ericsson paid Saudi state-firm staff and fixers for $700m of contracts
rank: Employees of a Saudi state-owned enterprise
d: Ericsson, the Swedish telecoms equipment maker, paid people who could sway a Saudi state-owned enterprise, and later paid for the enterprise's staff to travel. In 2012 and 2013 its Saudi branch paid about $40 million through false consulting deals with two individuals who could influence the enterprise, and it received nine contracts worth over $700 million. From 2015 to 2017 the branch paid for leisure trips, including for family members, for employees of the enterprise in order to win orders, and earned at least $40.54 million from that customer. These facts came out in the US Securities and Exchange Commission's December 2019 case. Ericsson's combined US settlement exceeded $1 billion across several countries.
inside: A foreign equipment maker paid people with influence over a Saudi state firm and funded its employees' holidays, and the firm's orders and contracts went to Ericsson.
cite: Miller & Chevalier, FCPA Winter Review 2020 (summarising US DOJ and SEC filings); Phillips & Cohen, largest FCPA settlements

n: Ericsson funded gifts and agents around Chinese state telecom customers
rank: Staff of Chinese state-owned customers
d: Ericsson, the Swedish telecoms equipment maker, spent money on staff of its Chinese state-owned customers, and on agents connected to them, to win business. From the early 1990s it kept an expense account of about $19.5 million for gifts, travel and entertainment for those customers. After it restricted third-party agents in 2013, executives used false service contracts to keep paying agents with ties to the customers, a second scheme of $31.5 million that ran to 2016. The conduct formed part of the case the US resolved in December 2019, in which Ericsson's Egyptian subsidiary pleaded guilty. A summary of the case says the schemes won contracts from state entities, without listing the Chinese contracts one by one.
inside: A foreign equipment maker spent money on staff of Chinese state-owned customers and agents tied to them, in order to win those state customers' telecoms contracts.
cite: Miller & Chevalier, FCPA Winter Review 2020 (summarising US DOJ and SEC filings); SEC release via Newsfile, Dec 2019; JD Supra on the Ericsson resolution; Phillips & Cohen, largest FCPA settlements

n: Ericsson's Vietnam slush fund paid agents and cash gifts to state customers
rank: Staff of Vietnamese state-owned customers
d: Ericsson, the Swedish telecoms equipment maker, ran off-the-books money in Vietnam to pay people around its state-owned customers. From about 2011 to 2015, Ericsson units used a consultant to build slush funds, meaning money kept outside the normal accounts. The money went to sub-agents for state-owned customers, to third parties who would not have passed background checks, and to cash gifts for customers. The US Justice Department put the total at $4.8 million and the Securities and Exchange Commission at about $11.4 million. The conduct was part of the December 2019 US case against Ericsson. A summary of the case says the schemes won contracts from state entities, but it does not list the Vietnamese contracts.
inside: A foreign equipment maker used hidden funds to pay agents and give cash to staff of Vietnamese state-owned customers, in order to win those customers' business.
cite: Miller & Chevalier, FCPA Winter Review 2020 (summarising US DOJ and SEC filings); Phillips & Cohen, largest FCPA settlements

n: Alstom paid an Indonesian MP and power-firm head for a $118m contract
rank: Member of parliament; head of the state electricity company
d: Alstom, the French power and rail engineering group, got bribes to a senior Indonesian member of parliament and the head of the state electricity company to win a $118 million contract for Alstom Power and the Japanese trader Marubeni. Consultants were used to disguise the payments. Alstom and three subsidiaries resolved a US case with the Justice Department in December 2014. Charges against a former senior Alstom executive, Lawrence Hoskins, were brought in July 2013, and in November 2019 a jury convicted him on 11 of 12 counts. Later rulings in his case are not covered here.
inside: A foreign engineering group paid an Indonesian MP and the state electricity chief through consultants, and the state contract worth $118 million went to its own consortium.
cite: Miller & Chevalier, FCPA Winter Review 2020 (summarising US DOJ and SEC filings)

n: US firm paid Russian uranium exporter's official Mikerin for TENEX contracts
rank: TENEX official Vadim Mikerin
d: Transport Logistics International, a Maryland transport company, paid Vadim Mikerin, an official at Russia's TENEX, to secure contracts with TENEX. TENEX is the sole supplier and exporter of Russian uranium and enrichment services. The payments went through shell companies and offshore accounts in Latvia, Cyprus and Switzerland, backed by fake invoices. Mikerin was sentenced to four years in prison, and the company agreed to pay $2 million in March 2018. On 22 November 2019 a Maryland jury convicted the company's former president, Mark Lambert, on some charges and acquitted him on three bribery-law counts and on money laundering. Any later appeal is not covered here.
inside: An American transport firm paid an official inside Russia's state uranium exporter through shell companies, and the exporter's contracts went to the firm.
cite: Miller & Chevalier, FCPA Winter Review 2020 (summarising US DOJ and SEC filings)

n: Teva paid a Russian official to win sales in state health auctions
rank: State health departments
d: The US Justice Department says executives of Teva, the Israeli drug maker, and staff at its Russian subsidiary paid a high-ranking Russian official to boost sales of its drug Copaxone in health ministry auctions from 2010 to at least 2012. Teva also paid a senior Ukrainian health ministry official about $200,000 between 2001 and 2011 to influence drug registrations, and its Mexican subsidiary paid government doctors to prescribe Copaxone. On 22 December 2016 Teva agreed to a $283 million criminal penalty under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, the US law against bribing foreign officials, and about $236 million to the Securities and Exchange Commission. The Russian subsidiary agreed to plead guilty. The sources do not name the officials.
inside: A foreign drug maker paid a high-ranking Russian official to boost sales in health ministry auctions, and paid officials or doctors in Ukraine and Mexico, the US Justice Department says.
cite: US Justice Department, 22 Dec 2016; Phillips & Cohen, largest FCPA settlements

n: Unaoil's Steven Hunter agreed to bribe a Libyan official for bid secrets
rank: Libyan official (office not given in the source)
d: Unaoil, a Monaco-based firm that acted as a go-between for oil companies, tried to get confidential bidding information from inside Libya by paying an official. Steven Hunter joined the conspiracy in 2009 and in May 2010 agreed to bribe a Libyan official for that information. He then used a secret email account to direct a bribe payment. Hunter pleaded guilty on 2 August 2018. Unaoil's Cyrus and Saman Ahsani pleaded guilty on 25 March 2019, in a case announced that October. Prosecutors said they had acted for 25 companies, including Rolls-Royce and SBM Offshore, with bribes reaching officials in several countries. The source does not name the Libyan official or the tender.
inside: A go-between for oil companies agreed to bribe a Libyan official to hand over confidential bidding information, which Libya's state was meant to keep from bidders.
cite: Miller & Chevalier, FCPA Winter Review 2020 (summarising US DOJ and SEC filings)

n: Bribes of $2.97m to PetroEcuador officials kept a businessman's contracts
org_label: Company of Ramiro Andres Luque Flores
who: Company of Ramiro Andres Luque Flores
rank: PetroEcuador officials
d: Money was paid to officials at PetroEcuador, Ecuador's state oil company, to obtain and keep contracts for a company owned by the Argentine businessman Ramiro Andres Luque Flores. Frank Roberto Chatburn Ripalda admitted in a US court in October 2019 that he conspired, between 2013 and 2015, to pay those officials at least $2,970,080. He was sentenced to 42 months in prison in December 2019. In the same case Arturo Escobar Dominguez and Marcelo Reyes Lopez received 48 and 53 months as recipients of the money, and Jose Luis de la Paz received 36 months as a payer. The source does not name the specific contracts.
inside: A private contractor's money reached officials inside Ecuador's state oil company, and they gave and kept PetroEcuador contracts for that company, a US court case established.
cite: Miller & Chevalier, FCPA Winter Review 2020 (summarising US DOJ and SEC filings)

n: Atlanco's chief convicted over payments for Honduran police supply contracts
rank: Honduran officials (police supply contracts)
d: Atlanco, a uniform supplier based in the US state of Georgia, paid bribes to Honduran officials to obtain contracts to supply the police. In September 2025 a federal jury in the Southern District of Florida found its owner and chief executive, Carl Zaglin, guilty of conspiracy to commit money laundering, which means agreeing with others to move or hide money from crime. The US Justice Department says he arranged hundreds of thousands of dollars in bribes for contracts worth more than $10 million with TASA, naming two former TASA directors, Francisco Cosenza Centeno and Juan Ramon Molina. In December 2025 he was sentenced to eight years in prison and ordered to forfeit over $2 million.
inside: An American uniform supplier paid Honduran officials, and contracts to supply the country's police went to the supplier, a US jury found in 2025.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 3 Dec 2025; The Anti-Corruption Report, 22 Oct 2025

n: Israel's agent inside Lebanon's state mobile firm Alfa jailed
rank: Employee (executive or technician) at state-owned mobile firm Alfa
d: Israeli intelligence had an agent inside Alfa, Lebanon's state-owned mobile phone firm, a Lebanese military court found when it convicted Charbel Qazzi, called an executive by Ynet and a technician by the telecoms minister. He was arrested in June 2010 during a wider hunt for Israeli agents. Lebanese newspapers reported that he confessed to installing programs and electronic chips supplied by Israel in Alfa's transmission stations, and Hezbollah MP Hassan Fadlallah claimed he had worked for Israel since 1996. Prosecutors said his information helped Israel during its 2006 war with Hezbollah. In December 2011 the court gave him seven years' hard labour; prosecutors had asked for death. Hezbollah's leader linked the spy arrests to the inquiry into Rafik Hariri's killing, which used phone data.
inside: Israel, an outside state, had an employee inside Lebanon's state mobile company passing information to it, and reportedly placing its equipment in the network, according to the court case.
cite: Ynet News, 22 Dec 2011; Arutz Sheva (Israel National News), 1 Jul 2010; Ynet News, 2010

n: Lebanon arrested 100+ suspected Israeli agents, some in army and telecoms
rank: Army and security personnel, state telecom staff
d: Lebanese prosecutors say Israeli intelligence recruited people inside Lebanon's security forces and telecoms companies, and a sweep to find them began in April 2009. Lebanon is technically at war with Israel, so such contact is a serious crime. By September 2011 more than 100 people had been arrested, including members of the security forces and telecom employees, and by January 2012 at least five of those convicted had been sentenced to death. The accused included Colonel Shahid Tournieh, who told a military tribunal that he was not an agent and that his first confession was untrue. A former employee of the state telecoms operator Ogero was also charged. Officials said many suspects identified targets bombed in 2006, and ministers agreed to report the matter to the UN Security Council.
inside: Lebanese prosecutors allege that Israel, a foreign state, recruited army, security and telecoms staff, who then passed it information their institutions were meant to keep from it.
cite: Ynet News/AFP, 3 Sep 2011; Arutz Sheva (Israel National News), 1 Jul 2010 and 25 Jan 2012; Ynet News, 2010; VOA, 2010

n: Aoun party figure and ex-general Fayez Karam jailed over Israeli contacts
rank: Senior figure in the Free Patriotic Movement; retired brigadier general
d: Israeli intelligence had a source inside Lebanon's Free Patriotic Movement, the Christian party allied with Hezbollah, a Lebanese military court found. The source was Fayez Karam, a retired general who had run the army's anti-terrorism and counter-espionage unit in the 1980s and was close to party leader Michel Aoun. He was arrested in 2010, the first political figure caught in the probe into Israeli spy networks. Prosecutors said he met Israeli officers abroad after a fugitive introduced him to them in Paris, and passed on information from meetings between his party and Hezbollah. In September 2011 the court gave him two years for contacting Israeli intelligence and passing political information, but did not find him guilty of spying. The sentence was upheld in January 2012.
inside: Israel, a foreign state, got a senior figure in a Lebanese party allied with Hezbollah to pass it political information about his party and Hezbollah, a military court found.
cite: Ynet News/AFP, 3 Sep 2011; Arutz Sheva (Israel National News), Aug 2010 and 25 Jan 2012

n: US says Hezbollah paid and used Lebanese transport and finance ministers
rank: Minister of Public Works and Transport; Minister of Finance
d: The US Treasury says Hezbollah, Lebanon's Iran-backed armed movement and political party, paid and used two Lebanese ministers. In September 2020 it sanctioned Youssef Fenianos, the former transport and public works minister, and Ali Hassan Khalil, finance minister from 2014 to 2020. Treasury alleged that Fenianos took hundreds of thousands of dollars in 2015 for political favours, helped steer government contracts worth millions to Hezbollah-owned firms, and got Hezbollah sensitive documents from the Special Tribunal for Lebanon, the court trying Rafik Hariri's killing. It alleged that Khalil moved money from ministries to Hezbollah-linked bodies in ways that avoided US sanctions and exempted a Hezbollah affiliate from most taxes on imported electronics. These are US accusations, not court findings. Khalil's Amal Movement rejected the sanctions.
inside: The US Treasury alleges Hezbollah, an armed movement, paid ministers who then gave its companies state contracts, tax breaks and access to sensitive tribunal documents.
cite: Al Jazeera, 8 Sep 2020; The National, Sep 2020; Times of Israel, 8 Sep 2020; Annahar, 9 Sep 2020

n: Leaked emails tied UN rights official Kompass to Morocco; he denied it
rank: Director of field operations, UN human rights office
d: Leaked emails attributed to Morocco's UN ambassador in Geneva, Omar Hilale, suggested that Morocco had people inside the UN human rights office who served it on Western Sahara, the territory Morocco controls and whose human rights monitoring it has long sought to limit. An anonymous Twitter account published the emails in late 2014. They showed Hilale boasting that he had several people in his pocket, including Anders Kompass, the office's third-highest-ranking official. UN investigators looked into whether Kompass had shared confidential information with Morocco. Kompass denied it, and in 2015 the investigators said they had found no evidence and closed the case, then reopened it. By December 2015 it was unclear whether the inquiry continued. A UN panel separately cleared Kompass over his disclosure of child-abuse reports to France.
inside: Leaked emails allege a Moroccan ambassador had UN human rights staff working for his country's position on Western Sahara. The named official denied it and investigators initially found no evidence.
cite: Foreign Policy, 12 Jun 2015 and 17 Dec 2015; Inner City Press, 14 Nov 2014

n: Morocco's spy service allegedly paid Orly border police intelligence chief
rank: Head of border police information unit, Orly airport
d: French investigators say Morocco's secret service paid the police captain who ran the border police's information unit at Orly airport near Paris. He is accused of passing 100 to 200 confidential files between 2014 and 2017, through the head of an airport security firm, in return for cash and free holidays; €17,000 reached his and his wife's account. Notes on trips by Algerian ministers were found at the middleman's home. He is also accused of giving badges that let passengers, including one on a radicalisation list, avoid border checks. An anonymous tip-off in 2016 started the case. In 2020 the captain, his wife and the middleman were sent to trial, with a warrant out for the Moroccan agent. His lawyer said he acted in France's interest. No verdict was found.
inside: French investigators allege Morocco's spy service paid a French border police chief, who then handed it confidential files on travellers and let passengers bypass border checks.
cite: The Local France/AFP, 26 Aug 2020; Bladi.net citing Le Parisien, 2020; TSA Algérie citing Le Parisien; Middle East Monitor citing Libération, 2017

n: Berlin police officer suspected of giving Turkey dissidents' addresses
rank: Berlin police officer
d: A Berlin police officer was suspected of working for Turkish intelligence by giving a Turkish embassy employee the addresses of exiled opponents of Turkey's government, the Berlin newspaper Tagesspiegel reported in September 2018, citing unnamed sources. The paper said MIT, Turkey's National Intelligence Organisation, had been trying to recruit public servants in Germany. Berlin's interior minister, Andreas Geisel, confirmed an investigation but gave no details and said there was no sign of danger to Berliners with Turkish roots. Police chief Barbara Slowik said she would remove the officer if the claims were substantiated. Federal prosecutors, who handle espionage cases, had not taken the case over at that point. The report appeared as President Erdoğan visited Germany. The sources cited do not show how the case ended.
inside: A German newspaper alleged that Turkey's intelligence service obtained a Berlin police officer's help, so police information served Ankara's tracking of exiled opponents. No outcome is reported.
cite: Hürriyet Daily News/AP, 28 Sep 2018; Stockholm Center for Freedom citing Tagesspiegel, 27 Sep 2018

n: Fresenius paid Saudi state doctors and officials who approved dialysis products
rank: Public doctors; officials on the state dialysis-product review body
d: German dialysis company Fresenius Medical Care got its money inside Saudi Arabia's public health system by paying state-employed doctors and government officials. US regulators say that over five years from 2007 its Saudi distributor made more than $4.9 million in improper payments. Recipients included high-ranking officials at a Saudi technical body that reviewed and approved dialysis products for government tenders, the public contests for state purchases. Staff also arranged false bids for dialysis machine tenders. The company gained more than $40 million. The case came out through US enforcement under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, the law against bribing foreign officials. In March 2019 Fresenius agreed a $231 million settlement with the US Justice Department and Securities and Exchange Commission covering this and other countries.
inside: A foreign medical company paid the Saudi officials and state doctors who approved products for government tenders, so state purchasing decisions favoured the company.
cite: SEC Actions on In the Matter of Fresenius Medical Care AG, 29 Mar 2019; CFO.com, Apr 2019; Constantine Cannon, 2019

n: Fresenius bribed chief kidney doctor at Moroccan military hospitals
rank: Chief nephrologist, two state military hospitals
