d: German dialysis company Fresenius Medical Care bribed the chief nephrologist, or kidney specialist, at two Moroccan state-owned military hospitals to win contracts there, US regulators found. Under US anti-bribery law this doctor counted as a government official. Over four years from 2006, a senior officer and a sales manager in Germany ran the scheme, and the US Justice Department said bribes were paid through a sham commission. Fresenius earned more than $2.3 million in revenue from it. After a whistleblower reported the matter in 2012, company officials delayed an investigation for about two years, and staff destroyed records and deleted computer files. The company paid a $231 million settlement in 2019 covering this and other countries.
inside: A foreign company paid the doctor who ran kidney care at Moroccan military hospitals, so that public hospital contracts for dialysis centres went to the company.
cite: SEC Actions on In the Matter of Fresenius Medical Care AG, 29 Mar 2019; CFO.com, Apr 2019; Constantine Cannon, 2019

n: Fresenius gave Turkish public doctors free stakes for sending it business
rank: Publicly employed doctors
d: German dialysis company Fresenius Medical Care got its money into Turkey's public health service by giving publicly employed doctors free shares, US regulators found, and those doctors then sent it business from their public employers. Between 2005 and 2014 its Turkish unit set up four joint ventures with such doctors. A joint venture is a business co-owned by two parties. The doctors did not pay for their shares, and some shares were held in other people's names. The company benefited by more than $1 million. The arrangement was part of a wider case under the US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, the law against bribing foreign officials, settled in 2019 for $231 million across several countries.
inside: A foreign company gave state-employed doctors free hidden shares in clinics, and those doctors then directed business from their public employer to the company.
cite: SEC Actions on In the Matter of Fresenius Medical Care AG, 29 Mar 2019; CFO.com, Apr 2019; Constantine Cannon, 2019

n: Bahrain court: cell funded from Iran and Iraq chose soldier to kill army chief
org_label: Bahraini militant cell funded from Iran and Iraq
who: Cell funded from Iran and Iraq
rank: Serving soldier, Bahrain Defence Force
d: A Bahraini military court said a militant cell funded by people based in Iran and Iraq chose a serving soldier in the Bahrain Defence Force to assassinate its commander-in-chief, Field Marshal Khalifa bin Ahmed Al Khalifa. Case files say the cell's recruiter picked the soldier for the killing, which did not take place. On 25 December 2017 the court sentenced six men to death, including the soldier, jailed seven and acquitted five; eight were tried in their absence. Four death sentences, the soldier's among them, were upheld in April 2018, and the king then commuted them to life in prison. Bahrain accuses Iran of backing Shia militants, which Tehran denies. Rights groups said civilians were wrongly tried in military courts and alleged torture. The verdict was the first official mention of the plot.
inside: Bahrain's military court alleges a cell funded from Iran and Iraq recruited a soldier inside the armed forces to kill their commander. Rights groups dispute the trial's fairness.
cite: Daily Tribune (News of Bahrain), Dec 2017 and 2018; AP via KSL, 25 Dec 2017; Reuters via VOA, Dec 2017; The National, Dec 2017; ADHRB, 26 Dec 2017

n: Saudi court: Iran ran spy cell including ex-defence and interior ministry staff
rank: Former defence and interior ministry employees
d: A Saudi court found that Iranian intelligence ran a spy cell in Saudi Arabia, and Saudi media said many of the accused were former employees of the defence and interior ministries. Thirty-two people were tried: 30 Saudi Shia Muslims, one Iranian and one Afghan, detained from 2013. They were accused of passing Iran military and security information, including numbers of aircraft and bases, and of recruiting spies, in return for cash and goods. On 6 December 2016 the court sentenced 15 to death and 15 to prison, and acquitted two. Iran denied involvement. Amnesty International called the trial farcical, saying defendants were held without warrants, questioned without lawyers and pressed to sign confessions. Human Rights Watch said 11 men from the case were among 37 executed on 23 April 2019.
inside: Saudi prosecutors allege Iran recruited Saudis, including former defence and interior ministry staff, to pass it military secrets. Iran denies it and Amnesty calls the trial unfair.
cite: AP via Daily Herald, 6 Dec 2016; Arab News, Dec 2016; Iran Times, Dec 2016; Amnesty International, Dec 2016; Human Rights Watch, 24 Apr 2019

n: US says Palau Senate President Baules took bribes for Chinese interests
rank: President of the Senate
d: The US alleges that China-based interests paid the head of Palau's Senate to advance their aims inside the country's government. On 10 February 2026 the State Department barred Hokkons Baules and his family from the US, saying he accepted bribes for supporting 'government, business, and criminal interests from China'. Palau hosts US airstrips and radar sites. Reuters reported in 2025 that three Palauan officials said Baules phoned a customs officer after a Chinese investor allegedly arrived with $119,000 in undeclared cash; Baules said he did not recall it. He denies wrongdoing, says he was accused because he helped Chinese investors, and says Palau's authorities could charge him if they have evidence. China called Reuters's claims fabricated.
inside: The US government alleges China-based interests bribed Palau's Senate president, so that a top lawmaker supported their aims while holding office; he denies it.
cite: Island Times on US State Department designation, Feb 2026; Reuters investigation via Baird Maritime, 30 Apr 2025

n: FICAC charges Jason Zhong with bribing Fiji's land trust officials
rank: iTaukei Land Trust Board officials
d: Fiji's anti-corruption commission, FICAC, alleges that businessman Jason Zhong bribed officials of the iTaukei Land Trust Board, the body that manages land owned by Fiji's indigenous people. Reporting by OCCRP and the Fiji Times in late 2024 said Zhong had earlier convictions, in 2005 for a methamphetamine laboratory and in 2012 for trafficking Thai women, and was named in a 2020 police briefing on a suspected crime network. It also said iTaukei Affairs Minister Ifereimi Vasu is his friend and business partner in ginger farming, and that the two flew to Hong Kong together in March 2024. Vasu has not been charged, and the reports do not say he took part in any bribery. The outcome of the trial could not be confirmed.
inside: Prosecutors allege a man with criminal convictions paid officials at the board controlling indigenous land, buying influence inside the body that decides how that land is used.
cite: OCCRP and Fiji Times via In-depth Solomons, 2 Dec 2024; PINA, 28 Nov 2024

n: Chinese firm's executives tried to bribe Fiji's top finance official
rank: Permanent Secretary for Finance
d: Two men from China Huashi Enterprise Fiji Limited, Chen Xue Liang and De Chuan Zhao, tried to pay the most senior civil servant in Fiji's finance ministry to help their business. Prosecutors, who described them as the company's chief executive and accountant, said they offered Permanent Secretary John Prasad money and tea on 28 July 2009, seeking help with a water project in Savusavu. Early reports gave the sum as $60,000; reports of the plea give $6,000. They pleaded guilty to bribery in 2010. The defence said they did not know gifts were illegal and acted without company authority. Justice Salesi Temo gave each three years in prison, one to serve and two suspended, and a $10,000 fine.
inside: Executives of a foreign firm offered cash to the top civil servant in Fiji's finance ministry, seeking a public water contract; they later admitted the attempt in court.
cite: Fijivillage court reports, 2010

n: Hawaii engineering firm bribed Micronesian aviation official for contracts
org_label: Frank James Lyon's Hawaii engineering company
rank: Department of Transportation, Communications and Infrastructure official
d: A Hawaii engineering and consulting company paid officials in the Federated States of Micronesia to win and keep government contracts. US prosecutors said that from 2006 to 2016 the firm, owned by Frank James Lyon, gave cash, vehicles, gifts and entertainment to officials, in connection with FSM contracts worth nearly $8 million. One recipient, Master Halbert, oversaw aviation programmes, including airport management, in the FSM transport department; the payments were carried from the US to Micronesia. Lyon pleaded guilty to conspiring to break the US law against bribing foreign officials and got 30 months in prison. Halbert pleaded guilty to conspiring to launder money and got 18 months, both in 2019.
inside: A foreign contractor paid a government official overseeing Micronesia's airports and other officials, so the firm could win and keep government engineering contracts for a decade.
cite: US Department of Justice press releases, May and Jul 2019

n: Foreign timber group gave PNG forests minister Ted Diro a secret stake
rank: Minister for Forests
d: A Singapore-based timber group with Malaysian principals, Angus, secured Papua New Guinea's forests minister as a hidden partner. Reporting by PNGi on the late-1980s inquiry led by Judge Tos Barnett says Ted Diro, minister from November 1985, secretly held about 35% of Angus PNG through a trust and in February 1986 ordered that the company be given a timber permit, over the objections of senior officials. Angus rented an apartment from his company and paid for a trip to Singapore and Malaysia. Barnett found Diro knew of and helped plan a scheme to shift profits offshore. In October 1991, as deputy prime minister, Diro was convicted by a leadership tribunal of 81 counts of misconduct and resigned.
inside: A foreign logging group gave the minister in charge of forests a secret share and benefits, and he then overrode his own officials to hand that group a timber permit.
cite: PNGi Central, 5 Feb 2019, on the Barnett inquiry; Wikipedia, Ted Diro

n: Barnett inquiry: logging firms bribed PNG politicians and leaders
rank: Politicians and provincial leaders
d: Some logging companies paid politicians and leaders in Papua New Guinea to log forests while ignoring laws, an official inquiry found. Prime Minister Paias Wingti appointed Justice Thomas Barnett in May 1987, and the report, released in July 1989, found corruption, fraud and incompetence at every level of the forest industry. Barnett described companies in New Ireland province acting 'with the self assurance of robber barons'. According to a 1991 account, someone tried to kill Barnett, evidence held by the Ombudsman was stolen, and a fire destroyed more at the Anti-Corruption Office. Only two of the nine volumes were printed.
inside: An official inquiry found logging firms paid politicians and leaders, so that those meant to protect Papua New Guinea's forests let the companies break forestry law.
cite: Green Left, 20 Mar 1991

n: PNG inquiry: officials worked with loggers on land leases across 5m hectares
rank: Land and forestry agency officials
d: Logging companies gained control of more than five million hectares of Papua New Guinea, over a tenth of the country, through farm leases known as SABLs, with help from officials. A government inquiry reported in 2013 that 'developers and people with vested interests have hijacked' the scheme and cited 'greed and corruption at all levels'. Global Witness says nearly all the operations were run by foreign companies, largely linked to Malaysian nationals, and that the inquiry recommended 42 of the 46 leases it reviewed be revoked, or suspended and renegotiated. Global Witness says it does not allege fraud by Rimbunan Hijau, a Malaysian firm whose subsidiary used a lease. In 2014 it reported no prosecutions.
inside: Officials sometimes colluded with those claiming the leases, according to accounts of the inquiry, so customary land passed to foreign-run logging operations under leases meant for farm projects.
cite: Global Witness briefing, Nov 2014; PNG Exposed via farmlandgrab, 3 Mar 2014; Lowy Institute, 3 Mar 2016; Devpolicy, 10 Dec 2013

n: Malaysian loggers reported to fund Solomon Islands MPs to reach ministries
rank: Government MPs; Forests and Finance ministries sought
d: An unnamed logging-industry source alleged in 2008 that at least six Malaysian logging companies backed a new Solomon Islands party in order to reach key ministries. As reported in the Solomon Times, citing the National Express, sixteen government MPs were each paid $50,000 to join the National Alliance Party, led by Honiara businessman Bobo Dettke. The source said the firms wanted influence over the Finance, Forests and Environment ministries, where foreign advisers had made it harder to get tax breaks on log exports. Dettke allegedly gave the prime minister a letter from the MPs asking for a particular minister for forests; he appointed someone else. The claims were not independently verified.
inside: A source alleged logging firms paid MPs to join a party so that they could gain influence over the ministries that tax and license logging; the claim was not verified.
cite: Solomon Times, 28 Oct 2008

n: Earth Movers logging boss convicted of trying to bribe Solomons customs
rank: Customs officials at Noro port
d: A businessman from a Malaysian logging firm was convicted of trying to pay Solomon Islands customs officers. Radio New Zealand reported in May 2004 that Alex Wong was arrested and appeared in the Honiara Magistrate's Court, accused of offering a bribe to customs officials at Noro port in Western Province for his company, Earth Movers. He was convicted in September 2004 and sentenced to three years in prison. The High Court refused him bail that December, and heard his appeal in March 2005, when his lawyers said the evidence was too weak to convict. The result of the appeal could not be found, and the amount was not reported.
inside: A court convicted a logging firm's head of offering money to customs officers at the port, seeking to have the officers who check goods there act for his company.
cite: Radio New Zealand, 25 May 2004 and 31 March 2005; Wong v Regina [2004] SBHC 135 via PacLII

n: Solomons ex-minister: colleagues sought approval for Chinese miner for cash
org_label: Chinese prospecting company and Malaysian loggers
rank: Minister for Mines and Energy (acting)
d: A former Solomon Islands acting minister for mines said two fellow ministers asked him to approve a Chinese prospecting company's application just before an election, telling him they would each be paid SI$50,000 and that the money could help their campaigns. The account comes secondhand from writer Transform Aqorau, in a chapter published by ANU Press, and the ministers are not named. Aqorau also describes Malaysian loggers throwing a bundle of cash onto a forestry legal adviser's car seat, which a commissioner told him to return, and a logging company set up by a firm's employee and a local consultant who was a serving MP. No payment was confirmed.
inside: A former minister's account has colleagues seeking his approval for a foreign mining firm in return for campaign money, an attempt to buy a licence decision from inside cabinet; it is unconfirmed.
cite: Transform Aqorau, 'Crisis in Solomon Islands: foraging for new directions', ANU Press

n: Developer paid Casey councillors almost A$1.2m to promote his rezonings
org_label: John Woodman and his developer clients
rank: City of Casey councillors
d: A property developer's money reached councillors who decide planning in Melbourne's southeast, Victoria's anti-corruption commission, IBAC, found in its Operation Sandon report of July 2023. It found City of Casey councillors Sameh Aziz and Geoff Ablett accepted almost A$1.2 million in payments and support for promoting the interests of developer John Woodman, whose proposals included rezoning Cranbourne West land to raise its value. They repeatedly failed to declare the conflict. Woodman also gave over A$470,000 to Labor and Liberal between 2010 and 2019. Woodman says there is no evidence of improper influence. IBAC sent evidence to prosecutors and made 34 recommendations, including taking planning powers from councils.
inside: A developer paid sitting councillors, the commission found, and they then pressed his rezoning proposals on the council that was meant to judge those proposals fairly.
cite: IBAC Operation Sandon report as reported by The New Daily/AAP, 27 Jul 2023; The Mandarin, 31 Jul 2023

n: Eddie and Moses Obeid and NSW minister convicted of conspiring over a coal licence
rank: NSW minerals minister
d: Labor MP Eddie Obeid and his son Moses conspired with a New South Wales minister over a coal exploration licence at Mount Penny. The state's anti-corruption commission, ICAC, examined a 2008 tender run by minerals minister Ian Macdonald covering Obeid land in the Bylong Valley, and in 2013 found Obeid and Macdonald corrupt. In October 2021 the NSW Supreme Court jailed Macdonald for nine and a half years, Eddie Obeid for seven and Moses for five. The family reportedly took A$30 million. ICAC also found five businessmen acted corruptly. The Obeids denied wrongdoing when ICAC reported. Appeals failed in October 2023, and on 4 February 2026 the High Court unanimously dismissed their further appeals, so the convictions stand.
inside: A family with a business stake conspired with a minister over a coal licence decision, so a public resource was awarded to serve its private profit.
cite: InDaily, 31 Jul 2013; Yahoo News UK report on the sentencing, Oct 2021; High Court of Australia, Obeid v The King [2026] HCA 1, judgment summary, 4 Feb 2026

n: NSW MP Maguire ran a firm from parliament for Chinese and developer deals
org_label: G8wayInternational, property developers and Chinese business associates
rank: NSW MP for Wagga Wagga
d: A New South Wales MP used his office to serve a company he secretly profited from and clients who paid him, ICAC found in its Operation Keppel report of June 2023. Between 2012 and 2018 Daryl Maguire effectively ran G8wayInternational from parliament, took a fee for introducing a Chinese provincial party secretary to the premier, misused a parliamentary friendship group to help associates in a Shenzhen business body, and took commissions from developers, including for introducing Chinese developer Country Garden to a developer with a site. Country Garden says it has zero tolerance for illegal behaviour. A separate conviction for misleading ICAC was quashed on appeal in March 2026. In July 2026 a jury found him guilty of conspiracy over bogus visa applications; the sentence could not be confirmed.
inside: Developers and Chinese business contacts gained a sitting MP as a paid go-between, the commission found, so his parliamentary office worked for their deals and his own income.
cite: ICAC Operation Keppel as reported on inkl; Daily Advertiser timeline; Region Riverina, 17 Jul 2026; AAP, Jul 2026; Apartments.com.au, Jul 2018

n: ICAC: Canterbury councillors and planning chief corrupt over development
rank: Canterbury City councillors and director of city planning
d: New South Wales' anti-corruption commission found senior figures at a Sydney council acted corruptly in a planning office developers depended on. ICAC's Operation Dasha report of March 2021 found councillors Michael Hawatt and Pierre Azzi and planning director Spiro Stavis engaged in serious corrupt conduct by using their posts dishonestly and partially. It also found general manager Jim Montague acted corruptly in appointing Stavis. It recommended that prosecutors consider charges against the three, and against developers Charbel Demian and Marwan Chanine. A separate ICAC report said Hawatt agreed with an MP to share commissions from developers introduced to Canterbury sites. Court outcomes could not be confirmed.
inside: Councillors and the planning chief who ruled on development acted corruptly, the commission found, while one councillor agreed to share commissions from developers seeking sites in the same area.
cite: The New Daily, 22 Mar 2021; NSW Greens on ICAC report, 22 Mar 2021; inkl on Operation Keppel

n: Crime Commission assistant director Standen plotted with drug trafficker
rank: Assistant director, NSW Crime Commission
d: A drug trafficker turned informant, James Kinch, had a senior crime fighter in New South Wales working with him. Mark Standen, assistant director of the NSW Crime Commission, the state body that investigates major crime, was found guilty by the NSW Supreme Court in 2011 of conspiring to import and supply about 300 kg of pseudoephedrine, a methamphetamine ingredient, and of conspiring to obstruct justice. The offences allegedly ran from 2006 to 2008, with food wholesaler Bill Jalalaty. The shipment turned out to hold no pseudoephedrine. He was sentenced to 22 years, with 16 non-parole, lost his appeal in 2015 and was granted parole in May 2024. One legal commentary alleges Kinch paid Standen A$300,000 to A$500,000.
inside: A trafficker's network won over the senior official running major investigations at a state crime agency, who then conspired with it to import drug ingredients and obstruct justice.
cite: OCCRP, Aug 2011; Sydney Criminal Lawyers commentary; SBS, 13 Aug 2015; NSW State Parole Authority, 17 May 2024

n: Businessmen paid Queensland minister Nuttall in secret; he was jailed
org_label: Businessmen Ken Talbot, Harold Shand, Brendan McKennariey
who: Mining magnate Ken Talbot and other businessmen
rank: Queensland minister (Health, Primary Industries, Industrial Relations)
d: Businessmen paid a serving Queensland cabinet minister for years. Gordon Nuttall, a minister from 2001 to 2005, was convicted in July 2009 of corruptly receiving almost A$360,000 from mining magnate Ken Talbot and solicitor Harold Shand, and was jailed for seven years. Talbot's share was almost A$300,000 in 35 payments. Talbot died in an air crash in June 2010 before trial, and the charges were dropped; Shand was convicted in 2011 and got 15 months. In 2010 Nuttall was convicted again, for taking A$152,700 from businessman Brendan McKennariey, who received government money as a subcontractor on programmes run by Nuttall's departments. The Queensland Crime and Misconduct Commission investigated. The reports do not spell out what Talbot received in return.
inside: Businessmen secretly paid a sitting minister, and one of them also received public money through contracts commissioned by that minister's departments, so public office served private payers.
cite: Crime and Corruption Commission Queensland outcome page and news release, 17 July 2009; Wikipedia, Gordon Nuttall and Ken Talbot

n: Defector alleges Chinese spies offered A$1m to make Bo Zhao an MP
rank: Federal parliament candidacy
d: A defector alleged that a Chinese intelligence group set out to place an agent in Australia's parliament. Nine's 60 Minutes reported in November 2019 that the group offered A$1 million to Bo 'Nick' Zhao, a Melbourne car dealer and Liberal Party member, to run for the seat of Chisholm. Claims came from former agent Wang Liqiang, whom Shanghai police call a convicted fraudster. Zhao told ASIO, Australia's security service, and was found dead in a hotel room in March 2019. In October 2020 a coroner found he intended to end his own life and found no evidence that a third party was involved. ASIO said it was investigating. Melbourne businessman Brian Chen, reportedly the go-between, denies it. The plot claims were not independently confirmed.
inside: A defector alleges Chinese intelligence offered money for a Liberal Party member to win a seat, aiming to have its own person inside parliament; nothing shows the plan went further.
cite: 3AW, 25 Nov 2019; Asia Times, Nov 2019; The New Daily, 29 Nov 2019; Coroners Court of Victoria, 29 Oct 2020

n: Contractor paid Auckland Transport manager over $1m in bribes for road work
rank: Senior manager, Rodney District Council and Auckland Transport
d: An engineering contractor paid a senior public manager at the bodies that bought its road services in Auckland. Stephen Borlase, director of Projenz Ltd, gave undisclosed payments, travel, accommodation and entertainment to Murray Noone, who held senior management posts at Rodney District Council and then Auckland Transport, the region's transport agency. Projenz held the contracts to maintain and renew the road network in those areas. Bribes passed between 2005 and 2013 and totalled more than $1 million, New Zealand's Serious Fraud Office said. In February 2017 the High Court jailed Borlase for five and a half years and Noone for five; a third man, Barrie George, got home detention.
inside: A road contractor secretly paid a senior manager at the public bodies buying its services, and held their road maintenance contracts while he took the money.
cite: NZ Serious Fraud Office, 22 Feb 2017

n: Mitsubishi Hitachi paid a Thai Transport Ministry official 11m baht
rank: Transport Ministry official (port clearance)
d: Executives of the Japanese power-equipment maker Mitsubishi Hitachi Power Systems paid a Thai Transport Ministry official 11 million baht in February 2015 to get favourable treatment when unloading cargo. The firm held a 30-billion-baht government contract to supply a gas-fired power plant in Nakhon Si Thammarat, and the cargo had failed clearance conditions. The case came out in Japan's first plea bargain, in which the company avoided indictment by cooperating. In September 2019 a Tokyo court gave former executive Satoshi Uchida a suspended 18-month term. In July 2020 the Tokyo High Court replaced it with a ¥2.5 million fine, finding he failed to stop the bribe, and he appealed. Thailand's anti-corruption commission recommended charges against four or five officials, none laid by 2019.
inside: A Japanese company's cash reached a Thai ministry official to get favourable treatment for its power-plant cargo at the point of unloading, Tokyo courts found.
cite: Bangkok Post/Kyodo, 13 Sep 2019; Japan Times, 21 Jul 2020; MLex, 4 Aug 2020

n: Rolls-Royce money reached Thai Airways staff and Thai state agents
rank: Thai Airways employees; ex-chairman charged
d: The British engine maker Rolls-Royce paid middlemen so that some of the money reached employees of the state airline Thai Airways and agents of the Thai state, who were expected to favour its engines. A statement of facts in a British court, published in January 2017 when Rolls-Royce settled with prosecutors, put payments to these "regional intermediaries" at about US$36.3 million between 1991 and 2005. Thailand's anti-corruption commission then investigated. In August 2022 it found against former finance minister Thanong Bidaya, who had chaired the airline, and a former finance vice-president. The attorney general declined to prosecute, so the commission went to court itself. On 29 April 2025 a Thai corruption court dismissed the case, finding the evidence too weak to convict the two men.
inside: Rolls-Royce admitted paying intermediaries so that people inside Thailand's state airline would favour its engines; a Thai court dismissed the anti-graft commission's case against a former chairman in 2025 for lack of evidence.
cite: Bangkok Post, 26 Sep 2024; Bangkok Post/AP, Jan 2017; The Nation, 29 Apr 2025; The Thaiger, 29 Apr 2025

n: Rolls-Royce allegedly paid $11m in kickbacks over Thai energy firm PTT
rank: state energy firm PTT
d: The British engine maker Rolls-Royce is alleged to have paid about US$11 million (388 million baht) in kickbacks over contracts for equipment and services at PTT, Thailand's state-owned oil and gas company. The allegation came from the US Department of Justice after Rolls-Royce's bribery settlement in January 2017. In March 2017 the secretary-general of Thailand's National Anti-Corruption Commission, Sansern Poljeak, said politicians were likely to have had a hand in it. In 2024 the commission said four former executives of PTT's subsidiary PTTEP were guilty of corruption over compressor buying at the Arthit gas field, a commission finding rather than a court verdict. In May 2025 it cleared seven PTT executives on two other projects, citing insufficient evidence of bribery.
inside: US prosecutors' disclosures allege that Rolls-Royce's money went into winning contracts at a Thai state energy company; Thailand's anti-graft body found against four ex-executives on one project and cleared seven on others.
cite: Bangkok Post, 14 Mar 2017; Offshore Technology, 1 May 2024; The Nation, 19 Oct 2025

n: Thai deputy finance minister quit over alleged scam-network payments
rank: Deputy Finance Minister
d: A newsletter called Whale Hunting alleged that Chinese-Cambodian criminal networks got money to the family of Thailand's deputy finance minister, Vorapak Tanyawong. It reported that his wife was paid US$3 million in cryptocurrency in 2025 by networks he had been tasked to investigate on a government committee, and that he was once listed as an adviser to BIC Bank, a Cambodian bank linked to an alleged laundering network. Vorapak, who took office the previous month, resigned in October 2025 after the prime minister demanded a written explanation. He denied the claims and called them politically driven. A Thai court has since agreed to hear two of his seven criminal defamation complaints against the newsletter's co-founder Tom Wright. The reports name no decision of his that helped a scam group.
inside: A newsletter alleges that scam networks paid the wife of the minister assigned to help investigate them; he denies it, and no decision serving them has been shown.
cite: AFP via Arab News, Oct 2025; Saksith Saiyasombut, 22 Oct 2025; Committee to Protect Journalists, 8 Oct 2026

n: Thai district chiefs allegedly took bribes to make Chinese nationals citizens
org_label: Thai identity-document brokers and Chinese clients
rank: district chiefs and village headmen
d: Chinese nationals running illegal businesses in Thailand allegedly bought their way into Thai citizenship through local officials. Investigators allege that district chiefs, deputy district chiefs and village headmen took bribes to issue permanent-residence certificates and grant citizenship. The probe began when an identity-fraud ring was broken up in Wiang Haeng district, Chiang Mai, and the network also allegedly opened nominee bank accounts. In November 2025 police arrested a 44-year-old Chinese man on a warrant for helping officials abuse their authority, the 25th suspect. He told investigators he paid 1.5 million baht for a card so he could do business more easily. Documents usually cost 800,000 to over 1 million baht.
inside: Police allege that money from Chinese nationals running illegal businesses reached Thai local officials, who then used their offices to register those people as Thai citizens.
cite: Khaosod English, 22 Nov 2025

n: AVG's owner paid Vietnam's communications minister $3m over MobiFone deal
org_label: Audio Visual Global (AVG), Pham Nhat Vu
rank: Minister of Information and Communications
d: Pham Nhat Vu, owner of the private pay-TV company Audio Visual Global (AVG), paid Vietnam's communications minister Nguyen Bac Son US$3 million after the state-run phone company MobiFone agreed to buy 95 per cent of AVG. The confidential contract, signed in late 2015, was worth nearly VND8.9 trillion (US$383.7 million), and AP reported a price inflated almost ten times. Inspectors began checking in July 2017 and the deal was cancelled in March 2018. In December 2019 a Hanoi court gave Son life in prison and his successor as minister, Truong Minh Tuan, 14 years. MobiFone's former chairman got 23 years, and Vu got three years for giving bribes.
inside: A private company owner paid a minister over a state phone company's purchase of his firm at a reportedly inflated price, and a Hanoi court convicted them.
cite: Tuoi Tre News, 28 Dec 2019; AP via VOA, 28 Dec 2019

n: Online gambling ring had two senior Vietnamese police chiefs as backers
rank: head of General Police Department; head of high-tech crime police
d: Operators of the Rikvip online gambling websites had two senior police chiefs covering for them inside Vietnam's Ministry of Public Security. The sites, opened in 2015, drew up to 42.9 million players and VND9.85 trillion in revenue in 28 months. The court found that Phan Van Vinh, head of the General Police Department, and Nguyen Thanh Hoa, head of the high-tech crime police, covered up its activity. Vinh had signed the decision setting up the ring leader's firm, CNC, a shell company of the ministry. In November 2018 a court jailed Vinh for nine years and Hoa for ten for abusing power. Ring leader Nguyen Van Duong told the court he gave both men large sums, which they denied.
inside: A gambling ring's operators had the chiefs of cybercrime police and the general police department on their side, so the force meant to catch them covered for them.
cite: Viet Nam News, 30 Nov 2018; Tuoi Tre News, 30 Nov 2018

n: Blackgold shareholder paid Indonesian lawmaker and minister over Riau-1 plant
rank: deputy chair of parliament's seventh commission; social affairs minister
d: Businessman Johannes Budisutrisno Kotjo, a shareholder of Blackgold Natural Resources, paid two politicians of Indonesia's Golkar Party to help his firm win the Riau-1 coal power plant project at the state electricity company PLN. A court found he paid lawmaker Eni Maulani Saragih and Idrus Marham, then social affairs minister, Rp 4.75 billion. The Corruption Eradication Commission arrested Eni at Idrus's home in July 2018, and she was sentenced to six years in March 2019. Idrus was also convicted. Prosecutors also charged PLN's president director Sofyan Basir with arranging meetings for the deal, but the Jakarta Corruption Court acquitted him of all charges in November 2019.
inside: A coal investor paid a lawmaker and a minister to speed a state power-plant contract towards his firm; the court convicted them but acquitted the state utility's chief.
cite: Kontan/Jakarta Post, 24 Jun 2019; Jakarta Post, 4 Nov 2019; Republika, 21 Mar 2019; Wikipedia (Eni Maulani Saragih)

n: Tender cartel allegedly paid into Malaysia's army procurement, up to its chief
rank: Chief of Army and procurement officers
d: Malaysia's anti-corruption commission (MACC) suspects that companies bidding for army procurement contracts formed a cartel and paid officers to rig tenders, reaching former army chief Muhammad Hafizuddeain Jantan. In January 2026 the MACC said it was investigating 26 companies, detained 17 company directors and seized 2.4 million ringgit in cash it believes was linked to bribery. It detained Hafizuddeain and his two wives on 7 January. The Vibes reported an alleged organised bribery system in army procurement. On 22 and 23 January prosecutors charged him with six counts of money laundering, over 2.12 million ringgit and a further 145,000, and he pleaded not guilty. His wife Salwani Anuar faces five counts and denied the first four. The cases will be tried together; no verdict was found.
inside: Investigators allege that firms bidding for army contracts paid officers up to the army chief so that tenders went their way; the former chief pleads not guilty.
cite: OCCRP, 8 Jan 2026; The Vibes, Jan 2026; Free Malaysia Today and Malay Mail, 22-23 Jan 2026; Malaysiakini, 23 Jan 2026; The Edge, 30 Mar 2026

n: Smuggling syndicate allegedly paid Malaysian military officers for intelligence
rank: armed forces officers
d: A smuggling syndicate working from the Strait of Malacca down to Johor allegedly paid Malaysian Armed Forces officers for sensitive military information. Malaysia's anti-corruption commission (MACC) said in August 2025 that raids under Op Sohor had led to the arrest of five military officers, two of them former officers, and five civilians. Each officer is alleged to have received RM30,000 to RM50,000 per smuggling operation. The commission estimates the syndicate moved narcotics, cigarettes and other contraband worth up to RM5 million a month. Its chief, Azam Baki, said the officers were supposed to share information with other enforcement agencies, and that leaks could seriously compromise enforcement. The source reports an investigation, with no verdict.
inside: The commission alleges that a smuggling syndicate paid military officers per operation for operational information, so that officers meant to safeguard national security helped it avoid enforcement.
cite: The Vibes, 14 Aug 2025

n: Chinese state firm allegedly used a Cambodian general's troops to clear coast land
rank: armed forces chief of staff Kun Kim
d: The US Treasury alleges that Union Development Group, a Chinese state-owned company, used a local company and Cambodia's military to obtain and clear land. It says the firm got a 99-year lease in 2008 on the Dara Sakor project, almost 20 per cent of Cambodia's coastline, by forming a local company as leaseholder, and that ownership later reverted to Chinese hands. It says the military used violence to help clear the land and that Kun Kim, a senior general and former armed forces chief of staff, benefited financially. Treasury imposed sanctions on the company. Cambodia and China rejected the allegations, and a ruling-party spokesman said the state development council had reviewed and approved the master plan.
inside: The US alleges that a Chinese state company's local leaseholder and a senior general's financial interest got Cambodia's military clearing coastland for it; both governments reject this.
cite: AP via KSL, 16 Sep 2020 (citing US Treasury); US Treasury press release sm1121, 15 Sep 2020

n: FARC agent posed as a student inside Colombia's war college to plant a bomb
rank: Escuela Superior de Guerra (student cover)
d: The FARC, Colombia's largest guerrilla army, got an agent inside the Escuela Superior de Guerra, the school for senior military officers in Bogotá. Marilú Ramírez Baquero, who ran intelligence and communications for the FARC's Antonio Nariño urban network, posed as a student and gathered the information needed for an attack. On 19 October 2006 a Ford Explorer carrying 60 kilos of explosive was parked inside the school and set off, injuring several people. Bogotá's High Court upheld a 27-year sentence. In 2020 Colombia's peace tribunal, the JEP, granted her an amnesty; on 8 April 2022 its appeals section annulled it because victims had not been properly notified, and ordered the process restarted.
inside: A guerrilla army placed an intelligence agent inside the military's own staff college as a student, and what she learned there was used to put a car bomb inside it.
cite: La FM, Bogotá High Court ruling upholding sentence, 28 Jul 2016; Noticias RCN, JEP annuls amnesty, 8 Apr 2022

n: Civilian adviser to AUC paramilitaries became deputy head of Colombia's DAS
rank: Deputy director, DAS
d: José Miguel Narváez, whom former commanders of the AUC paramilitary army describe as their civilian adviser, was deputy director of the DAS, Colombia's state intelligence agency, from June to October 2005. Ex-commanders Don Berna, Ernesto Báez and El Alemán said he lectured in their camps and handed over lists of people to pursue or kill. Courts found he urged AUC leader Carlos Castaño to order the 1999 murder of the journalist Jaime Garzón, and the Supreme Court upheld that 26-year sentence in February 2021. A Medellín court also gave him 28 years for instigating the 1999 kidnapping of Senator Piedad Córdoba, after he gave Castaño recordings of her calls. Narváez denies any link to the AUC.
inside: Courts found that a man tied to the AUC's leader urged him to order killings, and ex-commanders call him their adviser; he also held the state intelligence agency's second post.
cite: Noticias RCN, profile of Narváez; Asuntos Legales, Supreme Court upholds sentence, 8 Feb 2021

n: Clan del Golfo ally Matamba allegedly paid an army colonel to move troops
rank: Commander, Batallón Boyacá, and active-duty soldiers
d: Prosecutors say the Cordillera Sur, a cocaine group in Nariño allied to the Clan del Golfo and led by Juan Larinson Castro, alias Matamba, had Colombian army officers working for it. They allege retired colonel Harry Gómez Tabares, former commander of the Batallón Boyacá in Pasto, took about 50 million pesos a month to move troops away from cocaine routes and warned of operations. Five serving soldiers, including a captain, were charged with him. Retired colonel Róbinson González del Río allegedly recruited soldiers and passed on troop movements. Radio reports also named retired general Leonardo Barrero, who has not been charged and denies any link. Matamba was killed in a police operation in May 2022.
inside: Prosecutors say a cocaine group paid an army battalion's former commander monthly, so that troops meant to stop it moved off its routes and it received warning of operations.
cite: El País (Cali), citing Fiscalía hearings and Blu Radio; InSight Crime, on the escape and military links, Mar 2022

n: Police captain accused of helping Matamba walk out of Bogotá's La Picota jail
rank: Police captain; La Picota prison staff suspected
d: Authorities say police and prison insiders helped the trafficker alias Matamba, leader of a Clan del Golfo-allied group, escape La Picota, a maximum-security jail in Bogotá, on 18 March 2022 while he awaited extradition to the United States. He left dressed as a guard of INPEC, the prison service. Days later the unnamed duty inspector was arrested, accused of leaving a door open. In March 2023 an anti-kidnapping unit captured police captain Luis Eduardo Duque Casas, accused of providing the vehicle. He pleaded not guilty, and by August 2023 he and two others faced trial; no verdict was found. A former soldier testified that other police officers drove Matamba out of Bogotá. Matamba was found dead in May 2022.
inside: Authorities allege a trafficker awaiting extradition used police officers and prison staff to leave a maximum-security jail, so those paid to hold him worked to free him.
cite: Noticias Caracol, 14 Mar 2023; Blu Radio, 31 Aug 2023; El Universal, 16 Mar 2023; Infobae, 20 Mar 2022; InSight Crime, Mar 2022; Publimetro, 18 Mar 2022

n: Medellín's security chief convicted over dealings with La Oficina crime group
rank: Secretary of Security, Medellín
d: La Oficina de Envigado, Medellín's main crime group, had a line into the city hall official responsible for security, prosecutors said. Gustavo Villegas, Medellín's security secretary under Mayor Federico Gutiérrez, was arrested on 4 July 2017. The prosecutor said he passed privileged information to jailed bosses, especially Edison Rojas, alias Pichi. Villegas reached a plea deal admitting abuse of office for meeting Oficina leaders, and in May 2018 Medellín's High Court upheld 33 months in prison and 81 months' ban from office. The Attorney General's Office objected that the deal did not reveal the truth. Gutiérrez said his administration fought the group and that Villegas was arrested over an unreported extortion attempt.
inside: Prosecutors said a crime group's jailed bosses received privileged information from the city official in charge of fighting them; he admitted meeting its leaders while holding the post.
cite: El Espectador, High Court upholds sentence, May 2018; Infobae, 9 Mar 2022

n: Peace-court prosecutor took money to delay ex-FARC Santrich's extradition
rank: Support prosecutor, JEP peace tribunal
d: Prosecutors say emissaries of Jesús Santrich, a former FARC commander wanted by the United States, paid a prosecutor inside the JEP, the tribunal set up by the peace deal to judge the war. Carlos Julián Bermeo was filmed taking cash in a Bogotá hotel in 2019, in transactions said to reach US$40,000, and investigators said he agreed to delay Santrich's extradition by at least three months. In September 2022 a court convicted him of bribery at first instance and sentenced him to eight years, while acquitting him of conspiracy and influence peddling. Bermeo said he would appeal. A fugitive, he was recaptured in Bogotá on 15 March 2024 with US Marshals support. No appeal result was found.
inside: Prosecutors say people acting for a former guerrilla leader paid a prosecutor inside the peace tribunal to slow his extradition case; a court convicted the prosecutor of taking the bribe.
cite: Noticias RCN, 9 Sep 2022; Vanguardia, 15 Mar 2024; El Colombiano, Mar 2024

n: Buenaventura port smugglers allegedly had a prosecutors' team leader
org_label: Buenaventura port smuggling and drug networks
rank: CTI team coordinator, Attorney General's Office
d: Prosecutors allege that smuggling networks linking Colombia's main Pacific port, Buenaventura, with Cali and Bogotá had a man inside the CTI, the Attorney General's Office's investigative police. Francisco Javier Martínez, alias Pacho Malo, coordinated the CTI team in Buenaventura that handled drug and smuggling cases. Undercover CTI agents gathered material on him from 2020 to 2022. He was arrested in Medellín on 22 February 2024 for criminal conspiracy. The agents also said deputy attorney general Martha Mancera and another senior official favoured him. An inquiry into Mancera was closed in January 2024 for lack of evidence and reopened in May 2025. She denies the claims and says the agents are lying.
inside: Prosecutors allege smuggling networks had the very officer leading local drug and contraband inquiries; agents claim senior prosecutors shielded him, which remains unproven and is denied.
cite: Vanguardia, capture, 22 Feb 2024; El Tiempo, inquiry reopened, 24 May 2025

n: AUC commander Mancuso allegedly chose the rectors of the University of Córdoba
rank: Rector and governing board, state university
d: The AUC paramilitary army under Salvatore Mancuso allegedly took control of the University of Córdoba, a state university in Montería, by pressing its governing board over who became rector. Recordings raised in Congress by Gustavo Petro in 2004 reportedly show Mancuso pressing board members over the 2000 vote. On 18 February 2003 board members, unions and the acting rector met him at a camp in Santa Fe de Ralito; four who attended later voted for Claudio Sánchez Parra as rector. Victims' lawyers count over 277 abuses against the university community and say collective agreements were ended. In 2008 Mancuso confessed to murders of staff and students. Prosecutors sent Sánchez to trial in 2019; the sources cited give no verdict or defence.
inside: Prosecutors and victims allege a paramilitary commander pressed a state university's board to elect his preferred rector, so its leadership and labour policy served the armed group.
cite: Semana, 8 May 2004; El Heraldo, 15 Feb 2019

n: Ex-commander says AUC gained votes on the University of Sucre's board
who: AUC, Héroes de Montes de María bloc
rank: Governing board, state university
d: A former AUC paramilitary commander says his bloc copied what Salvatore Mancuso did at the University of Córdoba and got inside the University of Sucre, a public university in Sincelejo. Edwar Cobos, alias Diego Vecino, told a Justice and Peace prosecutor in May 2011 that between 2001 and 2005 the group had the votes of the students' and graduates' board representatives. He named Jáder Castilla and Yahir Acuña, then a city councillor and later a member of the Chamber of Representatives, said this helped elect Rafael Peralta as rector, and said the group proposed its vice-rector in exchange for those votes. The prosecutor said he would send copies for criminal inquiries. The report carries no response from Acuña and no verification.
inside: A former paramilitary commander claims his group won board votes at a public university to choose its rector and vice-rector; this has not been shown in court.
cite: El Heraldo, 9 May 2011

n: Convicted Magdalena governor Trino Luna told peace court of AUC control there
rank: Governor of Magdalena, 2004-2007
d: Trino Luna Correa, governor of Magdalena department from 2004 to 2007, was convicted in the 'parapolítica' scandal, the prosecutions of politicians allied to the AUC paramilitary army. In July 2022 Colombia's peace tribunal, the JEP, accepted him and he pledged to explain the AUC's influence over public administration, its control of elections in Magdalena and its funding by local businesses. He also made claims about national figures, including that the AUC financed the campaign of Mario Iguarán, Attorney General from 2005 to 2009, through commanders Macaco and Jorge 40. The JEP told him he must provide evidence for his statements. Those claims are unproven; the report carries no reply from those he named.
inside: A governor convicted over paramilitary ties has told a tribunal that the AUC influenced Magdalena's administration and elections; his wider claims about national officials remain unproven.
cite: Publimetro, on the JEP's decision of 12 Jul 2022, 14 Jul 2022

n: Mancuso told peace court the DAS gave his men targets at Córdoba's university
rank: DAS state intelligence collaborators
d: Salvatore Mancuso, a former AUC paramilitary commander, told Colombia's peace tribunal, the JEP, in Montería in May 2023 that staff of the DAS, the state intelligence agency, worked for his group. He said the DAS supplied information about professors' supposed guerrilla links at the University of Córdoba, on which the group decided to kill three named teachers and students. He also said the DAS ran illegal phone taps and moved his men in Córdoba and Norte de Santander, and that he had DAS collaborators from 1988 and 1989. He said the group had also infiltrated the student body through a student leader. The report gives Mancuso's account only, with no independent check or reply.
inside: A paramilitary commander testifies that state intelligence staff gave his group names and transport, so agency information chose whom his men killed; this is his account.
cite: El Universal (Cartagena), 17 May 2023

n: Paraguay's arms-control officers accused over guns for PCC and CV; Brazil acquitted four
who: Arms network supplying PCC and Comando Vermelho
rank: Directorate of War Material (DIMABEL)
d: Prosecutors in Brazil and Paraguay allege an arms-trafficking network had officers at DIMABEL, the Paraguayan military agency that controls and registers weapons, to supply Brazilian buyers, chiefly the PCC and Comando Vermelho gangs. In November 2025 Brazilian prosecutors reported that a federal court had sentenced four officers (a general, a colonel, a captain and a lieutenant) to terms of up to 7 years 6 months. Paraguayan press reported in April 2026 that all four were acquitted, with a Brazilian regional federal court clearing General Jorge Orué Roa and Colonel Bienvenido Fretes, and Brazil dropped their extradition. Paraguayan prosecutors allege those two and General Arturo González Ocampos took gifts or payments linked to the importer International Auto Supply. A judge ordered trial in May 2025; no verdict was found.
inside: Prosecutors allege officers in the agency licensing weapons imports helped, for gifts or payments, a network whose guns were meant for Brazilian gangs; a Brazilian court acquitted four of them.
cite: Ministério Público Federal (Brazil), 6 Nov 2025; ABC Color, 7 Dec 2024, 9 May 2025 and 21 Apr 2026; Última Hora, 21 Apr 2026

n: Clan Rotela allegedly bribed guards and set shifts at Paraguay's Tacumbú
rank: Guards and managers, Tacumbú prison
d: The Clan Rotela, a Paraguayan crime group led by Armando Rotela, allegedly took over the running of Tacumbú, the country's main prison, by bribing and threatening its staff. Former Justice Minister Ángel Barchini testified that guards protected the clan under threats and bribery. A guard said staff lost control in 2021 and clan members decided shift changes. Prison director Luis Esquivel says his security chief pressed him to open the gates during a revolt on 10 October 2023, when he was seized and stabbed. About 2,500 police and soldiers retook the jail on 18 December 2023, and over 300 phones were seized. Prosecutors indicted Rotela and eight others in December 2024; in May 2025 a judge sent the case to trial.
inside: Prosecutors and witnesses say a crime group bribed and threatened prison staff until it set guards' shifts, so the staff protected the gang they were guarding.
cite: ABC Color, on the indictment, 22 Dec 2024; Última Hora, 27 Jun 2025

n: Trafficker 'Tavi' Celis funded Paraná's mayor, then got a municipal unit
rank: Mayor, councillor and security official, Paraná
d: A drug-selling group led by Daniel 'Tavi' Celis got inside the city government of Paraná, capital of Argentina's Entre Ríos province, by financing the 2015 campaign of Sergio Varisco, who won knowing where the money came from, a court found. Once elected, Varisco, councillor Pablo Hernández and security official Griselda Bordeira let the clan keep trafficking and gave it unrestricted control of Municipal Unit No. 2. On 30 December 2019 a federal court convicted 26 people, sentencing Varisco to six and a half years and Celis to 13. The federal cassation court confirmed the verdicts in December 2020. Varisco and Celis denied wrongdoing. Six other defendants were acquitted.
inside: A drug group paid for a mayor's campaign; judges found that in office he and his officials let it keep trading and gave it a municipal unit.
cite: La Capital, 31 Dec 2019; El Litoral, 22 Dec 2020

n: Montonero guerrilla served as a conscript inside Formosa's army regiment
rank: Conscript, Regimiento de Infantería de Monte 29
d: The Montoneros, an Argentine guerrilla movement, had one of their own inside an army regiment before attacking it. According to Infobae's account, drawing on Ceferino Reato's book, Luis Roberto Mayol was a Montonero who had served as a conscript at Regiment 29 in Formosa. On 5 October 1975 about 50 Montoneros tried to seize 200 weapons there, planning to bring in attackers on a hijacked airliner. They expected little resistance, but conscripts fought back. Infobae counts 32 dead, including 10 conscripts; El Litoral counts 28. The sources do not set out exactly what Mayol passed on.
inside: A guerrilla movement had a member serving as a conscript in the regiment it raided for weapons; published accounts call him its infiltrator, without detailing his role.
cite: Infobae, 27 Nov 2018; El Litoral, on Operación Primicia; Wikipedia, Operation Primicia

n: Tupamaros recruited a sailor who opened Uruguay's naval training centre
rank: Second-class sailor, Centro de Instrucción de la Marina
d: The Tupamaros, Uruguay's urban guerrilla movement, had a sailor working for them inside the navy's training centre in Montevideo. According to an account in the Cuban journal Pensamiento Crítico, second-class sailor Fernando Gorin (also spelled Garin), on guard duty that night, gave the signal in late May 1970, disarmed the roof sentry and helped subdue the duty petty officer. Militants identifying themselves as police were let in. They locked up the personnel and left with over 300 long arms. Uruguayan police files, held in the Sitios de Memoria archive, list about 300 rifles, 170 revolvers and 30 pistols taken, and date the raid 27 May; the journal says 29 May. Gorin went underground. Fernán Pucurull, a Tupamaro named as a raider, was killed days later.
inside: A guerrilla movement recruited a serving sailor, who used his guard post to open a naval base to its fighters, so the navy's own weapons went to the movement.
cite: Pensamiento Crítico no. 43, Havana, Aug 1970; Sitios de Memoria Uruguay, file on Fernán Pucurull

n: US says Venezuelan diplomat Ghazi Nasr al Din used his post to fund Hizballah
rank: Chargé d'affaires in Damascus; embassy post in Lebanon
d: The US Treasury said in June 2008 that Hizballah, the Lebanese armed movement, had a supporter inside Venezuela's diplomatic service. Ghazi Nasr al Din had been chargé d'affaires at Venezuela's embassy in Damascus, then director of political aspects at its embassy in Lebanon. Treasury said he used his position as a diplomat, and as president of a Shi'a Islamic centre in Caracas, to support Hizballah financially. It said he advised donors on fundraising, gave them bank details so deposits went directly to Hizballah, and arranged members' travel, including a January 2006 trip to Caracas. He was designated under US terrorism sanctions, with Fawzi Kan'an and two travel agencies. This is a US finding, not a court verdict.
inside: The US Treasury says an armed movement's supporter sat in Venezuela's diplomatic service and used that post to raise money for it and arrange its members' travel.
cite: US Treasury press release hp-1036, 18 Jun 2008

n: Communist and MIR ties to Venezuelan officers behind the 1962 Carúpano rising
rank: Marine battalion and National Guard officers
d: Venezuela's Communist Party (PCV) and the Revolutionary Left Movement (MIR) had links with serving officers who rose against President Rómulo Betancourt in Carúpano on 4 May 1962. Captain Jesús Molina Villegas, Major Pedro Vegas Castejón and Lieutenant Héctor Fleming Mendoza led a marine battalion and a National Guard detachment. Accounts name PCV and MIR figures involved, including Congressman Eloy Torres and Douglas Bravo. Loyal forces retook the town within a day; one count gives 56 dead and over 400 arrested. Betancourt suspended the activities of both parties by decree, and a second rising followed at Puerto Cabello a month later.
inside: Two left-wing parties had ties with serving officers, who then turned their units against the government, according to accounts of the rising.
cite: El Ciudadano, on the Carupanazo; Wikipedia, El Carupanazo

n: Illegal gold miners allegedly got tip-offs from Peruvian police: 96 officers in 37 cases
rank: Peruvian National Police, sub-officers to colonel
d: Police officers in Peru have been accused of working for illegal gold-mining networks, according to an Ojo Público report on cases reviewed by the Police Disciplinary Tribunal. From 2019 to 2024 at least 37 cases implicated 96 officers, 36 of them in La Libertad, home of the Pataz mining area, where 13 mine workers were killed. Officers were accused of leaking operations to miners, stealing gold and altering custody of seized ore. They included a colonel and two commanders. Cases rose from 2 in 2019 to 16 in 2024, but only six ended with sanctions fully upheld, and eight ended in acquittal. Illegal miners also use a government registry, Reinfo, to avoid controls.
inside: Disciplinary cases accuse police officers of leaking operations to illegal miners and tampering with seized ore, so that officers sent to stop the mining served it instead.
cite: Ojo Público via Actualidad Ambiental, 28 May 2025; La República, 15 Sep 2026

n: Peru's police chief accused of selling protection to gold miners
who: Informal gold miners and a mining firm
rank: Head of Arequipa police region; later national commander
d: Witnesses allege that informal gold miners in Arequipa had Víctor Zanabria on their side when he led the region's police; he later became commander general of Peru's National Police. The Sunday programme Panorama, reported by RPP in May 2025, cited an anonymous officer and a protected collaborator. They claim he belonged to a group selling police protection in mining disputes, tipped off armed miners before operations, and took payment in cash and gold, and that officers listed at Arequipa posts really worked at a mine for 250 soles a day. Zanabria replied that the Public Ministry archived the case because the collaborator gave a date when he was in Jordan. The claims come from unnamed sources and were not independently verified.
inside: Unnamed witnesses claim gold miners paid a regional police chief for protection and warnings; he says prosecutors closed the case, and nothing is proven.
cite: RPP, citing Panorama, 12 May 2025

n: Bolivia probed whether police warned trafficker Marset before he fled in 2023
rank: Anti-narcotics force (FELCN) and Santa Cruz police
d: Bolivia's government investigated in 2023 whether the Uruguayan cocaine trafficker Sebastián Marset had help inside its police. Marset left Santa Cruz on 29 July 2023. Four days later he sent a video thanking Ismael Tito Villca, director of the FELCN, the anti-narcotics force, for alerting him to leave in time. Villca firmly denied it. Government Minister Eduardo del Castillo said he could not rule out police help and that prosecutors and even judges might have favoured Marset. Villca and two other senior officers testified as witnesses, and the police high command publicly backed Villca. Marset's video is a trafficker's own claim; the report cited shows no finding against any officer.
inside: A minister said a trafficker may have had help inside police and courts, after he thanked the anti-drug chief for a warning; this is unproven, and police backed the chief.
cite: Montevideo Portal, 29 Aug 2023

n: Airbus money reached SriLankan Airlines' chief via his wife's shell firm
rank: Chief executive of state-run SriLankan Airlines
d: Airbus, the European planemaker, used a shell company to pay the head of state-run SriLankan Airlines during the 2013 sale of 10 aircraft. The UK Serious Fraud Office's 2020 settlement with Airbus described a US$2 million bribery arrangement through a Brunei firm in the name of chief executive Kapila Chandrasena's wife. Sri Lanka's bribery commission alleges the money went further. Chandrasena reportedly said Rs 60 million reached former president Mahinda Rajapaksa, then retracted this, alleging intimidation; he was found dead in May 2026. Prosecutors allege Rs 100 million reached his son Namal, who denies it and was in remand from September 2026. The order for four A350s was terminated at a reported US$116 million.
inside: Airbus paid the chief of the state airline buying its planes; Sri Lankan investigators allege the money also reached the president's family, which Namal Rajapaksa denies.
cite: News 1st, 12 May 2026; Daily FT, 9 May and 30 Sep 2026, and 6 Oct 2016; EconomyNext, 4 Sep 2026; The Sunday Times (Sri Lanka), 13 Sep 2026; Daily FT, 20 Mar 2026

n: SNC-Lavalin accused of bribing for Padma Bridge job; executives acquitted
rank: Communications minister and Bridges Division officials (alleged)
d: The World Bank accused SNC-Lavalin, a Canadian engineering firm, of conspiring to bribe Bangladesh's communications minister Syed Abul Hossain and other officials to win the consultancy job on the Padma Bridge. In June 2012 the bank cancelled its US$1.2 billion credit, citing a corruption conspiracy. None of this was proven. Bangladesh's Anti-Corruption Commission cleared all the accused in September 2014. In Canada, a judge excluded the wiretap evidence, prosecutors called no evidence, and in February 2017 three former SNC-Lavalin executives were acquitted. The bank also barred the firm from its projects for 10 years. Bangladesh finished the bridge with its own money in 2022.
inside: The World Bank alleged a Canadian firm tried to buy a minister and officials to win a state bridge contract, but Bangladeshi and Canadian proceedings cleared the accused.
cite: The Daily Star (Bangladesh), Feb 2017; Wikipedia, Padma Bridge graft scandal (World Bank statements, 2012)

n: Medical colleges allegedly paid India's health ministry staff and inspectors
org_label: Private medical college owners and middlemen
rank: Health Ministry officials, National Medical Commission inspectors and board member
d: Owners of private medical colleges allegedly paid officials inside India's Health Ministry and the National Medical Commission (NMC), the body that decides which colleges may teach doctors. In July 2025 the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) named 34 people, among them eight ministry officials, a National Health Authority official, five NMC inspection doctors and board member Jeetu Lal Meena. The CBI alleges ministry staff photographed confidential files and sold inspection dates and inspectors' names. Colleges could then prepare ghost teachers, fake patients and tampered fingerprint attendance. Three inspectors allegedly took Rs 55 lakh for a favourable report on one institute. Eight people were arrested, and none of the allegations has yet been proven in court.
inside: The CBI alleges private college owners paid ministry staff and inspectors for leaked inspection files and favourable reports, so the regulator of doctor training served those it regulates.
cite: PTI via The Week, 4 Jul 2025; Medical Dialogues, 7 Jul 2025

n: Rolls-Royce accused of paying Indian officials over Hawk jet deal
rank: Unnamed Defence Ministry, HAL and tax officials (alleged)
d: Rolls-Royce, the British engine maker, is accused of paying intermediaries whose money reached Indian public servants during India's purchase of Hawk trainer jets. In May 2023 the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) booked the company, its then India director Tim Jones and arms dealer Sudhir Choudhrie, along with unidentified officials of the Defence Ministry and Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL). Its case says tax officials were paid to block inquiries, and that about GBP 1.85 million went to an intermediary to retrieve a seized list of agents, which could have ended the contract. A 2017 UK court judgment found Rolls-Royce concealed its Indian intermediaries from 2005 to 2009. The Indian allegations have not been tested in court.
inside: The CBI alleges Rolls-Royce's money reached defence and tax officials through intermediaries, so that purchases and tax inquiries inside the Indian state served the company.
cite: ThePrint, 29 May 2023 (citing the CBI FIR and Southwark Crown Court judgment of 17 Jan 2017)

n: Kashmir police officer Davinder Singh caught driving Hizbul militants
rank: Deputy Superintendent of Police, Jammu and Kashmir
d: Davinder Singh, a Deputy Superintendent of Police in Jammu and Kashmir, is accused of working for Hizbul Mujahideen, an armed group fighting Indian rule in Kashmir. On 11 January 2020 police stopped a car on the Srinagar-Jammu road and found him with two Hizbul militants; weapons and explosives were recovered. The National Investigation Agency's July 2020 charge sheet alleges he sheltered a commander in Jammu, moved militants in his own vehicle and helped obtain arms from across the border. It also alleges Pakistani High Commission officials in New Delhi were grooming him for sensitive information. The Lieutenant Governor dismissed him in May 2021. The reports cited give no trial verdict.
inside: Prosecutors say an armed group and Pakistani officials had a serving police officer on their side, using his rank and vehicle to protect and move militants.
cite: The Quint, 6 Jul 2020 and 21 May 2021; The Wire, 6 Jul 2020

n: About 80 Kashmir state staff dismissed as alleged militant collaborators
rank: Police, prisons, schools, hospitals, J&K Bank and other state bodies
d: Authorities in Jammu and Kashmir say armed groups such as Hizbul Mujahideen and Lashkar-e-Taiba have supporters on the state payroll, and about 80 employees were dismissed in the five years to October 2025. Those removed include two sons of Hizbul's leader, who officials say handled its funding, plus constables alleged to have given militants inside information, teachers, a prisons deputy superintendent and a J&K Bank chief manager. A task force set up in April 2021 selects cases. Article 311 of the Constitution lets the government dismiss staff without an inquiry on security grounds, so the allegations are not tested first. Politician Mehbooba Mufti and trade unions call the dismissals arbitrary.
inside: Officials allege armed groups kept people in state jobs who passed information and handled funds for them; the dismissals came without inquiry, so most claims remain unproven.
cite: Scroll, Jul 2021; Kashmir Life, 6 Nov 2023; ETV Bharat, 30 Oct 2025; IBTimes India

n: Serving Pakistani navy officers helped militants try to seize a frigate
rank: Pakistan Navy officers at Karachi Naval Dockyard
d: Serving Pakistan Navy officers worked with militants to try to seize the frigate PNS Zulfiqar at Karachi Naval Dockyard on 6 September 2014. The attackers came aboard in uniform showing service cards. Al-Qaeda's South Asian branch claimed the attack and said it meant to turn the ship's missiles on American and Indian naval vessels, though the Pakistani Taliban also claimed it. A closed navy tribunal sentenced five officers to death in 2016 for terrorist links, mutiny, conspiracy and bringing weapons into the dockyard. One officer's father said the charge named Islamic State links. The navy has refused to release its inquiry report. In December 2024 the Islamabad High Court lifted a stay on the executions.
inside: A militant group had serving navy officers on its side, and a navy tribunal found they conspired and brought weapons into the dockyard to seize a warship.
cite: Nukta, Dec 2024; Asia Times, Jun 2016; The Express Tribune, May 2016

n: Energy firm staff charged over papers taken from India's oil ministry
rank: Petroleum ministry files, via paid suppliers and government staff
d: Executives of Indian energy companies are accused of paying for confidential papers taken from the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, which sets rules and awards for their industry. In February 2015 Delhi Police arrested staff of Reliance Industries, Reliance ADAG, Essar, Cairn India and Jubilant Energy. The April 2015 charge sheet named 13 people, including two men described as government employees and a casual defence ministry worker. Police said two brothers, arrested outside Shastri Bhavan, the building housing the ministry, were paid Rs 2.5 lakh a month for documents. Charges were theft, trespass, forgery and conspiracy; the Official Secrets Act was not then used. The reports cited give no trial outcome or company statements.
inside: Police allege energy firms' staff paid for confidential papers from the ministry that governs them, with government workers among those charged in the scheme.
cite: Free Press Journal; The Quint; The News Minute, 18 Apr 2015; Business Standard/IANS, 20 Apr 2015; Millennium Post, 20 Apr 2015

n: Gold smugglers allegedly reached Kerala chief minister's top civil servant
org_label: Gold smuggling network using UAE consulate baggage
rank: Principal secretary to Kerala's chief minister
d: A gold smuggling network allegedly had help from M. Sivasankar, principal secretary to Kerala's chief minister. In July 2020 customs officers found about 30 kg of gold in diplomatic baggage addressed to the UAE consulate, which is normally cleared without inspection. They arrested P.S. Sarith, a former consulate employee, who named Swapna Suresh, another former employee. Investigators alleged Sivasankar pressed customs to clear baggage without checks and took commission on a state housing scheme. He was arrested in October 2020, spent 98 days in jail, and had his suspension revoked in January 2022. In April 2023 the Kerala High Court refused him bail in the housing case; in January 2024 the Supreme Court granted medical bail without ruling on the merits. No verdict was found.
inside: Investigators allege smugglers got the chief minister's senior aide to press customs to pass their consignments; the reports cited show no court finding on that allegation.
cite: ThePrint, Dec 2020; The News Minute, 5 Jan 2022; Onmanorama, 13 Apr 2023; DT Next, 19 Jan 2024

n: Police tipped off gangster Vikas Dubey before he ambushed eight officers
rank: Chaubeypur police station and senior Kanpur police
d: Gangster Vikas Dubey had police in Uttar Pradesh's Kanpur district passing him information, a state inquiry found. Shortly after midnight on 3 July 2020, eight policemen who went to arrest him in Bikru village were ambushed with gunfire from rooftops. Dubey was killed by police on 10 July. A three-member Special Investigation Team then reported a nexus between police, administration officials and Dubey. Its 3,500-page report said officers gave him tip-offs, that his phone records showed policemen in regular contact over the previous year, and that police failed to secure convictions in his pending cases. It recommended action against 80 police personnel and left the decision to the government.
inside: A crime boss had police officers in contact and on side, and the state inquiry found their tip-offs and inaction protected him instead of enforcing the law.
cite: The Week, 5 Nov 2020

n: Staffer at India's Moscow embassy accused of passing secrets to ISI
rank: Security assistant, Indian embassy in Moscow
d: Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), its main spy agency, allegedly paid a Ministry of External Affairs employee posted at India's embassy in Moscow for confidential information. The Uttar Pradesh Anti-Terrorist Squad arrested Satendra Siwal, 26, on 3 February 2024 after summoning him to its Meerut unit while he was home on leave. He joined the service in 2018 and went to Moscow in 2021; ThePrint describes him as multi-tasking staff, and a ministry source as a security assistant. The squad says he had passed strategically sensitive information to ISI operatives since 2021. The report gives no amount for the payments. The report cited does not cover any trial.
inside: Police say Pakistan's spy agency paid a foreign ministry employee inside an Indian embassy, so information the ministry was meant to protect went to Pakistan.
cite: ThePrint, Feb 2024

n: HAL fighter-jet plant supervisor arrested as alleged ISI source
rank: Assistant supervisor, HAL Aircraft Division
d: Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), its main spy agency, allegedly obtained information from inside Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL), the state-owned firm that builds India's military aircraft. In October 2020 the Maharashtra Anti-Terrorism Squad arrested Deepak Shirsath, 41, an assistant supervisor who had worked for 15 years at HAL's Aircraft Division near Nashik. Police say he sent details of Indian fighter aircraft, the factory at Ozar, the nearby airbase and restricted areas over WhatsApp and social media. An officer said he confessed; that claim comes from police. A case was registered under the Official Secrets Act, and phones and memory cards went for forensic testing. The report cited does not give a verdict.
inside: Police allege Pakistan's spy agency recruited a long-serving supervisor inside India's state military aircraft maker to pass it details of fighters and the plant.
cite: Scroll, 9 Oct 2020

n: Two Indian ordnance factory staff accused of leaking output data to ISI
rank: Junior works manager and chargeman at ordnance factories
d: Pakistani agents allegedly recruited staff inside two Indian ordnance factories, the plants that make ammunition and weapons for the armed forces. In March 2025 the Uttar Pradesh Anti-Terrorism Squad arrested Ravindra Kumar, a chargeman at Hazratpur in Firozabad, and Kumar Vikas, a junior works manager at Kanpur. Both allegedly dealt with a social media contact called 'Neha Sharma', which police believe was a false identity. Police say they passed production reports, stores records, requisitions, machine layouts and staff attendance sheets, for money. Kumar Vikas was booked under the Official Secrets Act. The squad says Pakistani handlers use such identities to approach central government staff. The reports cited do not cover any trial.
inside: Police allege Pakistani intelligence used a fake online identity and money to recruit staff at two arms factories, who then sent it production data.
cite: The Week, 15 Mar 2025; India TV, 19 Mar 2025

n: Engineer with Mumbai naval dockyard access accused of spying for Pakistan
rank: Contractor's engineer with access to Mumbai naval dockyard
d: A Pakistani intelligence operative allegedly recruited an engineer whose job, the police say, gave him access to warships at the naval dockyard in south Mumbai. The Maharashtra Anti-Terrorism Squad arrested Ravindra Verma, 27, of Thane on 28 May 2025. He worked as a junior service engineer for a defence technology firm and went aboard naval ships and submarines. The squad alleges an agent posing as a woman on Facebook drew him in, and that he sent sketches, diagrams and audio notes about warships and submarines in return for money from accounts in India and abroad. Verma pleaded innocence in a bail application, saying the allegations must be proven at trial.
inside: Police allege a Pakistani operative recruited a contractor's engineer with access to the navy's dockyard to pass it details of ships and submarines; he pleads innocence.
cite: PTI via The Week, 25 Jun 2025

n: Coast Guard boat welder allegedly paid Rs 200 a day by Pakistani handler
org_label: Pakistani handler using the name Sahima
rank: Welder working on Coast Guard boats at Okha jetty
d: A Pakistani handler allegedly recruited a welder who worked on Indian Coast Guard boats at Okha jetty in Gujarat. The Gujarat Anti-Terrorist Squad announced the arrest of Deepesh Gohel, 33, on 29 November 2024. Police say a Facebook contact called Sahima, who claimed to work for the Pakistan Navy, approached him about seven months earlier. He allegedly sent the names and movements of ships stationed at Okha for Rs 200 a day, with about Rs 42,000 moving through his associates' accounts. Gujarat police reported a similar arrest in Porbandar a month before. He was booked for criminal conspiracy against the state. The reports cited do not cover any trial.
inside: Police allege a Pakistani handler paid a worker with access to Coast Guard boats to report which ships were at the base and how they moved.
cite: Free Press Journal/ANI, 30 Nov 2024; News Arena India; Patrika, May 2025

n: Cochin Shipyard subcontract workers accused of leaking navy ship data
rank: Insulation workers at Udupi Cochin Shipyard
d: Pakistani handlers allegedly recruited subcontract workers at Udupi Cochin Shipyard, part of the Indian shipbuilder Cochin Shipyard, to send them details of naval ships. The chief executive of Cochin Shipyard reported a security breach at Malpe police station in Karnataka in November 2025. Police then arrested Rohit and Santri, insulation workers employed by the subcontractor Shushma Marine. They allege Rohit sent ship identification numbers, repair schedules and details of sensitive infrastructure, continuing after a transfer with Santri's help. A third man was later held for allegedly supplying SIM cards and one-time passwords for the WhatsApp accounts. All three face Official Secrets Act charges, and none has been proven in court. Police reported a further arrest in February 2026.
inside: Police allege Pakistani handlers recruited a subcontractor's staff working inside a state shipyard, who passed them details of naval vessels under repair there.
cite: Scroll, Dec 2025; ETV Bharat, Feb 2026

n: Rajasthan official, a former minister's ex-aide, accused of working with ISI agents
rank: Assistant administrative officer, district employment office
d: Police in Rajasthan allege that Shakur Khan, an assistant administrative officer at the employment office in Jaisalmer, a district on the Pakistani border, passed sensitive information to Pakistan's Inter-Service Intelligence (ISI). Police arrested him in June 2025 after detaining him on 28 May.
