They say he kept in contact with staff at Pakistan's High Commission in New Delhi, including one expelled by India that May, visited Pakistan without reporting it, met ISI agents and sent information over WhatsApp. He had been personal assistant to former minister Saleh Mohammed; Congress said that link does not implicate the minister. The arrest came amid a wider wave of at least 16 spying arrests.
inside: Police allege a Rajasthan government employee in a border district dealt with Pakistan's spy agency and its embassy staff and sent them sensitive information.
cite: Scroll, 4 Jun 2025

n: Embraer paid $800,000 to win a jet sale to Mozambique's state airline
rank: Transport Minister; state airline LAM
d: Brazilian aircraft maker Embraer paid $800,000 in bribes to secure the sale of two aircraft to LAM, Mozambique's state airline, in 2009. The money was booked as "sales commissions" and paid in two $400,000 instalments to Xihivele, a shell company set up by the go-between Mateus Zimba, through an account in Portugal. In September 2021 Maputo City Court sentenced the former transport minister, Paulo Zucula, and Zimba to ten years each, and ordered them to pay Mozambique 70.7 million meticais. Both defence teams planned to appeal. LAM's former chairman, Jose Viegas, was acquitted for insufficient evidence and an expired time limit; the attorney general said it would appeal. Embraer admitted paying bribes in several countries and paid about $225 million in US and Brazilian fines.
inside: A foreign aircraft maker sent bribes through a shell company while Mozambique's state airline bought its planes, and a court jailed the transport minister and the go-between.
cite: MarketScreener/AIM, 14 Sept 2021; ch-aviation, Sept 2021

n: Chinese timber traders claimed Mozambique's agriculture ministers helped them
rank: Minister of Agriculture (current and former)
d: Chinese timber traders told undercover investigators that they benefited from help by Mozambique's agriculture ministers, whose ministry oversees the forests, according to a February 2013 report by the Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA), a campaign group. EIA linked the trader Mofid to minister Jose Pacheco and the trader Senlian to his predecessor Thomas Mandlate. A trader, Liu Chaoying, said Pacheco was "like brothers" with him and came to him for money. Both ministers denied involvement. EIA put 2012 lost revenue at almost $30 million. Prosecutors opened an investigation. EIA's 2014 follow-up said the anti-corruption office, apparently prompted by donors, found no evidence that Mozambicans held shares in either firm, and called officials' role in illegal exports beyond its scope. Mofid's licence was suspended for a year.
inside: EIA alleges Chinese log exporters had the ministers who oversee Mozambique's forests on their side, so smuggled timber left the country untaxed; both ministers denied it.
cite: EIA, 3 May 2013; EIA, First Class Crisis, July 2014; Wood Floor Business, 2013

n: Mofid accused of paying Mozambique customs and forest agents at Pemba
rank: Customs and forest checkpoint agents
d: Mofid, a Chinese-linked timber company in northern Mozambique, was accused of paying state agents to get its timber through. In January 2017, days after a ban on raw log exports took effect, the reporting outlet Oxpeckers described about 30 containers from Mofid and its associate Peng Pai being loaded at Pemba harbour. Drivers said the cargo had no export permits and alleged that customs agents were paid to offload it. An unnamed employee alleged that Mofid's general manager, Vicky Lau, paid cash to agriculture and environment agents at checkpoints for seized illegal timber. The provincial agriculture department had cancelled Mofid's licence, but the report alleged it kept operating through other companies. Lau and Mofid did not answer questions. The report mentions no charges.
inside: Drivers and an employee allege a timber firm paid customs and forest agents, so the officers meant to stop illegal logs let them through or sold them on.
cite: Oxpeckers (Estacio Valoi), 10 Jan 2017

n: Chinese timber firms allegedly bribe officials along Mozambique's export route
rank: Officials on the timber route; ruling Frelimo party
d: Chinese timber businesses pay Mozambican officials to move wood to port, according to a May 2024 report by the Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA), a campaign group. A former official, quoted anonymously, described sharing in the bribes. EIA says inspections of protected rosewood rarely happen because of corruption, and that the ruling Frelimo party gains campaign funds from Chinese investment, making it reluctant to crack down. China takes more than 90% of Mozambique's wood despite a log export ban in place since 2017. EIA also estimates that about 30% of timber from Cabo Delgado province comes from insurgent-held forests, a claim analysts dispute. China's embassy in Washington and the environment minister did not answer VOA. An attorney general's report to parliament links forest crime to corruption.
inside: EIA alleges Chinese timber firms pay Mozambican officials, so those officials move banned wood to port and inspections of protected rosewood rarely happen.
cite: VOA, 17 May 2024, citing EIA

n: Mukula rosewood traffickers allegedly reached Zambia's president and ministers
rank: President's circle, ministers, state forestry firm ZAFFICO
d: Timber traffickers supplying China allegedly used Zambia's state forestry company, ZAFFICO, as cover and shared profits with people around President Edgar Lungu, according to the Environmental Investigation Agency's 2019 report "The Mukula Cartel". Mukula is a protected rosewood. EIA named Lungu's daughter Tasila, Lands Minister Jean Kapata and Justice Minister Given Lubinda. It estimated over 50 containers a month left illegally from June 2017 to May 2019, with about $7.5 million a year in bribes and informal fees, and said a Chinese trader gave $40,000 worth of campaign outfits. The government denied it and Kapata called the report fake. Tasila Lungu, Lubinda and Kapata sued EIA in 2021; Lungu later withdrew. Transparency International Zambia says most prosecutions are still ongoing.
inside: EIA alleges timber traffickers paid their way to Zambia's ministers and a state company, which then covered their log exports; the officials named deny it.
cite: Daily Monitor/AFP, Dec 2019; Lusaka Times repost of EIA, The Mukula Cartel, 2019; Transparency International Zambia

n: Hong Kong businessman Sam Pa allegedly funded Zimbabwe's spy agency
rank: Central Intelligence Organisation
d: Hong Kong-based businessman Sam Pa, a member of the Queensway Syndicate, gave Zimbabwe's Central Intelligence Organisation (CIO), the state spy agency, money and equipment in return for access to diamonds, cotton and property, according to CIO sources quoted in a June 2012 Global Witness report. One CIO document put the support at $100 million and 200 pick-up trucks. Global Witness, a campaign group, said CIO members jointly controlled a company with Pa, Sino Zimbabwe Development, and called the money apparent off-budget financing, meaning it sat outside the state budget. On 14 April 2014 the US Treasury sanctioned Pa and the company, citing their role in undermining democracy and facilitating corruption. The Global Witness summary records no reply from Pa, the company or the CIO.
inside: Global Witness alleges a foreign businessman paid Zimbabwe's spy agency and went into business with its members, winning access to diamonds and other sectors.
cite: Global Witness, 11 June 2012, with April 2014 update on US Treasury sanctions

n: Malawi police food contractor paid K145m into an account the president signed
rank: Police finance director; ruling party account
d: Businessman Zameer Karim's company Pioneer Investments won a 2015 contract to give Malawi's police 500,000 ration packs, and a leaked Anti-Corruption Bureau report alleged it then paid MK145 million into a ruling party account. President Peter Mutharika was its sole signatory. The report, leaked in June 2018, alleged Karim sought a 20% price rise, and that loans of about MK3.8 billion were taken with police as guarantor using a forged signature. Karim also claimed K466 million extra. Karim and police finance director Innocent Bottoman were charged and pleaded not guilty; Bottoman died in July 2021. Mutharika called the money an honest donation. The party refunded it and later apologised when a civil appeal was withdrawn. In October 2021 the High Court ordered the trial resumed; no verdict was found.
inside: The Anti-Corruption Bureau alleges a contractor got an inflated police food deal with a police finance chief's help, then paid money into the president's party account.
cite: amaBhungane/Daily Maverick, 1 Apr 2019; The Nation (Malawi); The Nation (Malawi), 21 Oct 2021

n: Malawi minister accused of favouring maize trader Transglobe, then acquitted
rank: Minister of Agriculture
d: A presidential inquiry found that Malawi's agriculture minister, George Chaponda, acted suspiciously in favour of a private maize trader, Transglobe, during a food shortage reported to affect 6.5 million people. The inquiry, led by retired Chief Justice Anastasia Msosa, found he personally asked the state grain buyer Admarc to buy from Transglobe, and that Zambia then licensed Transglobe for half of a 100,000-tonne contract. It said the timing could not be put down to coincidence and did not rule out corruption. Chaponda was arrested on 19 July 2017 with Transglobe's representative Rashid Tayub. A magistrate acquitted him in 2018 on charges including illegally holding foreign currency at his home, and the High Court later upheld the acquittal.
inside: An inquiry found a minister pressed a state grain buyer on behalf of a private trader and suggested possible corruption, but a court acquitted him.
cite: The Nation (Malawi) on the Msosa commission report; The Nation on High Court ruling

n: German firm and Lesotho minister accused of forging a solar deal past Cabinet
rank: Minister in the Prime Minister's Office
d: Lesotho's anti-corruption directorate charged Robert Frazer, head of the German company Frazer Solar, and former minister Temeki Tšolo with fraud and abuse of power over a solar deal signed in September 2018. Prosecutors allege they forged the deal after Cabinet declined to approve it and told Tšolo to send it to the energy ministry. Tšolo denies signing and says his signature was forged. The sources cited report no bribe. Lesotho's High Court declared the agreement unlawful in November 2022, but an arbitrator had awarded the company about €50 million, and it pursued Lesotho's water royalties and assets in Belgium and Mauritius. In May 2026 Lesotho's Court of Appeal revived the prosecution, and South Africa's Supreme Court of Appeal sent Lesotho's challenge to the award back for reconsideration.
inside: Prosecutors allege a foreign company and a minister together pushed through a contract Cabinet had not approved, leaving Lesotho facing a €50 million claim from the company.
cite: AllAfrica, 25 May 2026; Public Eye (Lesotho), 11 Nov 2022 and 8 Oct 2024; The Reporter (Lesotho), 4 July 2021

n: Nuctech's alleged $12.8m 'commission' to a Namibian commissioner's firm ended in acquittals
rank: Public Service Commission member
d: Namibian prosecutors alleged that Chinese state-owned scanner maker Nuctech inflated the price of a roughly $55.3 million deal with the finance ministry so it could pay at least $12.8 million in "commission" to Teko Trading. Teko was owned by Teckla Lameck, a serving member of the Public Service Commission, which oversees state employment, and her partner Jerobeam Mokaxwa. Prosecutors said Teko had no role in the deal. The Anti-Corruption Commission arrested them and Nuctech's Africa representative, Yang Fan, in July 2009. Nuctech had been led until 2008 by Hu Haifeng, son of China's then president, though the case did not allege he was involved. The three were later found not guilty of fraud and corruption.
inside: Prosecutors alleged a Chinese firm paid millions to a company owned by a Namibian public service commissioner on a state deal, but the three accused were acquitted.
cite: AFP via Solar Daily, 21 July 2009; The Namibian; NBC News Namibia

n: Lesotho's deputy army commander says security staff help famo gangs
rank: Security agency and police members
d: Members of Lesotho's security agencies escort and associate with famo gangs, deputy army commander Matela Matobakele said in July 2024, without naming any soldier. Famo is a Basotho music style whose rival groups are blamed for killings. He spoke after a famo musician and a radio presenter working for peace between the groups were shot dead in Maseru on the weekend of 20 July 2024. An earlier police minister, Lepota Sekola, had also said some officers were allegedly involved in the gangs. Reports describe strong relations between some gangs and the All Basotho Convention and Democratic Congress parties; the ABC leader denied receiving money from one. In 2024 the government outlawed 12 famo groups. No officer is named in these sources.
inside: Lesotho's own deputy army commander says members of the security agencies escort criminal famo gangs, putting state officers at the gangs' service; he named nobody.
cite: Lesotho Times, 27 July 2024; Africa Press Lesotho; City Press, 18 Sept 2022; Transformation Resource Centre monthly report, June 2024

n: Mining minister took $8.5m from China International Fund, US jury found
rank: Minister of Mines and Geology
d: Executives of China Sonangol and China International Fund (CIF), Chinese-linked companies, paid Guinea's mines minister, Mahmoud Thiam, $8.5m to win rights in the country's mining sector. Thiam, minister in 2009 and 2010, negotiated many terms of a joint venture with CIF. Sam Pa, head of CIF, sent $3m to Thiam's Hong Kong account about two weeks before the shareholders' agreement was signed. The bribes aimed to secure the companies' place as first shareholder in a national mining company that would take over Guinea's stakes in mining projects. A New York jury convicted Thiam of money laundering, and in August 2017 he received seven years in prison. A US appeals court upheld the judgment in August 2019.
inside: Chinese-linked companies paid the minister negotiating with them, and he used his post to steer Guinea's government into agreements giving those companies rights over its mining stakes.
cite: US Department of Justice, 25 August 2017; US Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, United States v. Thiam, 5 August 2019

n: Panalpina and oil firms paid Nigeria Customs officials to ignore import rules
who: Panalpina, Shell, Transocean, Tidewater, Noble, GlobalSantaFe
rank: Nigeria Customs Service officials
d: Panalpina, a Swiss freight company, and oil-sector firms paid officials of the Nigeria Customs Service through brokers to set aside import rules, according to US regulators. From about 2002 to 2007, GlobalSantaFe paid for documents showing its drilling rigs had left Nigerian waters, when they had never moved. Noble obtained eight temporary import permits with false papers. Tidewater reimbursed a broker about $1.6m for such payments, and a Shell unit used a broker to obtain preferential customs treatment. Invoices called the bribes 'special handling' or 'local processing' fees. In November 2010 the firms settled with the US Justice Department and Securities and Exchange Commission. The total for all seven companies in the settlements exceeded $236m.
inside: Foreign companies paid customs officers through brokers, so Nigeria's customs officials supplied false papers and set aside import rules for those companies' rigs and vessels.
cite: US Securities and Exchange Commission, 4 November 2010; National Law Review, 'Record FCPA settlements', 2010

n: Parker Drilling paid an agent to influence a Nigerian customs panel
rank: Temporary Import Panel on customs duties
d: Parker Drilling, a Houston drilling company, paid an agent to influence a Nigerian government panel that was reviewing its customs and tax compliance. Nigeria set up the Temporary Import Panel in late 2002 to check whether its customs service had collected the duties owed. The panel fined Parker $3.8m. From January to May 2004 Parker sent the agent $1.25m instead of paying. The agent reported spending part of it on items including entertaining officials, and his emails mentioned contacts at the Ministry of Finance, the State Security Service and the president's office. The fine fell to $750,000. In April 2013 Parker agreed to an $11.76m penalty under a deferred prosecution agreement, in which charges are dropped if it complies, and paid the US securities regulator $3.05m plus $1.04m in interest.
inside: A US drilling company paid an agent $1.25m to influence the government panel judging it, and the panel's $3.8m fine against the company was cut to $750,000.
cite: US Department of Justice, 16 April 2013

n: Airbus used an official's relative in Ghana plane deals; Ghana found no bribery
rank: High-ranking elected official (identified and cleared in Ghana's inquiry)
d: UK court papers said Airbus hired a close relative of a high-ranking elected Ghanaian official as its business partner while selling Ghana C-295 military transport planes. Ghana signed for two aircraft in August 2011. Commissions of about €5m were allegedly promised or paid. When the arrangement failed Airbus's checks, staff allegedly routed payments through a Spanish company with no Ghana links. Airbus agreed a record £3bn settlement with France, the UK and the US in 2020, covering several countries, including failure to prevent bribery in Ghana. In August 2024 Ghana's Special Prosecutor closed its inquiry, finding no evidence that John Mahama, identified as the official, took bribes, and no basis to say he was induced to favour Airbus. It also cleared the relative and his associates.
inside: UK court papers allege Airbus placed a decision-maker's relative as its paid partner to win Ghanaian aircraft purchases; Ghana's Special Prosecutor found no evidence of bribery and charged nobody.
cite: Citi Newsroom, February 2020 (UK court statement of facts); Office of the Special Prosecutor of Ghana report, 8 August 2024, via Modern Ghana; Ghana News Agency, 9 Aug 2024

n: Latin American cocaine cells paid off Guinea-Bissau's military, GI-TOC reports
rank: Senior military figures
d: Latin American cocaine traffickers were paying Guinea-Bissau's military for protection by about 2006, according to the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), a research group. Its 2022 study says each of three trafficking cells was 'protected by, and paying off, the military'. It says that by the 2005 elections 'military and political protection of the trade went right to the top'. It reports that senior military figures consolidated their control of the bulk transit of cocaine and kept a share of the profits, reportedly between 13% and 15%. The report names no individual for these payments. These are the group's findings from its sources, and not a court verdict.
inside: GI-TOC reports that foreign cocaine traffickers paid Guinea-Bissau's military for protection, so army figures guarded and then took a share of the traffickers' transit trade.
cite: Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), 'Cocaine politics in West Africa: Guinea-Bissau's protection networks', 2022

n: Sanctions: Mali ruling-party MP coordinated armed blockade of peace talks
who: Arab Movement of Azawad (MAA), pro-government wing
rank: Member of the National Assembly
d: Mohamed Ould Mataly sat in Mali's National Assembly for the party of President Keita, the RPM, while being an influential member of an armed group, the pro-government wing of the Arab Movement of Azawad (MAA). He was a former mayor of Bourem and its member of parliament. The UN listed him in July 2019 for obstructing Mali's 2015 peace deal. According to the listing summaries, he and the MAA wing's military chief of staff coordinated an armed blockade of regional consultations in Gao in November 2018, which stopped discussion of key parts of the deal. The UN imposed a travel ban, then an asset freeze on 19 December 2019. The US and EU followed with sanctions.
inside: An influential member of an armed group held a ruling-party seat in parliament, and sanctions listings say he helped organise an armed blockade that stopped talks on the peace deal.
cite: UN Security Council Mali sanctions list, via Hong Kong SFC, December 2019; Kharon Brief, December 2019; Arab News/AFP, 10 July 2019

n: Sanctions: armed-group member advised Kidal's governor, controlled aid
who: HCUA, an armed group in the CMA coalition
rank: Special adviser to the Governor of Kidal
d: Ahmed Ag Albachar, an influential member of the armed group HCUA, became special adviser to the Governor of Kidal in northern Mali in early 2018, according to the UN sanctions list. He also chaired the humanitarian commission of Kidal's regional administration. The list says he mediated between the Coordination of Movements of Azawad (CMA), the rebel coalition, and Ansar Dine, a designated terrorist group. Sanctions findings summarised by Kharon, a sanctions research firm, say he used his role to control all aid and development projects in the region and to intimidate and extort aid organisations. He co-owned a transport company that NGOs were authorised to use in Kidal. The UN listed him in July 2019 and froze his assets that December.
inside: A member of an armed group held a post advising the regional governor, and sanctions findings say he used his position to control and extort aid projects in Kidal.
cite: UN Security Council Mali sanctions list, via Hong Kong SFC and Government of Jersey annex; Kharon Brief, December 2019

n: Papers said Nigerian generals aided Boko Haram; defence chiefs denied it
rank: Ten generals and other senior officers (unnamed, reported)
d: Nigerian newspapers reported in June 2014 that courts-martial had found ten generals and five other senior officers guilty of giving arms and information to Boko Haram, the Islamist armed group. The Leadership daily, citing unnamed military sources, named none of them. Defence headquarters said there was 'no truth whatsoever' in the report. The Interior Minister, Abba Moro, told the BBC the trials were 'good news'. Soldiers had told AP that some senior officers were helping the group, and officers' information allegedly helped it ambush convoys and attack barracks. John Campbell of the US Council on Foreign Relations wrote that the credibility of the claims remained unresolved. The sources cited show no published verdict or names.
inside: Newspapers alleged senior army officers secretly supplied Boko Haram with arms and information, helping it attack troops; the Defence Headquarters denied this and no officer was publicly named.
cite: Al Jazeera, 4 June 2014; Council on Foreign Relations, John Campbell, 5 June 2014

n: Nigerian army commander said soldiers were selling arms to Boko Haram
rank: Soldiers and a brigade commander (unnamed)
d: Nigerian soldiers sold arms and ammunition to Boko Haram, the armed group they were fighting, according to the army's own commander in the north-east. Maj-Gen Lucky Irabor said in 2016 that some soldiers had been making the sales, calling them a betrayal of the Nigerian people. Three weeks earlier the army had said a tribunal was trying 16 officers and troops for offences including theft and sale of ammunition. A front-line soldier told AP his brigade commander was on trial in secret in Maiduguri, and that his artillery brigade had received only one of 21 anti-aircraft guns assigned to it. The army was investigating the guns. The sources do not report a verdict or say where the guns went.
inside: Boko Haram's money reached soldiers inside the Nigerian army, the theatre commander said, and they sold it army weapons and ammunition meant for use against the group.
cite: AP via The Herald, September 2016

n: Nigeria held 18 soldiers and 15 police over alleged arms sales to militants
who: Boko Haram, ISWAP and criminal buyers (alleged)
rank: Serving soldiers and police officers
d: Serving Nigerian soldiers and police officers have been arrested on suspicion of selling arms to the armed groups they were sent to fight, according to a Daily Trust article listing the cases. On 29 May 2025, Operation Hadin Kai, the army's north-east campaign against Boko Haram and its offshoot ISWAP, arrested 18 soldiers and 15 police officers for allegedly selling arms to terrorists and other criminals. On 2 September 2025 a lance corporal in Marte, Borno State, was arrested with 711 rounds he allegedly meant for terrorists. On 27 September a soldier and a police officer were held over arms allegedly being smuggled to Boko Haram and ISWAP. These are allegations, and the article reports no outcome.
inside: The arrests allege that armed groups obtained weapons through paying soldiers and police officers who were posted to fight them and had access to security force arms.
cite: Daily Trust, 'Soldiers, stop the gunrunning', 2025

n: Salt Lake City's 2002 bid paid cash and favours to IOC members
org_label: Salt Lake City Olympic bid committee
rank: International Olympic Committee members
d: The International Olympic Committee's members vote on which city hosts the Olympic Games. The committee that wanted the 2002 Winter Games for Salt Lake City spent over $16 million and flew more than 70 of the roughly 100 IOC members to Utah. Members' relatives were given jobs at First Security Corporation Bank, arranged by Spencer Eccles, and helped into the University of Utah by Jim Jardine, while Intermountain Health Care made medical facilities and treatment available during visits. The scandal broke on 24 November 1998 with a report on a letter showing tuition paid for a member's child. The IOC expelled six members, four resigned and ten more were sanctioned, the first corruption expulsions in its history. Bid leaders Tom Welch and David Johnson were acquitted of all US charges in December 2003.
inside: A city's bid committee put money, jobs and university places in the hands of the officials who voted on hosting, and the vote went its way.
cite: IOC Ad Hoc Commission report, 1999; New York Times, 6 December 2003, on the acquittal of Welch and Johnson
undone: Five organisers were tried in the United States and acquitted in December 2003.

n: CONCACAF president Jeffrey Webb pleaded guilty and forfeited $6.7m
org_label: Traffic and other sports marketing companies
rank: President of CONCACAF and FIFA vice-president
d: CONCACAF, based in Miami, governs football in North and Central America and the Caribbean and sells tournament rights such as the Gold Cup. Jeffrey Webb, its president and a FIFA vice-president, was among 14 officials charged on 27 May 2015 in the US racketeering case built around sports marketing companies paying football officials for media and marketing contracts. He pleaded guilty on 23 November 2015 to racketeering conspiracy, wire fraud conspiracy and money laundering conspiracy, and agreed to forfeit more than $6.7 million. Prosecutors estimated about $150 million in bribes across the case, at least $110 million of it tied to the 2016 Copa America Centenario. FIFA banned him from football for life in September 2016, and his sentencing was postponed repeatedly.
inside: Marketing firms' money reached the president of the confederation that sells regional tournament rights, and those contracts were steered to the payers.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 3 December 2015, on the EDNY superseding indictment and guilty pleas

n: Colombia's football federation chief Luis Bedoya admitted FIFA bribes
org_label: sports marketing companies in the US FIFA case
rank: FIFA executive committee member and CONMEBOL vice-president
d: Luis Bedoya led Colombia's national football federation, sat on FIFA's executive committee and was a vice-president of the South American confederation CONMEBOL. He waived indictment and pleaded guilty in the United States on 12 November 2015 to a two-count information charging racketeering conspiracy and wire fraud conspiracy, in the case over payments by sports marketing companies for tournament rights, and agreed to forfeit all funds on deposit in his Swiss bank account, among other funds. No amount has been given for that forfeiture. Reuters reported in May 2016 that he was banned from football for life. He cooperated with prosecutors and no sentence has been reported. On his own admission he took money from firms doing business with the competitions he helped govern.
inside: Rights-buying companies paid a man who voted inside FIFA and CONMEBOL, so decisions on their contracts were taken by someone on their payroll.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 3 December 2015, on Bedoya's 12 November 2015 guilty plea; Reuters, 6 May 2016, on the life ban

n: UNOPS executive director accused of steering $60m to a businessman's firms
rank: Executive director, UN Office for Project Services (UNOPS)
d: The UN Office for Project Services, UNOPS, manages construction and procurement projects for the UN system. US prosecutors allege that Vitaly Vanshelboim, a Ukrainian who joined the UN in 1992 and became a UNOPS executive director, took bribes to divert nearly $60 million in agency funding to companies linked to British businessman David Kendrick. A UN tribunal valued his benefits at over $3 million and ordered him to repay $58.8 million. He was sacked in January 2023 and arrested in Alicante in March 2025. On 21 October 2025 Spain's National High Court approved extradition on three of six charges: bribery as an agent of an organisation receiving federal funds, honest-services wire fraud and money laundering. His lawyers had three days to appeal; no transfer to US custody has been reported.
inside: Prosecutors say a businessman's payments bought a senior UNOPS official, who then sent the agency's project money to that businessman's firms.
cite: Associated Press, 21 October 2025, on Spain's National High Court extradition ruling (read via infonews.ca); EFE report of the same ruling

n: Nigeria's election staff jailed over cash before the 2015 vote
rank: INEC deputy director and a second commission official
d: Nigeria's Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, runs elections and its staff count and collate the votes. On 28 June 2019 the Jigawa State High Court in Gumel, before Justice Yusuf Birnin-Kudu, convicted two INEC officials on three of six counts and discharged them on the other three. Auwal Jibrin, a deputy director in Dutse, was jailed for six years and Garba Ismaila for seven. The court found that Jibrin and Ismaila dishonestly received 45 million naira out of 250 million naira handed out in Jigawa State before the 2015 presidential election. The EFCC says that money came from about $115 million disbursed by the then petroleum minister Diezani Alison-Madueke, who has not been convicted in the matter, and that it was meant to influence the result.
inside: Money the anti-corruption agency traced to a serving minister was paid to the officials running the vote count, so the commission's own staff worked to shape the result.
cite: EFCC press release, June 2019, and ICIR Nigeria, 1 July 2019, on the 28 June 2019 judgment

n: Football boss Mamic accused of paying three Croatian judges for rulings
rank: Judges of the Osijek County Court
d: USKOK, Croatia's anti-corruption office, indicted six defendants at the Zagreb County Court: the football executive Zdravko Mamic, his brother Zoran, Osijek County Court judges Darko Kruslin, Zvonko Vekic and Ante Kvesic, and Natasa Sekulic, on bribery, influence-peddling and money-laundering charges. The case began when Mamic, after his conviction became final, sent USKOK a USB drive accusing the three judges. Prosecutors say he met Vekic between 2017 and 2019 in Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Dubai, met Kruslin at Maksimir stadium in November 2016, and gave Vekic at least 370,000 euro for himself, Kruslin and Kvesic, who allegedly promised an acquittal, a dismissal of charges and the return of a 7 million kuna guarantee. Kruslin had presided over the chamber that sentenced Mamic to six and a half years for siphoning 116 million kuna from Dinamo Zagreb.
inside: Prosecutors say a football executive facing trial paid judges in the court hearing his cases, so the court's decisions would be made to suit him.
cite: N1 (Croatia), 7 June 2023; USKOK indictment; no trial verdict found as of November 2026

n: Malta's ex-PM and hospital concession bosses charged over privatised hospitals
org_label: Vitals Global Healthcare and Steward Health Care
rank: Prime Minister, chief of staff and a former minister
d: Maltese prosecutors charged former prime minister Joseph Muscat, former chief of staff Keith Schembri and former minister Konrad Mizzi, with 19 other people and companies, over the 2015 contract handing three public hospitals to private concessionaires. Charges include money laundering, fraud, conspiracy, bribery and corruption in public office. Steward Malta Management's legal representative, David-Joseph Meli, was charged with corrupting Muscat, Schembri and Mizzi. A magistrate's four-year inquiry produced a 1,200-page report, and charges were filed on 28 May 2024. A civil court had already annulled the concession, citing fraud and collusion between the concessionaires and senior officials. All pleaded not guilty, Muscat calling the charges laughable. The charges have not been tried; in February 2026 a court turned down Muscat's human rights application over how he was drawn into the inquiry.
inside: A court found the hospital concessionaires and senior officials colluded; prosecutors say the companies paid the prime minister's circle, who then handed them public hospitals.
cite: OCCRP, May 2024; Malta magisterial inquiry; civil court annulment; The Maltese Herald, 20 February 2026

n: Aprilia's mayor arrested over alleged mafia vote deal; council dissolved
rank: Mayor and council of Aprilia
d: Lanfranco Principi, mayor of Aprilia in the Lazio region south of Rome, was placed under house arrest in July 2024 on charges of political-mafia electoral exchange and external complicity in a mafia association. Political-mafia electoral exchange is the Italian offence of trading votes delivered by a criminal group for favours from the person elected. In April 2025 the Italian cabinet dissolved Aprilia's council for conditioning by organised crime, the decree's own ground, and appointed an extraordinary commission for eighteen months. Caserta in Campania and Badolato and Casabona in Calabria were dissolved in the same decree. The charges are not proven.
inside: Prosecutors say a mafia group delivered the votes that elected the mayor and in return had a say over the town hall it had helped fill.
cite: L'Indipendente, 19 April 2025; Council of Ministers decree

n: Court convicts nine over cocaine moved through Portugal's Leixoes port
rank: Port employees at Leixoes
d: Portugal's public prosecutors charged 13 people and one company with criminal association, drug trafficking, possession of a prohibited weapon and money laundering, and Porto's criminal investigation court sent them to trial. Prosecutors said employees of the port of Leixoes, near Porto, were paid 10,000 and 40,000 euro to help move cocaine, and a diver and an importer from Brazil were among the defendants. Those two challenged the case for procedural nullities and insufficient evidence; the court rejected the challenge. Seizures at Leixoes of 78 kilograms in May 2023 and 91 kilograms in October 2023 were valued at about 4.2 million euro. On 17 July 2026 the Porto court convicted nine of the 13 defendants, acquitted four, imposed terms from suspended sentences to 17 years and fined the company 48,000 euro.
inside: Prosecutors said a cocaine network bought the help of the port's own workers, so the people handling containers moved the drugs through for it.
cite: Portugal Resident on the Porto Regional Attorney General's Office indictment; Observador, 17 July 2026, on the judgment

n: UN panel: UAE pays Yemeni brigades and controls the guard forces at its own bases
rank: Amaliqah Brigades, Guards of the Republic, Tihamah Brigades and base guard forces
d: The UAE originally recruited, trained and paid most of the forces affiliated with the Southern Transitional Council, a situation the UN Panel of Experts on Yemen said had evolved since 2015, and found in January 2021 that it had scaled down its direct control over most of them. The Amaliqah Brigades, Guards of the Republic and Tihamah Brigades are all provided with some payments by the UAE; some brigades also draw salaries from Yemen's government. A footnote records the Panel's finding that the UAE directly controls the Yemeni guard forces at its own bases at Balhaf and Rayyan. Yemen's government told the Panel that Emirati money and weapons continued to reach the Security Belt and Shabwani Elite Forces. The UAE told the Panel it does not support any unilateral action by any party to the conflict.
inside: UN investigators say a foreign state pays units inside Yemen's own forces and directly commands the guard forces at its own bases.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2021/79 (25 January 2021), paras. 31-32 and 52 and footnote 13

n: Foreign service paid an Azerbaijani to get back into its spy agencies
rank: Reserve officer of the state security service
d: Azerbaijan's State Security Service said in December 2018 that Bahruz Yusifzade, a reserve officer who had left the state security service, arranged meetings with officers of a foreign special service, who reached him through a foreign national he had himself once recruited. The service said he was instructed to seek a position inside Azerbaijan's intelligence agencies and was found to have taken money from foreign intelligence services. He was arrested and prosecuted for treason under article 274 of the criminal code. The country behind the recruitment was not named. The account comes from the State Security Service alone; no independent account of the case, and no trial outcome, has been published.
inside: Azerbaijan's State Security Service says a foreign spy service paid a former officer and told him to win a post back inside its intelligence agencies.
cite: Trend.az, 'State Security Service unveils multi-stage espionage against Azerbaijan', 27 December 2018

n: Iran paid a serving Israeli soldier to photograph army bases
rank: Soldier, Givati Brigade, Israel Defense Forces
d: A soldier in the Israeli army's Givati Brigade was arrested in September after allegedly being in contact with Iranian intelligence from about July 2025 and sending photographs and video of sites in Israel, including the inside of army bases, together with information on weapons the army uses. Prosecutors say he did it in exchange for financial compensation. The investigation was run by the Shin Bet internal security service, the investigative military police and the defence ministry's security directorate, and a court cleared the details for publication in January 2026. He is charged with contact with a foreign agent, passing information to the enemy, impersonation and obstruction of justice. The case has not yet been decided.
inside: Prosecutors say Iranian intelligence paid a serving soldier to photograph inside the bases he was posted to and send the pictures out.
cite: Tzvi Jasper, Jerusalem Post, 15 January 2026 (mirrored by Yahoo News)

n: US prosecutors say $10m from South Africa's 2010 bid reached FIFA's Jack Warner
rank: FIFA vice-president
d: FIFA's executive committee members voted on World Cup hosts. US prosecutors allege that before the vote, officials of FIFA, the South African government and the bid committee were prepared to arrange for $10 million to be paid to the Caribbean Football Union to help South Africa win the 2010 tournament. Because the bid could not pay from government funds, the indictment says the money came from FIFA funds for the tournament and was wired from a FIFA account in Switzerland in three payments on 2 and 31 January and 7 March 2008, into accounts controlled by Jack Warner, a FIFA vice-president, in the name of the Caribbean Football Union. Warner has maintained his innocence. Trinidad and Tobago's High Court stayed his extradition in September 2025, finding it flawed, and permanently halted it in July 2026; he never stood trial.
inside: Prosecutors say a national bid got millions into the accounts of the FIFA official who controlled a bloc of votes.
cite: US Department of Justice indictment, Eastern District of New York, May 2015, as analysed by Daily Maverick, 27 May 2015

n: Honduras: CONCACAF chief Hawit and federation head Callejas admit bribes
org_label: sports marketing companies in the US FIFA case
rank: CONCACAF president; president of the Honduran football federation and member of FIFA's Television and Marketing Committee
d: Alfredo Hawit, a Honduran who became president of the regional confederation CONCACAF and a FIFA vice-president, was arrested in Zurich on 3 December 2015 on suspicion of bribery, at the hotel where seven officials had been arrested that May, and later pleaded guilty in the US case in which sports marketing companies paid football officials for media and marketing rights. Rafael Callejas, a former president of Honduras who ran the Honduran football federation and sat on FIFA's Television and Marketing Committee, also pleaded guilty, in a plea the Department of Justice announced in March 2016. Callejas died in US custody on 4 April 2020, before he could be sentenced. The wider prosecution brought 41 arrests and charges against 18 individuals and two corporations, with bribes estimated at $150 million.
inside: Companies that bought football rights paid two Honduran officials, one of them CONCACAF's president, and both admitted taking the money.
cite: US Department of Justice press releases, 11 April 2016 (plea by a former high-ranking FIFA and CONCACAF official) and 28 March 2016 (plea by the former president of the Honduran soccer federation), as listed in the 2015 FIFA corruption case file

n: Costa Rica's federation president Eduardo Li pleaded guilty in FIFA case
org_label: sports marketing companies in the US FIFA case
rank: President of the Costa Rican football federation; FIFA executive committee member-elect
d: Eduardo Li was president of Costa Rica's national football federation and had been elected to FIFA's executive committee when he was arrested in May 2015. He pleaded guilty in the United States on 7 October 2016, admitting he had taken more than $500,000 in bribes. The prosecution described sports marketing companies, among them Traffic, paying officials of CONCACAF and its member federations for the rights to matches and tournaments, including qualifying games sold by national federations. Li's plea is one of more than a dozen guilty pleas by football officials and executives in the same investigation, which the US estimated involved about $150 million in bribes across the whole case. He has not been sentenced and has asked the US court to vacate the conviction.
inside: Marketing companies' money reached the head of Costa Rica's federation, whose body sold the match rights those companies bought.
cite: Associated Press, 7 October 2016; US Attorney, Eastern District of New York, court records

n: A contractor paid the finance director of a US Africa development agency
rank: Director of Financial Management, US African Development Foundation
d: The US African Development Foundation is a federal agency that funds enterprises in Africa. On 30 January 2026 federal prosecutors charged its director of financial management, Mathieu Zahui, by criminal information with accepting gratuities from a foundation contractor and lying to a federal investigator. Prosecutors said the contractor, who owned a Kenya-based company, paid him $12,000 in cash. From June 2020 to December 2023 Zahui arranged for the foundation to route payments to its vendors through that company, including invoices for work the company did not perform, approved mark-ups of 17 to 66 per cent, and caused at least $617,625 to be paid to it. He denied receiving any benefit when interviewed in 2024. He pleaded guilty on 23 February 2026 and was sentenced on 27 May 2026 to four months in prison and a $12,000 forfeiture.
inside: A contractor's cash bought the official who controlled the agency's payments, and he routed the agency's money through that contractor's company.
cite: US Attorney, District of Columbia, press releases, 30 January 2026 (charge) and 27 May 2026 (sentencing)

n: Bangladesh's former election chief arrested over the 2018 'midnight' vote
rank: Chief Election Commissioner
d: After Sheikh Hasina's government fell, her main opponent, the BNP, filed a case on 22 June 2025 against KM Nurul Huda, chief election commissioner at the 2018 general election, and three other former chief commissioners from the Awami League years, accusing them of a farcical election. Huda was reportedly seized from his Uttara home by a mob, assaulted and handed to police. The prosecution says he helped keep Hasina in power, told local officials to stuff ballot boxes at night and declare the governing party the winner, and misused funds. Police sought a 10-day remand; a court granted four days on 23 June 2025. Huda told the court the election was controversial but the commission was not responsible, that he had not broken his oath and that its authority ends with the gazette. He was refused bail on 2 July.
inside: The case alleges a governing party controlled the officials heading the election commission, who then ordered the count fixed in its favour.
cite: Prothom Alo, 24 June 2025; The Financial Express (Dhaka), 2 July 2025

n: Novomatic accused of buying a seat on Casinos Austria's board for an FPO man
rank: Chief financial officer, Casinos Austria
d: In March 2019 Peter Sidlo, a Freedom Party (FPO) district councillor in Vienna with no gaming or executive experience, was made chief financial officer of Casinos Austria, a company one third owned by the Austrian state through its holding company OBAG, with Novomatic then holding 17.19 per cent as another large shareholder (it no longer holds a stake). Years later, in early 2026, Austria's corruption prosecutor, the WKStA, charged Johann Graf, founder of the gambling machine maker Novomatic, former Novomatic chief executive Harald Neumann, and Heinz-Christian Strache, then vice-chancellor and FPO leader, with trading in influence, and asked for a corporate fine against Novomatic. Prosecutors allege Graf and Neumann supported Sidlo's appointment in return for the FPO pushing the government to open the casino market and repeal Vienna's ban on gaming arcades. Novomatic calls the allegations groundless.
inside: Prosecutors say a gambling firm helped put a party loyalist into a state-owned casino company's boardroom in exchange for laws the firm wanted changed.
cite: Casino.org, 3 March 2026; World Casino Directory, 2 March 2026, on the WKStA indictment filed at the Vienna Regional Court for Criminal Matters (Causa Casinos)

n: Five Greek border police charged with running crossings for smugglers
rank: Special border guard unit, Evros border
d: Five officers of a special border guard unit in north-eastern Greece were arrested in Didymoteicho and held in custody pending trial, accused of working with four smugglers of undetermined nationality operating from Turkey. Authorities said the officers helped with at least 12 crossings bringing in at least 100 people, and took a share of what the smugglers charged. Internal affairs had been watching them since October 2022, and wiretapped calls produced more than 2,000 pages of transcripts; about 26,000 euro in cash and nearly 60 mobile phones were seized when they were arrested. They testified before an examining magistrate in Orestiada in June 2023, and the case had not been tried as of that date.
inside: Prosecutors say a smuggling ring had the border guards themselves on its payroll, so the unit guarding the crossing arranged the crossings for it.
cite: Associated Press / WTOP, June 2023

n: Tremestieri Etneo council dissolved after ex-mayor's vote-exchange sentence
who: Mafia group (none named for this town in the source)
rank: Mayor and council of Tremestieri Etneo
d: The Italian cabinet dissolved the council of Tremestieri Etneo, a town in the province of Catania in Sicily, for mafia infiltration on 27 March 2025, together with San Luca in Calabria and Poggiomarino in Campania. A few days earlier its former mayor, Santi Rando, had been sentenced at first instance to eight years for political-mafia vote exchange at the 2015 municipal election, the offence of obtaining votes through a criminal group in exchange for favours once in office; an Italian first-instance sentence is not final. Dissolution hands a town to government commissioners and is ordered when an inquiry finds organised crime has conditioned the administration. San Luca, dissolved for confirmed criminal-organisation conditioning, had seen no candidates stand at its June 2023 municipal elections.
inside: A court has sentenced the former mayor at first instance over votes exchanged with a mafia group, and the government dissolved the council.
cite: L'Indipendente, 19 April 2025, which reports the 27 March 2025 dissolutions in background

n: Houthi defence procurement chief attached to the Tehran office
who: Houthi supply network operating from Iran (per the UN Panel)
rank: Director of procurement, Houthi-appointed Ministry of Defence
d: Major General Muhammad Ahmad al-Talibi is director of procurement at the defence ministry run by the Houthi authorities in Sanaa. The United Nations Panel of Experts on Yemen said in October 2024 that he is attached to the Houthi office in Tehran and is in charge of the illicit shipment of materiel to the Houthis through a network of individuals and entities, and that he arranges training for Houthi combatants in Iran. The Panel places him in a liaison cell monitoring transfers from Iranian naval ports. Its case study 6 says that in 2022 he ordered the relocation to Djibouti of a Yemeni customs broker who was facilitating clearance of smuggled materiel; an annex to the same report dates the broker's move to August 2023. Press material annexed to the report notes that Tehran has always denied arming the Houthis.
inside: UN investigators say the man buying weapons for the defence ministry in Sanaa is attached to an office in Tehran, so purchasing serves the supply route from Iran.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2024/731 (11 October 2024), paras. 77-79 and case study 6; the Iranian denial from press material annexed to the same report

n: MAN manager accused of paying Turkmenistan's state oil chief 8.4m euros
org_label: A former manager of MAN GHH Gas & Oil
rank: Head of the state oil company Turkmennebit
d: German prosecutors say a former manager of the engineering group MAN, not publicly named, transferred 8.4 million euros (about $9.3 million) between 2002 and 2007 into accounts controlled by Saparmammet Veliev, then head of the state oil company Turkmennebit. A 1999 decree of the leader Saparmurat Niyazov had already ordered Turkmennebit to let MAN build a compressor station worth 233 million German marks (about $126 million) in oil fields near the Iranian border. He was charged in 2011; the trial opened in late 2016, was postponed for his ill health and resumed in Munich in December 2019, where the defence asked that it be stopped as time-barred. He said corruption was the norm in Turkmenistan and that key decisions predated his 2000 arrival. Veliev was dismissed in 2005 and died in prison in October 2017 serving 24 years for corruption.
inside: Prosecutors say a German contractor's manager put money into the accounts of the man running the state oil company overseeing MAN's compressor-station work.
cite: RFE/RL, 'Former German Manager On Trial For Bribing Of Turkmen Oil Officials', 11 December 2019

n: Myanmar's home affairs minister investigated over scam-syndicate bribes
rank: Minister of Home Affairs and chair of the anti-scam supervisory committee
d: Lieutenant General Tun Tun Naung, home affairs minister in Myanmar's military government, chaired the Central Supervisory Committee on Combating Telecom Fraud and Online Gambling, the body set up to eliminate scam centres, formed on 10 December of the preceding year. He had earlier served as minister of border affairs. Mizzima reported that he had come under investigation for allegedly taking bribes from illegal online scam syndicates, and that he was removed as home affairs minister on 31 January 2025, a year after taking the post, with the National Defence and Security Council returning him to his original military duties. The report gives no evidence for the allegation, no charge has been made public, the syndicates were not named, and its sources say he has not been given a new assignment.
inside: One report says the scam operators paid the minister who chaired the committee set up to close their centres, with no evidence given.
cite: Mizzima, 'Former Home Affairs Minister investigated for alleged ties to online scam operations', undated copy at mizzimaenglish.blogspot.com

n: Three Israeli soldiers and a civilian charged with working for an Iranian handler
rank: Three serving soldiers and a civilian
d: The Haifa District Prosecutor's Office charged three Israeli soldiers and a civilian in May 2026 with working for an Iranian intelligence handler. Prosecutors say the soldiers are suspected of having acted for the handler before they enlisted, and that some approached the handler on their own initiative to carry out missions. The group photographed and sent images of train stations, shopping centres and security cameras, and material on the Israeli Air Force's Technological College in Haifa, where some of them had studied. They were asked to obtain weapons, and some damaged property as part of the tasks. One defendant recruited the others. The four were arrested in March after an investigation by the Shin Bet, military intelligence's Unit 8200, the Israel Police's Lahav 433 unit and the military police. The case has not been decided.
inside: Prosecutors say some were already acting for an Iranian handler before they enlisted, so the service had recruits inside the army.
cite: JNS, 'Civilian, three IDF soldiers charged with spying for Tehran', 9 May 2026

n: Marketing firms bought CONMEBOL's president Juan Angel Napout
org_label: Traffic, Torneos y Competencias and Full Play
rank: President of CONMEBOL and FIFA vice-president
d: CONMEBOL, in Luque outside Asuncion, runs South American football and sells the television and marketing rights to its tournaments. A Brooklyn jury convicted Juan Angel Napout, its president and a FIFA vice-president, of racketeering conspiracy and two counts of wire fraud conspiracy on Friday 22 December 2017, in a verdict announced by the Department of Justice on 26 December. Prosecutors showed that principals of the marketing companies Traffic, Torneos y Competencias and Full Play paid him millions of dollars for his support on rights to editions of the Copa America, and that on the Copa Libertadores rights Torneos paid through Full Play as an intermediary. A third defendant, Manuel Burga of Peru, was acquitted. Judge Pamela Chen remanded Napout, sentenced him to nine years in August 2018, and the Second Circuit upheld the conviction in June 2020.
inside: Marketing companies put bribe money in the pocket of the man running South American football, and the rights to its tournaments went to them.
cite: US Attorney, Eastern District of New York, press release, 26 December 2017, on the jury verdict of Friday 22 December 2017; sentencing August 2018; United States v. Napout (2d Cir., June 2020)

n: Chile's football federation president Sergio Jadue pleaded guilty
org_label: sports marketing companies in the US FIFA case
rank: President of Chile's ANFP (national football association) and a CONMEBOL vice-president
d: Sergio Jadue ran Chile's ANFP, the national football association, and was a vice-president of CONMEBOL, the South American confederation that sells the rights to the Copa America and Copa Libertadores. Waiving indictment, he pleaded guilty in the United States on 23 November 2015 to a two-count information of racketeering conspiracy and wire fraud conspiracy, in the case in which the marketing companies Traffic, Torneos y Competencias and Full Play paid officials for those rights, and he agreed to forfeit all funds in his US bank account. FIFA banned him from football for life in May 2016. His US sentencing has been postponed repeatedly, most recently in October 2023, and he has not been sentenced. A Santiago court later closed the separate Chilean case against him as time-barred.
inside: Marketing companies' payments reached the head of Chile's football association, who also held a vice-presidency at the confederation selling those tournament rights.
cite: US Attorney, Eastern District of New York, court records; Reuters, 23 November 2015; La Tercera on the Chilean case being closed

n: Nicaragua's federation head and FIFA officer Julio Rocha pleaded guilty
org_label: sports marketing companies in the US FIFA case
rank: President of the Nicaraguan football federation; FIFA development officer
d: Julio Rocha Lopez was president of Nicaragua's football federation and later a FIFA development officer. He pleaded guilty in the United States to racketeering conspiracy and wire fraud conspiracy, each carrying up to 20 years, in a case the Department of Justice announced on 7 December 2016. The prosecution concerned sports marketing companies paying officials of CONCACAF and its member federations for the rights to matches and tournaments. Rocha's plea put the scheme inside FIFA's own development arm. He was banned from football for life about two months before he died of cancer in January 2018, under house arrest in the United States and due to be sentenced in Brooklyn federal court on 2 February. He was never sentenced.
inside: Rights-buying firms paid an official who had run Nicaragua's federation and then held a FIFA development post, placing their interests inside both bodies.
cite: US Attorney, Eastern District of New York, release of 7 December 2016; Inside World Football, 15 January 2018

n: Traffickers' payments reached the head of Mexico's Interpol office
rank: Head of Mexico's Interpol National Central Bureau
d: Each country's national central bureau connects its police to Interpol, through which forces exchange information across borders. In the 2008 Mexican investigation called Operation Clean House (Operacion Limpieza), Ricardo Gutierrez Vargas, director for international police affairs and Interpol at Mexico's Federal Investigative Agency and, according to an Interpol website, head of the country's Interpol National Central Bureau, was put under house arrest on suspicion of passing police information to traffickers. Rodolfo de la Guardia Garcia, the agency's former second-in-command, was held over a suspected leak to the Sinaloa cartel for monthly payments. The former federal police commissioner Gerardo Garay and three other Public Safety Department officials were also detained, on allegations that were not disclosed. Interpol sent a team to check whether its database information had reached cartels. Both Interpol chiefs were later acquitted, prosecutors unable to support the charges.
inside: Prosecutors suspected traffickers were paying the officials who ran Mexico's link to international policing, turning that channel to the gangs' use; both were later acquitted.
cite: Associated Press via NBC News, 2008 (undated copy); El Universal, 27 February 2014, for the acquittals

n: 41 Romanian police and customs officers indicted over cigarette route
org_label: Cigarette-smuggling network running loads from Serbia
rank: Moravita customs post and border police
d: Romania's anti-corruption prosecutors indicted 41 police and customs officers working at the Moravita crossing, on the country's western border with Serbia. Prosecutors said the officers took money to wave through an organised cigarette-smuggling operation, which moved loads worth about 3.3 million euro. Officers were allegedly paid between 100 and 900 euro per shift, and the smuggling ran almost daily. One officer was already in temporary arrest. On the prosecutors' case, the smuggling network had bought the control function at the crossing itself.
inside: Prosecutors say a smuggling ring paid almost the whole staff of a border post, so the officers meant to search lorries let its cigarettes through.
cite: HotNews.ro, 16 June 2011

n: Bulgaria's gambling regulators charged as members of Bozhkov's crime group
rank: State Gambling Commission - head of control activities and a commission member
d: Bulgarian prosecutors charged the State Gambling Commission's head of control activities and a former commission member, identified by the court only as T.M. and P.G. and named in local media as Todor Markov and Plamen Georgiev, with taking part in an organised criminal group headed by the gambling businessman Vasil Bozhkov. The commission licenses and inspects betting operators. Police raided it twice in January 2020, questioned 16 officials, and both men were placed under house arrest in February 2020. Bozhkov, charged in absentia with extortion and attempted bribery after leaving the country, denies wrongdoing and called the accusations ridiculous; no response from the two regulators is reported. He returned in August 2023, and in April 2024 prosecutors sent the case to court, with nine co-defendants including officials of the now-dissolved commission.
inside: Prosecutors say Bulgaria's richest gambling operator had the regulator's own inspection chief inside his criminal group, so the body policing him answered to him.
cite: OCCRP, 13 February 2020; Bulgarian National Radio, 23 April 2024

n: Russia's GRU sought Slovak parliament's secret reports via an MP's aide
rank: Parliamentary staff and classified annual reports
d: Slovak police charged Bohus Garbar, a former correspondent for the pro-Russian website Hlavne spravy, with espionage and bribery, announced with Special Prosecutor Daniel Lipsic on 15 March 2022. Police said that from about April 2021 he was an intelligence contact for Russia's GRU, whose officers worked under diplomatic cover at the Russian embassy, and that he sought parliament's classified material, including the annual reports of Slovakia's secret services, through Jozef Mihalcin, an assistant to a lawmaker, and Bohus M., in the Slovak Intelligence Service until the end of 2021. Both were released without charge. Four Slovaks were accused in all; Lipsic said Garbar and a second defendant, Pavel Bucka, accused of passing NATO material since 2013, could face four to 13 years. In 2023 the court approved a plea bargain: three years suspended for three, and a 15,000 euro fine.
inside: Russian military intelligence used a journalist to reach a parliamentary aide and an intelligence service officer, to get the secret annual reports of Slovakia's spy agencies.
cite: Radio Slovakia International (STVR), 15 March 2022 and 1 March 2023

n: Poggiomarino mayor arrested over alleged mafia pact; council dissolved
rank: Mayor and council of Poggiomarino
d: Maurizio Falanga, then mayor of Poggiomarino in the province of Naples, was arrested in October, accused of taking part in a political-mafia pact - the Italian offence of trading votes delivered by a criminal group for favours from the person elected. On 27 March 2025 the Italian cabinet dissolved the town's council for mafia infiltration and handed it to government commissioners. Dissolution is ordered when an official inquiry finds that organised crime has conditioned a local administration's decisions. Poggiomarino was one of several councils in Campania, Lazio and Calabria dissolved in the same period. The allegations against Falanga have not been proven in court.
inside: Prosecutors say a mafia group and the mayor struck a deal over votes, so the town hall's decisions were open to the group that helped elect him.
cite: L'Indipendente, 19 April 2025 (reporting the 27 March 2025 cabinet session)

n: UN panel: Hezbollah-linked expert said to guide Houthi revenue committee
rank: Adviser to the Houthi committee on revenue and military spending
d: The United Nations Panel of Experts on Yemen reported in October 2024 that a special committee had recently been set up to augment the Houthis' revenue and to plan military spending, including on weapons, allegedly under the guidance of a high-profile expert known as Abu Radwan, linked to the Radwan forces of the Lebanese armed movement Hizbullah. He reportedly provides advice on increasing customs duties, taxes, levies and telecommunications tariffs, and enhanced collections from telecommunications companies by almost 35 per cent. The same report places General Abdulreza Shalai of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Quds Force, and his deputy, a senior Hizbullah cadre, in the Houthi command and control structure, advising and assisting Abdulmalik al-Houthi. The report records no response from Hezbollah.
inside: UN investigators say a Hezbollah-linked expert is alleged to guide the committee raising Houthi customs duties, taxes and telephone tariffs and planning military spending.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2024/731, paras. 72 and 108 (October 2024)

n: Fake research jobs used to recruit Philippine defence staff for China
rank: Civilian employees of the defence department, navy and coast guard
d: Philippine investigators said in March 2026 that civilian employees connected to the Department of National Defense, the navy and the coast guard had been recruited through fake freelance research work: an official called it a closed case involving 'these three', though the report names four. People posing as staff of research organisations approached them after seeing their resumes on networking sites like LinkedIn, commissioned geopolitical analysis, then asked about troop rotations and roll-on/roll-off resupply schedules for the BRP Sierra Madre at Ayungin Shoal and personnel names at West Philippine Sea detachments. They reportedly passed material for more than two years, paid up to 100,000 pesos through e-wallets, messages hidden in a modified Tetris app. The National Security Council tied the operation to China; investigators believe it was state-linked. No charges have been reported, and officials believe other recruits remain.
inside: Investigators say handlers posing as research clients paid defence and coast guard staff, so insiders passed out the navy's resupply plans.
cite: Daily Tribune, 'Spy recruitment ABCs targeting Pinoys bared', 8 March 2026

n: Taliban men inside Afghan army and police killed 115 troops in three months
rank: Soldiers and police inside the Afghan National Defence and Security Forces
d: Insider attacks are cases in which Afghanistan's security forces are targeted by Taliban infiltrators within their ranks. The Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction, the US auditor of Afghan war spending, reported on 30 April 2021 that such attacks rose 82 per cent in the first quarter of 2021 and that casualties from them roughly doubled. Coalition figures cited in the report counted 31 insider attacks in those three months, killing 115 Afghan military personnel and wounding 39. SIGAR said some of the underlying data is classified. All attacks on Afghan security forces were up 37 per cent on the same period a year earlier. The government fell in August 2021.
inside: The Taliban got its own fighters enlisted in the army and police, so soldiers on the state's payroll attacked the forces they had joined.
cite: SIGAR, Quarterly Report to the United States Congress, 30 April 2021, as reported by Al Jazeera

n: Launderers used a Citibank manager inside the bank in Singapore
rank: Relationship manager, Citibank Singapore
d: Wang Qiming, a relationship manager at Citibank in Singapore - the employee who opens and handles client accounts - was sentenced to two years in October 2025, the longest in the city's largest money-laundering case, in which about 3 billion Singapore dollars was seized. The court heard that he helped Su Baolin, a convicted launderer, open an account and handle illicit cash, and forged transaction documents, cheating Citibank of over 8.5 million Singapore dollars in deposits. He pleaded guilty to four of ten charges and his lawyer said he would appeal the sentence, arguing he took only 700 to 800 Singapore dollars commission per transaction and did not benefit; the judge found he had deliberately disguised the source of funds. Singapore's regulator penalised nine financial institutions over lapses in the case, including the local units of Citigroup and Julius Baer.
inside: The syndicate's money came through a banker inside Citibank who opened its accounts and faked the paperwork the bank used to check clients.
cite: Bloomberg, 'Ex-Citi Banker Gets Longest Sentence in Singapore Launder Case', 23 October 2025, republished by SWI swissinfo.ch

n: Brazil's football federation chief Jose Maria Marin took rights bribes
rank: President of the Brazilian Football Confederation (CBF)
d: The Brazilian Football Confederation, the CBF, runs football in Brazil and sells the rights to its competitions. Jose Maria Marin, its former president, was convicted in federal court in Brooklyn in December 2017 of racketeering conspiracy, three counts of wire fraud conspiracy and two counts of money laundering conspiracy. The court heard that Traffic and the Brazilian marketing company Klefer paid him over the Copa do Brasil, the CBF's own cup competition, and that he accepted or agreed to accept millions of dollars in bribes in connection with the media and marketing rights to the Copa America and Copa Libertadores. He was sentenced on 22 August 2018 to four years in prison, a $1.2 million fine and $3,335,593 in forfeiture, and FIFA banned him from football for life in April 2019.
inside: Companies buying the rights to Brazilian and South American tournaments paid the head of the federation that sells the rights to its own competitions.
cite: US Attorney, Eastern District of New York, press releases, 26 December 2017 and 22 August 2018

n: Venezuela's football federation president Rafael Esquivel pleaded guilty
org_label: sports marketing companies in the US FIFA case
rank: President of the Venezuelan football federation 1988-2015; vice president of CONMEBOL
d: Rafael Esquivel was president of Venezuela's national football federation from 1988 to 2015 and was vice president of CONMEBOL, the South American confederation, when he was arrested on 27 May 2015 in the US racketeering case. On 10 November 2016 he pleaded guilty in federal court in Brooklyn to racketeering conspiracy, three counts of wire fraud conspiracy and three counts of money laundering conspiracy, admitting he had taken millions of dollars in bribes from sports marketing companies in connection with the sale of media and marketing rights to tournaments including the Copa Libertadores and the Copa America. He agreed to forfeit more than $16 million. FIFA banned him from football for life in November 2017. No sentence has been reported.
inside: The companies buying South American tournament rights paid Venezuela's federation president, who was also a vice president of the confederation selling those rights.
cite: US Attorney, Eastern District of New York, press release, 10 November 2016

n: US Imagina bribed Caribbean and Central American football officials for rights
rank: Officials of the Caribbean Football Union and four Central American federations
d: US Imagina, a Florida media company previously known as Media World and majority-owned by the Barcelona group Mediapro, buys sports media rights. On 10 July 2018 it pleaded guilty to two counts of wire fraud conspiracy over two senior executives' part in schemes to pay more than $6.5 million in bribes to officials of the Caribbean Football Union and four Central American federations for rights to World Cup qualifying matches. It paid $5,279,000 in forfeited proceeds, a $12,883,320 fine and $6,655,000 in restitution to those federations, about $24.8 million in all. Its chief executive Roger Huguet and the executive Fabio Tordin had pleaded guilty, their pleas unsealed in December 2015. Gerard Romy, co-chief executive of Mediapro, was indicted on 53 counts in March 2020 and was still at large as of 2024; those charges are untested.
inside: A broadcaster paid the football officials who controlled the rights it wanted, so the people selling those rights were working for the buyer.
cite: US Attorney, Eastern District of New York, press release, 10 July 2018

n: Indonesia's ruling party bribed an election commissioner for a seat
rank: Commissioner of the General Elections Commission (KPU)
d: Indonesia's General Elections Commission, the KPU, decides who takes seats in the national parliament. On 25 July 2025 the Jakarta Corruption Court sentenced Hasto Kristiyanto, a senior figure in the governing Indonesian Democratic Party of Struggle, to three years and six months in jail and a 250 million rupiah fine for bribery. The judges found he handed 400 million rupiah, about $24,500, to the KPU commissioner Wahyu Setiawan to get a seat vacated by a lawmaker-elect's death in March 2019 given to a fellow party member, Harun Masiku. He was acquitted of obstruction of justice over the search for Masiku, a fugitive since January 2020. His party said the prosecution was politically motivated. Parliament approved an amnesty on 31 July 2025, he walked out of prison the next day, and the KPK then ended the case.
inside: A governing party's cash bought a serving election commissioner, so the body that allots parliamentary seats awarded one to the party's man.
cite: Jakarta Post, 25 July 2025; Antara, 2 August 2025; Indonesian police news service, 2 August 2025

n: 66 officers at Romania's Siret border post indicted over smugglers' bribes
org_label: Organised smuggling networks at the Ukrainian border
rank: Siret customs post and border police
d: Anti-corruption prosecutors sent 62 border police officers and four customs officers from the Siret crossing, on Romania's border with Ukraine, for trial at the Suceava Appellate Court. They were charged with taking bribes, offering bribes and supporting criminal networks. Prosecutors said the police officers received or accepted money and goods worth 3,643,513 lei so that organised crime networks could pass the crossing without being checked. Forty-nine of those charged were in temporary arrest, that is pre-trial detention, and 17 were at liberty. Prosecutors alleged that the networks had bought the cooperation of officers at the post. The charges were untested when the file was sent to court, and the outcome of the Suceava case has not been traced.
inside: Prosecutors say smuggling networks paid dozens of officers at one border crossing, so the state's own checks there worked for the smugglers.
cite: Mediafax / HotNews.ro, 27 April 2011

n: Bulgarian prosecutor arrested as part of the Balbuzanov crime group
rank: Prosecutor, Pleven Regional Prosecutor's Office
d: Dimitar Zahariev, a prosecutor at the Pleven Regional Prosecutor's Office, was arrested on 6 June 2017 inside the Palace of Justice in Sofia, where he was due to appear in a trial. The Specialized Prosecutor's Office accused him of providing logistics to an organised criminal group headed by Kamen Balbuzanov, known as 'The Hook', which investigators said had been broken up at the end of 2016; he also faced a charge of blackmailing a local doctor. An employee of the prisons department was taken into custody in Pleven in the same case, accused of threatening a witness. A prosecutor decides which cases are brought and how they are run, so a criminal group with a prosecutor inside can shape whether its own members are charged. Last known position: the June 2017 arrest; the later outcome is unverified.
inside: A crime group is alleged to have had a serving prosecutor working for it, giving it a say inside the office that decides who gets charged.
cite: The Sofia Globe, 6 June 2017; BNT, 6 June 2017

n: Caserta city council dissolved for Camorra infiltration
rank: City council and departments of a provincial capital
d: The Italian cabinet dissolved the city council of Caserta, a provincial capital near Naples, for Camorra infiltration in 2025 and put an extraordinary commission in charge of the city for 18 months. Italian law allows a council to be dissolved when an inquiry finds that organised crime has conditioned its decisions. Inspectors had been inside the administration since the previous August. The inquiry pointed to figures connected to the Belforte clan backing the coalition that won the election. Two former members of the city executive, Massimiliano Marzo and Emiliano Casale, an official, Francesco Biondi, and eight others, including council employees and businessmen, are under investigation for alleged corruption, falsification and vote-buying; those allegations are untested. The mayor, Carlo Marino, called the decision political and said he would challenge it before the TAR Lazio.
inside: Inspectors found a Camorra clan's people had backed and reached inside a city administration, so council decisions and jobs were shaped to suit the clan.
cite: L'Indipendente, 19 April 2025; Council of Ministers decree

n: Bosnia's special police chief held over drug cartel ties
rank: Head of the Federation Special Police Unit; acting director of the Federation Police Directorate
d: On 22 April 2024 Bosnia's State Investigation and Protection Agency detained 22 people in Operation Black Tie 2 on suspicion of organised crime, drug trafficking and money laundering. Oslobodjenje named Mustafa Selmanovic, head of the Federation's Special Police Unit, and Vahidin Munjic, acting director of the Federation's Police Directorate, among them; Dnevni avaz named businessmen and a hospital manager in Zenica. Several special police officers are alleged to have acted as bodyguards for Edin 'Tito' Gacanin in 2016. The US Treasury blacklisted his 'Tito and Dino' clan in March 2023, alleging close links to the Kinahan cartel. Rotterdam sentenced him in absentia in November 2023 to seven years and a one million euro fine; arrested in Dubai in 2022 and bailed in January 2024, his whereabouts are unknown. No charges have been traced.
inside: Suspects detained on suspicion of drug trafficking and money laundering included the heads of the federation's special police unit and police directorate, whose officers allegedly guarded the cartel's leader.
cite: OCCRP, April 2024; SIPA, RFE/RL

n: UN sources place a Quds Force general over Houthi military commands
rank: Adviser to the Houthi leader, supervising aerospace and naval forces
