d: Several confidential sources told the United Nations Panel of Experts on Yemen, in its October 2024 report, that General Abdulreza Shalai of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Quds Force plays a predominant role: operating under the title jihad assistant, he advises and assists the Houthi leader Abdulmalik al-Houthi and allegedly supervises the aerospace forces, meaning missiles and drones, the naval forces and all military regions, along with mobilisation and logistics. His deputy is described as a senior Hezbollah cadre, and the Panel reports that Hezbollah takes part in Houthi decision-making. The Panel also reports that Iraqi armed groups have sent experts and combatants to Yemen since 2015, and that the Popular Mobilization Forces recently trained about 80 Houthi combatants at the Bahbahan centre in Jurf al-Sakhr, in Iraq.
inside: UN investigators report a foreign officer at the top of the Houthi command, where Iran's Quds Force is said to shape its missile and naval forces.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2024/731, paras. 14, 20 and 72 (October 2024)

n: Azerbaijan's security service says a ministry department head spied for foreign agencies
rank: Department head, Ministry of National Security
d: Azerbaijan's State Security Service said in December 2018 that Zakir Ismayilov, born in 1959, who had been a department head and held other senior posts in the former Ministry of National Security, was recruited by foreign intelligence agencies under a pseudonym and passed them information from his posts, personnel information and other secret data while in office. After retiring in 2015 he is said to have reported on changes in Azerbaijan's security agencies and on methods that could be used against them. He was arrested and prosecuted for treason under article 274 of the criminal code. The service did not name the country involved, and named a second man, Bahruz Yusifzade, prosecuted under the same article. The claim rests on the service's own statement; the accused's response and the outcome are not known.
inside: Azerbaijan's security service says a foreign spy service recruited a serving department head inside its own ministry, who passed out personnel files and other secrets.
cite: Trend.az, 'State Security Service unveils multi-stage espionage against Azerbaijan', 27 December 2018

n: 78 Lao border officers disciplined for waving Chinese nationals through
rank: Police and immigration officers at the Boten checkpoint
d: Laos disciplined 78 officers, 77 serving police and immigration officers and one former officer, for taking bribes to let Chinese nationals enter and leave the country at the Boten crossing on the Chinese border without visas or passports. Most of those punished worked in the Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone in Bokeo province, a gambling and tourism hub for Chinese visitors, although the Boten checkpoint itself sits in Luang Namtha province. A notice from the Luang Namtha provincial police on 7 June 2023 set out the penalties: five officers lost their Lao People's Revolutionary Party membership and their jobs or pensions, and 73 were suspended from the party for six months, demoted or moved. All had to sign notes acknowledging the penalty. A provincial official told Radio Free Asia it was kept quiet because of the many ongoing investigations.
inside: People paying to cross unchecked had bought the officers at the border post, so Laos's own immigration control let them in and out unrecorded.
cite: Radio Free Asia, 'Laos punished 78 border security officers for bribery in June', 6 November 2023

n: Fish exporter and a Tunisian customs officer jailed over false exports
rank: Customs executive at the Dhehiba border post
d: The financial-corruption chamber of the Tunis Court of First Instance sentenced a former customs executive posted at the Dhehiba crossing to five years in prison, and the owner of a group of companies exporting tuna and sardines to seven years, in a judgment delivered late on 2 October 2025. They were convicted of misuse of office and falsification of customs documents for private interests, to the detriment of the administration: the officer had applied the customs revenue office stamp to two declarations recording exports of tuna and sardines that had never passed through the Dhehiba post, giving them an appearance of regularity. Neither man was named in the ruling as reported. The report rests on a single judicial source, and no appeal outcome has been traced.
inside: An exporter had the customs officer at the border stamp paperwork for shipments that never crossed, so the state certified exports that did not exist.
cite: Diwan FM, reported by Tunisie Numerique, 'Tunisie - Corruption douaniere: 5 ans de prison pour un ancien cadre, 7 ans pour un homme d'affaires', 3 October 2025

n: Suppliers put a UN procurement chief on their payroll for contracts
rank: Chief of the Commodity Procurement Section, UN Procurement Division
d: Sanjaya Bahel ran the commodity procurement section of the UN Procurement Division, which buys goods and services for the organisation's operations worldwide. A jury convicted him on 7 June 2007 of mail and wire fraud, conspiracy and accepting corrupt payments, and on 1 April 2008 he was sentenced to 97 months in prison. He had helped companies owned or represented by the businessman Nishan Kohli and his relatives win contracts worth tens of millions of dollars, giving them inside information, advice on bid prices and help with UN problems, and ghost-writing their correspondence with the UN. In return he received cash, first-class flights, a computer and a discounted three-bedroom apartment, benefits worth hundreds of thousands of dollars. He forfeited $103,500 and the apartment.
inside: Suppliers paid the official who decided UN purchases, so the UN bought from them on terms he shaped from inside the buying office.
cite: US Attorney, Southern District of New York, sentencing release, 1 April 2008

n: World Bank staff took kickbacks to steer Africa contracts to Swedish firms
org_label: Swedish consultants and companies in World Bank tenders
rank: World Bank trust funds manager and task manager
d: The World Bank lends money for projects in poorer countries and its staff manage the contracts. Ramendra Basu, a World Bank trust funds manager, conspired between 1997 and 2000 with a Swedish consultant and others to steer Bank-financed contracts for work in Ethiopia and Kenya to particular Swedish companies, taking $127,000 in kickbacks. He also helped the consultants bribe a Kenyan government official, arranging a $50,000 wire transfer abroad for the official's benefit. Basu pleaded guilty on 17 December 2002 and was sentenced on 22 April 2008 to 15 months in prison. A colleague, task manager Gautam Sengupta, pleaded guilty to the same charges in February 2002 and was sentenced in February 2006. Sweden prosecuted and convicted the consultants.
inside: Contractors paid World Bank staff who chose who won Bank-funded work, so the loans bought services from the firms that paid them.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 22 April 2008

n: Romania's ex-transport minister held over a firm's state contract
rank: Former Minister of Transport; director of the Romanian Automobile Registry
d: Romania's National Anticorruption Directorate (DNA) detained Razvan Cuc, a former Social Democrat transport minister, on 16 December 2025 on suspicion of complicity in bribery. Prosecutors say Cuc acted as go-between for the businessman Catalin Buse, whose company held a contract with the Romanian Automobile Registry, the state body that certifies vehicle roadworthiness. At issue was renewal of a framework agreement worth 23 million lei for maintaining vehicle inspection equipment. Prosecutors say Cuc assured the Registry's director, Mihai Alecu, that he would receive 6 per cent of the contract's value, more than 1.3 million lei, and that the three meetings took place between September and November 2025. Homes in Bucharest and Ilfov county were searched. Nothing is proven.
inside: Prosecutors say a company seeking a state contract used a former minister to offer the state agency's own director a cut, so the renewal would go its way.
cite: Romania Insider, 17 December 2025; DNA statement

n: Houthis run Yemenia Airways through loyalists and hold its $100m
rank: Operational management of the state airline
d: Yemenia Airways is Yemen's state-owned airline; its board of directors sits in Aden under the internationally recognised government. The United Nations Panel of Experts on Yemen reported in October 2024 that the Houthi movement took over the running of the company in Sanaa through loyal staff and refused to recognise the Aden board, and that aircraft were detained at Sanaa airport on 25 and 26 June 2024. On instructions from the Houthi-appointed finance ministry, the central bank branch in Sanaa told commercial banks to suspend the airline's payments, leaving about 100 million dollars of its money under Houthi control for more than a year.
inside: An armed movement put its own people in charge of a state airline whose legal board sits elsewhere, and the company's cash then stayed in its hands.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2024/731, paras. 115-118 (October 2024)

n: Foreign bidders and two Nepali telecom regulators convicted over contract
org_label: Nuemera SDN Berhad, Namaste Global Communication and OSI Consulting joint venture
rank: Chairmen of the Nepal Telecommunications Authority
d: Nepal's Special Court convicted two former chairmen of the Nepal Telecommunications Authority, Digambar Jha and Purushottam Khanal, a Malaysian national, Mohammad Nur Amin, and a joint venture of the Malaysian firm Nuemera SDN Berhad, Namaste Global Communication of Singapore and OSI Consulting of India, on 6 March 2025. The authority regulates telecoms and was setting up a Mobile Device Management System to stop grey-market phone imports. In June 2019 it disqualified the lowest bidder, which had offered 7.66 million dollars, and gave the contract to the joint venture. Nepal's anti-corruption commission alleged inflated cost estimates, manual bids in breach of the procurement law, fabricated documents and collusion to hide the partners' shortcomings. The court put the loss to the state at 232 million rupees. Fourteen other defendants were acquitted.
inside: A foreign consortium got the regulator's own chairmen to disqualify the cheapest bidder and hand it the phone-tracking contract instead.
cite: Kathmandu Post, 'Court convicts Nepali officials, foreign firms in MDMS corruption case', 7 March 2025

n: Seven Kuwaiti judges jailed for taking gifts from a laundering suspect
rank: Seven serving judges
d: Kuwait's Court of Cassation upheld seven-year prison terms for seven judges who took vehicles and gifts from Fouad Salehi, an Iranian national arrested by the interior ministry in August 2020 and accused of money laundering and of bribing Kuwaiti officials. Investigators said his communications linked him to ten judges. It was the first time Kuwait lifted judicial immunity, and the Court of Appeal ordered the seven dismissed from the bench and the gifts returned. Two businessmen were given twelve years each with fines, a lawyer ten years and a government department head seven. One judge's acquittal was upheld. The ruling was reported in October 2023.
inside: A money-laundering suspect handed cars and gifts to serving judges, putting his network inside the court that would decide cases touching it.
cite: Gulf News, 'Kuwait landmark verdict: Seven judges sentenced to seven years over bribery scandal', 20 October 2023

n: Huawei and ZTE men convicted over $10m to a former Algerie Telecom executive
rank: former Algerie Telecom executive
d: An Algerian court sentenced two ZTE executives, Dong Tao and Chen Zhibo, and Huawei's Xiao Chunfa to ten years in jail in their absence for corruption and influence peddling, with international arrest warrants issued, fines of three million dinars each and a two-year ban on the firms from public tenders. Mohamed Boukhari, a former executive of the state operator Algerie Telecom, and a businessman, Chami Madjdoub, each got 18 years and a five million dinar fine over suspicious payments and money laundering between 2003 and 2006. The report alleges the Chinese executives paid $10m into offshore accounts set up by Madjdoub for Boukhari. The Register attributes these details to the French-language site Presse-DZ and does not independently verify them.
inside: Two Chinese telecoms suppliers allegedly routed $10m to an executive of Algeria's state operator, whose contract decisions then favoured them.
cite: The Register, 12 June 2012, citing Presse-DZ

n: Chinese loggers reported bribing Congolese officials over concessions and over-quota logging
org_label: Wan Peng and Booming Green (Booming Group)
rank: officials controlling forest concession allocation and harvest oversight
d: The Environmental Investigation Agency's October 2024 report examines two Chinese-owned loggers in the Democratic Republic of the Congo: Wan Peng, and Booming Green, of the Booming Group. An insider said Wan Peng obtained a concession during the moratorium on new industrial concessions, in place since 2002, by buying an old concession and bribing officials, saying "Yeah, we have bribed the General, equivalent to the military chairman in China", which the report calls an apparent reference to General Gabriel Amisi Kumba without independently confirming it. Another insider described payments to cover over-quota harvesting and misdeclared species, without naming recipients. A government audit dated January 2024 documented illegalities at two Wan Peng subsidiaries, Congo King Baisheng and Congo Sunflower, including acquisition through influence peddling and through violation of the relevant regulations, and a fraudulent concession acquisition by Booming Green in Mai-Ndombe.
inside: Logging firms allegedly paid officials to obtain concessions during a moratorium and to cover harvesting above quota and misdeclared species.
cite: Environmental Investigation Agency, 'Until the Last Log', October 2024

n: Armed group commander Johnson Olony made one of South Sudan's deputy army chiefs
rank: Deputy Chief of Defence Forces, SSPDF (one of several such posts)
d: The United Nations Panel of Experts on South Sudan reported, in its final report dated 1 July 2025, that Johnson Olony was appointed an SSPDF Deputy Chief of Defence Forces in January 2025, one of several such posts, and that his Agwelek forces are being integrated into the army. The Panel says the appointment carried responsibility for dismantling illegal checkpoints and disarming civilians, and that his presence in Malakal in February 2025 led to further mobilisation among local youth. Reporting that he had been deployed to disarm Nuer youth and seize checkpoints along the Sobat River came from local observers, corroborated by photographs on file with the Panel. The army has continued integrating defectors from the National Salvation Front and the Agwelek forces under Olony, who secured an agreement of his own in 2023.
inside: An armed group's commander was made one of the army's deputy chiefs and his own fighters were integrated into its ranks.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on South Sudan, final report S/2025/442, 1 July 2025

n: Wagner proxies given ministerial posts in the Central African Republic
rank: livestock minister; delegated minister for disarmament
d: The Sentry's June 2023 report says Hassan Bouba, appointed livestock minister in the Central African Republic, has been acting as a Wagner proxy, and that Hamza Gilbert Toumou Deya was awarded the position of delegated minister in charge of disarmament for working in the interest of President Faustin-Archange Touadera and Wagner. It also says a former anti-Balaka member nicknamed Yarkopa was appointed head of Unite 124, a unit the report says has not been publicly acknowledged, with several sources saying the Wagner-linked figure Wananga helped secure the appointment. The report says Wagner's top country representatives also serve as Touadera's special advisers. Its findings rest largely on confidential documents and interviews with named and unnamed sources.
inside: A foreign paramilitary group's proxies were given cabinet and command posts, the report says, including a livestock minister it describes as acting for Wagner.
cite: The Sentry, 'Architects of Terror', June 2023

n: Four Jamaican narcotics detectives charged under the Anti-Gang Act
org_label: Unnamed criminal organisation cited in the charge
rank: Firearms and Narcotics Investigation Division detectives
d: Four members of the Jamaica Constabulary Force's Firearms and Narcotics Investigation Division, Detective Sergeant James Dawes, Detective Corporal Tamela Anderson, Detective Constable Shane Givans and Constable Lakarie Barrett, were charged on 8 April 2025 after a ruling by the Director of Public Prosecutions earlier that week. The charges are facilitating the commission of a serious offence by a criminal organisation, forgery, uttering forged documents and perverting the course of justice. It is alleged that in 2023 the officers were investigating a Trelawny woman for suspected drug trafficking and she was taken into custody; her mother said a policeman told her the daughter would be released if money was paid, and she was freed without charge. It was reportedly discovered that the four accused had prepared the forged document used to release her.
inside: Prosecutors say serving narcotics detectives forged a document to free a trafficking suspect, and charged them with helping a criminal organisation from inside the police.
undone: Each officer was offered J$2m bail at the Supreme Court, after an application by attorneys Christopher Townsend and Chadwick Berry, and the case was set to return to court on 21 May 2025. Their lawyer argued there is no evidence of gang involvement.
cite: Radio Jamaica News (RJR), 10 April 2025

n: Costa Rica arrests two judges and an investigator over a trafficking group
rank: criminal court judges and an OIJ agent
d: Costa Rican prosecutors arrested two criminal judges, named only by the surnames Valverde and Ramirez, one of whom reportedly coordinates the Pococi criminal court, and an agent of the Organismo de Investigacion Judicial, the judicial police, surnamed Rojas. The arrests were made on 1 September 2026 in a raid on the Juzgado Penal de Pococi, in Limon province. The Fiscalia Adjunta de Probidad, Transparencia y Anticorrupcion says the three used their posts to collaborate with the group led by Alejandro Arias Monge, known as Diablo, who was captured on 24 July 2026 in Sarapiqui, and which it describes as trafficking drugs locally and internationally. It is investigating whether they accepted gifts and neglected their duties. The suspected offences are procuring impunity in drug cases, bribery, bribe-giving and misuse of public resources.
inside: Prosecutors say a trafficking group reached inside a criminal court and the judicial police, so judges and an investigator worked to keep its members out of prison.
cite: Observador.cr, September 2026

n: Palau land authority chairman accused of leasing to a Chinese national for payment
org_label: Chinese national leasing Palauan public land
rank: chairman of Aimeliik's State Public Land Authority; Speaker of the House of Delegates
d: The US State Department's 2023 human rights report for Palau says local media covered the chairman of Aimeliik's State Public Land Authority, Clarence Sriderio Renggulbai, reporting that he leased land in September 2022 to a Chinese national without proper approvals and received direct payment. The same report says that on 4 August the Office of the Special Prosecutor charged House of Delegates Speaker Sabino Anastacio with misconduct in public office for leasing land without a business license. The report gives no amounts, does not name the lessee, and gives no outcome for either matter. The accounts were also collected in a U4 Anti-Corruption Helpdesk review of corruption in Pacific island countries, which does not name the officials.
inside: A Chinese national is reported to have paid a Palauan state land authority chairman directly, and public land was leased without the proper approvals.
cite: US Department of State, 2023 Country Report on Human Rights Practices: Palau; also U4 Anti-Corruption Helpdesk, Caitlin Maslen, 3 February 2026

n: US money-laundering charges: bribes alleged to have won CLAP food contracts
org_label: Contractors led by Alvaro Pulido Vargas
who: contractors led by Alvaro Pulido Vargas
rank: Venezuelan officials including Jose Gregorio Vielma-Mora
d: A five-count indictment returned by a federal grand jury in the Southern District of Florida on 7 October 2021 and unsealed on 21 October 2021 charged five people with one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering and four counts of money laundering, over CLAP, described by the Justice Department as a Venezuelan state-owned and state-controlled food and medicine distribution programme. Prosecutors allege that from about July 2015 until at least 2020 Alvaro Pulido Vargas, also known as German Enrique Rubio Salas and 'Cuchi', Emmanuel Enrique Rubio Gonzalez, Carlos Rolando Lizcano Manrique and Ana Guillermo Luis paid bribes to Venezuelan officials, including their co-defendant Jose Gregorio Vielma-Mora, to obtain CLAP contracts and inflated the costs to pay the bribes. The bribery is alleged underlying conduct, not a charge.
inside: Prosecutors say the contractors paid officials inside Venezuela's state food programme, which then handed them the contracts to feed the country.
undone: The Justice Department announced on 11 October 2026 that Pulido Vargas was in the Southern District of Florida to face the 2021 charges, with an initial appearance set for 13 October 2026. Each of the five counts carries a maximum of 20 years. No disposition is recorded for the other defendants.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 21 October 2021; US Department of Justice press release 26-1168, 11 October 2026

n: Yara offered a fertiliser ministry official's son a paid engagement
rank: Additional Secretary and Financial Adviser, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers
d: In the same case, Norway's Supreme Court set out that Yara International's then chief legal officer and a colleague offered a representative engagement to the son of an Indian official who was Additional Secretary and Financial Adviser in the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers and a government-appointed board member of KRIBHCO, a fertiliser cooperative 67 per cent owned by the Indian state. The offer was linked to the father's position: a US$250,000 lump sum plus 50 cents per tonne of Yara fertiliser sold in India. A later draft replaced the lump sum with US$3 million, payable in US$1 million instalments for 2007 to 2009. On 16 October 2007 US$1 million went to a Hong Kong account of Krystal Holdings & Investments Limited, a British Virgin Islands company whose beneficiaries were the spouses of the official and his son.
inside: Yara's money was aimed at an official who advised India's fertiliser ministry and sat on a state-owned producer's board, to strengthen Yara's position there.
cite: Supreme Court of Norway, HR-2017-1776-A, judgment of 15 September 2017 (official English translation)

n: Banker settled SEC case alleging $2.5m reached Ghanaian officials and MPs over a power plant
org_label: Asante Berko and a Turkish energy company
who: a Turkish energy company and the banker Asante Berko
rank: members of the Ghanaian parliament and officials approving a power plant
d: The US Securities and Exchange Commission charged Asante Berko, a former executive of a foreign-based subsidiary of a US bank holding company, on 13 April 2020 with violating the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act's anti-bribery provisions. According to the complaint, filed in the Eastern District of New York, Berko arranged for his client, a Turkish energy company, to send at least $2.5 million to a Ghana-based intermediary, which used the money to bribe Ghanaian government officials into approving an electrical power plant project. The intermediary is alleged to have paid more than $200,000 to various other officials, and Berko to have paid more than $60,000 himself to members of Ghana's parliament and other officials. The SEC also alleged he misled his employer's compliance staff about the intermediary's role, and said those staff kept the firm out of the transaction.
inside: The SEC says a banker channelled a client's money to Ghanaian MPs and officials so they would approve the power plant his client wanted built.
undone: Berko consented to a final judgment on 23 June 2021, permanently enjoining him from violating the FCPA anti-bribery provision, Section 30A of the Exchange Act, and ordering $275,000 in disgorgement plus $54,163.92 in prejudgment interest, $329,163.92 in all. The litigation release records no admission.
cite: US Securities and Exchange Commission press release 2020-88, 13 April 2020; SEC litigation release 25121, 23 June 2021

n: Church circulated notices recruiting believers as Diet members' secretaries
rank: secretary to a House of Representatives member
d: Shimbun Akahata obtained notices it says Unification Church members circulated in spring 2013 among second-generation believers, recruiting them as secretaries to members of Japan's House of Representatives. One, headed House of Representatives secretary recruitment, said a young believer already working as a secretary to a lower house member had made contact, and asked readers to introduce candidates, describing the lawmaker, not a believer, as strict and as promising for a party's future plans. Neither notice names the lawmaker or the party. Another, addressed to students wanting to become politicians, relayed that a lower house member elected in Kanagawa prefecture - written with a question mark - was looking for secretaries. The paper reported that the church has sent believers as election campaign workers and secretaries, and that its sources say it sought to get close to LDP and other lawmakers.
cite: Shimbun Akahata, 17 October 2022
inside: The church circulated notices recruiting second-generation believers into jobs as lawmakers' secretaries, seeking to place its people in Japan's parliamentary offices.

n: Chinese timber group Dejia reported bribing Gabonese ministers
rank: government ministers in Gabon and the Republic of Congo
d: A 2019 report by the Environmental Investigation Agency, a campaign group, said Dejia, described as one of China's most influential groups of affiliated timber companies in Africa, regularly bribed Gabonese and Congolese ministers to access timber concessions and manage them without controls. Mongabay, reporting the claim in May 2023, said the agency also found that illegally sourced Dejia timber reached the European Union and the United States, and that the practices cost Gabon millions of dollars.
inside: A Chinese timber group is reported to have paid ministers who hand out logging rights, so its concessions were granted and left unchecked.
cite: Mongabay, 10 May 2023, citing Environmental Investigation Agency, Toxic Trade: Forest Crime in Gabon and the Republic of Congo and Contamination of the U.S. Market (2019)

n: Haftar-linked men took over Benghazi's Bank of Commerce and Development
org_label: Khalifa and Saddam Haftar's circle and the financier Ahmed Gadalla
rank: chairmanship and de facto control of a commercial bank
d: The Sentry's April 2026 report says figures linked to Field Marshal Khalifa Haftar's forces forced the founder of Benghazi's Bank of Commerce and Development, Jamal Tayeb Abdel Malek, to surrender his shares in 2022. Wassim al-Zway, a Haftar loyalist, became chairman on paper, while the report says genuine authority flowed to Saddam Haftar's circle and to the Dubai-based financier Ahmed Gadalla, who rose to become the bank's de facto chief. Russia's state printer Goznak had begun shipping billions in dinar banknotes to Haftar's camp as early as May 2016, roughly 14 billion dinars entering circulation this way, and after 2023 occasionally smuggled pallets of high-grade notes into Libya. Injections of unauthorised dinars reached about 10 billion in circulation as of October 2025, mainly in two categories of new 50-dinar notes, which the report says Gadalla oversaw distributing.
inside: An armed faction's financiers took a commercial bank's shares and chairmanship, so its money and banknote supply served the Haftar family's forces.
cite: The Sentry, 'Eastern Libya's Top Money Man', April 2026

n: Uganda police convicted of guarding a gold fraud syndicate's refinery
org_label: alleged gold fraud syndicate around Real Sunnex Ltd
rank: four police constables, called counter-terrorism officers in the article's photo caption
d: Uganda's Police Disciplinary Court convicted four police constables on 29 August 2026 after they left their assigned beats and, police say, self-deployed to support a gold fraud syndicate, guarding an illegal gold refinery linked to a $4m fraudulent transaction. Police Spokesperson Kituuma Rusoke said two of them, Kulutu Ayubu and Waiswa Benon, were recommended for dismissal and two, Waiswa Siraj and Emorut Razak, for discharge. A Dubai-based businessman complained in July 2025 that Asiimwe Moses and others operating under Real Sunnex Ltd had taken $4m from him in a bogus gold deal, and police said the syndicate was preparing to take a further $4m. A sting led to 16 arrests, and the four officers and 12 civilian suspects are being processed for criminal trial; no denials are reported.
inside: A fraud ring had serving police officers guarding its fake-gold refinery, so state force protected the swindle instead of stopping it.
cite: Daily Monitor (Uganda), 31 August 2026

n: Wagner firms granted CAR mining permits; report says they shaped mining law
rank: mining ministry decisions and state mining company GEMINCA
d: The Sentry's June 2023 report says Wagner-affiliated companies Lobaye Invest, Midas Ressources and Diamville were granted mining licences and export authorisations in the Central African Republic, which the report calls de facto authorisations to exploit and loot the country's wealth in exchange for protecting Faustin-Archange Touadera. It says the exploitation permit for the Ndassima deposit was transferred to Midas in 2020, apparently without legal basis, and that Midas reportedly obtained a decree and a mining convention, the decree confirming the allocation of a 25-year gold exploitation permit; a note from the mines minister to Touadera in December 2020 described Midas as a Russian company. It also says Wagner attempted to influence the revision of mining legislation, citing a confidential document by alleged Wagner authors recommending that the state control artisanal miners and make state company GEMINCA the main buyer.
inside: Wagner's companies were granted state mining permits by decree, and The Sentry says Wagner worked to shape the mining law that would govern them.
cite: The Sentry, 'Architects of Terror', June 2023

n: Bahamas defence force officer sold patrol positions to traffickers
org_label: Cocaine conspiracy prosecuted in the Southern District of New York
rank: chief petty officer, Royal Bahamas Defence Force
d: Darrin Alexander Roker, 56, a former chief petty officer in the Royal Bahamas Defence Force, pleaded guilty in a New York court to one count of cocaine importation conspiracy. He told the court he gave traffickers information on where Bahamian law enforcement vessels were so their boats could avoid interception, and prosecutors say he was paid 20,000 dollars. He is the first of thirteen defendants to plead guilty. Prosecutors allege the conspiracy moved tons of cocaine through the Bahamas into the United States between 2021 and 2024 and also included police officers; Chief Superintendent Elvis Nathaniel Curtis and former sergeant Prince Albert Symonette are accused of taking bribes to move shipments through Nassau. Roker faced up to twenty years and a $1 million fine.
inside: Traffickers paid a serving naval officer for the positions of Bahamian patrol boats, turning the force meant to stop them into their lookout.
undone: At a hearing on 21 January 2026 before Judge Gregory Woods, Roker was sentenced to 48 months in prison. Prosecutors had sought at least five years and called his stage-four metastatic prostate cancer a powerful mitigating factor.
cite: Eyewitness News Bahamas (undated), 'Former Defence Force Officer Pleads Guilty in U.S. Cocaine Smuggling Case'; sentence from ZNS Bahamas, 22 January 2026, and Tribune242, 19 January 2026

n: Operation Leviathan: traffickers' people inside Costa Rica's Moin container port
org_label: Cocaine export network using the Moin container terminal
rank: border police officers and terminal staff at Moin
d: Costa Rica's organised crime prosecution unit, FAEDO, says a network used the Moin container terminal at Limon, operated by APM Terminals, to ship cocaine to Europe and the United States. Investigators say ten border police officers let containers in and out without triggering alerts, allegedly for payment, alongside thirteen private security officers, twelve tractor-unit drivers, crane operators and operational supervisors. The group charged about $250,000 a shipment, whatever the quantity of cocaine, hiding loads under 60 kilos in refrigeration units or removing containers, loading them at properties in Limon and returning them, a method investigators call mete y saca. The investigation has run since 2023; on 28 July 2026 the Fiscalia, with the PCD and OIJ, carried out 65 raids and 43 arrests. The reporting does not accuse APM Terminals itself.
inside: Prosecutors allege border police and terminal staff at Costa Rica's main container port were paid to let the network's containers pass unchecked.
cite: Observador.cr, 28 July 2026

n: Alstom Power paid Lithuanian power station officials and politicians
rank: officials of a state power station and senior politicians
d: Alstom Power Ltd, the British arm of the French engineering group Alstom, pleaded guilty at a London court on 10 May 2016 to conspiring to corrupt officials at a Lithuanian power station and senior Lithuanian politicians. The Serious Fraud Office said the Alstom companies paid more than EUR 5 million in bribes across the investigation, to secure EUR 325 million of contracts, including two Lithuanian contracts worth EUR 240 million, one of them to upgrade the burners at the Lithuanian Power Plant, and falsified records to get past anti-bribery checks. Alstom Power Ltd was ordered to pay GBP 18,038,000 in total: a GBP 6,375,000 fine, GBP 10,963,000 compensation to the Lithuanian government and GBP 700,000 in prosecution costs.
inside: Alstom's money reached officials of a state power station and senior politicians, who then awarded the firm EUR 240 million of Lithuanian power contracts.
undone: Two men had been jailed on this charge set as of December 2018: John Venskus (3 years 6 months, sentenced 4 May 2018) and Goran Wikstrom (2 years 7 months, sentenced 9 July 2018, plus GBP 40,000 costs). Nicholas Reynolds, Alstom Power's former global sales director, was convicted at Blackfriars Crown Court on 19 December 2018 and sentenced on 21 December 2018 to 4 years 6 months, with GBP 50,000 in costs.
cite: UK Serious Fraud Office, 'Five convictions in SFO's Alstom investigation into bribery & corruption to secure EUR 325 million of contracts', 19 December 2018; SFO, 'Former Alstom Power Global Sales Director sentenced to 4.5 years for corruption', 21 December 2018

n: Scoular paid Mexican border inspectors to pass its grain trains
org_label: The Scoular Company, a US agricultural trader
rank: Mexican officials inspecting shipments at the border
d: The Scoular Company, an agricultural supply chain company based in Omaha, Nebraska, entered a three-year deferred prosecution agreement with the US Justice Department on one count of conspiring to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act. Between 2013 and 2019 Scoular authorised third-party customs brokers to bribe Mexican officials at the border so that its trains of corn and other products would cross despite inspections that found dirt, soil and other impurities. The brokers paid about $2,000 per train and invoiced the money back to Scoular as reinspection fees. In all Scoular authorised more than $400,000 in bribes and avoided more than $6.5 million in fees and costs, and agreed to pay a $9,769,521 penalty and $414,351 in forfeiture. Scoular received no credit for voluntary disclosure, the department said, because it did not disclose the conduct voluntarily and in time.
inside: The firm's brokers paid Mexican border inspectors, so the state's own inspection decisions let its failed grain shipments through.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 17 July 2026

n: SNC-Lavalin paid $22.5m to the McGill hospital's chief and a manager
rank: chief executive and a senior manager of the McGill University Health Centre
d: The McGill University Health Centre is a public hospital group in Montreal. According to an agreed statement of facts, the engineering firm SNC-Lavalin paid $22.5 million that Arthur Porter, the centre's chief executive, and the senior manager Yanai Elbaz received to rig the bidding on the $1.3 billion contract to build a new hospital; Porter funnelled the money through a shell company and Elbaz received his share through his own shell company. Elbaz pleaded guilty in December 2018 to accepting a bribe and was sentenced to 39 months. The former SNC-Lavalin executive Riadh Ben Aissa was sentenced to 51 months for using forged documents. The former chief executive Pierre Duhaime pleaded guilty on 1 February 2019 to helping a public servant commit breach of trust. Porter died in 2015 while a fugitive in Panamanian custody.
inside: The contractor's money bought the hospital's own chief executive and a senior manager, who then shaped the tender so the firm won the building contract.
undone: On 1 February 2019 a Quebec judge accepted a joint Crown and defence recommendation and sentenced Duhaime to 20 months of house arrest, 240 hours of community service and a $200,000 donation to a fund compensating crime victims, with no jail time; 14 of the 15 original charges against him were withdrawn.
cite: The Canadian Press via Global News, 1 February 2019; sentence from CBC News, 1 February 2019

n: Prosecutors allege Equalize paid serving police and tax-police officers for database files
rank: Guardia di Finanza marshal; state police superintendent and inspector; Carabinieri NCO
d: Milan prosecutors allege that the private intelligence firm Equalize had serving officers of Italy's state agencies on its payroll to pull confidential files. Named as suspects in October 2024 were Giuliano Schiano, a Guardia di Finanza maresciallo assigned to the DIA in Lecce; Marco Malerba, a Polizia di Stato sovrintendente at the Rho-Pero commissariato; Roberto Bonacina, a Polizia di Stato ispettore at the border police office at Orio al Serio airport; and Saverio Penna, a Carabinieri non-commissioned officer in the investigative unit in Milan. Open reported that Schiano and Malerba were regularly paid by the investigations firm for non-public information about the targets of the dossier operations, drawn from the interior ministry's SDI database and the tax agency's Punto Fisco system, and that Malerba's son was hired off the books.
cite: Open, 27 October 2024; Il Sole 24 Ore, 21 July 2026 (en.ilsole24ore.com/art/equalise-trial-of-74-defendants-accused-of-spying-on-over-800-people-AJH5yLR)
inside: Prosecutors say a private firm put serving police and tax-police officers on its payroll so state databases were searched for its paying clients.
undone: In July 2026 Milan prosecutors sought trial for 74 defendants in the 'clients' strand of the case, with 832 people named as alleged victims of the spying.

n: US and UK sanction Kamlesh Pattni over bribes in Zimbabwe's gold trade
org_label: Kamlesh Pattni's gold and diamond network
rank: officials in Zimbabwe (Al Jazeera reported bribery at the national gold refinery)
d: The United States and the United Kingdom sanctioned the Kenyan-British businessman Kamlesh Pattni, freezing assets, confiscating property and imposing travel bans, reported on 10 December 2024. The US Treasury listed 27 companies and individuals in his network and said he had allegedly bribed officials in Zimbabwe for illicit profits from its gold and diamond trade. Al Jazeera's 2023 undercover investigation reported bribery at Zimbabwe's national gold refinery and smuggling through Harare airport. Pattni told undercover reporters that his Zimbabwean businesses relied on political support from President Emmerson Mnangagwa and that an employee paid the president regular bribes; Mnangagwa did not respond to requests for comment. Pattni denied involvement in money laundering and denied criminal wrongdoing in Kenya, saying he was never convicted there, and said he believed the undercover reporters were investors.
inside: A foreign gold dealer allegedly bribed Zimbabwean officials, and Al Jazeera reported bribery at the state refinery and smuggling through Harare airport.
cite: Al Jazeera, 10 December 2024

n: Libyan state bank's $300m deposit backed loans to a Haftar fixer's firms
org_label: Ahmed Gadalla's companies and Haftar-aligned bankers
rank: the last central bank governor under Qadhafi, later aligned with the Haftar family, as chairman of a UAE bank; Libyan Foreign Bank guarantee deposit
d: The Sentry's April 2026 report says Farhat Benqdara, the last central bank governor under Qadhafi, later aligned with the Haftar family, became chairman of Al-Masraf, the Arab Bank for Investment and Foreign Trade in Abu Dhabi, in 2018 with the support of the central bank governor Sadiq al-Kabir, whose votes through the state-owned Libyan Foreign Bank helped secure the post. In 2019 Al-Masraf lent $300m to three Dubai companies linked to the financier Ahmed Gadalla: JTA General Trading LLC, al-Mored Oasis General Trading LLC and AMAA General Trading LLC, backed by a $300m Libyan Foreign Bank guarantee deposit. The report says the money funded Haftar's failed Tripoli offensive and likely bankrolled Wagner mercenaries. Benqdara attributed about $375m in 2020 impairment charges to Covid-19, which the report says masked the truth. Gadalla did not respond to The Sentry's request for comment.
inside: One faction's man chaired a foreign bank while a Libyan state bank's deposit backed the loan, so public money financed their own war, the report alleges.
cite: The Sentry, 'Eastern Libya's Top Money Man', April 2026
undone: A $70m partial repayment was made in 2021, leaving about $230m of the loan outstanding as of January 2025.

n: US sanctions Liberia's chief prosecutor over bribes to drop cases
org_label: money launderers and criminal suspects paying for case outcomes
rank: Solicitor General and Chief Prosecutor of Liberia
d: On 15 August 2022 the United States Treasury designated three senior Liberian officials under Executive Order 13818. It said Sayma Syrenius Cephus, then Solicitor General and Chief Prosecutor, received bribes to have individuals' cases dropped, worked to halt money laundering investigations for personal financial gain, shields money launderers and helps clear them through the court system, and had intimidated other prosecutors in an attempt to quash investigations. It also named Nathaniel McGill, Minister of State for Presidential Affairs and Chief of Staff to President George Weah, who Treasury said accepted kickbacks for steering contracts to firms in which he had an interest, and Bill Twehway of the National Port Authority, who Treasury said diverted $1.5 million in vessel storage fees into a private account and awarded a Port of Buchanan cargo contract to a company he secretly formed.
inside: Paying people facing prosecution bought the office that decides prosecutions, so Liberia's own chief prosecutor dropped their cases, Treasury says.
cite: US Department of the Treasury, press release, 15 August 2022; Executive Mansion of Liberia, 16 August 2022
undone: President George Weah suspended the three men with immediate effect on 16 August 2022 to let them face investigation, naming each one's principal deputy to act in their place.

n: Ethiopia charges fuel traders and the petroleum authority's deputy chief
org_label: fuel trading companies, including Yegna Petroleum
rank: Deputy Director General, Petroleum and Energy Authority
d: Ethiopian federal prosecutors charged 13 people, including senior officials and business figures, over fuel contraband, before the Federal High Court, reported on 7 May 2026. The first defendant is Dibara Fufa, Deputy Director General of the Petroleum and Energy Authority; others include Shumalem Birhane, director general of a fuel supply enterprise, Bereket Worku, and the unnamed owner and manager of Yegna Petroleum. Prosecutors allege officials issued unauthorised fuel purchase permits and helped sell 466,058 litres of white diesel to gold producers, gave one defendant access to more than 1.2 million litres without legal justification, removed 1.9 million litres from oversight, and that the Yegna Petroleum owner obtained a distribution licence illicitly. The losses alleged are 8.4m, 22.5m, 21.3m and 17.8m birr, over 70 million birr in all. The hearing was adjourned to 18 May 2026 for preliminary objections.
inside: Prosecutors say fuel traders worked through the officials who issue permits, so the regulator's own decisions opened the taps for them.
cite: Fidel Post (Ethiopia), 7 May 2026; Capital (Ethiopia), 10 May 2026

n: Bahamas customs officer charged over payments from a contractor
rank: chief customs revenue officer
d: Pamela Williams, a chief customs revenue officer with the Bahamas Customs Department who had been stationed in Exuma, was charged on 19 May 2026 in Freeport Magistrate's Court with 77 counts covering 58,045 dollars: nineteen counts each of bribery, extortion, money laundering and fraud by false pretences, and one of fraudulent breach of trust. Prosecutors allege that between March 2023 and April 2025 she solicited and obtained payments without lawful authority while a public servant, including 56,320 dollars by cheque from Costal Systems Bahamas Ltd for unauthorised services and 1,725 dollars by three cheques from Geoffrey C. Lawes. She was not required to plead; bail was refused, with leave for her attorney to apply to the Supreme Court, and the matter was adjourned to 26 September for voluntary bill of indictment proceedings. These are allegations.
inside: Prosecutors allege a contractor paid a senior customs officer $56,320 by cheque for services she had no lawful authority to give.
cite: The Tribune (Nassau), 20 May 2026

n: Two ex-PDI officers convicted of feeding a Chilean ketamine gang
rank: detectives, Policia de Investigaciones
d: Two former officers of Chile's investigative police, the Policia de Investigaciones, were convicted at the Arica guarantee court after accepting the facts in an abbreviated procedure. Leoncio Oporto Duhart used his institutional login on the police BRAIN system to look up active arrest warrants against two men identified as leaders of Los Kussy Boys and passed the information on by messaging app, with photographs of evidence from police cases including seized cash; 2,200,000 pesos was paid into his account. He was convicted of criminal association, improper passive bribery, disclosure of secrets and illegal possession of firearm parts and ammunition, and received about five years. Claudio Solans Marchant ran a price list for reserved police information with a minimum price of 300,000 pesos, and was convicted of criminal association, active bribery and illegal firearm possession, receiving just over four years.
inside: A drug gang paid a serving detective for police warrants and evidence, so Chile's investigative police warned the traffickers it was meant to catch.
cite: El Desconcierto opinion column, 7 August 2026, citing El Mostrador

n: Odebrecht paid Ecuador's Comptroller General over $10m to drop fines
rank: Comptroller General
d: Carlos Ramon Polit Faggioni was Ecuador's Comptroller General, the official charged with guarding public funds against fraud. A federal jury in Miami convicted him on 23 April 2024 of conspiracy to commit money laundering, concealment money laundering and transactions in criminally derived property. The US Justice Department said that between 2010 and 2015 he solicited and received over $10 million in bribes from the Brazilian construction group Odebrecht, and in exchange removed fines and did not impose fines on Odebrecht's projects in Ecuador. In about 2015 he also took a bribe to help a businessman win state insurance contracts. From about 2010 until at least 2017 a conspirator acting at Polit's direction moved the bribe money through Florida companies registered in the names of friends and associates, often without their knowledge, and to buy and renovate Florida real estate.
inside: Odebrecht's money captured the official meant to audit it, so Ecuador's own spending watchdog cancelled the fines on the firm's projects.
cite: US Department of Justice press releases, 24 April 2024 (conviction) and 1 October 2024 (sentencing)
undone: He was sentenced to ten years in prison on 1 October 2024 and ordered to forfeit $16.5 million.

n: Okokrim charges Petronor unit over bribes tied to Congo's president
org_label: A Norwegian subsidiary of Petronor E&P ASA
rank: the President of Congo and close family members
d: Okokrim, Norway's economic crime authority, said on 26 January 2026 it had indicted two Norwegian citizens for gross corruption and gross accounting violations, and a Norwegian company for gross corruption. The company is a wholly owned subsidiary of Petronor E&P ASA, listed in Oslo. Okokrim says that from 2016 onwards the accused applied for and obtained a share in oil licences in the Republic of Congo, and that bribes of particularly high value are linked to the President of Congo and his close family. Norway has no jurisdiction over the recipients, so their liability was not considered. The case began with a suspicious transaction to a bank in Monaco; Monaco's financial intelligence unit investigated, then requested legal assistance from Norway. Okokrim closed separate market manipulation suspicions against the individuals, the company and Petronor's former chairman without charges, for insufficient evidence.
inside: Okokrim alleges bribes of particularly high value are linked to Congo's president and his close family, and the Norwegian company then obtained a share of the country's oil licences.
cite: Okokrim press release, 26 January 2026

n: Canadian firm's bribes aimed at a Philippine police equipment deal
rank: officials deciding a Philippine National Police procurement (no post or official named in the release)
d: Ultra Electronics Forensic Technology Inc., a Montreal company, was charged with two counts of bribing officials of the Republic of the Philippines under section 3 of Canada's Corruption of Foreign Public Officials Act and one count of fraud under section 380 of the Criminal Code. The conduct ran from 2006 to 2018, aimed at securing the procurement of a ballistic identification system for the Philippine National Police. The Superior Court of Quebec published a remediation agreement on 16 May 2023: the company pays a penalty of $6,593,178, a surcharge of $659,318 and forfeits $3,296,589, and must follow an anti-bribery programme supervised for four years by an external auditor it pays for. The prosecution is stayed and the charges are to be withdrawn once the company meets its obligations, which include reporting to the Public Prosecution Service on implementation.
inside: The company paid Philippine government officials over twelve years in a scheme aimed at winning the national police force's contract for a ballistic identification system.
cite: Public Prosecution Service of Canada news release, 17 May 2023

n: SAP fined $222m; bribes offered to Tanzania Ports Authority officials
rank: top officials of the Tanzania Ports Authority
d: The German software company SAP was fined $222m by US authorities over bribery of government officials in several African countries, including Tanzania, in a report dated 15 January 2024. The article says SAP is linked to offering bribes to top officials at the Tanzania Ports Authority, the state body running the country's ports, in 2014/2015 to win a tender, and is alleged to have colluded with Tanzania Ports Authority insiders to obtain preferential treatment on other government deals that were meant to go to competitive bidding. The report does not name the officials or the tender, and says SAP offered bribes without stating whether payments were received. No response from the company appears on the page. The underlying US resolutions with SAP SE were announced on 10 January 2024.
inside: A software supplier is alleged to have colluded with insiders at the state ports authority to obtain preferential treatment on deals meant for competitive bidding.
cite: The Citizen (Tanzania), 15 January 2024; underlying US Department of Justice and SEC resolutions with SAP SE, 10 January 2024

n: Report says Haftar-aligned chairman used Libya's National Oil Corporation for the family
org_label: Khalifa Haftar's Libyan Arab Armed Forces network
rank: chairman of the National Oil Corporation
d: The Sentry's April 2026 report says Farhat Benqdara, the last central bank governor under Qadhafi who became a key economic adviser to Field Marshal Khalifa Haftar and his sons in 2018, chaired Libya's National Oil Corporation from 2022 to 2025, and that the Haftar family used the corporation to help get around the United Nations arms embargo on Libya, including securing an Irish private military contractor. The report says the NOC sold crude to the Chinese trader Unipec in August 2022 at what it calls an abnormal discount, and says separately that stages of a Chinese drone acquisition programme were financed not through monetary payments but through illicit oil schemes. Haftar's forces did not respond. The Sentry says it used interviews, documentary research and financial forensic analysis, and that some sources are not named.
inside: An armed faction's own adviser ran the state oil company, so its oil sales and contracts were used to arm that faction, the report says.
cite: The Sentry, 'Eastern Libya's Top Money Man', April 2026

n: Prosecutors say company payments reached Botswana's mining minister
org_label: Sieyuan Electric Botswana and New Energy Company
who: Sieyuan Electric and New Energy Company
rank: Minister of Mineral Resources, Green Technology and Energy Security
d: Court filings by Botswana's Directorate on Corruption and Economic Crime, reported on 31 December 2025, allege that more than five million pula in kickbacks reached Lefoko Maxwell Moagi, then mining minister, from companies dealing with his ministry. Prosecutors allege 4,706,000 pula moved into a Wisecreatives Investments account from New Energy Company and Riders, and that payments of 117,500 pula on 30 August 2024 and 300,000 pula hours later allegedly bought him cattle from a Ghanzi farmer. In mid-2024 Moagi reportedly approved and signed eight base-metal prospecting licences for New Energy. Sieyuan Electric Botswana, a contractor on projects under his ministry, allegedly had its executives arrange the cattle purchases. Charges fall under the Corruption and Economic Crime Act and the Proceeds and Instrumentalities of Crime Act (money laundering); the Director of Public Prosecutions has moved to immobilise Moagi's assets.
inside: Companies seeking licences and power contracts allegedly paid the minister who signs them, and he then signed eight licences for one of them.
cite: The African Mirror, 31 December 2025, citing DCEC court filings

n: Global Fund: bid collusion needed a Madagascar procurement official
org_label: malaria grant suppliers bidding to Madagascar's health programme offices
rank: procurement unit official at the health projects support office (UGP)
d: The Office of the Inspector General of the Global Fund, which finances health programmes, investigated procurement under five malaria grants to Madagascar and released its report on 3 January 2014, having begun work in April 2012. Reviewing $12.2m of about $70.8m disbursed, it found non-compliant expenditure, over-priced goods and collusion among suppliers, with about $1.16m of non-compliant spending including $462,670 of over-pricing. In a 2010 restricted national tender for indoor residual spraying supplies and equipment, run by UGP, the government's support office for health sector projects, contracts worth $640,146 were compromised, with slightly more than half charged above market rates; the Inspector General said such practices needed the collusion of a procurement unit official. SALAMA was removed as a principal recipient and its grant is in closure.
inside: Suppliers rigged bids for malaria contracts, which the inspectors said required an official inside the UGP, the government's support office for health sector projects, to work with them.
cite: Aidspan / Global Fund Observer, 8 January 2014, on the Global Fund OIG report of 3 January 2014

n: Operation Lobo: security firm Senase accused of paying state security staff
rank: security directors, officers and coordinators at state utilities and agencies
d: Dominican prosecutors accuse the private guarding company Senase, Servicio Nacional de Seguridad Integral S.R.L., of paying 108,080,359.92 Dominican pesos in bribes to security staff inside state bodies so its contracts were kept in force, paperwork moved quickly and objections or audits were avoided. The accusation covers 2012 to 2025, names ten people and four companies, and charges bribery, criminal association, fraud against the state and money laundering. Those accused include the company's representative Quilvio Bienvenido Rodriguez Gonzalez, former security directors of the electricity distributors EdeSur and EdeEste, former security officers at EdeNorte, a member of EdeEste's security department, a former security director and a former security assistant at the child-care agency Inaipi, and a former security coordinator at the health insurer Senasa. The operation began in July 2025; prosecutors filed the accusation and requested trial, which has not been reached.
inside: Prosecutors say a guarding company put money in the pockets of the officials who oversaw its own contracts, so state bodies kept buying from it unchecked.
cite: Acento (Santo Domingo), 15 July 2026, Ministerio Publico accusation in Operation Lobo

n: Samoan immigration officer jailed for selling passports to non-Samoans
rank: assistant immigration officer
d: David Nomeneta Uaine, a former assistant immigration officer from Tuana'i, was convicted in Samoa's Supreme Court on 28 charges including corruption, bribery, forgery and using false documents, and was sentenced by Justice Tafaoimalo Leilani Tuala-Warren to four years in prison, all sentences concurrent. While in post in 2016 and 2017 he lodged and processed six applications for Samoan passports for people who were not Samoan; five were approved. He was allegedly paid with money sent to him from overseas, which the judge described as not significant amounts but as going to him personally, and the judge found the offending premeditated, sophisticated and deliberate, spread over six months, with his level of criminality high. The Samoa Observer brought the passport sales to the immigration office's attention in September 2017.
inside: Buyers abroad paid an immigration officer to push through Samoan passports for people with no right to them, using the state's own document system.
cite: Samoa Observer, 31 May 2019 (sentencing date confirmed by RNZ Pacific, 31 May 2019)

n: J&F bribed BNDES and Petros executives and a legislator for state finance
rank: BNDES and Petros executives and a senior legislative official
d: J&F Investimentos S.A., the Brazilian company behind meatpacker JBS, pleaded guilty on 14 October 2020 in federal court in Brooklyn to conspiring to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and agreed to pay a criminal penalty of $256,497,026. The US Justice Department said the conspiracy ran from 2005 to 2017, and that between 2005 and 2014 J&F engaged in a bribery scheme involving more than $148 million in corrupt payments to high-level Brazilian officials, including a then high-ranking executive at BNDES, Brazil's state development bank, which provided hundreds of millions in financing. A high-ranking executive of the state-controlled pension fund Petros was paid more than $4.6 million for approving a merger benefiting J&F, and J&F paid approximately $25 million to a high-ranking official in the legislative branch to secure hundreds of millions of dollars of financing from Caixa Economica Federal.
inside: J&F's payments reached executives inside Brazil's state development bank and a state pension fund, which approved its financing and a merger, and a legislator who secured it financing from Caixa.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 14 October 2020

n: Strukton paid $31m through an agent for Riyadh metro work
rank: a high-ranking member of the ruling family
d: The Dutch public prosecution service said on 30 March 2026 that the construction company Strukton had accepted a settlement of 10 million euro over foreign bribery of officials and forgery of documents in the building of a metro line in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. Between February 2013 and June 2021 Strukton paid about US$31 million to a company acting as its agent, in order to bribe a high-ranking member of the ruling family; the payments helped Strukton win part of the metro contract. Its final export credit insurance application to Atradius Dutch State Business N.V. stated it had paid the agent US$1.5 million when the agreed amount was US$27.5 million, concealing the bribe payments; Strukton also gave false information to its external auditor. The investigation into several former employees is complete and prosecutors intend to charge some of them.
inside: Strukton paid about $31m to an agent in order to bribe a senior member of the Saudi ruling family, and won part of the Riyadh metro contract.
cite: Openbaar Ministerie (Netherlands) news release, 30 March 2026

n: IT firm paid a Frankfurt chief prosecutor for the state's data work
org_label: A German IT company and its owner
rank: chief public prosecutor in Frankfurt, a corruption investigator
d: Frankfurt's regional court convicted an IT entrepreneur of bribery in twenty cases on 17 December 2025, giving him an 18-month suspended sentence and confiscating 44,200 euro; the verdict is not yet final. The court heard that the city's former chief public prosecutor, himself a corruption investigator, awarded contracts to firms in which he secretly held a stake, among them the man's company, which had been doing his data backup and processing work for about two years, and in autumn 2014 told him to pay one euro for every billed hour or get no more orders. He paid in cash withdrawn from his private account, about once a quarter and in sums of 1,000 to 5,000 euro, roughly 66,000 euro in all, handed over on walks in a park, until the prosecutor was arrested in summer 2020.
inside: A senior Frankfurt prosecutor demanded a cut of every billed hour from an IT firm he kept giving the state's data contracts.
cite: hessenschau (Hessischer Rundfunk), 17 December 2025
undone: The prosecutor was sentenced to six years in spring 2023 and released on probation in December 2025. A business partner received almost three years and a prosecutor who worked with him was fined. Hessen is suing for 6.6 million euro, the revenue the IT firm earned from his orders in the offence period.

n: Church renaming allowed after 18 years; church-linked editor bought the minister's tickets
rank: Minister of Education; Agency for Cultural Affairs
d: In 2015 the Agency for Cultural Affairs, part of Japan's education ministry, let the Unification Church register a new name, the Family Federation for World Peace and Unification. Jiji Press reported on 5 August 2022 that Kihei Maekawa, head of the agency's religious affairs division in 1997 and vice education minister in 2015, told an opposition-party hearing at the Diet that the agency reversed an 18-year policy of not accepting renamings, that he was overruled, that he was 100 per cent sure the intent behind it was that of the education minister Hakubun Shimomura, and that external power was at work. Shimbun Akahata reported on 4 September 2022 that an editor of the church-linked paper Sekai Nippo bought 40,000 yen of tickets to Shimomura's fundraisers in 2013 and 2014. Shimomura said in 2022 that he felt responsible for the renaming.
cite: Jiji Press, 5 August 2022 (Maekawa testimony); Shimbun Akahata / Japan Press Weekly, 4 September 2022 (https://www.japan-press.co.jp/s/news/?id=14271); The Japan Times, 5 August 2022
inside: A church-linked paper's editor bought tickets to the education minister's fundraisers, and his ministry reversed an 18-year refusal to let the church change its name. No source connects the two.

n: RSF-linked firms took a majority stake in Sudan's Al Khaleej Bank
org_label: companies linked to the Rapid Support Forces (RSF)
rank: majority shareholding in a commercial bank
d: Companies linked to Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, a paramilitary force led by the Dagalo family, bought a majority stake in Al Khaleej Bank in Khartoum in 2019, according to a report by The Sentry published in October 2025. A Dubai firm, Al Jil Alqadem General Trading, held bank shares; the report says Abdulrahim Dagalo owned that firm and that by late 2024 it was held by Mazin Fadlalla and Abozer Habib. In a Treasury release of 31 January 2024 the United States described Al Khaleej Bank as an essential part of the RSF's efforts to finance its operations. The report rests on interviews, documentary research and corporate registry records in the UAE and Sudan, with some sources unnamed for their safety. It says Abozer Habib declined to comment, citing legal proceedings, and that Mazin Fadlalla did not respond.
inside: An armed force bought control of a commercial bank through front companies, so a licensed bank's accounts and transfers served its war financing.
cite: The Sentry, October 2025

n: Logging firms paid South Sudan's army, security and intelligence officers
org_label: logging companies, including Santos Petroleum and Timber Ltd and Aguet Trading (the Panel identified at least three South Sudanese and Ugandan companies)
rank: SSPDF, National Security Service, Military Intelligence and county officials
d: The final report of the United Nations Panel of Experts on South Sudan, dated 1 July 2025, says that in some cases individual foreign businesspeople have been identified as the owners and financiers of illegal logging, and names the companies Santos Petroleum and Timber Ltd and Aguet Trading. It says logging deals were negotiated directly with communities, county officials and security forces, including the SSPDF, the National Security Service, Military Intelligence and the opposition SPLA-IO, depending on the area, and cites a document from December 2023 in which a company agreed to pay local officials $5,000 per truck. Local chiefs and communities might receive only a few hundred dollars, with the rest going to county officials and security actors. The Panel reports these findings for 2023 to 2025.
inside: Timber operators reportedly paid county officials and the army, intelligence and security services they negotiated logging deals with.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on South Sudan, final report S/2025/442, 1 July 2025

n: Charges dropped against Ugandan officers accused of spying for Rwanda
rank: seven serving army and police officers
d: Seven senior Ugandan security officers were accused of allegedly sharing classified information with Rwandan authorities. The case was heard by the General Court Martial at Makindye in Kampala, chaired by Brigadier General Robert Freeman Mugabe. On 16 April 2024 prosecutors told the court they had instructions to discontinue all charges, and the officers were freed. The report names no formal charge beyond that allegation. The visible portion of the report does not say what information was said to have been shared, or why the case was dropped, and the allegations were never tested at trial.
inside: Prosecutors alleged Rwanda was receiving classified Ugandan material from serving officers inside Uganda's army and police; the charges were later dropped.
cite: New Vision (Uganda), 17 April 2024

n: Arms dealer's company held power of attorney for Niger's defence ministry
org_label: Aboubacar Hima's arms companies (TSI, Brid A Defcon)
rank: power of attorney on behalf of the Ministry of Defence
d: A confidential audit by Niger's army inspectorate, reported by OCCRP, found that TSI, a company founded by the Nigerien arms broker Aboubacar Hima, gained power of attorney on behalf of the Ministry of Defence, giving the ability to approve weapons deals and issue end-user certificates. Before receiving that power, Hima had already issued Russia's Rosoboronexport an end-user certificate for the ministry in 2018. The audit covered about $1bn of military spending from 2011 to 2019 and found problems in contracts worth over $320m; Hima handled at least three quarters of the purchases reviewed, about $240m. Companies run by a second intermediary, Aboubacar Charfo, used fake bids, and the audit said the winner was known in advance. Hima's lawyer, Marc Le Bihan, declined to answer questions, said Hima could not be reached and was not being prosecuted over the auditors' report.
inside: An arms dealer's company was given the ministry's own signing power, so it could approve and certify the weapons deals he was selling.
cite: OCCRP, 6 August 2020, citing Niger's Inspection Generale des Armees audit

n: Panama's presidential guard and prosecution staff convicted in an airport cocaine ring
rank: officials of the SPI, the Ministerio Publico, Senan and private airport security
d: The investigation began in 2021. At trial, which opened on 1 June 2025, judges Kathia Rodriguez, Ilka Castillo and Raul Vergara found twenty defendants guilty of conspiracy to traffic drugs and three of those also guilty of money laundering, as reported on 24 July 2026. Those convicted include officials of the Servicio de Proteccion Institucional, which guards the presidency, the Ministerio Publico, the air and naval service Senan, and private security at Tocumen airport. The network was led by Fernando Mendoza. Insiders changed the colillas, or identifying tags, on suitcases bound for terminals in France, Spain and other European countries.
inside: A trafficking network had officials of the presidential guard, the prosecution service, the air and naval service and airport security working inside Tocumen.
undone: Sentences had not been set when the verdict was reported. The court must still fix each one, and they are expected to range between 8 and 12 years.
cite: La Prensa (Panama), 24 July 2026

n: Samoan national jailed for bribing a New Zealand immigration contact
rank: staff contact, Immigration New Zealand office in Samoa
d: In April 2025 a Samoan national was jailed for four years at Auckland District Court and ordered to pay $4,000 to the victims, after pleading guilty to twelve representative charges: five of aiding and abetting breach of visa conditions, six of exploitation of unlawful migrants and one of corruption of a public official. RNZ reported that the person had bribed a contact at Immigration New Zealand's office in Samoa for favourable treatment on visa applications for those workers. The person's name was suppressed on an interim basis. A U4 Anti-Corruption Helpdesk overview of corruption in Pacific island countries records the case as bribing a government official and helping others to break visa rules.
inside: A broker paid a contact inside New Zealand's immigration office in Samoa, so visa applications got favourable treatment and workers entered illegally.
cite: RNZ, 7 April 2025; U4 Anti-Corruption Helpdesk, Caitlin Maslen, Overview of corruption and anti-corruption in Pacific island countries, 3 February 2026

n: Trader accused of bribing Venezuela's state food buyer CASA
rank: officials of the state food company CASA and PDVSA joint ventures
d: US prosecutors alleged that Naman Wakil, a Syrian national and lawful permanent resident living in Miami, paid bribes from 2010 until at least September 2017 to officials of CASA, the Venezuelan state-owned and state-controlled company that buys food for the country, and to officials of joint ventures between the state oil company PDVSA and foreign firms in the Orinoco belt. The Justice Department said the bribes won at least $250 million in contracts to sell food to CASA and to do business with the PDVSA joint ventures, including at least $30 million in highly inflated contracts to supply those joint ventures. He was arrested in Miami on 3 August 2021 and charged with conspiring to violate and with violating the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and with money laundering. The allegations were never tested at trial.
inside: Prosecutors said the businessman's bribes reached buyers inside Venezuela's state food company and the PDVSA joint ventures that then awarded him contracts.
undone: Wakil died in his sleep on 24 July 2023, before his trial; his lawyer Howard Srebnick confirmed the death to Voice of America. On 8 January 2025 US District Judge Melissa Damian entered final judgment in a civil forfeiture action, forfeiting over $20 million in proceeds of the scheme to the United States. The 2025 forfeiture release describes Wakil as a Venezuelan national; the 2021 charging release called him a Syrian national.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 4 August 2021; US Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida, 10 January 2025; Voice of America, 25 July 2023

n: Yara's bribe to the son of Libya's de facto oil minister
who: Yara's former chief legal officer, acting on behalf of Yara International ASA
rank: de facto oil minister and chair of the National Oil Corporation
d: Yara International ASA is an Oslo-listed fertiliser group, 36.2 per cent state-held. Norway's Supreme Court ruled on 15 September 2017 in the case of Yara's former chief legal officer, convicted of gross corruption. Norwegian courts found that in about early 2007 he agreed, on Yara's behalf, to pay at least US$4.5 million to the son of the man who was Libya's de facto oil minister and chair of the board of the state-owned National Oil Corporation, with which Yara was negotiating. About US$1.5 million was paid into a Swiss account on 29 March 2007, prepaid through the subsidiary Nitrochem and recovered through excess invoicing between October 2007 and May 2008. It coincided with a heads of agreement signed in April 2007. The Court of Appeal raised his sentence to seven years and the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal, upholding it.
inside: Yara's money went to the family of the man running Libya's state oil company, to win his goodwill in the deal he was deciding.
cite: Supreme Court of Norway, HR-2017-1776-A, judgment of 15 September 2017 (official English translation)

n: Church papers describe Hagiuda as its hotline into the LDP
rank: LDP acting secretary-general; former Minister of Economy, Trade and Industry
d: Tansa reported on a 3,212-page set of internal Unification Church reports to the church's World Headquarters that it calls the TM Report. The TM Report casts Koichi Hagiuda, now LDP acting secretary-general and a former trade and education minister, as a hotline between the church and the Liberal Democratic Party. Eiji Tokuno, then president of the Unification Church in Japan, wrote in a September 2020 report that he had met Prime Minister Shinzo Abe five times, that Hagiuda arranged the meetings and was usually present, and that one, on 2 July 2019, was to ask the church to support the candidate Tsuneo Kitamura in the upper house election. Hagiuda's secretary said on 31 January 2026 that he has no direct connection to the church as an organisation, but may have met people from an affiliated group called the Family.
cite: Tansa, The True Mother Files, 27 January 2026 (Japanese original 1 February 2026)
inside: Church records cast a senior LDP figure as its standing channel into the party leadership, arranging meetings with the prime minister and asking the church for votes.
undone: The church's public relations department called the documents extremely lacking in credibility on 16 January 2026.

n: Businessman's money reached Benin's presidential guard commander
rank: head of the presidential guard
d: Olivier Boko, a businessman and long-time friend of President Patrice Talon, and Oswald Homeky, a former sports minister, were each sentenced to 20 years in prison by the financial crimes and terrorism court in Cotonou for conspiracy against state security and corruption of a public official. Special prosecutor Elonm Mario Metonou said Homeky was arrested in September 2024 while handing six bags of money to the head of the presidential guard, Colonel Djimon Dieudonne Tevoedjre, who told the court Homeky had contacted him to foment a coup. The three men, including Boko's brother-in-law Rock Nieri, convicted in absentia, were ordered to pay 60 billion CFA francs ($95m) in damages. Defence lawyers walked out before the verdict; opposition figures accuse Talon of using the courts against opponents.
inside: A businessman's money was handed to the officer commanding the president's own guard, prosecutors say, to turn that unit against the president.
cite: Africanews, 31 January 2025

n: Russian officers placed over CAR's presidential security and police
rank: security adviser to the president; Russian control of the police security partnership
d: A report by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, published in February 2025, says Vitali Perfilev operated in 2023 as a security adviser to President Faustin-Archange Touadera, dealing with security and military matters. It says that from December 2023 Denis Pavlov, presented as a diplomat but in reality an officer of Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service, took control of the security partnership with the General Directorate of the Central African National Police; Canada sanctioned Pavlov in February 2024. The report says Wagner took control of the Ndassima gold mine through Midas Ressources, sanctioned by the United States in June 2023, and quotes a Ministry of Mines official saying operations there have been totally opaque, with ministry staff unable to carry out environmental checks.
inside: Russian intelligence and Wagner men sit inside the presidency's security circle and run the police partnership, so Central African security decisions follow Moscow.
cite: Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, February 2025

n: Wahda Bank issued $55m in uncovered cheques under a Haftar financier's sway
org_label: Ahmed Gadalla and the Haftar family network
rank: board seat and reported tacit control of a commercial bank
