d: The Sentry's April 2026 report says that in May 2024 Benghazi's Wahda Bank issued certified cheques worth about 300 million dinars, roughly $55m, across 151 accounts without sufficient funds, in what it calls zero-clearing incidents. Multiple sources described the Dubai-based financier Ahmed Gadalla as holding tacit control of the bank at the time, and the report says he sits on its board. In a separate episode in April 2024, Benghazi's National Commercial Bank approved letters of credit worth 400 million dinars, about $88m, without matching dinar deposits, with paperwork involving a Turkish company linked to Fauzi al-Muqla, whose wife is the sister of Saddam Haftar's wife; sources say Gadalla already held sway over that bank. Wahda Bank, the National Commercial Bank and Muqla did not respond.
inside: A faction's financier sat on bank boards and reportedly controlled them, so banks created money and credit for people close to the Haftars.
cite: The Sentry, 'Eastern Libya's Top Money Man', April 2026

n: Wagner officers took command of Central African army units
rank: command of army battalions and the presidential guard
d: The Sentry, an investigative group, reported in June 2023 that an internal note of November 2021 by the European Union's External Action Service said most deployed units of the Central African Armed Forces were operating under direct command or supervision by Wagner mercenaries. The report says Wagner has exclusive control over some units, including Territorial Infantry Battalion 7, made up of former self-defence group members and ex-militiamen incorporated in early 2021, and that military sources described battalions 8 to 12 as largely controlled by Wagner. All 11 military sources it spoke to said Russian commanders give operational orders outside the capital. A former executive said of Wagner's country head Vitalii Perfilev: 'Vitali has the full green light on the army, he does not ask Touadera for approval.'
inside: A Russian paramilitary company's officers command Central African army units, so the state's own soldiers take orders from a foreign private force.
cite: The Sentry, 'Architects of Terror', June 2023

n: Importer bribed a Vanuatu customs officer to let a container pass
rank: customs border officer
d: Zhiqiong Huang pleaded guilty in Vanuatu's Supreme Court to two counts of corruption and bribery of officials under section 73(2) of the Penal Code, and was convicted on both. She handed customs border officer Jules Sesai 1,500,000 vatu in cash on 25 July 2025 to help release container APZU 2114608, consigned to Santo Nambawan Stores, and offered a further 1,000,000 vatu that month to steer him against physically inspecting it. On 28 July she telephoned customs officer Pakoa Tom asking him to cancel the inspection. The inspection went ahead on 6 August 2025 and found undeclared cigarettes, with duty assessed at 143,820,550 vatu. She was sentenced on 24 March 2026 to 24 months on each count, twelve months immediate and twelve suspended, and fined 1,000,000 vatu.
inside: An importer paid a customs border officer to release and not inspect her container, so the checks that would have found undeclared goods were called off.
cite: Public Prosecutor v Zhiqiong Huang, Supreme Court of Vanuatu, 24 March 2026

n: Florida supplier's $532,000 bought Bolivia's Minister of Government
org_label: A Florida-based equipment supplier and its owners
rank: Minister of Government
d: Arturo Carlos Murillo Prijic was Bolivia's Minister of Government, the cabinet post in charge of the police and internal security. The US Justice Department says he received at least $532,000 in bribes from a Florida-based company in return for helping it secure a contract worth about $5.6 million in 2019 to supply tear gas and other non-lethal equipment to Bolivia's Ministry of Defense. He was charged in the Southern District of Florida on 7 December 2021, pleaded guilty on 20 October 2022 to conspiracy to commit money laundering with a Foreign Corrupt Practices Act violation as the underlying offence, and was sentenced to 70 months in prison. A related case charged Sergio Rodrigo Mendez Mendizabal, Luis Berkman, Bryan Berkman and Philip Lichtenfeld.
inside: A US supplier's payments put Bolivia's security minister on its side, and he helped it win a $5.6 million state order for tear gas.
cite: US Department of Justice, case page United States v. Arturo Carlos Murillo Prijic

n: SAP bribed Indonesian fisheries ministry and telecoms agency officials
rank: Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries and a state telecoms agency
d: SAP SE, the German business software company, admitted that between about 2015 and 2018 it paid bribes through agents to Indonesian officials to gain advantages on contracts with Indonesian government bodies. The US Justice Department named two of those bodies: Kementerian Kelautan dan Perikanan, the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries, and Balai Penyedia dan Pengelola Pembiayaan Telekomunikasi dan Informatika, a state-owned and state-controlled telecommunications and information accessibility agency. SAP was charged in the Eastern District of Virginia with conspiring to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and entered a three-year deferred prosecution agreement announced on 10 January 2024, paying a criminal penalty of $118.8 million and administrative forfeiture of $103,396,765. The same resolution covered a separate scheme in South Africa.
inside: SAP's agents paid officials inside an Indonesian ministry and a state telecoms agency, which then bought the company's software.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 10 January 2024

n: UK brokers paid Ecuador's state insurers' chairman $2.8m for reinsurance
org_label: Tysers Insurance Brokers and H.W. Wood, UK reinsurance brokers
who: UK reinsurance brokers Tysers and H.W. Wood
rank: chairman of Seguros Sucre and Seguros Rocafuerte
d: Two British reinsurance brokers, Tysers Insurance Brokers Limited and H.W. Wood Limited, agreed on 20 November 2023 to three-year deferred prosecution agreements with the US Justice Department on charges of conspiring to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act. Between 2013 and 2017 they agreed, through employees and third-party agents, to pay about $2.8 million in bribes to the then chairman of two Ecuadorian state-owned insurers, Seguros Sucre S.A. and Seguros Rocafuerte S.A., and to three other Ecuadorian officials, in order to win and keep reinsurance business. Tysers paid a $36 million penalty and forfeited about $10.5 million; H.W. Wood paid $508,000 because it could not pay more. Juan Ribas Domenech, former chairman of both insurers, pleaded guilty on 16 September 2020.
inside: The brokers' money reached the chairman of two Ecuadorian state insurers, who then steered their reinsurance business to the two firms.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 20 November 2023

n: Gorrin accused of bribing officials for PDVSA currency contracts
rank: high-level officials deciding PDVSA currency contracts
d: A federal grand jury in the Southern District of Florida indicted Raul Gorrin Belisario, a Venezuelan television news network owner, on 23 October 2024 on one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering. US prosecutors allege that between 2014 and 2018 he and others paid bribes to high-level Venezuelan officials to obtain foreign currency exchange loan contracts with PDVSA, Venezuela's state-owned energy company, then moved the proceeds through the US financial system and foreign bank accounts using shell companies, buying real estate, yachts and other luxury items in Florida. The Justice Department called it a $1.2 billion laundering scheme and over $1 billion in ill-gotten gains. Gorrin remains a fugitive and the indictment is an allegation.
inside: Prosecutors say Gorrin's bribes bought senior officials' decisions inside Venezuela's state oil company, which handed his side lucrative currency contracts.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 23 October 2024

n: Balt paid a senior doctor at a French state hospital to buy its devices
org_label: Balt SAS, a French medical device maker
rank: a physician in a senior role at a state-owned public hospital
d: The US Justice Department announced in March 2026 that it had resolved a foreign bribery investigation into Balt SAS, a medical device company headquartered in France, over payments to a physician who served in a senior role at a state-owned public hospital in France. Because Balt reported itself, cooperated and made changes, the department declined to prosecute and Balt agreed to pay about $1.2 million in disgorgement; France's Parquet National Financier reached a coordinated resolution. A grand jury in California indicted David Ferrera, an executive at Balt's US subsidiary, and Marc Tilman, a consultant, on 4 March 2026. Prosecutors allege that from about 2017 into 2023 they paid the official so the hospital would buy Balt's embolization coils.
inside: The company's payments reached a senior doctor inside a French public hospital, who then had the hospital buy that company's medical devices.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, March 2026

n: Berlin senator convicted after an agency staged her wedding free
rank: Senator for Health, Care and Gender Equality
d: Berlin's regional court convicted Dilek Kalayci, the city state's former Senator for Health, Care and Gender Equality, of passive bribery on 4 April 2025. In 2019 she had a Berlin advertising agency plan and organise her wedding, including invitation cards, worth 6,240 euro, and the agency never invoiced her. The court found that her department then hired the same agency for a campaign to recruit nursing staff, a contract she personally influenced, and that the agency received about 250,000 euro from the department in 2020 and 2021. Kalayci received a suspended sentence of one year and six months and had 6,240 euro confiscated; the agency head, Thomas E., received one year and three months, suspended. The verdict can still be appealed.
inside: An advertising agency's free work on a minister's wedding bought her influence, and her department then awarded that agency a 250,000 euro campaign contract.
cite: Landgericht Berlin I press release 13/2025, 4 April 2025

n: Deere's Thai unit bribed the air force and two road departments
org_label: Deere & Company (John Deere) and Wirtgen Thailand
rank: officials of the Royal Thai Air Force, Department of Highways and Department of Rural Roads
d: The US Securities and Exchange Commission announced on 10 September 2024 that Deere & Company, the Illinois maker of agricultural and heavy equipment, would pay nearly $10 million to settle charges under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act. From at least late 2017 through 2020 its wholly owned subsidiary Wirtgen Thailand bribed Thai government officials at the Royal Thai Air Force, the Department of Highways and the Department of Rural Roads to win multiple government contracts, and also paid employees of a private company. The bribes took the form of cash, international travel and visits to massage parlours, and were booked as legitimate expenses. The subsidiary made about $4.3 million in profits. Deere paid about $5.4 million in disgorgement and interest and a $4.5 million penalty without admitting or denying the findings.
inside: The firm's Thai subsidiary paid officials inside the air force and two roads departments, which then awarded it their government equipment contracts.
cite: US Securities and Exchange Commission press release 2024-124, 10 September 2024

n: Philips China's staff shaped hospital tenders with hospital directors
rank: public hospital directors handling procurement
d: The Securities and Exchange Commission announced on 11 May 2023 that Koninklijke Philips N.V., the Amsterdam-based medical technology group, would pay more than $62 million over sales of medical diagnostic equipment in China. The SEC found that a district sales manager at Philips China gave funds to a hospital director to help with procurement, and that employees discussed tailoring technical specifications with hospital directors so that only Philips China and two other manufacturers would qualify. Employees, distributors or sub-dealers also prepared extra bids using rival manufacturers' products to make public tenders look legitimate and meet the minimum number of bids required under Chinese law. Philips paid $15 million in civil penalties and more than $47 million in disgorgement and interest without admitting or denying the findings.
inside: The company's staff worked with directors inside Chinese public hospitals to write tender specifications only its own equipment could meet.
cite: US Securities and Exchange Commission press release 2023-92, 11 May 2023

n: A $2.7m bribe scheme reached Ukraine's Supreme Court chief
rank: Chairman of the Supreme Court and Grand Chamber judges
inside: A businessman's money reached the head of Ukraine's highest court, which then overturned the ruling and returned the plant's shares to Ferrexpo AG, restoring his control.
d: Kostiantyn Zhevaho, a businessman, sought to bribe Grand Chamber judges of Ukraine's Supreme Court to overturn a 2022 appellate ruling that took Poltava Mining and Processing Plant shares from Ferrexpo AG and so from his control. The bribe totalled $2.7m, of which Chief Justice Vsevolod Kniaziev knew of $2m; it passed through the lawyer Oleh Horetskyi, who also entered a plea agreement, and the notary Kyrylo Horburov. Kniaziev had a hearing delayed while the money was collected, and after the Grand Chamber overturned the ruling on 19 April 2023 he joined another judge's dissent to conceal his interest. He was detained on 15 May 2023 after $1.34m was delivered to his flat.
undone: On 8 June 2026 the High Anti-Corruption Court approved a plea agreement and jailed Kniaziev for five years with confiscation of property and a three-year ban on judicial and law-enforcement posts, the term reduced below the statutory eight to twelve years because he cooperated and testified against other participants.
cite: Transparency International Ukraine, 'Unprecedented Case: Head of the Country's Highest Judicial Body Receives Custodial Sentence for Corruption'

n: Kremlin advisers worked inside Moldova's Socialist Party
rank: advisers to the president and senior Socialist Party figures
inside: Russian operatives advised Moldova's then governing party and its president's campaign and funded pro-Russian parties, pressing party members to take guidance from Moscow; Treasury says the effort failed.
d: On 26 October 2022 the US Treasury designated nine individuals and 12 entities over Russian interference in Moldova, saying its efforts to influence Moldova's 2020 and 2021 elections had failed. It said Olga Grak and Leonid Gonin had advised former president Igor Dodon during the 2020 campaign, and that Yuriy Gudilin and Grak pressured members of the Party of Socialists to accept Russian guidance by promising to weigh in favourably with the Russian Presidential Administration. Treasury said Russia-based businessman Igor Chayka worked with Kremlin press secretary Dmitry Peskov on plans to undermine President Maia Sandu, and that the Russian government used Chayka's companies as a front to funnel money to collaborating political parties, some of it earmarked for bribes and electoral fraud. Gudilin, a political technologist and former FSB officer, was designated for coordinating election influence in 2020 and 2021.
cite: US Department of the Treasury press release, 26 October 2022

n: Onyshchenko's gas firms got tax deferrals from Ukraine's tax chief Nasirov
rank: Head of the State Fiscal Service
inside: A member of parliament's gas companies got the head of Ukraine's tax service to grant unlawful tax deferrals, and examinations found the state may have lost over two billion hryvnia.
d: NABU alleges that the then member of parliament Oleksandr Onyshchenko organised a scheme in which gas from the state producer Ukrgazvydobuvannya was sold through fictitious exchanges to companies he controlled at below-market prices and resold at market rates. Prosecutors say Roman Nasirov, head of the State Fiscal Service, Ukraine's tax and customs authority, issued unlawful instructions granting three of those companies instalment repayment of tax debt and subsoil use fees; regional directorate heads submitted false reports claiming the companies faced bankruptcy risks when no such risks existed. Two forensic economic expert examinations confirmed that his actions between May 2015 and March 2016 may have caused the state to forfeit over UAH 2 billion in revenue.
undone: Nasirov was convicted of abuse of office in late 2025, the case file giving both 31 October and 4 November, and sentenced to six years' imprisonment, a UAH 17,000 fine and a three-year ban on holding certain posts. His co-defendant Volodymyr Novikov, a former State Fiscal Service department head, was acquitted, and a forgery charge against Nasirov was dropped in September 2023 on the statute of limitations, leaving the conviction resting on abuse of office alone. On 2 April 2026 the appeal chamber partly granted the defence appeals and amended the verdict, removing references to Liudmyla Solotva's testimony and recalculating pre-trial detention, but left the sentence unchanged; the Supreme Court opened cassation proceedings on 9 April 2026, so the conviction is not final. A separate charge of taking a UAH 722 million bribe, joined with proceedings against his father-in-law Oleksandr Hlimbovskyi, is pending.
cite: Transparency International Ukraine, HACC case file 52017000000000218

n: Developer leased 18 hectares near Kyiv after cadastre data changed
rank: officials of the regional State Land Cadastre
inside: A developer allegedly had officials inside the state land register change the records, so the register itself delivered a large lease to his company.
d: NABU's report on its investigations records a case, exposed in September 2025, in which officials of the regional State Land Cadastre allegedly manipulated cadastral data so that a company controlled by a developer obtained a lease over 18 hectares of land near Kyiv, where the Stolychnyi market is located. The report values the land at UAH 160 million. The cadastre is the official register of land plots, their boundaries and permitted uses, so altering its entries can change what may be built on a site and who may use it. The plots were then split among nine strawmen who resold them to companies linked to the same developer, and were seized at the request of SAPO. The developer, the former MP said to be involved and the cadastre officials are all unnamed in the report, and the allegations are unproven.
cite: National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine, investigations section of its report for the second half of 2025

n: Cyprus report: Rybolovlev's lawyers hired a judge's wife; officials helped
rank: president of Nicosia District Court; deputy attorney general; Limassol CID head
d: Cyprus's Anti-Corruption Authority report, titled 'Mafia State' after Makarios Drousiotis's book, covers seven cases. Days after interim orders of 9 and 14 October 2013 favoured clients of Andreas Neocleous & Co, among them Dmitry Rybolovlev, the firm hired the wife of Nicosia District Court president Charis Solomidou on 1 November 2013. His 9 July 2014 recusal ruling named her employer as A. Neocleous Trust Company Ltd; investigators concluded, on the balance of probabilities, that he intentionally concealed it. Former deputy attorney general Rikkos Erotokritou did not forward the police file on the complaint against Elena Rybolovleva to the attorney general, and ensured it went back to police quickly, contrary to standard procedure. Former Limassol CID head Ioannis Sotiriadis allegedly delayed returning her passport. It recommends criminal investigation of Solomidou for bribery and Rybolovlev for influence peddling, and finds no guilt.
inside: Cyprus's Anti-Corruption Authority found a Russian businessman's law firm put a judge's wife on its payroll and reached prosecutors and police, so decisions went the firm's clients' way.
cite: Politis (en.politis.com.cy), Michalis Hadjistylianou, 17 June 2026

n: Mauritius drugs inquiry tied a minister and a deputy speaker to traffickers
rank: Minister for Gender Equality; Deputy Speaker
d: The Commission of Inquiry on Drug Trafficking in Mauritius, chaired by the former judge Paul Lam Shang Leen, opened on 15 November 2015, questioned more than 300 people, released its findings in late July 2018 and called for further in-depth investigations. Roubina Jadoo-Jaunbocus, a lawyer and Minister for Gender Equality, resigned after the commission accused her of meeting jailed traffickers who were not her clients, and alleged she was complicit in money laundering and had arranged a money transfer to a trafficker. Deputy Speaker Sanjeev Teeluckdharry, like her a member of the governing MSM, resigned after being implicated. The prime minister said both disputed the findings and would take legal action, and that Jadoo-Jaunbocus could return to her post if she cleared her name in court.
inside: An official inquiry alleged a serving minister had met jailed traffickers who were not her clients and had helped move money for one; she and the deputy speaker both resigned.
undone: On 13 August 2024 the Privy Council allowed an appeal by Coomaravel Pyaneandee, a lawyer criticised in the same report (Pyaneandee v Lam Shang Leen [2024] UKPC 27), declaring that passages about him on pages 232-233 breached fairness and natural justice because he was never told the gist of the case against him, and ordering that they be disregarded and a link to the judgment be added to the published report. Whether any court challenge, prosecution or reinstatement followed for Jadoo-Jaunbocus or Teeluckdharry could not be confirmed.
cite: Africanews, 28 July 2018

n: San-Pedro's criminal police chief convicted in a cocaine network
rank: commissaire of the criminal police, San-Pedro
inside: A trafficking ring had the officer who ran criminal investigations in the port city on its side, so the police force meant to stop the cocaine was part of it.
d: Karamoko Dosso, a former commissaire of the criminal police in the Ivorian port city of San-Pedro, was among nineteen people convicted of drug trafficking and criminal association by the pole penal economique after a record seizure of more than two tonnes of cocaine in Abidjan and San-Pedro in April 2022. Thirteen appealed. The Abidjan appeal court confirmed ten-year sentences for five of them, including Miguel Devesa, a former Spanish police officer described as the network's organiser, and reduced five sentences to five years, Dosso's among them and that of Cesar Ouattara, a former regional elected official from San Pedro. Three defendants were acquitted, among them a cook, Bartolo Priolo, and four companies, including Italia Service, were acquitted of tax fraud; Italia Service's director, Maurizio Coco, said he had served 37 months in custody before the acquittal.
undone: Devesa's lawyer, Me Zakaria Toure, called the sentence harsh and announced an appeal to the Court of Cassation, so the sentences are not final.
cite: Fraternite Matin via AllAfrica, 29 July 2025, on the Abidjan appeal court ruling of 28 July 2025 (the article itself gives no year)

n: Brunei's major crimes chief took a Malaysian contractor's pickup truck
org_label: Liew Say Koo (Say Koo (Liew) construction and L & E Contractor)
rank: head of the Major Crimes Investigation Unit, Royal Brunei Police Force
inside: A barred Malaysian contractor got the head of the police major crimes unit to press immigration to let him back in, in exchange for a vehicle.
d: Superintendent Hj Khairur Rijal Hj Abu Salim, former head of the Royal Brunei Police Force's Major Crimes Investigation Unit, was convicted of corruption and abuse of power at the Magistrate's Court in Bandar Seri Begawan in a judgment delivered on 31 January 2019. The court found he corruptly accepted a Toyota Hilux from Liew Say Koo, a Malaysian contractor, in exchange for helping him re-enter Brunei after he had been barred following a two-year prison sentence for a 2007 conviction for killing his wife. Of 36 re-entry requests sent to immigration between 2011 and 2013, 14 went while the officer was abroad on training. He said he had borrowed the vehicle over three years as an unmarked surveillance car and that Liew was a police informant; the magistrate found it was modified to stand out and Liew's informant role exaggerated.
undone: Sentencing of Khairur Rijal was deferred, the court taking two weeks from the verdict to consider it; this source does not record the sentence imposed and no later source for it could be found. Liew Say Koo was sentenced to 18 months for abetting.
cite: The Scoop (Brunei), 1 February 2019

n: Airline's $35,000 bribe to four Kyiv Court of Appeal judges
rank: four judges of the Kyiv Court of Appeal
inside: Prosecutors say four appeal judges received $35,000 from an airline's representative to release two aircraft held as evidence, so the court's decision served the company rather than the case.
d: Ukraine's anti-corruption bureau NABU and the specialised prosecutors SAPO allege that four judges of the Kyiv Court of Appeal received $35,000, offered by Tetiana Polishchuk, a representative of Aircompany Constanta PrJSC, to cancel the seizure of two An-74TK-100 aircraft held as evidence in a case about obstructing the armed forces. The seizure of one aircraft was lifted in November 2023, and the judges, Viacheslav Dziubin, Ihor Palenyk, Viktor Hlynianyi and Yurii Slyva, were detained on 29 November 2023; searches reportedly found $10,000 with Dziubin, $25,000 with Palenyk and $8,300 each with Slyva and Hlynianyi. The High Council of Justice removed them from judging and later dismissed all four. SAPO referred the case to court on 20 September 2024; the register shows proceedings continuing through May 2026 with no verdict. The allegations are unproven.
cite: Transparency International Ukraine, HACC case No. 991/10365/24 (proceeding No. 52023000000000547)

n: Businessman's $20m in bribes to Armenia's finance minister
rank: former Minister of Finance
inside: A businessman allegedly paid Armenia's finance minister more than $20m, and in return his company is said to have been given favourable tax treatment.
d: On 8 July 2024 the US Department of Justice announced a settled civil forfeiture action over a Holmby Hills mansion in Los Angeles bought in 2011 by a trust benefiting the sons of Gagik Khachatryan, then Armenia's most senior official for taxes and customs and later finance minister. The sons called the money loans; the United States alleges the loans, repeatedly extended without repayment, were covers for bribe payments. Gibson Dunn's FCPA review names the payer as the businessman Sedrak Arustamyan, said to have paid more than $20m in exchange for favourable tax treatment for his company. The United States will sell the property, keep 85% of the net proceeds and pass the rest to the sons. The alleged payments are the subject of pending criminal prosecutions in Armenia.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 8 July 2024; Gibson Dunn, '2024 Year-End FCPA Update'

n: Company founder convicted of bribing a Kazakh state enterprise branch head (ruling not final)
who: a private company bidding on boiler-house work
rank: head of a branch of a state-owned enterprise
inside: A company's owner paid an official running part of a state enterprise to get a favourable state review, but the scheme was stopped before the review was given.
d: A court in Astana convicted three people over a bribe offered to secure a favourable state review for a project to reconstruct 21 boiler houses. According to Orda.kz, the founder of a private company offered 73.5 million tenge in total, and a middleman passed 12.2 million tenge of it to a government official who headed a branch of a state-owned enterprise. The offer was made in the autumn of 2024 and law enforcement exposed the scheme before the deal was completed. All three defendants pleaded not guilty and asked for acquittal: the businessman was given eight years, the official eleven years and the intermediary eighteen months. The report, published on 9 July 2025, says the ruling had not yet come into legal effect, and no appeal outcome is recorded.
cite: Orda.kz, 9 July 2025

n: A network of 200 firms was shielded inside Ukraine's State Tax Service
org_label: a money-laundering hub operating 200 controlled firms
who: operators of a network of 200 controlled firms
rank: the former head of the State Tax Service and the deputy head of the Poltava Regional Tax Office
inside: Operators of a network of 200 paper companies were allegedly shielded by the former head of the national tax service, so the service ran no audits.
d: NABU's report for the second half of 2025 records a case about a money-laundering hub with billion-hryvnia turnovers, whose members operated a network of 200 controlled firms that mass-produced fictitious tax invoices so other businesses could cut their tax. The report says the operation was shielded by the former head of Ukraine's State Tax Service and the deputy head of the Poltava Regional Tax Office, who helped the hub's companies obtain favourable rulings and guaranteed that no tax audits or control measures would be conducted. It puts the forged sales at UAH 15 billion between 2020 and 2023, 'scheme-based' VAT at more than UAH 2.3 billion, and the tax revenue shortfall at UAH 147 million. The officials are not named and no payment to them is stated. The allegations are unproven.
cite: National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine, report for the second half of 2025, investigations section (the page's own footer and archive URL instead say 2026)

n: Cyprus law firm bribed the deputy attorney general; he was jailed, the firm fined
rank: Deputy Attorney General of Cyprus
d: In February 2017 the Assize Court found Rikkos Erotokritou, Cyprus's former deputy attorney general, guilty of bribery, abuse of power, corruption and conspiracy, and sentenced him to three and a half years for bribery and eighteen months for abuse of power. The Andreas Neocleous law firm LLC, then one of the island's largest, was convicted of bribery, conspiracy and corruption and fined 70,000 euros; the founder's son, Panayiotis Neocleous, received two and a half years, and Andreas Kyprizoglou, a partner in Erotokritou's own firm, eighteen months suspended for conspiracy to defraud. The prosecution argued that efforts to ensure a raid on the Providencia trust went unpunished showed a conspiracy between Erotokritou and Panayiotis Neocleous over Erotokritou's application to have his loan written off. The investigation began after attorney general Costas Clerides ordered a probe in 2015.
inside: A large law firm bribed the state's second-ranking prosecutor; prosecutors said he worked to keep a raid on the Providencia trust from being punished.
undone: The Supreme Court heard the appeals in December 2017 and was to rule separately on whether Erotokritou held constitutional immunity from prosecution, which could have collapsed the case; neither source records the outcome. President Anastasiades pardoned Panayiotis Neocleous in 2018.
cite: Financial Mirror, 15 December 2017; OCCRP

n: Monaco's top judge charged over a 136 million euro award to developer Caroli
rank: President of the Supreme Court of Monaco
d: Didier Linotte, who led Monaco's Supreme Court for eleven years until Prince Albert II dismissed him in August 2023, was charged in June 2025 with corruption, influence peddling and illegal taking of interest in an organised group. The charges concern a 2020 Supreme Court ruling, which Linotte sat on, ordering the Monegasque state to pay the developer Caroli nearly 136 million euros plus interest after Monaco cancelled the Esplanade des Pecheurs development. He was held in police custody for 48 hours, then released under judicial supervision and barred from leaving Monaco. The case stems from the anonymous 'Dossiers du Rocher' allegations published in 2021. Linotte denies wrongdoing and plans to challenge the charges; his lawyer Pascal-Pierre Garbarini called the claims a 'fairy tale' and noted that five of seven judges approved the ruling.
undone: Linotte's lawyer has filed motions with Monaco's court of appeal and a complaint to the European Court of Human Rights.
inside: Prosecutors say a property developer reached the head of Monaco's highest court, whose ruling then ordered the state to pay the developer 136 million euros.
cite: Monaco Life, 27 June 2025

n: Cocaine traffickers paid a Salvadoran prisons aide for favours, prosecutors say
rank: aide in the General Directorate of the Bureau of Prisons
d: Wilfredo Hernandez Molina, for about a decade an aide to El Salvador's vice minister of security Osiris Luna Meza and an assistant in the prisons directorate on $2,500 a month, was arrested on 30 May 2023 on bribery accusations and illicit association, with a prisons fish-farming instructor, Mario Chavarria Ayala. Prosecutors say they sold early release, improved living conditions, unauthorised family visits and entry to Mariona prison, where visits had been suspended since 2020, a transfer to the private Baptist Hospital for detained trafficker Marvin Antonio Ramos (the report gives both 18 March 2022 and 18-20 January 2022), and funeral leave for Angel Alexander Bonilla Carranza. In a wiretapped call Walter Ramos said a visit would cost $5,000 to $6,000. He had no formal authority over prison staff; the report attributes his influence to his closeness to Luna.
inside: Prosecutors say traffickers' payments reached an aide inside the prisons directorate, so the prison service granted them visits, hospital stays and leave other inmates could not get.
undone: El Faro reported the case in July 2023 and no later outcome is recorded; the same report notes that two earlier investigations into Hernandez Molina never went to trial.
cite: El Faro, July 2023

n: Business associates' gifts bought favour from Brunei's work pass chief
org_label: business associates, including Daiecharm Deco Sdn Bhd and BT Employment Agency
who: business associates, including Daiecharm Deco and BT Employment Agency
rank: Senior Chief Immigration Officer, Head of the Work Pass Section
inside: Business owners who needed work passes gave gifts to the officer heading the work pass section, and the court found he showed them preferential treatment.
d: Seruji bin Haji Setia, a former Senior Chief Immigration Officer and head of Brunei's Work Pass Section, the unit that approves permits for foreign workers, was found guilty on 12 October 2024 on five counts of graft under Section 165 of the Penal Code, Chapter 22, and sentenced on 28 October 2024 to three years in prison, effective from his remand date of 12 October. The court heard he was given carpets, sofa cushion covers, car seat covers and BND100 in cash on multiple occasions by business associates, including the managing director of Daiecharm Deco Sdn Bhd and the manager of BT Employment Agency, and found that he had shown preferential treatment to certain business owners, which it called a severe abuse of authority. The report does not say which payer gave what, nor which work-pass decisions were involved.
cite: Borneo Bulletin, 28 October 2024

n: Hotels and an events firm bought favour inside Brunei's tourism ministry
org_label: two hotels and an event management company
who: two hotels and an event management company
rank: Deputy Permanent Secretary for Tourism, Ministry of Primary Resources and Tourism
inside: Two hotels let the tourism ministry's deputy secretary defer his bills and the court found he favoured them in return; an events firm paid into his own account.
d: Wardi Mohd Ali, Deputy Permanent Secretary for Tourism at Brunei's Ministry of Primary Resources and Tourism until his suspension in February 2021, was found guilty on 23 July 2025 of misconduct in public office under section 12B of the Prevention of Corruption Act, Chapter 131. The Magistrate's Court found he had been or remained favourably disposed to two hotels in return for being allowed not to pay immediately on checking out between 18 June 2020 and 23 February 2021, accumulating unpaid invoices of about BND5,000, and that he let an event management company organising an event with the ministry under his purview transfer funds into his personal account three times. Prosecution witnesses said his position was a factor in the hotels' decisions to defer payment. The court called his actions deliberate, without reasonable justification and a serious abuse of power.
undone: The court revoked his bail. Sentencing submissions were set for 30 July 2025 and the sentence is not recorded in this source; the offence carries a fine of up to BND30,000 and/or up to seven years in prison.
cite: Borneo Bulletin via The Star (Malaysia), 24 July 2025

n: Suppliers' alleged $500,000 bribe for a Ukrainian deputy minister
org_label: EPG LLC and Techno Train LLC
rank: Deputy Minister of Communities and Territories Development (the case file also calls him former Acting Minister)
inside: Prosecutors say contractors' money was meant for a deputy minister so that ministry procurement went to predetermined suppliers at inflated prices.
d: Prosecutors allege a bribe of USD 500,000 intended for Vasyl Lozynskyi, a deputy minister in Ukraine's Ministry of Communities and Territories Development, whom the case file also calls former acting minister. USD 400,000 of it was brought from Lviv by Roman Kitner, who allegedly collected part of the bribe there from Ihor Politar; the source of the remaining USD 100,000 is not established. The money is tied to alleged kickbacks of 7 to 10% on 2022 heating-season equipment purchases: the Cabinet transferred UAH 1.68 billion, of which UAH 1.41 billion went to procurement by the state institute UkrNDIvodokanalproekt under direct contracts with predetermined suppliers at prices allegedly inflated by 25 to 30%. Co-defendants include Serhii Kryvyi of Techno Train LLC, who allegedly used his controlled companies, and his subordinate Mykhailo Lukashyk, who allegedly prepared the inflated bids.
undone: The case file says Lozynskyi was detained on 21 January 2023 while receiving a bribe, though its own narrative says NABU searched the intermediary and he was not able to receive the money. He was dismissed on 22 January 2023 and released on UAH 2.5 million bail on 21 July 2023. The trial opened at the High Anti-Corruption Court on 16 May 2024 and is still running; the only verdict on file is the approval, on 18 December 2024, of the plea agreement of Oleksandr Kroshko (also spelled Kroshka), former director of EPG LLC, who admitted giving a bribe. On 21 January 2026 the court severed and suspended the case of co-defendant Mykhailo Lukashyk, who was serving in the military. Lozynskyi is charged under Articles 368(4) and 369(4) of the Criminal Code.
cite: Transparency International Ukraine, HACC Decided case file, proceeding No. 52022000000000280 (HACC case No. 991/4139/24)

n: Russian bank and officials got inside Kyrgyzstan's Keremet Bank
who: Russian state bank PSB and Russian officials
rank: Keremet Bank management and ownership
inside: Russian officials and a sanctioned Russian state bank coordinated with officials inside a Kyrgyz bank, and the state sold control of it to a firm linked to a Russian oligarch.
d: On 15 January 2025 the US Treasury designated OJSC Keremet Bank of Kyrgyzstan under E.O. 14024, as amended by E.O. 14114, for conducting or facilitating significant transactions, or providing services, involving Russia's military-industrial base. Treasury said that since at least summer 2024 Keremet Bank officials have coordinated with Russian officials and the sanctioned Russian state bank Promsvyazbank on a sanctions evasion scheme under which Keremet would facilitate cross-border transfers on PSB's behalf; neither the Keremet nor the Russian officials are named. It said the Kyrgyz Ministry of Finance sold a controlling stake in the bank in 2024 to a firm strongly linked to a Russian oligarch with ties to the Russian government, intending to create a sanctions evasion hub. Treasury also said the US-designated Russian-Moldovan oligarch Ilan Shor was involved in discussions about the bank's role.
cite: US Department of the Treasury press release, 15 January 2025

n: Ukraine's court administration chief jailed over a company's Supreme Court case
who: Forvater Plus LLC, the company whose case was at issue
rank: Head of the State Judicial Administration of Ukraine
inside: An intermediary's payments reached the official running Ukraine's court administration over a company's Supreme Court case; the court then partly granted the company's appeal.
d: Oleksii Salnikov was acting head of Ukraine's State Judicial Administration, which runs the courts' finances and staffing, from September 2021, formally appointed in April 2022 and dismissed in December 2023. Investigators say the former businessman Oleksii Honchar, the prosecution's key witness, approached him about a case before the Supreme Court's Administrative Cassation Court in which Forvater Plus LLC challenged the geology service's inaction over its application for a special subsoil permit without auction. They say Salnikov told him on 27 February 2023 that the case could be settled for $5,000, and that on 5 March 2023, under law enforcement supervision, Honchar handed him $5,000 at a restaurant and, after Salnikov said a further sum was needed, another $2,500 shortly afterwards. The court partially granted the company's appeal in December 2023.
undone: On 6 August 2025 the High Anti-Corruption Court convicted Salnikov of abuse of influence under Article 369-2(2), having acquitted him of fraud under Article 190(2) and reclassified the incitement-to-bribery charge brought under Article 369(4), and sentenced him to three years in prison with a three-year ban on holding posts in state and local government bodies. The defence argued the case was a provocation and that the money was for a vehicle for the Armed Forces. The parties were expected to appeal to the HACC Appeals Chamber, and no appeal outcome is recorded, so the conviction is not final on this source.
cite: Transparency International Ukraine, HACC Decided analytics on the Salnikov verdict

n: Prosecutors say a supplier's 1.9m lari reached Georgia's defence minister and PM
who: a businessman supplying the military hospital
rank: Minister of Defence and former Prime Minister
inside: Prosecutors say a supplier's cash reached the defence minister and the prime minister, and that the ministry's classified bidding was rigged on the minister's orders.
d: Georgia's Prosecutor's Office charged Juansher Burchuladze, defence minister from 2021 to 2024, and his relative Vasil Mkheidze in September 2026 over the ministry's purchase of medical equipment for the Giorgi Abramishvili Military Hospital under classified procurement rules in late 2022. Prosecutors say Mkheidze demanded a 10% cash kickback on the contract value; the businessman hesitated and sought guarantees from higher authorities, and Burchuladze allegedly reached an understanding with then prime minister Irakli Garibashvili, who demanded his own cut and vouched for the chosen businessman. They say 1,900,000 lari was paid in instalments, Mkheidze keeping 400,000 and passing 1,500,000 to the minister, who kept 750,000 and passed 750,000 to Garibashvili. Burchuladze allegedly ordered his then deputy Giorgi Khaindrava and procurement chief Vladimer Ghudushauri to rig the bidding. Across three contracts GEL 18,484,960 was charged against a market value of GEL 11,499,705.
undone: Former prime minister Irakli Garibashvili has been charged in the same matter. Burchuladze is charged under Article 338 of the Criminal Code and Mkheidze under Articles 25 and 338, and both are already serving sentences in separate criminal convictions. Both have proposed guilty pleas: Burchuladze five years, three in prison and two suspended, with a GEL 1,000,000 fine; Mkheidze four years and two months, one year two months in prison and three years suspended, with a GEL 100,000 fine. The prosecution says both cooperated and will seek summary judgment at the initial hearing, and puts the damage to the state at GEL 6,985,255.
cite: First Channel Georgia (1TV), 8 September 2026, reporting the Prosecutor's Office

n: El Salvador's ex-attorney general jailed for faking a case to favour businessman Rais
who: Enrique Rais, the businessman prosecutors say was favoured
rank: Attorney General of El Salvador
d: On 22 August 2025 the Tribunal Tercero de Sentencia in San Salvador sentenced Luis Antonio Martinez Gonzalez, El Salvador's former attorney general, to ten years in prison: five for procedural fraud and five for failing to investigate. Prosecutors had asked for fifteen. The prosecution service accused Martinez of favouring the businessman Enrique Rais by using false evidence in cases involving the lawyer Mario Calderon, who represents the querella, and Claudia Herrera, a victim in the proceedings. Also convicted were Julio Adalberto Arriaza Gonzalez, former director of the Fiscalia's office for the defence of society's interests, who got five years for fraude procesal after his charge was changed from actos arbitrarios, and Francisco Grimaldi, who got six for fraude procesal under concurso real, having been tried for two separate cases. Asked about the ruling, Martinez said 'no comment'.
undone: The sentence is first-instance and no appeal outcome has been checked. The report records no verdict for Enrique Rais, whose role is the prosecution service's accusation rather than an adjudicated finding. The verdict came nine years to the day after Martinez and Rais were first arrested in the case in 2016.
inside: Prosecutors say the attorney general used the national prosecution service's own cases, built on false evidence, to favour the businessman Enrique Rais.
cite: Diario El Mundo, 22 August 2025

n: Document fixers allegedly bribed staff inside Malta's identity agency for ID cards
rank: officials of Identita, Malta's identity agency
d: Identita, formerly Identity Malta, is the Maltese state agency that issues identity cards and residence permits. Former member of parliament Jason Azzopardi alleges that officials there helped non-EU nationals obtain valid ID cards and residence permits on false documents, putting the number at 18,000; sources privy to Identita's workings reportedly dispute that the number is as high as that, and said the agency had long been aware of fake identity cards. He names the car dealer Bernard Attard as a broker who allegedly asked non-EU nationals for bribes running into thousands of euros, and alleges that Marija Spiteri, who worked at the agency's Brexit desk, used to input the foreign nationals' details into the system and let them into the office through a side door after hours so their photographs could be taken.
undone: Azzopardi filed a 59-page sworn statement requesting a magisterial inquiry, and the request was granted. A magistrate ordered police to investigate two Identita officials over possible perjury after their testimony contradicted each other. Police charged three Egyptian nationals with fraudulently obtaining ID cards; two pleaded guilty and were jailed six months each, while the third, Moustafa Ata Moussa Darwish, did not plead guilty and his case is ongoing. Identita said it had flagged the case against some individuals through internal checks and passed it to the police, and when asked whether internal reviews had flagged wrongdoing by its own officials said only that it is cooperating with the police. It is unclear whether police are investigating any current or former employees.
inside: A former MP alleges that a ring selling papers paid staff inside the state identity agency, so it issued real ID cards and residence permits to the ring's clients.
cite: MaltaToday, report by Kurt Sansone (the page carries no publication date)

n: Indian technicians captured traffic inside Mauritius Telecom's cable station
rank: Baie-Jacotet submarine cable landing station
d: Mauritius Telecom is the island's main, state-controlled telecommunications company, and the Baie-Jacotet landing station in the south of the island is where the SAFE submarine cable carrying Mauritius's internet traffic comes ashore. A report by Girish Guddoy, Chief Technical Officer, revealed by Teleplus (Defimedia.info), says that on 15 April, with no year given on the page, a team of Indian technicians connected their tools to several internet links on the SAFE cable at the station and carried out a two-minute data capture on each, and that 'once the data capture was done, the tools used were removed'. The report says Guddoy informed the chief executive, Sherry Singh, immediately afterwards; it was submitted before Guddoy's own resignation and handed to Mauritius Telecom's acting chief executive. The article calls the sniffing alleged.
inside: Indian technicians were allegedly inside the state telecoms company's cable landing station, connecting tools to the country's main internet links and capturing data from each.
cite: Le Mauricien, 22 July 2022

n: Brunei narcotics officer fed his drug supplier the bureau's secrets
rank: Assistant Narcotics Officer II, Narcotics Control Bureau
inside: A drug supplier had a source inside the drug squad, an officer who passed on confidential bureau information seven times, seeking cut-price drugs and to shield him from enforcement.
d: Muhammad Ali Iskandar bin Mustapha, an Assistant Narcotics Officer II in Brunei's Narcotics Control Bureau, disclosed confidential bureau information to his drug supplier on seven occasions between June and August 2023, seeking drugs at a reduced price and to shield the supplier from enforcement action. The supplier is not named and the report does not say whether money changed hands. He denied the charge on 19 March, then pleaded guilty on 26 December, and was sentenced on 7 January 2025 to two years and eight months in prison under section 12(B) of the Prevention of Corruption Act (Chapter 131), with two further offences taken into consideration. The sentence was reported the following day.
cite: Borneo Bulletin, 8 January 2025

n: Eight airport police charged over a trafficking network at Dakar's airport
org_label: a Senegalese and Sierra Leonean trafficking network
rank: police officers serving at Blaise Diagne International Airport
inside: A trafficking network allegedly paid officers on duty at the international airport 20,000 CFA francs a head to board travellers, making border policing part of the route.
d: Eight police officers serving at Blaise Diagne International Airport, outside Dakar, were arrested and charged on 4 December 2020 with complicity in migrant trafficking, document fraud and corruption, in a case the Brigade de Recherches de Faidherbe built against a network described as run by Senegalese and Sierra Leonean nationals and said to have operated between Diamniadio and the Boune road. According to hosts and facilitators in the case, the officers helped travellers board flights for 20,000 CFA francs a person. Police found 87 women from Sierra Leone and Guinea who were to be taken from the airport and employed, reportedly as prostitutes or domestic workers, in the Gulf countries, and who said they had each paid more than 7,000,000 leones. The officers were granted provisional release pending a hearing on the merits; the drivers were placed in pretrial detention.
undone: The status is as of December 2020: the officers were charged and granted provisional release pending a hearing on the merits, and no outcome of that hearing is recorded six years on. Ndarinfo is relaying a report by Liberation; the Liberation original was not retrieved.
cite: Ndarinfo, 7 December 2020, citing Liberation

n: Coal buyers and hauliers paid officials inside Mongolia's state coal firm
org_label: coal buyers, transport companies and Chinese intermediaries
rank: Erdenes Tavan Tolgoi management, customs and border officials
inside: Coal buyers and haulage firms allegedly worked with managers inside Mongolia's state coal company and with customs officers, so state coal was sold and shipped on terms that suited them.
d: State coal company Erdenes Tavan Tolgoi was alleged to have undervalued coal against its market price in offtake contracts with Bodi International LLC, while transport companies were alleged to have overvalued their services. Bottlenecks at the railway, customs and the border militia gave officials opportunities to demand bribes. Thousands protested in Sukhbaatar Square in front of parliament in December 2022, and a former chief executive of the company, Gankhuyag Battulga, was charged with money laundering along with 11 others.
undone: By October 2025 the Prosecutor's Office reported 124 cases investigated against 156 individuals and three legal entities, 108 individuals charged, 88 found guilty, five sentenced to between two years and five years and nine months in prison, 80 fined, and 63 barred from public office for two to seven years, with 20 trials pending and 40 investigations continuing. Those figures are aggregate for the coal case and are not tied to the named company officials or firms above.
cite: U4 Anti-Corruption Resource Centre, 'The coal theft case', U4 Brief 2024:4, 27 February 2024; The Star (Go Go Mongolia/ANN), 7 October 2025, thestar.com.my/aseanplus/aseanplus-news/2025/10/07/five-people-sentenced-to-prison-and-80-fined-for-coal-crimes-in-mongolia

n: FSB paid a Ukrainian cabinet secretariat department head for secret files
rank: head of a department of the Cabinet of Ministers Secretariat
inside: Russia's security service recruited and paid a department head inside the office that serves Ukraine's government, so secret files from his own desk went to Moscow.
d: Ukraine's SSU reported on 21 June 2022 the detention of a department head in the Cabinet of Ministers Secretariat and a directorate head at the Chamber of Commerce and Industry. The SSU said the FSB recruited the first man in 2012 during a trip to Russia and tasked him with collecting secret material, printed or photographed onto a flash drive, including the state of Ukraine's defences, the arrangement of the state border, and the personal data of law enforcement officers. The chamber official was his liaison, meetings arranged through a closed Telegram channel, and sent the material to Russia through encrypted channels. The FSB reportedly paid $2,000 to $15,000 per task at meetings in temporarily occupied Crimea or abroad, where the chamber official usually collected the money, paying the cabinet official his share in Kyiv.
undone: Both men were declared suspects of treason under Article 111 of the Criminal Code, which carries 12 to 15 years, and were remanded in custody. The cited report is from June 2022 and carries no trial result; the current stage is unverified.
cite: Hromadske, 21 June 2022, reporting the Security Service of Ukraine

n: Food firm's $55,000 bribe freed its invoices inside Kharkiv's tax office
rank: head of a department of the Main Directorate of the State Tax Service in the Kharkiv region
inside: A company's money was offered to a department head inside the regional tax office so that the commission would take the firm off a risk list and unblock its trading.
d: On 18 January 2024 Ocean Foods LLC was placed on the tax service's list of taxpayers meeting risk criteria, blocking its tax invoices and nearly halting its business. A company representative asked Olena Zubko for help; she had no authority and brought in Vitalii Hovorukha, who offered $55,000, to be shared among those involved, to an acquaintance heading a department of the Main Directorate of the State Tax Service in Kharkiv region, so the commission would delist the company. Searches followed on 14 February and property was seized on 12 March. Both signed plea agreements with the specialised anti-corruption prosecutor on 12 August 2024, the trial opened on 19 August, and both were convicted of aiding and abetting bribery on 21 August - the case page also gives 22 August - receiving one-year and two-year probationary terms with assigned duties.
cite: Transparency International Ukraine, HACC case file 52024000000000324

n: Fenech paid Malta's police anti-money-laundering chief, prosecutors say
rank: head of the police anti-money-laundering unit
d: Ray Aquilina, former head of the Maltese police's anti-money-laundering unit, was committed to trial in February 2025 with businessman Yorgen Fenech. Aquilina faces corruption, perjury, leaking official secrets and money laundering; Fenech complicity in corrupting a public officer and money laundering. Aquilina was arrested in 2021 in a probe into officials who had potentially leaked sensitive information about the Daphne Caruana Galizia murder investigation to suspects, including Melvin Theuma. Investigators examined a planned sale of a flat in Birzebbuga to Aquilina, which Fenech was suspected of facilitating while about to be investigated over his ownership of the offshore company 17 Black; his parents were to appear as buyers and would later donate the property to him. Magistrate Rachel Montebello ruled they must stand trial; Fenech, Aquilina and the notary Mario Bugeja, also charged with money laundering, all pleaded not guilty.
inside: Prosecutors say a businessman under investigation got the police officer heading the money-laundering unit onto his side, so police work served him instead of the inquiry.
undone: The cited report covers the February 2025 committal ruling only; no trial date or verdict has been confirmed since.
cite: The Malta Independent, 12 February 2025

n: UK charges Peter Virdee with bribing Antigua's tourism and energy minister
rank: Minister of Tourism, Economic Development, Investment and Energy
d: Britain's National Crime Agency charged Peter Virdee, 50, also known as Hardip Singh, with bribing a foreign public official, named in the charge as Asot Michael, a Member of Parliament and Government Minister of Tourism, Economic Development, Investment and Energy for Antigua and Barbuda. Virdee's company PV Energy Ltd was charged with failing to prevent bribery over the same conduct, which the agency says took place between January 2015 and July 2017 and was intended to benefit PV Energy. Virdee appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court on 23 May 2024 and was bailed to appear at Southwark Crown Court on 20 June 2024. The agency described the investigation as multi-million pound, gave no bribe figure, and hedged only that it is alleged.
inside: A British energy company is accused of paying Antigua's energy minister, so the minister's decisions on power projects would serve the company.
undone: Virdee and PV Energy pleaded not guilty in a London court, reported on 9 July 2025; no trial outcome has been reported.
cite: National Crime Agency press release, 23 May 2024 (via wired-gov.net republication; the NCA newsroom original could not be opened); Global Investigations Review, 9 July 2025

n: PdVSA and FMLN mayors co-owned Alba Petroleos; its boss became vice-minister
rank: deputy foreign minister; 18 municipal mayors
d: Alba Petroleos was set up in El Salvador in 2006 as a joint public-private venture: Venezuela's state oil company PdVSA held 60 per cent and eighteen FMLN mayors 40 per cent, financed by Venezuelan loans to the mayors between 2010 and 2015. InSight Crime calls Jose Luis Merino, an FMLN political commission member, the primary middleman between the FMLN and the Venezuelan government and Alba's public face, with his brother Sigfredo the listed founder while Merino controlled it behind the scenes. In late October 2016 President Salvador Sanchez Ceren had Foreign Minister Hugo Martinez create an ad-hoc post for Merino, which became a vice ministry of foreign affairs.
inside: A foreign state oil company owned a Salvadoran firm jointly with serving mayors, and its chief go-between was then made a deputy foreign minister.
undone: In June 2017 fourteen members of the US Congress from both parties asked the US Treasury to investigate Merino under the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Designation Act. Responding to earlier accusations by Senator Marco Rubio in 2016, the FMLN condemned what it called defamatory and baseless claims against one of its best leaders; the article reports no response from Merino to the 2017 letter.
cite: InSight Crime investigation, 2018 (updated 2025)

n: Brunei immigration officer paid to wave travellers out of the country
rank: immigration officer
inside: An outsider paid an immigration officer to break the rules she enforced, so border control worked for whoever paid rather than the state.
d: Hajah Nurul Huda, also known as Hajah Rusiati binti Abdullah, a former Brunei immigration officer, pleaded guilty to four charges under Section 6(a) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, Chapter 131, and was sentenced to two years in prison, two charges running consecutively and two concurrently. She took BND500 in bribes, in cash and by bank transfer, from an Indonesian national between October 2023 and July 2024, bypassing immigration rules so foreign nationals could leave Brunei without the required re-entry permits. Malaysian Immigration at the Miri ICQ found discrepancies in a foreign national's travel records and a person concealed in a vehicle, and referred the case to Brunei's Anti-Corruption Bureau. Her defence cited her early plea, cooperation and the small sum; the judge said corruption, however small the amount, is contagious and cannot be taken lightly.
cite: Borneo Bulletin (Fadley Faisal), 'Ex-immigration officer jailed for corruption', April 2025; the page carries no printed date beyond a site header of 15 April 2025 and says the sentence was passed the previous day

n: Kyiv judge Chaus took bribe money to fix a criminal verdict
who: a defendant seeking a suspended sentence
rank: judge of the Dniprovskyi District Court of Kyiv
inside: Money from outside the court reached a judge so that a defendant before him would be given a suspended sentence instead of prison.
d: Mykola Chaus was a judge of the Dniprovskyi District Court in Kyiv. Transparency International Ukraine records that an investigation opened in August 2016 after NABU caught him accepting a bribe, and that he was convicted in 2023 of soliciting a bribe of $100,000; its account gives the sum caught in 2016 as $150,000 and does not reconcile the two figures. The benefit was a suspended sentence for a pensioner accused of trading diphenhydramine. The case was referred to court in November 2021. He was sentenced to ten years in prison with full confiscation of property, reduced on appeal in 2025 to eight and a half years, and the case is under cassation review. The record does not say who handed over the money.
cite: Transparency International Ukraine, 'Real prison terms for real crimes: which high-level officials have been convicted'

n: Money allegedly aimed at prosecutors and judges to close a NABU case
org_label: a suspect in a NABU case
rank: a prosecutor of the Prosecutor General's Office, with SAPO officials and HACC judges named as targets
inside: A man under investigation allegedly paid a prosecutor and lawyers to buy decisions from the prosecutors and judges handling his own case, turning the anti-corruption system against itself.
d: NABU's report on its investigations records a case in which a prosecutor of the Prosecutor General's Office, together with two lawyers said to have acted as intermediaries, allegedly took money from a suspect in a NABU case to have that case closed, through bribes said to be intended for officials of the Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office and judges of the High Anti-Corruption Court. The report says the sum demanded rose from $2 million to $3.5 million and that $200,000 was received, between February and September 2025, and that the scheme was exposed in October 2025. SAPO supervises corruption prosecutions and the High Anti-Corruption Court tries them, so these are the bodies meant to be beyond reach. Those involved are not named and the allegations are unproven.
cite: National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine, investigations section of its semi-annual report

n: Waste firm Helector bribed Cypriot mayors and planning officials
rank: mayor of Larnaca; municipal financial controller; town planning engineers
d: Helector, a waste management company that ran the landfills at Marathounda in Paphos and Koshi in Larnaca, was convicted in February 2020 of bribing Cypriot public officials. The case involved 83 charges of bribery, corruption, conspiracy and money laundering: the company overcharged municipalities by reporting higher waste volumes, and officials took bribes to look the other way. Convicted with it were Andreas Louroudjiatis, the former mayor of Larnaca, who received five years in prison; Demetris Patsalides, financial controller of Paphos municipality; and town planning engineers Michalis Pantis and Giorgos Koullapis. Helector was fined 201,000 euros. On 20 July 2022 the Supreme Court rejected all the appeals and convicted a further town planning engineer, Antonis Kourouzides, whom the lower court had acquitted.
inside: A waste contractor paid the municipal and planning officials who were supposed to check its invoices, so the councils kept paying it for waste it had not handled.
cite: Cyprus Mail, 20 July 2022

n: Brunei logistics firm's manager had a customs inspector bribed
rank: customs inspection officer, Royal Customs and Excise Department
inside: A freight company reached into the customs service that inspects its cargo by having its own staff bribe the inspecting officer.
d: Chin Chee Vun, 55, then general manager of the freight company Sivli Logistics Sdn Bhd, was convicted of instigating a subordinate to bribe a customs inspection officer in Brunei's Royal Customs and Excise Department, part of the Ministry of Finance and Economy, in October 2021. A Senior Magistrate's Court had acquitted him; the Public Prosecutor appealed, and the High Court in Bandar Seri Begawan reversed the acquittal and sentenced him to 24 months in prison, reported in September 2024. The report does not state the amount involved or what the company gained, and records no response from him.
cite: The Star (Malaysia), 25 September 2024, on the Brunei High Court ruling

n: Glencore bribed officials of Cameroon's state oil and refining firms
rank: officials of Société Nationale des Hydrocarbures (SNH) and Société Nationale de Raffinage (SNR, also known as Sonara)
d: Glencore, a commodity trader, paid bribes to officials of Société Nationale des Hydrocarbures and Société Nationale de Raffinage, Cameroon's state oil and refining companies, for favourable treatment in the allocation and sale of crude and the purchase of oil products. The English court's sentencing remarks put the Cameroon bribes at EUR 10,532,712 between 1 March 2012 and 1 March 2015: EUR 4,187,820 disguised as service fees under an agent's contract, and EUR 6,344,892 in cash drawn from Glencore's Swiss cash desk. Glencore's UK arm pleaded guilty at a London court in June 2022 to seven counts, five of them bribery counts, and was fined £182,935,392 in total, of which £56,881,245 was for the Cameroon count. The judge said: “I am making no findings of any kind against any specific individual”; individuals remained under Serious Fraud Office investigation, uncharged.
cite: Sentencing remarks, R v Glencore Energy UK Ltd, judiciary.uk; UK Serious Fraud Office case page, updated 1 May 2026
inside: A trading company's cash reached officials inside Cameroon's state oil and refining companies, which then gave Glencore favourable terms on the country's crude.

n: Eswatini registrar gave an alleged South African crime boss an identity
rank: assistant regional civil registrar, Ministry of Home Affairs
d: Nonhlanhla Malambe, an assistant regional civil registrar in Eswatini's Ministry of Home Affairs, was found guilty of dishonesty and corruption by Eswatini's civil service commission over a scheme to give citizenship documents to Vusimuzi ‘Cat’ Matlala, a South African businessman described as an alleged underworld figure. On 12 February 2024 she registered a birth certificate for ‘Vusimuzi Dlamini’, entered as a replacement of an older version, which the commission said created a false impression that the registration was long-standing; an ID card followed on 20 February. The certificate falsely named Thembi Christinah Zulu as his mother. Interpol asked Eswatini to verify the ID number after Dlamini was arrested in South Africa; audits linked the account used to Malambe. The state alleges Matlala used it to pose as an Eswatini prince; he denied holding an Eswatini ID before South African MPs.
cite: TimesLIVE, 24 October 2026
inside: Eswatini's civil service commission found an assistant registrar guilty of corruption over a manufactured birth certificate and ID card for Vusimuzi ‘Cat’ Matlala, an alleged South African underworld figure.

n: Angola's central bank and sovereign fund moved $500m to a London firm
org_label: Jorge Gaudens Sebastião and a private foreign company headquartered in London
who: a private foreign company headquartered in London
rank: Governor and managing director of Banco Nacional de Angola; president of the Sovereign Fund
d: Angola's Supreme Court convicted four men in August 2020 over the irregular transfer of US$500 million from the central bank, Banco Nacional de Angola, to a private foreign company headquartered in London, said to be for a strategic investment fund for projects in Angola. José Filomeno dos Santos, president of the Sovereign Fund of Angola and a son of the former president, received five years in all for fraud and influence peddling. Valter Filipe, the former central bank governor, was convicted of continued embezzlement and fraud; the reports give no sentence for him. António Samalia Bule, its former managing director, got five years, and the businessman Jorge Gaudens Sebastião six. All were acquitted of money laundering.
inside: A private company headquartered in London received a US$500m transfer out of Angola's central bank; the Supreme Court convicted the bank's governor, its managing director and the sovereign fund's president.
undone: The defendants' extraordinary appeal of unconstitutionality suspended the ruling, and on 3 April 2024 the Constitutional Court declared the 2020 conviction unconstitutional, finding breaches of legality, the presumption of innocence, the adversarial principle and the rights of defence, chiefly the Supreme Court's refusal to admit a letter from former president José Eduardo dos Santos, and removed the fraud-by-defraudation count from the framework. The Supreme Court plenary reheard the record, including that written testimony, and on 9 July 2024 reinstated the convictions, holding that the former president's authorisation of the transfer did not exclude the defendants' responsibility; two judges dissented.
cite: Ver Angola (Lusa), 29 November 2021; Ver Angola, 4 April 2024; Ver Angola, 9 July 2024

n: US sanctions Liberia's presidential chief of staff over investors' bribes
org_label: investors and business owners dealing with the Liberian government
rank: Minister of State for Presidential Affairs and Chief of Staff to the President
d: On 15 August 2022 the US Treasury designated three senior Liberian officials under Executive Order 13818, which builds upon and implements the Global Magnitsky Act. One was Nathaniel McGill, Minister of State for Presidential Affairs and Chief of Staff to President George Weah. Treasury said McGill is credibly accused of taking bribes from potential investors, bribing business owners, taking kickbacks for steering contracts to companies in which he held an interest, and manipulating public procurement processes in order to award multi-million dollar contracts. It says he solicited bribes from government office seekers and regularly distributes thousands of dollars in undocumented cash to other government officials. Also designated were Solicitor General and Chief Prosecutor Sayma Syrenius Cephus and the National Port Authority's managing director Bill Twehway. The release records no response from any of them.
inside: Treasury says bribes from investors and business owners reached the chief of staff to Liberia's president, who it says steered and rigged state procurement.
undone: allAfrica reported on 9 December 2023 that McGill, by then senator-elect for Margibi County, had earlier been sanctioned by the United States. Whether the designation is still in force was not confirmed.
cite: US Department of the Treasury press release, 15 August 2022; allAfrica, 9 December 2023

n: Prosecutors say a borrower's 1.7m birr bribe reached a Commercial Bank of Ethiopia chief
org_label: an unnamed borrower of the Commercial Bank of Ethiopia
rank: Vice-President, CBE Noor, Commercial Bank of Ethiopia (described in the report as the former CBE Noor executive)
d: Federal prosecutors charged Nuri Hussein, vice president for CBE Noor, the Commercial Bank of Ethiopia's interest-free banking unit, with receiving 1.7 million birr in bribes, in cash and in kind, from a borrower in order to facilitate a loan; the report also calls him the former CBE Noor executive. They accuse him of abusing his official authority and of making the proceeds appear legitimate, and charge his sister-in-law, Rihana Workineh, with helping present the payments as lawful. The charges were put on 31 March 2026 before the Fourth Anti-Corruption Bench of the Federal High Court's Lideta Division, which ordered Nuri kept in custody after his lawyers asked for more time to file objections, and adjourned to the following week. He had earlier been granted bail, upheld by the Federal Supreme Court. No plea is recorded.
inside: Prosecutors say a borrower's money reached the executive who ran the state bank's interest-free arm, and that the loan the borrower wanted was then facilitated.
cite: Addis Fortune, hearing of 31 March 2026

n: Financier Mpinganjira tried to buy Malawi's election-case judges
rank: High Court judges sitting as the Constitutional Court
d: Thomson Mpinganjira, founder of FDH Financial Holdings Limited and one of the richest people in Malawi, faced six charges under the Corrupt Practices Act and was convicted on 10 September 2021 on two counts of offering an advantage to a public officer under Section 24(2), the officers being Justices Michael Atanazio Tembo and Healey Potani. AFP reported that he was recorded offering financial inducements to one of the judges sitting as a Constitutional Court in the challenge to Malawi's 2019 presidential election, the allegation being that he sought their support for the then president, Peter Mutharika; the court found widespread irregularities and ordered a fresh election. High Court Judge Dorothy DeGabrielle sentenced him to nine years on each count, concurrently.
inside: A financier's money was offered to the judges deciding a presidential election case, to swing the court's ruling to the sitting president.
undone: Then president Lazarus Chakwera pardoned him under Section 89(2) of the Constitution on 6 July 2025, as one of 37 inmates pardoned during the Independence celebrations, and his appeal to the Supreme Court of Appeal was withdrawn by a notice dated 15 September 2025.
cite: Nation (Malawi) on the withdrawal of the appeal; AFP via Nile Post, 6 October 2021

n: Smugglers paid Kosovo border police to wave contraband trucks through
rank: border police officers serving in the Leposavić area
d: Smugglers moving goods between Serbia and Kosovo used serving Kosovo border police to let their lorries through unchecked. In January 2019 the BIRN programme Justice in Kosovo broadcast footage filmed at two petrol stations and a retail store in Leposavić of officers taking bribes of up to €200 to pass contraband lorries; the prosecution alleged 20 to 150 euros per vehicle, shared with the officers on duty. In May 2020 the Special Prosecutor's Office charged 33 people, mostly Kosovo police, with offences including illegal firearms possession, but later dropped the bribery counts. On 27 October 2023 the Basic Court in Prishtina convicted 13 of the accused officers, the report giving the number of accused as both 19 and 20, imposing 23 years in total, terms from three years to 18 months, and two-year bans on public office after release.
undone: Of the rest, six were acquitted for lack of evidence, one had charges withdrawn, 11 accused were separated from the case and one defendant died; the bribery counts in the May 2020 indictment had already been dropped.
inside: A cross-border smuggling network had Kosovo's own border police on its side, so the state officers meant to search its lorries let them through instead.
cite: Prishtina Insight (BIRN Kosovo), 27 October 2023

n: Three Serbian interior ministry members convicted of aiding Šarić's group
rank: members of the Ministry of the Interior (MUP)
d: Three members of Serbia's Ministry of the Interior, which runs the police, were convicted of aiding the criminal group of Darko Šarić, the head of an international criminal organisation, of abuse of official position and of disclosure of confidential information. In April 2025 Šarić was sentenced to six years in prison for planning a murder and discrediting a cooperating witness, in proceedings brought against him and his associates. Radio Slobodna Evropa set the verdict alongside an earlier episode: in 2014 five heads of police administrations were removed after Šarić named one of them in court as a corrupt policeman, the state leadership citing their alleged involvement in politics and the media and alleged contacts with the drug dealer then on trial; the dismissed officers said it was a staged media campaign by criminals.
inside: A drug-trafficking organisation had interior ministry members passing it confidential information, and a court convicted three of them for helping it.
undone: The report, a June 2026 retrospective, does not name the three, give their posts or sentences, or say whether the April 2025 verdict is final or under appeal.
cite: Radio Slobodna Evropa (RFE/RL), 2 June 2026

n: Finnish border guard paid to hand police files to a convicted drug offender
org_label: Timo Erkki Sakari Tulokas, convicted separately in a large drug case
who: a convicted drug offender buying police data
rank: border guard (rajavartija, also called merivartija in the report) in a military post, Finnish Border Guard
d: On 30 August 2024 Helsinki District Court sentenced Jim Markku Koskenmäki, serving in a military post in the Finnish Border Guard since 1995, to two years and six months for breach of official secrecy, aggravated dereliction of duty, aggravated bribe-taking, an aggravated firearms offence and a drug use offence, and stripped him of his military rank. The court found that Timo Erkki Sakari Tulokas, who the previous year had received more than ten years in a separate large drug case, asked him to search official registers for secret material on serious and organised crime, including live investigations, and paid him at least €1,820, and that Koskenmäki's aim was to further organised criminal activity. The two agreed that he would report any investigative measures aimed at Tulokas or at people Tulokas named. Koskenmäki denied most charges and Tulokas all of his.
