inside: A man convicted in a large drug case paid a serving border guard for the police's own files on organised-crime investigations, including live ones.
undone: The 30 August 2024 judgment was not legally final and could be appealed to the court of appeal; Tulokas received eight months, for aggravated bribery and incitement to breach of official secrecy and to aggravated dereliction of duty. No appeal-court ruling was found.
cite: Yle, 30 August 2024

n: Carabinieri report far-right group's proselytism reaching serving Italian soldiers
rank: three serving Italian Army soldiers posted in or near Turin
d: Carabinieri investigators in Turin reported that serving Italian Army soldiers were increasingly often present at a far-right group's meeting place, which the paper frames as a hypothesised neo-fascist proselytism that would have reached armed-forces circles. The inquiry into “La Barriera – Avanguardia Torino” sent seventeen activists to a preliminary hearing on 11 March 2026 on charges of apologia di fascismo, the Italian offence of glorifying fascism, over Fascist-era rituals and slogans and racist and antisemitic remarks at its gatherings. Months of surveillance by the Carabinieri's ROS unit of the venue recorded soldiers described in the reports as holding extremist views. Three on active service in or near Turin were identified; one, the case papers say, is reported to have attended an operational meeting with two leaders and, in autumn 2024, to have taken part in some initiatives. None was investigated.
inside: Investigators report that serving army soldiers, described as holding extremist views, turned up ever more often at a neo-fascist movement's Turin meeting place; one took part in its activities.
cite: Il Fatto Quotidiano, 6 March 2026

n: Icelandic billionaire accused of paying a serving police officer to spy
org_label: Björgólfur Thor Björgólfsson and the security firm PPPSF
rank: traffic warden, Reykjavík Metropolitan Police
d: Lúðvík Kristinsson, a traffic warden with the Reykjavík Metropolitan Police, has been relieved of duty, and Iceland's state prosecutor is investigating evidence that he carried out paid private surveillance while on police duty between September and December 2012, logging about 60 hours of it; the firm logged about 850 hours over the three months. RÚV's investigative programme Kveikur reported that the billionaire Björgólfur Thor Björgólfsson allegedly financed the surveillance through PPPSF, a security firm founded by two former police officers, Jón Óttar Ólafsson and Guðmundur Haukur Gunnarsson, with the lawyer Birgir Már Ragnarsson alleged to have brokered it. Those watched were former Landsbanki shareholders behind a class action over the bank's 2008 collapse; Björgólfsson allegedly wanted to know whether the businessman Robert Wessman was behind it.
cite: Iceland Monitor, April 2025, reporting RÚV's Kveikur
inside: A billionaire litigant allegedly paid a serving Reykjavík police officer, through a private security firm, to watch his legal opponents in 2012 while the officer was on police duty.

n: US Treasury says Tagwirei's gifts to Zimbabwe's leaders won state contracts
rank: President and First Vice-President; senior government officials
d: On 5 August 2020 the US Treasury designated the Zimbabwean businessman Kudakwashe Regimond Tagwirei and Sakunda Holdings, where he is chief executive officer and a founding director, for being owned or controlled by him. Treasury said he has utilized his relationships with high level Zimbabwean officials to gain state contracts, and that he provided high priced items, such as expensive cars, to senior-level Zimbabwean government officials. A government audit prompted a 2019 parliamentary inquiry after about $3 billion disbursed under Command Agriculture, a state farm subsidy championed by President Emmerson Mnangagwa and largely financed by Sakunda, could not be accounted for. Designating him again on 4 March 2024, Treasury said Mnangagwa has benefited from his corrupt network and that he has provided high-value gifts to senior members of the government to gain access to resources.
inside: The US Treasury says a businessman's cars and high-value gifts to senior Zimbabwean officials won his company state contracts, and that the president benefited from his corrupt network.
cite: US Department of the Treasury press releases, 5 August 2020 (sm1082) and 4 March 2024 (jy2154, https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/jy2154)

n: Botswana's top civil servant jailed over a pension fund deal
rank: Permanent Secretary to the President
d: Carter Morupisi, Botswana's Permanent Secretary to the President, was found guilty of money laundering and corruption by the High Court in Gaborone, before Judge Mokwadi Gabanagae, on 16 November 2022. The South African businessman Tim Marsland, described as his alleged corruptor, is alleged to have given him a Toyota Land Cruiser worth about 700,000 rand in exchange for facilitating a 500 million pula transaction from the Botswana Public Officers Pension Fund to the asset manager Capital Management Botswana; the vehicle was forfeited to the state. On appeal, reported 7 December 2024, the Court of Appeal sentenced him to 18 months for money laundering and to five and seven years on the corruption counts, to run concurrently; a 130,000 pula fine imposed at trial was to be refunded if paid.
inside: An asset manager's principal is alleged to have given Botswana's top civil servant a Land Cruiser, and he facilitated the 500 million pula pension fund transaction that paid the firm.
undone: Marsland, who was fighting extradition from South Africa, allegedly shot and killed himself at his home in Kliprivier, Gauteng, on 10 April 2025; an inquest was opened.
cite: Botswana Daily News, 7 December 2024; The African Mirror, 8 December 2024 and on Marsland's death in 2025

n: Chinese firm's proprietors paid Gambia's fisheries chief to free detained vessels
rank: Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Fisheries
d: Dr Bamba Banja, permanent secretary at the Gambia's fisheries ministry, accepted 100,000 dalasi from a Chinese private company in September 2018 to free a vessel detained for illicit fishing. The High Court, before Judge B.A. Bakre, convicted him of economic crime, official corruption and a public officer receiving property to show favour. He was given a two-year mandatory jail term, a fine of one million dalasi for causing economic loss to the government or two further years in jail, 100,000 dalasi or one year, and 50,000 dalasi or six months. He denied the allegations in his defence. The Point, reporting the conviction of 8 March 2023, said the money came from the proprietors of Golden Lead Company Limited, who wanted their detained vessels freed.
inside: A Chinese company's payment reached the civil servant running Gambia's fisheries ministry, in exchange for freeing a vessel detained for illicit fishing.
undone: President Adama Barrow pardoned Banja and 36 others on 19 January 2024.
cite: The Standard (Gambia), 9 March 2023; The Point (Gambia), 9 March 2023 (https://thepoint.gm/africa/gambia/headlines/ex-ps-banja-jailed-fined-d1000000) and on the pardon (https://thepoint.gm/africa/gambia/headlines/barrow-pardons-ex-ps-banja-others)

n: Kenya's anti-counterfeit chair charged over payments from two companies
org_label: Hongda Automotive Limited and UNIPRO Limited
rank: board chair, Anti-Counterfeit Authority
d: On 17 November 2025 Kenya's Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions announced it had approved a bribery prosecution of Josephat Kabeabea, board chair of the Anti-Counterfeit Authority, which polices fake goods, under section 6(1)(a) read with section 18 of the Anti-Bribery Act No. 47 of 2023; the Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission had recommended charges on 14 November. The commission says that after visits to Hongda Automotive Limited's premises on 10 and 11 November, Kabeabea sought 5 million shillings from its proprietor, a Chinese national, to halt the investigation and avoid arrest; the demand was reportedly cut to 1 million, then 300,000, then 150,000 shillings, which he is alleged to have received, paid through a mobile number believed to belong to his personal driver. It alleges he earlier demanded 10 million shillings from UNIPRO Limited and received 8 million.
inside: Investigators say two companies' payments reached the chair of the agency that polices counterfeits, in exchange for dropping its investigations; the commission says the Hongda investigation is still open.
undone: He pleaded not guilty at the Milimani Anti-Corruption Court to receiving a bribe and to acquiring proceeds of crime, and was released on a 2 million shilling bond or 1 million shilling cash bail, with the case returning to court on 8 December 2025.
cite: Capital FM (Nairobi), 17 November 2025, via allAfrica

n: Freetown customs officers demanded a bribe to clear an exporter's container
org_label: Sigismond Tommy Mei, operations assistant at Bollore Logistics; container of exporter Juan Ruiz
who: a freight forwarder and a mineral exporter
rank: customs officers at Queen Elizabeth II Quay
d: Akmed Karim and Mary Banya, Sierra Leonean customs officers of the National Revenue Authority formerly stationed at Queen Elizabeth II Quay in Freetown, were convicted on two counts of soliciting and accepting an advantage under section 28(2) of the Anti-Corruption Act No. 12 of 2008. On 28 February 2019 they solicited 2.5 million old leones from Sigismond Tommy Mei, an operations assistant at Bollore Logistics, to clear a 40-foot container owned by Juan Ruiz, an American businessman. The High Court, before Justice Aiah Simeon Allieu, a Court of Appeal judge sitting as a High Court judge, convicted them on 18 December 2025 and sentenced each to three years in prison or a fine of 60,000 new leones. Both had pleaded not guilty. Premier Media reported that a third officer charged over Ruiz's boat was acquitted.
inside: A freight forwarder's payment reached two customs officers at Freetown's main quay, who had refused to release an American exporter's container until it was paid.
cite: Sierra Leone Anti-Corruption Commission press release ACC/PR/25/020, 23 December 2025; Premier Media (Sierra Leone), 19 December 2025, on the judgment of 18 December 2025

n: Illegal gambling ring paid Kosovo police economic-crime investigators
rank: investigators, Kosovo police directorate for economic crimes and corruption
d: Prosecutors allege an illegal gambling operation paid two investigators in the Kosovo police unit meant to investigate economic crime to leave it alone. Lavdim Osmani and Lutfi Menxhiqi were arrested in February 2020, Osmani while taking 1,300 euros in a sting. The June 2020 indictment alleged they agreed in November 2019, with the cooperating witness D.H., not to investigate illegal gambling, took 1,500 and then 3,000 euros from Driton Berisha, and 3,000 more in January 2020, and that Menxhiqi passed on planned inspections. In February 2022 the basic court in Pristina jailed them for six and a half and five and a half years and fined each 4,000 euros; the court of appeals annulled that judgement in May 2023 and ordered a retrial. Both pleaded not guilty at the retrial; in January 2025 Menxhiqi said he never took the money.
inside: Prosecutors say gambling operators bought the two police investigators assigned to economic crime, so the unit meant to shut them down protected them instead.
undone: At the retrial, reported on 30 April 2025, the Pristina court again convicted both, jailing Osmani for six years and Menxhiqi for five, fining each 4,000 euros and barring them from public office for five years; the verdict could be appealed within 30 days.
cite: Transparency International, Corruption cases with social impact in the Western Balkans and Turkey (case updated January 2025); Periskopi, 30 April 2025, on the retrial verdict

n: Police say Puls club's people paid Štip tax inspectors to hide inspections
org_label: owners of the Puls nightclub in Kočani
rank: tax controllers and inspectors, Public Revenue Office regional directorates
d: Police say the people behind the Puls club in Kočani paid tax officials to warn them of inspections; a fire there on 16 March 2025 killed 60 people. On 20 November 2025 the Kočani police announced eight arrests and charges against eleven, three detained earlier. Two tax controllers at the Regional Tax Inspectorate in the Štip directorate, D.P. and D.D., were reported for receiving a bribe under Article 357 after abusing their access to data on unannounced inspections to warn the club's responsible person in exchange for unlawful gain and gifts; that person, M.J., son of the club's actual owner, was reported for giving a bribe, and the owner, D.J., for forgery. Six more tax officials in Štip and Strumica were reported for abuse of office for enabling Puls and the MMMM Cafe to avoid inspections and skip proper fiscalization.
inside: Police say the club owner's son paid tax controllers inside the Public Revenue Office, so officials with access to inspection plans tipped the club off instead.
cite: Ministry of Interior, Republic of North Macedonia, press release, 20 November 2025; Euronews, 4 April 2025, on the fire

n: Montenegrin police and intelligence officers jailed with the Kavač clan
rank: a former intelligence officer and a police officer
d: Two Montenegrin security officials were convicted alongside the leader of the Kavač clan, the Kotor-based group originally allied with the Škaljari clan in smuggling South American cocaine into Europe. In a verdict OCCRP reported on 24 July 2026, a special panel of the Higher Court in Podgorica, using intercepted messages from the Sky app, handed the clan's fugitive leader Radoje Zvicer 40 years in absentia for aggravated murder and other charges, and sentenced ten co-defendants, a combined 148 years. Petar Lazović, a former intelligence officer, received 20 years and was also convicted of smuggling for financial gain, fined 100,000 euros and ordered to forfeit 32,000 euros; Ljubo Milović, a fugitive police officer, received 19 years, was fined 100,000 euros and ordered to forfeit 31,800 euros. OCCRP reported that the feud between the two clans has allegedly corrupted police and politicians.
inside: A cocaine-trafficking clan had a police officer and an intelligence officer among its co-defendants, and a court jailed both on drug and smuggling charges.
cite: OCCRP, 24 July 2026

n: Bitumen supplier paid Thimphu city officials to sign for undelivered barrels
rank: engineer and procurement officer, Thimphu Thromde
d: Bhutan's Anti-Corruption Commission found in 2019 that an engineer and a procurement officer at Thimphu Thromde, the capital's municipal administration, had allegedly colluded with Bhutan Bitumen Industries over short deliveries of bitumen emulsion. On an order of 75 barrels the company was asked to keep 25 back and to deposit Nu 75,000 into the officials' accounts; they verified and paid the bills for all 75, and the Commission found the deposit was made. The same pattern followed on two further orders. The two officials were charged with two counts of abuse of functions, three company officials with two counts of participating in an offence, and the money was to be restituted. The company also faces ten counts of active bribery of foreign public servants, over alleged payments of Nu 3 M to Sikkim officials, and three counts of tax evasion.
undone: The Commission forwarded the case to the Office of the Attorney General in October 2019. No prosecution, plea or verdict has been reported since, and a search found no later outcome, so the charges remain untested allegations.
cite: Bhutan Broadcasting Service, 16 October 2019
inside: A supplier allegedly put money into the bank accounts of the city government's own buyers, who then signed off and paid for bitumen the company had never delivered.

n: Treasury says Zimbabwe's president shields gold and diamond smugglers and takes bribes
org_label: unnamed gold and diamond smuggling networks (no payer named in the release)
who: unnamed gold and diamond smuggling networks (no payer named in the release)
rank: President of Zimbabwe
d: On 4 March 2024 the US Treasury designated 11 people and three companies in Zimbabwe under the Global Magnitsky order, the same day it ended its older Zimbabwe sanctions programme. Treasury said President Emmerson Mnangagwa gives gold and diamond smugglers a protective shield, directed officials to sell gold and diamonds in illicit markets, and takes bribes in exchange for his services; the release names no payer. He was designated both for corruption and as a leader or official of an entity whose members engaged in serious human rights abuse. The businessman Kudakwashe Tagwirei, designated in August 2020, reportedly gave high-value gifts to senior members of the government. Obey Chimuka, Fossil Agro and Fossil Contracting, designated in December 2022 under E.O. 13469, were re-designated under E.O. 13818: Chimuka for acting for Tagwirei, Fossil Contracting for being controlled by Chimuka.
inside: Treasury says Mnangagwa gives smugglers a protective shield and takes bribes for it, and has directed officials to sell gold and diamonds in illicit markets; the release names no payer.
cite: US Department of the Treasury press release, 4 March 2024

n: Businessman accused of offering Namcor managers N$2.5m over fuel stations
rank: managers, since described by the paper as former managers, of Namcor, the state petroleum corporation
d: Namcor is Namibia's state-owned National Petroleum Corporation. In July 2022 its trading arm, Namcor Petroleum Trading and Distribution, bought the rights to nine service stations at Namibian Defence Force bases from Enercon Namibia for N$53.2 million. The state alleges that Peter Elindi, then an Enercon shareholder, offered N$2.5 million that month to two Namcor managers, Cedric Willemse and Jennifer Hamukwaya, since described by the paper as former managers, to induce them to abuse their positions and facilitate the purchase. Elindi is also charged with fraud, prosecutors alleging he misled Namcor into believing he could sell stations encumbered to the Ministry of Defence and Veterans Affairs until 2031. Namcor sued Enercon in the High Court in April 2024, seeking to void the agreement and recover the money. Elindi, one of nine accused, denied the bribe allegation, calling the case a witch-hunt.
undone: The report covers a bail hearing. Elindi and his eight co-accused have not been tried: no plea, verdict or sentence is reported, and the page carries no date of its own.
inside: Prosecutors say a fuel company's shareholder offered two managers of Namibia's state oil firm N$2.5m so it would buy his nine filling stations.
cite: The Namibian, bail hearing report (no date on page)

n: Gold scheme paid a Kenyan senator $700,000, investigators report
who: Zandi, named in the report as handing over the cash
rank: Senator, later Speaker of the National Assembly
d: A September 2023 report by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, drawing on an account by a Kenyan gold transporter and broker and on what the report calls an apparent internal report by Kenyan security services that the researchers could not independently verify, concerns a non-existent 4.6-tonne gold consignment known as Zlivia, supposedly transported to Nairobi in February 2018. It says that in Dubai Moses Wetang'ula, then a senator, reportedly asked for US$2 million, claiming it was demanded by a senior Kenyan cabinet secretary to secure the consignment's release, and that in January 2019 Zandi handed over US$700,000 in cash to him and the businessman Zaheer Jhanda. Jhanda, contracted to handle the consignment's documentation, taxes and customs, said he was hired only for advisory services. Both men had previously denied wrongdoing; Wetang'ula called the affair a non-issue.
undone: Police gave notice of warrants in June 2020, but the researchers found no evidence of any detention. No charge, trial or verdict has been reported, and Wetang'ula was elected Speaker of the National Assembly in late 2022 and still held the post.
inside: A fake-gold scheme's cash reached a senator who, the report says, asked for US$2 million in Dubai to get the consignment released, citing a demand from a senior cabinet secretary.
cite: Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, 'All that glitters', September 2023

n: Addax paid $2.1m to a Nigerian state oil manager over drilling rights
rank: General Manager, Upstream Division, Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation
d: Paulinus Okoronkwo, a dual US-Nigerian citizen, was general manager of the upstream division of the Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC), the state oil company. In October 2015 Addax Petroleum, a Swiss-based Sinopec subsidiary, wired $2,105,263 into his Los Angeles law firm's client trust account, described as consultancy fees for a settlement with NNPC over Addax's drilling rights. The engagement letter bore a fake Lagos address, and prosecutors said the trust account created the false impression that the money belonged to a client; they said it was a bribe for his influence over more favourable terms. A jury convicted him in August 2025 of three counts of transactional money laundering and one each of tax evasion and obstruction of justice. He was sentenced to 87 months in prison, with $923,824 restitution to the Internal Revenue Service and $1,039,997 forfeited.
undone: The sentence was announced on 23 February 2026, and the State Bar of California suspended his law licence in January 2026. The release records no appeal and no charge against Addax.
inside: An oil company's $2.1m, routed through a law firm, reached the state oil manager handling its drilling-rights settlement, US prosecutors said.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Central District of California, press release, 23 February 2026

n: Trucking director accused of paying a Zambian provincial official K8,000
rank: Deputy Permanent Secretary for Copperbelt Province
d: Zambia's Anti-Corruption Commission said in a release dated 6 January 2025 that it had arrested Yusuuf Saiid Abdidahir, 45, a director of Gaban Trucking and Trading Limited, and charged him with one count of corrupt practices under the Anti-Corruption Act No. 3 of 2012, for allegedly offering 8,000 kwacha to the Deputy Permanent Secretary for Copperbelt Province, who is not named. The money was allegedly offered to influence the release of a truck and two trailers the Zambia National Service had impounded in Ndola over an attempt to smuggle 1,392 bags of mealie meal into the Democratic Republic of Congo. The truck was later handed to the Zambia Revenue Authority. The commission said the conduct took place between 1 November and 27 December 2024, and that Abdidahir had been released on bond and would appear in court.
undone: No court outcome has been reported. A search for developments after the January 2025 charge found no plea, trial, conviction or acquittal, so the charge remains untested.
inside: A haulier allegedly offered money to the unnamed deputy head of a provincial administration so that his smuggling-seized truck would be let go.
cite: Zambia Anti-Corruption Commission media release, 6 January 2025

n: Head of Moldova's Central Customs Bureau detained over payments to clear imports
org_label: unnamed payers (the source identifies no importers or companies)
who: unnamed payers (the source identifies no importers or companies)
rank: head of the Central Customs Bureau
d: On 21 May 2025 Moldova's National Anti-corruption Centre and prosecutors in Bălți announced that they had detained the head of the Central Customs Bureau and a customs broker in a case of passive corruption in aggravating circumstances. According to preliminary data of the investigation, the two, with other people whose identity the centre said could not be disclosed, allegedly received over 40,000 dollars in several instalments to facilitate the passage of goods across the customs border, including goods for the Transnistrian segment, and to omit detection of multiple legal violations. A close relative of the accused, alleged to have acted as an intermediary, was later detained for 72 hours, as was the head of the Căușeni internal customs post, and financial means of about 1.1 million lei were detected.
undone: The case was still under investigation by prosecutors in Bălți at the centre's June 2025 update. No indictment, trial or court decision has been reported, and no payer has been named.
inside: Investigators say unnamed payers, with the bureau's own head, allegedly bought the passage of imports across Moldova's customs border and the overlooking of breaches.
cite: National Anticorruption Centre, Republic of Moldova, press releases of 21 May 2025 and 25 June 2025 (the 21 May date appears in the companion release on the intermediary's arrest)

n: Spain's Supreme Court dissolved ANV as an instrument of ETA
rank: 337 council seats in the Basque Country and 93 in Navarre
d: On 17 September 2008 the Supreme Court's Sala 61 ruled unanimously, the court's president saying there were no dissenting opinions, to outlaw Acción Nacionalista Vasca (ANV) and wind it up, on suits by the Fiscalía and the Abogacía del Estado; the dissolution of its municipal groups follows from the ruling, with the details left to the execution phase. The same proceeding concerned the Partido Comunista de las Tierras Vascas (PCTV), which the government's final reports likewise called an instrument of ETA. The Abogacía del Estado argued ANV was a “mere instrument or tool of ETA-Batasuna”, and a pendrive seized from an alleged ETA member, Gorka Murillo, headed “Elecciones 2007. Pasos a dar en el ámbito jurídico”, reportedly showed Batasuna directing ANV's candidacy process and campaign for the 2007 municipal elections.
undone: The Constitutional Court dismissed ANV's amparo appeal against the Supreme Court judgment, dated 22 September 2008, in STC 31/2009 of 29 January 2009, leaving the party's dissolution final.
inside: Spain's courts found an armed separatist movement was running a party that held hundreds of council seats, putting its people inside local government.
cite: Legal Today (Europa Press), 17 September 2008; later outcome: Tribunal Constitucional, STC 31/2009, 29 January 2009

n: Crime bosses got Macedonian passports from interior ministry staff
org_label: Škaljari clan and other criminal organisations
who: Škaljari clan and other crime groups
rank: eleven staff of the interior ministry's administrative affairs department
d: In April 2021 the opposition party VMRO-DPMNE, citing a whistleblower, said ministry employees had issued documents to organised crime figures, among them Jovan Vukotić, head of Montenegro's Škaljari clan, who received a passport in December 2017 as “Georgi Andonov”; the party said about 200 of the false-identity documents, issued between December 2017 and January 2021, went to people in criminal organisations. Within a week prosecutors charged eleven people, ten with abuse of office and authority and one with instigation, officials of the ministry's administrative affairs department in Skopje; the case covered 215 passports, 214 to foreign nationals and one to a North Macedonian citizen. Seven admitted guilt, five at the first hearing on 5 May 2021 at the Basic Criminal Court in Skopje; the court imposed seven prison sentences of one to three years and four suspended sentences.
undone: Transparency International's page says the appellate court upheld the sentences but gives no date, and no later source confirming that outcome could be found; first-instance sentencing was reported in June 2021.
inside: Criminal organisations obtained real state passports under false names from officials inside the interior ministry, so the state itself concealed who they were.
cite: Transparency International, Corruption cases with social impact in the Western Balkans and Turkey, 'The Double Affair' (case updated August 2021)

n: Bhutan trading firm's bribe fixed an agriculture ministry tender
rank: Senior Livestock Production Officer, Ministry of Agriculture and Forests
d: Samten, chief executive of Sai Trading Partner, paid Nu 1 million to Tshewang Tashi while Tshewang was a Senior Livestock Production Officer at Bhutan's Ministry of Agriculture and Forests. According to the Anti-Corruption Commission's investigation in 2017 and 2018, the payment was to obtain privileged information and fix the tender for a modern hatchery project in Samrang, Samdrupjongkhar. Samten got technical specifications and drawings for hatchery equipment from a foreign company and passed them to Tshewang on a USB drive, and Tshewang then made sure the tender document matched those specifications. The Thimphu District Court sentenced both men to three years and six months in 2022. Tshewang said the money was repayment of a loan from Samten. Both appealed and sought bail.
cite: The Bhutanese, 25 August 2022
inside: A trading company's owner paid a ministry officer for inside information, and the ministry's tender was then written to match the equipment specifications his firm supplied.

n: Armed exile movement recruited serving Rwandan army soldiers
org_label: P5 Platform and the National Liberation Front (FLN)
rank: serving privates and corporals of the Rwanda Defence Force
d: Rwanda's Military High Court in March 2021 convicted Maj. (Rtd) Habib Mudathiru and about 30 others over an armed campaign against the government, among them serving soldiers of the Rwanda Defence Force. Mudathiru was found guilty of terror-related charges including joining a criminal group and conspiracy against an established government or the President; he admitted training fighters of the P5 Platform, which the report says had declared war on Rwanda's government, and got 25 years. Pte Muhire Dieudonné, an RDF soldier accused of desertion and of creating and recruiting for an armed group, also got 25 years, and Cpl Dusabimana Jean Bosco 18 months for covering up. Mudathiru denied forming the groups, saying he was ‘just a recruit like others’.
cite: KT Press, 25 March 2021; The New Times, 25 March 2021
inside: An armed exile movement that had declared war on Rwanda drew serving soldiers into its ranks, one of them accused of recruiting fighters from inside the army.

n: Hauliers allegedly paid customs officers at Moldova's Leușeni post
org_label: passenger and parcel carriers crossing from Romania
rank: officials of the Leușeni–Albița and Cahul–Oancea customs posts
d: Moldova's National Anti-corruption Centre says carriers crossing from Romania were paying the customs officers on two of the country's main border posts to skip their checks. On 28 January 2026 the centre, with prosecutors in Cahul, announced searches at the Leușeni–Albița and Cahul–Oancea posts and the detention for 72 hours of seven Customs Service officials in what it called a systemic corruption case. The suspects are alleged to have systematically demanded, and received, sums of up to €1,000 from passenger and parcel carriers so that vehicles were not put through customs control and goods entered Moldova without customs clearance. Several episodes of demanding and receiving money were documented during the investigation. The centre said the inquiry continues to identify others involved, and that those concerned are presumed innocent.
inside: Investigators say hauliers were paying the customs officers on Moldova's Romanian border, so the state's own checkpoints let their loads in uninspected.
cite: National Anticorruption Centre, Republic of Moldova, press release, 28 January 2026

n: Alexion paid doctors on Turkey's health ministry commissions
rank: health care providers sitting on Ministry of Health commissions
d: Alexion Pharmaceuticals agreed on 2 July 2020 to pay more than $21 million to settle US Securities and Exchange Commission charges over payments in several countries. The SEC's order says Alexion's Turkish subsidiary paid health care providers employed at state-owned healthcare institutions who sat on commissions in Turkey's Ministry of Health, the commissions that reviewed and approved patient applications for its drug Soliris. From 2012 to 2015 over $100,000 went to or at the request of providers on those commissions, and over $15,000 to one provider from 2012 to 2014; that provider was the decision maker for the reimbursement criteria for the blood disorder aHUS. The order puts the gain in Turkey at over $6.6 million. It names no city and no individual official.
cite: US Securities and Exchange Commission cease-and-desist order, Release No. 34-89214 (File No. 3-19852), 2 July 2020
inside: Alexion's payments reached doctors sitting on the Turkish health ministry commissions that approved prescriptions of its drug Soliris, and the order puts its gain in Turkey at over $6.6 million.

n: Alexion paid advisers to Russia's health ministry over its drug's budget
rank: chief non-staff specialist advisers to the Ministry of Health
d: Alexion Pharmaceuticals agreed on 2 July 2020 to pay more than $21 million to settle US Securities and Exchange Commission charges. The SEC's order says Alexion's Russian subsidiary paid health care providers employed at state-owned healthcare institutions, some of whom served in official roles at regional and federal level, to influence regional budget allocations and increase approved prescriptions of its drug Soliris. Payments exceeded $1 million from 2011 to 2015. Two of the providers were chief non-staff specialist advisers to the Ministry of Health; one was tasked with advising on including Soliris on a drug list, another with developing a list of rare diseases. In one region in 2013, patients requiring Soliris were allocated 52 per cent of the regional health budget. The order names no city.
cite: US Securities and Exchange Commission cease-and-desist order, Release No. 34-89214 (File No. 3-19852), 2 July 2020
inside: Alexion paid advisers to Russia's health ministry and officials in a region, and the budget allocated to its drug and the number of approved prescriptions rose.

n: Bailiffs' chamber chief accused of paying Hungary's justice state secretary
org_label: György Schadl and the Hungarian Chamber of Court Bailiffs
rank: State Secretary, Ministry of Justice; Ministry of Justice bailiff appointments
cite: bne IntelliNews, 20 February 2023; Index.hu report on the Budapest Metropolitan Court hearing, 17 March 2026
who: György Schadl, head of the bailiffs' chamber
d: György Schadl, president of the Hungarian Chamber of Court Bailiffs, is accused of paying Pál Völner, the state secretary at the Ministry of Justice who oversaw bailiffs, at least 83 million forint between May 2018 and July 2021. Bailiffs enforce debts and are appointed through the ministry. Prosecutors say Völner pushed for the appointment of bailiffs Schadl wanted and sought state support for one of his firms, and that Schadl took more than 924 million forint in kickbacks from bailiffs he helped appoint. Völner resigned in December 2021 and his immunity was lifted. Of 22 charged, ten admitted guilt and got suspended terms in May 2023, reduced on appeal. Schadl and Völner deny the charges; their trial opened in February 2023 and was still running in March 2026.
inside: The head of the bailiffs' chamber is accused of paying the justice ministry official who supervised bailiffs, and the ministry then appointed the bailiffs he wanted.

n: US says Belize's security minister was bribed over immigration papers
org_label: Payers for Belizean immigration documents (not named in the release)
who: Unnamed payers; separately the convicted fuel-fraud financier Lev Dermen
rank: Minister of National Security
d: On 15 November 2022 the US State Department designated John Saldivar, Belize's national security minister until November 2020, under section 7031(c) of its appropriations act for involvement in significant corruption. It said it had credible information that while in office he accepted bribes in exchange for improperly facilitating the acquisition of Belizean immigration documents, and that he misused a US-donated Coast Guard boat for personal gain. The release names no payer, and the bar covers his immediate family. Separately, at the February 2020 US trial of the fuel-fraud financier Lev Dermen, the cooperating witness Jacob Kingston testified that Dermen handed Saldivar US$25,000 in Miami; Dermen was sentenced to 40 years in April 2023. Saldivar says he is innocent, denies any part in immigration corruption and calls the Miami money campaign finance he spent on sports projects in his Belmopan constituency.
inside: The US State Department says Belize's national security minister took bribes to get Belizean immigration documents issued, though its release names nobody who paid.
cite: US Department of State designation, reported by Channel 5 Belize and Breaking Belize News, 15 November 2022; Breaking Belize News, 11 April 2023 (Kingston's trial testimony and Dermen's sentence); Jamaica Observer, 25 November 2022 (Saldivar's denial)

n: Spanish state arms exporter convicted of bribing Cameroonian officials over navy contracts
org_label: Defex S.A. and Aresa Marine S.L.
who: Defex S.A., the Spanish state's arms export company
rank: Cameroonian officials and authorities (not individually named in the judgment); one senior government official identified only by his wife's surgery
d: Defex S.A., the arms export company majority-owned by the Spanish state through SEPI, supplied Cameroon's government between 2005 and 2013 with patrol boats for maritime surveillance, spare parts, repair accessories and training, under project PRE174. On 28 February 2023 Spain's Audiencia Nacional found that Defex's commercial director Manuel I.S. and Oscar L.S. of the subcontractor Aresa Marine paid gifts and favours to Cameroonian officials, authorities and people close to them to win their goodwill and to obtain and keep the contracts running. The gifts included trips, hotel stays and cosmetic surgery for the wife of a senior Cameroonian government official, paid for by Defex as main contractor. Both men were sentenced to two years for corruption in international business transactions. Defex, by then in liquidation, was acquitted because the conduct ended before a 2015 reform made state-owned companies criminally liable. The court's release names no individual Cameroonian official and gives no sums.
inside: A Spanish state arms firm paid trips, hotel stays and surgery to Cameroonian officials, and Cameroon's government awarded and kept running its naval supply contracts.
undone: Spain's Supreme Court confirmed the acquittal of Defex on 24 September 2026 and set aside the fine imposed on the subcontractor, while upholding the two-year sentences on both men.
cite: Audiencia Nacional, Sala de lo Penal, Seccion Tercera, press release of 28 February 2023 (ECLI:ES:AN:2023:819); Tribunal Supremo, Sala de lo Penal, press release of 24 September 2026

n: British oil firm paid the salaries of the Somali ministry negotiating its contract
rank: Director General and Deputy Director General, Ministry of Petroleum; directors of exploration, planning, oil management and legal affairs; a member of the production-sharing negotiating team
d: Soma Oil & Gas, a British company chaired by the former Conservative leader Michael Howard, signed a capacity-building agreement with Somalia's Ministry of Petroleum in April and May 2014 and then paid the salaries of ministry staff while negotiating its own contract with that same ministry. The UN Monitoring Group on Somalia and Eritrea documented USD 490,000 transferred to the ministry's Central Bank account and USD 295,800 paid to fourteen named officials by February 2015, among them the director general, his deputy and a director on the production-sharing negotiating team; six of them were drawing their civil service salaries at the same time. Two weeks after the terms were agreed the minister extended Soma's survey area to include a block it could then bid for, and Soma's was the only one of eight contracts reviewed by the Financial Governance Committee on which no action was taken. The Group called the payments a likely quid pro quo. Soma said no connected person had been paid under the agreement; the petroleum minister called them basic support salaries and said Soma got nothing for them.
inside: A British oil company paid the wages of the Somali ministry officials negotiating its own contract, and that ministry then widened the area it could drill in.
undone: The Serious Fraud Office opened an investigation in July 2015 and closed it on 14 December 2016, saying there were reasonable grounds to suspect corruption offences but insufficient evidence to provide a realistic prospect of conviction.
cite: UN Monitoring Group on Somalia and Eritrea, annex on Soma Oil & Gas, July 2015; UK Serious Fraud Office statement closing the Soma Oil & Gas investigation, 14 December 2016 (https://www.sfo.gov.uk/?p=14498)

n: German submarine makers bribed Greece's defence minister and procurement chief
who: Ferrostaal and the HDW submarine consortium
rank: Minister of National Defence; deputy head of defence ministry procurement; managing director, Skaramangas shipyard
d: In 2000 Greece ordered three Type 214 submarines from the German firms HDW and Ferrostaal for EUR 1.26 billion and took a fourth in 2002. In December 2011 a German court fined Ferrostaal EUR 40 million and convicted two of its senior managers, Johann-Friedrich Haun and Hans-Dieter Muehlenbeck, who were fined and given suspended terms, for bribes paid to win the order. In June 2017 Bremen prosecutors found the sensor supplier Atlas Elektronik had paid as much as EUR 13 million in commissions; it gave up EUR 48 million in profits. In Greece, defence minister Akis Tsochatzopoulos was convicted in October 2013 of laundering about USD 75 million in bribes tied to the submarines and a Russian missile purchase, and jailed for 20 years; the bribery charges themselves were time-barred. Sixteen co-defendants were convicted with him, including his wife and daughter. He denied the charges throughout. Antonis Kantas, deputy head of defence procurement, admitted taking bribes and testified; an appeal court in January 2019 convicted him, the managing director of the Skaramangas shipyard the consortium had taken over, and three others, and acquitted a ministry official.
inside: German arms firms paid Greece's defence minister and its deputy procurement chief, and Greece bought four German submarines for 1.26 billion euros.
cite: World Peace Foundation, Compendium of Arms Trade Corruption (Tufts University), 'The Greek Submarine Scandal'; OCCRP, 'Greece: Former Defense Minister Convicted of Money Laundering', October 2013; Bremen Public Prosecutor's Office statement, June 2017; Corruption Tracker case file

n: Siemens paid Greece's transport minister, who approved its OTE contract
rank: Minister of Transport and Communications; director of Siemens Greece
d: Siemens was found in 2006 to have kept EUR 1.3 billion in off-book funds used for bribes on international tenders, and paid about EUR 1 billion in fines in 2008 to settle the investigations. In Greece, an Athens court convicted Tassos Mantelis, transport and communications minister from 1996 to 2000, of money laundering in July 2017, giving him an eight-year suspended sentence and a EUR 50,000 fine for concealing 450,000 deutsche marks received from Siemens through a third party. The money was tied to his approval of a contract between Siemens' Greek unit and the state-controlled telecoms company OTE. He had told a parliamentary committee in 2010 that he took money from Siemens while in office, calling it a campaign donation. Ilias Georgiou, who ran Siemens in Greece at the time, received a twelve-year suspended sentence for money laundering and was barred from leaving the country. A 2011 Greek parliamentary report put the cost to the state at at least EUR 2 billion.
inside: Siemens paid Greece's transport minister, who approved its Greek unit's contract with the state telecoms company; an Athens court convicted him of laundering the money.
undone: Siemens agreed in 2012 to pay Greece about EUR 170 million in compensation and invest a further EUR 100 million to keep its Greek subsidiary running, subject to ratification by parliament. A case against other former Siemens Greece executives has run since 2015.
cite: OCCRP, 'Ex-Greek Minister Sentenced for Money Laundering in Siemens Scandal', July 2017; Global Legal Post reporting the Financial Times on the settlement terms; Greek parliamentary committee report, 2011

n: Ferrostaal managers admitted bribing Portuguese officials over a submarine order
org_label: German Submarine Consortium (HDW, Thyssen Nordseewerke, MAN Ferrostaal)
who: MAN Ferrostaal and the German Submarine Consortium
rank: Portuguese officials, not named by any court; alleged recipients include a defence minister's party, an honorary consul and a rear admiral
d: Portugal signed for two Type 209 submarines from the German Submarine Consortium of HDW, Thyssen Nordseewerke and MAN Ferrostaal in 2004, at a base price of EUR 769 million that rose to EUR 833 million, with an offsets package of EUR 1.2 billion for Portuguese industry. In December 2011 two former Ferrostaal executives, Hans-Dieter Muehlenbeck and Johann-Friedrich Haun, pleaded guilty in Germany to bribing Greek and Portuguese officials with EUR 62 million in all, of which EUR 1.6 million went to Portugal; both were fined and given suspended terms, and Ferrostaal agreed with prosecutors to pay a EUR 140 million fine. No court has named a Portuguese recipient. Reporting and authorised wiretaps pointed to more than EUR 1 million reaching accounts of the party of defence minister Paulo Portas, EUR 1.6 million to the honorary consul Juergen Adolff in Berlin and EUR 1 million to an unnamed rear admiral; a Munich court convicted Adolff in 2014 and an appeal court acquitted him in 2015.
inside: Two German arms executives admitted paying 1.6 million euros to Portuguese officials over a submarine order, though no court has said which officials took it.
undone: A Portuguese court acquitted all ten people charged over falsified offsets invoices in 2014, and prosecutors closed the investigation that December, citing difficulty obtaining evidence and the expiry of the limitation period. Nobody in Portugal was convicted.
cite: World Peace Foundation, Compendium of Arms Trade Corruption (Tufts University), 'German Submarine Sales to Portugal'; Munich court proceedings of December 2011 and the 2015 appeal as reported there

n: Siemens bribed Bangladesh's telecom board and a minister for a mobile deal
rank: Bangladesh Telegraph & Telephone Board; Minister of Posts & Telecommunications
d: Siemens paid Bangladeshi officials to win a mobile telephone contract from the Bangladesh Telegraph & Telephone Board, the state body that then ran the country's phone network. The US Department of Justice said that from May 2001 to August 2006 Siemens Bangladesh caused at least $5,319,839 to be paid to officials through purported consultants, to get favourable treatment in bidding on the project; the contract was worth about $40.9 million. The SEC complaint says the money went under sham consulting agreements for services never performed, and that recipients included the board's director of procurement, a government minister and the son of the then prime minister. Siemens Bangladesh pleaded guilty in Washington on 15 December 2008 and was fined $500,000.
inside: A German engineering firm's money reached the state telephone board's procurement director and a minister, and the board then awarded Siemens the mobile contract.
undone: Siemens AG pleaded guilty the same day to books-and-records and internal-controls offences and was fined $448.5 million, paid $350 million in disgorgement to the SEC and 395 million euros to the Munich Prosecutor General.
cite: US Department of Justice press release 08-crm-1105, 15 December 2008; SEC v. Siemens AG, complaint, US District Court for the District of Columbia, case 1:08-cv-02167, 12 December 2008; SEC litigation release LR-20829, 15 December 2008

n: Siemens paid Israel Electric Corporation's senior managers for power plants
rank: senior deputy director general and department heads, Israel Electric Corporation
d: Siemens bribed senior managers of the Israel Electric Corporation, the state-owned company that generates and supplies almost all of Israel's electricity, to win turbine and power plant work. The SEC complaint says that from 2002 to 2005 Siemens paid about $20 million to a former director of the company in connection with four contracts worth about $786 million, routed through a consultant owned by the brother-in-law of the chief executive of Siemens Israel. The Tel Aviv District Court sentenced five former company officials on 13 June 2017 under plea bargains: David Cohn, a former senior deputy director general, took $500,000 and was jailed for 45 months; Haim Brenner took $430,000 and was jailed for 33 months.
inside: Siemens' payments reached the managers of the state electricity company who shaped its tenders, and the company then awarded Siemens power plant contracts worth hundreds of millions.
undone: Globes reported on 2 May 2016 that Siemens agreed to pay a 160 million shekel penalty to the Israeli government and to appoint an external inspector to supervise its activities in Israel, and that its lawyers said the district attorney chose to refrain from filing a criminal suit against Siemens in favour of a settlement. The 2017 plea bargains did not cover Siemens Israel, which remained a defendant, and a sixth IEC official, David Elmakis, was not covered and his case was still being heard.
cite: Globes, '5 former IEC execs jailed over Siemens affair', 13 June 2017; Globes, 'Siemens to pay Israel NIS 160m penalty', 2 May 2016; SEC v. Siemens AG, complaint, US District Court for the District of Columbia, case 1:08-cv-02167, 12 December 2008; Israel Electric Corporation, SGX bond filing (registered office, Haifa)

n: Siemens paid kickbacks to Iraq's electricity and oil ministries
rank: Ministry of Electricity and Ministry of Oil
d: Under the United Nations oil-for-food programme, which let Iraq sell oil to buy humanitarian goods, Iraqi ministries demanded a ten per cent kickback from suppliers, dressed up as an 'after-sales service fee' for services never provided. The SEC complaint says four Siemens units took part across 42 contracts, paying about $1.7 million in kickbacks on revenues of more than $124 million and profits of about $38.2 million. Siemens France signed twelve power station contracts with the Ministry of Electricity and paid about $321,745, with cash deposited into a Jordanian bank account held by two Iraqi officials. Siemens Turkey paid about $1,243,119 on twenty contracts, in cash so that no names appeared on paper. Osram's Middle East unit paid about $89,250 on contracts with state companies under the Ministry of Oil.
inside: Siemens units paid secret percentages to Iraqi ministries that then bought their equipment, with the inflated prices billed to the United Nations escrow account.
undone: Siemens AG settled with the SEC and pleaded guilty in Washington on 15 December 2008, paying a $448.5 million fine and $350 million in disgorgement; the SEC said the contracts had been inflated by ten per cent without telling the United Nations.
cite: SEC v. Siemens AG, complaint, US District Court for the District of Columbia, case 1:08-cv-02167, 12 December 2008; SEC litigation release LR-20829, 15 December 2008; US Department of Justice press release 08-crm-1105, 15 December 2008

n: Siemens bribed officials of Moscow's World Bank traffic project unit
rank: senior officials, Moscow Project Implementation Unit
d: Siemens paid officials of the Moscow Project Implementation Unit, the quasi-governmental body running the city's World Bank-funded Third Ring Road traffic control project, to win the $27 million contract to build the system. The SEC complaint says that from 2004 to 2006 Siemens units paid about $741,419 in bribes, of which at least $600,000 was funnelled to senior officials of the unit. About $313,000 went to a business consultant who was at the same time a technical consultant to the unit; at least $141,419 of that bought favourable treatment in the tender, including the specifications, advance tender documents and the evaluation of bids. Siemens also colluded with a competitor that inflated its bid, then hired it at about $800,000.
inside: Siemens paid a consultant who also advised the city project unit, so the unit wrote the tender terms and judged the bids in Siemens' favour.
undone: On 2 July 2009 the World Bank Group announced a settlement in which Siemens Russia faces up to four years' debarment over the Moscow Urban Transport Project, Siemens AG and its affiliates accepted a voluntary two-year bar on Bank business to 31 December 2010, and Siemens agreed to pay $100 million over 15 years for anti-corruption work.
cite: World Bank Group press release, 2 July 2009; SEC v. Siemens AG, complaint, US District Court for the District of Columbia, case 1:08-cv-02167, 12 December 2008; SEC litigation release LR-20829, 15 December 2008

n: Siemens paid Nigeria's telecoms and power officials for $130m contracts
rank: Nigeria Telecommunications Limited and the Ministry of Communications
d: Siemens paid Nigerian officials to win four telecommunications projects worth about $130 million from Nigeria Telecommunications Limited, the state phone company, and the Ministry of Communications. The SEC complaint puts suspicious payments in Nigeria at about $12.7 million, of which at least $4.5 million were bribes; a senior figure at Siemens Nigeria said that in 2000 and 2001 bribes commonly ran at 15 to 30 per cent of contract value, documented through fictitious consultancy agreements, with cash withdrawn from Siemens cash desks and hand-carried to Nigeria. About $2.8 million went through a bank account in Potomac, Maryland held in the name of the wife of a former Nigerian vice president. About $172,000 of watches was bought for officials recorded as 'P.' and 'V.P.'.
inside: Siemens' cash reached officials of the state telephone company and the communications ministry, and those bodies then awarded it four contracts worth about $130 million.
undone: Vanguard reported that Attorney General Mohammed Adoke ordered the EFCC to end its case against Siemens after the company agreed to pay a 7 billion naira fine, and that the EFCC then arraigned four former officials on a 16-count charge before Justice Danlami Senchi at the Abuja High Court: Maigada Shuaibu, a former Power Holding Company of Nigeria director, Edwin Moore Momife, a former M-Tel chief executive, Emmanuel Chukwuemeka Ossai, a former NITEL general manager of finance, and Mahmood Sadiq Mohammed, a former permanent secretary of the Federal Ministry of Power and Steel. All four pleaded not guilty and were granted bail. They were convicted, but in June 2014 the Court of Appeal in Abuja overturned the convictions and acquitted all four, holding that the EFCC could not establish a lawful case because the Siemens officials named as co-conspirators had never been charged or declared wanted.
cite: SEC v. Siemens AG, complaint, US District Court for the District of Columbia, case 1:08-cv-02167, 12 December 2008; SEC litigation release LR-20829, 15 December 2008; Vanguard (Nigeria), 'Siemens bribery: AGF orders EFCC to end case', https://www.vanguardngr.com/?p=114352; humanipo, 'Nigerian court frees telecoms boss over Siemens bribe', 2 June 2014

n: Siemens paid a senior Pemex official to settle refinery cost claims
rank: senior official, Petroleos Mexicanos
d: The SEC complaint says that in late 2004 two Siemens units made three payments totalling about $2.6 million to a politically connected business consultant in order to settle claims for cost overruns on three projects to modernise refineries of Petroleos Mexicanos, the Mexican state oil company known as Pemex. Some of the money passed from the consultant to a senior Pemex official who was in a position to influence the settlement. The then chief executive of Siemens' Mexican regional company knew of and approved the payments, and the supporting invoices described services that were not provided or were only vaguely described. Part of the work was performed by a Siemens subsidiary in Atlanta, and US Export-Import Bank financing supported some of the contracts.
inside: Siemens' money reached the Pemex official who could decide its cost-overrun claims, so the state oil company settled those claims on terms that suited Siemens.
undone: Siemens consented to a final judgment without admitting or denying the allegations; the court entered judgment on 15 December 2008 and Siemens paid $350 million in disgorgement to the SEC. The SEC complaint does not name the Pemex official.
cite: SEC v. Siemens AG, complaint, US District Court for the District of Columbia, case 1:08-cv-02167, 12 December 2008; SEC litigation release LR-20829, 15 December 2008

n: Siemens paid Vietnam's health ministry officials for medical equipment
rank: Ministry of Health
d: The SEC complaint says Siemens' medical division paid $183,000 in early 2005 and $200,000 in early 2006 in connection with about $6 million of medical device sales on two projects involving Vietnam's Ministry of Health. The payments went through an intermediary linked to a group of Hong Kong consultants, were routed through a United States correspondent bank to accounts in Singapore, withdrawn in cash and carried to Vietnam. Project calculation sheets described them as relating to 'room preparation'. A former chief financial officer of Siemens Limited Vietnam described collecting an envelope holding $183,000 in cash at a Singapore hotel and leaving it at Hanoi airport with the head of the medical division in Vietnam, who was handling the contract talks with ministry officials.
inside: Siemens' cash was carried to Hanoi for the health ministry officials negotiating its contracts, and the ministry then bought about $6 million of Siemens equipment.
undone: Siemens consented to a final judgment without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, entered on 15 December 2008, and paid $350 million in disgorgement; the complaint does not name the ministry officials.
cite: SEC v. Siemens AG, complaint, US District Court for the District of Columbia, case 1:08-cv-02167, 12 December 2008; SEC litigation release LR-20829, 15 December 2008

n: Siemens agreed payments to Vietnam's defence ministry for a GSM tender
rank: Ministry of Defence officials; Vietel
d: The SEC complaint says that in 2002 Siemens' communications division paid about $140,000 in connection with a tender worth about $35 million to supply GSM mobile network equipment and services to Vietel, a government-owned telecommunications provider founded by Vietnam's Ministry of Defence. Two payments totalling $140,000 went to a Siemens business consultant's account in Singapore and then through a United States correspondent account, and the complaint says they likely reached Ministry of Defence officials. A fax of June 2002 described an agreed payment of eight per cent of project value to Defence Ministry officials and fourteen per cent to Vietel officials. Siemens lost the tender before making further payments, so no contract followed.
inside: Siemens agreed shares of the contract value for defence ministry and state telecoms officials deciding the tender, though the complaint says only that the money likely reached them.
undone: Siemens lost the tender. It consented to a final judgment without admitting or denying the allegations, entered on 15 December 2008.
cite: SEC v. Siemens AG, complaint, US District Court for the District of Columbia, case 1:08-cv-02167, 12 December 2008; SEC litigation release LR-20829, 15 December 2008

n: Siemens bribed Enel's managers in Italy for two gas turbine contracts
rank: managing member of Enelpower's board; managing director of ENEL Produzione
d: Siemens paid managers inside the Enel group, Italy's largest electricity company and partly owned by the Italian state, to win gas turbine orders. The Landgericht Darmstadt convicted two men on 14 May 2007: Andreas Kley, former finance chief of Siemens' power generation division, who received two years' probation, and Horst Vigener, a freelance consultant, who received nine months'; the court ordered Siemens to pay 38 million euros in forfeited profits. The Federal Court of Justice judgment of 29 August 2008 records that the money went to the managing member of the board of Enelpower S.p.A. and to the managing director of ENEL Produzione S.p.A., and that Siemens won the La Casella order worth about 132.5 million euros and the Repowering order worth 205.6 million euros.
inside: Siemens paid the Enel group managers who awarded turbine orders, and those managers then placed two contracts worth more than 330 million euros with Siemens.
undone: On 29 August 2008 the Bundesgerichtshof (case 2 StR 587/07) held that the pre-2002 bribery offence did not cover bribery aimed solely at foreign competitors, recharacterised one of Kley's convictions as breach of trust, quashed the other bribery conviction and his sentences, quashed the judgment against Vigener, and set aside the 38 million euro forfeiture against Siemens, remanding the case to another chamber of the Landgericht Darmstadt.
cite: Bundesgerichtshof, judgment of 29 August 2008, 2 StR 587/07; Jurist, 'German court finds former Siemens officials guilty of bribery', May 2007; IndustryWeek, 'Former Siemens managers get probation for corruption charges', 14 May 2007; Enel, ISO 14001 certificate for Enel Produzione S.p.A. (registered office, Viale Regina Margherita 125, Rome)

n: Siemens bribed a Chinese city hospital's deputy director for an MRI sale
rank: deputy director and head of radiology, Songyuan City Central Hospital
d: The SEC complaint says that in May 2006 Siemens paid $64,800 in connection with the sale of a $1.5 million magnetic resonance imaging system to the Songyuan City Central Hospital in China, one of five Chinese-owned hospitals the complaint describes Siemens' medical division paying agents over. The payment went first to a United States bank account and then to an intermediary's account in Singapore. A project calculation sheet signed by the then chief financial officer of Siemens' medical division in China described it as 'expenses (commission)', but the complaint says the intermediary provided no service beyond passing on bribes. In or around March 2008 the hospital's deputy director, who also headed its radiology department, was convicted of corruption in China, including taking a $60,000 bribe from a Siemens salesperson over the sale, and was sentenced to fourteen years in prison.
inside: Siemens' commission reached the hospital's deputy director, who also ran its radiology department, and the hospital then bought a $1.5 million Siemens scanner.
undone: The hospital official was sentenced to fourteen years in prison in China. Siemens consented to a final judgment without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, entered on 15 December 2008.
cite: SEC v. Siemens AG, complaint, US District Court for the District of Columbia, case 1:08-cv-02167, 12 December 2008; SEC litigation release LR-20829, 15 December 2008

n: Swissport money reached SAA staff before its ground-handling contract
org_label: Swissport and JM Aviation South Africa
rank: SAA head of procurement and SAA Technical procurement and board figures
d: The ground-handling firm Swissport signed a service level agreement with JM Aviation South Africa, which was paid R28.5-million; a month later South African Airways concluded a five-year ground-handling contract with Swissport. The State Capture Commission, reporting in January 2022, said payments of that money to individuals were likely kickbacks. R20-million went to Jamicron, owned by businessman Daluxolo Peter, R2.5-million went to BMK Attorneys and was used the next day to pay for two luxury cars for SAA's head of procurement Lester Peter, and R2.5-million reached businessman Vuyisile Ndzeku's private account. The report records that R1.139-billion was paid to Swissport without any contract being in place. The Commission asked the prosecuting authority to consider charging Ndzeku, Lester Peter, advocate Nontsasa Memela and Swissport.
inside: An airport services contractor routed money to people inside the state airline, and the airline then handed it a five-year ground-handling contract.
undone: Julian Aires, president of JM International, pleaded guilty in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia to conspiring to breach the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, the charge covering about US$2.7-million paid to South African officials over two 2016 SAA transactions; sanction was still pending. No South African trial of the people the Commission named had been reported.
cite: Judicial Commission of Inquiry into State Capture, Part 1 (handed over 4 January 2022), as reported by BizNews, 12 January 2022, and Daily Maverick, 5 January 2022; ch-aviation on the US Department of Justice charge

n: Guptas bought Denel's armour supplier, then got its board replaced
rank: Denel board chairmanship and chief executive
d: Denel is South Africa's state-owned arms manufacturer. In 2013 Gupta associate Salim Essa bought a 74.9 per cent stake in VR Laser, one of Denel's largest suppliers of armoured steel, through his company Elgasolve. The State Capture Commission found this "shows that the Guptas bought control of a significant supplier of armoured steel to Denel", acquired "using it as a vehicle with which to capture Denel". In 2015 public enterprises minister Lynne Brown replaced the board without consulting her department's officials; the new board under Daniel Mantsha suspended chief executive Riaz Saloojee, the chief financial officer and the company secretary, then paid them to leave. The Commission said those actions aimed at "facilitating the capture of Denel by the Guptas". Three contracts went to VR Laser in 2014 and 2015.
inside: A family that controlled Denel's armour supplier through an associate had the minister install a board which removed the executives resisting it, and contracts followed.
undone: The Commission recommended that law enforcement investigate the three VR Laser contracts for breaches of the Public Finance Management Act, and that the Legal Practice Council be made aware of its findings against Mantsha and investigate how he was readmitted as an attorney and whether he is fit and proper to practise. Denel has struggled to pay staff salaries because of its financial troubles.
cite: Judicial Commission of Inquiry into State Capture, Part 2 Vol 2 (1 February 2022), as reported by News24 via Polity, 2 February 2022, and TimesLive, 3 February 2022

n: Free State paid R255m for asbestos work; the contractor paid its head
org_label: Blackhead Consulting and Diamond Hill joint venture
rank: head of the Free State human settlements department
d: In 2014 the Free State provincial human settlements department set aside R255-million to strip asbestos from the roofs of provincial houses, after accepting an unsolicited proposal from the Blackhead Consulting and Diamond Hill joint venture with no competitive process. About R255-million was paid and, according to the State Capture Commission, no asbestos was removed. The Commission found the joint venture was not qualified for asbestos removal despite claiming it was, and called the project "a considerable scam from its inception", meant to unlawfully benefit a business consortium and certain officials. Blackhead's Edwin Sodi paid R650,000 towards a property for the department's head, Nthimotse Mokhesi, which the Commission found was a reward or inducement or both.
inside: A contractor paid the official who ran the provincial housing department, and the department then handed its unqualified joint venture a R255-million job without competition.
undone: Sodi paid R600,000 into a car dealership account in December 2015 marked "TZ"; the Commission was not persuaded by his and former national director-general Thabane Zulu's explanation and said it "may well have been a bribe". Magashule and sixteen co-accused face fraud, corruption, money laundering and Public Finance Management Act charges in the Free State High Court before Judge Phillip Loubser; the trial has been delayed more than five years, and on 23 January 2026 the Constitutional Court partly overturned his order freeing a co-accused.
cite: Judicial Commission of Inquiry into State Capture, Part 4 Vol 2 (29 April 2022), as reported by Daily Maverick, 29 April 2022; Business Day, 26 January 2026

n: Estina, fronted by a Gupta salesman, took R280m from Free State farming
rank: head of department and MEC, Free State agriculture
d: The Free State provincial agriculture department paid more than R280-million to Estina for a dairy project at Vrede. The State Capture Commission found the payments unlawful and the intended black farmer beneficiaries sidelined. Estina had R16 in its bank account when it received a R30-million prepayment in June 2012, arranged by the provincial agriculture MEC Mosebenzi Zwane; its only director was a sales manager at a Gupta company, and the Commission wrote that it "had no experience whatsoever in farming". The contract was cancelled in 2014 but the department kept paying until 2016. The Commission said departmental head Peter Thabethe, who signed without competitive bidding or due diligence, "must be held both criminally and civilly liable".
inside: A family's own employee fronted the company a provincial department paid R280-million, and the department's head and MEC pushed the money out for it.
undone: The Commission said Zwane pursued the Guptas' agenda and that premier Ace Magashule "would have also been pursuing the agenda of the Guptas", and asked law enforcement to investigate both. On 7 August 2024 Judge Celeste Reinders struck the criminal case against Zwane, Thabethe, former chief financial officer Seipati Dhlamini, Gupta associates and eight companies off the Free State High Court roll for unreasonable delay. The prosecuting authority said it would reinstate it.
cite: Judicial Commission of Inquiry into State Capture, Part 6 Vol 1 (22 June 2022), as reported by Daily Maverick, 23 June 2022 and 8 August 2024

n: Free State paid Gupta associate's Nulane R25m for a study it farmed out
rank: accounting officer and head of rural development, Free State agriculture
d: On 7 October 2011 the accounting officer of the Free State agriculture department, Limakatso Moorosi, approved a request to appoint Nulane Investments without a tender; the request had been drafted on the chief financial officer's instruction and recommended by the head of rural development, Peter Thabethe. Nulane, whose sole director and shareholder was Iqbal Sharma, was contracted on 28 October 2011 for R24,984,240 to produce a feasibility study, and subcontracted the work to Deloitte for about R1.5-million. Nulane then paid R19,070,934 to Gateway, a United Arab Emirates company that rendered it no services, and the prosecution traced money through Islandsite Investments and an Absa cash management system of which Atul Gupta was the manager with unlimited access.
inside: Officials waived the tender for a company owned by a family's associate; prosecutors say most of the state's money then flowed into accounts that family controlled.
undone: On 21 April 2023 Acting Judge Nompumelelo Gusha of the Free State High Court discharged seven accused under section 174 of the Criminal Procedure Act and acquitted Moorosi, who had not applied for discharge, calling the state case "still born". On 12 June 2025 the Supreme Court of Appeal set that order aside, found numerous errors of law and said "this was a failure of justice", ruling that the accused may be retried for the same offences before a different judge. Thabethe's acquittal on the Public Finance Management Act count was left standing.
cite: The State v Thabethe and Others (839/2023) [2025] ZASCA 88, Supreme Court of Appeal, 12 June 2025

n: SABC carried the costs of the Guptas' media business for six years
rank: SABC chief operating officer and senior executives
d: The South African Broadcasting Corporation is the state broadcaster. The State Capture Commission found that Jacob Zuma helped the Gupta family launch the newspaper The New Age and the television channel ANN7 in 2010 and used his office to steer contracts to them; his son Duduzane held 30 per cent of Infinity Media, which housed both. From 1 April 2011 to 31 March 2017 the SABC carried most of the production and broadcast costs of the Guptas' business breakfast briefings while the Gupta companies took the financial and publicity benefit, and the contract was repeatedly extended outside National Treasury procurement rules. The Commission put the SABC's loss at R4.3-million and asked that it be recovered.
inside: A family's newspaper and television channel had the state broadcaster pay to make their programmes, through executives who kept extending the deal outside procurement rules.
undone: The Commission recommended that chief operating officer Hlaudi Motsoeneng "face an investigation by law enforcement agencies to prosecute him" over the wasteful extensions, and that the SABC consider civil proceedings against The New Age and Infinity Media, including Duduzane Zuma. It also found the SABC sold ANN7 two thousand minutes of archive footage at R70 a minute instead of R100 and was never paid the R420,000 owed.
cite: Judicial Commission of Inquiry into State Capture, Part 5 Vol 2 (22 June 2022), as reported by Daily Maverick, 23 June 2022

n: Vossloh used a front firm to win PRASA's R3.5bn locomotive contract
rank: PRASA chief executive and tender procurement
d: The Passenger Rail Agency of South Africa awarded a locomotive contract worth about R3.5-billion to Swifambo Rail Leasing in March 2012. Vossloh, described in the judgment as a Spanish locomotive company, had advised PRASA in 2011 and in July 2011 sent PRASA's chief executive Lucky Montana a memorandum recommending a hundred locomotives, but could not tender itself because it is not based in South Africa. Swifambo was created twenty days before it tendered and its only obligation was to accept delivery and hand the locomotives over. The Supreme Court of Appeal held that "Swifambo's real role was undoubtedly to enable Vossloh to become the real bidder for the tender". At Montana's instruction a man with no relevant qualifications drew specifications that suited Vossloh's locomotives but left them too high for South African lines.
inside: A foreign manufacturer that could not bid advised the rail agency, whose chief executive is alleged to have had specifications drawn to fit its trains; a shell company bid instead.
undone: The Johannesburg High Court found in July 2017 that the specifications breached PRASA's procurement policy and set the contract aside; the Supreme Court of Appeal dismissed Swifambo's appeal on 30 November 2018. The State Capture Commission recommended in June 2022 that prosecutors seriously consider charging Montana and board member Sfiso Buthelezi, and speed up the prosecution of Swifambo director Auswell Mashaba.
cite: Supreme Court of Appeal, Swifambo Rail Leasing v PRASA, judgment 30 November 2018, as reported by GroundUp via Daily Maverick, 4 December 2018; Judicial Commission of Inquiry into State Capture, Part 5 Vol 2 (22 June 2022), as reported by Daily Maverick, 23 June 2022 (https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2022-06-23-chief-justice-calls-for-special-commission-to-investigate-prasas-implosion/)

n: Siyangena funded PRASA chief's homes and won R5.5bn in contracts
rank: PRASA chief executive and senior managers
d: Siyangena Technologies supplied and maintained station access and security systems for the Passenger Rail Agency of South Africa under contracts worth about R5.5-billion, work that began around the 2010 World Cup. In October 2020 three judges of the Gauteng High Court in Pretoria set aside every agreement between PRASA and Siyangena on PRASA's own application. The judgment found chief executive Lucky Montana steered an unsuitable contract, "not fit for purpose", past the safeguards meant to protect public money, reportedly helped by PRASA employees Luyanda Gantsho, Chris Mbatha and Jabulani Sindane. It held that "the evidence is irresistible" that Siyangena was providing the backing for the purchase of homes for Montana, and that Gantsho was given a beachfront apartment at Ballito.
inside: A supplier paid for the rail agency chief executive's houses and a manager's flat, and the agency then gave it billions of rands in station contracts.
undone: The court found Siyangena "complicit to the corruption, impropriety and maladministration" and ordered it to pay costs, and appointed an independent engineer to value the work done against what had been paid. The Supreme Court of Appeal dismissed Siyangena's appeal with costs on 1 November 2022. The State Capture Commission recommended in June 2022 that the Hawks finalise their investigations into possible criminal conduct, such as the Siyangena and Swifambo deals, as soon as possible.
cite: Gauteng High Court, Pretoria (North Gauteng High Court), judgment of October 2020, reported by GroundUp, 9 October 2020; Supreme Court of Appeal media summary, Siyangena Technologies v PRASA (487/2021) [2022] ZASCA 149, 1 November 2022; Judicial Commission of Inquiry into State Capture, Part 5 Vol 2, as reported by Daily Maverick, 23 June 2022

n: Willbros and Bilfinger paid NNPC officials $6m for a gas pipeline job
rank: NNPC and NAPIMS officials
d: The Houston pipeline company Willbros and its German joint-venture partner Bilfinger inflated their bid for the $387m Eastern Gas Gathering System pipeline in the Niger Delta by three per cent to cover bribes. US prosecutors say that from late 2003 to March 2005 they paid, promised or authorised more than $6m to officials of the Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation, the state oil company, and of its subsidiary National Petroleum Investment Management Services, to a senior official of Nigeria's federal executive branch and to members of a Nigerian political party. Willbros paid a $22m penalty in 2008 and Bilfinger $32m in 2013. The consultant Paul Novak was jailed for 15 months in 2013; two Willbros executives were jailed in 2010 and a former Willbros International executive, Kenneth Tillery, remains a fugitive.
cite: US Department of Justice press releases, 11 December 2013 (Bilfinger SE), 3 May 2013 (Novak sentencing) and 19 December 2008 (Tillery and Novak indictment)
inside: A pipeline consortium's cash reached officials of Nigeria's state oil company, which then awarded and kept the contract whose price had been padded to pay them.

n: Willbros agreed to pay PetroEcuador officials $300,000 over a pipeline job
rank: PetroEcuador and PetroComercial officials
d: The US indictment unsealed in Houston in December 2008 charged that James K. Tillery, a former Willbros International executive, the consultant Paul Novak and other Willbros employees in South America agreed to pay about $300,000 to officials of PetroEcuador, Ecuador's state oil company, and of its subsidiary PetroComercial.
