The aim was a $3m job rehabilitating about 16 kilometres of gas pipeline from Santo Domingo to El Beaterio, where PetroComercial was the client. A former Willbros executive, Jim Bob Brown, pleaded guilty in 2006 to a conspiracy covering both the Ecuadorean and the Nigerian payments and was jailed for 12 months and a day in 2010. The $22m penalty Willbros paid in 2008 covered bribes in both countries. Tillery remains a fugitive.
cite: US Department of Justice press releases, 19 December 2008 and 3 May 2013
inside: An American contractor agreed to pay officials of Ecuador's state oil company so the pipeline repair job went to the firm paying them.

n: Armor Holdings paid an agent to steer UN body-armour contracts its way
rank: United Nations procurement
d: The US Securities and Exchange Commission complaint of 13 July 2011 alleged that Armor Holdings' British subsidiary, Armor Products International, paid a third-party intermediary at least 92 times, about $222,750 in all up to late 2006, with the understanding that part of the money would be offered to a United Nations official who could help steer business to the subsidiary. The intermediary is alleged to have priced a bid after learning from a UN procurement official about competitors' non-public bids. The United Nations, which buys body armour for peacekeepers, awarded the subsidiary a multi-year contract in October 2001 and a three-year contract in August 2003, extended for a year in 2006, bringing about $7.1m in revenue. Armor, by then owned by BAE Systems, paid $5.69m to the SEC without admitting or denying the allegations and $10.29m to the Justice Department.
cite: SEC Litigation Release 22037, 13 July 2011 (SEC v. Armor Holdings Inc., D.D.C. 1:11-cv-01271)
inside: An armour maker paid an intermediary on the understanding part would be offered to a United Nations buyer, and the UN then awarded it peacekeeping contracts.

n: Lockheed paid an Egyptian MP $1m to win a C-130 aircraft sale
rank: member of Egypt's People's Assembly
d: Lockheed pleaded guilty on 27 January 1995, before US District Judge Marvin Shoob in Georgia, to conspiring to break the bribery provisions of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and to falsifying its books, and agreed to pay $24.8m. It admitted that in October 1990 it wired $1m to a Zurich account of Dr Leila Takla, a member of the People's Assembly of Egypt from 1987 to 1990, labelling the money a termination fee when it was really payment for her influence in winning the sale. The contract, signed in April 1989 and worth about $79m, supplied Egypt with three C-130 Hercules transport aircraft and was paid for with US military financing grants. A retired Lockheed executive, Allen Love, had pleaded guilty a week earlier.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 27 January 1995 (plea of Lockheed Corporation and Allen R. Love)
inside: Lockheed paid a member of Egypt's parliament for her influence over the state's purchase of its transport aircraft, and the sale went to Lockheed.

n: Thomson-CSF's agent paid a Taiwanese navy captain over a frigate deal
rank: navy captain, naval procurement
d: Taiwan bought six Lafayette-class frigates from France in 1991 for about $2.8bn. The affair began with the death in 1993 of Captain Yin Ching-fen, head of Taiwan's naval procurement directorate, who had been gathering evidence of irregularities; an outside coroner concluded he had been murdered. Navy captain Kuo Li-heng was convicted of taking bribes from Andrew Wang, the agent of the seller Thomson-CSF, and in April 2014 his 15-year sentence became final, though he did not return to prison because of time already served on a separate sentence. Six other senior naval officers charged with corruption were acquitted, and Kuo's brother was convicted of money laundering. Wang, indicted in absentia in 2000 over the murder, died in Britain in 2015. In 2010 an ICC arbitration found Thomson-CSF had breached the contract's anti-corruption clause and awarded 630m euros, upheld in 2011.
cite: CNA (Focus Taiwan), 16 April 2014, on the final 15-year sentence; CNA, 10 July 2025, on Kuo Li-heng's death; World Peace Foundation, Compendium of Arms Trade Corruption: Taiwan's Lafayette Frigate Affair, for the wider case
inside: Thomson-CSF's agent paid a captain in Taiwan's naval procurement directorate, so the office that specified and bought the warships was taking money from the firm selling them.
undone: Swiss authorities have frozen about $730m in accounts linked to Wang and Kuo, and Taiwan is still pursuing recovery. Kuo died of cancer aged 73, reported on 10 July 2025.

n: Rheinmetall commissions funded bribes to Greek defence officials
rank: Greek defence ministry armaments officials, incl. the deputy armaments director
d: Antonis Kantas, deputy armaments director at Greece's defence ministry from 1997 to 2002, told Greek anti-corruption investigators from late 2013 that he had taken about $13m in bribes across several arms contracts, and Greek courts later gave him suspended sentences. On 11 December 2014 the Bremen public prosecutor's office announced an administrative fine of 37.07m euros on Rheinmetall Defence Electronics, final since 10 December, over the ASRAD air-defence deal: the prosecutors allege that more than 20m euros in commissions paid for the mediation of a Greek sales agent partly funded bribes in the millions to Greek officials, hidden through the agent's London shell company and further accounts in Switzerland. A Munich court separately convicted a former Krauss-Maffei Wegmann marketing executive of tax evasion linked to bribery over the PzH-2000 howitzer sale and fined the company.
cite: Staatsanwaltschaft Bremen press release No. 13/2014, 11 December 2014; World Peace Foundation, Compendium of Arms Trade Corruption: Greek Land Forces and German Bribery (https://sites.tufts.edu/corruptarmsdeals/greek-land-forces-and-german-bribery/)
inside: German arms firms' commissions to a Greek agent partly funded bribes to defence ministry officials deciding the air-defence and howitzer purchases, Bremen prosecutors allege.
undone: Bremen charged at least five former Rheinmetall employees in February 2017 and its investigation of Atlas Elektronik employees continued. Germany's Federal Court of Justice ruled in May 2017 that the Munich sentence and fine were too lenient and ordered a retrial; in June 2019 the Munich court raised the company fine to 500,000 euros and confirmed a sentence of one year and three months.

n: Greek court punished 17 over bribes on Ericsson's radar aircraft sale
rank: defence ministry armaments and procurement officials
d: Greece chose Ericsson's Erieye airborne early-warning radar in December 1998 and signed in July 1999 for four systems, usually put at about $575m with its aircraft. In 2000 about 116m Swedish kronor, roughly $13m, went to a company of the Greek businessman Thomas Liakounakos; prosecutors' documents reported in 2016 say it went to a shell company owned by Yannis Sbokos, the ministry's procurement secretary general. In May 2018 a Greek court gave Liakounakos a 16-year suspended sentence, sentenced the former deputy armaments chief Antonis Kantas to 10 years, which one account describes as suspended, punished 15 other co-defendants and awarded the state 48.4m euros. Sbokos is serving a life sentence on two money-laundering counts. No investigation had been opened in Sweden, where bribery carries a ten-year time limit.
cite: World Peace Foundation, Compendium of Arms Trade Corruption: Ericsson's Sale of Radar Systems to Greece, citing E. Tsiliopoulos, 'Heavy sentences for defendants in the SONAK military procurement scandal', New Greek TV, 3 May 2018
inside: A Swedish supplier's money reached the officials who ranked Greece's radar options, and the state bought the system whose agent was paying them.

n: Caso Mirage: a broker's commissions reached Chilean air force officers
rank: senior Fuerza Aerea de Chile officers
d: Chile bought 25 Belgian Mirage aircraft in 1994. After a seven-year investigation, the Chilean judge Omar Astudillo ruled, in a decision reported on 3 February 2017, that the Czech businessman Carlos Honzik had delivered about $15m in commissions to senior officers of the Fuerza Aerea de Chile over the purchase, and traced $6,285,567 to an account in Liechtenstein that Honzik had opened to distribute the money. Retired general Jaime Estay was convicted as an accomplice to embezzlement of public funds for receiving $65,000 in illegal commissions and barred from public office for three years. Honzik's widow, Henriette Bahna, was convicted as an accessory and lost funds held in a Swiss bank, but was acquitted of money laundering. Two other retired officers were acquitted.
cite: El Mostrador, 3 February 2017, on Judge Omar Astudillo's ruling in the Caso Mirage
inside: An arms middleman's commissions went to senior officers of Chile's air force, the service that chose and paid for the aircraft he was selling.

n: Gupta-linked adviser helped rewrite Transnet's loco case, cost rose R16bn
rank: Transnet transaction adviser; group chief financial officer
inside: The Gupta network's adviser was brought into Transnet's procurement without a tender and, the Zondo Commission found, helped rewrite the case for a R16bn increase that it linked to kickbacks.
d: Transnet, South Africa's state-owned rail and ports company, set out to buy 1,064 locomotives. McKinsey was appointed in July 2012 to advise on the purchase. Regiments Capital was brought in later, without the procurement process Transnet's rules required. Chief financial officer Anoj Singh signed a contract with Regiments on 23 January 2014 and, less than two weeks later, an addendum purporting to transfer McKinsey's rights to it; the Zondo Commission into state capture found that transfer invalid and found a later payment of R79.23m had no legal basis. The Commission found Regiments helped rewrite the business case, approved on 25 April 2013, that lifted the project's cost from R38.6bn to R54.5bn, and linked the extra R16bn to more than R7bn in kickbacks laundered through Hong Kong and Dubai.
undone: Molefe, Singh, Gama, Regiments directors and others were charged in 2022 with fraud, corruption, money laundering and breaches of the Public Finance Management Act. The trial due to begin on 2 February 2026 did not start, and in October 2026 the accused asked the Johannesburg High Court to strike the case off the roll for unreasonable delay; judgment was reserved to 26 November 2026. Charges against McKinsey and Trillian Asset Management were withdrawn before trial, and McKinsey Africa paid R1.115bn into the Criminal Assets Recovery Account under a December 2024 agreement with the prosecuting authority. Transnet and the Special Investigating Unit asked the High Court in March 2021 to set aside all four locomotive supply contracts; the former General Electric contract for 233 diesel locomotives was set aside by the Pretoria High Court on 14 April 2025 and the other three remain pending.
cite: Judicial Commission of Inquiry into State Capture (Zondo), Part 2 Vol 1, 1 February 2022, as reported by Daily Maverick (22 April 2026) and Moonstone (August 2026); South African government media statement, 9 March 2021; TimesLIVE, 16 April 2025; Business Day, 19 October 2026; EWN, 22 October 2026

n: China South Rail paid the Guptas' fixer 21% on Transnet locomotives
org_label: China South Rail (CRRC) and Salim Essa's Tequesta Group
who: China South Rail and Salim Essa
rank: Transnet locomotive supply contracts; adviser's seat at Transnet
inside: The Chinese manufacturer's commissions went to the fixer whose advisory firm sat inside Transnet's procurement, and Transnet then bought from it without open tender.
d: Transnet, South Africa's state rail company, gave China South Rail (CSR) three locomotive orders: 95 electric locomotives in an accelerated tender in 2012, on a contract reconciled at about R2.7bn; 100 more for which reporters found no evidence of an open tender; and 359 electric locomotives in the split tender announced on 17 March 2014, a split Transnet's chief financial officer credited to its adviser Regiments. On 18 May 2015 Salim Essa, the Gupta family's main fixer, signed a contract in Shenzhen with CSR's Hong Kong arm entitling his Hong Kong company Tequesta to an advisory fee of 21% of the R18.1bn locomotive contract, about R3.8bn; the document said CSR would not require any proof of delivery of the services. Payments ran through Hong Kong and Emirati companies.
undone: The Zondo Commission recommended that Essa be investigated over contracts from 2012 to 2016 that it said produced at least R7.34bn in kickbacks to companies he or the Guptas controlled. Transnet and the Special Investigating Unit asked the High Court in March 2021 to set aside the four 1,064 locomotive supply agreements, arguing that CSR's and China North Rail's parent company had concluded kickback agreements with Regiments Asia and Tequesta. The former General Electric contract was set aside on 14 April 2025; the CSR, China North Rail and Bombardier agreements remain before the court. Essa has not been charged; he has been in Dubai since 2017, and the prosecuting authority said in 2026 that it was still waiting for replies to mutual legal assistance requests to the United Arab Emirates, Hong Kong and China. Through his lawyers Essa denied wrongdoing and said he has never been charged, indicted or convicted of any criminal offence in South Africa or elsewhere.
cite: amaBhungane and Scorpio GuptaLeaks, 1 June 2017; South African government media statement, 9 March 2021 (Transnet/SIU review application); TimesLIVE, 16 April 2025; Daily Maverick, 20 May 2026

n: Transnet paid Trillian R93.48m for a loan it had not worked on
who: Trillian, linked to Salim Essa and the Gupta network
rank: lead arranger on Transnet's R12bn loan; acting group chief executive
inside: A Gupta-linked adviser took the lead-arranger seat on Transnet's loan and was paid a success fee for work the inquiry found it had not done.
d: Transnet raised a R12bn syndicated 'club loan' from a group of banks to help pay for its 1,064 new locomotives. Trillian, a firm Eric Wood helped set up after leaving Regiments Capital and which the Zondo Commission placed in the network around the Gupta family's fixer Salim Essa, replaced JP Morgan as lead arranger on the loan and was paid a success fee of R93.48m, against an original Regiments proposal of R50.2m. Transnet's board acquisitions and disposals committee approved the cession of Regiments' contracts to Trillian on 10 May 2016, on a memorandum from Siyabonga Gama, then acting group chief executive; treasurer Phetolo Ramosebudi had recommended the appointment, which an investigation found breached the Public Finance Management Act. The Commission found Trillian had not done the work.
undone: The Commission recommended that Trillian's appointment be investigated. Gama, Brian Molefe, Anoj Singh, Regiments directors Niven Pillay and Litha Nyhonyha, Albatime's owner Kuben Moodley and others are accused in the state capture case enrolled in 2022 in the Johannesburg High Court, where the R93.4m paid to Trillian Asset Management forms part of the charges. The trial set for 2 February 2026 did not start; in October 2026 the accused asked the court to strike the case off the roll for unreasonable delay, and judgment was reserved to 26 November 2026. Charges against Trillian Asset Management itself were withdrawn before trial.
cite: Judicial Commission of Inquiry into State Capture (Zondo), Part 2 Vol 1, 1 February 2022, as summarised by Moonstone (August 2026); Corruption Watch report on Zondo Commission hearings, 16 May 2019; Business Day, 19 October 2026; EWN, 22 October 2026

n: Gupta-linked Regiments ran Transnet's swaps and its pension fund's money
who: Regiments Capital and Regiments Fund Managers
rank: Transnet treasury adviser; asset manager of the Transnet Second Defined Benefit Fund
inside: The Gupta network's adviser was handed Transnet's treasury and its pensioners' fund without a tender, and the swaps it arranged lost both money while earning it fees.
d: Regiments Capital, the advisory firm linked to the Gupta family's fixer Salim Essa, was appointed without a procurement process to advise Transnet on interest-rate swaps, which fix the interest on borrowings, on about R23bn of locomotive loans. Its sister firm Regiments Fund Managers managed assets for the Transnet Second Defined Benefit Fund, the pension fund for retired rail staff, then used as the counterparty to further swaps. Acting chief financial officer Garry Pita backed the deals, over the deputy treasurer's written objection of December 2015. Transnet's acting group chief executive told the Zondo Commission there was no procurement process for the swaps and that Pita was not authorised to appoint Regiments. The Commission's recommendation 104 cited over R1.5bn in realised losses and R229m in fees to Regiments.
undone: The Commission's recommendation 104 called for Ramosebudi, Eric Wood and the Regiments companies to be investigated with a view to prosecution. A 2019 restraint order over the assets of Wood, Niven Pillay and Litha Nyhonyha was increased to R1.685bn in May 2022, adjusted for R639.1m Regiments had paid to the pension fund. In December 2023 the Johannesburg High Court sequestrated Wood's estate in a claim by the fund over bond transactions it says took R349m from it. The Financial Sector Conduct Authority debarred Wood and Pillay from financial services for 18 years on 30 July 2026. The criminal case against them is still before the Johannesburg High Court.
cite: Judicial Commission of Inquiry into State Capture (Zondo), Part 2 Vol 1, 1 February 2022, as summarised by Moonstone (August 2026); Daily Maverick, 17 May 2019 and 22 April 2026

n: A Gupta associate on Transnet's board as the minister handpicked its chief
who: Gupta family network and Salim Essa
rank: Transnet board seat and bid adjudication committee; group chief executive
inside: The minister handpicked a Transnet board including a business partner of the Guptas' associate, and chose as chief executive the candidate the Commission found the Guptas wanted.
d: Transnet is South Africa's state rail and ports company. In November 2010 public enterprises minister Malusi Gigaba handpicked candidates for a new Transnet board, among them Iqbal Sharma, who in 2012/14 was the business partner of the Gupta family's associate Salim Essa; Sharma was later promoted to control Transnet's bid adjudication committee, which decides who wins its tenders. In February 2011 Gigaba handpicked Brian Molefe as group chief executive, passing over Mandla Gantsho, who the Zondo Commission into state capture found had scored higher in the interviews. The Gupta-owned newspaper The New Age had reported the appointment as imminent months before it was made, in an article published in December 2010.
undone: The Commission found that Gigaba knew Molefe was the candidate the Guptas wanted in the post, and that Molefe, Gama, Singh and Sharma were instrumental in the capture of Transnet between 2011 and 2018; it recommended that all four be investigated and possibly prosecuted for corruption. Molefe, Singh, Gama and former chief procurement officer Thamsanqa Jiyane were charged over the locomotive contracts, and on 18 November 2025 the Investigating Directorate Against Corruption added Gigaba as the fifth accused, alleging that between November 2010 and May 2014 he repeatedly accepted undisclosed cash from members of the Gupta family. The case was moved to the Gauteng High Court in Johannesburg and had not come to trial by late 2026.
cite: Daily Maverick, 5 February 2022; Corruption Watch reports on the Zondo Commission, 28 May 2019 and February 2022; National Prosecuting Authority statement, 6 October 2025; The Citizen, 31 January 2026; Business Day, 19 October 2026

n: Neotel paid a Gupta front R75.6m as Transnet signed off its contracts
who: Neotel, through the Gupta-linked firm Homix
rank: Transnet group chief financial officer; network equipment and service contracts
inside: A supplier's money went to a front company tied to the Gupta network, and Transnet's own finance chief approved the purchases those payments were attached to.
d: Neotel, a South African telecoms operator, paid R75.6m to Homix, a front company the Zondo Commission treated as part of the Gupta family's network. R34.53m went on 3 April 2014, tied to a Transnet purchase of Cisco network switches and routers through Neotel, and R41.04m on 27 February 2015, tied to a master service agreement with Transnet. Neotel's auditors were told the second payment was for a single day's work resolving a negotiating impasse, and the Commission found no documentary evidence supporting the first payment and that neither Neotel executive could describe the work Homix had done. Transnet approved the Cisco request on 21 February 2014, up to R305m, signed off by chief financial officer Anoj Singh. The Commission said both transactions appeared to have had corrupt intent.
undone: Deloitte, Neotel's auditor, told the company to report the transactions and later reported irregularities to the auditors' regulator; Werksmans Attorneys investigated for Neotel, and chief executive Sunil Joshi and chief financial officer Steven Whiley left. On 19 May 2015 Transnet's acting chief executive Siyabonga Gama wrote to Neotel's chairman N Srinath saying Transnet was comfortable and confident in its procurement and that Homix had played a similar advisory role; the Commission said the letter exposed his dishonesty and that he had essentially vouched for Homix. The Commission recommended referring the matter to law enforcement.
cite: Judicial Commission of Inquiry into State Capture (Zondo), Part 2 Vol 1, 1 February 2022, as reported by TechCentral, 2 February 2022

n: Transnet's chief overturned an IT tender for a Gupta-linked bidder
rank: Transnet group chief executive; network services tender
inside: The minister had put the Gupta network's fixer on the partner firm's board, and Transnet's chief executive then overturned the scores to hand that bid the contract.
d: Transnet, South Africa's state rail and ports company, put its computer network services out to tender, drawing bids from Neotel, Telkom, Dimension Data, T-Systems and Vodacom. Neotel ranked first at R1.363bn; T-Systems came third at R1.737bn. The award to Neotel was signed on 30 October 2013 by an acting executive while group chief executive Brian Molefe was on an overseas trip, and on his return Molefe reversed it in favour of T-Systems, which was bidding with state-owned Broadband Infraco, to whose board public enterprises minister Malusi Gigaba had appointed the Gupta family's associate Salim Essa. Transnet's Gerhard van der Westhuizen told the Zondo Commission that Molefe instructed him to write a memorandum supporting the reversal, and that counting T-Systems' late R248m discount would have breached Transnet's procurement policies.
undone: Transnet's internal structures, acting on legal advice, and an external audit both found the reversal unfair and outside internal procurement protocol. Molefe later revoked it and the contract returned to Neotel. T-Systems subcontracted the rental and equipment-sales parts of an earlier master service agreement to Zestilor, a company owned by Essa's wife Zeenat Osmany, which was paid more than R3m in monthly instalments between August 2012 and mid-July 2015. In February 2017 Transnet awarded an information technology data services tender to T-Systems although Gijima scored highest, on what the Commission called a spurious basis; that award was reversed in Gijima's favour in court. T-Systems sold its South African business to Gijima in October 2017.
cite: Corruption Watch report on Zondo Commission hearings, 28 May 2019; Business Day, 2 February 2022; Daily Maverick, 10 October 2022 and 20 May 2026

n: Güralp Systems paid a senior figure at a Korean state geoscience institute
rank: senior posts at the Korea Institute of Geoscience and Mineral Resources
d: Güralp Systems, a British maker of seismic monitoring equipment, paid a man the court calls Dr Chi, who held senior posts at the Korea Institute of Geoscience and Mineral Resources (KIGAM), a government-funded research institute, and in 1999 headed its Earthquake Research Centre. The approved judgment records $1,034,931 paid between 2003 and 2015, in cash and by transfers to a US bank account, invoiced as technical consultancy. In return he recommended the firm's equipment to other Korean public bodies, shaped equipment specifications to match its products, advised it to inflate the list price submitted to the procurement body and not to offer Korean discounts, and passed it a competitor's pricing and presentation. The company's Korean revenue rose from about £20,000 to over £1.45m.
cite: Approved judgment, Southwark Crown Court (Mr Justice William Davis), 22 October 2019; Serious Fraud Office case page; Guralp Systems Ltd v Director of the Serious Fraud Office [2026] EWHC 37 (Admin), 13 January 2026
inside: A British equipment maker paid a senior figure inside Korea's state geoscience institute, which then wrote specifications and prices that suited its products.
undone: Güralp Systems entered a five-year deferred prosecution agreement requiring it to disgorge £2,069,861, with no financial penalty. None of that money was paid: the High Court recorded in January 2026 that non-payment was an agreed breach of the agreement, and the Serious Fraud Office's application to the Crown Court, made on 21 November 2024, continues. Three former employees stood trial at Southwark Crown Court: Andrew Bell was acquitted on 18 December 2019 and Dr Cansun Güralp and Natalie Pearce were found not guilty on 20 December 2019.

n: Ultra Electronics agents paid Algiers airport authority officials
rank: director general and officials of the Algiers airport authority SGSIA
d: Ultra Electronics, a British defence and security electronics group, agreed a deferred prosecution agreement with the Serious Fraud Office over its bid for an IT project at Algiers airport, awarded by the airport authority, Société de Gestion des Services et Infrastructures Aéroportuaires (SGSIA). The agreed statement names SGSIA's director general Tahar Allache and officials Mohamed Amine Kheider and Achour Omar Aboudil, and records two agents engaged in June 2016 on commissions totalling about 30 per cent of contract value, split between them. One agent said he had paid Aboudil and Kheider from his own pocket; the statement does not show company funds reaching them, and records payments to the agents of £21,933 on 13 September 2016 and EUR 5,485 on 15 September 2016. SGSIA did not award it to Ultra.
cite: Statement of Facts and approved judgment, R v Ultra Electronics Holdings Ltd, Crown Court at Southwark (Mr Justice Hilliard), 1 May 2026
inside: A British contractor's paid agents worked on named officials inside the state airport authority that was choosing the winner, to have the contract steered its way.
undone: The DPA, approved on 1 May 2026, runs three years and carries a £10,083,150 penalty and £4,804,831 in costs, with no disgorgement because the Algerian bids were lost. The court made no findings of fact and no findings of any kind against any individual; some individuals denied involvement.

n: Ultra Electronics' agents courted Algeria's ICT ministry chief
rank: director general of the Ministry of Post and Information and Communication Technologies
d: The second Algerian count in Ultra Electronics' deferred prosecution agreement concerns Algeria's public key infrastructure project, run by the Ministry of Post and Information and Communication Technologies (MPICT). The agreed statement of facts names the ministry's director general Ahmed Berbar, for whom an iPhone was bought as a thank-you gift, given, the statement says, because the request for proposals had been supplied outside the standard process. It also names Moussa Benhamadi, a former MPICT minister and a director of the Algerian group Condor Electronics, who was given a consultancy agreement worth $1.5m; a draft supplementary agreement of $4m went to an agent. The statement says it can properly be inferred that the agreements were to facilitate corrupt payments. The consortium's bids in 2016 and 2017 failed.
cite: Statement of Facts and approved judgment, R v Ultra Electronics Holdings Ltd, Crown Court at Southwark (Mr Justice Hilliard), 1 May 2026
inside: A British contractor's gift reached the ministry official running the tender, who had supplied the bid papers early, while consultancy money went to a former minister.
undone: The DPA was approved on 1 May 2026 for three years, with a £10,083,150 penalty and £4,804,831 in costs across all three counts. The court made no findings against any individual, and no individual admitted the conduct.

n: Colas Rail put Malaysian officials on its bid vehicle's board and payroll
rank: boards of Prasarana and MRT Corp contract decisions
d: Colas Rail Asia, the Malaysian arm of the French rail contractor Colas Rail, part of Bouygues, settled with France's financial prosecutor over work on Kuala Lumpur's urban rail lines. The convention records that an intermediary introduced its local director to two influential Malaysian public officials, a man and his father, while another separately approached a member of a Malaysian royal family. Companies linked to the two officials were hired on success fees to extract delay compensation from Prasarana, the transport operator, and the three men were made directors or officers of, and paid by, the joint venture set up to bid for the MRT2 line awarded by the state-owned Mass Rapid Transit Corporation. The prosecutor says the sums were illicit commissions allowing kickbacks to Malaysian decision-makers.
cite: Convention judiciaire d'intérêt public, Parquet national financier and Colas Rail Asia Sdn Bhd, 17 March 2026, validated by the president of the tribunal judiciaire de Paris on 19 March 2026
inside: A French contractor paid serving Malaysian officials and seated them on its own bid company, which then won state rail contracts and extra payments.
undone: Colas Rail reported itself in June 2017 after its own finance department found unjustified spending. Illicit commissions of €18,399,710 were identified; the company obtained MYR 298.6m (€65.8m) in variation orders and claims and the MRT2 contract worth about €147m, which was later novated away. The fine was €29,745,974, with a three-year compliance programme supervised by the French anti-corruption agency.

n: Oberthur money reached an adviser steering Bangladesh's ID card award
rank: adviser to the Prime Minister, controlling the Election Commission's award committee
d: Oberthur Technologies, the French secure document maker now called Idemia France, settled with France's financial prosecutor over Bangladesh's national smart identity card contract. The Bangladesh Election Commission tendered in April 2014 for 70 million cards, worth $113m and partly World Bank financed, awarding it to Oberthur in December 2014. The convention says a Bangladeshi intermediary was likely to have obtained the technical specifications in advance and to have manipulated the tender, and that the investigation identified a high-level public official, an adviser to the Prime Minister, under whose control the Election Commission's award committee acted and who pushed the order up from 70 to 90 million cards. His promised reward was €730,000, paid in March 2015 against a false training invoice, plus a share of €2,408,158 in hologram payments.
cite: Convention judiciaire d'intérêt public, Parquet national financier and Idemia France, 20 June 2022, validated 7 July 2022
inside: A French card maker's money was routed to an adviser in the prime minister's office who controlled the election body's award committee and enlarged its order.
undone: Idemia acknowledged the facts and paid a public interest fine of €7,957,822. The case began with a referral from Britain's National Crime Agency in July 2017. The World Bank separately excluded the former Oberthur entities from its tenders; its integrity compliance officer lifted that exclusion in May 2020.

n: Oberthur's banknote commissions reached a governor of Angola's central bank
rank: governor of the Banco Nacional de Angola
d: Idemia France, previously Oberthur Technologies, settled with French prosecutors over banknote printing for the Banco Nacional de Angola, Angola's central bank. The convention records that the printing was invoiced through two Hong Kong companies set up in 2003 by executives of the Oberthur parent, and that a Brazilian agent representing the group in Angola was paid commissions of 35 per cent of the sums received from the central bank, through a Panama company holding an account in Madeira. The Hong Kong vehicles took $100,755,000 from the bank for printing between 2007 and 2011, and €25,420,841 more for running its cash office. Bank records obtained from Portugal show that on 2 June 2009 the Panama company transferred $855,328.15 to a governor of the central bank who had left office that April.
cite: Convention judiciaire d'intérêt public, Parquet de Paris and Idemia France, 2 June 2025, validated 27 June 2025
inside: A French printer's commission money reached a governor of Angola's central bank, the body buying its banknotes and paying for its services.
undone: The investigation began with an anonymous letter in February 2011; the case was widened to active and passive bribery of foreign public officials in March 2017 and Idemia was placed under formal investigation in June 2019. Idemia acknowledged the facts for November 2007 to September 2011 and paid a public interest fine of €15,541,130.

n: Doris Group's Angolan partners held Sonangol officials' interests
rank: executive of the state oil company Sonangol and its consortium representative
d: Doris Group, a French offshore oil and gas engineering firm, settled with France's financial prosecutor over contracts in Angola. Sonangol, the state oil company and sole concession holder, vetted bidders for the oil companies' tenders and recommended who should win. Angolan law required majority local ownership, and in 2008 Doris gave 51 per cent of its Angolan subsidiary to three individuals. The convention says the material passed to the prosecutor suggested these shareholders carried the interests of Angolan public officials, notably of Sonangol, and that one had a privileged relationship with a Sonangol executive who also sat as its representative on a research consortium, passing him information from his post. That executive was the beneficial owner of a company paid over $1m for Luanda offices that were never occupied.
cite: Convention judiciaire d'intérêt public, Parquet national financier and Doris Group SA, 9 June 2022, validated 7 July 2022
inside: A French engineering firm gave most of its Angolan arm to men said to hold officials' interests, reaching a Sonangol executive inside the body that vetted its bids.
undone: Shell companies owned by one shareholder invoiced Doris for consultancy and other services around four engineering contracts won between 2013 and 2016, worth about 2 per cent of their value; the prosecutor says the payments were intended to be passed on to Angolan officials of Sonangol. The margin was €2,770,793 and the public interest fine €3,463,491. The French investigation followed two referrals from US judicial authorities in 2018 and 2019.

n: Technip's partner reached a GNPC executive deciding Ghana's oilfield awards
rank: senior executives of the Ghana National Petroleum Corporation
d: Technip, the French energy engineering group, settled with France's financial prosecutor over contracts won in 2008 and 2009. In Ghana, a joint venture including the state-owned Ghana National Petroleum Corporation (GNPC) was formed to develop an offshore oilfield and put the work out to tender. Two Technip salesmen took on a local commercial partner who had privileged contacts with GNPC's leadership, and he introduced them to a senior GNPC executive who took part in awarding the tendered contracts. The convention says documents suggest that executive took part in negotiating the partnership contract signed in March 2009 and that financial commitments were made to him through it. Technip UK paid the partner's company $6,952,030 between 2009 and 2011, equal to 1 per cent of the contract value.
cite: Convention judiciaire d'intérêt public, Parquet national financier and Technip Energies France SAS and Technip UK Ltd, 22 June 2023, validated 28 June 2023
inside: A French engineering group paid a go-between to reach a senior executive inside Ghana's state oil corporation who sat in on awarding the contracts it won.
undone: The convention says part of the sums paid to the partner would have been passed on to three GNPC executives, and that a third party was compensated for making the introduction; the wording is hedged throughout. The resulting installation and supply contracts brought Technip UK €368m and Technip France €113m between 2008 and 2011. The combined fine for Ghana and Equatorial Guinea was €208,938,000.

n: Technip money was meant for Equatorial Guinea's oil secretary of state
rank: Secretary of State for Mines and Hydrocarbons
d: The second country in Technip's French settlement is Equatorial Guinea, where a consortium including the state company GEPetrol was formed in 2008 to exploit oil and gas and put work out to tender. The convention says the same commercial partner used by Technip in Ghana had privileged contacts with the son of the president of Equatorial Guinea, who at the time was the country's secretary of state for mines and hydrocarbons, and that he arranged a meeting between that official and a Technip salesman in London in 2009. A partnership contract signed in August 2009 led to $2m being paid to the partner's company between 2010 and 2012, which, the prosecutor says, was to cover its running costs and be distributed to the official.
cite: Convention judiciaire d'intérêt public, Parquet national financier and Technip Energies France SAS and Technip UK Ltd, 22 June 2023, validated 28 June 2023
inside: A French engineering group paid a go-between sums the prosecutor says were meant for the minister in charge of oil, while a state consortium awarded the work.
undone: Technip UK signed a flexible materials installation contract with a consortium member in November 2009 and subcontracted manufacture to Technip France; the two earned €59m and €34m between 2009 and 2012. The prosecutor's wording is hedged, and the convention records no finding against the official. The fine covering both Ghana and Equatorial Guinea was €208,938,000, split €154,792,000 to Technip UK and €54,146,000 to Technip France.

n: French betting supplier paid the head of Mali's state tote for its contract
org_label: Périphériques et Matériels de Contrôle (Carrus group)
rank: chief executive of PMU Mali
d: Périphériques et Matériels de Contrôle, a French maker of betting terminals and systems in the Carrus group, settled with France's financial prosecutor over a contract with PMU Mali, the Malian horse-race betting operator. PMU Mali is a mixed-economy company 75 per cent owned by the Malian state and supervised by the ministry of economy and finance. The contract to supply, install and run its betting system and terminals was signed in January 2007 without any prior competitive tender, with the company's deputy general manager on one side and PMU Mali's chief executive on the other. Investigators established that the French firm paid that chief executive €78,972 in unjustified sums between 2008 and 2011, described in transfers as air fares, fees or expenses, though he had never worked for it.
cite: Convention judiciaire d'intérêt public, Parquet national financier and Périphériques et Matériels de Contrôle SAS, 10 February 2026, validated 18 February 2026
inside: A French supplier paid the chief executive of Mali's state betting company, which had awarded it the contract to supply and run its betting system without a tender.
undone: The case began with a TRACFIN money-laundering report in December 2015. Separate payments to the executive's son for terminal maintenance were examined and not found to be fraudulent. The company admits the facts; the advantage was put at €335,000 and the public interest fine at €499,150, with a compliance programme supervised by the French anti-corruption agency. The executive led PMU Mali from 2004 to 2014.

n: Uniform supplier's fixers linked to an adviser in Gabon's defence ministry
rank: economic and financial affairs adviser in the defence minister's office
d: SOTEC, a Gabonese construction and services company, settled with the Paris prosecutor over its role as local representative for a French maker of military uniforms, which won a 2005 contract worth €7.5m to supply uniforms and equipment to Gabon's security forces. SOTEC was paid €180,480 in 2007 and 2008 and COGEM €91,440 between 2004 and 2009, for smoothing dealings with Gabonese administrations. The convention says their work formed part of a scheme of bribery of foreign public officials through facilitation payments and undue commissions, and that the investigation identified a Gabonese official, an economic and financial affairs adviser attached to the defence minister's office who held the power to commit spending, as likely to have received undue advantages from their activity.
cite: Convention judiciaire d'intérêt public, Parquet de Paris and SARL SOTEC, 1 July 2024, validated 10 July 2024
inside: A French uniform maker's local fixers were paid to work the defence minister's office, where an adviser with spending power is said to have received undue advantages.
undone: The investigation began with a TRACFIN report in June 2007 about a €394,843 transfer and became a judicial investigation in 2015. Work subcontracted for €394,843, for 1,700 uniforms for the Gabonese police, was rebilled to the defence ministry at €2,084,763.60. The prosecutor treats the facts as complicity in active bribery of foreign public officials, and the wording about the official is hedged. SOTEC paid a public interest fine of €520,000.

n: China Harbour's cash reached Bangladesh's roads division secretary
rank: Secretary, Road Transport and Highways Division
d: China Harbour Engineering Company, a state-backed Chinese contractor, sent about 5 million taka in foreign currency to the secretary of Bangladesh's Road Transport and Highways Division, after Nazrul Islam took that post on 15 October. The company had been selected by the Chinese government to widen the 226km Dhaka-Sylhet highway, with bidding under way. The secretary reported it and the ministry returned the money to the Chinese embassy in Dhaka with a letter. Finance Minister A.M.A. Muhith disclosed the offer in January 2018, said the firm was blacklisted and that it "might have offered the money for future favours". He put the sum at "maybe 50 lakh", saying he had forgotten it. Bangladesh suspended bidding and decided to fund the road itself. China Harbour could not be reached for comment.
inside: A Chinese state contractor bidding for a highway put money into the hands of the civil servant heading the division that would award the work.
undone: The money was handed back to the Chinese embassy and the bidding was suspended; no prosecution of the company or of any official was reported, and the road transport minister said officials would not be punished.
cite: Prothom Alo, 17 January 2018; The Daily Star, 16 January 2018; Agence France-Presse via South China Morning Post, 17 January 2018

n: 500.com paid Japanese Diet members over its casino resort bid
rank: a member of the House of Representatives who was also vice-minister of land, infrastructure, transport and tourism and state minister for integrated resorts, his aide, and other Diet members
d: 500.com, a Chinese online lottery company now called BIT Mining, wanted a licence for an "integrated resort", a casino and hotel complex, in Japan. Between 2017 and 2019 it paid cash, sham consulting and lecture fees and luxury trips to a member of Japan's National Diet, the national parliament, who also held a government post covering infrastructure, transport and tourism, to his aide and to other Diet members. Consultants hand-delivered cash to officials' offices in Tokyo. Prosecutors put the payments at about $1.9 million; regulators put total improper payments at about $2.5 million. The lawmaker and his aide were convicted in Tokyo in 2021. The company never obtained a licence, and in November 2024 agreed a $10 million criminal fine, $4 million of it met by a civil penalty.
cite: SEC administrative order 34-101649, 18 Nov 2024; US Department of Justice criminal Information, United States v. BIT Mining Ltd, No. 24-cr-744 (D.N.J.), filed 18 Nov 2024; SEC press release 2024-180, 18 Nov 2024
inside: A gambling company's money got inside Japan's parliament, reaching a lawmaker who also held the government's infrastructure and tourism post, his aide and other members, to win its casino bid.

n: Moog's Indian unit agreed a bribe with a Hindustan Aeronautics buyer
rank: Hindustan Aeronautics procurement official
d: Moog Inc., an American maker of precision motion-control parts, let its Indian subsidiary, Moog Motion Controls, pay bribes to win public business. Hindustan Aeronautics Limited, India's state aerospace and defence manufacturer, put actuators out to tender in April 2021. One of its officials was recorded asking for 2.5 per cent, or one per cent immediately; the order does not say what of. The agreed bribe was ten lakh rupees, about 1,000,000 rupees. Hindustan Aeronautics awarded the subsidiary a $1,399,328 contract in November 2021. A distributor issued a fabricated invoice for 1,540,000 rupees in January 2022, and in March 2022 the subsidiary paid that distributor about $18,614. Moog settled with US regulators on 11 October 2024 for $1,683,815, without admitting or denying the findings.
cite: SEC administrative order 34-101307, 11 Oct 2024
inside: An American parts maker's Indian unit agreed a bribe with a buyer inside India's state aerospace manufacturer, which then awarded it a $1.4 million actuator contract.

n: Moog's Indian unit paid to get on India's railway approved supplier list
rank: Research Design and Standards Organization official
d: Moog Motion Controls, the Indian subsidiary of the American parts maker Moog Inc., signed a liaison agreement with an agent in July 2020 under which he would obtain South Central Railway business for ten per cent of any contract value. Employees used the agent to get on to the supplier list of the Research Design and Standards Organization, the body under India's Ministry of Railways whose approval a firm needs before it may bid, and separately discussed bribing its officials to eliminate competitors. One was recorded saying an official wanted one per cent. The Moog brand was added to the list for an upcoming South Central Railway tender in August 2020, and a $34,323 contract followed in September 2020.
cite: SEC administrative order 34-101307, 11 Oct 2024
inside: An American parts maker paid an agent to reach officials of India's railway standards body, seeking a supplier listing and a rival's removal; its Indian unit then won railway work.

n: Vendors paid PDVSA's purchasing arm Bariven for payment priority
org_label: vendors Roberto Rincon and Abraham Shiera
rank: the PDVSA "management team", including Bariven's president and general manager
d: Bariven S.A. buys equipment for PDVSA, Venezuela's state-owned oil company. From in or about 2011 until at least 2013, two vendors, Roberto Rincon and Abraham Shiera, paid PDVSA's "management team", including Bariven's president and general manager, 10 per cent of all payments they received from PDVSA, in return for priority over other vendors in being paid and help winning further PDVSA business. Nervis Villalobos, a former Venezuelan vice-minister of energy, brought them the offer. The money moved through accounts at Banco Espirito Santo in Portugal, held in the names of officials' relatives, friends and close associates, set up by Paulo Casqueiro Murta, an employee of a Swiss wealth management firm; about $25.9 million in bribes passed through them. Shiera pleaded guilty in March 2016 and Rincon in June 2016.
inside: Suppliers' kickbacks reached the managers who decide purchases at Venezuela's state oil company, so their own invoices were paid first and they got help winning more work.
cite: Plea agreement and criminal Information, United States v. Casqueiro Murta, No. 4:17-cr-00514 (S.D. Tex.), filed 21 and 20 May 2024; US Department of Justice press releases, 23 March 2016 and 16 June 2016

n: Surys's benefits reached the director of Ukraine's state passport printer
rank: former director, state enterprise Polygraph Combine
d: Polygraph Combine prints Ukraine's passports and identity cards for the state. Its former director demanded improper benefits from Surys, the French firm that designed the security features, and in return Surys was allowed to supply the plant. The money ran as royalties to an Estonian company, Ou Feature, controlled by the director: about 7 million euros between 2018 and 2021, while Polygraph transferred more than 22 million euros to Surys and bought materials at four to six times their original cost. France's financial prosecutor settled with Surys on 8 July 2025 for a fine of 18,363,007 euros plus 3.37 million euros to the Ukrainian state, treating the conduct as bribery of a foreign public official. The former director is a suspect in Ukraine and is presumed innocent.
cite: French National Financial Prosecutor's Office, judicial public interest agreement with Surys, signed 8 July 2025 and validated by the Paris Judicial Court on 3 September 2025; National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine, 23 May 2025
inside: A French supplier's benefits reached the director of Ukraine's state passport printer, which went on buying its security materials at several times their cost.

n: AAR paid an agent to win South African Airways Technical work
rank: officials at South African Airways Technical
d: AAR Corp, a US aviation services company, paid South African officials through an agent to win an aircraft-component support contract with South African Airways Technical, the maintenance subsidiary of the state carrier South African Airways. The US Justice Department said the payments ran from 2015 to 2020. On 19 December 2024 AAR accepted a non-prosecution agreement and agreed to pay more than $55 million, covering this and a parallel scheme in Nepal, from which it made nearly $24 million in profit in total. The South African agent pleaded guilty.
inside: An aviation company paid an agent to reach officials at the state airline's repair arm, which then gave it the component support contract.
cite: US Department of Justice, 19 Dec 2024

n: Airbus's intermediaries had contacts inside Taiwan's China Airlines
rank: contacts within China Airlines, including a member of its board
d: China Airlines is Taiwan's state-owned airline. On 22 January 2008 it agreed to buy fourteen A350 aircraft from Airbus. France's financial prosecutor found Airbus engaged two intermediaries on the campaign. The first, on a contract backdated to December 2008, had contacts inside the airline who passed him confidential information about the negotiations, which were still ongoing; he received 5.75 million euros from accounts linked to an Airbus subsidiary in the UAE. The second acknowledged being close to a board member who supplied campaign information, and received more than two million dollars in 2013. The prosecutor considered the facts could constitute bribery of a foreign public official, did not establish the materiality of the advisory services, and does not say money reached anyone inside the airline.
inside: Airbus paid intermediaries who had contacts inside Taiwan's state airline, including a board member, feeding out confidential information on the negotiations so the seller knew the buyer's position.
cite: French National Financial Prosecutor's Office, judicial public interest agreement with Airbus SE, 29 January 2020, section 5 (paragraphs 110-126), official English translation

n: Chinese firm part-owned by his wife had a researcher inside Japan's state institute
org_label: Chinese chemical company linked to the researcher's family
rank: Senior researcher, National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology
d: Quan Hengdao worked about 25 years at Japan's National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology, a state research agency, latterly as a senior researcher. On 25 February 2025 the Tokyo District Court convicted him under the Unfair Competition Prevention Act, case 2023 (wa) No. 1278, and imposed two years and six months suspended for four years, with a fine of 2 million yen. He had emailed out the institute's synthesis know-how for heptafluoroisobutyronitrile, a fluorine compound. Japan's industry ministry records that his wife was the main shareholder of the foreign company that used the know-how and was that company's representative, and that he chaired a firm with a capital tie to it. Reporting places the company in Beijing. He was arrested in June 2023; no one else was charged.
inside: A Chinese company whose main shareholder was the researcher's wife had him inside Japan's state research institute, emailing its synthesis know-how out to its staff.
cite: Japan Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, iPLNet forum materials, 24 June 2025, recording the Tokyo District Court judgment of 25 February 2025, case 2023 (wa) No. 1278; California Insider/AP, 'Chinese researcher convicted in Japan for leaking tech secrets to Chinese firm', 2 March 2025

n: US sanctions say a Dominican senator's firms won Haiti's reconstruction contracts
org_label: Constructora Hadom and other firms of senator Felix Bautista
who: Dominican construction firms of senator Felix Bautista
rank: Prime Minister, Ministry of Planning and External Cooperation, tender evaluation committee
d: Felix Bautista is a Dominican Republic senator. In June 2018 the US Treasury designated him for significant acts of corruption in the Dominican Republic and Haiti, saying he used his connections to win Haitian post-disaster reconstruction contracts and that a company linked to him was paid over 10 million dollars for work it had not completed. Treasury designated five Dominican firms it said he owned or controlled, among them Constructora Hadom SA. Haiti's Senate PetroCaribe commission reported in 2017 that Constructora Hadom SA held the 33.77 million dollar Legislative Palace contract, signed by prime minister Jean-Max Bellerive on 8 November 2010 though the firm was three months old and failed the tender's five-year experience rule. The commission found the planning ministry broke procurement rules across six restricted tenders worth 348 million dollars, and records no payment to any official.
inside: US sanctions say a Dominican senator used his connections to win Haiti's rebuilding contracts; Haiti's own inquiry found his firm given work it was not eligible for.
cite: US Department of the Treasury, 'Treasury Sanctions Two Individuals and Five Entities Under Global Magnitsky', 12 June 2018; Federal Register vol. 83 no. 248, 28 December 2018, Global Magnitsky annual report; Senate of the Republic of Haiti, Rapport de la Commission Speciale d'Enquete sur le Fonds PetroCaribe, October 2017, pp. 438-439 and the analysis of six restricted-tender contracts

n: Sicpa admitted paying a public agent while running Brazil's drinks-tax counters
rank: a public agent, unnamed in the agreement; the police operation indicated tax authority servants and mint employees
d: Sicobe was Brazil's beverage production control system: counters fitted to bottling lines that reported output to the Receita Federal, the federal tax authority. Casa da Moeda do Brasil, the state mint, held the contract and Sicpa supplied it. In July 2015 the Federal Police searched the mint, the tax authority and Sicpa's Brazilian headquarters in Operacao Vicios, after the mint's own presidency complained that employees were steering a retender back to Sicpa. The finance ministry said there were indications of about 100 million reais paid to tax authority servants and mint employees, on a contract that had billed more than 6 billion reais over six years. On 7 June 2021 Sicpa do Brasil and Ceptis signed a leniency agreement with the comptroller general and the solicitor general worth about 762 million reais, covering undue advantages paid to a public agent between 2009 and 2015. The agreement names no official and no contract.
inside: Sicpa admitted paying a public agent from 2009 to 2015 while supplying the system Brazil's mint and tax authority used to count drinks output and tax it.
cite: Controladoria-Geral da Uniao, 'CGU e AGU celebram acordo de leniencia com as empresas SICPA e CEPTIS no valor de R$ 762 milhoes', 7 June 2021; Agencia Brasil, 'Operacao Vicio investiga fraudes em contratos envolvendo a Casa da Moeda', 1 July 2015; Metropoles on the Swiss Office of the Attorney General decision of 27 April 2023

n: Spain's state arms exporter charged over commissions on an Angolan police contract
org_label: Defex S.A. and the Cueto-Defex joint venture
who: Defex S.A., the Spanish state's arms export company
rank: Angolan authorities and public officials, none named in the order; the contract counterparty is the General Command of the National Police
d: Defex S.A. was Spain's state-owned arms exporter. On 13 July 2018 Audiencia Nacional judge Jose de la Mata closed his investigation in a 275-page order finding grounds to prosecute 27 people and three companies for international corruption, embezzlement, money laundering and criminal organisation. The central contract was signed on 12 June 2008 between the Cueto-Defex joint venture and the General Command of Angola's National Police, for police equipment worth over 152 million euros, of which just over 59 million went on actually supplying it. The judge describes about a third of the contract transferred for local services in Angola that were never carried out, and 41,464,729 euros moved to Luxembourg and Angola as distributions of illicit commissions to Angolan authorities and officials. Two further supplies went to the Presidential Security Unit. Oral trial was opened on 20 May 2019 and no verdict has been given.
inside: Spain's state arms exporter is charged with paying commissions to Angolan authorities to win a 152 million euro equipment contract with the national police command.
cite: Audiencia Nacional / Consejo General del Poder Judicial press releases, 'El juez ve indicios para juzgar a 27 personas y a la sociedad Defex por los contratos de Angola', 13 July 2018, and 'El juez abre juicio oral a Defex y a su excupula directiva por los contratos de material policial con Angola', 20 May 2019

n: Iraq's bomb squad chief jailed for taking a bribe from fake-detector sellers
org_label: British sellers of the ADE 651 detector
who: British sellers of fake explosive detectors
rank: head of the Interior Ministry's bomb squad department
d: Iraqi checkpoints were equipped with hand-held wands sold as explosive detectors, chiefly the British-made ADE 651. The wands have no working detection mechanism; they were based on a novelty product costing about 20 dollars and sold for thousands each. Iraq spent close to 60 million dollars on them. In 2012 Major General Jihad al-Jabri, head of the Interior Ministry's bomb squad department, was convicted of accepting a bribe from the British manufacturers and jailed for four years. The published accounts do not give the amount, and his case did not address whether the wands worked. Two British sellers were convicted of fraud in separate trials in Britain the following year. Iraq banned the devices in 2016, after a bombing in Baghdad that July.
inside: The British sellers of a fake explosive detector paid the officer who headed Iraq's interior ministry bomb squad, the department that put the wands on its checkpoints.
cite: Associated Press, 'Iraq finally bans fake bomb detectors after July 3 blast', carried by VOA News, 2016

n: India blacklisted six arms firms over bribes to its ordnance factories chief
org_label: Israeli Military Industries, Singapore Technologies, Rheinmetall Air Defence, Corporation Defence of Russia, TS Kisan and Co., RK Machine Tools
who: six Indian and foreign arms suppliers
rank: Director General, Ordnance Factories Board
d: The Ordnance Factories Board ran India's state arms and ammunition factories and bought their machinery and technology. In 2009 the Central Bureau of Investigation registered a case and arrested its former Director General, Sudipto Ghosh, alleging that he and other officials took bribes from suppliers and promised them defence contracts in return. A charge sheet followed in June 2010. The Defence Ministry first froze dealings with seven firms named in the case; the Delhi High Court set that order aside for want of natural justice, and after show-cause notices and reports from the CBI, the Central Vigilance Commission and the Law Ministry, the ministry barred six firms from any dealing with it for ten years: Israeli Military Industries, Singapore Technologies, Rheinmetall Air Defence, Corporation Defence of Russia, TS Kisan and Co. and RK Machine Tools. The firms denied the allegations. No trial outcome has been published.
inside: Suppliers' money is alleged to have reached the officer running India's state arms factories, who then promised them the factories' contracts.
cite: Deccan Herald, 'Defence ministry blacklists 6 companies', reporting the Defence Ministry's ten-year debarment and the CBI's 2009 case and June 2010 charge sheet

n: Airbus paid intermediaries close to Gaddafi's circle over a Libyan airline sale
rank: a representative of the Libyan government who was Muammar Gaddafi's chief of cabinet, and Gaddafi's son
d: On 2 November 2006 a subsidiary of EADS, later Airbus, agreed to sell twelve aircraft to Afriqiyah Airways, Libya's state airline, after negotiations with Libyan government representatives at the Farnborough air show. France's financial prosecutor found the contract was obtained through two intermediaries paid 2 million and 4 million euros because of their closeness to Gaddafi's chief of cabinet and to his son. The second said he had acted as a facilitator between Airbus executives and the son, and that the 4 million was routed through a Lebanese company created for that purpose alone so that his commissions would not be visible; an Airbus slide recommending the payment noted no external due diligence had been done, and the company approving it did so the same day. The prosecutor considered the facts could constitute bribery of a foreign public official and does not say money reached anyone inside the airline or the government.
inside: Airbus paid two intermediaries chosen for their closeness to Gaddafi's chief of cabinet and his son to win a twelve-aircraft order from Libya's state airline.
cite: Convention judiciaire d'interet public, Parquet national financier and Airbus SE, validated by the vice-president of the tribunal judiciaire de Paris on 30 November 2022, section IV.1 on the Libyan sales campaign

n: Airbus routed a success commission through shell firms over Kazakh space contracts
rank: Kazakh public authorities, approached through a businessman close to the president
d: In January 2009 Astrium, an Airbus company, was chosen as strategic partner by KazCosmos, Kazakhstan's national space agency, and went on to sign contracts with the state company Kazakhstan Gharysh Sapary for two Earth observation satellites and a satellite assembly and test centre. France's financial prosecutor found that from June 2008 Airbus's international operations unit brought in two intermediaries, one engaged mainly to introduce to Airbus an influential Kazakh businessman close to the president so that he would intercede with the Kazakh public authorities. A comfort letter promised that intermediary 30,000 euros a month and 3 per cent of the satellite contract; 696,253 euros was paid to his Tunisian company, and the unit then sought to get around Airbus's own compliance procedures, routing the promised success commission through an Irish company held by Isle of Man entities and linked to a Hong Kong structure whose ultimate beneficiary he was. The prosecutor considered the facts could constitute bribery of a foreign public official.
inside: Airbus engaged an intermediary to reach a businessman close to Kazakhstan's president so he would intercede with the authorities awarding the space contracts, and hid the commission in shell companies.
cite: Convention judiciaire d'interet public, Parquet national financier and Airbus SE, validated by the vice-president of the tribunal judiciaire de Paris on 30 November 2022, section IV.2.1 on the Astrium sales campaign

n: Eurocopter paid a French senator's travel and an associate's firm over Kazakh sales
rank: a French senator, member of the France-Central Asia interparliamentary friendship group, holding an official mission letter signed by the President of the Republic
d: In October 2010 the Kazakh government chose Eurocopter, part of Airbus, as its strategic partner for helicopters, and signed agreements with the state-owned Kazakhstan Engineering and a protocol with the Kazakh defence ministry for forty-five EC145 aircraft. France's financial prosecutor found no success-fee consultant on this campaign, but that Eurocopter's management had sought the support of a French senator who sat in the France-Central Asia friendship group and held an official mission letter signed by the President of the Republic. He was kept informed of the negotiations, helped arrange meetings between Kazakh officials and Airbus, and had the costs of two official trips to Kazakhstan met by Eurocopter. He was also involved in an agreement of June 2011 paying 85,000 euros for services between January 2010 and June 2011 to a company part-owned by someone close to him, which staff inside Airbus disputed had been provided and which bypassed its compliance process. The prosecutor considered the facts could constitute bribery of a public official.
inside: Airbus's helicopter arm met a French senator's travel costs and paid 85,000 euros to a firm part-owned by an associate of his, while he arranged its meetings with Kazakh officials.
cite: Convention judiciaire d'interet public, Parquet national financier and Airbus SE, validated by the vice-president of the tribunal judiciaire de Paris on 30 November 2022, section IV.2.2 on the Eurocopter sales campaign

n: France's former intelligence chief used state resources for LVMH and was jailed
rank: former head of the domestic intelligence service, later the company's security consultant
d: Bernard Squarcini headed France's domestic intelligence service, the DCRI, now the DGSI, from 2008 to 2012, and was afterwards hired as a security consultant by the luxury group LVMH. On 7 March 2025 a Paris court convicted him of using public resources for the company's benefit and of complicity in the unlawful surveillance of Francois Ruffin, then an activist and later a member of parliament, and of staff at his publication Fakir, who were planning to disrupt an LVMH shareholders' meeting and were making a film about the group. He was sentenced to four years with two suspended and fined 200,000 euros, and said he would appeal. Nine others were tried with him. LVMH itself had settled in December 2021 under a judicial public interest agreement of 10 million euros; its chairman testified in November 2024 that he knew nothing of the surveillance, which he said an associate who died in 2018 had ordered.
inside: A luxury group had the man who ran France's domestic intelligence service turning its resources on the journalists and the activist-turned-MP who were targeting it.
cite: Reuters, 'Former French spy chief found guilty of misusing public resources to aid LVMH, fined 200,000 euros', 7 March 2025, carried by Malay Mail; Fortune, 'Bernard Arnault tells court he was completely unaware', 28 November 2024; Le Club des Juristes, report on the convention judiciaire d'interet public, Annex 3, recording the LVMH CJIP validated 17 December 2021

n: Bouygues contractors' invitations reached the Annecy hospital director
org_label: Bouygues Bâtiment Sud-Est and Linkcity Sud-Est
rank: director of the Centre hospitalier Annecy Genevois, who chaired the tender jury
d: The Centre hospitalier Annecy Genevois is a public hospital in Haute-Savoie. Between 2016 and 2018 it awarded Bouygues Bâtiment Sud-Est contracts worth 32 million and 3.3 million euros before tax and sold its subsidiary a plot for 5.5 million, all for a new long-term care building. A regional audit chamber referral in December 2021 led to a criminal inquiry, which found the hospital's director had accepted invitations from staff of the winning companies between 2015 and 2018. On the 32 million euro contract the jury he chaired left out price and delay, worth 40 per cent of the score, and ranked the Bouygues-led group first on architecture alone, worth 15 per cent, where the hospital's own analysis had placed it last.
inside: A construction group's hospitality reached the hospital director who chaired its tender jury, and he ranked its bid first on a criterion worth 15 per cent.
cite: Convention judiciaire d'intérêt public, Parquet national financier with Bouygues Bâtiment Sud-Est and Linkcity Sud-Est, validated by the tribunal judiciaire de Paris on 17 May 2023, sections II.2.a to II.2.c and paragraphs 37 and 46; public interest fine 7,964,000 euros

n: A waste firm's gifts reached the Orne council president over a landfill
rank: president of the Conseil général de l'Orne and his chief of staff
d: Guy Dauphin Environnement applied in 2006 to the Orne prefecture to open a tip for shredded car waste at Nonant-le-Pin. Between 2007 and 2013 the company sought the help of the president of the Orne department council and of his chief of staff to steer public decisions its way. The president approached the regional environment directorate, the prefect, an adviser at the Élysée and the ecology minister. In return the company took him to lunches and dinners and on a helicopter flight over Mont Blanc, considered putting him on its supervisory board, and discussed 10,000 euros towards a book under his name. His chief of staff added a favourable opinion to the council's official reply to the environment directorate before sending it, and leaked the company a copy.
inside: A waste company's hospitality and a book deal reached the department council president, whose chief of staff added a favourable opinion to the council's official reply.
cite: Convention judiciaire d'intérêt public, Parquet national financier and Guy Dauphin Environnement, validated by the tribunal judiciaire de Paris on 17 May 2023, paragraphs 7 to 30 and 39

n: Builders paid a Martigues housing company agent for its contracts
org_label: Omnium group, including Société d'Isolation et de Peinture Omnium
rank: a general-duties employee of SEMIVIM, partner of its property director
d: SEMIVIM is the part-public housing company of the town of Martigues. A Marseille drug-trafficking investigation turned up payments to a man employed there since 2008 as a general-duties agent, who was also the partner of the company's property director. Investigators found he had set up a system of corruption in the award of SEMIVIM's works contracts. The Omnium group's deputy general manager told them the man had offered him contracts for money, saying his partner was SEMIVIM's director. The group paid nearly 550,000 euros against false subcontracting invoices the employee himself supplied, along with two trips, materials and gift vouchers. Omnium won lots 1 and 3 of the Paradis Saint Roch estate refurbishment, worth nearly 5.5 million euros. The fine across the group was 1.7 million euros.
inside: A building group's cash and gifts reached an employee of the town's housing company, who steered its refurbishment contracts to the group through false invoices.
cite: Convention judiciaire d'intérêt public, parquet of the tribunal judiciaire de Marseille and Société d'Isolation et de Peinture Omnium, validated 22 December 2023, section II and the public interest fine section

n: Paprec's gifts to two waste chiefs brought its subsidiaries contracts
rank: mayor of Compiègne, who also chaired the agglomeration and the Oise waste syndicates, and the president of the SIREDOM waste syndicate
d: Between 2013 and 2022 the president of Paprec Group, its vice-president and its director of institutional relations obtained from the mayor of Compiègne the award to Paprec subsidiaries of a household waste collection contract published in 2013 and a sorting centre contract published in 2016. The mayor also chaired the agglomeration and the Oise waste syndicates that let them. In return Paprec supported a riding association chaired by the mayor's wife. Between 2014 and 2016 it obtained from the president of SIREDOM, the waste body for Essonne and Seine-et-Marne, two concessions for its eco-centre network, in return for hiring his son and placing a communications contract with an agency run by a friend of his director general of services.
inside: A waste group's money for a mayor's wife's association and a job for a syndicate president's son brought its subsidiaries the contracts those two men awarded.
cite: Convention judiciaire d'intérêt public, Parquet national financier and Paprec Group, validated by the tribunal judiciaire de Paris on 11 February 2025, sections II.B.2 and II.B.3 and the public interest fine section

n: Egis Avia paid a go-between over Sonatrach's Oran terminal contract
org_label: Egis Avia, part of the Egis group
rank: Algerian public officials able to influence the award, and the son of the interior minister
d: A search of the French engineering firm Egis Avia in 2013 seized seven invoices totalling 390,640 euros from Amphora Consultant Ltd, an offshore company. Each described only work on a terminal at Oran under Egis Avia's contract with Sonatrach, Algeria's state oil company. Also seized was that contract, signed on 25 March 2009 for 3,969,800 euros to build an annexe to the Oran terminal, which provided for no consultant at all; no record of Amphora's work was found. Amphora's owner was to take 10 per cent if the contract was signed. From its account 115,000 euros was withdrawn in cash and 12,000 euros went to the son of Algeria's interior minister. Investigators concluded the money could have been used to approach Algerian officials able to influence the award.
inside: Prosecutors found a French engineering firm's payments to an offshore go-between could have been used to reach Algerian officials able to influence Sonatrach's contract award.
cite: Ordonnance de validation d'une convention judiciaire d'intérêt public, president of the tribunal de grande instance de Paris, procureur de la République financier and SAS Egis Avia, 10 December 2019, parquet file 14 153 000 230, published by the Agence française anticorruption

n: An EDF buyer took commissions from contractors for power-plant work
org_label: Kaefer Wanner, SET Environnement and Poujaud
rank: a buyer in EDF's purchasing department, treated in law as entrusted with a public service mission
d: On 1 July 2011 the security director of the French electricity utility EDF told the central criminal police of a corruption system that had run for years inside the company's purchasing department. A contractor's director had reported that a buyer there was asking for commissions in exchange for awarding or renewing contracts. Phone intercepts were authorised from November 2011, and in February 2012 a judge allowed an undercover operation in which an agent brought the cash the buyer had asked for. Several contractors had paid him for maintenance contracts on thermal power stations. Kaefer Wanner paid several hundred thousand euros between 2004 and 2011, in cash through foreign companies that sent it false invoices and in trips and building work. SET Environnement paid 136,621.28 euros and Poujaud about 29,000 euros.
inside: Contractors' cash, trips and building work reached the buyer inside EDF's purchasing department who awarded and renewed their power-station maintenance contracts.
cite: Conventions judiciaires d'intérêt public, procureur de la République of the tribunal de grande instance de Nanterre with SAS Kaefer Wanner (signed 15 February 2018, validated 23 February 2018), SAS Set Environnement (signed 14 February 2018, validated 23 February 2018) and SAS Poujaud (signed 4 May 2018, validated 25 May 2018), published by the Agence française anticorruption

n: A builders' cartel bought two Petrobras directorates and split its contracts
org_label: The 'Clube' cartel of Brazilian construction groups
rank: the Supply directorate and the Engineering and Services directorate of Petrobras
d: Petrobras is Brazil's state-controlled oil company. From about 2004 to 2014 the largest Brazilian construction groups ran a cartel they called the Clube, which federal prosecutors list as sixteen companies, among them Odebrecht, UTC, OAS, Camargo Correa, Andrade Gutierrez and Engevix. It settled in advance which of them would win Petrobras's biggest works, and paid the company's own directors a percentage of each contract to keep the arrangement running. Prosecutors put that share at between 1 and 3 per cent. One account of supply-side works sets it at 2 per cent: half to the supply director Paulo Roberto Costa and half split between the services directorate and a political party. Costa was arrested in 2014 and convicted, and the services director Renato Duque was charged too.
inside: A cartel of builders paid two Petrobras directorates a percentage of every contract, and the state oil company's biggest works were shared out among them in advance.
cite: Ministerio Publico Federal, Procuradoria da Republica no Parana, denuncias naming the sixteen-company 'Clube' cartel, its member groups and its operators; Tribunal de Contas da Uniao, Acordao 2106/2024-Plenario, on the percentages paid to the Supply and the Engineering and Services directorates; Petrobras Form 20-F for 2014 filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, on what the company calls the payment scheme and the cartel members, and on the officials charged; and the leniency agreements the Controladoria-Geral da Uniao and Advocacia-Geral da Uniao concluded with the Odebrecht group (9 July 2018, R$2,727,239,997.64), OAS (14 November 2019, R$1,929,257,982.37), Andrade Gutierrez (18 December 2018, R$1,489,361,135.32), Camargo Correa (31 July 2019, R$1,396,128,459.76), UTC (10 July 2017, R$574,658,165.21) and the Engevix group (12 November 2019, R$516,301,313.70)

n: Keppel's agent paid Petrobras officials and a party for 13 rig contracts
rank: Petrobras officials and the then governing party
d: Keppel Offshore & Marine, a Singapore rig builder, won work from Brazil's state oil company Petrobras by paying its officials through an agent. The US Justice Department said that from at least 2001 to 2014 Keppel paid about 55 million dollars in bribes to Petrobras officials and to Brazil's then governing party, to win thirteen contracts with Petrobras and with Sete Brasil, a rig supplier.
